He hasn't made much progress at Double-A this year, a telling sign that probably caps his ceiling as a fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sanchez signed with the D-backs for $50,000 as a 17-year-old out of the Dominican Republic in January 2023, and entering 2026, he’s yet to post a seasonal ERA above 4.00 during his steady climb through the lower Minors. In 2025, his 2.40 ERA in 105 innings between Single-A Visalia and High-A Hillsboro was best among D-backs Minor Leaguers (min. 100 IP) and ranked 10th among MiLB hurlers who met that requirement. He accomplished that despite striking out only 88 in that span. The right-hander returned to the Northwest League for his age-20 campaign in ’26 and poured on the strikeouts at much better rates, furthering his push into Arizona prospect prominence. The 5-foot-10 hurler shows a pair of promising pitches in his four-seam fastball and sweeping slider. The heater comes in at 92-94 mph, giving it just below MLB average velocity, but it plays above that with cut-ride action and enough induced vertical break to keep it consistently above bats. The mid-80s breaking pitch comes with high spin and good horizontal movement and has regularly fooled batters, getting both ample whiffs and chases early on this season. Sanchez has worked on incorporating a bridge cutter and a changeup, though the latter hasn’t quite helped him fend off splits issues against lefties at this stage of his career. Starting from the extreme first-base side of the rubber, Sanchez has steadily improved his control numbers throughout his time as a pro, aided by opponents expanding the zone against the slider in particular. He lacks the power stuff to blow his arsenal past opponents, and given his size, it’s unlikely that will ever come, so he’ll need to keep locating well. The results are becoming undeniable though, and he looks more like a possible backend MLB starter with each passing year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels may have a reputation of drafting college players who can get pushed to the big leagues in a hurry, but they broke away from that script when Day 3 of the 2023 Draft commenced. They had some bonus pool money left over to sign Wimmer -- a toolsy but raw high school shortstop from South Carolina -- away from his commitment to The Citadel as their 11th-round pick for close to $400,000. He got his feet wet with a handful of games in the Arizona Complex League. It's likely going to require patience for Wimmer to grow into his raw tools. He’s a plus quick-twitch athlete and right-handed hitter who can use the whole field. His swing works and there might be some power to tap into in the future if he can add some strength to his lean frame. An above-average runner, he shows good instincts on the basepaths. While there’s work to be done on his footwork defensively, there’s some confidence he can stick at shortstop in the long run. It’s possible the Angels will move him around the diamond some, but don’t be surprised to see him stick up the middle -- at second or in center field -- if shortstop doesn’t work. He’s a bit like a piece of unmolded clay, one that the Angels can dream on becoming a Rodin.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Cool Breeze" Corey was a reliever at Division-II Wingate who the A's began to stretch out as a long reliever and spot starter in 2024, before more solidly committing to developing him as a starter in 2025, when he worked 123 innings (including his Fall League frames). Avant still has some reliever risk because of his below-average control - he only walked 10.5% of opponents in 2025, but his underlying strike-throwing was worse than that, and he's tended to be in the 13% or above area dating back to college - but he is built like a starter at a broad-shouldered 6-foot-4, and he deserves a longer developmental runway since we're talking about a small school guy who barely pitched in college because he was deployed as a reliever. 
Avant throws hard; he was parked in the 93-97 mph range last year, though his fastball's downhill plane sucks some of the effectiveness out of that pitch. Conversely, the higher slot helps add depth to Avant's slider, which has great velocity for a standard gyro-style offering. Whether Avant can continue to start will depend on the development of his splitter/sinker, an 87-91 mph offering that he actually has decent feel for locating, but that lacks big movement. Automatic pitch tagging thinks a lot of his splits are two-seamers, so it's tough to tell exactly how many of them he threw last year, but the number is something like twice what he did in 2024, though still only 200 of them across the entire season. He looks like he takes great care of himself, and he's an engaged teammate who was often watching his fellow A's arms with intense focus as everyone got underway this spring. It's probably more likely that Avant is a reliever in the end, but even if that's the case, he'll be a draft-and-develop feather in the cap of the A's. They should continue with the starter track for another two seasons at least, and decide more about his path when his 40-man roster deadline arrives after the 2027 season.

fangraphs.label: FanGraphs 2026 Pirates Top 50
fangraphs.text: Diamond, with his Pirate appropriate facial hair, is an oft-injured righty who, when healthy, has been an excellent reliever since he permanently transitioned to the role after the 2024 season. Granted, he’s only thrown about 50 career relief innings (and that’s counting two Arizona Fall League stints) because of persistent injury, including two IL stints already at the start of 2026. Diamond is currently healthy and really humming in Altoona, where he’s been in the 93-97 mph range and bending in hellacious sliders. He’s moved toward the third base side of the rubber this year, and the angle on his stuff has become tougher for hitters to match. Diamond’s frequent injuries cloud his future, but from a pure stuff standpoint, he is a standard middle-inning righty who should debut next year if he can remain healthy for the rest of this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres are one of the most heavily involved -- if not the most heavily involved -- teams in Mexico as part of the international signing process. That’s where the club headed to sign Serna in January, two months before the southpaw turned 17. Serna gained some international notoriety at the 2024 WBSC U15 World Cup in Colombia, where he struck out 12 and allowed only one earned run on one hit and four walks in seven innings against the host nation. He signed for $1 million. The 6-foot-3 southpaw throws free and easy from a smooth delivery, and while he only sits 88-91 mph with his fastball now, he has the size to add strength and get that velocity up to at least Major League average in the years to come. His best present pitch is an upper-70s slider with short, controllable depth, and it should help fuel any immediate Minor League success. There’s a feel for a low-80s changeup too, though he barely used it in the World Cup. Serna excelled on the international stage because he could hit his spots at an advanced level, and he was willing to go right after hitters. The Padres brought up his strike throwing on signing day as the most exciting part of the early profile, and if Serna can sharpen his stuff with physical maturity -- not a given considering the wide error bars on young arms -- he could be a midrotation option in the Majors in the next decade.

fangraphs.label: FanGraphs 2026 Twins Top 50
fangraphs.text:
Sprock is a compact, multi-positional prospect with quick hands and a punchy, line drive swing. He went to high school in New Jersey at Rick Porcello ’s alma mater, then was an excellent small conference two-way player at Elon, where he played both corner infield positions and started as an underclassman before shifting to relief as a junior (he bumped 96). A young-for-the-class prospect, the Twins began toying with a catcher conversion for Sprock late last summer, something they’ve leaned into this season. It’s working. Sprock has pretty quickly become a good receiver, ball-blocker, and thrower while still playing some corner infield and left field. His current trajectory suggests that catcher will be his best defensive position very soon.

Though he’s not likely to make much impact at the plate, Sprock’s short, punchy line drive swing generates enough contact that he’s an interesting offensive prospect for a catcher. It’d be nice for him to continue in a multi-positional role as he climbs the minors (he isn’t a great third baseman) because it adds fun window dressing to his profile, but it isn’t especially important to Sprock’s big league future, which early on looks like it’ll be as a contact-oriented backup catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kouba spent his first two college seasons at North Central (Texas) CC and opened 2021 in Dallas Baptist's bullpen, pitched his way into the rotation by midseason, earned all-Missouri Valley Conference honors and became a 12th-round pick. He doesn't dazzle anyone with his stuff but compensates by being the best strike-thrower in the system. He was named Double-A Texas League pitcher of the year in 2023 and finished the season in Triple-A. Kouba's fastball sits at 89-92 mph and tops out at 94 but doesn't get hit hard because he has all the traits the Astros target with pitchers: low release height, flat approach angle, significant extension in his delivery. It also plays up because he keeps batters off balance with his best pitch, a solid low-80s changeup with fade and sink. He has a pair of ordinary breaking balls, a sweeping low-80s slider he uses vs. righties and an upper-70s curveball he employs against lefties. With his combination of deception and control, Kouba could be a No. 5 starter. His stuff works better than it grades because he mixes his pitches well, commands his fastball and throws his secondary offerings for strikes. He was in line to get an opportunity if Houston needed rotation help in 2024 before missing two months with an elbow injury that didn't require surgery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds are always active players on the international market and it was no different during the 2024 international signing period. They focused much more on bats, with seven of their top bonuses – all six figures or more – going to hitters. Down the list was Torres, a six-foot right-hander who got $30,000 to sign with the organization when the period opened in January of that year. He was among the Dominican Summer League’s leaders in ERA, WHIP and batting average against, then came stateside in 2025 and was equally dominant over 38 1/3 Arizona Complex League innings. While a bit undersized, Torres is strong and stocky and his intriguing combination of feel for pitching and solid all-around stuff points to a future as a starter. He has three usable pitches, all of which are average but could be better as he progresses. His fastball sits in the 91-94 range, and he’s shown the ability to maintain his velocity throughout outings, he spins a low-80s curve very well and has good feel for an 85-87 mph fading changeup. All of his offerings play up because he’s shown a very strong feel for throwing them all for strikes, especially for his age. He’s walked just 1.9 per nine in his brief pro career heading into 2026, with the hopes of him having at least above-average command in the future. He’s yet to show he can answer the bell in a full-season rotation, but the Reds are bullish on his ability to start long term. Other organizations have definitely noticed his early success as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Coley faced plenty of adversity in his college career at Rhode Island, striking out in more than half his at-bats as a freshman in 2019, losing most of the 2020 season to the pandemic, missing all of 2022 because of a school credit snafu and half of 2023 after breaking his jaw in a collision at first base. He homered eight times and stole six bases in 25 games last spring, graduated with a mechanical engineering degree and signed with the Marlins for $50,000 as a 17th-rounder. He made his pro debut by batting .265/.395/.480 in Single-A and helping Jupiter win the Florida State League title. Coley's bat speed and strength rank among the best in the system and create plus raw power. A right-handed hitter, he looks to make the most of it by launching balls to his pull side, though his approach also yields strikeouts and rolled-over groundballs. More raw than most 23-year-olds because he had only 305 at-bats in five years in college, he could do a lot of damage if he learns to be more selective. He didn't run much at Rhode Island but Coley possesses plus speed and swiped nine bases in 10 tries during his 33-game pro debut. His quickness allows him to cover plenty of ground of center field and he has solid arm strength that could improve a tick if he cleans up his throwing motion. Besides his tools, he draws raves for his intelligence and work ethic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rivas earned NCAA Division II All-America accolades at Indianapolis in 2022 before transferring to Mississippi, where he was the Rebels' best starter as a junior before missing all of 2024 following Tommy John surgery. The Yankees still drafted him in the 16th round because they were intrigued by the deception of his pitches. He returned to the mound last year and recorded a 3.38 ERA with a .166 average-against and a 31 percent strikeout rate while advancing from Rookie ball to High-A. Rivas doesn't fool hitters with a riding fastball that sits at 90 mph and maxes out at 92, but he utilizes it well enough to set up a pair of baffling secondary pitches. He does an excellent job of killing spin on a low-80s changeup with splitter action that generated a 41 percent chase rate and 57 percent swing-and-miss rate in his pro debut. Hitters also consistently swung over the top of his tight low-80s slider. Though Rivas spent his first pro season as a starter, he profiles better as a tricky left-handed reliever. He has to nibble with his below-average heater and get chases with his slider and changeup, so only a third of his pitches landed in the strike zone last year. His competitive makeup also would work well out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Wisconsin high schooler with a big fastball, Snead started his college career at Wichita State, but then moved on to Tennessee where, as a sophomore, he helped the Volunteers win the 2024 Men's College World Series, picking up a key save and hold in the Finals. He came out of the bullpen again as a junior, but his combination of a full arsenal and ability to throw strikes could give him the chance to start, something the Angels no doubt were contemplating when taking him with their compensation pick following the third round of the 2025 Draft. There’s no doubt that Snead can throw hard -- he sat around 95-97 mph and touched triple digits. But the heater often lacked life, with sink over carry, so if he wasn’t locating it down in the zone well, it was very hittable. He’s already gotten to work on differentiating his two- and four-seamers (which often blended together), as well as improving his low-90s cutter. His low-80s curve evolved into his best secondary offering in 2025. There’s also a mid-80s slider and low-90s changeup in Snead’s bag of tricks, though he didn’t pull them out often. He has a bit of a slinky delivery coming from a low three-quarters slot, and while he finds the strike zone, it’s control over command. The Angels could give him a chance to start out of the gate, knowing that he could also develop into a late-inning reliever with better fastball characteristics.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Of all the pitchers taken in the 2025 Rule 5 Draft, Winquest might have the best long-term chance to remain a starter. The former eighth rounder out of UT-Arlington reached Double-A in 2025 and worked 106 total innings with a 3.99 ERA. He’s a bouncy 6-foot-2, and has both starter-quality athleticism and physicality at a well-composed 205 pounds. Winquest also consistently locates his 94-97 mph fastball to the up-and-arm-side quadrant of the zone where it plays best, and then bends in several different breaking balls - cutters, curveballs and sliders - off of that pitch. He’s better at landing his breakers in the zone than he is at dotting them for chase, and he’s comfortable pitching backwards, which he may need to do against big league lefties since he lacks a changeup. 
Winquest's control gives him a good chance to stick on the Yankees' roster, and his pedigree as a minor league starter puts him in position to provide length in the event that he makes the team. He can lean on his fastball/curveball combo an inning at a time and work in the other breaking balls if he eventually returns to starting. Either way, he should be a solid, lower-ceiling contributor to a pitching staff for the next several years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De la Rosa signed with the Yankees out of the Dominican Republic for $400,000 last April, receiving the third-highest bonus given to any left-hander on the 2025 international market. He quickly stood out with his stuff and strikes during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, drawing immediate trade interest. Three months after he turned pro, the Giants acquired him in a four-prospect package in exchange for Camilo Doval. De la Rosa works with a 92-94 mph fastball that reaches 96 with significant carry as well as armside run. Both of his secondary pitches also show promise. He throws both a tight slider and a sweepier version in the low 80s, and his fading changeup is a tick harder. While De La Rosa has three legitimate pitches and posted a 7 percent walk rate in his first taste of pro ball, there are questions about his ability to remain a starter in the long run. He's undersized and works uphill with some funk in his arm action, though his delivery provides deception without costing him control. If he does land in the bullpen, he has the upside to work in a late-inning role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Right-hander Nehomar Ochoa Sr. pitched in the Expos system from 2003-05 until falling off a horse and injuring his shoulder, and his son was born in Venezuela shortly before his career ended. The younger Nehomar moved to the United States at age 10 and blossomed into a physical and toolsy outfielder at a Houston high school before signing with the local Astros for $300,000 (double slot value) as an 11th-rounder in 2023. In his first full pro season, he slashed .222/.317/.359 with 10 homers and 17 steals in 103 games as the second-youngest batting qualifier (age 18) in the Single-A Carolina League. Extremely physical at 6-foot-4 and 230 pounds, Ochoa has a quick right-handed swing and at least plus raw power that plays mostly to left field because of his pull- and launch-heavy mindset. He has enough natural pop to hit 25 or more homers per season without swinging for the fences. He'll have to moderate his approach as he advances because he chases too much and is overmatched by breaking balls from righties. Very athletic for his size, Ochoa has average speed and is aggressive on the bases. He's still a work in progress as a corner outfielder, but he has the quick reactions to become at least an average defender and may get a trial in center field. He has plus arm strength, reaching 95 mph with his fastball as a prep pitcher and throwing out 12 runners in 76 starts in right field last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In 2024, the Mariners signed Chia-Shi Shen out of Chinese Taipei. They hit that pitching market again in 2025, signing Lin for $460,000 when the signing period opened in January. A former two-way player who pitched well in international competition, Lin looked really good in Spring Training after signing, but then wasn’t able to make his pro debut because of a lat strain, though he did get some innings in the bridge league at the end of the year, once again raising expectations. Lin had played both the infield and outfield previously, and he brings that athleticism to the mound. The 5-foot-11 right-hander has the chance to have a full starter’s repertoire, with his splitter the standout pitch. It flashes plus and can fall off the table with excellent depth while also throwing a distinct changeup. His fastball sits around 92-93 mph, but he’s shown the ability to reach back for more, and there could be more velocity in the future. He has some feel to spin with a more traditional slider, though it’s behind the other offerings, and there’s been some talk of adding a sweeper to his mix. Lin’s athleticism helps him repeat his delivery and find the strike zone consistently. His stuff may never wow anyone, but his feel for pitching and full array of offerings gives him the chance to start, with the Mariners getting to see what he’s like in competition this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After showing the ability to command his fastball and miss bats with his secondary pitches as a freshman at Cloud County (Kan.) CC and a sophomore at Nebraska, McConnaughey positioned himself as an early-round pick in 2025. But his elbow gave out after three starts last spring and required Tommy John surgery in March. He still rated as the top prospect in the Cornhusker State and went in the fourth round to the Rangers, signing for a below-slot $495,825. McConnaughey's fastball sits in the low 90s and peaks at 95 mph, though it plays up a bit because he can ride it up in the zone and sink it down at the knees. He can manipulate his low-80s slider, landing a tight version for strikes and getting chases by burying them in the dirt or sweeping them away from righties. He also has good feel for a tumbling 82-85 mph changeup that neutralizes left-handers. McConnaughey has an easy, clean delivery that he repeats well, allowing him to place his pitches where he wants. Pitchers often throw harder after adding strength during the Tommy John rehab process, and adding more velocity to his present polish would raise his ceiling. Scouts praise his mound presence and work ethic.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Tunink enticed scouts with his left-handed stroke and athleticism as an Illinois high schooler, his strong Notre Dame commitment clouded his signability in the 2024 Draft. The Dodgers floated him down to the eighth round and were able to land him for $412,500, the equivalent of fifth-round money. He earned Arizona Complex League All-Star honors in his pro debut last summer after finishing fourth in the Rookie circuit in wRC+ (152), slugging (.550) and OPS (.967), but he also struck out at a 30 percent rate. Tunink's bat speed, growing strength and propensity for driving the ball in the air to his pull side generate high exit velocities and plus raw power. He's not overly aggressive in terms of chasing pitches, but he has holes in his swing that lead to too many in-zone misses. Viewed as more of a hit-over-power guy as an amateur, he flipped that projection in the ACL. Tunink features at least plus speed that makes him a basestealing threat and a solid center fielder. He has below-average arm strength and didn't record an assist in 35 outfield starts last year.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Mariano is a switch-hitting middle infielder who draws Ozzie Albies starter kit comparisons from his most ardent proponents. He slashed .336/.466/.580 with more walks than strikeouts in his second DSL season after adding relevant physicality between years one and two. Mariano is built like a wiry defensive back. He's undersized but is definitely bigger than his listed 5-foot-7, 140 pounds, and his gorgeous swing is actualized to get to the modest power he currently has. This isn't a super projectable hitter likely to fit at a premium position (Mariano has experience at several positions, but our sources think second base is his best fit) and grow into big power, but Mariano is a special athlete who worked hard to add meaningful strength, and he's a skilled enough hitter that he might be able to punch above his weight. He's a high priority target on the 2026 Arizona Complex circuit.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants have signed a number of intriguing arms on the international market in the last few years, including Rodriguez for $10,000 as a 19-year-old out of Venezuela in 2025. He carved up Rookie-level Dominican Summer League hitters in his pro debut, logging a 2.41 ERA with a .138 opponent average and 46 strikeouts in 41 innings. He has continued to impress after coming to the United States and pitching in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League in 2026. Rodriguez operates at 92-94 mph and touches 96 with a fastball that features sinking and tailing action. He backs it up with a hard, short slider in the mid 80s. He also shows the making of an average low-80s changeup with some fade. At 5-foot-11 and 212 pounds, Rodriguez is more physical than projectable. He has a simple delivery with a low release height, and his control is improving as he gains more experience. He has a chance to pitch in the back of a big league rotation if he can upgrade his secondary pitches and command.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Between COVID and a medical redshirt season, Franklin was a sixth-year senior at Missouri in 2023 with ugly surface numbers and an uglier delivery when the Sox took a $10,000 flier on him in the 10th round. But his short-armed, vertical riding mid-90s heater has always piled up whiffs, and while the right-hander is entering his 40-man platform year at age 27, it also comes on the heels of a season that saw him strike out 35.3% of hitters in 56.1 innings while finishing the year at the end of the Triple-A bullpen. The Sox have added a Garrett Crochet-esque leg kick to keep Franklin’s weight back in his delivery, which has had mixed success in allowing his arm to get on time (11.2% walk rate). Given his heater's sub-70% in-zone contact rate, Franklin has been extremely fastball-heavy throughout his pro career, but most recently he has leaned on a mid-80s splitter as his primary secondary, which alternates gorgeous finishes and arm-side misfires.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Jerzembeck missed his final two years at South Carolina recovering from a TJ and later a stress fracture in his elbow. He was nasty on the backfields this spring, executing a lateral attack with a tailing mid-90s fastball and late-biting slider. Jerzembeck's delivery has NC-17 violence and his recent injury history is severe, making him a likely reliever. Early this year he's done a mix of starting and long relieving at Myrtle Beach. His changeup has enough tail and sink to give him a third projected bat-missing pitch, and he can tweak his slider to play more like a cutter. There's a starter's mix here, and Jerzembeck (who is underdeveloped from a reps standpoint) has pretty solid feel for location, but his delivery is just too messy to project him in the rotation. He should be a reliable long reliever instead.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heuer had some of the best physicality and projectable fastball velocity in the 2023 Draft, but he turned down the Guardians as a 16th-rounder to attend Texas Tech. He served as the Red Raiders' No. 1 starter and pushed his fastball to 98 mph last spring, but he also logged a 6.28 ERA as a Draft-eligible sophomore. That didn't deter the Yankees, who signed him for an over-slot $400,000 in the eighth round. Heuer operates at 93-95 mph with cut and carry on his fastball, which is effective up in the zone but gets pounded when he doesn't command it well. His mid-80s slider with sweeping action can be a solid offering when it's on, though he has trouble landing it for strikes and it sometimes flattens over the heart of the plate. His mid-80s changeup with fade and depth was his most effective offering as a sophomore, though he didn't use it much. Scouts don't love Heuer's delivery, which features a short arm action, high release point and some crossfire. He presently has fringy control and below-average command, which may make him more of a reliever than a starter in the long run. If he doesn't make it in baseball, he has his own livestock business with his brother and raised ewes that won grand champion titles at the 2020 and 2022 Georgia National Fairs.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies targeted college pitching in the 2025 Draft, using 13 of their 20 selections on that demographic. Their first six picks were all college arms, with Tallon the last of the half-dozen. The big left-hander spent three years at Duke, almost entirely as a reliever, showcasing swing-and-miss stuff albeit without the ability to command it consistently. A 12.5 career K/9 rate for the Blue Devils stood out and the Phillies took a chance on his bat-missing arm in the sixth round, signing for right around slot. While there was some talk about Tallon being given the chance to start out of the gate, it’s looking like he’s going to be a reliever to kick off his pro career. The 6-foot-5 southpaw is all about his unhittable fastball, a pitch he threw more than 70 percent of the time last year at Duke. It sits in the low 90s and tops out at just 95 mph, but it elicited a miss rate of 34 percent and a 35-percent chase rate in 2025 thanks to a deceptive delivery and a low release height. He’ll need to improve his breaking ball, though his cutter-like slider did miss bats at times. Tallon did throw a mid-80s changeup now and again in college, but will likely focus on his top two pitches as a professional reliever. He needs to harness his command after walking 4.7 per nine last year, but if he can do that and improve his ability to spin the ball, he could move pretty quickly through the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kohn immediately claimed a role in Mississippi State's bullpen as freshman before missing all of 2023 following Tommy John surgery. He showed average stuff when he came back as a starter and went undrafted in 2024, then improved his stuff and strike-throwing as a redshirt junior last spring. One of the best fourth-year collegians in the 2025 Draft, he went in the fourth round and will make his pro debut this year. Though Kohn's fastball has pedestrian velocity at 91-95 mph, hitters don't see it coming out of his low three-quarters arm slot and flat approach angle, and he has the aptitude to work it with carry up in the zone or spot it down at the knees. He also has advanced command of a sweeping low-80s slider that he can locate on either side of the plate. While he works almost exclusively with those two pitches, he does show a promising low-80s changeup with fade that could give him a third solid offering. Kohn improved his athleticism in 2025, allowing him to get down the mound better and repeat his delivery more consistently. That led to improved extension and deception as well as control and command. He has a high floor as a three-pitch lefty starter with advanced feel for his craft and strong mound presence.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants drafted Heliot Ramos in the first round out of the Leadership Christian Academy (Guaynabo, P.R.) in 2017, then went back there six years later to take Ortiz in the 13th round. He impressed with his athleticism on the U.S. high school showcase circuit and continued to do so in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League the last two years. Promoted to Single-A last August, he banged up his knee running into the outfield wall in his first game, ending his 2024 season. Ortiz isn't very physical, so he focuses on making contact and getting on base. He has good feel for his right-handed swing and the strike zone and looked more comfortable against pro pitching during his second stint in the ACL. He did a better job of turning on pitches and lifting them last summer, so he could grow into 12-15 homer power once he fills out his 5-foot-11 frame. Ortiz earns plus grades for his speed, arm and center-field defense. He has the mentality and aptitude to steal bases, and the instincts enhance his range in center. His arm is stronger than most at his position, adding to his credentials as the system's best defensive outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Watson utilized a low slot at Virginia Commonwealth before the Yankees selected him in the 15th round in 2021. Following his lackluster first full pro season in Single-A, they had him drop down further and overhaul his arsenal. The changes paid off as he led all Minor League relievers (minimum: 60 innings) with a 1.58 ERA and ranked second with a .138 opponent average while reaching Double-A. Watson creates unique deception as a 6-foot-7 sidearmer with an upright delivery. Batters struggle to barrel his fastball, which parks at 90-92 mph and tops out at 94 but features tremendous carry and armside run. He has scrapped a tight slider and a changeup and now works with a mid-80s cutter that shows flashes of becoming a solid offering and a fringier 78-82 mph sweeper. The new arm slot not only upgraded Watson's stuff, but he's also throwing more strikes. The changes also helped him log a .393 OPS against left-handers in 2023 after they teed off on him for a 1.019 OPS the year before. He could reach New York in 2024 if his unusual look can continue to baffle hitters in Triple-A.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Gomez is a stout lefty with a really strong lower body and a clean, deceptive arm action. Though he's a little shorter than most big league starters, the consistency and ease of his delivery gives him the look of a guy who can take the ball every fifth day. His arm stroke hides the baseball from the hitter until very late, when Gomez's hand appears from behind his head and suddely a 93 mph fastball is backspinning toward the dish. All of Gomez's pitches play up a tad because of his delivery, and his changeup has exciting long-term projection because of it. Though neither of Gomez's breaking balls is especially nasty, they consistently finish in effective (and different) locations. His pitch mix features weapons that finish in all four qudrants of the zone, and though he is definiely a control-over-command type, it's enough to consider Gomez a future backend starter. He won't turn 21 until the middle of 2026, but his build is relatively maxed out and he's more of a polished prospect than one with big long-term projection. The 2026 season is Gomez's 40-man platform year and the Guardians, who acquired him from the Mets in exchange for international pool space, might try to push him to Double-A at some point to see if he merits addition after the season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly was a two-sport standout who didn't stop playing football until his senior year of high school. He was on scouts' radars in southern California but headed to pitch at UC Irvine. Although Injuries interrupted his progress over his two first years with the Anteaters, a chance to move into their rotation in March of his junior year allowed him to take off. He landed in the fourth round of the 2025 Draft, and while he didn't pitch officially after signing, he got in some good work during instructs. An athletic 6-foot-5 right-hander, Kelly entered pro ball with three pitches and might now have four at his disposal. The Rockies are hoping there might be another tier of velocity to reach with his fastball, which currently sits in the 91-94 mph range, occasionally touching 96. It has some good metrics with some ride and finish to the pitch. But Kelly's really all about the spin. His upper-70s curve has 11-to-5 shape and regularly tops 3,000 rpm, and he can miss bats with his low-80s changeup as well. During instructs, he found a slider grip that works for him, giving him a fourth pitch that could be Major League average. Kelly started throwing better quality strikes when he became a starter during his junior year, and the hope is that trend continues. He has the pitch mix to start and will be given the opportunity to stick in a rotation if he can hold the zone consistently throughout his outings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thach could have started his pro career out of high school when the Giants took him in the 18th round in 2022, but the great-nephew of Hall of Famer Catfish Hunter headed to UNC Wilmington instead. He's all over the Seahawks' record books, setting the freshman home run mark (15) in 2023 and then the single-season record with 27 as a sophomore. The power kept showing up with wood bats in the Cape Cod League (eight homers), but enthusiasm dampened a bit when the pop didn't show up as much in 2025. Still, his 54 career homers are a school record, and the Rockies took a flier in the eighth round of last summer's Draft, going a bit over slot to bring him into the fold. He got off to a very good start during his first full season of pro ball with Single-A Fresno. The big left-handed hitter offers an intriguing combination of strength and bat speed coming from his 6-foot-4 frame that provides optimism he can send the ball a long way and catch up to good velocity. He hits the ball very hard, registering high exit velocities and his well-above-average raw power can show up to all fields, though most of his home run thump comes to his pull side. He doesn't strike out a ton, especially given his power, but he does chase out of the zone too much, something that will have to improve as he moves up the ladder. A former two-way player who was up to 90 mph on the mound, Thach's well-below-average speed almost certainly limits him to first base, though he has seen a little time in right field as a pro. He'll have to keep getting to that raw pop to profile well in either corner spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brailer Guerrero was the big name in the Rays’ 2023 international signing class, but they may have landed another player to watch in Monzon. The infielder from La Guaira, Venezuela, was signed for $300,000 by Rays scouts Marlon Roche and William Bergolla. Initially viewed as a defensive-oriented shortstop who could also make contact at the plate, he immediately performed well in the Dominican Summer League as a 17-year-old and jumped onto the prospect radar. Monzon is one of the Rays’ best young players coming out of the DSL, and his .281/.395/.421 batting line reflects some of the things he does well. His hit tool stands out ahead of his power, which is more gap to gap at this point, but he controls the strike zone well from the left side of the plate and he ultimately had more walks (35) than strikeouts (30) in 205 plate appearances during his 46-game professional debut. Considering he was signed as a glove-first prospect, it’s an especially interesting offensive profile for someone his age -- but he’s obviously yet to be tested by even Florida Complex League pitching. Monzon played 25 games at shortstop, 10 at third base and nine at second last season. He’s a shortstop for at least the short term, with above-average actions, solid instincts in the field and enough arm to hold down the spot. The question is more about how he grows physically, as he bulked up quickly to 6-foot and 160 pounds with some projection remaining on his frame. If he gets bigger, it’s more an issue of lateral quickness and whether he’s better suited for one of the other infield positions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Girton played three springs at Texas Tech but never found a regular spot in the rotation -- an injury-marred 2022 didn’t help -- and transferred to Oklahoma in '24. Ten of his 16 appearances with the Sooners were starts, but success was still limited with a 7.32 ERA, 47 strikeouts and 31 walks in 35 2/3 innings. The Mets selected him in the 10th round -- two rounds after taking OU teammate Ryan Lambert -- and signed him for below slot at $122,500. Girton dominated High-A Brooklyn in his first full season, posting a 2.59 ERA with 91 strikeouts in 76 1/3 innings, before slowing down in his final four starts with Double-A Binghamton. The 6-foot-1 right-hander pitches with bounce in his delivery and throws from a high three-quarters slot. His four-seam fastball can move in the mid 90s and acted like a downright weapon with cut-ride action at the top of the zone, getting whiffs on one-third of opponents’ swings against it across both levels in 2025. Girton works with two slider variations -- a mid-80s sweeper with a ton of horizontal break and a tighter upper-80s option that practically acts like a cutter. He has talked about adding a splitter but went to very little offspeed last season. Luckily for him, the sweeper can backfoot lefties well and helped fend off splits issues. Girton really struggled to deliver consistent strikes in school and looked to correct course midseason in ’25, only to struggle again after his move to the Eastern League. He’s already entering his age-24 season and might not have too long of a leash for starting, now that he’s seen the upper Minors, unless the control is ironed out or he finds a split/change. Even so, the fastball/sliders could put him on the fast track to Queens on their own.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Pacheco has had early-career success as a rookie ball starter, with 1.19 WHIP in 62.1 career innings. He throws hard, with his fastball residing in the 93-96 mph range through most of 2025 as he worked four to five innings per start. Pacheco's arm action is explosive, and he generates six-and-a-half feet of extension even though he's only six feet tall. He's been able to throw strikes despite his delivery featuring a good bit of effort, and he's walked just 6.5% of opposing hitters since signing. His arm action (and ability to kill spin) allows for lots of projection on his power changeup, which currently lives in the 86-90 mph range. His breaking ball is a blunt 80-mph curveball that might morph into a harder slider/cutter with time. It'd be easier to project Pacheco as a starter if he were a bigger athlete; it's rare for righties this size to wind up in a big league rotation. But he throws hard, throws strikes, and should have at least one viable secondary weapon at peak (the changeup), which would allow him to be a reliable middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fisher redshirted at Mississippi in 2020, helped Walters State (Tenn.) CC make the Junior College World Series in 2021 and cranked 18 homers (including two grand slams in one game) at Charlotte in 2022 but went undrafted because of worries about his stroke and strikeout tendencies. Then he set 49ers marks for single-season (30, third in NCAA Division I) and career homers (48), including a record six while winning MVP accolades at the Conference USA tournament, powering his way into the fourth round. He batted .273/.396/.500 with five homers in 31 games in Single-A in his pro debut. There's nothing subtle about Fisher's approach. He stands upright at the plate and looks to launch balls to his pull side with an uphill left-handed stroke. His combination of bat speed and strength, extreme pull-focused mentality and high exit velocities led one amateur scout to call him the mid-major version of Kyle Schwarber. Though he ranked fifth in D-I with 64 walks and generally makes good swing decisions, his mentality results in a lot of strikeouts and some difficulties against non-fastballs. Fisher isn't the prettiest runner, but he has surprisingly solid speed and succeeded on all 15 of his steal attempts between college and pro ball last year. His athleticism should translate into defensive ability as well, but he's just adequate as a corner outfielder with an average arm. A part-time catcher in junior college, he played mostly right field at Charlotte and in his debut but is better suited for left.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taurek redshirted his freshman year at St. Mary’s in 2023, then played sparingly the next season. He made it count in 2025, earning second-team All-West Coast Conference honors while hitting .328 with 11 homers and helping the Gaels win the WCC tournament and reach NCAA Regional play. The Mariners liked his swing enough to take a $150,000 flier on him in the 13th round of the Draft, and he went out and hit some more, posting a .336 average over 27 games with Single-A Modesto during his pro debut. The one thing that seems certain about Taurek is that he can make a lot of contact with a chance to hit at this level. He’s small and compact and so is his right-handed swing, with simple mechanics and direct to the ball action. He does not strike out much -- just 9.5 percent with the Gaels in ‘25 -- and while he’s very aggressive at the plate and doesn’t walk a ton, he also limits chase. He’s not all that projectable from a physicality standpoint, and it’s unclear whether he’ll have that much impact. Taurek is a bit of a tweener defensively. He doesn’t have enough speed to play center field regularly -- he played left exclusively at St. Mary’s, and that’s where he spent most of his time during his pro debut. But he doesn’t have enough thump to profile as an everyday guy in a corner. The right-right undersized profile is a tough one, but he’s swung the bat well enough to make him interesting.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Michigander during his high school days, Steensma headed to Boone, North Carolina, home to Appalachian State, for college ball. After pitching out of the bullpen as the Mountaineers' closer, racking up seven saves as a freshman in 2023, he moved into the rotation as a sophomore, finishing among the Sun Belt Conference top 10 in a host of pitching categories. An elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery in December 2024 kept him off the mound in '25, but a combination of Mariners scouts and their analytics department saw enough potential from his performance the year prior to take him in the ninth round of last July's Draft. Now healthy, he got off to a very good start during his pro debut at Single-A in 2026. A strong 6-foot-4 right-hander, Steensma has a potential four-pitch mix that gives him a chance to start. While his fastball sits 92-93 mph and touches 95, it plays up and misses bats thanks to riding life that comes as a result of the combination of good extension and low release height. His tight mid-80s slider has ticked up since his college days and could be an out pitch in time. He'll mix in an 80 mph curve, and while he does have a potentially serviceable changeup, he wasn't throwing it much at the outset of his pro career. The Mariners are bullish about Steensma because he's still learning how to mix his pitches effectively. He was throwing a ton of strikes out of the gate, with the organization thinking he could have future plus command. They don't want to put unfair expectations on him, but the Mariners have done excellent development work with formerly injured college arms taken later on Day 2 of the Draft, like sixth-rounder-turned-All-Star Bryan Woo.

fangraphs.label: bos2026may
fangraphs.text: Bravo popped onto the radar because of his 2025 data (he posted an 88% contact rate during his debut season), and would have based on his visual scouting look in Florida this year, albeit for entirely different reasons. On paper, Bravo looks like a slappy contact hitter with special feel for the barrel but no power (16% hard-hit rate). In person, he has a bloodthirsty low-ball swing with an epic finish in the dirt behind him. He also looks like a prospect with strikeout risk, as his front foot is often bailing down the first base line when he swings, and his scoopy bat path leaves Bravo vulnerable to elevated fastballs away from him. When he gets a ball in his wheelhouse on the inner third of the dish, his swing looks like that of a baby Darryl Strawberry. Because the BoSox FCL roster is chock full of shortstops, Bravo’s reps there have been limited, but he’s looked competent on the opportunities he’s gotten. The incongruity between Bravo’s scouting look as a hitter versus his DSL data from last season is fascinating, but not deleterious. Most of what’s happening here is positive and exciting, giving the Red Sox yet another fun young infielder to monitor.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Arias is a twitchy, medium-framed outfielder who runs well enough to develop in center field. He swings pretty hard, but it requires a good bit of effort for him to do so, creating risk that he'll whiff more as he climbs. His $1.2 million deal with the Dodgers was one of the earlier handshake agreements in the class.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Van Dam was a ninth-rounder out of NC State, a promising righty who slipped in last year's draft in part because Tommy John surgery wiped away the end of his sophomore and most of his junior season. It didn't take long for his modest draft position bonus to look out of step with his talent. 
Van Dam is an above-average athlete with good body control and a very loose arm swing. After throwing well in front of Eric last fall, he looked good again on the backfields this spring, sitting 95-96 with average carry and limited tail on his fastball. He flashes a plus curve, and while he doesn't throw his slider much, his feel for spin suggests he could have a pretty good one of those as well. Van Dam maintains arm speed on his change, which makes it projectable, even if he’s not yet generating the kind of movement likely to miss a bunch of bats. He isn't especially deceptive, as his arm stroke and delivery are long and timeable, and if I had one nagging thought about my in-person look, it was that hitters seemed to make surprisingly good contact against him. That could also just be a coincidence, because Van Dam’s stuff and control look big league-caliber. 
Kansas City is using him in a multi-inning relief role out of the gate, an understandable choice to manage his innings in his first full season after surgery. In the long run, Van Dam has a shot to start. It’s possible his fastball won't have the same zip or that he'll be too hittable in that role, but for now you can dream on a no. 4 with a mid-to-high-leverage fallback. Good scouting from the Royals here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz signed with the Yankees for $75,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2022 and was one of several standouts on a prospect-laden team in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League last summer. The youngest batting qualifier in the circuit at age 17, he led the FCL with 47 RBI and ranked second with 10 homers. The Marlins acquired him in a three-team trade in March, sending Jon Berti to New York and also receiving outfield prospect Shane Sasaki from the Rays. After looking launch-happy and passive during his 2022 pro debut, Cruz displayed a better approach and more power last year. His quick left-handed stroke produces loud contact when he connects, and he could grow into plus pop if he fills out his projectable frame and adds more polish as a hitter. He controls the strike zone fine for a teenager, but his aggressiveness leads to less-than-ideal contact. Cruz presently has solid speed but is still learning to make the most of it on the bases and in the outfield. He's not an instinctive defender and spent most of his FCL time in right field, where he displays solid arm strength. To make it in center, he'd need to improve his reads and routes while retaining his quickness as he matures physically.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Green showed off an exciting power-speed combination across three seasons at Cal by swiping 45 bases and crushing 34 home runs in 151 games. The A’s had plenty of looks at those raw tools while scouting him just down the road over the years and were thrilled to land him in the fourth round of the 2024 Draft, going over slot value to sign him for $1 million. Getting his feet wet at Single-A Stockton last year, he hit .289 with an .832 OPS, three homers, eight doubles and nine stolen bases in 24 games. Green falls in line with recent A’s Draft picks such as Denzel Clarke and Henry Bolte who stand out for their exciting raw tools. The ball really jumps off the bat with his ability to drive it to all fields, and the A’s still believe there is more raw power he will tap into. The big concern has always been his lack of consistent contact, as his strikeout rate hovered around 30% in college, which could be attributed to his unorthodox mechanics at the plate. But the A’s have been encouraged by his improvements in that respect, and he has shown a decent eye by drawing a fair amount of walks. A plus runner who can cover a ton of ground with a solid arm, Green has a chance to stick in center field, though some scouts see an eventual move to left. The A’s saw Green as a first-round talent with a ceiling that is just about as high as any other prospect in the organization, but he will have to overcome the swing-and-miss issues that plagued him throughout his amateur career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fairly anonymous when he signed with the Yankees for $30,000 out of Venezuela in 2022, Ramirez batted .319 in two seasons in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League before attracting attention in his U.S. debut last year. He earned Florida Complex League All-Star accolades after ranking second in the Rookie-level circuit in hitting (.348) and on-base percentage (.447) and fourth in OPS (.960). The Marlins acquired him as part of a three-prospect package for Jazz Chisholm Jr. at the Trade Deadline last July. Ramirez employs a leg kick at the plate and makes consistent contact with a disciplined approach and a compact right-handed stroke. He's learning to turn on pitches but hits a lot of ground balls and may not provide more than 10-12 homers per season. Though he puts the bat on the ball with ease, he makes good swing decisions and draws a healthy amount of walks. Ramirez's solid speed plays better on the bases than in the field, though he's not a prolific basestealer. His average arm and range are best suited for second base, though he spent the majority of his time last year at third base, where he committed nine errors in 36 starts. He also has seen action at left field and shortstop and projects as a utilityman with a sparkplug mentality.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: James signed for $2.5 million rather than head to Ole Miss and was assigned to Low-A Fredericksburg to start his pro career in 2026. Part of the crowded infield contingent there, he has played a mix of second base, third base and left field as of list publication. A terrific low-to-the-ground athlete, James can be slow to approach grounders and makes some plays unnecessarily close at first base. This is more an issue of polish and the speed of pro ball rather than talent, and he should still become a good infielder with time. While it was obvious that James had a power-over-hit skill set as a draft prospect, the degree to which that is true is coming into greater focus. He is pummeling pitches with power when he connects, but he's struggling to make adjustments to pro sliders. James can really run, he's strong, and he has power to both gaps. He's a fun, toolsy dev project who is probably going to take a while to mature on both sides of the ball.

fangraphs.label: 2025draft
fangraphs.text: Athletic shortstop with impressive power. Muscular, but loose and mobile. Terrific low-to-the-ground defender, has the arm strength for shortstop but needs to polish accuracy. Strikeout issues plagued him on the showcase circuit, where he ran a 69% contact rate. Swing is loose and explosive but isn't always well-connected or well-timed. Bottom-hand dominant swing that works best when James can get extended. Thunderous power in his wrists and hands. Defensive fit at shortstop should allow room for elevated strikeouts as long as James is getting to power. Right tail outcome is akin to a Trevor Story type of offensive performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: James had the look of a potential first-round pick after showing out as an underclassman on the showcase circuit and with Team USA’s 18-and-under team in 2023 but couldn’t replicate that same level of success in the summer before his senior year, including going 1-for-12 with six strikeouts at the East Coast Pro Showcase. He rebounded a bit in the spring at Davie County HS and won Gatorade’s Player of the Year honors in North Carolina as a result. Some scouts thought he was headed to Mississippi, but the Nationals selected him in the fifth round and signed him for $2.5 million, tied for the second-highest bonus in their 2025 class. A 6-foot infielder, James added weight going into his Draft year, trading off athleticism for strength in the process. With that additional impact, he profiles as a possible 20-homer hitter, especially if he can maintain his bat speed on the pro side. The focus on driving the ball also came with a regression in swing decisions, and he bit on a good number of non-fastballs outside the zone during his 2024 showcases. His right-handed swing has looked smoother in the past, and getting back to those mechanics would help his ability to hit for average in the pros. James has the actions, hands and above-average arm strength to handle shortstop, but his fringy speed limits his range on the dirt. With Eli Willits also in the organization, James is more likely to be a better fit at second or third base, and his arm could even work in a corner outfield spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves had a compensation pick after the fourth round of the 2025 Draft after losing Max Fried to free agency. They used it to pick up Williams, a middle infielder who was coming off a solid junior season at East Carolina, finishing with 14 homers and an OPS over 1.000 before going 8-for-20 and being named to the all-tournament team at the NCAA Greenville Regional. He signed for just under $500,000, a bit under slot, becoming the earliest-drafted hitter from the Pirates program since Connor Norby was a second-rounder in 2021. Williams brought his solid approach from the left side of the plate with him during his relatively brief 28-game pro debut last summer with Single-A Augusta. He could be an average hitter in the future with solid on-base skills and strike zone control. He drew more walks than strikeouts in his last year of college, part of what helped him get to his power more, with his over-the-fence pop coming mostly to his pull side. His debut with Augusta was solid, but the Braves think the underlying data points to even better contact rates to come. A plus runner who swiped 22 bases in 25 tries last year at East Carolina, Williams could have a potentially intriguing power-speed combination in the future. Where he ends up defensively is still up in the air. He played second and third in college, and his arm might be a tad short for the hot corner. His best bet long term to stick in one spot might be as an offensive-minded player at the keystone. But he’ll likely move around some, with center field one day not out of the question for a more likely utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The most advanced prospect in Miami's 2022 international crop, de la Cruz turned pro for $150,000 out of the Dominican Republic. Making his U.S. debut last summer, he needed just two starts in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League to earn a promotion to Single-A. The only 18-year-old to work double-digit innings in the Florida State League, he held his own with a 4.57 ERA and 42 strikeouts in 43 1/3 innings. While de la Cruz still is refining his entire repertoire, both his fastball and curveball show the potential to become plus pitches once fully developed. His riding fastball parked at 92-95 mph and touched 97 before he tired late in his first full pro season, and he should add more velocity as he fills out his projectable 6-foot-3 frame. His mid-70s curveball has good shape with plenty of depth and some horizontal action but also would benefit from more power. De la Cruz's changeup has some interesting fade, though it gets too firm in the mid-80s and he needs to use it more often so he can refine it. He's not as physical as Edward Cabrera was as a teenager, but he reminds some club officials of their big league starter with his repertoire and delivery. His control was spotty versus much older competition in the FSL but should be fine as he adds more strength and experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After putting himself on the Draft radar with three solid years at South Florida, Boser transferred to the University of Florida and boosted his stock as a senior with an impressive season. Entering the 2025 MLB Draft on MLB Pipeline’s Top 250 list, Boser landed with the A’s as an 11th-round pick. Ahead of his first full season as a pro, he got his feet wet with 32 games at Single-A Stockton. Boser has an intriguing profile as a hitter. He’s got some power to all fields and showed he can do some damage with the bat in college with good bat speed and balance at the plate. There’s also a bit of swing-and-miss to his game, which he’ll have to improve to tap into that power as a pro. Boser fits the mold of a versatile utility player who can provide strong defense at multiple positions that the A’s traditionally value highly, similar to past prospects such as Jeremy Eierman and Max Schueman. He has a good, accurate arm that should allow him to get plenty of reps at shortstop, third base and second base. He also worked to improve his athleticism in college, and that shows through on the bases as a decent runner. There is a solid floor here as a productive super-utility type, and the A’s liked what they saw from him at first glance.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Sando thrived as a junior reliever at Santa Clara and then struggled as a senior starter and spent his first full pro season in the bullpen. After an early-2025 demotion to Low-A, he pitched so well that the Reds not only elevated him back to Dayton, but also moved him into the rotation there. Sando thrived, twirling some impressive six-inning outings late in the year, and was again promoted, this time to Double-A. 
Sando is a control-over-command southpaw with a low-three-quarters delivery that helps his fastball play up. He bullies the zone with uphill fastballs and can land both his slider and changeup for strikes, but neither of those pitches is especially nasty. You could consider Sando a swingman candidate for 2027, though it's more likely he winds up as a bullpen's second or third lefty.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
The old saw about how long levered guys sometimes just need extra time to grow into their bodies can be a little frustrating because there’s not much you can do but wait and hope. It’s still early in the season, but we may be seeing that at play with Gongora. The lefty always threw strikes in college, but after a rough year in that department in 2025, he’s posted a tiny 1.97 BB/9 through his first seven starts at Double-A. He’s probably running hot and his command is still progressing - on video, it isn't unusual to see him alternate a perfectly placed breaking ball with a heater 18 inches from the target - but it’s impressive nonetheless, and his control drives a backend starter projection. 
Gongora has a classic starting pitcher’s four-pitch mix. Out of a high slot, he works with a low-to-mid-90s fastball, straight with a bit of carry. He has two functional breaking balls, a lovely 1-7 curve and a harder two-plane slider. He used his change less often than the breakers last year, but it too has good action and arm speed, and projects average. Unlike a lot of Orioles arms, Baltimore hasn’t overhauled too much with Gongora. He’s slowed the cadence in his delivery in pro ball, and to Brendan's eye he looks a little more limber. But the O’s have kept his high slot, and the tweaks to his offspeed pitches have been minor. That continuity has perhaps been helpful as he’s developed in pro ball, and it also means there’s runway ahead to play with a cutter, a split, or something else if the current mix proves hittable. As is, he’s having success at Double-A - 3.66 ERA, 40 strikeouts, two homers allowed in 32 innings across seven starts - and projects as a backend starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tommy John surgery ended Patteson’s 2022 college season early at Central Florida, but the Royals were convinced enough in their scouting of him and his makeup that they still drafted him in the fifth round that year. It took Patteson time to come back from the injury and start to make an impact, but his stuff shot up in 2025. He made 13 starts in High-A with a 1.99 ERA, while holding batters to a .199 average. He finished the year with 11 appearances (eight starts) in Double-A, where he had a 4.41 ERA. Patteson’s fastball hovered around 90-92 mph over the past few years, but once he got to Double-A in ‘25, he started running it up to the mid 90s and touching 97. The velo spike, which was more about a return to his pre-TJ form, also helped his main breaking ball become more firm as a mid-80s average slider that tries to be gyro but can get a little sweepy. Patteson also throws a curveball with good depth and feel to land it for strikes. His best weapon, though, is a mid-80s changeup with plus potential. Patteson throws strikes and has a clean delivery, hiding the ball well with short arm action. Lauded for his pitchability and being a student of the game, Patteson might be a late bloomer but is really coming into his own now that he’s reached the upper levels. He needs to show more consistency at Double-A and continue to refine his secondaries, but if the stuff continues to look like what it did there in ‘25, he has back-end rotation potential. The Royals might try him in the bullpen to see whether the stuff ticks up even more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Cardinals for $200,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2019, Saladin still didn’t see the Dominican Summer League until 2021 due to the pandemic and repeated the level after becoming a starter in 2022. He moved stateside in 2023 and enjoyed a breakout season in 2024 with a 2.62 ERA that ranked second among St. Louis Minor League full-season qualifiers. He also struck out 134 and walked 33 over 123 innings between Single-A and High-A. He was Rule 5-eligible in the offseason but went unprotected and unpicked due to his distance from the Majors. Standing only 5-foot-11, Saladin still stands out for his fastball that comes out of a low release height and has a flat vertical approach angle, causing more swing-and-miss than expected for most four-seamers. The pitch played in the 92-94 mph range in the Florida State League but lost some steam late with Peoria, understandable considering Saladin’s workload. His mid-80s changeup comes with enough armside run and deception off the fastball to get some whiffs too and hold lefties relatively at bay. A low-80s slider and upper-70s curveball aren’t at the same standard. Saladin kept his walk rates fairly low at both levels in 2024, and while he relies on some chase on all of his pitches (particularly the changeup), he has the control to remain a starter. Despite his Rule 5 status, the hurler is only entering his age-22 season and should get heavier 40-man consideration if he enjoys repeat success in 2025.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Hampu was a great find in the 2024 draft, as you don't normally get a flamethrower with a razor-sharp slider in the 18th round. There’s some effort to his delivery, and he can spray the ball around, but while he'll never have great command, he was actually a fair strike-thrower after a rough April last season. The former Governor is even a little deceptive, as a glove throw just prior to release is distracting and helps his already considerable stuff play up further. The developmental key going forward is getting his change and slider in good locations more consistently. Hitters did absolutely nothing with either of them last year, but he had too many noncompetitive misses to fully leverage their effectiveness. There’s work ahead, but Hampu has big league stuff, and modest improvements in his control will put him on track to reach his middle relief projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thompson spent his first three years of collegiate ball with Division III North Carolina Wesleyan and transferred to UNC Greensboro for the 2024 season. He spent two additional years with the Spartans and closed out his time there with a 3.79 ERA and 87 strikeouts in 61 2/3 innings as a reliever. The Blue Jays took him in the eighth round as a fifth-year senior sign, and his $5,000 bonus was the lowest in Toronto's 2025 class. Thompson popped nicely at Single-A Dunedin with one run allowed and 15 K's in 13 2/3 innings after the Draft, and he has joined the High-A Vancouver staff in his first full season, showing enough stuff to get his first extended starting look since 2023. The 6-foot right-hander has already taken nice steps forward in his professional development under the Blue Jays' guidance. His fastball velocity is up a bit in his first full season, sitting 93-95 mph, and he can staple the four-seamer to the top of the zone from a lower-than-average release height, making it tough for High-A hitters to pick up. Thompson also works with a promising upper-80s slider with harder action, and he's folded in a sweepier breaker in '26 too (one he calls a curveball but is likely closer to a sweeper). He's struggled to land his upper-80s changeup in the zone. It might be more of a command-over-control profile for Thompson moving forward. He can place the ball in the right spot to miss bats consistently, but if batters can learn to lay off the fastballs up and the sliders down, Thompson could find more trouble the higher he climbs. As it sits early in '26, he's been a K-BB% standout with a possible back-end starter profile and another potential win for the improved Toronto pitching department.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It has been well documented several times on the current Angels' Top 30 that this organization likes rolling the dice on high-end high school pitchers in later rounds of the Draft. In 2025, they did it five times, acquiring a group that included LaCourse in Round 6, making him the first Michigander prep pitcher to be taken in the top 10 rounds since Brock Porter was a fourth-rounder in 2022. The Angels went about $120,000 over slot to sign the right-hander away from his commitment to Michigan State. LaCourse’s size, projection and feel for spin all stood out to the Angels scouting staff. The 6-foot-3 starter routinely hits elite spin rate levels with his slider, registering consistently north of 3,000 RPMs with what could be a true out-pitch in time. While he had touched 93-94 mph in short stints in high school, he was more around 88-92 mph with his fastball as a starter, though Angels player development staff have been pleased to see that his velocity is starting to creep up. He throws the heater with a lot of spin for good carry up in the zone to miss bats. His changeup has also improved under pro supervision in the early going. A strong athlete who played basketball in the winter and shortstop when he wasn’t pitching as a prepster, LaCourse does an excellent job of filling up the strike zone with all of his offerings. If the early gains are for real and he can continue to add strength and velocity, he could turn into an inning-eating starter in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davis never could claim a regular turn in Oklahoma State's rotation, battling injuries and his control and command while logging a 5.61 ERA in three seasons. As a junior, he missed fall practice after breaking his collarbone in a fishing accident and lost a month last spring to shoulder issues. But he was still a 6-foot-9 right-hander with power stuff, so the White Sox selected him in the fifth round last July and signed him for an over-slot $587,500. Davis can work at 94-97 mph and touch 100 with his fastball, which features more downhill plane than armside run, so it can get hit when he doesn't command it. His tight upper-80s slider climbs as high as 92 mph, and he can turn it into a harder cutter. His mid-80s changeup lacks consistency but will flash some intriguing fade and tumble. With room to add more strength to his huge frame, Davis could add even more velocity. He still has starter upside, but to get there he'll have to prove he can stay healthy and keep his long limbs in sync well enough to put his pitches where he wants them. If he does head to the bullpen, he has the fastball and slider to fill a late-inning role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rangers paid eight of the nine largest bonuses in their 2022 international class to Venezuelans, including $247,500 to Torres. He ranked third in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League with 23 steals and fifth with seven homers in his U.S. debut last summer, the only player in the league to place in the top five in both categories. He was overmatched in a 10-game promotion to Single-A as an 18-year-old, going 4-for-37 (.108) with 18 strikeouts. Torres has one of the quickest bats among Rangers farmhands, and the loft in his left-handed stroke and his growing strength produce some of the best raw power. There are some questions about how much contact he'll make because his swing can get long and uphill, and he didn't do much damage against southpaws last year. He does display some characteristics of a good approach, mostly concentrating on balls from gap to gap and showing reasonable patience for a teenager. Torres flashes plus straight-line speed but projects to be more of an average runner once he fills out his 6-foot-3 frame. He steals more with savvy than quickness, so he likely won't be as much of a factor on the bases at higher levels. He's an average defender with similar arm strength in left and right field and at first base, the three positions he played (in order of frequency) in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lindsey took a truly unique path to the Rays’ Minor League system. He pitched for two years at Walters State (Tenn.) CC and struggled a bit the following season at UNC Charlotte, at which point he decided to give up baseball. He took a job digging ditches and repairing roads and took the spring of 2022 off, but coaching a youth team renewed his love of the game. He pitched in the Appalachian League that summer, transferred to Tennessee and pitched his way into the Volunteers' rotation. He wound up being their most reliable starter, logging a 2.90 ERA in 21 outings, and went to the Marlins for a below-slot bonus of $340,000 in the fifth round of the 2023 Draft. He only made two professional starts in the Florida Complex League before Miami flipped him to Tampa Bay alongside Erick Lara and Jake Mangum for Calvin Faucher and Vidal Bruján. Lindsey added velocity across the board as a fifth-year college pitcher last spring, and he’s now a power sinker/slider-type starter who covers the entire width of the plate and hides the ball well before throwing from a lower arm slot. His fastball sits in the mid-90s with the potential to reach back for more. But the Rays were more enamored with his slider, a tight upper-80s breaker that can tick above that while landing in the zone for strikes or outside for chases. It’s a different profile for the Rays, who often target pitchers with big fastballs that carry up in the zone. Lindsey also throws a curveball and a lesser-used changeup, giving him a starter’s arsenal. He also has the physical strength to log innings in the rotation. He could evolve to handle a variety of roles for the ever-creative Rays, with the ceiling of a starter and a solid floor as a sinker/slider reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scull’s father, Antonio, won three Olympic medals playing as a first baseman for Cuba. Anthony started his own path in baseball by signing with the Angels for $235,000 in September 2021. It took a while for the outfielder to show the Angels anything, getting into just 10 games in the Dominican Summer League after signing, then missing most of the 2022 season with a shoulder injury sustained when diving for a ball in the outfield. He did play a full slate of Arizona Complex League games in 2023, showing glimpses of some playable tools. Scull has a strong and athletic frame with the ability to do some damage from the left side of the plate. He makes a lot of hard contact, registering some of the better exit velocities in the lower levels of the Angels' system. He doesn’t strike out a ton, but he can be a bit too aggressive at the plate. It’s more of a line-drive swing right now, but there’s raw power to tap into with the potential to hit around 15 homers annually once he matures physically and with his approach. An above-average runner, Scull can play all three outfield spots with an average arm. He saw more time in center field than anywhere else in 2023 and he does have a chance to stay there should he develop into a regular at one position. A more likely outcome is for him to be a solid fourth outfielder type who moves around and provides a left-handed bat off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A seventh-round pick in 2022 out of Iowa, Williams has always been an upside play on his long-term power. Nicknamed “The Iowa Meat Truck”, you won’t find a larger human being in the Blue Jays’ organization … or many organizations. Listed at 6-foot-5, 255 pounds, Williams looks even larger than that in the box, but it hasn’t turned into the eye-popping power numbers you’d expect just yet. He homered 14 times in 2023 (83 games) and 11 times last season (87 games), but with a strong finish and a successful stint in the Arizona Fall League, there’s buzz in the system about him finally unleashing more of that pop. Outside of Vladimir Guerrero Jr., there may be no player in the organization who hits the ball harder than Williams.
