He’s still a proper hitter, fully capable of shooting a line drive when the situation calls for it, but the Blue Jays are eager to get Williams taking more shots in the right counts. There’s also been a focus on getting him to drive the ball in the air more often. While Williams is a sturdier defender at first base than you’d expect, all of the upside here is clearly and fully tied to his bat. The Rowdy Tellez comps are easy, and given the breakout season Tellez had at Double-A New Hampshire in 2016, you’ll probably be hearing more of them. Similar to outfielder Dasan Brown, whose value leans on elite speed and defense, Williams gets on this list because he does one thing extremely well. He’ll need to hit his way to the top, but there’s a chance he does just that. He’s already an organizational favorite and would be a fan favorite in Toronto if he ever puts on that uniform.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies had spent $6.1 million of their close to $6.7 million international bonus pool as the 2026 season opened, but they knew they wanted to land Park, a projectable 17-year-old right-hander from South Korea, to their organization. So they traded Griff McGarry to the Dodgers and Andrew Baker to the Rockies for a total of $750,000. That gave them enough room to sign Park for just over $1.2 million in May and keep him from being one of the top pitchers in the KBO Draft. Park wanted to pursue a career in the United States rather than head to the top league in Korea, and now he'll get his chance. He's still growing and now stands at 6-foot-3 and 195 pounds with as many as five pitches in his arsenal. Throwing from a three-quarter slot, he can get up to 94 mph with his fastball, generally sitting in the 91-93 range, with late ride at the top of the zone. He can also run and sink it occasionally against right-handed hitters. He has feel to spin two distinct breaking pitches in his curve and slider, the latter registering 2,800 rpm spin rates. He has a changeup and splitter for offspeed options to kill spin -- using the fading change more frequently -- against hitters on both sides of the plate. The Phillies really like Park's ease of operation on the mound, showing an ability to repeat his delivery. He's athletic, with a feel to pitch and an ability to execute that belies his years. That gives him a very good chance to start long-term, and given how much strength he can add to his frame, there's excitement about his ultimate ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez has built a reputation for outstanding bat-to-ball skills ever since his high school days in Georgia. He brought them with him to Georgia Tech, where he hit .332 and had a .932 OPS the spring after finishing second in the Cape Cod League with a .331 average. The skillset intrigued the Pirates enough for them to take him in the fifth round of the 2022 Draft and he continued to do his thing, hitting .325 during his pro debut in Bradenton. He quickly made his way from Bradenton to High-A Greensboro while he continued to build on his hit-over-power profile. The left-handed-hitting outfielder has a fairly high floor because of his knack for contact and lack of strikeouts, especially when combined with his plate discipline and willingness to draw walks. What’s lacking thus far has been impact; his exit velocities have been a little light and he’ll need to find a way to add more physicality and drive the ball more without sacrificing his contact skills. Gonzalez is a better baserunner than his average speed would indicate, and those instincts make him a thread on the basepaths. The lack of speed makes it seem unlikely that he can stick in center field, and he’s seen time in all three outfield spots. If he can’t play center, the offensive profile without more extra-base thump is a little tougher, but his feel for hitting gives the chance to perhaps be a fourth or fifth outfielder.

fangraphs.label: bos2026may
fangraphs.text:
Romero ranked 37th on the 2022 Draft Board and was selected 24th overall, where he got a $2.3 million bonus to forego his commitment to LSU. At the time, scouts viewed him as one of the draft’s more polished prep hitters, a sweet-swinging middle infielder who might not stick at shortstop. Lower back stiffness sidelined him for most of 2023 and those issues persisted into 2024. He played well at High- and Double-A after returning to the field and reached Triple-A last season. He struggled there, hitting for some power but also striking out 30.2% of the time. So far this year, the strikeouts are under control but the power has vanished.

Let’s start with the positives. Romero has big raw power and generated plus measurable exit velocities as a 21-year-old last year. He does so with limited obvious effort, just a small hand loop for a load. Evaluators of all stripes love to see this kind of power in a controlled, fairly short-levered swing. Statistically and visually, though, there are a few red flags lurking here. Romero’s trouble with secondaries jumps off the page immediately, as he whiffed on spin more than 40% of the time last season. Swing-and-miss in general was a problem, as his contact rate was below 70% (the big league average is 75%). He’s also prone to chasing, particularly with two strikes. Visually, he doesn’t seem to get the A-swing off all that often. He lets it fly on pitches at the belt and lower middle in, but he otherwise tends to look off balance or use a gentler, sometimes inside-out cut on pitches on the outer half.

At third base, Romero’s hands are pretty good but the rest of the package looks light. At his speed, he isn’t especially rangy, and both his throwing accuracy and the time it takes him to get rid of the ball are below average. He’s also playing some second base, which redistributes some of the pressure from the latter issue onto the former.

Ultimately, Romero is going to go as far as his power takes him. It’s a potential carrying tool, and can play like one even if he’s an otherwise flawed hitter. That would require a big change in his approach, though, as he’s more of an aggressive hitter than a guy who militantly hunts his pitch. At 22, he’s young enough to take a step forward here, and perhaps positive walk and strikeout rates in Worcester are an early sign that he’s trending that way. He projects as a power-first utility player, with unusual thump for a guy who can cover second base.

fangraphs.label: 2025report
fangraphs.text:
Romero ranked 37th on the 2022 Draft Board and was selected 24th overall, receiving a $2.3 million bonus to forego a commitment to LSU. High school Romero was viewed as one of the draft's more polished prep hitters, a sweet-swinging middle infielder who might not stick at shortstop. Lower back stiffness sidelined him for most of 2023 and those issues persisted into the start of 2024. When he was finally deemed healthy in the middle of May, the Red Sox effectively skipped Romero over Low-A (he only played there for a month in 2023) and sent him straight to Greenville. He hit well enough there to earn a late-season promotion to Portland, and all told in 2024, Romero slashed .271/.312/.509 with a terrifyingly low walk rate (5%). He's back in Portland and has a strong surface-level statline, including twice as many walks. 
Look under the hood and Romero is more of a mixed bag. While his baseline chase rate has backed off, he's still expanding at a 50% clip with two strikes, which is nearly two standard deviations worse than the big league average. He's also running a sub-70% contact rate as of list publication, which only a handful of qualified big leaguers carry each year (the major league average is 77%). He has issues covering the outer third, and swings underneath a ton of fastballs finishing away from him. Romero still has a good-looking low-ball swing and the explosive hitting hands that made him an exciting draft prospect. He has impressive all-fields power for a hitter his age and is pulverizing the ball when he actually makes contact. 
His build is fairly mature for a 21-year-old athlete, and Romero's mobility on defense isn't great; he takes quite a while to turn the baseball around to first base. His throwing stroke and accuracy also look a little odd (Romero has an over-the-top arm slot atypical of an infielder), and he takes a while to get rid of the baseball. There was a point last year when this could have reasonably been explained as rust coming off of injury, but we're a good distance away from that now. There's a chance Romero doesn't stick on the infield at all, and even if he does, he's going to be below average. There's enough lefty pop here to consider Romero a priority prospect, but he's got some risk indicators, both visually and from a data standpoint.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text:
Romero ranked 37th on the 2022 draft board and was selected 24th overall, receiving a $2.3 million bonus to forego a commitment to LSU. High school Romero was viewed as one of the draft's more polished prep hitters, a sweet-swinging middle infielder who might not stick at shortstop. Lower back stiffness sidelined him for most of 2023 and those issues have persisted into the start of 2024. When he was finally deemed healthy in the middle of May, the Red Sox effectively skipped Romero over Low-A (he only played there for a month last year) and sent him straight to Greenville. 
Romero still has a good looking low-ball swing and the explosive hitting hands that made him an exciting draft prospect. His mobility on defense isn't great, and he takes quite a while to turn the baseball around to first base. His throwing stroke and accuracy also look a little odd (Romero has an over-the-top arm slot atypical of an infielder), and he takes a while to get rid of the baseball. Whether this is just rust or is the result of continued back discomfort or physical changes caused by it, we just won't know until Romero gets more time to air out as a pro prospect. 
Romero's 40-man timeline is such that he and Boston have through the 2026 season to get things on track; that's still plenty of runway. If I were an actual team thinking about Romero from a trade standpoint, it would be tougher to rank him this highly; teams aren't falling over themselves to acquire a teenager with recurring back issues. But this is a "hold" on where Romero's FV grade was as a draft prospect. I am more inclined to let Romero's late-season look - once he's had an opportunity to fall into a routine and get some traction - drive any sort of FV update during the next list cycle.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: While not a lock to stay at shortstop due to middling range and actions, Romero had among the more advanced hit tools in the 2022 high school class, able to impact pitches all over the strike zone. He ranked 37th on the 2022 draft board and was selected 24th, where he received a $2.3 million bonus to forego a commitment to LSU. Lower back stiffness has sidelined him for all of 2023 as of list publication, though Romero is expected to start playing rehab games on the complex shortly. He projects as a strong-side platoon infielder who's capable at second and third base.

fangraphs.label: 2022draft
fangraphs.text: While not a lock to stay at shortstop due to middling range and actions, Romero has among the more advanced hit tools in the 2022 high school class, able to impact pitches all over the strike zone. Based on where hitterish middle infielders were picked in 2021, he fits near the comp round.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Romero family produces talented hitters: sisters Sierra and Sydney were college softball stars, while younger brother Mikey was the 24th overall pick in the 2022 Draft. Signed for a well-below-slot $2.3 million, he was hampered by persistent back issues in his first two full pro seasons but finally was completely healthy and played a career-high 111 games in 2025. He led the system with 54 extra-base hits and 76 RBIs while reaching Triple-A at age 21, but he also struck out at a 27 percent clip. Considered one of the best pure hitters in his prep class, Romero concentrated on working the ball from gap to gap as an amateur. He changed his approach after he put his back issues behind him, focusing on using his quick left-handed stroke to launch balls in the air to his pull side. He has added about 20 pounds since turning pro and now has plus raw power, but his aggressive approach leads to a lot of chases and empty swings, especially against non-fastballs. Romero has slowed down as he has added muscle, though his high baseball IQ helps him play quicker than his below-average speed. Signed as a shortstop, he has fringy range and average arm strength. He saw most of his action at third base last season but his tools fit better at second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox spent three straight first-round picks on California prep middle infielders: Nick Yorke (2020), Marcelo Mayer (2021) and Romero (2022). The younger brother of former college softball sensations Sierra and Sydney Romero, Mikey signed for a well-below-slot $2.3 million as the 24th overall pick. Persistent back issues that included a stress fracture limited him to 34 games in his first full pro season and sidelined him until mid-May in 2024, but he finally got healthy afterward and hit his way to Double-A at age 21. Romero earned acclaim as one of the best hitters in the 2022 high school class by focusing on making contact from gap to gap with a quick left-handed stroke. He showed an entirely different approach last year, relinquishing control of the strike zone while aggressively looking to launch balls to his pull side. He has added about 20 pounds since turning pro and become more of a power-over-hit guy with some opposite-field thump on occasion. Romero's high IQ helps his tools play up on the bases and in the middle infield. He's an average runner who's more likely to take an extra base than steal one. His actions, range and arm are all average at shortstop, where he finds a way to make plays, but they're better suited for second base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After drafting Marcelo Mayer fourth overall in 2021, the Red Sox took his good friend and fellow California prep shortstop Romero with the 24th overall choice a year later. The younger brother of former college softball superstars Sierra and Sydney Romero, he signed for a well-below-slot $2.3 million. After a strong pro debut, he played in just 34 games last year because of persistent lower-back issues. One of the best hitters in the 2022 high school class, Romero concentrates on making contact from gap to gap with his quick left-handed swing. He wasn't at his best at 2023, when his back problems underscored his need to add strength to his 5-foot-11 frame. He won't be a slugger but more muscle could create 15-homer power and would ease concerns about how much impact he'll offer at the plate. When healthy, Romero has average speed and plays quicker than that thanks to his high baseball IQ. Many scouts believe that his average range and arm aren't enough to make him a regular shortstop, but Boston believe his finely tuned internal clock and quick release give him a shot. Mayer likely will push him to second base when they're both in Boston, and Romero could be a solid defender at the keystone whose quick hands would help him turn double plays.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox have used their first-round pick in each of the last three Drafts on sweet-swinging high school middle infielders from California: Nick Yorke (17th overall) in 2020, Marcelo Mayer (fourth) in 2021 and Romero (24th) last July. Romero also joined Gerrit Cole, Cole Winn and Garrett Mitchell as first-rounders who played at Orange (Calif.) Lutheran HS. Signed for $2.3 million, he comes from a family of hitters that also includes a pair of former college softball superstars in older sisters Sierra and Sydney. Romero's quick left-handed swing and mature approach gave him some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the 2022 prep class. He focuses on making contact from gap to gap and isn't very physical, leading to some concerns about how much impact he'll provide at the plate. He does have bat speed and hitting aptitude and has gotten stronger in the last year, so he should be able to provide 15-20 homers on an annual basis. There are also questions about Romero's ability to stay at shortstop, though that may not matter much in the long run with his good friend Mayer also in the organization. He has average speed and arm strength, leaving both tools light for the position, but he compensates with advanced instincts and a quick release on throws. He does show good actions at short and is a polished defender with reliable hands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After his high school career in Champaign, Illinois, Munroe stayed in-state to keep playing at the junior college level, setting both single-season and career home run records at John A. Logan College. He parlayed that to an invite to play for Louisville in 2025 and continued to perform with an OPS over 1.000 and a spot on the College World Series All-Tournament Team. The Angels took him in the fourth round of last summer's Draft, signing him for an under-slot bonus of just less than $600,000. He got his professional feet wet with a dozen games in the California League after signing and got off to a solid start with High-A Tri-City in his first full season. Munroe is a 6-foot-2 right-handed hitter who has shown a feel to hit throughout his college career and early on with the Angels. With more of a choppy approach as an amateur, even though he found the seats at that level, he profiles more as a contact-first bat with good plate discipline, one who uses the whole field with some gap power, though he was showing some over-the-fence juice early in 2026. A below-average runner who didn't show much in the way of quick-twitch athleticism at Louisville, there were some concerns about his ability to stick at third base at the pro level. So far, though, he's shown off average defensive tools with an average arm, giving him the chance to stick at the hot corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia, a cousin of Wilmer Flores (both the Giants infielder and the Tigers pitching prospect), joined the Mets system out of Venezuela in June 2021 and made it to full-season ball last year with mixed results. His 5.04 ERA in 80 1/3 innings between Single-A St. Lucie and High-A Brooklyn didn’t quite pop, but he did strike out 106 batters in that span. His 31.9 percent K rate in the Florida State League ranked third among the 46 pitchers on the circuit with at least 60 frames. The 6-foot right-hander throws a 92-94 mph two-seam fastball (topping out at 96.7) out of a low slot that lower-level batters just found difficult to pick up, leading to a strong whiff rate and some weak contact. He primarily paired that with a low-80s sweeping slider that gave him an option with good gloveside break as compared to the armside movement of the two-seamer. He showed the occasional low-80s curveball and mid-80s changeup too, but he understands which pitch is his bread and butter. Garcia walked 14.6 percent of batters faced between those two levels. That’s a slight improvement from 15.6 percent in 2022 but an example of why many believe he’ll remain in a relief role. He’ll still only be 21 years old as he heads back to the High-A level, and there are some in the organization who believe he’s on the precipice of a breakout as he continues to rack up K’s and finetune his command with more stateside experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tom Candiotti rode the knuckleball to a 16-year career in the Major Leagues. His son, Clark, utilizes a very different arsenal that took him on an interesting ride as a college player. Candiotti played for five schools in five years between St. Mary’s (2020), Vernon (Junior) College (2021), Grayson County Community College (2022), Wichita State (2023) and finally Arizona (2024). He was a Pac-12 All-Conference selection after posting a 3.39 ERA with 103 strikeouts in 95 2/3 innings with the Wildcats, and that helped push him to Padres with the 135th overall pick in the '24 Draft, where he signed for $80,000. The 6-foot-4 right-hander has the look of a durable starter. He added fastball velocity between his time at Wichita State and Arizona, averaging around 93 mph with the latter while touching 96. The heater can feature good carry, eliciting chase above the zone. Candiotti, however, leaned even more heavily on his 83-85 mph slider, throwing it 45 percent of the time and using it against batters from both sides. It has sharp, short movement, allowing him to wear out the gloveside half of the plate. He mixed in a 78-82 mph curveball for a different breaking look and barely used his mid-80s changeup in ’24. Candiotti did a great job of throwing strikes in each of his last two collegiate seasons, but a significant portion of that was getting batters to expand the zone. That ability will be tested against pro bats. There is a certain temptation to throw Candiotti in the bullpen because of his age -- he'll be 24 entering his first full season -- but given his late college trajectory, he could have a fighting chance to stick in future rotations, too.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners’ activity in the 2024 international signing period started with Dawel Joseph being the headliner, getting $3.3 million in January. Six months later, they added Shen, signing the Taiwanese right-hander, for $175,000 in July. Pitching at age 21, Shen was rolled out cautiously, making his debut in the Arizona Complex League last May. After 28 dominant innings over seven appearances, he earned a bump up to full-season ball for nine more starts. Right out of the gate, Shen displayed a feel for commanding all three of his pitches. His fastball sits in the low 90s, touching 95 mph now and again, and he throws it with sink to help get ground ball outs. His mid-80s changeup also gets weak contact on the ground and gets a lot of chase. He can spin an 81 mph slider decently, and it missed bats at the lower levels, but a little more power could make it even nastier. Shen filled up the strike zone in both stops during his debut, though he was getting too much of the plate during his time in Modesto. Some added strength to his 6-foot-3 frame would help not only that slider, but all of his offerings trend upwards. He has back-of-the-rotation potential based on his pitchability and projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dumesnil looked like he could be a high-round Draft pick after an eye-opening sophomore season at Cal Baptist, including a .362/.440/.702 slash line with 19 homers, and an All-Star season in the Cape Cod League, hitting .311 and leading the circuit in steals (26). A difficult junior season changed his momentum, but the Tigers snagged him in the eighth round, signed him for $214,300 and immediately put him at Single-A, where he made an impact for Lakeland in the Florida State League playoffs. Strong and athletic, the 6-foot-2 Dumesnil showed the ability to hit with power in college, but his 2025 season came with struggles against spin, notably sliders, and inconsistent power. Both of those continued in Lakeland, where he hit fastballs well but not for much power while whiffing on breaking balls. He’s not a fluid runner but has enough speed and aggressiveness to swipe bases, which he did often in a small sample size for the Flying Tigers. Dumesnil’s speed does help him cover ground in the outfield and he’s shown he can be solid at all three spots defensively. Some feel he can play center long term, but others feel he’s best suited for a corner, with left being a better option because of his fringy arm strength. Even with the struggles he’s had, the Tigers will try to get him back to 2024 Cape form.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 While Joswa Lugo received the highest bonus of any player from the Angels’ signing class at the start of the 2024 international signing period, De La Rosa received the most of any pitcher signed by the organization, getting $300,000 to get his pro career started. He did that in the Dominican Summer League and put his best foot forward out of the gate, finishing with a 2.79 ERA, .211 BAA and a 9.9 K/9 rate in a typically hitting-friendly environment. At 6-foot-4, the hope is De La Rosa can develop into an innings-eating workhorse-type starter. His fastball maxes out at 96 mph and typically sits 91-94, though the hope is more velocity will come as he matures. He has a solid 77-82 mph slider that flashes above average and could develop into an out pitch. There’s an upper-80s changeup in there, but it’s too firm and it’s behind the other two offerings. For his first time out, De La Rosa did a decent job of being in and around the strike zone. He’ll be just 18 as he comes stateside for the 2025 season and he’s a long way away, but with improved command and velocity to go along with a solid third pitch, he has a big league starter ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Montgomery was well-known as an Orlando-area high schooler and slotted in at No. 34 on MLB Pipeline’s 2020 Draft rankings. The shortened Draft and his strong commitment to Florida State kept him from being drafted that year, but he never found consistent success with the Seminoles as a starter or a reliever. The Padres still took him in the 11th round in 2023 and signed him for $200,000. Montgomery needed Tommy John surgery after only three appearances with Single-A Lake Elsinore in '24, and he didn’t return to a mound in an official setting until the 2025 Arizona Fall League, where he allowed two earned runs, struck out seven and walked seven in 10 1/3 frames. He has opened his age-23 season as a starter with High-A Fort Wayne. The 6-foot-1 right-hander showcases both a four-seamer and sinker. He can sit 92-95 mph with the heat, though he’s been below that at times in the cold Midwest League this spring. The sinker has decent tail running in on righties, while the four-seam will flash promising ride, and both were significant chase pitches in the AFL. His 83-86 mph slider is back as a whiff generator in 2026, flashing enough depth to look like a potential above-average offering, while his upper-80s changeup lacks enough separation to be a serious weapon against lefties at this stage. Montgomery had control problems dating back to his first year in Tallahassee but has actually tightened up his command coming out of his TJ recovery and rehab, enough to keep getting starting looks. He’s already facing Rule 5 eligibility this upcoming offseason though, and unless there’s a significant jump in stuff in 2026, he might not be far off from seeing if the sinker-slider combo can play up as a righty-heavy option in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After getting $600,000 to sign with the Pirates out of the Dominican Republic at the start of the 2019-20 international signing period, Terrero couldn’t play until 2021 because of the pandemic. He showed off a solid approach during his Dominican Summer League debut that year, then posted an .890 OPS in the Florida Complex League when he came to the United States for the first time. He was streaky during his full-season debut in 2023, fading down the stretch, but showing off some of his offensive potential. With a smaller frame, Terrero has yet to display a ton of impact from the left side of the plate. But there were some gains in terms of exit velocity last year, which gave the Pirates hope there could be more of that to come with some pop to his pull side. He’s made a ton of contact in his brief career, though his strikeout rate did climb a bit in Single-A Bradenton. He tends to have a consistent approach and draws walks, with a 13 percent walk rate in 2023. Terrero runs well enough to steal some bags, and it also gives him the potential to stick in center field. He’s an average defender there now who still needs to work on his reads and routes. He’s actually a plus defender in an outfield corner, but he’s not going to have the kind of offensive impact teams like to see from that spot, which could make him a bit of a tweener if center doesn’t work out.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
Araujo is a bat-first catching prospect who had an awesome 2025 DSL debut during which he slashed .289/.377/.528 with 21 extra-base hits in 45 games. He's a medium-framed, short-levered hitter whose top hand drives the explosion of his swing, facilitating lots of loud pull-side contact. Araujo can flatten his bat path to cover the top of the zone or use a more uphill angle to scoop low pitches. 
Because of his youth and inexperience, Araujo is currently a very raw defensive catcher and is not a lock to stay back there. He played a lot of first base in 2025, too, though that was due as much to Philly's DSL catching depth as it was Araujo's own shortcomings. If he doesn't develop as a catcher, then Araujo's modest size (think Ty France's body) would likely cap his power and, it follows, his ceiling as a first baseman. For now, he's a talented young hitter who'll be tested by Florida complex arms as an 18-year-old in 2026.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: A native of Taiwan, Huang signed for $210,000 prior to the 2025 season. From a pitchability perspective, he was as advanced as anyone you’ll find on the complex. With a well-honed motion, Huang absolutely peppered the zone with three pitches, showing touch and feel to complement plus control. The stuff is less eye-catching. He'll touch 95 but sits in the low 90s, and his secondaries project average. The underlying foundation means things could get pretty interesting if he finds a little more velo. I'm not projecting it, though, and see Huang as more of a low-leverage arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally recruited as a catcher by Boise State, Buxton moved to the mound with the Broncos, redshirted in 2019 and pitched in just four games during the shortened 2020 season. Boise State dropped baseball afterward, so he transferred to Lipscomb, where he led the Atlantic Sun Conference with seven wins in 2022 before getting drafted in the 15th round that July. He reached Double-A for one start at the end of his first full pro season and soaked up more experience in the Arizona Fall League afterward. Buxton relies heavily on his fastball, a power sinker that operates at 93-95 mph, reaches 97 and creates a ton of groundball contact -- his 2.06 groundout/airout ratio would have ranked fourth in the Minors last year if he had enough innings to qualify. He can flash a solid low-80s slider with nice sweep at times but he struggles to land it in the zone. He has made some strides with an 82-85 mph changeup with similar sink to his heater, and it could become an average offering if he uses it more often. To remain a starter, Buxton will need to throw more strikes. His control improved a bit during his six weeks in High-A last summer but remains fringy at best. He could wind up fitting toward the back of a big league rotation or wind up as a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of Georgia's best prep pitching prospects in 2019, David slid to the Diamondbacks in the 35th round amid signability concerns and opted to attend Auburn instead. He never pitched for the Tigers during the pandemic-truncated 2020 season before bouncing from Gordon State (Ga.) JC to Northwest Florida State JC to NAIA program Southeastern (Fla.) before the Astros drafted him in 2024's 10th round as a fifth-year senior. He moved from Single-A to Double-A in his first full pro season, compiling a 3.47 ERA with 87 strikeouts in 85 2/3 innings. David's fastball parks at 95-96 mph and peaks at 98, and he maintained that velocity throughout 2025. It features carry and armside run. His tight mid-80s slider doesn't get a lot of chases but does generate a lot of in-zone swings and misses, and he can turn it into an 89-91 mph cutter on occasion. After focusing primarily on his heater and slider in college, he has worked on incorporating a low-80s curveball and an upper-80s changeup with depth but has trouble landing both for strikes. There's effort in David's delivery that has prevented him from throwing consistent strikes, so he's more of multi-inning reliever than a starter in the long run. He spent the first two months of 2025 in the rotation at Single-A Fayetteville before shifting to the bullpen. He'll pitch at age 25 this season, and the less challenging role will accelerate his timetable to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were two Indiana natives on the World Cup-winning US 18-and-under national team in 2022: Max Clark and Tilly. While Clark went third overall to the Tigers in the 2023 Draft, Tilly was unselected as MLB Pipeline’s No. 208 prospect in the class and headed to Auburn instead. He pitched primarily out of the bullpen in his two years in the SEC and sported a 5.48 ERA with 58 strikeouts in 46 innings as a Draft-eligible sophomore last year. The Mets took him in the seventh round and signed him for above slot at $397,500 to keep him from heading back to school. The Mets have early interest in developing Tilly as a starter because of his interesting pitch mix. His fastball sits at 92-94 mph, touching 97, and because of the average velocity, he was willing to go liberally to his secondaries in his final season on campus. Since his amateur days, Tilly has earned praise for the high spin rates on his low-80s slider, and he’s developed his mid-80s splitter into arguably an even better pitch, one with enough dip and movement to cause lefties fits. Tilly also worked in another high-spin curveball in the mid 70s with Auburn but saved it mostly for early counts. Tilly walked 13.4 percent of the batters he faced in his two years at Auburn -- a rate that would keep anyone in the bullpen early in their collegiate career -- but the Mets believe there’s untapped pitchability there, especially if they can tame some of his spinnier options. There’s a good chance Tilly would have gotten starting looks as junior anyways, and now that can happen under the eye of a New York organization that has specialized in pitching development in recent years.

fangraphs.label: FanGraphs 2026 Twins Top 50
fangraphs.text:
Lares pitched well as a rookie ball starter in 2022 and 2023, then had strong peripheral stats in 2024 despite a bloated ERA. He missed 2025 recovering from an elbow surgery and returned this season not long before list publication, with two rehab outings and then a promotion straight to Cedar Rapids. That’s perhaps a sign that the Twins aren’t messing around with assessing Lares, who is in his 40-man platform season.

Lares is an athletic, undersized lefty who can execute the heck out of a good slider. It has lovely length and two-planed movement in the 81-85 mph range, the kind commonly found on good specialist relievers. Because Lares throws strikes like a starter, is a starter-quality athlete, and has a gorgeous arm action that gives his changeup meaningful long-term projection, the Twins could justifiably develop him as a starter, take things a bit slow this year, stretch him out, and then have more of a two-season plan to assess whether he can be part of their 2028 40-man mix. Then there’s the version where you put him in the bullpen toward the end of this year (or in a winter league) and see if his otherwise vulnerable fastball ticks up enough to make him an immediate in-house bullpen candidate. He’s projected to the bullpen here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Roberts went undrafted after his junior year at Utah in 2023, when he batted just .266 with three homers over 46 games, but he started to show out for Mankato in the Northwoods League that summer (.346/.476/.555), creating some momentum for himself. He built on that with a Pac-12 All-Conference nod after slashing .356/.430/.562 with seven homers in 55 games for the Utes as a senior. His 33 steals were most among Pac-12 players. The Padres selected him in the seventh round and signed him for just $10,000, but Roberts continued to show out with a .340/.414/.470 line in 24 games with Single-A Lake Elsinore in his first taste of the Minors. Roberts cuts a stunning figure in the field at 6-foot-5, 205 pounds, and he moves exceptionally well for that size, notching 60-yard dashes in the 6.5-second range. He was a perfect 14-for-14 in steal attempts during that short run in the California League, and the Padres don’t have much doubt that his speed will continue to play as he reaches higher levels. With those wheels, Roberts is a comfortable fit in center field and has just enough arm for the position, too. That said, the left-handed hitter hasn’t been a huge power threat despite his size, though San Diego officials were intrigued by the good weight he put on during in his first offseason. He struggled to make contact against sliders and changeups as a senior and will need his speed to help run high BABIPs that can make up for some of the contact issues. Roberts already enters his first full season at age 24 and doesn’t have a long runway, but his best skills could be useful in the Majors in short order.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Seven years after the Tigers took a Draft flier on a college pitcher with mixed results a year removed from Tommy John surgery (Tarik Skubal), they went a similar route with Leys, who missed the 2024 season recovering from surgery before taking the mound for the University of Maine in 2025. Leys won America East Pitcher of the Year with a 2.69 ERA and 74 strikeouts in 67 innings, better than his first two seasons with the Black Bears. The Tigers drafted him in the fourth round, five rounds earlier than Skubal, and signed him for $574,900. While Leys isn’t big for a pitcher, he has a quick, fluid delivery with a big leg kick and a three-quarters arm angle. His fastball can touch 96 mph, setting up a slider and a changeup both in the low 80s. Leys greatly improved his strike throwing and command upon his return from surgery, cutting his walk rate in almost half from his first two seasons while ticking up his strikeout rate. The Tigers have been aggressive at times starting out college pitchers in full-season ball, and could do the same with Leys, who made an impression in Spring Training. If he can hold his command while adding more swing-and-miss, he could force his way up the system quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees' decision to select Jackson in the fifth round last July drew criticism after reports surfaced that he drew a swastika on the dorm room of a Jewish student when he was a freshman at Nebraska in 2021. He transferred to South Mountain (Ariz.) CC as a sophomore and spent his final two college seasons at Utah, where he was charged with impaired driving in 2024. He batted a combined .363/.455/.577 and earned first-team all-conference honors in his two years with the Utes before signing for a well below-slot $147,500. A left-hander who made consistent hard contact despite an aggressive approach in college, Jackson was unusually passive in High-A during his pro debut. He usually crushes fastballs but had trouble making contact against in-zone heaters last summer, though he may have been overwhelmed by his challenging assignment. He has the ingredients for at least 15-homer power, especially if he can learn to elevate more pitches. Jackson was more impressive defensively in his first taste of pro ball. He displays smooth actions, solid range and plus arm strength, leaving no doubt he can remain at shortstop. He has average speed with good baserunning instincts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fontenelle bounced around during his college days, starting at the University of Washington in 2021, then moving to McLennan Junior College the following year and then on to Texas Christian for his Draft year in 2023. He went to the College World Series that year and finished with an OPS over 1.100, helping him land in the seventh round with the Angels. In a very unsurprising development for anyone who follows the organization, Fontenelle went up to Double-A to start his first full season and was playing well when his season ended after just 22 games after a slide into second caused both a dislocated ankle and fractured fibula. He made it back to play in the Arizona Fall League, where he really struggled to shake off the rust at the plate. A big switch-hitter the Angels think just fell through the cracks as teams focused on Horned Frogs teammate Brayden Taylor, Fontenelle has the chance to fit the corner-infield profile well offensively. When he’s healthy, he can hit the ball very hard with excellent exit velocities. He didn’t swing and miss much in college with a solid overall approach, and while his strikeout rate ticked up during his pro debut and in the AFL, it’s too small of a sample size to draw any conclusions there. Fontenelle has only played third with the Angels, and while he’s big and a below-average runner, he has good instincts (which help him steal some bases despite the lack of quickness) and actions, with enough arm to have a chance to stick at the hot corner. He’s played first base and even a little left field in the past, so there are some options should a move be needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 10th-round selection by the A’s in the 2024 MLB Draft out of Boston College, Leary underwhelmed a bit in his first taste of pro ball upon joining the organization. His first full season as a pro went much better, as he began the year at Single-A Stockton and earned a promotion to High-A Lansing, where he held his own over a 33-game stint. Between the two levels, Leary hit .269 with a .798 OPS in 126 games. Leary has above-average power potential which showed up in stints last season, with an ability to hit to all fields after working with the A’s to tighten up his swing. He can draw a decent amount of walks, but his 130 strikeouts last year highlight some swing-and-miss issues that will need to be corrected for him to fully take advantage of that power. Leary might be one of the better baserunners in the entire organization, evident by his 56 stolen bases in ‘25 while getting caught only eight times. Defensively, he can move around well, but his below-average arm likely limits him to left field, though the A’s plan to work with him on his quickening up his release to see if his positional versatility could expand to the other two outfield spots. The A’s are still trying to figure out just what type of player Leary might end up being, but there were some encouraging signs in his first full year.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text:
At $275,000, Almonte was a fairly big signing for a pitcher on the international market. He’s a big, physical righty, a little tightly wound and not especially twitchy, but strong with an innings-eater's build. He has a long, circular arm path, loose enough to project on his command, though he’s a little wild right now. 
Almonte has four pitches that all at least flash average. He touches 97 with the fastball and sits 93-95 early in starts. He has average carry or a tick more on the four-seamer and can also hit the box with a sinker. The slider is his best secondary, a sweeping, low-to-mid-80s offering that ran a 40% miss rate in the DSL. While his curve can run into the slider and the change doesn’t consistently have a ton of fade, he’ll execute often enough to project four viable offerings at maturity. He’s eons away and a lot can go wrong, but you can dream on a no. 3 or 4 starter, while the arm strength and slider feel give him a relief fallback.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dominican-born Reyes' $450,000 bonus was the fifth-highest given to a pitcher on the 2024 international amateur market. He broke into pro ball by not allowing a run in four June starts in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, striking out 17 and walking just two in 16 innings. He came down with a tired arm and worked just one more frame in the next two months as the Red Sox had him concentrate on gaining strength. Reyes already can park in the low 90s and reach 94 mph with run and sink on his fastball while exerting little effort, and he could operate in the mid-90s once he fills out his extremely projectable 6-foot-5 frame. Just 18, he already has the makings of a pair of solid mid-80s secondary pitches in a slider and a fading and sinking changeup. Boston may have him add a cutter to his arsenal as well. Quite advanced for his age, Reyes does a nice job of keeping his long limbs in sync and producing a clean delivery that he repeats well. In his pro debut, he not only provided strikes but also showed the ability to command his pitches and manipulate their shapes. He'll need time to add muscle and develop, but his combination of stuff and pitchability gives him one of the higher ceilings among Red Sox pitching prospects.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Yeager has an above-average two-pitch mix. He gained five ticks on his slider from when I first saw him in early 2024 to when I caught him again last summer. Suffice to say, that's hard to predict and he deserves a lot of credit for the transformation. His fastball ticked up a bit as well, and he now touches 99; the velo is enough to miss bats even though he doesn't get a lot of extension. His slider flashes plus and is a tight bender that appears more firm than sharp to my eye, but hitters look bad against it, and missed on more than 40% of their swings last year. The arsenal is shallow and the stuff isn't quite late-inning loud, but Yeager has enough in the holster to project as an optionable reliever. Sometimes those guys turn into long-term middle relievers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lara wasn’t a big-time prospect when the Marlins signed him for just $85,000 out of the Dominican Republic as part of their international signing class in January 2023. But his performance as a 17-year-old in the Dominican Summer League caught the Rays’ attention, and they landed him from Miami as part of a three-prospect return for infielder/outfielder Vidal Bruján and reliever Calvin Faucher. This could be the latest in a long line of moves in which the Rays have acquired a young Complex League prospect and watched him take off. Lara, hailing from Bani, has excellent bat speed and a loose, whippy swing from the left side of the plate that allows him to drive the ball well. He had enough skills and polish to perform in his professional debut in the DSL, slashing .305/.416/.445 with 23 walks and 37 strikeouts in 154 plate appearances. He’s skinny, at 6-foot-2 and 165 pounds, but he could develop above-average power as he fills out his frame. Where Lara lands defensively is another question. He started most of his games at shortstop last year, and he has the arm strength to handle the left side of the infield. It’s not out of the realm of possibility that he’ll stick at the six, but if he gets big enough, he might be a better fit at third base and could be athletic enough to handle a spot in the outfield. He’ll likely spend the season at the Rays’ Spring Training complex, first for extended spring camp then in the Florida Complex League. The Rays love his upside, but it’ll be years before his developmental path is totally clear.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It’s been a long winding path for Mejia, who started his college career by redshirting at Arizona in 2019, then transferred to Pima Community College in 2020, but made just five starts there because of the pandemic. The right-hander went to New Mexico State after that, mostly relieving in 2021 then stepping into the rotation in 2022. He signed for $100,000 as an 11th-round pick that summer, spent all year with High-A Rome in 2023 and then had another solid, and durable, season with Double-A Mississippi in 2024. Mejia’s feel for pitching and the ability to mix his offerings to keep hitters off-balance stands out more than any of his pure stuff. His fastball averaged around 92 mph last year and maxed out at 94 mph. It doesn’t feature a ton of life, but he commands the pitch consistently. His low-80s slider is his go-to pitch, and he threw it almost as much as his heater in 2024, missing bats at a 42-percent clip. His 83-84 mph changeup is a decent third offering and he’s been working on a splitter as well. The 6-foot-3 Mejia does a nice job of repeating his delivery and has a history of throwing strikes, especially in 2022 with the Aggies and during his first pro season. His walk rate did jump a bit in 2024, but he’s posted consistently, topping 120 innings in each of his two full seasons. His ceiling is probably as a No. 5 type starter because of the lack of wow stuff, but he’s close to showing if it can work in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a Panamanian pipeline to Georgia Premier Academy (Statesboro, Ga.) highlighted by Guardians 2019 first-rounder Daniel Espino, Rodriguez was one of the older prep prospects (19 years, seven months) in the 2023 Draft. The Cubs didn't mind his age because they had some third-round grades on him, and they took him in the 13th round. His development has progressed more slowly than expected, but he finally reached Double-A at the end of last season. Rodriguez operates at 92-95 mph and touches 99 with his fastball, but he's often tentative with it because it lacks good shape and gets whacked when it grabs too much of the plate. He shows much better feel for strikes with his upper-80s changeup that fades and sinks. Like the rest of his arsenal, his tight mid-80s slider plays as an average pitch. Rodriguez works solely out of the stretch with a low release height that creates some deception. He has improved his strike-throwing every season as a pro, though his control and command still need more work if he's going to succeed as a starter. He gets more ground balls than he misses bats and is more likely to wind up in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Colon grew up in Puerto Rico and came to the United States for his senior year of high school in the Miami area. He caught the attention of the Reds, who had some bonus pool money left over as Day 3 began in 2024. They went about $100,000 over the post-10th-round slot to sign him in Round 11. He learned a lot in going to full-season ball during his first full season in 2025, then returned to Daytona and was making big strides in the Florida State League to kick off 2026. A strong and athletic right-hander who is about an inch taller and 20 pounds heavier than his listed height and weight, Colon has future rotation potential if he can improve his command. Right now, he leans heavily on his fastball-split-change combination. It's a plus heater that currently sits around 96 mph and touches 98 mph, getting outstanding induced vertical break on the pitch to elicit strong swing-and-miss rates. He can kill spin and gets good horizontal action on his upper-80s changeup that also can miss bats. His slider thrown at about the same velocity continues to improve. Colon is athletic on the mound, with a short stride that leads to less-than-optimal extension. In addition to rounding out his arsenal with a dependable breaking ball he trusts, Colon needs to continue to improve his control and command. He showed some improvement in that regard to kick off 2026 and he gets high marks for his maturity at age 20, providing optimism he can figure things out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Karpathios played both ways in his one season at Maryland’s Harford Community College in 2022, and the Padres (via area scout Danny Sader, who scouted Jackson Merrill from the same area) preferred his bat. Looking to go pro rather than stay in school, Karpathios signed with San Diego as a nondrafted free agent that July, just one month after his 19th birthday. While he was a decent performer early in his career, his big breakout came in 2025, when he hit .249/.357/.413 with 15 homers and 73 walks in 124 games between High-A and Double-A. Karpathios ended the year with time in the prospect-rich Arizona Fall League. The Pennsylvania native stands tall from the left side of the box before getting into a leg kick. He rarely chased pitches outside the zone during the 2025 regular season despite increasing his overall swing rate a tad. His exit velocities were loud with a 90th-percentile EV of 105.8 mph, leading to a jump in home-run production. He can hit the ball well to all fields too, although he went the opposite way more than he pulled the ball once he reached Double-A. Getting the barrel out front more often will be a focus when he returns to the upper levels, or else he’s probably limited to 15ish homers per season. Karpathios also whiffs at high levels against non-fastballs, and he swung and missed more across the board in the Fall League (albeit after a long summer). A below-average runner, he has experience in all three outfield spots but is the best fit in right, thanks to his above-average arm strength. Ahead of his Rule 5 decision year, Karpathios is trending toward a lefty bench bat/fourth outfielder, and that’d be a nice development win for an NDFA signing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dettmer spent three years as a mainstay at Texas A&M, showing glimpses of exciting stuff -- highlighted by seven shutout innings in the Men's College World Series as a sophomore in 2022 -- albeit with very mixed results. Excitement for his junior year dissipated when he got hit hard and struggled with his command in 2023. His size and potential were enough for teams to consider on Day 2 of the Draft, and the A's nabbed him in the fifth round, but he proceeded to throw in just four games during his first full season because of bone spurs in his elbow. He topped 100 innings in 2025, though he again got knocked around, but he started to figure things out and have some success in 2026, earning a bump to High-A for the first time in May. Like he did with the Aggies, Dettmer's stuff starts with a heavy power sinker, a fastball up to 96 mph thrown with good sink that elicits a very good ground-ball rate. His slider -- a low-80s breaker that misses a decent amount of bats -- offers more sweep than it did in the past. He works in a low-80s changeup that can be effective as well. While he's yet to be tested at higher levels, it has been encouraging to see Dettmer throw more quality strikes this year than he has previously. He's learning that his stuff is plenty good enough to get outs and he's been more in attack mode instead of working more passively to induce contact with his sinker. He could be coming around at just the right time, as the pitching pendulum swings back towards hurlers who feature sinkers thanks to hitters who have adjusted to four-seamers with carry up in the zone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers swiped Pacific Northwest prep pitchers away from Oregon State commitments in consecutive Drafts. The more recent, Swanson, was a two-sport star in Washington, the son of a high school basketball coach who was the top-ranked high school player in the state. The Tigers drafted Swanson in the ninth round and wooed him to pro ball with an above-slot $722,500 bonus. Swanson’s athleticism has allowed him to blossom as a pitcher at a later stage than others. His fastball ranged from the low-to-mid 90s in high school but is more of a power offering with carry since working with the Tigers’ pitching department to refine his delivery. His high-spin slider has a lot of movement and depth. His changeup needs work but could be the difference between starting and relieving. The Tigers drafted Swanson fully knowing he could take longer to develop but believing in the athlete and competitor. His introduction to pro ball will be delayed after he underwent Tommy John surgery ahead of the 2025 campaign, knocking him out for what would have been his first full season.

fangraphs.label: FanGraphs 2026 Twins Top 50
fangraphs.text: Caraballo had an exciting pro debut in the Giants system (.264/.432/.442) last year even though he was 16 for the entire season; he came to Minnesota in exchange for access to Daniel Susac via the second pick in the Rule 5 Draft. The Twins promoted Caraballo to the FCL and he’s off to another hot start, especially from a slugging standpoint. His lefty swing especially is geared for launch. It has the classic low ball look, and Caraballo’s hands have precocious strength to them. Whether he will be able to cover elevated fastballs as he climbs the minors is in doubt, as lefties with this kind of bat path often struggle with that, and Caraballo is sporting a sub-70% contact rate as a lefty stick so far in his career. He also has work to do on defense. Caraballo is a conspicuous pitch framer, and when he completes his exchange enough to get off a throw, he does so without great pace. None of these issues are so bad to conclude he can’t catch, but he’s green enough that he couldn’t catch at an affiliate right now without it being an issue, though that’s normal for a 17-year-old. For now, consider Caraballo a low-and-slow bat-first project who might have the power of a primary catcher at peak.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Cutter: 45 | Control: 50 | Overall: 40 Dalena shares an alma mater of Montoursville Area (Pa.) HS with Mike Mussina and was mentored by the Hall of Fame pitcher growing up in the Keystone State. After a stint at Monmouth in 2021-22, he played both ways at Division II Shippensburg in 2023, turned toward pitching in ’24 and posted a 3.36 ERA and a 1.17 WHIP with 99 strikeouts in 83 innings as a graduate student in ’25. The Padres took him in the sixth round, making him the first Shippensburg player selected since 2018 and the highest since 1999, and signed him for $10,000. Dalena made three brief appearances for Single-A Lake Elsinore in his pro debut. The 6-foot-3 right-hander is entering his age-24 campaign in his first full season but has some upside given his limited background. He was sitting mid-90s with impressive ride up in the zone after signing, and it’s a pitch he uses to set up the rest of his repertoire. It’s likely to be a true north-south look with an upper-70s curveball that drops off the table and a low-80s slider that stands out more for its drop than sweep. The deuce has better action and got more whiffs in his final collegiate season, but finding a consistent preferred breaking pitch will be a priority in ’26. Dalena also worked with a cutter and a changeup, the latter of which he struggled to command in his brief pro look in the California League. Dalena has a history of landing multiple pitches in the zone though, and he’d come up in offseason trade talks with other clubs intrigued by his early mix. He must prove his stuff can play beyond Division II, but the quality of the arsenal could make him a quality low-money, middle-round sign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Van Scoyoc comes from Iowa baseball royalty, with a grandfather who was a coach immortalized in the film “The Final Season,” a dad who played pro ball and a brother who was drafted by the Phillies in 2019. Connor was committed to Arizona State after earning Iowa Gatorade Player of the Year honors, but the Angels went well over slot, giving him $400,000 in the 11th round of the 2018 Draft to keep him from heading to campus. He didn’t make much noise over his first couple of years, but he found some success in A-ball in 2022 and got some exposure in the Arizona Fall League. He was pitching well at High-A in 2023 when he was sent to the Rockies in exchange for Mike Moustakas and he finished the year with eight starts at Double-A. A 6-foot-6 right-hander, Van Scoyoc could have a three-pitch mix that gives him the chance to start. His fastball averages around 92 mph, though he can reach back for a few more ticks on occasion. It can be an effective pitch because of it’s cut and sink, a reason why he produces solid ground-ball rates. He’s shown the ability to spin a decent upper-70s curve that can flash above-average at times. He has a mid-80s changeup, but he doesn’t throw it much and it’s well behind the other two offerings. Pitchers this size can often find it difficult to repeat their delivery and Van Scoyoc struggled with finding the zone consistently in the early stages of his career. He improved dramatically on that front in 2022 and was a decent strike-thrower in '23. He was left unprotected from the Rule 5 Draft last offseason and wasn’t selected, making this a big year for the 24-year old.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Clarke tied for the Division I lead with 23 homers as a junior for South Carolina in 2021, apt timing considering he missed much of his sophomore campaign the previous year due to the pandemic. The Brewers selected him in the 10th round that summer and signed him below slot at $75,000. The right-handed slugger was a solid performer between High-A and Double-A his first full season, finishing with 14 homers and a 116 wRC+ in 99 games, but truly took off in a return to Biloxi this summer with a Southern League-best 26 homers and an .889 OPS that placed third on the circuit. A strong Arizona Fall League campaign solidified the breakout. Power, power, power -- that’s long been Clarke’s calling card and will continue to be the closer he gets to Milwaukee. His uphill swing enables the pop to play as 50.2 percent of his batted balls were flyballs in 2023, but it also can affect his overall contact rate as he struck out 29.2 percent of the time. Clarke balances the punchouts with a lot of walks, but even he’s admitted he needs to get to the power earlier in counts to keep the offensive profile balanced. A well-below-average runner, Clarke initially impressed Brewers officials with his improvements behind the plate, but he’s still viewed as a long-term first baseman, especially as he plays next to Jeferson Quero and bumps into William Contreras’ shadow. He has decent arm strength but lacks accuracy on throws, leading to a 10.3 percent caught-stealing rate in 2023. A full-time right-right first baseman has a high offensive bar to clear, but Clarke just might have the power to handle it. If he can serve as a third catcher on the roster too, all the better.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the Braves didn't shy away from big-ticket players during the 2023 international signing period -- they did get outfielder Luis Guanipa for $2.5 million -- they did some excellent bargain shopping as well. Shortstop John Gil signed for $110,000 and Antonio received only $10,000 to join the organization from his home country of Colombia. Brought along slowly, he saw more time in relief than as a starter during his debut in the Dominican Summer League after signing and again when he came stateside for the Florida Complex League in 2024, though he did reach the Carolina League that summer. He took a big step forward in 2025 as a starter back with Augusta, topping 90 innings, but wasn't able to build off of it when a Spring Training elbow injury led to Tommy John surgery that knocked out his 2026 season. Strong, athletic and compact, Antonio's velocity and stuff all ticked up in 2025. He has a four- and two-seamer, throwing the former up the zone and the latter with sink, and it averaged close to 94 mph and touched 98. His mid-80s slider is his most consistent secondary offering, missing bats at a solid clip. He uses a low-80s splitter that's effective at times, though he struggles to land it for strikes. When healthy, Antonio has been a solid strike-thrower overall, and his sinker and splitter are particularly effective in getting ground-ball outs. He'll be only 21 when he returns to the mound at some point in 2027 and it will be interesting to see if the velocity and strikeout gains he showed in '25 return when he's 100 percent.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Merejo was born in Florida and grew up there before moving to the Dominican Republic late in his high school career and signing for $340,000 in 2023. He followed up a strong pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League by coming to the United States at age 18 last year. After beginning the season in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, he concluded it by batting .282/.372/.466 in the final month Single-A as one of the Carolina League's youngest players. Unlike most of the Guardians' international signings, Merejo stands out more for his power than his hitting ability. His physicality and the bat speed in his right-handed stroke produce plus raw pop, and he taps into most of it by concentrating on driving balls in the air to his pull side too. He has some feel to hit and is willing to take walks, though he'll have to tone down his approach because it leaves him vulnerable to non-fastballs. Most of Merejo's value will come from his bat. Though he stole 11 bases in 77 games last year, he's a below-average runner who's probably limited to first base. He committed 10 errors in 53 starts there in 2024 while also getting time on the outfield corners, where he displayed solid arm strength but substandard range.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros paid the two highest bonuses in their 2025 international class to a pair of players who trained together in Santo Domingo, D.R. Cuban outfielder Kevin Alvarez signed for $2 million, while Venezuelan infielder Manzueta turned pro for $847,500. The latter slashed .224/.405/.392 with 42 walks in 47 games during his pro debut as one of the youngest players (age 16) in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Manzueta stands out with his advanced feel for the barrel and his control of the strike zone. He has a sound right-handed stroke and recognizes pitches well. He won't be physically imposing and needs to add strength to his 5-foot-10 frame, but his ability to turn on pitches and square them up gives him some sneaky power that could translate into 12-15 homers per season. While Manzueta trained as a shortstop, his below-average speed and average arm strength aren't suited for the position. He played there briefly in the DSL while spending most of his time alternating between second base and third base. He profiles best at the keystone and could wind up a utilityman who derives much of his value from his on-base skills.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Mason Martin, a former Pirates farmhand who ranked fourth in the Minors with 35 homers in 2019, Martin also stands out with his well-above-average raw power. Signed for an over-slot $250,000 in 2023 as an 11th-rounder from a Washington high school, he struggled for two years in Rookie ball before doing more damage in Single-A last year and drawing significant trade interest from other clubs. He earned Carolina League all-star honors after leading the Single-A circuit in extra-base hits (43) and ranking second in slugging (.440) and third in homers (12) and OPS (.783). Martin can drive the ball out of the park to all fields with an impressive combination of bat speed and strength, and he hits the ball harder and farther than most Rangers farmhands. In 2025, he did a better job of attacking hittable pitches in early counts and launching them in the air to his pull side, allowing him to make better use of his pop. How much he'll be able to tap into his 25-30 homer upside at higher levels will depend on his ability to improve his swing decisions and handle secondary pitches. Though Martin stole 15 bases in as many attempts last year, he has fringy speed with good instincts on the bases. He has limited range and below-average arm strength, relegating him to left field and diminishing his value outside of the batter's box. He's adequate at first base and can fill in in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While fellow infielder Nestor Miranda was the Tigers’ headline signing of the 2024 international class, Dickson had the better introduction to pro ball after signing for $400,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He was one of the more impressive performers for the Tigers in the Dominican Summer League and earned a spot in the DSL All-Star Game. Dickerson has a lanky, athletic build with a solid swing that becomes more formidable as he physically matures. He had a leg kick when he signed, but the Tigers worked to quiet his stance. He was pull heavy in the DSL with a high rate of ground balls and fly balls and good extra-base power without a home run, but his aggressive approach was tempered by a good eye at the plate for his age. He’s an opportunistic baserunner whose high stolen-base total in the DSL came with a good success rate. He moves well at shortstop but could move positions as he fills out. Dickson’s success in the DSL should move him to the Florida Complex League as an 18-year-old. He has the tools to become a promising prospect, but his physical maturation will have a big impact on his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Olson earned second-team all-Big Ten Conference honors and an invitation to try out for the U.S. national team as a Nebraska sophomore in 2022. He boosted his Draft stock with a strong performance against Michigan in front of a crowd of scouts last April and went in the fourth round, where he signed for a well below-slot $460,000. He made just one brief appearance after turning pro. A finesse left-hander, Olson has his most success when he's in command of his breaking pitches. His mid-70s curveball has a lot of downer break but lacks power and rarely lands in the zone, while his low-80s slider is more reliable in terms of strikes and chases. His fringy low-90s fastball peaks at 95 mph and doesn't miss many bats, and his mid-80s changeup has depth but gets too firm. Olson features a high-three-quarters arm slot and provides consistent strikes with all of his pitches except for his curve. He's physically maxed out at 6-foot-4 and 230 pounds, so he's unlikely to add significant velocity. He has a decent floor as an end-of-the-rotation starter with little margin for error with his stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: St Joseph’s most successful product has been left-hander Jamie Moyer, who spent a quarter century in the big leagues. There’s been one other catcher, Brian O’Keefe, who touched the Majors in 2022-23, but Cossetti is hoping to be the next. After four years at the Philadelphia-based school, Cossetti certainly didn’t hurt his stock with a strong showing in his second stint in MLB’s Draft League in 2022, helping him land in the 11th round of that year's Draft. He posted a .960 OPS across two levels of A ball in 2023, with a 163 RC+ that placed second among all catchers with more than 300 plate appearances, before finishing up with a defense-focused stint in the Arizona Fall League. Cossetti has the chance to be a productive right-handed hitter because he has a solid combination of strength and approach at the plate. He limits strikeouts and draws a ton of walks, getting him into better counts where he did fairly consistent damage. He registers high exit velocities, and there’s good power he should be able to continue to get to. Whether he can defend well enough to stay behind the plate is more of a question. He’s improved his arm strength to average, and he works very hard at his craft, but he’ll need to keep grinding to become an adequate receiver. The Twins don’t want to bet against his work ethic, but they’ll also keep getting him some reps at first base to get his bat in the lineup more regularly.

fangraphs.label: 2026report
fangraphs.text: Sales' pro debut - 94.2 innings combined between the Tigers and Nats systems (he was in the Kyle Finnegan trade), 2.85 ERA, 26% K%, 7.3% BB% - marked his second consecutive season approaching 100 innings with starter-quality strike-throwing. He has begun 2026 on the IL with a vague upper body injury that, according to a source, is related to his torso rather than his arm. Healthy Sales has two nasty breaking balls in a cutter and slider that both generated plus miss in 2025. He can throw a slower curveball into the zone and uses it more often against lefties, who had a .750 OPS against him last year. The next box Sales needs to check to continue projecting as a starter is an offspeed pitch that will help keep lefties off of his back. As his repertoire is currently constituted, he should be a good middle reliever who'll face righties as often as possible.

fangraphs.label: 2025updated
fangraphs.text: Short and slight, the UNC-Wilmington product has been touching the 95-96 mph band with greater regularity as his first pro season has worn on, but it takes some delivery violence to get there and Sales doesn’t get whiffs from the downhill plane his release point creates. Sales’ supination allows him to shape a cutter and mid-80s slider, with the latter showing potentially above-average two-plane break. He lacks a changeup, and the .347/.402/.493 line Low-A lefties have managed against Sales reflects that. A control-over-command approach has fed into the 22-year-old’s impressive 6.5% walk rate, but the slider is good enough with maturing velocity to project Sales to handle some seventh innings down the road.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers signed a then 17-year-old Aquino for only $16,000 out of the Dominican Republic on the first day of the 2021 international period and have seen him steadily climb the ranks one level a year since. After stints on the Dominican and Arizona Complex circuits, the right-hander posted a 2.75 ERA and 1.26 WHIP with 86 strikeouts over 88 1/3 frames for Single-A Carolina this summer. That inning output more than doubled his total from 2021 and '22 combined (78 1/3), so Milwaukee officials found it particularly promising that Aquino was still growing into himself toward the end of his age-20 campaign. Aquino shows largely average fastball velocity around 92-94 mph but can crank it up as high as 96 at times. His low-80s slider is his best pitch with impressive two-plane movement that can drive his whiff rate. Despite averaging less than a K per inning, his 14.5 swinging-strike percentage was ninth-best among 29 Carolina Leaguers with at least 80 innings in 2023. The vertical drop, in particular, can make the breaker look closer to a curveball at times, but it’s still effective. Aquino’s mid-80s changeup remains behind the other two offerings, and without a quality third pitch, lefties batted .288 with a .381 OBP off the hurler in 2023. The 6-foot righty found the zone with better regularity as the season wore on, walking only five batters in his final six outings (27 IP). More disciplined upper-level hitters could hold off chasing the diving sliders out of the zone, pushing that walk rate back up in years to come, but the improvements at least help Aquino’s odds of starting for now. Even so, his best chance of being an impact Major Leaguer might be as a two-pitch reliever who leans into his best tools in shorter appearances.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2025 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2023 NCAA Division II player of the year after batting .408/.506/.901 with a school-record 28 homers at Point Loma Nazarene (Calif.), Christian transferred to San Diego for his Draft year. The Toreros' best power prospect since Kris Bryant, he slashed .364/.460/.828 with 26 homers to win West Coast Conference player of the year honors. He played briefly in Single-A after signing for $397,500 as a fifth-rounder. Christian's 6-foof-5, 225-pound frame gives him tremendous strength and leverage, and his right-handed stroke provides plenty of bat speed and loft. That combination results in well above-average raw power that allows him to smash balls out of any part of the ballpark. He does come with an aggressive approach and swing-and-miss concerns, especially against non-fastballs, and he struggled to produce with wood bats in college summer leagues. Christian moves well for his size, displaying fringy speed with decent instincts on the bases. After playing first base at Point Loma Nazarene, he moved to right field at San Diego and spent most of his short pro debut in left field. He has adequate range and average arm strength on the outfield corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cohen spent five years at George Washington and was the Colonials' best starter in the final three before signing for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent in 2022. Since missing the first half of the 2024 season with a back strain, he has been one of the most unhittable relievers in the Minors during the past two years, logging a 1.62 ERA and .155 opponent average. Though the Yankees declined to protect him on their 40-man roster this offseason, he slipped through the Rule 5 Draft and will compete for a big league bullpen job in 2026. Cohen's money pitch is a tight mid-80s slider that hitters can't lay off or catch up to when it ventures into the strike zone. His fastball is fairly ordinary, ranging from 92-94 mph and reaching 96 with nice carry at times but also below-average command that can make it vulnerable. His mid-80s changeup with fade and sink can be a solid offering at it's best. Cohen hides the ball well with an up-tempo, upright delivery with a high leg kick. While his mechanics provide deception, they also hamper his control and have resulted in a 12 percent walk rate in pro ball. He profiles more as a middle reliever than a high-leverage option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2026 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ortiz slugged .771 with 34 homers in his two years at Walters State CC in Tennessee and showed out nicely in separate stints in the Appalachian (2023) and MLB Draft Leagues (2024) to establish himself on the Draft radar. The Cardinals took him in the 16th round and dipped a little into their bonus pool to make him a JUCO signing for $200,000.
