fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text:
After two years in the GCL (another Canadian high schooler further down this list was developed the same way), Balazovic spent the spring of 2018 in Extended and then skipped the Appy League and went right to Low-A. He dominated there, striking out 78 in 61.2 innings while walking just 18. He throws an unusually high number of strikes for such a lanky, young, cold-weather arm with a somewhat violent delivery, and he gets nasty vertical action on his breaking ball despite a mediocre spin rate. 
There's still some visual discomfort with Balazovic's mechanics, but he's throwing strikes early in his career and hasn't been injured. He'll move up this list with a full year of innings at his 2018 level of performance. For now he at least projects as a reliever, but has a puncher's chance to be a No. 4 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2024 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After signing with the Dodgers for an over-slot $247,500 in the 11th round of the 2017 Draft, Amaya quickly made an impression with his plate defense and plate discipline. He set a career high with 17 homers and reached Triple-A in 2022 before the Marlins acquired him in a trade for Miguel Rojas in January 2023. He made his big league debut over four games with Miami last June, but got designated for assignment this April and traded to the Astros for right-handed pitching prospect Valente Bellozo. Amaya is a quality defender at shortstop with smooth actions, quick and sure hands, a solid and accurate arm and a good internal clock. He has average speed but solid range and is working to enhance his first-step quickness so that he can cover more ground. He's also quite capable at second and third base. A right-handed hitter, Amaya is at his best when he keeps his stroke under control and focuses on getting on base. He added strength during the pandemic layoff, which enhanced his power but also has led to lapses where he starts hunting home runs and chasing pitches. He makes consistent contact when he swings at strikes and could provide on-base ability with 15 homers per year if he maintains a disciplined approach.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers signed Amaya out of a suburban Los Angeles high school for an over-slot $247,500 in the 11th round of the 2017 Draft, and his plate discipline and defense quickly made him an organization favorite. He bounced back from his worst pro season in 2021 to hit a career-best 17 homers between Double-A and Triple-A last year before the Marlins acquired him for Miguel Rojas in January. He could be Miami's shortstop of the very near future and for the long term. Amaya is most effective when he employs a controlled right-handed stroke and concentrates on getting base. He got stronger during the pandemic layoff, but his newfound power can get him into trouble when he starts hunting home runs and chasing pitches. He settled down more in 2022 and projects as a .250 hitter with 12-15 homers per season and plenty of walks. That type of production would be more than enough to make Amaya a big league regular at shortstop, because he's a quality defender. Not only does he have quick, reliable hands and a strong, accurate arm, but his high baseball IQ and nonstop energy allow him to get the most out of his physical tools. He also is an asset at second and third base and would be a useful utility man if he doesn't hit enough to play regularly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The grandson of former Dodgers middle-infield prospect Frank Amaya, Jacob signed for an above-slot $247,500 out of a suburban Los Angeles high school in the 11th round of the 2017 Draft. His keen batting eye and his glovework quickly made him an organization favorite, and he bounced back from his worst season as a pro in 2021 to hit a career-high 17 homers in 2022. The Marlins acquired him in a January deal for Miguel Rojas. Amaya walked nearly as much as he struck out in his first three pro seasons, but he got away from his approach in 2021 after homering five times that April and seeking more power. He's most effective when he employs a controlled right-handed stroke and focuses on hitting line drives and getting on base. He could hit .260 with 12-15 homers per season if he can refrain from chasing pitches; he did show more discipline in 2022. Even when he slumped, Amaya continued to provide quality glovework at shortstop. His high baseball IQ and constant energy allow him to maximize his tools and play faster than his average speed. His quick, reliable hands and a strong, accurate arm help make him a plus defender at shortstop and will serve him well in a projected utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The grandson of Frank Amaya, a middle infielder in the Dodgers system during the late 1950s, Jacob signed for an above-slot $247,500 as an 11th-rounder in 2017. He stood out at the National High School Invitational that spring but his commitment to Cal State Fullerton scared off several clubs. When he made his full-season debut in 2019, he ranked second in walks (74) and seventh in OPS (.775) in the low Class A Midwest League at age 20 and batted .563 in the high Class A California League postseason. Amaya possesses one of the best batting eyes in the system and hit .273 with nearly as many walks as strikeouts during his first three pro seasons. He has a sound right-handed swing and a mature, all-fields approach. He's making harder contact as he continues to get stronger but likely will be more of a doubles threat than a home run hitter. Amaya's high baseball IQ and nonstop energy allow him to make the most out of his tools and play faster than his average speed on the bases and in the field. He has quick, reliable hands and a strong, accurate arm, and he's the best infield defender among Dodgers prospects. He's a legitimate shortstop who also has seen action at second and third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Frank Amaya was a middle infielder with a keen batting eye who played in the Dodgers system in the late 1950s, and his grandson Jacob is following in his footsteps six decades later. He impressed scouts at the 2017 National High School Invitational but a Cal State Fullerton commitment clouded his signability and dropped him to the 11th round, where he received an above-slot $247,500 bonus. He finished second in walks (74) and seventh in OPS (.775) as a 20-year-old in the low Class A Midwest League in 2019, then batted .563 in the high Class A California League playoffs. Amaya has outstanding strike-zone judgment and rarely chases pitches out of the strike zone. Add in his sound right-handed stroke, feel for the barrel and all-fields approach, and he has the ingredients to become a solid hitter. He has gotten stronger since turning pro, displays occasional power to all fields and could become a 12-15 homer threat if he launches the ball in the air more often. An average runner, Amaya has a high baseball IQ and constant energy that help him play faster than his pure speed on the bases and in the field. He has a strong, accurate arm and quick, reliable hands. He projects as a solid defender at shortstop, perhaps plus at second base and also has seen brief action at third base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Amaya impressed scouts at the 2017 National High School Invitational but concerned them with his commitment to Cal State Fullerton. He fell to the 11th round and the Dodgers, for whom his grandfather Frank was a Minor League shortstop in the 1950s, before signing for an over-slot $247,500. After a so-so pro debut, he was one of the best hitters in the Rookie-level Pioneer League last summer before earning a promotion to low Class A at age 19. Amaya spent his first pro offseason concentrating on getting stronger and hit the ball with more authority in 2018. He has a sound right-handed swing with advanced feel for the barrel, controls the strike zone well and uses the entire field. He has some gap power but hasn't fully tapped into it because he tends to hit the ball on the ground. An average runner, Amaya has outstanding instincts that allow him to play quicker than that on the bases and in the middle of the infield. He has solid arm strength and a nose for the ball, projecting as at least an average defender at shortstop and perhaps plus at second base. Club officials love his constant energy and work ethic.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text: Amaya is a skills-over-tools infielder whose versatility and ability to play shortstop should enable a utility infield role in the near future. Amaya doesn't have the huge physical tools of a premium shortstop defender (he's more average there), but his hands and actions are exceptional and make him a plus defender at the other infield positions. A lack of physicality and power will limit his offensive impact, but Amaya has a great eye for the strike zone, as well as an idea of which pitches he can drive for doubles. He's got a short, punchy swing you can't beat with velo alone, and Amaya has run plus contact rates again in 2024. In his final option year, Amaya should end up in a steady on-roster role as a sixth infielder within the next year.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Amaya is a skills-over-tools infielder whose at-bat quality and viability at shortstop should enable him to play a utility infield role in the near future. A lack of physicality and power will limit his impact, but Amaya has a great eye for the strike zone, as well as an idea of which pitches he can drive for doubles. He's got a short, punchy swing you can't just beat with velo. His hands were uncharacteristically inconsistent at the end of 2022, but Amaya has historically been a plus hands and actions shortstop with average range and arm strength. He is likely to debut in 2023, especially if Joey Wendle continues to struggle.

A lack of physicality and power will limit his impact, but Amaya has a great eye for the strike zone, as well as an idea of which pitches he can drive. He's got a short, punchy swing you can't just beat with velo. He'll hit a bunch of doubles. Instinctive and fundamentally sound, Amaya projects as a utility infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Alton (Ill.) High not only produced the tallest man in recorded history (8-foot-11 Robert Wadlow) but also one of the tallest pitchers currently in the Minors, the 6-foot-8 Hudson. When the Cubs went over slot to sign him for $1.1 million as a third-rounder in 2015, they knew his development would require patience and time. He has progressed more slowly than expected, though he did finish 2017 by going 7-0 with a 3.39 ERA in his final 11 starts. Hudson had trouble repeating his delivery and maintaining strength during his first full pro season in 2016, when his fastball often sat at 86-88 mph and his curveball lost its normal bite. He looked more coordinated and better prepared to handle the rigors of pro ball in 2017, when he worked from 87-94 mph with his heater and unleashed some hammer curves at times. His fastball plays above its velocity with its sink and the extreme angle his big body creates, resulting in a 3.1 groundout/airout ratio that ranked second in the Minors last year. Hudson's extra-large frame has plenty of projection remaining, so it's possible that both his fastball and curve become plus pitches. His changeup has less upside but is an effective third pitch. He's starting to translate the athleticism he displayed in high school basketball to the mound, which helped him cut his walk rate from 6.3 per nine innings in 2016 to 3.8 last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Illinois' best high school pitching prospect since the Astros made Mike Foltynewicz a first-round pick in 2010, Hudson signed for $1.1 million as a third-rounder in 2015. He's a product of Alton (Ill.) High, which graduated the tallest man in recorded history (8-foot-11 Robert Wadlow) in 1936, and Hudson towers over most players at 6-foot-8. He had a rough first full season as a pro, recording a 5.06 ERA in the short-season Northwest League as his mechanics and control got out of whack. Hudson has the potential for a well-above-average fastball and curveball. He has a ton of projection remaining in his skinny frame, which should mean more power for a heater that already can reach 94 mph with sink and a curve that can be a hammer in the upper 70s. Neither pitch was at its best when he had trouble maintaining his normal three-quarters arm slot last summer, when he often pitched with an 86-88 mph fastball and lost some faith in a diminished curveball. Hudson knows he needs to work on his changeup and overemphasized it at times last year. He has good athleticism and body control for his size, so he's equipped to figure out his delivery and improve his control and command. His ceiling remains sky-high, though it may take him longer to develop than initially expected.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text: Hudson was slow to develop big league velocity as a Cubs prospect, and it took him eight seasons to debut. He's a gigantic, low-ish slot reliever with a low-90s fastball that tends to induce abnormally high chase rates because hitters are so uncomfortable with Hudson's release point. His stuff is otherwise pretty generic and he's likely to play an up/down role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Now in his third organization after being drafted by Cleveland in 2016, Taylor was part of Kansas City's return for Whit Merrifield in the August 2022 trade with the Blue Jays. Things started to click for Taylor in Double-A in 2021, when he hit .294 with a career-high 16 home runs and 30 stolen bases. He was off to a solid start in 2022 in Triple-A but missed half the season with an oblique injury. He didn’t make his Royals debut until the Arizona Fall League, but the club saw enough to add him to the 40-man roster in the offseason to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. Taylor is a toolsy player, with a good combination of speed and power for a second baseman. His natural bat speed is enticing, but he’s still learning to control it and remains aggressive at the plate. Taylor is working with the Royals’ hitting department on the strike zone, letting pitches get deeper before committing, as well as in-game adjustments that will enable his bat-to-ball skills to play. Even at 5-foot-8 and 160 pounds, he does have power in his swing, but that can lead to holes if he’s trying to hit it over the fence. There is value solely in putting the ball in play for him because of his plus-plus speed and ability to run the bases. Taylor is a better defender at second base with his quick instincts, but he can be an average defender in the outfield. The Royals have moved Taylor around the infield and outfield this year to increase his versatility. His speed and defense can give him a utility role in the big leagues, with everyday playing time dependent on whether it clicks offensively. Taylor has gotten sporadic Major League time in KC as that versatility has opened up holes for him with the big club.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafted by Cleveland out of Corona High School in 2016, Taylor debuted in the Rookie Arizona League as a 17-year-old and in ’17 advanced to the short-season level. That’s the summer he was traded to the Blue Jays along with Thomas Pannone for reliever Joe Smith, a deal that could still pay off for Toronto. In ’18, Taylor spent the full season in Low-A, hitting .228, then continued into ’19 hitting just .216 in High-A. Finally, in ’21 with an assignment to Double-A, Taylor’s physical gifts began to click. He hit .294 with a career-high 16 home runs, an .888 OPS and 30 stolen bases, showing the all-around skillset the Blue Jays had been waiting on. In the midst of a steady Triple-A season, Taylor was traded to the Royals at the Trade Deadline in a swap that sent Whit Merrifield north of the border. With a combination of speed and some power for a second baseman, Taylor excites the organization with his natural bat speed. The next step will be trusting that bat speed, allowing pitches to get a bit deeper in the zone before committing. His overall approach and in-game adjustments will be part of this next step, too, but the raw tools continue to be tantalizing. Defensively, Taylor was solid enough at second base, but he spread his focus to play third, shortstop, center field and left field in Double-A in ’21. If he can prove to be a competent defender in a utility role, that only gives him more paths up the ladder. Left off the 40-man roster this past offseason, Taylor still has a chance to impress from Triple-A at some point in ’22. Between defensive versatility and his speed, which remains his best tool, Taylor can create an opportunity for himself in a few different ways. While the Blue Jays believed that ’21 was the true Taylor, it’s now on Kansas City to develop him into a potential fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 10th-round Draft pick by the Indians out of the California prep ranks in 2016, Taylor, who signed for $125,000, showed advanced hitting ability during his pro debut and continued to do so the following year in the Class A Short-Season New York-Penn League, where he owned a .300/.328/.467 slash line when the Tribe dealt him and lefty Thomas Pannone to Toronto for reliever Joe Smith at the July Trade Deadline. Advancing to full-season ball in 2018, Taylor impressed his new organization with his blend of power and speed as he totaled 48 extra-base hits and 44 steals over 121 games in the Midwest League. Taylor's wiry frame is loaded with quick-twitch athleticism. It translates to good bat speed and better-than-expected power at the plate, with Taylor showing he can consistently impact the baseball. Those qualities, along with his feel for controlling the zone, give him a chance to be at least an average hitter, with power that should play in games more often as he becomes more physical and improves his pitch recognition and selectivity. A plus runner, Taylor's 44 steals in 2018 were good for a share of third place in the Midwest League, but he will need to improve his reads and jumps after he was thrown out 16 times, the second-highest total in the circuit. Taylor's athleticism shows at second base, where he profiles as an average defender. He has good range, quick feet and above-average arm strength. There's first-division regular upside if it all clicks for Taylor, and he also has a fairly high floor with his blend of hitting ability, patience and speed at an up-the-middle position.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text:
Taylor was drafted by Cleveland and traded to Toronto as part of a package for reliever Joe Smith, then was sent to the Royals as part of last year's Whit Merrifield deal. He played his way onto the Royals 40-man with a great Arizona Fall League run (he played better than his statline), broke camp with Omaha in 2023, and, after parts of eight seasons in pro ball, made his big league debut in the middle of June. 
Taylor can impact the game in a host of ways, mainly with his blazing speed. He barely looks like he's touching the ground as he floats from base to base, and he's become a much more efficient basestealer during the last few years. Baseball's new rules should enable him to make an impact if/when he reaches base. A career .262/.350/.423 hitter in the minors, Taylor's feel to hit is comfortably below-average and he likely won't hit enough to be a true righty platoon option on a contender. He's an average second base defender but, despite his speed, Taylor's feel for center isn't good enough for him to play there regularly. Eric Young Jr. is my go-to comp for players who fit in this sort of role, a 2B/LF part-timer whose impact is situational.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Taylor's home run and steal totals from last season have undoubtedly made him a fashionable sleeper in statline-scouting fantasy circles. We'd caution against taking his batting line at face value. His measurable power is much closer to Mallex Smith/Richie Martin territory, which means he simply isn't strong enough at present to replicate his 2021 numbers in a big league environment. In that context, his swing decisions loom as a big concern. He's both passive and prone to swinging and missing, a combination that works among players with big pop but often proves fatal for anyone else. However, his speed and defensive chops - he started at least five games at five different spots, including the four hard ones - give him big league utility, particularly in the slim-bench era.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text:
Taylor signed with Cleveland for $125,000 in the 10th round in 2016 out of a southern California high school. The report then was an explosive, quick second baseman with some tools who could use some refinement. That's still mostly the report, but Taylor's 2018 full season debut was excellent, hitting above league average in the Midwest League as a 19-year-old most of the year, despite a .270 BABIP. Some players naturally have a lower BABIP, but Taylor is a player who should have a higher-than-normal BABIP given his plus speed (44 stolen bases in 2018), solid plate discipline (11% BB to 19% K), and surprising game power for his size and age (nine home runs and 32 doubles). 
Taylor can still make a boneheaded play defensively, use improper footwork at the keystone, or try to do too much at the plate, but the tools are here for a low-end everyday second baseman if things continue progressing.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: 2022 Robinson held the velo bump he first showed in '21 and polished his cutter enough that all three of his pitches now flash above average or better. This makes it more likely that he will be a foundational on-roster middle-inning reliever rather than an up/down option. Always walk-prone, glove-side feel for his cutter might help him carve that path, since poor control has also been part of Robinson's up/down projection of the last few years. He not only threw a better rate of strikes in 2022, but his cutter helped him generate a 63% groundball rate in 65 innings. Now on the 40-man roster, Robinson and his vertical-action fastball/curveball combination are set to debut in 2023.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Robinson experienced a velo bump in 2021 and averaged 93-94 with his fastball after sitting a couple ticks lower than that in 2019. He also added a cutter, but his stuff is not vicious enough to overcome 30-grade control and force his way onto a 40-man roster. He and his vertical-action fastball/curveball combination will likely play an upper-level relief depth role in 2022.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Robinson works in the low-90s with a flat-planed fastball that plays at the top of the zone, and a snapdragon, 12-to-6 curveball. He's not that projectable, but he's athletically built and has a good arm action. He needs to refine his strike-throwing pretty badly and it would be nice if he ended up throwing harder, but the repertoire works well together, and I think he has a good shot to be a big league bullpen piece. He's projected as an up/down reliever here.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A rare 23rd-round pick who signed out of high school, Robinson took a few years to find his footing in pro ball and started showing improved velocity heading into 2021. The improved stuff helped him post a 3.08 ERA with 62 strikeouts in 49 2/3 innings across three levels in that first post-pandemic season. He was even better last year, finishing with a 2.49 ERA and 84 K’s in 65 frames at High-A, Double-A and Triple-A while leading all Minor Leaguers with 25 saves. The Brewers added Robinson to the 40-man roster in November to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. Throwing from a near-extreme over-the-top delivery, Robinson can make for an uncomfortable at-bat with the way he puts his 93-95 mph fastball on top of hitters. Since the pandemic off year, the heater has a natural cut to it, and while it looks like a hard cutter, Robinson says it’s his natural fastball. All the same, the improvements helped fuel his 2022 successes, including a 63.2 percent ground-ball rate that was fourth-highest among 905 Minor Leaguers with at least 60 innings in 2022. He’ll also drop in a 79-82 mph curveball with solid spin rates and good bite that can hold off any batters sitting on the high cheese, and he’s been working on developing a slider with a longer tail to differentiate it from the cutting fastball. Robinson’s overall control improved last season, but his 11.3 percent walk rate – raised by a 12.9 mark in Triple-A – was still a touch high. Despite all the saves, his strike-throwing and overall quality of stuff point more toward a middle-relief role, and it’s one he could fill quickly in Milwaukee, given his run of success and newfound roster status.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers talked Robinson out of a University of South Florida commitment with a $125,000 bonus as a 23rd-round pick out of University High School (Orlando, Fla.) in 2017. The right-hander’s career sputtered in the early years as he didn’t pitch above Rookie ball, and he hadn’t posted an ERA below 5.50 at any level as a reliever. With the rubber about to meet the road in 2021, he showed an uptick in velocity last spring, throwing more in the low-90s. He rode that to climb three levels from Low-A to Double-A in his first taste of full-season ball. He finished 2021 with a 3.08 ERA, 62 strikeouts and 30 walks in 49 2/3 innings, but he was left off the 40-man roster when he became Rule 5-eligible in November. After throwing in the 94-96 mph range last spring, Robinson settled in closer to 92-94 as the 2021 season wore on. His delivery is very over the top, and the fastball can get right on top of batters (especially right-handers) as a result. He also sports a 12-to-6, upper-70s curveball that pairs really well with his elevated fastballs. An upper-80s cutter -- some systems read it as a slider -- provides another option to keep hitters off-balance. The big break on Robinson’s curve makes it difficult for him to earn calls in the zone, and a lack of consistent fastball command doesn’t help matters either. There’s a reason why Robinson has been in Minor League bullpens since signing. That said, he changed his trajectory in 2021, and it’s much easier now to see Robinson’s fastball-curve combo playing a useful role in a Major League bullpen someday.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Ingram was a Division-II senior sign by the Tigers in 2019 and was released after less than a year, having only pitched for the org in the GCL. He continued to pitch and work out at a facility in Georgia and was signed by the Angels in 2021; he has now ascended to Double-A. Though short, Ingram is an explosive on-mound athlete with a powerful delivery that gets the most out of his body. He only sits 92-93 mph, but his height and the shape of his fastball give it bat-missing carry, and his sweeping low-80s slider, which has near elite spin rates, is above average. Throw in a passable changeup and Ingram has the tools to work the middle innings - he isn't just a lefty specialist. It's probable that his 2022 walk rates (which were a career low) were an anomaly rather than a progression, but there's still enough here to keep big league hitters from crushing his fastball.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: There are a lot of moving parts to Sheehan's profile and he projects to be an impact multi-inning reliever when the dust settles. He's had a velo spike, added a second breaking ball, been moved back and forth between the bullpen and the rotation, and has dealt with a couple of injuries dating back to college, which limited him to just 28 innings prior to his draft year. At times, Sheehan's delivery seems deliberate and out of sync, which is largely where his relief projection comes from, though the balance and power he shows in his lower half and the way he gets down the mound are indicative of a special level of athleticism. After some early 2022 time on the IL, Sheehan was dominant late in the summer with Great Lakes, stringing together several good five- and six-inning starts in August before a promotion to Tulsa and a Fall League stint. His heater features big carry through the strike zone, making it a potential plus-plus pitch if he can sustain the mid-90s velo that comes and goes depending on how well synced his delivery is in a given start. Sheehan has leaned more on his changeup since turning pro. He threw more curveballs (a pitch that's been de-emphasized but that Sheehan still uses occasionally) than changeups in college, but the latter is what garnered more swings and misses. An invisible parachute pops out of the back of his changeup as it approaches the plate, and hitters flail over the top of it. Sheehan doesn't have great feel for his newer slider, but that pitch is still in the nascent stages of development; at times it's harder and looks cuttery, while at others it looks like a typical slider. From one point of view, Sheehan's history of injury and his atypical mechanical look funnel him toward the bullpen; from another, his ability to make adjustments on the fly despite relative inexperience might continue until he's a complete starting pitching prospect. In either case, Sheehan's stuff is going to play in the big leagues, and he's projected here as a multi-inning bridge.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Sheehan had a velo spike after the 2021 draft, going from sitting 91-94 mph in the Boston College rotation to sitting 94-97 in the Rancho bullpen; he struck out more than two batters per inning during his brief late-season run in pro ball. Sheehan's delivery at times seemed deliberate and out of sync while he was at Boston College, though the balance and power he showed in his lower half and the way he got down the mound indicated there might be more in the tank if he could get things dialed in. That seems to have happened, and his heater features big carry through the strike zone, making it a potential plus-plus pitch if he can sustain the mid-90s velo throughout a whole season. Now that Sheehan is in pro ball, expect more emphasis on his plus-plus changeup. He threw more curveballs than changeups in college but his changeup is what garnered more swings and misses. While the shape of Sheehan's loopy, mid-70s curve plays nicely off his fastball, an invisible parachute pops out of the back of his changeup as it approaches the plate, and hitters flail over the top of it. Injuries are part of the equation here. Sheehan only pitched 28 total innings as an underclassman at BC, then missed a few starts in his draft year and went on the IL early in 2022. He projects solely as a reliever in pro ball but could have late-inning impact if he sustains the velo bump.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After pitching just 28 1/3 innings in his first two years at Boston College, Sheehan became the Eagles' ace in 2021, setting a school record with 15 strikeouts in his penultimate start and finishing one whiff shy of the season mark with 106 in 76 2/3 innings. He has been even more unhittable since turning pro as a sixth-round pick and reached Double-A at the end of his first full pro season despite missing the first six weeks with mild arm soreness. He stood out in the Arizona Fall League with the induced vertical break on his fastball and his quality changeup, tore up Double-A for the first two months of the 2023 season and then broke into the big leagues with six no-hit innings against the Giants. Sheehan's fastball sat at 91-94 mph in his final college season but now operates at 94-97 and reaches 99, and his low release point and the extension in his delivery create outstanding carry up in the strike zone. He entered pro ball with advanced feel for his changeup, which arrives in the low 80s before diving at the plate. The Dodgers had him mostly shelve a soft curveball in favor of a short low-80s slider has made a jump this year to become a solid third pitch. Sheehan has the upside of a mid-rotation starter but has a number of things to check off his to-do list to get there. He has refined a reliable breaking ball, but he still has to improve his strike-throwing and prove he's durable enough to handle a 150-inning workload. If he can't, he could be a multi-inning relief weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Krook was set to sign with the Marlins for $1,587,700 as a supplemental first-round pick in 2013 before a post-Draft physical raised concerns about his shoulder and killed the deal. He went to Oregon instead and dominated as a freshman before blowing out his elbow and having Tommy John surgery. Control problems dogged him when he returned to the Ducks in 2016 and continued to do so in pro ball after he signed for $500,000 as a fourth-rounder. Krook can be completely unhittable at his best. He has outstanding life on a 92-94 mph fastball that can reach 96 and seems to dive when it arrives at the plate. His curveball can be a plus-plus pitch with power and depth, his slider shows flashes of becoming a plus offering and his changeup is solid at times. The Giants will be patient with Krook and intend on developing him as a starter. They had him focus on fastball command during instructional league, though his pitches have so much action that they're hard to control even when he repeats his mechanics. If he can't harness his stuff well enough to stay in the rotation, his fastball/curveball combo could still make him a high-leverage reliever.

fangraphs.label: 2024report
fangraphs.text: A 2013 first round pick of the Marlins out of high school, Miami flunked Krook’s post-draft physical and he ended up at Oregon, where he struggled with walks. The Giants took him in the fourth round in 2016 and traded him to the Rays as part of the Evan Longoria deal after the 2017 season. He spent the next several years doing a mix of starting and relieving while with Tampa Bay, again struggling with walks and declining velocity (mid-90s at peak, upper 80s more recently) while still showing big sinking action on his fastball and changeup to go with big break on his slider. The Yankees made him a minor league Rule 5 pick in 2020 and returned Krook to the rotation for a while, then put him in the Scranton bullpen in 2023. He was traded to the Orioles this spring. While his command is still well below average, the length and depth of his slider makes it a plus pitch, and his upper-80s fastball sinks enough to keep it off barrels (he surrendered just 10 hits total in 34 minor league innings in 2023, a number he nearly matched in four big league frames) and generate a ton of groundballs; both pitches are aided by his funky delivery. He doesn't throw strikes consistently enough to stick on an active roster permanently, but is still an optionable "look" reliever who can come up and give hitters fits.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: A 2013 first round pick of the Marlins out of high school, Miami flunked Krook’s post draft physical and he ended up at Oregon, where he struggled with walks. The Giants took him in the fourth round in 2016 and traded him to the Rays as part of the Evan Longoria deal after the 2017 season. He spent the next several years doing a mix of starting and relieving while with Tampa Bay, again struggling with walks and declining velocity (mid-90s at peak, upper 80s more recently) while still showing big sinking action on his fastball and big break on his slider. The Yankees made him a minor league Rule 5 pick in 2020 and returned Krook exclusively to the rotation. While his command is still well below average, the length and depth of his slider makes it a plus pitch, and his upper-80s fastball sinks enough to keep it off barrels and generate a ton of groundballs (55% GB% overall for Krook in 2022); both pitches are aided by his funky delivery. He doesn't have the command you ideally want out of a spot starter or multi-inning reliever, but his stuff is a great fit in either of those roles, especially the latter. He seems likely to begin 2023 as an optionable starter but could move into a bulk middle inning role throughout the year.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Krook has one of the best 88 mph fastballs in the minors due to its dramatic sinking movement, which makes it capable of missing bats despite below-average velocity. His arm angle and the shape of his fastball create a pitch that looks very similar to Zach Britton's sinker, but with much less zip. Though the Giants, who traded him to Tampa as part of the Evan Longoria deal, tried to develop Krook as a starter early in his career, a combination of injury concern (bad delivery, flunked physical coming out of high school, TJ in college) and lack of control made it likely that he'd eventually move to the bullpen, and that transition -- or at least to a role where Krook throws a number of innings typical of a reliever; he may be a candidate to 'open', but we don't know for sure -- is underway. Krook used to live in the low-to-mid-90s and his drop in velocity is perhaps a red flag, considering his medical history. But it plays even at this velocity, and so do his two breaking balls, which benefit from the deceptive ugliness of his delivery.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Mlodzinski started for most of his 2022 season at Double-A but was called upon for middle-inning relief on a few occasions, and though it was only a handful of appearances, he was more effective as a reliever than as a starter. He has a wide arsenal, including a changeup and a two-seamer, but tends to rely more heavily on pairing his riding fastball and curveball to keep hitters off balance. His curveball was his only secondary to induce an above-average chase rate. Spotty command and limited fastball utility push Mlodzinski into a multi-inning relief role.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Mlodzinski missed almost the entire 2019 college season due to a broken foot, then blew up on the Cape, where he was into the mid-90s with two above-average breaking balls. He was 95-98 mph with bat-missing life early in outings, and a 88-91 cutter/slider was his most-used secondary. He got lit up early in 2020, his draft year at South Carolina, when his slider wasn't as crisp and his fastball very liftable. While he dealt with a couple of stints on the IL, including one for a shoulder injury, Mlodzinski had a solid pro debut at (mostly) High-A, where he struck out more than a batter per inning across 14 starts. He picked up innings in the Arizona Fall League, where he sat 95-96 (harder than during the summer) with an 84-86 mph slider and changeup. His fastball still gets hit more than you might expect given how hard it is. This, plus his command, push him toward the bullpen for us, probably in a middle-inning role.
