mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a stress reaction in a lumbar vertebra limited him to six games as a Louisiana State sophomore in 2018, Smith bounced back the next year and went to the Yankees in the second round of the 2019 Draft. Clubs pursued him in trade talks as soon as he raked in his pro debut, and the Rangers landed him last July in a four-prospect package for Joey Gallo and Joely Rodriguez. He advanced to Double-A shortly after switching organizations and continued to hit, staying on course for a big league debut in 2022. Smith possesses some of the best bat-to-ball skills and strike-zone judgment in the Texas system, regularly delivering hard contact to all fields. He has a quick bat and began launching more balls in the air last season, giving him 20-homer upside, though he put too many grounders in play during his month in Double-A. He has solid to plus speed and the savvy to steal bases. Scouts debate whether Smith has enough range to stay at shortstop in the long run, and his chances probably ended when the Rangers signed Corey Seager and Marcus Semien this offseason. He's a reliable defender with soft hands, solid arm strength that plays up with a quick release and a finely tuned internal clock. He'll see time at second base, third base and the outfield this year as Texas determines where to fit his bat into its lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Smith started at third base on Louisiana State's 2017 College World Series runner-up team as a freshman before moving to shortstop the next year, when a stress reaction in a lumbar vertebra limited him to six games. He returned to lead the Tigers in all three slash categories (.346/.433/.533) as well as steals (20) in 2019, elevating himself into the second round of the Draft. He raked in his pro debut with the Yankees that summer and other clubs began asking about him in trade talks ever since -- until the Rangers landed him as the top prospect in the four-player package they received from New York for Joey Gallo and Joely Rodriguez this July. Smith has outstanding bat-to-ball skills, controlling the strike zone well while making hard contact to all fields. His bat speed and the loft in his left-handed stroke create solid raw power that could translate into 20-homer power as he gets stronger. He could provide a similar amount of steals thanks to his solid to plus speed and his instincts on the bases. While many scouts think Smith's range would fit better at second base, he has a chance to stick at shortstop. He's more of a steady than a flashy defender with reliable hands and a good internal clock that helps him get the job done. His solid arm strength plays up with his quick release.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A freshman starting third baseman on the Louisiana State team that finished second at the 2017 College World Series, Smith was slated to take over at shortstop as a sophomore, but a stress reaction in a lumbar vertebra limited him to just six games. He bounced back in '19 to lead the Tigers in all three slash categories (.346/.433/.533) as well as stolen bases (20). After signing for $976,700 as a second-round pick, he posted similar numbers at short-season Staten Island. Smith isn't flashy, but he manages the strike zone well and makes repeated hard contact to all fields. His bat speed and the loft in his left-handed swing give him solid raw power, and he could produce 15-20 homers annually if he can add some more strength. He also could deliver a similar amount of steals with his solid to plus speed and his savvy on the bases. Many scouts believe Smith's range fits better at second base, though he has a chance to stick at shortstop with his instincts and ability to make the most of his tools. He has reliable hands and his solid arm strength and quick release allow him to make all the throws. While he lacks a true plus tool, there are no obvious holes in his game either.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Declared ineligible for what would have been his senior season at Lake Worth (Fla.) High in 2017, Velazquez returned to his native Puerto Rico and caught the attention of the Cubs, one of the few clubs with an area scout (former big leaguer Edwards Guzman) on the island. A fifth-round pick, he flashed intriguing tools but didn't break out until 2021, when he led the system in extra-base hits (45), total bases (191), RBIs (73) and slugging (.496) while reaching Double-A. He continued to mash in the Arizona Fall League, where he was named MVP after topping the development circuit in homers (nine) and OPS (1.191), cementing a spot on Chicago's 40-man roster. Velazquez is loaded with bat speed and strength that has produced some of the best raw power and exit velocities in the system for a while. He spent his pandemic downtime honing his ability to identify and punish breaking pitches, which previously had been a weakness, and also toned down what had been a busy right-handed swing. He's still an aggressive hitter who will accrue strikeouts, but he's doing a better job of tapping into his pop and driving balls in the air to all fields. Though Velazquez lost a step as he has matured physically and now has just average speed, he uses it well on the bases and in the outfield. He swiped 17 bags in 19 attempts last season and continued to see action at all three outfield spots. A solid defender on the corners and more average in center, he has a strong arm that erased 16 runners in 121 games between the Minors and the AFL last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Velazquez was declared ineligible for his senior season at Lake Worth (Fla.) High in 2017, he moved back to his native Puerto Rico. The Cubs were one of the few clubs with a full-time area scout on the island (former big leaguer Edwards Guzman) and fell in love with his tools before signing him for an over-slot $400,000 in the fifth round. He struggled in his first taste of full-season ball in 2018 but fared much better last year, albeit while losing two months to an oblique injury. A right-handed hitter, Velazquez creates plus raw power to all fields and impressive exit velocities with his combination of bat speed and strength. He won't fully tap into it until he tones down his aggressive approach and reduces his propensity for groundball contact. He did a better job of making contact and using the opposite field in 2019 while working to do a better job of staying behind the ball rather than swinging for the fences. Velazquez had solid speed when he turned pro but has slowed a bit as he has begun to fill out and now is more of an average runner. He played all three outfield positions in 2019, spending most of his time in right field, and his quickness and instincts are better suited for the corners. He has the strong arm required in right and has made improvements with his defense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Velazquez played at Lake Worth (Fla.) High as a junior in 2016, then moved back to Puerto Rico after he was ruled ineligible. One of the few teams with a full-time area scout on the island (former big leaguer Edwards Guzman), the Cubs fell in love with his tools early and paid him an over-slot $400,000 bonus in the fifth round of the 2017 Draft. Overmatched in low Class A at the start of his first full pro season, he rebounded to finish fifth in the short-season Northwest League with 11 homers. Velazquez has the most raw power in Chicago's system, as well as some of the best bat speed, strength and all-around tools. He could pile up home runs by letting them come naturally, but instead he uses an overly aggressive and pull-happy approach. He struck out in 30 percent of his plate appearances during his first two seasons and he won't make enough contact to survive against more advanced pitching unless he makes some adjustments. While Velazquez can show solid speed out of the batter's box and plus speed underway, he has already lost a half-step as he has begun to mature physically and likely will wind up as an average runner. He has played all three outfield spots in pro ball and needs to improve his jumps and reads. His prodigious power and his strong arm fit the right-field profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Velazquez played at Lake Worth (Fla.) High in 2016 before getting declared ineligible and moving back to Puerto Rico. One of the few clubs with a full-time area scout on the island (former big leaguer Edwards Guzman), Chicago got on Velazquez early and were completely sold by the time he starred at the Excellence Games showcase last May. After turning pro for an over-slot $400,000 in the fifth round, he nearly led the Rookie-level Arizona League in homers (eight in 32 games) despite signing late and fighting hamstring issues. Velazquez has the best raw power and one of the quickest bats among Cubs prospects. He could deliver 30 or more homers annually from the right side of the plate, provided he makes enough contact. He's very raw at the plate with an aggressive, pull-heavy approach and struck out in 31 percent of his AZL plate appearances. While his power is his most obvious tool, Velazquez is far from a one-dimensional masher. He's a solid runner out of the batter's box and shows plus speed underway. He played all three outfield positions during his pro debut and should fit well in right field with his quickness and arm strength.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: It's appropriate to be skeptical of Fall League statistical performance due to the league's elevation, climate, and level of pitching, which was especially bad in 2021. But Velazquez has other stuff going on that lends greater legitimacy to his 2021 performance, which culminated in a cartoonish .385/.480/.712 line and a Fall League MVP award. Several swing changes (leg kick gone, more conservative toe tap implemented, hands not loading quite as deep, shorter stride) and improved physical conditioning were evident along with the uptick in offensive performance, and Velazquez's batted ball profile shifted in a meaningful way, as his groundball rate dropped from 50% to about 35%. Once a power-goof flier, Velazquez is now a substantively different player. We expect his plate discipline, which had been an issue for him and was much better in 2021, to regress to his career norms and for Velazquez to be a low-OBP hitter, which means he's still relatively volatile. He may have some lean years because of his approach, but there will be others when Velazquez hits 25 bombs while seeing fairly regular duty in right field. He and Alexander Canario are similar players likely competing for short-term reps in Chicago now that they're both on the 40-man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Espinoza was signed by Boston for $1.8 million during the 2014-15 international signing period, a record for a Venezuelan prospect, doubling the amount that Francisco Rodriguez received in 1998. After he’d ascended to become one of the top pitching prospects in baseball, the Padres acquired him for Drew Pomeranz during the 2016 All-Star break. But Espinoza's ‘17 season was over before it began. He opened the year on the disabled list and underwent Tommy John surgery in August. In ‘19, disaster struck twice, and Espinoza needed a second Tommy John surgery that April. Though he may be small in stature, there's nothing diminutive about Espinoza's stuff when healthy. His smooth delivery and lightning-quick arm produce a heater that can touch triple digits, though he typically worked in the 94-95 mph range with late movement. Espinoza's curveball shows plus potential but it lacked consistency at times, while his changeup, thrown with fastball-like arm action and considerable sink, gives him a true chance for three plus pitches. Beyond the stuff, Espinoza demonstrated advanced control and command. With Espinoza's second TJ surgery comes yet another setback in his once promising career. He'll still be 22 when he returns in 2020, but he also hasn't thrown a competitive pitch since '16 and has never pitched above the Class A level. On top of that, the right-hander will forever face questions about his durability. There’s a small measure of hope for the Padres that he might still be built into a starter, given his pitch mix. But it's only to fair to wonder whether Espinoza is ticketed for a bullpen role upon his return – perhaps later in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2018 Espinoza was signed by Boston for $1.8 million during the 2014-15 international signing period, a record for a Venezuelan prospect, doubling the amount that Francisco Rodriguez had received in 1998. His immediate success as a teenager against full-season competition caught the Padres' attention, and they acquired him for Drew Pomeranz during the 2016 All-Star break. Unfortunately for both Espinoza and the Padres, the right-hander's 2017 season was over before it began, as he opened the year on the disabled list with right forearm tightness before undergoing Tommy John surgery in August. Though he may be small in stature, there's nothing diminutive about Espinoza's stuff when healthy. His smooth delivery and lightning-quick arm produce a heater that can touch triple digits, though he typically works in the 94-97 mph range with late movement. Espinoza's curveball shows plus potential but lacked consistency at times in 2016, while his changeup, thrown with fastball-like arm action as well as considerable sink, gives the teenager a true chance for three plus pitches once he matures. Beyond the stuff, Espinoza repeats his mechanics well and demonstrates advanced control and command for a hurler his age. Espinoza had progressed to throwing bullpen sessions in July before it was announced he would require season-ending surgery. He's throwing from 120 feet as part of his rehab program and should soon be back on the mound, although the Padres are unlikely to deploy him during games until fall instructional league as they continue to exercise caution.

mlb_pipeline.text: 2017 The Red Sox landed Espinoza for $1.8 million during the 2014-15 international signing period, a new bonus record for a Venezuelan prospect and double the amount received by previous record holder Francisco Rodriguez in 1998. After reaching full-season ball at age 17, the precocious right-hander continued to impress with his combination of stuff and command last season at Class A Greenville, where he was stationed when the Red Sox dealt him to San Diego for Drew Pomeranz during the 2016 All-Star break. Unfortunately for Espinoza, his 2017 season was over before it began, as he opened the year on the disabled list with right forearm tightness before ultimately needing Tommy John surgery in August. Though he may be small in stature, there's nothing diminutive about Espinoza's stuff when healthy. His smooth delivery and lightning-quick arm produce a heater that can touch triple digits, though he typically works in the 94-97 mph range with late movement. Espinoza's curveball shows plus potential but lacked consistency at times in 2016, while his changeup, thrown with fastball-like arm action as well as considerable sink, gives the teenager a true chance for three plus pitches once he matures. Beyond the stuff, Espinoza repeats his mechanics well and demonstrates advanced control and command for a hurler his age. Espinoza had progressed to throwing bullpen sessions in July before it was announced he would require season-ending surgery. He could potentially return to the mound at the end of next season if all goes as planned with his recovery and rehab, though it wouldn't come as a surprise if San Diego pushed that back to 2019.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text:
Espinoza came to the Cubs as part of the Jake Marisnick trade, leaving a San Diego system in which he barely played despite spending several years in the org. The righty returned to an affiliated mound in 2021 for the first time since the spring of '17, having lost those years to two TJs and the pandemic. Before the trade, Espinoza’s starts had been capped at three innings, but after joining the Cubs, only one of his eight starts (five at High-A, three at Double-A) went fewer than three innings, with him typically lasting until the fourth or fifth. With this increase in his workload came an increase in his overall K-rate, but he also issued walks at a higher frequency than he had pre-trade, indicating that his command is still a primary concern in his profile. 
Before the start of the season, it looked like Espinoza had made some subtle tweaks to his delivery, lengthening his stride, squaring his hips to the plate on release, and throwing from a slightly higher arm slot. Over the course of his first few starts this season, he made another noticeable adjustment, transitioning from a leg kick that saw his heel lift straight off the ground, to a slower one with a straightened leg that curled underneath him. Within his first few starts with the Cubs, however, he'd returned to the simplified leg kick. It’s clear he’s still a work in progress, but the fastball and curveball still play nicely off one another, and the changeup is a bonus, though his command of all three still needs refinement.  
At peak prospectdom, Espinoza had All-Star stuff with command-driven relief risk. What he ends up becoming after nearly five years without an affiliated inning will be impacted by a) workload constraints and b) roster flexibility, or a lack thereof. We think he has a chance to start long-term because he's still just 24 and has the talent to generate swing-and-miss action on a couple of different pitches, though his stuff was down across the board in 2021. The Cubs usage of him after acquisition suggests they think he's a starter, too. He'll likely begin 2022 as injury depth.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Acquired from Boston for Drew Pomeranz in July 2016, Espinoza had only thrown 32 innings of affiliated ball for the Padres until, after a series of injuries and the pandemic, he was finally back to start 2021. I was at what was, to this point, Espinoza's last outing as a top prospect. It was his final spring training start of 2017, when he sat 94-97 and flashed a plus changeup and curveball during the course of a few breezy innings while a handful of scouts and Espinoza's parents watched. Between that outing and his first regular season start for High-A Lake Elsinore, he felt discomfort in his elbow and was shut down. After several weeks of rest and rehab, it was decided that he needed Tommy John surgery, which he had early in August. The timing wasn't great, and Espinoza missed all of 2018 working back from surgery, then re-tore his elbow during the spring of '19 and needed a second TJ; you know the rest. In his lone big league outing this spring, he sat 93-95 with very little feel to pitch, and the TV gun had him up to 97 in his first outing at Fort Wayne. Espinoza's delivery has changed a little bit. His stride is a little longer and slightly more open than before. Just from comparing video from 2016 and now, his hips are a little more square to the plate on release and his arm slot is a bit higher, though that could be the camera angles playing tricks on me. Hopefully this aids in his command and fastball playability (if there's indeed a new slot). At peak prospectdom, Espinoza had All-Star stuff with command-driven relief risk. What he ends up becoming after nearly five years without an affiliated inning will be impacted by a) workload constraints and b) roster flexibility. I think he has a chance to start long-term because he's still just 23 and has the talent to generate swing-and-miss action on a couple different pitches. Plus, I 'm betting on the Padres being granted an extra option year for Espinoza due to injury hardship, which gives him a little longer of a runway to rebuild an innings count and shake off whatever rust has accumulated since he last pitched consistently. I want to value Espinoza in an impact FV tier because of his pedigree and because some the dev context surrounding him is favorable. (Alternate site)

fangraphs.text: Acquired from Boston for Drew Pomeranz in July 2016, Espinoza has only thrown 32 innings of affiliated ball for the Padres since the deal. Espinoza was 94-97 and flashed a plus changeup and curveball during his final spring training start of 2017. Between that outing and his first regular season start for Hi-A Lake Elsinore, he felt discomfort in his elbow and was shut down. After several weeks of rest and rehab, it was decided that he needed Tommy John surgery, which he had early in August. The timing wasn’t great, and Espinoza missed all of 2018 working back from surgery, then re-tore his elbow during the spring of 2019 and needed a second TJ. He has front-end stuff but even if it returns, he’ll have missed three years of reps he desperately needed to polish his below-average control, increasing the likelihood that he's a reliever or backend starter.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Acquired from Boston for Drew Pomeranz in July 2016, Espinoza has only thrown 32 innings of affiliated ball for the Padres since the deal. Espinoza was 94-97 and flashed a plus changeup and curveball during his final spring training start of 2017. Between that outing and his first regular season start for Hi-A Lake Elsinore, he felt discomfort in his elbow and was shut down. After several weeks of rest and rehab, it was decided that he needed Tommy John surgery, which he had early in August. The timing wasn’t great, and Espinoza missed all of 2018 working back from surgery, then re-tore his elbow during the spring of 2019 and needed a second TJ. He has been spotted in a cast on the Peoria backfields. Espinoza has front-end stuff but even if it returns, he’ll have missed three years of reps that he desperately needed to polish his below-average control, increasing the likelihood that he's a reliever or backend starter.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Small has now had two consecutive seasons with lots of walks, and as he's aged into his mid-20s, it's become clear that he's not a great on-mound athlete, which makes it less likely those issues will improve. There are still two real big league weapons here, especially Small's devastating changeup, which has so much action that hitters often miss it even when it's in the zone. The utility of Small's low-90s fastball is bolstered by his deceptive, Kershaw-like arm stroke, the huge extension he gets down the mound, and his crafty array of different deliveries, which disrupt hitters' timing. Because he has two option years left, it's likely Small will continue to be developed as a starter in the short-term, and he and Janson Junk feel like the best taxi squad options on Milwaukee's 40-man. But Small's intermediate and long-term forecast includes fairly significant relief risk because of his track record of walks and his/Milwaukee's inability to find a third pitch (his breaking ball spin rate regressed by about 300 rpm since the last data load we sourced). Even if that's the case, Small still has impact potential if he sees a velocity boost in short outings. That would give him a truly plus fastball to go with the superlative cambio.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Small had a sketchy 2021 from a walk-rate perspective but still managed to amass a 1.98 ERA across 18 starts split between Double- and Triple-A. Despite the unusual spike in walks, Small's underlying in-zone fastball  rate was fine when he was at Triple-A Nashville and with Escogido, at 65% and 69% respectively. His heater lives off of carry and angle, and has gotten lots of in-zone whiffs to this point. It'll be more important for Small to locate more precisely at the top of the zone against big league hitters, because it is only 91-92 mph after all, and he stands the risk of being homer-prone if he's loose with his in-zone fastball command. Small's changeup is devastating, and it has consistent arm-side finish. He also does all sorts of crafty stuff, like varying his timing to the plate in several different ways, that disorients hitters. Some teams' proprietary, stuff-assessing metrics like the movement of Small's slider, but it's a below-average pitch visually, and of the thousand Ethan Small pitches logged by Synergy Sports, only two of them are swinging strikes induced by a breaking ball. He's a high probability no. 4/5 starter likely to seize a rotation spot sometime in 2022.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Small had a sketchy 2021 spring with the big club and walked an uncharacteristically high number of hitters early in the year, but his strike-throwing has been more in line with his historical rate lately. He blows his low-90s fastball (which has big carry) past opposing hitters. Small’s best secondary pitch remains his changeup. There were doubts about him ever finding a competent breaking ball when he was drafted and so far, his slider and curveball remain below average. But that there are now two distinct breakers here instead of just the one he had in college, and that's a meaningful development. Small also does all sorts of crafty stuff -- like varying his timing to the plate in several different ways -- that disorient hitters. He still projects as a No. 4/5 starter with a shot to make the back of the Top 100 as a 50 FV if the command and/or breaking balls tighten up.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Small is a mechanical doppelgänger for Clayton Kershaw and, like late-career Kershaw, he's blowing fastballs with mediocre velocity past opposing hitters because he hides the ball well and creates pure backspin, helping it carry at the top of the strike zone. Small has a bat-missing changeup but needs to find a better breaking ball to really max out as a prospect. He could be a 50 FV, league-average starter if he does, but otherwise is likely to slot toward the back of a rotation.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Small was eligible last year but made a jump this year to justify going in the top 5 rounds. He has average stuff, above average feel, sits around 90 and has 70 deception. One scout mentioned Ryan Yarbrough as a comparable pitcher, though Small is more of an four-seam, up in the zone type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2019 SEC Pitcher of the Year after fanning 176 in 107 innings at Mississippi State, Small got hot at the right time to vault himself into the first round, where Milwaukee took him 28th overall. His first full season was delayed due to the pandemic, but he didn’t skip a beat with a 1.98 ERA and 92 strikeouts in 77 1/3 innings in 2021, mostly at Double-A and Triple-A. His numbers regressed in his return to the Minors’ highest level (4.46 ERA, 1.36 WHIP in 103 innings back at Nashville) in 2022, but he did get a chance to debut with a pair of Major League starts -- neither of which lasted beyond the fourth inning. Small’s fastball typically only plays around 90-92 mph, touching 95, but it plays up because of the angular deception and extension coming from his 6-foot-4 frame. His changeup, hovering right around the 80 mph mark, remains his best pitch by far -- looking like the fastball out of the hand, only to slam on the brakes and dive below swinging bats before it reaches the plate. The Brewers have tried to get Small to find a breaking pitch, but his upper-70s slider just hasn’t become much of a weapon, and he doesn’t use it often as such. The southpaw’s walk rates have sat around 13-14 percent in the upper Minors, hurting his chances to start, and Major Leaguers hammered that point home by walking eight times in his 6 1/3 frames in The Show. In his age-26 season, Small has become a full-time reliever but one who can get outs against batters from either side.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After undergoing Tommy John surgery as a Mississippi State sophomore in 2017, Small was the SEC Pitcher of the Year in 2019 after leading Division I with 176 strikeouts in 107 innings, and that performance led the Brewers to take him 28th overall that June. His 2020 duty was limited to the alternate training site, and he roared into his first true full season in 2021, posting a 1.98 ERA with 92 strikeouts and 42 walks in 77 1/3 innings primarily at Double-A and Triple-A. Small was shut down for part of the summer with a strained tendon in his left hand, but he made up for the lost time with 20 additional frames in the Dominican Winter League. The 6-foot-4 southpaw’s fastball sits just in the low-90s, but it plays up because of good spin, deception and ability to work up in the zone. His changeup looks a lot like the heater out of the hand, only to dive low and armside for a healthy amount of whiffs. Small’s slider has moved ahead of his curve in terms of effectiveness, but neither looks much like an average pitch just yet. He’s thrown the fastball and change as much as 85 percent of the time because of that. Small’s control took a step back in 2021 as he issued free passes to 13.3 percent of the batters he faced. The Brewers chalked that up to facing more advanced hitters for the first time, and it was notable that the skill looked more average in the Dominican this winter. Small needs to throw strikes to keep himself in a starting role. The fastball-changeup could get him to be a No. 4/5, and if either breaking ball truly catches on, a higher rotation slot is possible.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Of the trio of left-handed pitching prospects in the Brewers’ Top 10, Small might not have the highest ceiling but he probably has the highest floor. After undergoing Tommy John surgery that wiped out his entire 2017 at Mississippi State, Small returned as a redshirt sophomore in 2018 and emerged as one of the most accomplished pitchers in college baseball, leading the Bulldogs to a College World Series appearance in '19 and winning Southeastern Conference pitcher of the year honors after finishing first and second among NCAA Division I hurlers with 176 strikeouts and 14.8 K/9, respectively. Hoping to reverse their history with touted college pitchers drafted in the first round (see: Eric Arnett, Taylor Jungmann, Jed Bradley), the Brewers took Small with their 2019 first-round pick and signed him for $1.8 million, below slot value for the No. 28 overall pick ($2.49 million). Early returns were promising. Small posted a 0.86 ERA and 36 strikeouts versus four walks over 21 innings that summer, mostly at low-A. He pitched at the team’s Alternate Training site in 2020 and was back in big league camp in ’21. Small’s fastball does not produce particularly big velocity since surgery (89-92 mph at the start of his pro career), but it plays up thanks to Small’s command, his deceptive and varied delivery with crossfire action, the extension from his 6-foot-3 frame, and his knack for going right after hitters, leading to surprising whiff rates and weak contact in the strike zone. Small sells his above-average changeup in the mid-70s with fastball arm speed, turning it over well to imparting late fading action on the pitch. Small also throws a curveball. None of those offerings stand out a’la Antoine Kelly’s fastball or Aaron Ashby’s slider, but Small’s polish and ability to fill up the strike zone should help him move quickly toward being an effective middle-of-the-rotation starter in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After undergoing Tommy John surgery that wiped out his entire 2017 at Mississippi State, Small returned to the mound as a redshirt sophomore in 2018 and quickly emerged as the staff ace. He was even better while pitching the Bulldogs to a College World Series appearance in '19, garnering Southeastern Conference pitcher of the year honors after finishing first and second among NCAA Division I hurlers with 176 strikeouts and 14.8 K/9, respectively. The Brewers took Small with their first-round pick that June and signed him for $1.8 million, below slot value for the No. 28 overall pick ($2.49 million). A dominant pro debut followed as Small compiled a 0.86 ERA and 36/4 K/BB over 21 innings, the majority of which he logged at Class A Wisconsin. While Small doesn't throw as hard now as he did pre-surgery, his fastball still is plenty effective. His 89-92 mph heater plays above its velocity because Small gets great extension over his front side from a delivery that has natural deception. Those qualities, along with his above-average fastball command, allow him to generate whiffs inside the zone as well as weak contact. Small sells his above-average changeup in the mid-70s with fastball arm speed, turning it over well to imparting late fading action on the pitch. Small’s curveball can have an inconsistent shape and often plays as more of a slurve than a true curveball, but even then, he throws it with good depth and mixes it well to keep hitters off-balance. Small’s control and command have greatly improved since his surgery and he can pound the strike zone with all three pitches. He has a simple delivery that he repeats well and knows how to create angle to the plate using his 6-foot-3 frame and high-three quarters arm slot. His delivery also has some crossfire action, adding to his deception, and he adeptly varies the tempo of his delivery. Small’s lack of a true plus pitch gives him more of a floor than ceiling, but he should be able to move quickly en route to Nos. 4 or 5-starter status in the Majors.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text:
Harris was a switch-hitting, two-way high school prospect who many teams preferred on the mound because of his mechanical grace and ease, his fastball's action and angle, and his curveball's depth. He stopped switch-hitting as a high school senior (he had good feel for contact as a righty hitter but was much less explosive than he was from the left side) and while many teams continued to prefer him on the mound, the Braves were one of the clubs that viewed him as a hitter, so blown away by his BP during a pre-draft workout that they didn't bother to ask him to pitch during it. 
After they picked him, Harris went to the GCL and raked. Not only was his on-paper performance fantastic (.349/.403/.514), but so was his underlying TrackMan data, as both Harris' average exit velo and hard-hit rates were well above the big league average. Exposed to a fair bit of 2021 big league spring training, Harris played well and produced some amazing individual highlights. He hit an oppo homer off of Peter Fairbanks and made a running catch in The Triangle at Fenway South, then went to High-A as a 20-year-old and hit .294/.362/.436 in his first full pro season. There were some yellow flag attributes revealed during that season, mostly that (like Cristian Pache and Drew Waters before him) Harris is apt to chase, which not only impacts his OBP but also his quality of contact. Partly because he tends to expand and partly because of his swing's previous mechanics (more on that momentarily), Harris has tended to hit the ball on the ground too often for his power to really play in games. Combine this with the notion that he may not be a long-term fit in center (though he's a short-term fit and the best center field defender on Atlanta's 40-man) because we're talking about a compact young man with a very low center of gravity and a bottom-heavy frame who is arguably already at physical maturity, and you have the reasons why Harris was just outside our offseason Top 100 rather than firmly entrenched in it. 
Harris was a doubles machine during the first five weeks of 2022 and the Braves decided that he should leapfrog Drew Waters when Adam Duvall's legs seemed overtaxed in center, which was bleeding into his offense. They altered his swing shortly after Harris was called up, in the middle of their late-May series in Arizona. Harris' hands start and are loading much lower now, which may prevent him from cutting down at the baseball quite so much. It's only been about two weeks since he's made the change, and of the balls he's put in play since, roughly 52% have been on the ground, which still isn't great, but the fact that he's continued to hit big league pitching as a 21-year-old who's making a swing change on the fly is incredible. It's too early to draw any real statistical conclusions about what kind of impact this swing change will actually have on Harris' power output. It may enable him to hit more homers and/or exacerbate some of issues Harris has already had with in-zone, letter-high fastballs. This will become a key development should he indeed have to move to a corner outfield spot. It has tended to serve us well to wait for hitters like this to make a swing change and yield results before totally pushing our chips in (recently rounding down on Garrett Mitchell and Jarren Duran feels correct so far, and waiting for Pete Crow-Armstrong to show prolonged results with his new swing does, too), while we've been punished for anticipating change (50'ing Travis Swaggerty from the get-go). Harris was a Pick to Click in anticipation of him making some of these adjustments this year, we just didn't think it would happen at the big league level. The foundation for Harris to be an integral role player is basically already here: at worst, even if he moves to a corner, he's an oft-used fourth outfielder (this is the area where ZiPS has had him projected) in the Joc Pederson mold (there are body type and swing similarities with Joc here), while he still has star-level ceiling if Harris stays in center and this swing change makes a real difference.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Harris was a switch-hitting, two-way high school prospect who many teams preferred on the mound because of his mechanical grace and ease, his fastball's action and angle, and his curveball's depth. He stopped switch-hitting as a high school senior (he had good feel for contact as a righty hitter but was much less explosion than from the left side) and while many teams continued to prefer him on the mound, the Braves were one of the clubs that viewed him as a hitter, so blown away by his BP during a pre-draft workout that they didn't bother to ask him to pitch during it. After they picked him, Harris went to the GCL and raked. Not only was his on-paper performance fantastic (.349/.403/.514) but so was his underlying TrackMan data, as both Harris' average exit velo and hard-hit rates were well above the big league average. Remember that these numbers are still from 2019, our last minor league season, but Harris' average exits were top 10 among teenagers, and only one of those ahead of him (Liover Peguero) clearly has a better chance of staying at an up-the-middle defensive position long-term. Exposed to a fair bit of 2021 big league spring training, Harris has played well and produced some amazing individual highlights. He hit an oppo homer off of Peter Fairbanks and made a running catch in The Triangle at Fenway South. He may not be a long-term fit in center because we're talking about a compact young man with a very low center of gravity and a bottom-heavy frame who is rapidly approaching physical maturity. Conversely, this is a short-levered hitter with seemingly innate feel for making impact contact all over the zone, and while there may be a frame-related cap on his raw power projection, the hit tool might enable Harris to outperform his raw juice in games. The industry knows less about Harris because aside from PG National, he did not participate in the big showcases before his draft year, and his first full season was lost to COVID. There's a slice of the industry that thinks elite players just perform all the time, with any kind of extended failure or statistical hiccup evidence that a player won't be elite. If that's true then Harris is one of a handful of players who has a chance to be elite because he technically hasn't failed yet, in part because he's had fewer opportunities to. He's a fantastic athlete who has looked like a terrific all-around baseball player when he's been able to play, and he's gone from a third rounder to someone who we value on par with a mid-first rounder in the span of two years. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text:
Harris would have been an elite college player with top-five round ability as both a hitter and a pitcher, but most scouts preferred him on the mound. He was used unusually during his senior spring, and some scouts think that he could be 90-93 with everything average to above within 12 months in a pro setting, counting on his quick arm, above average athleticism, and projectable frame, and accounting for his limited showcase presence and coaching in the projection. 
The Braves preferred Harris as a hitter most of the spring. He blew them away in a private pre-draft workout, showing plus raw power, making him a priority on draft day. He also beat expectations in his pro debut, and there's now some thought that he could be a center fielder as he gets more instruction, and may get faster as he gets stronger. There's no bad data to consider due to his lack of exposure before his draft spring, so some would see Harris as a comp round pick in a 2019 redraft. We won't really know his ceiling until he fails some, making him one of the biggest risers from the 2019 class thus far.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Harris would have been an elite college player with top-5 round abilty both as a hitter and pitcher, but most scouts preferred him on the mound. He was used unusually during his senior spring, and some scouts think within 12 months in a pro setting he could be 90-93 with everything average to above. But tis ounds like Harris blew the Braves away in a private workout and he might instead be deployed, full time, as an outfielder in pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Regardless of who’s in charge, the Braves have long prided themselves on drafting players from their own backyard. While most scouts liked Harris, a two-way talent from the Georgia high school ranks, as a left-handed pitcher, the Braves knew Harris wanted to hit and liked him better as a position player, so they took him as an outfielder in the third round of the 2019 Draft. He immediately responded to the faith they had in him by reaching full-season ball during his debut, then had a very successful season in High-A at age 20, including an invite to the Futures Game. Even the Braves have to admit Harris has gotten a lot better a lot faster than expected, though they saw improvement internally during 2020 and some of the gains showed up in the public eye in 2021. An aggressive hitter from the left side of the plate, Harris has shown an innate ability to make a lot of hard contact. There has been concern about his chase rate, but he made strides in that area in 2021, upping his walk rate considerably and seeing that rate decrease, all of which will help him tap into his raw power. The Braves feel Harris is one of the better defensive outfielders in the Minors, on par with Cristian Pache and Drew Waters. He has impressive instincts and a quick first step. While he’s not a pure burner, he gets very good reads and routes and the arm that made him an intriguing pitching prospect is plus from center field. Harris has rapidly become one of the more intriguing outfield prospects in baseball as he reaches the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the 2019 Draft approached, many teams saw Harris, who likely would have played two ways had he gone on to Texas Tech, more as a pitcher than a hitter. But much like they did with Austin Riley, whom most liked on the mound more than at the plate, the Braves were a bit of an outlier in liking Harris’ upside as a position player. So they drafted the Georgia prepster in the third round as an outfielder, then saw him hit well enough to get a large bump up to full-season ball. He was one of the youngest players at Atlanta's alternate site in 2020, then had a successful move to High-A that included a trip to the Futures Game. Outside of the players at the very top of the Braves’ Top 30, there might not be any prospect with as much upside potential as Harris. He has good bat speed and the ability to make hard contact from both sides of the plate. While he’s been more of a line-drive hitter, there is plus raw power to tap into as he improves things like pitch recognition, and it has started showing up a bit at the alternate site and in 2021. An instinctive plus runner, he should be able to steal bases. That speed also plays in the outfield, where he should have no problem manning center field for a long time. He played mostly center and right, where his plus arm looks good, during his pro debut and should keep seeing time in all three spots. The Braves love how well he’s competed so far, thinking it’s a harbinger of things to come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Braves have long loved finding talent in their own backyard and they were at it again when they drafted Harris in the third round of the 2019 Draft. A two-way player who could have gone on to both pitch and hit at Texas Tech, Harris was thought of more as a pitcher by most teams, but the Braves liked his bat and his athleticism. If his pro debut, where he raked in the Gulf Coast League and finished the season in full-season ball, is any indication, Harris and the Braves may have picked the right side of the ball. Harris is a bundle of tools, all a bit raw, though he certainly showed more with the bat during his debut than anticipated. The switch-hitter made consistent loud contact in the GCL, showing strength and bat speed. There’s plenty of raw power to tap into as well as he learns to refine his approach, which was pretty advanced for a two-way high schooler. Working on a gameplan at the plate and recognizing breaking stuff will allow him to tap into that pop more consistently. He has good instincts on the basepaths and the speed to be a threat as well as cover ground in the outfield. While there’s no reason to think Harris can’t play center field right now, he’ll likely see time in all three spots and he could outgrow the position. His plus arm that fired low-90s fastballs off the mound certainly would work in right field. Harris opened a lot of eyes during his pro debut, leaving the Braves excited for what he can do in his first full season of pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays drafted Winckowski in the 15th round out of a Florida high school in 2016 and he didn't reach full-season ball until three years later, when he led the system with a 2.69 ERA. After the 2020 pandemic shutdown, he stood out during instructional league that fall and got traded twice in the first two months of 2021, joining the Mets in a package for Steve Matz and to the Red Sox in a three-team swap that sent Andrew Benintendi to the Royals. The most advanced of the four prospects Boston landed in the Benintendi deal, he made two successful Triple-A starts at the end of last season and got added to the 40-man roster. Winckowski's velocity rose in his first year with the Red Sox, with his four-seam fastball sitting at 93-95 mph and 97 with good induced vertical break. His four-seamer does get straight at times, so he'll mix in some two-seamers in the low 90s with some sink down in the zone. His best offering is a power mid-80s breaking ball that he calls a slider but drops straight down like a curve, and he can morph it into a harder cutter. Winckowski requires a reliable third pitch to remain a starter and has come up with an upper-80s splitter that he uses as a changeup, though it doesn't have much velocity separation from his fastball and hasn't helped him keep left-handers in check. He throws strikes but also will need to improve his command in order to stay in the rotation. If he can't, his breaking ball could make him an effective multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 15th-round pick out of a Florida high school by the Blue Jays in 2016, Winckowski didn't reach full-season ball until his fourth year as a pro, when he was hampered by a finger injury. After impressing in instructional league last fall, he changed teams twice in the first two months of 2021, going to the Mets in a package for Steve Matz and to the Red Sox in a three-team swap that sent Andrew Benintendi to the Royals. The most advanced of the four prospects Boston received along with Franchy Cordero, he has made a successful jump to Double-A this season. Winckowski's velocity has risen a tick in his first year with his new organization and he's dealing with a 93-95 mph four-seam fastball that reaches 97 but can straighten out at times. He'll also mix in some low-90s two-seamers with some sinking action. He backs up his heaters with a power slider in the mid-80s and shows some aptitude for manipulating its shape. To succeed as a big league starter, Winckowski will need to refine a third pitch and improve his fastball command. He didn't have much success with a true changeup in Toronto's system and now employs more of an 89-91 mph splitter that shows some potential. He throws strikes and uses his 6-foot-4 frame and high three-quarters delivery to create downhill plane, but he needs to do a better job of locating his pitches.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Winckowski lived in the Others of Note section on past Blue Jays lists, sitting in the low-90s, wielding a good slider, and looking like a fringe middle reliever at the time. He was traded twice within a couple of weeks, first to the Mets as part of the Steven Matz trade, then to Boston as part of the multi-team Andrew Benintendi deal. Over the course of three years, he has added a better split/change and started throwing harder, and he sustained that velocity over 20 starts in 2021 before wrapping his year up in relief in the Arizona Fall League. Winckowski went from topping out around 94 mph to sitting there, and he sat 95-96 during short outings in Arizona. His best secondary pitch is a mid-80s "slider" that has such vertically-oriented shape that you may consider it a hard curveball. Those pitches don't always have big depth, but when they do, they look like ridiculous 85-86 mph curves and are clearly plus. Winckowski's changeup is also firm, often in the 89-92 mph range. He alters his release in a recognizable way when he throws it, but it still has enough movement to induce weak contact even when hitters aren't totally fooled. We tend to think he'll end up in the bullpen, but he has the stamina to give you length in the middle innings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sedlock took home Big Ten Conference Pitcher of the Year honors as a junior in 2016 after setting a new University of Illinois single-season strikeout record. He became the program's second straight first-round pick that June, following in the footsteps of 2015 No. 6 overall pick Tyler Jay, and signed for $2,097,200. Assigned to Class A Advanced Frederick for his first full season, Sedlock never rebounded after a shaky start, and a pair of stints on the injured list for a strained flexor mass in his right elbow limited his time on the mound. Things didn't go any better for Sedlock in 2018, when tingling in his fingers and shoulder soreness led a Thoracic Outlet Syndrome diagnosis and limited him to only 27 innings. But he was able to avoid surgery, spent the offseason rehabbing the injury and returned fully healthy in 2019 with a strong performance in the Carolina League. In the absence of his once-powerful stuff, Sedlock has really learned how to pitch, relying on his ability to command his two- and four-seam fastballs to both sides of the plate while effectively changing speeds and eye levels with his secondary pitches. His heater ranges from 90-93 mph, but his long arm action on the backside gives it some natural deception that enables him to miss bats and generate weak contact. His mid-80s slider is the better of his two breaking balls, while his changeup has been his most improved pitch in the wake of his injuries. That same long arm action does at times hinder his command, though Sedlock is generally around the zone with his four-pitch mix. Continuing to exercise caution with their former first-round pick, the Orioles will manage Sedlock's workload carefully in 2019, giving him extra rest during certain stretches of the season while also utilizing him as a piggyback reliever. While he's not going to be the type of impact prospect he once looked poised to become, Sedlock does appear to be back on track toward carving out a role as a back-end starter or long reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sedlock became the University of Illinois' second straight first-round pick in 2016, following in the footsteps of Tyler Jay, whom the Twins selected with the No. 6 overall pick in '15. Sedlock earned Big Ten Conference Pitcher of the Year honors in the spring after he set a school strikeout record by fanning 116 in 101 1/3 innings. He signed with the Orioles for $2,097,200 as the No. 27 overall Draft pick and had an impressive pro debut in the New York-Penn League, although he struggled with the move up to the Carolina League this season before landing on the disabled list in June with a right elbow strain. Sedlock's deep arsenal is headlined by his heavy fastball, which sits at 91-93 mph and reaches 96. The pitch has excellent sink and some arm-side action, which helps Sedlock to miss barrels and generate weak, ground-ball contact. His low-80s slider is his best secondary offering and helps him to miss bats, and he also demonstrates feel for both a curveball and changeup that have average potential. A good athlete who repeats his delivery with ease, Sedlock also receives raves from club officials for his makeup and competitiveness on the mound. Though he spent much of his college career in the bullpen, Sedlock has all of the ingredients to become a big league starter, with a strong, projectable frame, four average-or-better pitches and feel for throwing strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hicklen initially planned to play two sports at Alabama-Birmingham, but when the football program was shut down in 2015, Hicklen put his wide receiver dreams aside and focused on being an outfielder. He parlayed that into being a seventh-round pick and had a strong pro debut. When he was held back in extended spring training because of an outfield logjam, he sulked and struggled. To his credit, he put it behind him, hit his way out of Lexington once he was assigned, but then willingly returned there to help win a South Atlantic League title as the Legends' cleanup hitter after Seuly Matias got hurt. Hicklen's power-speed combination makes him a very intriguing prospect. He has plus raw power that is eye-popping when he is on time at the plate, and he'll have to continue to refine his approach in order to make enough contact to tap into that power. His speed is also a game-changer -- he finished third in the organization in stolen bases in just 104 games in 2018 -- and if it all comes together, he has 20-20 potential. His speed also gives him plenty of range to play center field, but he's likely destined for left field because of his below-average arm. The good news is he looks like he might have the offensive game to profile there.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Hicklen was a two-sport athlete of sorts at UAB, where he would have played football had the program been active while he was there. This means that he’s still only a few years into solely focusing on baseball, and those years have of course been interrupted. This is important context that explains Hicklen’s advanced age for his level and makes his performance markedly more noteworthy. Football shares enough athletic overlap with baseball that players who straddle the line between the two sports are often seen as having distinct advantages. But it's important to note that Hicklen was a quarterback in his football days, and while that has undoubtedly had a positive impact on his arm strength and other aspects of his hand-eye coordination, it doesn't inherently speak to his knack for outfield routes in the way it might had he been, say, a wide receiver, and his instincts in the outfield fall short of center-field quality, despite his speed. He spent all of 2021 at Double-A, where he slashed .243/.346/.434. So far this year in Triple-A, he’s improved in all three slash categories, but his strikeouts have ballooned to 38.8%. His swing is very short and linear, and while he generates sizable power anyway, his bat path doesn't really allow it to play. Much of his swing-and-miss this year is coming on fastballs in the middle of the zone, with his flat path passing just below them, though that may simply be a matter of adjusting to the higher level. He’s on track for a fourth outfielder role.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There's no change here: Hicklen needs to perform on paper this year. Even though he's 25, 2019 was only his second full year focusing solely on baseball, as he'd been a two-sport athlete of sorts at UAB, where he would have played football had the program been active while he was there. His statistical performance, despite his age, becomes much more impressive in this context. Hicklen has hit .280/.370/.470 as a pro. All of that has been in A-ball, save for the 2019 Fall League, during which he struggled. His swing is very short and linear and he generates sizable power anyway, but his bat path doesn't really allow it to play. Barring a very late jump in skills and instincts, he's a bench outfielder sort. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text:
Hicklen went to UAB planning to play both football and baseball, but the school's football program was shut down when he got to campus, and he was drafted and signed by Kansas City before it was reborn. He practiced with the team, but never suited up for a football game. 
2018 was his first year of full-time baseball and he hit .307/.378/.552 with 17 homers and 29 steals, albeit as a 22-year-old at Low-A. His strength/raw power and straight-line speed are what you'd probably expect from a college wide receiver, but Hicklen's compact, in-game swing prioritizes contact. He's predictably raw and somewhat stiff rather than graceful and coordinated but he has physical ability, he plays really hard, and there's a chance some of the skill-based parts of the game come to him in his mid-20s.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Indians' top signing in the 2014 international class, Gonzalez landed a $300,000 bonus out of the Dominican Republic. He excelled in his U.S. debut two years later, winning Arizona League MVP honors and topping the Rookie circuit in homers (eight) and slugging (.566). He since has continued to produce while advancing one level per year and has posted solid numbers in high Class A in 2019. Though he's extremely aggressive and rarely walks, Gonzalez consistently has hit for average in the lower levels of the Minors. He doesn't swing and miss excessively and he uses the entire field, but it remains to be seen if approach will work against more advanced pitchers. A right-handed hitter, he has plus raw power to all fields yet won't fully tap into it until he gets more selective hunting pitches he can punish. Gonzalez fits the right-field profile with his power potential and plus arm. He moves well for his size, projecting as an average defender even if he loses a half-step as he matures physically. He presently has average speed and isn't much of a factor on the bases.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $300,000 in 2014, Gonzalez struggled in his first taste of pro ball the following year, hitting just .203 over 70 games in the Dominican Summer League. He did anything but struggle in his 2016 U.S. debut, when he paced the Rookie-level Arizona League in both home runs (eight) and slugging percentage (.556) en route to the circuit's MVP Award. Advancing to Class A Short Season Mahoning Valley in 2017, Gonzalez continued to flash his offensive ceiling as a New York-Penn League midseason All-Star. Physically strong and mature for his age, Gonzalez possesses plus raw power to all fields from the right side of the plate and already understands how to get to it. With that big power comes a longer swing as well as swing-and-miss issues that are exacerbated by an aggressive approach and problems identifying spin. Those weaknesses have led some to worry about whether he will make enough contact to be successful at higher levels. Defensively, Gonzalez has prototypical right-field tools as a good athlete with modest speed and a cannon arm. With robust raw power as his calling card but concerns about his bat, Gonzalez is the definition of a high-risk prospect at this stage in his career. The potential is there, but he'll need to make many adjustments along the way.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30

With robust raw power but concerns about his bat, Gonzalez is the definition of a high-risk prospect at this stage in his career. The potential is there, but he'll need to make many adjustments along the way.

fangraphs.label: 2022graduates
fangraphs.text: Gonzalez maintained fairly even offensive performance as a prospect despite having one of the least-discerning approaches in all of pro baseball. He has huge raw power, a plus arm, and crude-looking bat control that makes has made his offensive skillset work despite his desire to swing at everything. It's almost unprecedented for a hitter this aggressive to sustain big league success but Gonzalez did so in the minors. His toolset is a traditional right field fit if it turns out his issues with chase aren't fatal to his offensive ability.

fangraphs.text: Injuries (including a TJ) limited De Los Santos to just 27 innings over a three-year span; 2019 was his first healthy, full season since '15. In 2019 he was back throwing hard and showing a typical middle relief fastball/slider combination. He's less procedurally advanced than the typical 23-year-old (as evidenced by his back-to-back balks in LIDOM this winter), which is perhaps unsurprising given his lack of reps. I have him in as an up/down reliever. (Fall Instructional League, LIDOM)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since signing with the Cardinals for $200,000 out of Panama in July 2016, Herrera has moved rather quickly through the St. Louis system with typically solid numbers across the board. He put himself on the cusp of the Majors in 2021 with a career-high 17 homers in 98 games with Double-A Springfield. He managed to make his Major League debut a year later, lasting 11 games with the big club. However, his offense and defense seemed to step back at Triple-A Memphis in 2022 as he posted a .268/.374/.396 slash line with six homers and just a 17.7 percent caught-stealing rate, sixth-lowest among the 17 International League backstops with at least 60 steal attempts faced. Herrera’s best offensive asset remains his discerning eye at the plate and his ability to protect the strike zone, as he proved with a 13.7 percent walk rate and 18.7 percent K rate at Triple-A. It’s when he makes contact that he’s run into trouble over the past year. Though he possesses at least average raw power, the right-handed slugger has struggled to lift the ball on contact, leading to grounders on more than half of his batted balls in 2022. The Cardinals have worked with Herrera on improving his blocking and framing since he signed, but his defense appears to have settled around fringy and he was a below-average framer during his small sample in the bigs. It was certainly telling that St. Louis, facing Yadier Molina’s retirement, chose to sign Willson Contreras to a five-year deal instead of handing the reins over to Herrera. But the backstop is still just entering his age-23 season and has some development time ahead of him to become a backup to Contreras or a lower-ceiling starter elsewhere.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Herrera has been pushed so aggressively since signing with the Cardinals for $200,000 out of Panama in July 2016 that it’s important to remember he’ll still only be 22 on 2022 Minor League Opening Day. He hit at least .330 in each of his first two seasons, produced a solid .284/.374/.405 over 106 games at two A-ball levels in 2019 and earned a 40-man spot in November 2020 after standing out at the alternate training site. The right-handed slugger’s .231 average at Double-A Springfield last season may seem like a steep drop, but it was driven in part by a .261 BABIP that was considerably lower than Herrera’s career numbers. He still took plenty of walks (13.7 percent BB rate) and showed improved ability to tap into above-average raw power with a career-best 17 homers in 98 games. In all, he was a league-average bat in a circuit where he was three years younger than the norm. Herrera can typically control the zone well -- no surprise for a catcher with a good eye -- and was starting to barrel balls better as 2021 wore on. He is a candidate to bat in the upper-.200s at the top level, should that trajectory continue. St. Louis officials have long been enthused by Herrera’s defensive growth and the work he’s put in on that side. His blocking has gotten better in the last two years, but there is still room to improve in that area. Once put on a throwing program by the Cardinals, Herrera now projects to have an above-average arm behind the plate. The Cardinals haven’t needed a Yadier Molina replacement yet, but they will after 2022. With solid tools across the board, Herrera could be the guy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cardinals have challenged Herrera at every stage in his career after signing the Panama native for $200,000 at the outset of the 2016-17 international period. He received a brief taste of the Double-A level in 2018 during his impressive U.S. debut, then advanced to full-season ball the next year to produce a .284/.374/.405 line between Class A Peoria -- where, at age 18, he was the Midwest League’s third-youngest player on Opening Day -- and Class A Advanced Palm Beach. Herrera performed well in that year’s Arizona Fall League, once again standing out as a younger player against the advanced competition, and he continued to improve at the Cardinals’ alternate training site in 2020 and earned a spot on the 40-man roster. The jump to Double-A proved troublesome initially in 2021, though once he settled in, he began to perform better in the second half. Herrera makes hard contact with a quick, compact right-handed swing. He knows how to use his hands to stay inside the ball and find the barrel, showing above-average raw power to his pull side during batting practice. He began to tap into that power more in the second half of 2021. Herrera has long demonstrated an advanced approach, recognizing spin well and controlling the zone better than most his age, with little swing and miss. Herrera’s most significant gains as a pro have come defensively. His blocking improved in 2020, thanks in part to the time he spent around Yadier Molina at the alternate training site, and his arm strength has continued to improve after the Cardinals put him on a throwing program early in his career. Herrera also earns high marks from club officials for his work ethic and dedication to improving on and off the field. A bilingual catcher, he began learning English early in his pro career and takes pride in communicating with his teammates and coaches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Herrera established himself as a promising hitter as an amateur during international events before signing with St. Louis for $200,000 at the outset of the 2016-17 July 2 period. The Panama native has added to that reputation in the pro ranks, hitting well at every stage in his career despite being a younger player at every stop. After batting .335 during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League and .348 in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League in 2018, Herrera advanced to full-season ball last season and produced a .284/.374/.405 line between Class A Peoria – where, at age 18, he was the Midwest League’s third-youngest player on Opening Day – and Class A Advanced Palm Beach. The Cardinals challenged Herrera with an Arizona Fall League assignment after the season, and he responded by batting .324 with more walks than strikeouts in 10 games. An advanced hitter for his age, Herrera combines bat speed with a compact swing to impact the ball consistently from the right side of the plate. He identifies pitches well, recognizing spin better than most teenagers, takes his share of walks and does not swing and miss all that often (7.4 percent in 2019). Herrera shows above-average raw power to his pull side during batting practice that should start to appear in games as he gets older and stronger. Scouts are increasingly bullish about Herrera’s power potential, with some seeing him as a future 15-plus homer threat who also hits for average and gets on base at a high clip. While Herrera’s defense is behind his bat, club officials are quick to note the strides he has made behind the plate in the past year, especially with regards to his blocking. His arm strength has ticked up to above average thanks to an offseason throwing program, and the hope is that it will allow him to better mitigate the running game at higher levels. Herrera’s receiving and catch-and-throw skills will require more time to develop, but he has the athleticism, aptitude and work ethic required to make the necessary gains.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 When Herrera signed with St. Louis for $200,000 out of Panama early in the 2016-17 international period, he had already established himself as an advanced hitter with strong performances in international events. He furthered that reputation during his professional debut by hitting .335 en route to honors as a Dominican Summer League All-Star, then raked at a .348 clip in 2018 while making his United States debut in the Gulf Coast League. And when Double-A Springfield needed a fill-in catcher at the end of the Minor League season, it was 18-year-old Herrera who got the call, and he held his own in his lone Texas League start. Herrera is an advanced hitter for his age, with a short, efficient swing and mature approach that has led evaluators to peg him as an average hitter. His swing is more conducive for driving balls into the gaps, though he could develop fringy over-the-fence pop as he adds strength and learns to leverage his swing a bit. He identifies pitches well, recognizing spin better than most teenagers, and generally does a good job controlling the strike zone. As with many teenage catchers, Herrera's bat is currently ahead of his defense. His blocking and receiving both will require some work, as will his management of the running game, but club officials believe Herrera can develop into an average defender thanks to his combination of tools, work ethic and makeup.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text:
Herrera was once considered the catcher of the future within the Cards system. He looked the part in the early days of his development, emerging rapidly after his signing in 2016. He's always performed at or above a league average level with the bat and is an especially gifted contact hitter for a catcher, but Herrera's defense has plateaued and remains below average across the board. The offseason signing of Willson Contreras was an indication not only that was Herrera no longer seen as surefire successor to Yadier Molina, but also that the Cardinals thought Contreras, who isn't a good defender, was fine enough to be a primary backstop while Herrera was not. When Contreras struggled early in 2023, the team did not turn to Herrera as a bandaid, even as he was hitting down in Memphis, and the Cardinals are carrying one more catcher on their 40-man roster (four) than is typical. 
A scouting rule of thumb is to give catchers who have any kind of offensive ability as much developmental runway as possible. The industry inventory behind the plate isn't exactly flush with good hitters, and lots of bat-first catchers take until they're deep into their 20s to polish their gloves enough to truly ascend to a primary role. Herrera's 2022 in-zone contact rates were incredible (89%) and he's historically been an above-average contact hitter with plus feel for the strike zone. An inside out swing means most of Herrera's fly ball contact goes to the opposite field, where he does mostly doubles damage. It's too much offense to consider Herrera merely a backup catcher prospect, but not enough for him to profile at another position if he doesn't improve back there. He's running out of option years and has to be traded or elevated to a big league role within the next year. He might initially be a part-time or backup catcher, but projects to have some seasons as an above-average offensive performer at the position later during his pre-free agency years.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text:
Herrera's bat-to-ball track record would be exciting regardless of what position he played, but it's rare for a catcher to be as deft with the barrel as he is, and it's the chief reason that he projects as St. Louis' heir apparent to Yadier Molina. While Herrera's hitting posture can get a little too upright and cause him to pull off of sliders away from him, including ones that finish in the zone, he is adept at making contact basically everywhere else, especially at the top of the strike zone. Herrera is also capable of doing all-fields damage when he gets extended on pitches on the outer third, and the hit/power combination here could make him one of the top 10 (or so) hitting catchers in the entire league. He also has uncommon athleticism for a catcher and generates home-to-first times close to 4.3 seconds at his fastest. 
Indeed, Herrera would just be a 55 FV prospect were he a better defender. Even as he's improved his receiving (average) and framing (below-average, at least to my eye, especially at the bottom of the zone), they're still not great, and his ball-blocking is even further behind and at times is a real problem. Things aren't so bad back there that Herrera will have to move to first base, but even though he's kissed the big leagues, he does need polish. He's only 22 and is now Molina's squire, so those issues should improve at least a little bit. Very likely to be a good everyday player, the strides Herrera can make on defense will determine just how good.

fangraphs.text: There's no change here as Herrera was only at the alt site: When I began sourcing data on the Cardinals system in 2019, I wasn't aware of a max exit velocity for a teenager in excess of 109 mph (Kristian Robinson, Marco Luciano, Luis Toribio) -- until I learned of Herrera's. It was surprising considering that Herrera is physically quite modest, and looked sluggish at times during that year's Fall League, but by that point he had played in three times as many games as he had the year before, and was likely exhausted. Regular season Herrera was a little leaner, twitchy, and athletic, and was an advanced defender with a mature approach at the plate. He also hit .286/.381/.423 as a 19-year-old catcher in the Midwest League. This guy checks all the proverbial boxes and looks like a well-rounded everyday catching prospect. (Alternate site)
