mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A transfer from Everett (Wash.) Community College to the College of Idaho, O’Brien became the first player from that NAIA school to be taken in the top 10 rounds when the Rays took him as a money-saving senior sign for $7,500 in the eighth round of the 2017 Draft. He looked like more than a bargain pickup when he pitched his way across two levels of A ball in 2018, then up to Double-A the following year, though the 2019 season ended early with elbow soreness. He hadn’t been pitching in 2020 when he was sent to the Reds for Cody Reed in late August. O’Brien was put on the Reds’ 40-man roster following the 2020 season because of his athleticism and the potential of his stuff, even if he wasn’t quite as electric at Reds instructs following the trade. O’Brien had added strength to his 6-foot-4 frame and was cranking his fastball up to 98 mph at times, sitting more in the 92-95 mph range in the past, though his fastball was more average last fall. Scouts differ on his breaking stuff, some preferring the shorter slider with bite, others preferring what they saw as a hard curve. The changeup is a work in progress, though he has been able to work in some usable ones at times. The slender right-hander has had fringy control and command, though the Reds liked his strike-throwing ability at instructs and think there’s still projection while loving his athleticism and makeup. There’s upside despite the fact he’s 26 and the Reds will let him keep working on his repertoire as a starter. They know that the fastball-breaking ball combination might play up out of the 'pen and other evaluators think that’s the best spot for him given his slender frame and effort in his delivery.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The grandson of Johnny O'Brien, who played in parts of six Major League seasons in the '50s, Riley O'Brien spent two years at Everett (Wash.) CC before transferring to NAIA College of Idaho and becoming the school’s highest-drafted player in 2017, when the Rays took him in the eighth round. The athleticism, size and raw potential that had endeared O’Brien to Rays amateur scouts began to show in his first full season, with the right-hander garnering All-Star honors in the Midwest League before finishing the season at Class A Advanced Charlotte. The Stone Crabs’ Opening Day starter in 2019, he dominated out of the gate to earn an early May promotion to Double-A Montgomery and continued to pitch well in the Southern League before a bout of elbow soreness prompted the Rays to shut him down in July. In August 2020, he was dealt to the Reds for Cody Reed. A plus athlete with a loose arm and projectable 6-foot-4 frame, O’Brien’s velocity has steadily improved as he’s added strength and gained experienced on the mound. After pitching with an upper-80s/low-90s fastball at the outset of his career, O'Brien comfortably sat 92-95 mph and bumped 97 during his breakout 2019 campaign. He's long shown feel for spinning the ball and can flash above-average to plus with both of his breaking balls. Most scouts like his slider, a swing-and-miss out-pitch with nasty bite, more than his curve, though the latter certainly has its moments. O’Brien also has feel for throwing a changeup that has average potential. While his control and command are both below average right now, O’Brien’s athletic delivery and clean arm action should allow him to make the necessary gains. He could have a mid-rotation future if can refine his secondary pitches and learn to throw more strikes. If that doesn’t work out, O’Brien could be a late-inning force on the strength of his fastball-breaking ball combo.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sanmartin’s pro career began way back in 2015, when the Colombian lefty signed with the Rangers for just $10,000 at the start of the 2015-16 international signing period. He’s been since traded twice, first to the Yankees in November 2017 and then to the Reds in January 2019 when Cincinnati also acquired Sonny Gray from New York. That 2019 season was the first time Sanmartin made it out of A ball and he had even more success in 2021, pitching his way from Double- to Triple-A before being called up to the big leagues for the first time in September. Sanmartin definitely falls under the “whole is greater than the sum of his parts” category. His fastball is fringy, averaging around 89 mph, topping out at 92 mph, though it plays up a bit because of deception and his ability to command the pitch very well. His best offering is his above-average changeup, giving him an excellent weapon against right-handed hitters, an offspeed pitch that led to a 44-percent whiff rate in Triple-A and the big leagues in 2021 and also elicited a lot of groundball outs. His 80-mph slider is average, but effective. All of Sanmartin’s stuff plays up because of his ability to command all three offerings in the strike zone and his strong feel for pitching. He has a limited ceiling because of the nature of his stuff, but he also has the chance to fill a number of roles, from No. 5 starter to lefty specialist and has impressed Reds staff with his willingness to take the ball at any time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sanmartin came to the Reds from the Yankees organization, along with pitcher Sonny Gray, during a Jan. 21, 2019 three-team trade. Before the Yankees, Sanmartin was with the Rangers, who had signed him for just $10,000 back at the start of the 2015-16 international signing period and had traded him to the Yankees after the 2017 season. Although he reached Double-A for the first time with the Yankees, Sanmartin opened 2019 at high-A Daytona and worked his way back to Double-A Chattanooga by midseason. He is a crafty left-hander with feel for his pitches and he has life on his fastball. He still needs to learn how to elevate that pitch a little better, however. He can’t just rely on his stuff, which what was doing at the lower levels. He also lacks a big out pitch. While he’s been a starter so far, Sanmartin projects more as a long reliever on the front end of a bullpen. He gets ground balls and has a good changeup. He possesses solid control but fringy command. Everything in his repertoire is borderline-average.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Sanmartin has been traded a couple of times, from Texas to New York and then to Cincinnati as part of the trade for Sonny Gray. He's a low-slot pitchability lefty who works east/west with command of his fastball. His changeup and slider are about average, with the slider doing well against lefties because of Sanmartin's arm slot. He's well-built and athletic, and the lateral action on his stuff helps him generate a lot of groundballs (55% in 2021), but we think his pure stuff limits him to a spot-starter type of role. With this level of athleticism and command, he'll probably pitch in the upper levels and the majors for a very long time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Crouse showed off first-round stuff and a super high-energy personality during his California high school days, and was taken by the Rangers in the second round of the 2017 Draft. Since then, he’s shown glimpses of that stuff while being shelved several times with different injuries with the Rangers and the Phillies, who acquired Crouse at the 2021 Trade Deadline. He made his big league debut that summer and got more work in during an Arizona Fall League stint but made just five Triple-A appearances in 2022 because of biceps tendinitis. It's hard to know exactly what Crouse can be after missing so much time, but when he has been healthy, he still shows four solid offerings. The velocity on his fastball has dipped because of the injuries, dropping down to an average of around 91 mph in his brief active time in 2022. His low-80s slider also lost some crispness, though it still missed bats and he can manipulate it when he’s feeling right. He has a fading changeup and more of a slower, truer curve as well. Crouse’s command and control has ebbed and flowed over his years in the Minors, though it’s more the injury history -- bone chips in his elbow with the Rangers, shoulder issues, and most recently, the biceps injury -- that point to a future as a reliever. He’ll likely work as a multi-inning guy in 2023 to build back up as the Phillies hope his stuff will tick back up with continued health and shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An electric, if a bit mercurial high school product from California, Crouse and his first-round stuff went in the second round of the 2017 Draft to the Rangers. He’s shown the ability to dominate Minor League hitters, but only in limited innings as bone spurs shelved him for parts of the 2019 season. He had them removed that offseason, sat out 2020, but came out throwing well in Double-A in 2021 and was part of the group sent to Philadelphia in return for Spencer Howard. Crouse made his big league debut at the end of the season and got some extra work in the Arizona Fall League, but missed nearly all of the 2022 season due to biceps tendinitis. Even though Crouse’s stuff backed up a little bit as the 2021 season wore on, he still has some big stuff that can get Major League hitters out. His velocity dipped a bit, but he was still averaging around 93 mph and touching 96 with riding life. His second plus pitch is his best one, a nasty mid-80s slider that can be a wipeout pitch. He started to throw it more again after his elbow was cleaned out. He’ll change the velocity on it, so it can have cutter-like action, or he can make it a bigger breaking ball. His fading changeup improved when he focused on that instead of his slider while battling the elbow issues and he can still fold in an average true curve. Ever since high school, because of Crouse’s high energy on the mound and effort in his delivery, there has been some reliever risk, with the injuries only adding to that potential move. He has thrown strikes for the most part and does have four legitimate pitches, so he does have the ingredients to start if he can stay healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Crouse had the stuff and performance track record to go in the first round of the 2017 Draft, but he also had a lot of moving parts and effort in his delivery and was emotional on the mound, so the Rangers were able to land him in the second. He worked just 162 1/3 innings in his first three seasons after signing him for $1.45 million, in part because he was limited by bone spurs in his elbow in 2019. He had them removed that October and then sat out alternate camp and instructional league in 2020 for undisclosed personal reasons that the club says aren't a concern. He was back and throwing well, handling a push up to Double-A in 2021, when he was sent to the Phillies in a Trade Deadline deal that also brought Kyle Gibson and Ian Kennedy to Philadelphia. It looks as if Crouse has regained the electric stuff he had when he was last fully healthy in 2018. His fastball sits at 92-97 and reaches 99 with riding life. His slider can be a wipeout pitch with mid-80s velocity and two-plane break, though it was less sharp and he used it less frequently in 2019 because it bothered his elbow. Relying less on his slider forced Crouse to spend more time on his changeup, which has the potential to become a solid offering with fade and sink, and he can also manipulate his breaking ball into more of a true curve to use as a fourth pitch. Though he still has a lot going on in his delivery, including some head whack, he keeps everything in sync and averaged just 2.0 walks per nine innings in 2019. He's entertaining to watch because he'll talk to himself, groom the mound a la Mark Fidrych and employ a Johnny Cueto shimmy, and some scouts think his energy would be best directed in a late-inning relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Crouse's stuff and track record of performance against quality competition could have landed him in the first round of the 2017 Draft as a California high schooler, but his volatile delivery and mound demeanor dropped him to the Rangers with the 66th pick. The Rangers have handled him carefully since signing him for $1.45 million and planned on turning him loose in Class A last year, only to have bone spurs in his elbow intervene. They kept him on an 80-90 pitch limit throughout the season, then shut him down in last August before he had surgery in October. When fully healthy, Crouse has a pair of well above-average pitches in his fastball and slider. His heater sits at 92-97 mph and peaks at 99 with riding life that keeps it off barrels, while his slider combines mid-80s velocity with two-plane break. He also can manipulate his breaking ball into more of a true curveball to give batters something else to think about. The bone spurs irritated Crouse when he threw his slider last year, so he used it less and spent more time working on his changeup, which improved and showed flashes of becoming a solid pitch with fade and sink. Though there still are a lot of moving parts and some head whack in his delivery, he repeats his mechanics and keeps them in sync, resulting in a career-best walk rate (2.0 per nine innings) in 2019. More animated than most pitchers, he'll talk to himself, groom the mound like Mark Fidrych and throw in a Johnny Cueto shimmy at times.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Few pitchers in the 2017 high school class could match Crouse's combination of stuff and track record of performance against top competition, but his volatile delivery and mound antics created enough concern that he lasted 66 picks in the Draft. Since the Rangers gladly pounced on him in the second round and signed him for an over-slot $1.45 million, he has been their best pitching prospect. He has pitched through bone spurs while making the jump to full-season ball in 2019 and plans to have surgery in the offseason. A true power pitcher, Crouse blows away hitters with a fastball that parks in the mid-90s and repeatedly hits 99 mph with riding life that makes it even more difficult to barrel. He backs it up with a wipeout slider with mid-80s velocity and two-plane depth, and he shows the aptitude to manipulate it into a true curveball to give batters a different look. His changeup can be too firm at times but shows flashes of becoming an average third offering with some fade. Crouse has a lot going on in his violent delivery, which finishes with some disconcerting head whack, yet he repeats it and keeps it in sync enough to find the strike zone on a regular basis. He's more animated than most pitchers, and he'll throw in a Johnny Cueto shimmy or groom the mound like Mark Fidrych at times. Though some scouts wonder if he can hold up as a starter, the Rangers are determined to develop him as one and believe he can become their ace of the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Crouse won the gold-medal game at the 18-and-under Pan American Championships with 11 strikeouts in seven one-hit innings in October 2016, then outdueled future Reds third-rounder Jacob Heatherly while showcasing the hottest fastball at the National High School Invitational last March. His stuff and his history of excelling against top competition led the Rangers to select him in the second round and sign him for an over-slot $1,450,000. He was nearly unhittable in his pro debut, recording a 41 percent strikeout rate and .109 opponent average in the Rookie-level Arizona League. Crouse has the potential for two well above-average pitches, starting with a mid-90s fastball with riding life that repeatedly topped out at 99 mph during his debut. He also flashes a wipeout slider, showing some feel to manipulate its speed and shape and turning it into a hard curveball at times. His fading changeup is a work in progress that can become an average third pitch with more velocity separation from his fastball. Though there's a lot of effort and moving parts in his delivery, Crouse repeats it well and everything comes together well enough for him to throw strikes. It may be difficult for him to have better than average command, but the Rangers are committed to developing him as a starter. He's extremely animated on the mound and has been known to groom the dirt a la Mark Fidrych or throw a shimmy into his mechanics like Johnny Cueto.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Crouse can still get by on funk and deception for an inning at a time. He has to mix in his slider and changeup liberally because his fastball has settled into the low-90s, but his slider and changeup quality and command are both sufficient for him to do so. He's an up/down reliever right now. Perhaps the more important, marco-level takeaway here is that sometimes this is where things end up for hard-throwing high schoolers, perhaps only for reasons of mechanical sustainability.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Part of the Kyle Gibson/Ian Kennedy/Spencer Howard trade, Crouse made his major league debut for the Phillies in their last home game of 2021 despite having previously made only one start above Double-A. His under-seasoning was perhaps most apparent in his command, as while his three offerings each displayed decent movement, he had difficulty locating any of them. He allowed two home runs - including one on the very first pitch of his big league career - and issued seven walks against just two strikeouts in his seven innings over two starts. Crouse's colorful, semi-eccentric, heavily-inked (imagine if Mark Fidrych was a Soundcloud rapper) mound presence can range from jovial to ultra-competitive, and everything in between, and he also has a disorienting release. Historically, Crouse has sprinkled shimmies throughout his windup, at times reminiscent of Johnny Cueto, Daisuke Matsuzaka, and quite frankly, Tyra Banks. He only pitched from the stretch in the big leagues and during Fall League looks, so the timing upset has been harder to come by and we're not sure it's there anymore. While the Phillies rotation situation makes it likely that Crouse will remain a starter for now, we think major league batters will be better at adapting to his delivery after they've seen him, and a multi-inning relief role may be a better fit for funk optimization purposes. He's also transitioned away from a traditional curveball to a firmer slider/cutter hybrid. That pitch rotates a few hundred rpm slower than his curveball but seemed to give hitters fits in the Fall League.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: The mercurial Crouse pitched through a bone spur in 2019 and still sat 92-95, about a tick below where he sat for me coming off biceps tendinitis earlier that spring, and he's been in the 92-97 range since then. It's the recent injury history paired with the industry's mechanical xenophobia that fuels the relief projection here, not Crouse's command or repertoire depth. His changeup now comfortably projects to average, while his fastball/breaking ball combination has been excellent since he was a high school underclassman. And even amid his injuries, Crouse has attacked hitters in games. On occasion, he incorporates all kinds of crafty veteran wrinkles into his delivery's cadence. An extra shoulder wiggle, a Travoltaian gyration of the hips, the occasional quick-pitch -- all sorts of things designed to take hitters by surprise. Lefties get a good look at his fastball because of Crouse's low slot, and the velo he would theoretically gain out of the bullpen (he was up to 102 out of the bullpen in a 2017 All-Star Game) would give him the margin for error he needs to not be crushed by them. I think he's a late-inning bullpen arm, for which his personality seems well-suited.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text:
Slowed by biceps tendinitis in the spring, Crouse's stuff was fine when he returned. He was touching 99 while throwing live BP, and sitting 92-96 during his starts in extended spring training. His 13-start Northwest/Sally League tour, during which he walked just 19 in 54 innings, was the first step toward quelling concerns about his viability as a starter, though we're still somewhat apprehensive here at FanGraphs. 
Crouse's repertoire depth is not the issue. Based on his pitch usage during instructional league, his changeup seemed to be a developmental priority, and he has indeed made progress with it. It now comfortably projects to average, while Crouse's fastball/breaking ball combination has been excellent since he was a high school underclassman. He incorporates all kinds of crafty veteran wrinkles into his delivery's cadence on occassion. An extra shoulder wiggle, a Travoltaian gyration of the hips, the occasional quick-pitch -- all sorts of things designed to take hitters by surprise. Scouts often sentence quirky, visibly fiery and emotional hurlers to late-inning duty, and we do think Crouse would thrive in such a role, but view these traits as positives. Crouse has a unique build and delivery, and is a very short strider whose 5-foot-4 extension sucks some of the perceived velo out of his fastball. This, plus the lower slot, might make him unusually vulnerable to lefties despite his velocity. This, his brief injury history, and still fringy command all contribute to a bundle of relief risk in our opinion.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: An athletic drop-and-drive style reliever with a tempestuous on-mound presence, Moreta makes heavy use of an upshot mid-90s fastball. It sat 95 mph and touched 99 in 2021 as he traversed Double- and Triple-A. His slider and changeup are both closer to average, and the absence of a plus secondary puts Morets in more of an up/down relief bucket than an integral role. He debuted late in 2021 and will likely spend most of this season working the middle innings for the rebuilding Reds.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ciuffo was the second catcher to be selected in the 2013 Draft, going to the Rays with the No. 21 overall pick. He stood out most for his offensive potential as an amateur, but as is the case with so many prep catchers, his bat has lagged behind his defense in the professional ranks. A hand injury sustained in June 2016 affected Ciuffo's development on both sides of the ball, but he returned fully healthy in '17 to enjoy his best all-around season, all of which he spent in Double-A. Left off the Rays' 40-man roster after the season, Ciuffo received a 50-game suspension in February after his second positive test for a drug of abuse. The Rays' defensive player of the year in back-to-back years, Ciuffo has made considerable strides in improving his blocking and receiving since signing. His plus arm strength and advanced catch-and-throw skills help him control the running game, a notion supported by his career caught-stealing rate of 46 percent in 263 games behind the plate. Meanwhile, club officials are quick to praise Ciuffo's leadership qualities and feel for handling a staff, even in the wake of his suspension. Ciuffo is less advanced from the left side of the plate, where he employs an up-the-middle approach and produces good bat speed. He did a better job controlling the strike zone in 2017 and had his walk rate jump to a full-season best 10.1 percent as a result. Ciuffo also began to tap into some of his raw power, as his seven home runs surpassed his career total (five) from his previous 253 games spanning four seasons. Even if Ciuffo's bat is merely average, he still stands to carve out a role as at least a big league backup based on his defensive merits.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ciuffo was the second catcher to be selected in the 2013 Draft, going to the Rays with the No. 21 overall pick. He stood out most for his offensive potential as an amateur, but his bat has come along slowly as a professional and now lags behind his defense. He began the 2016 season at Class A Advanced Charlotte and was in the midst of a breakout offensive campaign when a hand injury sent him to the disabled list in early June. He still made plenty of progress, especially behind the plate, and then made up for lost time in the Arizona Fall League before spending all of 2017 in Double-A. Left off the Rays' 40-man roster after the season, Ciuffo received a 50-game suspension in February after his second positive test for a drug of abuse. Ciuffo has made considerable strides in improving his blocking and receiving since signing. His plus arm strength and sound catch-and-throw skills help him control the running game, and he's thrown out exactly 50 percent of attempted basestealers in his career after posting a career-best 59-percent clip at Charlotte in 2016. Meanwhile, club officials are quick to praise Ciuffo's leadership qualities and feel for handling a staff. Ciuffo is less advanced from the left side of the plate, where he employs an up-the-middle approach and produces good bat speed, but needs to do a better job controlling the strike zone. Even if Ciuffo's bat fails to develop as hoped, the defense alone could make him a quality backup at the highest level.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Ciuffo was a first round pick out of a South Carolina high school in 2013 based on the strength of his arm and power, with his hitting and catching skills closer to average. That's still largely the report 5.5 years later, with the gap being that Ciuffo isn't quite offensively talented enough (a combination of plate coverage, loft and bat control) to hit for both leagues' average contact and power. The lesser offensive upside makes him more of a potential backup. He got a cup of coffee in 2018 and is currently the third catcher for the Rays, so he'll almost certainly get more big league time when there's a catcher injury or prolonged slump next season.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Coleman’s velocity reached a new level in 2021, when he was throwing 96-100 mph after having previously sat in the low-to-mid-90s. The velo bump earned him a call-up, and he impressed over a tiny 6.1 inning sample to close out the season. He’s stayed up in the big league bullpen ever since, and though he hasn't yet hit the same triple-digit heights as last year, he’s resting comfortably in the 97-98 mph range. He pairs the heater with a hard slider that has had more consistent finish in 2022, to the tune of a 17.2% swinging strike rate. But while his strikeout rate has been well above league average, his command has taken a hit and his walk rate has ballooned over the 20% mark. The fact that he’s remained a part of the big league roster (rather than being sent down for further development) indicates the club’s confidence in him finding his footing as he fine-tunes his strike-throwing.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: Coleman was an afterthought in the Tim Hill trade with San Diego. Edward Olivares (who also came over in the deal) had been hot leading up to the trade and Coleman had struggled when he was last seen, dealing with injuries and ineffectiveness. His velocity (93-96 as a starter at Missouri State) had dropped (90-92 toward the end of a rough 2019) and Coleman struggled with command. Back in 2021, his velocity has not only returned by has exceeded previous highs and he's now sitting 96-100 with a hard slider that doesn't always finish. The combination of injury history and lack of a consistent plus secondary weapon keeps Coleman out of the 40+ FV tier but he's become a high-probability big leaguer reliever by virtue of his velocity rebound.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Coleman is a muscular 6-foot-6 righty who body comps to NBA wing players like Andre Iguodala more closely than he does others in baseball. He has plus velocity, hitting as high as 97 mph with his heater in college. He also has a 55 or 60-grade slider at times, though some of his breaking ball effectiveness is a product of his lower arm slot. As you might guess, the combination of power stuff and an XL frame can lead to feel issues and trouble repeating the release point, which leads to control problems. The change is also behind, and Coleman realistically projects as a reliever. After two Hi-A appearances during which his velo was way down, he was sent back to Extended (but not put on the IL).

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a starter at Missouri State, Coleman had above-average velocity that would drop off late in games, so the Padres, who took Coleman in the fourth round of the 2018 Draft, moved him to the bullpen. While his numbers were good in his first two seasons, his velocity tumbled from 97 mph down to the upper 80s. Many wrote him off, but the Royals remained intrigued and selected him as the player to be named later in the Trevor Rosenthal trade in 2020. After an offseason searching for answers to the velocity drop, Coleman’s stuff jumped to another level in 2021, culminating in his MLB debut in late September. Coleman’s fastball now regularly sits 98-100 mph and has even flashed as high as 102 mph on radars last season. He complements that with a hard slider, and his work with the Royals’ pitching development team found a few more ticks of velocity on the pitch, making it more of a power slider than the looping shape it had before. Coleman is still working on consistency with the pitch, as well as his fastball command when he tries to blow it by hitters -- although he impressed in his short stint in the Majors with just one walk in 6 1/3 innings. The Royals have discussed working in a third offering as another look against lefties. With the obvious velocity, Coleman has the ceiling to be a dominant closer at the highest level, and his 6-foot-5 frame helps with that projection. How close he gets to that role will be about fastball command and slider consistency, but he factors into the Royals’ plans for their bullpen now and in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taken 12th overall in the 2017 Draft, Baz was the player named later alongside Austin Meadows and Tyler Glasnow in the Pirates-Rays trade that sent Chris Archer to Pittsburgh a year later. The Rays immediately got to work on making Baz their next big pitching prospect, and the early results showed in 2019 at Class A Bowling Green and the Arizona Fall League. After spending time at Tampa Bay’s alternate training site in 2020, Baz took another huge leap last summer as one of the Minors’ most dominant pitchers, posting a 2.06 ERA with 113 strikeouts and 13 walks in 78 2/3 innings at Double-A and Triple-A. He also mixed in a silver-medal-winning trip to the Olympics with Team USA. The Rays gave him his debut on Sept. 20 and made him their Game 2 starter in the ALDS. Baz was one of 12 Major Leaguers to throw 100 fastballs and average at least 97 mph and 11.4 inches or less of vertical movement, putting him on a list that includes Aroldis Chapman, Gerrit Cole and Jacob deGrom. That's why he threw it 54.5 percent of the time in the Majors. Baz’s mid-80s slider remains his best secondary, thanks to its bite that makes it a menace for right-handers. His low-80s, loopier curveball seemed like a distant fourth pitch in the past, but he threw it almost equal to the slider at the top level with similar whiff rates. His high-80s changeup is reserved almost exclusively for lefties. The 6-foot-2 hurler’s biggest gains came in the control department. His Minor League walk rate dropped from 10.8 percent in 2019 to 4.4 percent last summer, while his 8.7 K/BB ratio led the Minors (minimum 70 IP). Outside of some small improvements to his curve and change, there’s little polishing left to be done for Baz.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baz emerged as one of the hardest-throwing high school pitchers in the 2017 Draft as a Concordia Lutheran High (Tomball, Texas) senior, even generating some buzz as a possible top 10 pick. Pittsburgh ended up taking Baz with the No. 12 pick and signed him for $4.1 million, slightly above slot value. He had been in the Pirates’ system for a little more than a year when the organization sent him to Tampa Bay in August 2018 to complete the Chris Archer trade that had already netted the Rays Tyler Glasnow and Austin Meadows. Baz made a smooth transition to full-season Class A Bowling Green in 2019 and showcased his high-octane stuff after the season as one of the Arizona Fall League's youngest pitchers. He gained even more experience at the Rays’ alternate training site in 2020. From cleaning up his delivery to refining his pitch mix, Baz has only improved since he entered the Rays’ system. He scrapped his two-seam fastball and dialed back his curveball usage upon joining the organization in favor of a four-seamer that can touch triple digits and sits in the mid-90s and a hard, biting slider that is perhaps the best in Tampa Bay’s system. He can generate whiffs with both pitches, albeit while operating with fringy command, and he also shows the makings of having a solid changeup. Baz rounds out his arsenal with a fourth-pitch curveball that receives below-average grades from evaluators. The Rays worked with Baz to improve his delivery after acquiring him and he showed more control in 2019, walking one fewer batter per nine innings (4.1) compared to his first two seasons (5.1). That improved control and command took another jump in 2021, solidifying Baz’s place as one of the best pitching prospects in baseball when everything is working. If he can keep hitting his spots with premium stuff, he has the potential to lead future Tampa Bay rotations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baz lit up radar guns as a Concordia Lutheran High (Tomball, Texas) senior to establish himself as one of the hardest-throwing prep pitchers in the 2017 Draft. While there was buzz that he could be taken within the top 10 picks, Baz ended up going to the Pirates with the No. 12 pick and signed for $4.1 million, slightly over slot value. He was pitching well in the Rookie-level Pioneer League the following year when the Pirates sent him to Tampa Bay to complete the already lopsided Chris Archer trade. He made a successful transition to full-season ball in his first season with the Rays and then offered a glimpse of his high ceiling on the mound as one of the Arizona Fall League's youngest pitchers. Baz is the definition of a high-risk, high-reward pitching prospect because he has electric stuff but also well below-average control. He scrapped his two-seam fastball upon joining the Rays in favor of a four-seamer that sits in the mid-90s and routinely reaches triple digits, and he already commands it better than he did his two-seamer. Baz's curveball has taken a back seat to his swing-and-miss slider, a true plus offering in the mid-to-upper 80s with sharp biting action, and he shows the makings of developing a changeup that has at least average potential. In addition to refining his arsenal, Baz also has cleaned up his delivery since joining the Rays and walked one fewer batter per nine in his first full season (4.1) compared to his 2017-18 campaigns (5.1). He still has a long way to go in his overall development, and the Rays will handle him with care along the way, but the final product could be that of front-of-the-rotation starter. If that doesn't work out, Baz could serve as a shutdown bullpen piece with his lethal fastball-slider combination.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baz was a two-way standout at Concordia Lutheran (Texas) High, though it was the promise he showed on the mound that led some teams to peg him as a potential top-10 pick in 2017. The Pirates nabbed the Texas Christian commit at No. 12, gave him $4.1 million, a bit over-pick value, then sent him to the Gulf Coast League for his pro debut. He was pitching well in the Pioneer League when the Pirates sent him to the Rays in August 2018 as the player to be named in the Chris Archer trade. With his high-octane arsenal and remaining physical projection, Baz is the definition of a high-ceiling pitching prospect. Having scrapped his two-seam fastball in favor of a four-seamer, Baz consistently sits in the mid-90s and can reach back for triple digits, throwing his heater with late, riding life. He previously threw both a curveball and slider that often bled together, but now utilizes only the slider -- a plus offering that registers in the mid-to-upper 80s with devastating action that helps him miss bats. His changeup gives him another potential Major League-average pitch. While he has some violence in his delivery, Baz has the athleticism and clean arm action needed to make significant gains with his control and command. Patience will be key for Baz, and he's in good hands in a Rays organization that has a strong record of developing projectable young arms, with 2018 AL Cy Young winner Blake Snell representing their latest success story.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baz was a two-way standout at Concordia Lutheran High School in Texas who jumped into top 10 pick conversations for his pitching ability. The Pirates nabbed him at 12 and gave him $4.1 million, a bit over pick value, to sign him away from TCU, joining fellow Concordia product Ke'Bryan Hayes in the organization and making his brief pro debut in the Gulf Coast League. Baz was dealt to the Rays in August when he was announced as the Player to be Named Later in the trade for Chris Archer. Baz has a combination of deep repertoire and projection that gives him a very high ceiling. His fastball velocity picked up in his senior year. He'll sit at 92-96 mph and can reach back for 98 mph, with the ability to run and sink it while not losing velocity deep into his starts. He can miss bats with a plus cutter that he can turn into a true slider, and he also spins a distinctly different curveball. His changeup gives him another potential Major League average pitch. A solid athlete, Baz should be able to find the strike zone consistently as he refines his delivery. Patience will be key for Baz, and the Pirates know a thing or two about developing young pitching. With room to add strength to his athletic frame, Baz could slowly move up the right-handed pitching prospect ranks as he settles in to his pro career.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text:
Baz came into the 2021 season having never pitched above A-ball, but by the end of the year, his resume would include pitching before an empty Olympic ballpark, in a rowdy Yankee Stadium during a hotly-contested playoff chase, and on the postseason stage itself. The big story was Baz's improved control. Coming into 2021, he had a career 23.9% strikeout rate and 11.6% walk rate, which he bolstered with extreme velocity, including occasionally hitting triple digits. His low-effort, repeatable delivery has been changed so that Baz is throwing from the stretch all the time. 
Historically, Baz has presented two distinct versions of himself. The first is that of a starter who sits in the mid-90s with a four-pitch arsenal, the Baz that was present at the 2020 alternate site, where his lower velocity might be at least partially attributed to the less-competitive atmosphere. The other is that of a high-90s flamethrower with a more limited repertoire. In 2021, Baz combined the best of those profiles while in the minor leagues. He started the year at Double-A, where he struck out over 40% of the batters he faced against an absurd 1.6% walk rate – that’s just two batters in 32.2 innings. He was promoted in June and continued to dominate at Triple-A (with a brief hiatus to snag Olympic silver) before making his major league debut in September. He went five-plus innings in both of his first two big league starts, with his fastball velocity in the 96-98 mph range even into his later innings of work. But in his last start of the regular season against the Yankees, as well as his ALDS start against the Red Sox, he struggled to keep his pitch count down, unable to get big leaguers to chase with the same consistency he had against batters in the minors. He was also punished on several mistakes where he missed his location and left pitches over the heart of the plate. Still, no matter how hot the spotlight, Baz never seemed to sweat. That composure will be useful, even if he ultimately proves unable to more reliably miss bats multiple times through the order and ends up a high-leverage reliever. He had arthroscopic surgery in the spring of 2022, perhaps heightening those chances. No matter - reliever Baz would probably still be an elite closer.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Fastball velocities were down about a tick and a half on average across all of the alternate sites, which makes sense considering it was a non-competitive environment. Recall that the last we saw Baz, he was parked at 95-99 and touching 101 in the 2019 Fall League, working out of the bullpen with his fastball, curveball, and cutter/slider. He did not throw during Feb/March spring training and instead joined the team at the summer tuneup camp and then at the alternate site in Port Charlotte, where his velocity (according to a source not with the Rays) was more in the 93-96 range, which is where he pitched as a starter during the 2019 regular season. This could be because he was working as a starter at the alt site (he was back to throwing four pitches there, as the changeup came back) or because he was told to dial it down and throw more strikes, or because adrenaline doesn't really flow when nothing is on the line, or some combination of these factors. I'm not inclined to move Baz in light of this (obviously) because he's still only 21 and probably had a weird year like the rest of us. I'm still betting on his frame, athleticism, and stuff. Maturity will likely come with age, though I'm not sure better tactile feel for release and location will, so I still have Baz projected in a high-leverage relief role. (Alternate site)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: It's highly likely that Baz moves to the bullpen, where his unusually deep pitch mix could enable him to pitch multiple innings, though it's also possible the pitch mix gets whittled down and he works in single-inning relief. He pitched as a starter during the regular season but was bumping 100 out of the bullpen in the Fall League. The future fastball grade reflects the anticipated move.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Other than players who qualify under outdated rules about trading recent draftees, we can't think of a Player to be Named Later who had a stronger evaluation at the time of trade than Baz, who was part of the Chris Archer deal. The tightly-wound Baz has a repertoire tailored like Marcus Stroman's; it's four or five pitches, everything is hard, and his best stuff has glove-side action. Pitchers can succeed without changeups provided their breaking balls give them the tools to deal with opposite-handed hitters. Often, that's enabled by command. Baz's delivery is explosive but violent, and he may never have average command, let alone the command necessary to succeed without a change of pace pitch, or something to bisect the plate to his arm side. There's a chance he's a reliever but with three plus pitches, he could be elite in that role. If the command and/or a changeup develop, he fits in the middle of a rotation.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Martinez has had a two-tick velocity bump since 2019, his final year with Oakland, when he was sitting 89 mph and topping out at 92. He's now sitting 91-92 and can manipulate his fastball's shape, creating sink, ride, and even cut (usually 84-86 mph), which helps keep him off of barrels despite the below-average velo. Martinez's repertoire has east/west action. He has an athletic drop-and-drive delivery and a very low slot, creating a shallow approach angle that seems to benefit his slider the most. His slider has big lateral sweep and very little drop. In fact, the interaction of Martinez's release height and arm slot make it so some of his sliders, especially the ones that finish to his arm side, appear to be rising. He's a five-pitch long reliever/swingman.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text:
Frías rocketed from High-A to the big leagues in five short months last season. He's a power pitcher, with a sinking fastball that touches 98 mph, a tight and short slider, a split that tickles the 90s, and a 12-6 hook in the low-to-mid 80s. His offspeed is more good than great: While he doesn't have a reliable bat-missing secondary just yet, all three flash average and he has some feel for sequencing, particularly in pairing his heater and curve.
Between the end of 2019 and spring training last year, Frías cleaned up his delivery. It's still a little funky, with an unusual slow-fast-slow cadence as he starts his motion, lifts his leg, and drives toward the plate, but he's much more under control now and he threw plenty of strikes at Double-A. The big knock here is his movement profile. Frías works with a four-seamer out of an over-the-top slot, but his spin rate is well below average on that and all of his secondaries, so he probably won't miss as many bats as the velo suggests. That likely pushes him to relief in the end, where his heater should crest triple digits and he'll only need one of his offspeed pitches to tick up to project as a late-inning arm. There's also a modest chance he becomes a poor-man's Sandy Alcantara, where the stuff is too good to homer against consistently and he contributes as a grounder-generating innings eater.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: At times, Frías looks like a stiff, velo-only bullpen prospect. At others, he's competing in or near the zone with four (soon maybe to be three, as his slider was de-emphasized at the alt site) pitches, including a splitter that took a leap in quality in 2019. Frías has a vertical arm slot but his fastball has sink/tail, so it doesn't blow hitters away at the letters even though Frías throws it 94-98. The curveball has vertical depth and eats up hitters who are cheating on the velo, and it's a great first-pitch change of pace because of its depth. The movement profile of his fastball may not be the best for missing bats, but it's likely to be an impact pitch because of the velocity. He could end up with three average secondaries (there's a chance the split becomes better than that if it keeps improving) and enough strikes to start, making him a potential No. 4/5 starter or late-inning reliever. (Alternate site)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: At times, Frias looks like a stiff, velo-only bullpen prospect. At others, he's competing in or near the zone with four pitches, including a splitter that was much better in 2019. All four pitches give hitters a vastly different look. Frias' mid-90s fastball has tailing action and his curveball has vertical depth and eats up hitters who are cheating on velo, while the split has late bottom when it's on, and the slider has horizontal, cutting action. The movement profile of his fastball may not be the best for missing bats, but it's likely to be an impact pitch because of the velocity. He could end up with three average secondaries (there's a chance the split becomes better than that) and enough strikes to start, making him a potential No. 4/5 starter or late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Frias was a strong-armed third baseman when he signed out of the Dominican Republic for $50,000 in November 2015. Seeing the potential in that arm, the D-backs moved him to the mound early in his career and watched him blossom. He showed flashes of dominance in 2018 during his first stateside campaign and was the organization’s most improved pitching prospect in ’19, riding a jump in velocity and sharper secondary pitches up to Class A Kane County. Frias spent the bulk of 2021 in Double- and Triple-A, and while there are still bouts of inconsistency, he’s made noticeable strides. He put everything together in a seven-inning no-hitter for Double-A Amarillo on Aug. 1. He was called up in late September and made a trio of appearances in the Majors. A prototypical power pitcher with a combination of physicality and stuff, Frias generates big-time velocity with a lightning-quick arm. He touches 99 mph with a fastball that sits in the mid-to-upper 90s deep in starts. A spike curveball gives Frias a second plus pitch. It's thrown with huge vertical depth and hard 12-to-6 downer action that challenges right-handed hitters. He continues to make progress with that pitch, and his enormous hands enabled him to add a split-changeup in 2019. The pitch registers in the upper 80s and bottoms out as it nears the plate, giving him a potential weapon against left-handed hitters. Frias threw more strikes and also showed an ability to hold his velocity deep into starts in 2021. As he’s matured, he’s begun mixing his pitches and has become less of a thrower and more of a pitcher. That said, the D-backs moved him into relief for good this summer in the hopes that the fastball-curve combo can play up even more in short settings. If he can maintain the stuff and hone in on the control just a bit more, the right-hander could be a high-leverage bullpen option.
