mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lange, a Texas high school product, put his name on the map with a plus fastball that erupted in the spring preceding the 2020 Draft. He routinely sat in the upper 90s and touched 100 mph with his fastball, which vaulted him into the supplemental first round, where he signed with the Padres for $2 million as the 34th overall selection. Although he struggled a bit with his command in his pro debut, Lange showed his swing-and-miss stuff, striking out 29 over 22 innings in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. Lange's high-velocity fastball features both run and sink, but it’s the slider that truly has Padres officials excited. A mid-80s power slider with bite, the offering flashes plus and the 6-foot-4 right-hander has made big strides with the pitch since tweaking the grip. While it’s still inconsistent at times, it has the potential to become Lange’s best pitch. He’s also developing a changeup, but needs to further refine the pitch as he hardly needed to throw it against prep hitters. Lange added 25 pounds of muscle prior to the Draft and entered the Padres system with a lofty ceiling. In order to reach that ceiling he’ll have to improve his secondary pitches and tighten up his inconsistent command. It’s an encouraging sign that he’s already shown the ability to improve the slider and considering he’ll be just 20-years-old for the bulk of the 2022 season, Lange has time to refine his game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lange put his name on the map with a big-time fastball that erupted in the early spring preceding the 2020 Draft. He routinely hit the upper 90s and touched 100 mph, vaulting into the supplemental first round, where he signed with the Padres for $2 million as the 34th overall selection. After he made a rocky 2021 pro debut in Rookie ball, San Diego traded him to the Yankees for Luke Voit in March. Lange's fastball sits in the mid-90s and can feature both run and sink. He has the makings of a second power pitch in a slider that could become a plus mid-80s weapon with bite. The pitch is inconsistent, however, and should be a focal point of Lange’s as he begins to face pro hitters. He will also incorporate a changeup, which he rarely threw against high-school opposition. A quick-twitch athlete, Lange added 25 pounds of muscle in the offseason prior to the Draft and had one of the best bodies in the 2020 high school pitching class. He has a huge ceiling but will need time to reach it, given his unrefined secondary pitches and shaky control and command. His slightly unorthodox low-arm-slot delivery also raises a few question marks.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Howell was a toolsy junior college prospect with catalytic qualities, led by his supreme speed. After initial pro trials at shortstop in the Brewers system (he came to the Padres via last year's Victor Caratini trade), Howell began to play all over the diamond, including center field. He has really taken to center and it's basically the only position he plays now. Howell can really go get it out there, as his reads and range are both incredible. He's going to play in the big leagues by virtue of this skill alone, as outfielders with this level of defensive ability are very rare. Whether or not Howell will hit enough to have a bigger role remains to be seen, in part because his last two seasons have been marred by multiple injuries, including a 2022 wrist surgery. Indeed, he's currently on a rehab assignment for a shoulder injury. My pre-injury forecast had already put Howell in a one-tool bucket (though it's a very important tool) and sees him as a glove-only fifth outfielder.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Howell began the 2021 season on a tear and it looked as though something may have clicked for the toolsy former JUCO draftee, but his on-paper production took a dive after he spent 10 days on the shelf in June with an ankle injury. He slashed .210/.317/.399 split between High- and Double-A after that, which was still a league-average batting line. It came with a 34% strikeout rate, though, and ultimately the Brewers decided to leave Howell off their 40-man roster and expose him to the Rule 5 Draft that never was. Howell got consistent center field reps early in the 2021 season and at times made spectacular plays out there, before re-integrating the three infield positions he played early as a pro into his duties later in the summer. He has continued to play everywhere but first base since coming over from Milwaukee (along with Brett Sullivan) in the Victor Caratini trade. Howell doesn't have traditional infield arm utility, and he tends to hurriedly skip two- and three-hoppers over to first base when he's asked to make tough throws. While he could become a special outfield defender with continued reps, his limitations on the infield prevent him from projecting as a super utility type in the truest sense. He still has plenty of on-roster utility (speed, the raw power to run into one on occasion, being a defensive upgrade in the outfield) as a bench player.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text:
Howell popped onto my radar as a toolsy but raw AZL prospect who had just been a 12th rounder out of a junior college in Iowa. His speed was a serious problem for rookie-level defenses, which contributed to his BABIP-driven output there, but the quickness in Howell's hands was very apparent at that time. His defensive position was not. The Brewers tried him all over the infield, but in the intervening years he has moved to center field and is actually quite good there for how little he's played it. He has a chance to be plus there at maturity. 
As Howell's feel for defending has improved, so has his timing at the plate. He doesn't cover the outer half very well but he has a big, athletic move forward and great hand speed, and the improved timing has Howell doing much more damage than before. His pull% has skyrocketed from 33% in 2018 to 55% in '21, further indication that there has been an approach change here that's resulting in more power. He's run above-average walk rates as a pro and it's going to be important for Howell to continue to discern balls from strikes because he's very likely to end up with a 40-grade hit tool because of his hitting style. Even with a 40 bat, we're talking about a good defensive center fielder with power, and if ball/strike recognition can counterbalance what's lost with all Howell's swing-and-miss, he has a shot to be a regular. He compares similarly to guys like Sam Hilliard, Drew Stubbs, and other whiff-prone center field athletes.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Howell was a pleasant, toolsy, post-draft surprise whose combination of speed and crude bat control was too much for AZL defenses to deal with. He went to Low-A for his first full season and had less offensive impact, but still projects as a speedy, up-the-middle bench player.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Howell was a pleasant, toolsy, post-draft surprise whose combination of speed and crude bat control was too much for AZL defenses to deal with. A JUCO draftee would only turned 20 in September, Howell has some catalytic offensive qualities and a chance to play somewhere favorable on defense. He saw time at shortstop and third base during the summer and fall, but Eric and several scouts think he ends up in center field. Physical development will play a sizeable role in Howell's future, especially as far as his bat is concerned. He will be the age of a college sophomore in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Initially a 19th-round pick by the Royals in 2017, Howell climbed seven rounds in a year by going back to Kirkwood (Iowa) Community College and signed with the Brewers for $210,000. He showed signs of a breakout with 16 homers and 24 steals in 97 games between High-A and Double-A in 2021, and while he didn’t get added to the 40-man when Rule 5-eligible, he did capture the attention of the Padres, who acquired Howell in an early 2022 trade for Victor Caratini. Howell was off to a solid start at Double-A San Antonio, posting a 124 wRC+ in 48 games before suffering a wrist ligament injury that required surgery. Howell’s loudest tool by far is his plus-plus speed that’s always kept him on a prospect map in some way. While he’s never been overly aggressive on the basepaths, his skillset could take advantage of the new rules across the game geared toward encouraging stolen bases. Those wheels serve him well defensively, and it’s just a matter of finding him a regular spot. Both the Brewers and Padres liked giving him chances up the middle at center, second and short, but a below-average arm also meant he got 2022 looks in left field, where he can still cover lots of space. Offensively, Howell shows fast hands and around average raw power at the plate to go with a patient approach that helped him earn a .390 OBP in San Antonio. But his overall approach is heavy to the pull side, and he can struggle with swing-and-miss on breaking stuff. Even though he’s been passed over twice for 40-man spots, he still has a future as a fast and versatile right-handed-hitting option for San Diego.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Howell bet on himself by heading back to Kirkwood Community College in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, instead of signing with the Royals as a 2017 19th-rounder, and the move paid off when he slid up seven rounds a year later. He signed with the Brewers for $210,000. Howell’s breakout came in 2021 when he hit .248/.361/.465 with 12 homers and 20 steals in 69 games at High-A Wisconsin. His numbers dipped at Double-A (.235/.318/.429), and the Brewers chose not to protect the Rule 5-eligible speedster with a 40-man spot following the season. Prior to the 2022 campaign, the Padres acquired Howell and Brett Sullivan in exchange for Victor Caratini and cash. Howell’s plus-plus speed has made him a prospect since his early days. He’s an easy threat to steal 20-25 bags in any season and could exceed that if he gets even more aggressive on the basepaths. His overall athleticism is something the Padres enjoy taking advantage of when putting together a roster and lineup. The wheels absolutely play in center field, and if he had to stick in a position, that’s likely his best bet. But San Diego has liked the concept of keeping him moving around all three spots up the middle. The bat will be the big question. Howell shows fast hands at the plate, can take a walk and has at least average raw power. But his strikeout rate bloomed to as high as 39.6 percent at Double-A in 2021, and it will continue to be a problem. Now in his age-23 season, Howell is trending toward late-game pinch-runner/defensive replacement territory, but there still exists time and room for a larger utility role if he can find a way to make more contact.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text:
The extremely projectable Rodriguez's 2021 was about as exciting as a 12-inning pro debut can be. Quickly elevated to Low-A at age 18, Rodriguez was touching 97 mph from the left side and his fastball's riding action, as well as the vertical snap he was getting on his curveball, made him a prototypical power pitcher prospect. We entered 2022 looking for Rodriguez to hold the velocity he showed in 2021 across a larger innings count. Instead, he had Tommy John in March and missed the entire season. 
As of list publication, Rodriguez is now 14 months removed from surgery. He has progressed to throwing live BPs and supposedly looks quite good. If we take his 2021 stuff quality at face value and assume that's Rodriguez's true talent level, then he belongs next to Calvin Ziegler on this list. In part because the pandemic squashed what would have been his first pro season, Rodriguez has barely pitched as a pro, and when he was showing us 97 mph heat, he was coming off an extended period of rest and had only worked a dozen innings. It feels too aggressive to value him at that level right now, but if Rodriguez is sitting in the mid-90s again when he gets back into affiliated games, then he'll deserves a quick hook into an impact FV tier and maybe even to Brooklyn. The 2023 season was supposed to be his 40-man evaluation year, and if not for his surgery he would have been on pace to spend most of it at High-A and maybe make an argument to be added to the roster after the season. Now he's likely to spend most of the year in St. Lucie, first with the complex group and then the FSL roster.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: The extremely projectable Rodriguez belongs in the 40+ FV tier based on his combination of velocity (up to 97 mph), his fastball's riding action, and the vertical snap he gets on his curveball, but he had Tommy John in March and will miss all of 2022. The lefty-pitching prototype should be back in the middle of next summer and has one of the higher ceilings in this system.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Rodriguez, who signed for $2.6 million in 2019, is a feel and instincts center field prospect with advanced feel to hit and a medium frame. Though it caps his power projection, his modest size gives him a better chance of staying in center. He has table-setting, leadoff man characteristics, but is probably four or five years away from the big leagues. The lost minor league season meant the Dodgers sent most of their upper-echelon prospects to the alternate site and then Instructional League, which meant the Fall group skewed older. Rodriguez was not among them as he likely would have been in a typical year. He played instructional ball in the Dominican Republic instead, and still has a tweener fourth outfielder physical profile. But while he has a chance to make plenty of contact and exceed that role, his development has now been slowed by a year. (Dominican Instructional League)

Though it caps his power projection, Rodriguez's modest size gives him a better chance of staying in center field. fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Depending on the look, some scouts think he can play center field, others think he'll get bigger and shift to right field, but everyone sees a hit tool and power projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best Venezuelan prospect and one of the top all-around talents in the 2019 international class, Rodriguez signed for $2,667,500. The 2020 pandemic shutdown delayed his pro debut until last summer, when he homered four times in his first six games in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League before tailing off and finishing with a .216/.326/.367 line and a 31 percent strikeout rate. He spent the offseason working out with J.D. Martinez and Miguel Cabrera, which the Dodgers hope will spark a rebound in 2022. When Rodriguez signed, he projected as a hit-over-power center fielder with a line-drive, all-fields approach. He has gotten stronger and more aggressive since turning pro, looking to crush homers to his pull side with a longer right-handed swing while chasing too many pitches out of the strike zone and giving away too many at-bats. He needs to regain some discipline, get back to barreling balls more consistently and just let his pop come naturally. Rodriguez is starting to slow a bit as he has added muscle, earning average to solid grades for his speed. He didn't stick out on the bases or in center field during his debut despite a reputation for a high baseball IQ that allows him to get the most out of his tools. If he does have to shift to a corner, his solid to plus arm would play in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Los Angeles has landed the best Venezuelan prospect in each of the last three international classes, including signing Rodriguez for $2,667,500 in 2019. He was advanced enough to make his U.S. debut at age 17 last summer, but the coronavirus pandemic cancelled the Minor League season. Instead, he participated in the Dodgers' Dominican instructional league program. More advanced than most teenage hitters, Rodriguez has a mature approach that produces line drives to all fields. He has a definite hit-over-power profile from the right side of the plate, though his bat speed and ability to barrel balls could translate into 20 or more homers per season. He's starting to add strength and show some feel for driving balls in the air. With solid speed and a high baseball IQ, Rodriguez can steal some bases and has a chance to remain in center field. It's possible that he could lose a step as he matures physically, which could push him to an outfield corner. If that happens, his offensive upside and solid to plus arm would fit well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top Venezuelan prospect and one of the best all-around talents on the 2019 international market, Rodriguez signed with the Dodgers for $2,667,500. That's the largest bonus they've ever paid to a true amateur internationally, surpassing the $2.5 million they gave fellow Venezuelan Diego Cartaya in 2018. Like Cartaya, he should be advanced enough to make his U.S. debut at age 17. An advanced hitter for his age, Rodriguez uses a patient approach to lace line drives to all fields from the right side of the plate. His pure hitting ability stands out more than his power, though club officials believe his pop could manifest itself sooner than expected. With his bat speed and ability to put the barrel on the ball, he could hit 20 or more homers on an annual basis once he matures physically. Rodriguez has solid speed and a high baseball IQ, making him a threat to steal bases and giving him a good chance to remain in center field. It's possible that he could shift to a corner if he loses some quickness as he adds strength, but his bat and solid to plus arm strength would profile well in right field.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Goss continues to fill the zone with four pitches - a low-90s fastball, an average slider and split, a get-me-over curveball - and walked just 5% of opposing batters in 2022, making him a high-floor/low-ceiling prospect likely to pitch toward the back of a rotation eventually. His spin rates were abnormally high shortly after he entered pro ball (2,600 rpm on his fastball for a while!) but are now back down to his pre-draft levels, which is a bit of a sticking point in this evaluation. His on-mound athleticism and projected plus command should enable Goss' split/change to play like an above-average pitch at peak, and he shows consistent feel for creating tail and tumble on that pitch. Goss will be an interesting 2023 Rule 5/40-man candidate if he can sustain this level of performance amid an innings increase (Goss threw 100 frames in 2022) and against upper-level hitters.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Goss entered 2021 as a breakout candidate after he showed different stuff on paper during the prior season's instructs in the form of a significant spin rate spike. Both before the 2019 draft (data collection that occurred on the showcase circuit) and after, his fastball and the better of his two breaking balls spun at 2250 rpm and 2050 rpm, respectively. During 2020 instructs, his fastball spun at a whopping 2600 rpm while his breaking balls spun closer to 2400, and his changeup had much more velocity. Boots-on-the-ground scouts who saw instructs echoed the sentiments of the amateur side of the industry from before Goss was drafted: he can really pitch. He was a low-90s (touching mid-90s) changeup/command high schooler whose breaking balls relied on his deceptive slot to play, but his stuff had improved without detracting from his pitchability. With an improved breaking ball now in tow, there was hope Goss would move quickly. Instead, a shoulder impingement cost him almost all of 2021, and he made just four healthy starts in the FCL very late during the year. He then went to instructs, where he sat 92-94 mph and touched 96 with secondaries similar to 2020's, and he's been 91-94 so far during the spring of 2022. It was encouraging that his stuff was back, but the context of the look (Goss didn't have to deal with the grind of a whole season, and hasn't now for a couple of years) and Goss' developmental situation (he's 21 and has barely pitched in pro ball) put him in a significant relief risk area. His stuff isn't so nasty that he looks like a potential closer; instead, he is trending toward a multi-inning relief role.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: It appears as though Goss has had a pretty significant spin rate spike. Both before the 2019 draft (data collection that occurred on the showcase circuit) and after, his fastball and the better of his two breaking balls spun at 2250 rpm and 2050 rpm, respectively. But as I called around to see if Rays stuff had changed based on 2020 data, Goss came up. His fastball now spins at a whopping 2600 rpm while his breaking balls are spinning closer to 2400. He's also throwing his fastball a little bit harder and his changeup now has much more velocity and rests in the upper-80s. Boots-on-the-ground scouts who saw instructs echoed the sentiments of the amateur arm of the industry from before Goss was drafted: he can really pitch. He was a low-90s (touching mid-90s) changeup/command high schooler whose breaking balls relied on Goss' deceptive slot to play, but his stuff has improved without detracting from his pitchability. Pro scouts now think the breaking ball has a chance to be plus. This is a 2021 breakout candidate. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text:
In a draft demographic filled with wide-shouldered frames and traditional-looking deliveries, Goss stood apart from his 2019 prep pitching peers in many ways. He has a narrow, long-torso'ed frame, a flatter lower half, and a little bit of cross-bodied action to a delivery that resembles Luis Patiño's from a timing and sequencing standpoint. Goss' fastball has tough-to-square arm side tail created by his three-quarters arm slot, and its movement pairs well with his fairly advanced changeup, which seemed to evolve into a firm, mid-80s split once he was in pro ball. 
He has worked with two breaking balls in the past, both of which reside in the low-80s and have enough depth and movement to be considered future average pitches in a vacuum, but they lack raw spin and were consolidated after he signed. They may play better against righties if Goss' delivery proves tough for them to parse. There's some body/delivery relief risk perception throughout the industry -- some of which is delivery xenophobia, some of which is injury-related, though I think the mix and command are fine -- but otherwise Goss has fourth starter talent.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Goss is one of the more unique high school pitchers in the class, a plus athlete with a funky cross-body delivery, and a dynamic two-pitch mix.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays had high hopes for Goss when they selected the right-hander 36th overall out of Cypress (Texas) High School in the 2019 Draft and signed him for $2.05 million, the slot value for his Competitive Balance Round A pick, and you could argue he’s still only barely had a chance to show them what he’s capable of. He made nine appearances in his pro debut, sat out 2020 due to the canceled Minor League season then pitched only 10 1/3 innings in 2021 due to a shoulder injury. Goss didn’t require surgery on his shoulder despite tearing his labrum, and he handled a decent workload (101 1/3 innings) over 25 starts in his return last year. Remaining in Single-A all season, the starter posted a 4.00 ERA with 101 strikeouts and only 21 walks. It’s still unclear where Goss’ stuff will settle coming back from his injury -- shoulder rehab can be trickier than Tommy John rehab, in some ways -- and he pitched with lesser stuff last season than before his injury. But Tampa Bay saw the better version of Goss down the stretch and expects more of that after a normal offseason, which would give him a chance to reach his ceiling as a middle-of-the-rotation or back-end starter. Goss has an athletic 6-foot-3 frame that he harnesses well to repeat his delivery, consistently throwing strikes with good control. He throws a fastball in the low-to-mid 90s, touching 96, with backspin and riding life. He has a good feel for his changeup and throws a low-80s slider with late bite and two-plane depth. It’s a three-pitch mix that Goss commands well, but one that hasn’t yet been tested against upper-level competition -- even as his Rule 5 Draft eligibility looms at the end of 2023 -- due to the time he missed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The COVID-19 pandemic and a shoulder injury limited Goss to 27 1/3 innings during his first three professional seasons combined. The Rays selected Goss 36th overall out of Cypress (Texas) High School in the 2019 Draft and signed him for $2.05 million, which was the slot value for his Competitive Balance Round A pick. He made nine appearances in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, recording a 5.82 ERA with 16 strikeouts and only two walks in 17 innings, then had a 6.10 ERA with 12 strikeouts and no walks over four outings in complex-league ball last year. 2nd: The good news is that Goss did not require surgery on his shoulder despite tearing his labrum. He entered the 2022 season healthy, fully ready to go and has been fairly effective as a starter in Single-A. When healthy, Goss has his fastball sit in the low-to-mid 90s and touches 96 mph with backspin and riding life, and it’s reasonable to think he’ll add more velocity as he keeps growing into his projectable 6-foot-3 frame. He has a good feel for his changeup, but his slider is the most likely pitch to become a plus weapon. He throws that low-80s breaking ball with late bite and two-plane depth. Goss repeats his mechanics well and fills up the zone with control, command and understanding that were – when he entered the system -- considered to be advanced for his age and experience. He repeats his delivery well enough to command his arsenal, but he’ll have to prove it in game action after so little time on the mound as a pro. Perhaps his most valuable experience to this point came in the fall of 2020, after the Minor League season was canceled when he spent time pitching in front of the Rays’ staff during their instructional league camp. With Goss, Tampa Bay is betting on projection. It’s hard to reach those projections when you’re not pitching, but he has the arsenal, delivery and advanced feel to break out and reach his potential as a Major League starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Goss went nine picks ahead of his Cypress (Texas) High School teammate Matthew Thompson in the 2019 Draft, as the Rays selected Goss 36th overall and Thompson went to the White Sox shortly thereafter. Goss then signed with Tampa Bay for $2.05 million, which was the slot value for his Competitive Balance Round A pick, and made nine appearances in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, recording a 5.82 ERA with 16 strikeouts and only two walks in 17 innings. Shoulder issues kept him from pitching until the final month of the 2021 season. The right-hander was invited to the Rays’ instructional league camp last fall, giving him a chance to pitch in front of their staff despite losing what would have been his first full season to the pandemic. When healthy, Goss’ fastball sits in the low 90s and touches 95 mph with riding life, and it’s reasonable to think he’ll continue adding velocity as he grows into his projectable 6-foot-3 frame. He has a good feel for his changeup, but his slider is the most likely pitch to become a plus weapon. He throws that low-80s breaking ball with late bite and two-plane depth. Goss repeats his mechanics well and fills up the zone with control, command and understanding that are considered to be advanced for his age and experience. There’s still a long way to go considering his pro career only just began before the pandemic and this year's injury concerns, but he has the arsenal, delivery and advanced feel to break out and reach his potential as a Major League starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cypress (Texas) Ranch High was a popular destination for scouts last spring due to the presence of right-handers Matthew Thompson and Goss, both of whom were viewed as potential top-three-round picks in the 2019 Draft. While Thompson was more highly regarded entering the year and became the White Sox second-round pick, Goss outpitched him for the second straight spring to become the higher pick in June, signing with the Rays for slot value ($2.05 million) after they selected him in Competitive Balance Round A. Goss sits in the low-90s and has been up to 95 mph with a fastball that has riding life. It’s easy to envision the young right-hander throwing harder, perhaps even sitting in the mid-90s, once he grows into his very projectable 6-foot-3 frame. Goss had one of the better sliders in the high school ranks, a low-80s breaker with late bite and two-plane depth at times. He also has good feel for a changeup that he throws with similar velocity and some fade. Goss repeats his delivery well and is consistently around the plate, showing control and command that are advanced for his age. He’ll need to get stronger to handle the rigors of starting, but the athleticism, mechanics and stuff all point to a potential No. 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonaci celebrated his 16th birthday in 2018 by signing with the Red Sox for $290,000. He weighed just 140 pounds when he turned pro out of Venezuela, but has added at least 25 pounds of muscle five years into his pro career. In his first extended taste of full-season ball last year, he ranked second in the Single-A Carolina League in walks (89) and on-base percentage (.397) at age 19 and hit all six of his homers in the final six weeks. Though Bonaci has slowed as he has gotten stronger and is now a fringy-to-average runner, he remains one of the best infield defenders and has one of the strongest arms in the system. His instincts and quick first step still give him solid range to both sides at shortstop, though he played more second base last season as a teammate of 2021 No. 4 overall pick Marcelo Mayer. He also saw action at third and even played an inning in right field. A switch-hitter, Bonaci has been a different hitter in 2023 after being too passive and making too much soft contact in the past. Stronger and more aggressive than ever, he's turning on more pitches, hitting the ball with more authority and showing 15-homer potential. If he can keep this up, he'll provide enough offense to profile as an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonaci had to wait a week into the 2018 international signing period to turn 16 and become eligible to sign, landing a $290,000 bonus on his birthday. The Venezuelan carried just 140 pounds on his 5-foot-10 frame when he turned pro but since has added 25 pounds while still retaining his quick-twitch athleticism. He made his U.S. debut in 2021 and reinforced his reputation as one of the best infield defenders and strongest arms in Boston's system. A switch-hitter, Bonaci displays good bat-to-ball skills and a disciplined approach from both sides. While he won't be a slugger, he has enough hitting ability and bat speed to provide doubles power with 10-15 homers per year as he gets stronger and turns on more pitches. He understands that his focus is getting on base and doesn't try to do too much at the plate. Bonaci has slowed down to more of an average runner as he has started to mature physically, but his instincts help him play quicker than that and he stole 12 bases in as many attempts in 49 games last summer. He still moves well enough to have solid range at shortstop, though he might wind up getting more action at second base if he plays alongside 2021 first-rounder Marcelo Mayer. His double-plus arm strength is his loudest tool and enables him to make any throw needed at any infield position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonaci signed out of Venezuela for $290,000 on his 16th birthday in 2018, carrying just 140 pounds on his 5-foot-10 frame when he turned pro. While he's still not overly physical, he has added 25 pounds and played well on both sides of the ball during his 2019 pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, eliciting trade inquiries from other teams. While the coronavirus pandemic wiped out plans for his U.S. debut last year, he did come to instructional league and impressed there. A switch-hitter, Bonaci has good bat-to-ball skills and regularly produces line drives from both sides of the plate. He won't ever be a power threat, but he has the hitting ability and enough bat speed to provide some gap power as he gets stronger. He understands his limitations at the plate and focuses on employing a disciplined approach to get on base. Bonaci's loudest tool is a double-plus arm that allows him to make any throw needed at shortstop. He's a solid runner who's aggressive on the bases and covers plenty of ground at short, where he also displays smooth actions and soft hands. Advanced for his age offensively and defensively, he comes with a higher floor but lower ceiling than fellow shortstop and 2019 second-rounder Matthew Lugo.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bonaci had to wait a week into the 2018 international period to turn pro, receiving a $290,000 bonus on his 16th birthday. The Venezuelan carried just 140 pounds on his 5-foot-10 frame when he signed, and while he's still not very physical, he already has added another 20 pounds. He played well offensively and defensively during his 2019 pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, drawing trade inquiries from other clubs. A switch-hitter, he handles the bat well and makes regular line-drive contact from both sides of the plate. He still needs to get much stronger, and has the bat speed and hitting ability to provide some gap power when he does. He understands he won't be a slugger and instead focuses on maintaining a disciplined approach and getting on base. Bonaci has solid speed and an aggressive nature on the bases. His loudest tool is his plus-plus arm, which allows him to make every throw imaginable from shortstop. His smooth actions and soft hands should allow him to remain at the position, and he's a very reliable defender for his age.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Bonaci has impressed scouts with his bat since his amateur days in Venezuela. He has feel for contact, an advanced approach for his age, and the ability to drive balls into both gaps. Currently more of a doubles machine, Bonaci should get to 40-45 grade power as he ages into his 20s and projects as a total offensive package defined more by his lack of weaknesses than any particular strengths. He has outstanding defensive skills and a plus arm, but his frame has filled out since signing, leaving him a 40-grade runner who gets by at shortstop more on instincts and fundamentals than twitch. He has primarily played second base (where he's plus) during each of the last two seasons with some shortstop and third base mixed in, and he's dealt with rashes of inaccuracy throwing from the hot corner. A scrappy, grinder type of infielder who plays with big effort, Bonaci fits snugly in a utility infield role. His switch-hitting and defensive versatility will enable lots of favorable in-game matchups, or at least allow his manager to avoid unfavorable ones, since Bonaci can act as a platoon-neutral mid-game bat and then go to whatever position. He's a pretty good offseason 40-man candidate.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Bonaci has impressed scouts with his bat since his amateur days in Venezuela. He has feel for contact, an advanced approach for his age, and the ability to drive balls into both gaps. Currently more of a doubles machine, Bonaci should get to 40-45 grade power as he ages into his 20s and projects as a total offensive package defined more by his lack of weaknesses than any particular strengths. He has outstanding defensive skills and a plus arm, but his frame has filled out since singing, leaving him a 40-45 runner who gets by at shortstop more on instincts and fundamentals than twitch, and he might be better suited at second or third base in the end. Bonaci's most likely outcome lies somewhere between utility player and second division starter. He should make his full-season debut in 2022.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: He's much more physically mature than is typical for an 18-year-old, but Bonaci can hit. He's a switch hitter with rare feel for the barrel from both sides, which is especially remarkable considering his age. He has enough arm strength for the left side of the infield but, based on how thick he is at this age, he's at risk of losing the lateral agility needed to play the middle infield spots. He's very similar to recent Rule 5 pick Vimael Machin, and, like Machin, projects as a shift-aided role-playing infielder without quite enough in-game power production to play every day. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Bonaci is the big emerging sleeper on this year's list. He signed for $290,000 in the 2018 J2 class but has taken a significant step forward since then; team asked the Red Sox for him at the 2019 deadline, as many are covering the DSL with pro scouts now. Bonaci isn't huge at 5-foot-10 but has some raw power from both sides, including surprisingly high in-game exit velos. He figures to stick at shortstop because of premium arm strength and suitable lateral range. Boston didn't do traditional instructs during the fall, so Bonaci has still largely only been seen by scouts in the DR, making him a high-priority extended spring training evaluation in 2020.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Warren had an uncharacteristically rough start to the season at Wisconsin before heating up when the weather did. His season line looks awful, but he hit .284/.352/.600 during his final month with the Timber Rattlers before heading to Double-A and then the Fall League. While some of the excitement around Warren evaporated when the Brewers ended his return to catcher, he is still a well-rounded switch-hitter with plus on-base skills, and the longer track record of hitting that surrounds his rough 2022 still carries water when it comes to lining him up here on the prospect list. Warren has become a plus third base defender now that he's solely focused on that position. His range and body control are both plus, and so is Warren's arm from most throwing platforms. He's played some first base in the past, but looked rough there in the AFL when unexpectedly thrust into action due to injuries and departures on Glendale's roster. There's nothing close to prototypical 1B/3B power here, but the switch-hitting component and defense give him obvious on-roster utility. Ideally Warren will branch out to at least one more corner position and be a useful bench contributor.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Warren's playing time trended away from catcher throughout 2021 and after playing a C/1B/3B mix for much of the year, he caught just four times during the last six weeks of the season. Warren caught in high school but moved to the infield in college, and he's struggled with throwing and smothering errant pitches in a meaningful way. His best chance of entrenching himself in a big league role is if he can catch, even just a little bit, so it makes sense for him and the Brewers to continue to make it work. If not, then Warren will be limited to a switch-hitting, corner infield bench role, and his lack of power relative to other hitters in that space would make him a lower-end option in that regard.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Warren arrived to camp in amazing shape and looked stronger than he did last fall, either because he had added significant mass or because he struck me differently in close proximity on the backfields (I saw Milwaukee's instructs group at Chase FIeld in the fall). Either way, Warren's body looks like it can withstand the rigors of catching, which he's taking up again after playing the infield in college (Warren caught in high school). Warren has a contact-oriented approach derived from a very compact swing which features some wrist-flicking lift from the left side. His timing and fluidity have been better from the left side, too. The difference between this Warren and college Warren (who slugged just .406 in his draft year) is that that little wrist flick is generating big in-game power now. Warren has experience at all four infield spots (he's playing 1B/3B in addition to catching right now) and a track record of hitting, just not always for power. I think Warren has a chance to become an everyday catcher, and a very realistic fall back is a multi-positional role player who can sometimes catch, which is still very valuable.

fangraphs.label: 2020updated
fangraphs.text: Plus arm, can play any IF spot and was announced as a catcher, average speed, switch hitter, good instincts and feel for the game, contact approach derived from a very compact swing, some lift from the left side from which there is also more fluidity, swing is a little grooved and bat-to-balls skills are really thanks to how short the swing is.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers got creative by announcing Warren -- a shortstop out of Central Michigan -- as a catcher when they selected him in the third round of the 2020 Draft. The switch-hitter caught some in high school and had put himself on the map with a .502 OBP as a sophomore in 2019, followed by a productive trip to the Cape. The catching experiment seemed to wane in his first taste of the Minors, however, with Warren donning the tools of ignorance only three times in his final 39 games. He finished with a .258/.367/.442 line and 13 homers over 89 games between Low-A and High-A. The decision to move Warren away from catching and into the corner-infield spots was influenced, in part, by the Brewers noticing he made more impact offensively when he wasn’t being tasked at a more demanding defensive position. At his best, Warren can work deep counts that tax a pitching staff, and he’s capable of driving balls to the gaps with a short stroke from either side of the plate, though he’s a little more productive as a left-handed hitter. The power remains mostly in the park to this stage, but he has 15-20 homer upside if he can tap into his raw pop more. The Brewers like Warren’s hands on the infield, and there is a chance he could play some second base. In any event, he’ll need to hit even more if his future lies anywhere on the dirt, and Milwaukee has hope that that can happen the more catching gets put in the rearview.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers have been creative in recent years in an effort to find talented catchers, keeping an open mind about players without long track records at the position if they like the bat. Warren qualifies. He caught the attention of scouts with his hitting and on-base ability in the Mid-American Conference in 2019, then boosted his stock with a standout summer in the Cape Cod League. Primarily a shortstop at Central Michigan, he caught in high school and the Brewers announced him as a catcher when they selected him in the third round in 2020, making him the highest-drafted Chippewa since Kevin Tapani was a 1986 second-rounder. Warren signed for $575,000 and played over the summer in the Michigan pod of a pop-up independent league, allowing Brewers catching coordinator Charlie Greene to monitor Warren’s progress behind the plate. A switch-hitter with a sound, quick stroke from both sides and excellent hand-eye coordination, Warren makes repeated line-drive contact. He drives balls to the gaps more than over the fence and set a Central Michigan record with 22 doubles in 2019. He works deep counts and draws walks, and his fringy-to-average speed plays better than that on the bases because he's aggressive. There are mixed reviews of Warren's ability as a catcher, though he has the hands, arm and athleticism to make it work as he gains more experience -- and there is no doubt about his eagerness to master the position. The Brewers are committed to giving him a chance to stick there. His so-so range and funky arm action aren't particularly suited for shortstop, so he's received some looks at the corner infield spots with Low-A Carolina. In the worst-case scenario, he winds up in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Céspedes played for Cuba at the 2017 World Baseball Classic at age 19 before defecting two years later while the national team was in the independent Canadian American Association. The younger brother of two-time All-Star Yoenis Céspedes, he was cleared to sign in March 2020 but wanted to join the White Sox and waited until they had more money available in the next international period. Signed for $2.05 million in January 2021, he finished third in total bases (200) and sixth in steals (33) in the Double-A Southern League last year. His formidable strength and bat speed create well-above-average raw pop that plays to all fields, but Céspedes undermines himself with a grip-it-and-rip-it approach. His right-handed swing gets too long, leaving him vulnerable to quality fastballs, and he hasn't met a breaking ball he won't chase. He had the fifth-worst strikeout minus walk percentage (24.4) in the Minors in 2022 and would do more damage if he would just let his pop come naturally. Céspedes aggressiveness extends to the bases, where he uses his solid speed to steal when he gets the opportunity. He covers ground in center field but plays too shallow at times, reducing his effectiveness. His arm earns double-plus grades from some evaluators and would fit nicely in right field if he moves to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of two-time All-Star Yoenis Céspedes, Yoelqui played for Cuba at the 2017 World Baseball Classic before defecting two years later while with his nation's team in the independent Canadian American Association of Professional Baseball. Cleared to sign in March 2020, he wanted to sign with the White Sox and had to wait until they had more money available in the 2020-21 international period, landing a $2.05 million bonus in January 2021. Visa issues delayed his U.S. debut until mid-June, after which he batted .285/.350/.463 with eight homers and 18 steals in 72 games between High-A and Double-A. Céspedes added 20 pounds to his 5-foot-9 frame while training with his brother in advance of signing with a big league club, and his impressive bat speed and strength give him well above-average raw pop from the right side of the plate. He hit better than most scouts expected after a two-year layoff from competition, though his long swing and extremely aggressive approach lead to swing-and-miss issues that restrict his power in games. He struck out at a 28 percent clip in his debut while walking just 5 percent of the time, and his impatience grew as he homered just once in 46 Double-A and Arizona Fall League contests. Céspedes posts plus straight-line speed in workouts but is more average out of the batter's box and solid once he gets going. He has a nose for stealing bases but may not have more than average range in center field. His arm, which earns plus to double-plus grades, easily would fit in right field should he have to shift to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Yoenis Cespedes, Yoelqui played for Cuba at the 2017 World Baseball Classic and defected two years later while playing on Cuba's team in the independent Canadian-American Association. He added about 20 pounds to his 5-foot-9 frame while training with his brother in advance of joining a big league club, boosting his raw power and his prospect stock. He became eligible to sign in March 2020 but elected to wait until the subsequent signing period, accepting a $2.05 million bonus from the White Sox in January 2021. Cespedes' bat speed and strength give him well above-average raw power, though some evaluators wonder how much he'll be able to tap into it against quality pitching. His right-handed swing has a tendency to get long and uphill and he's overly aggressive at the plate. A younger, less physical Cespedes batted just .287/.351/.415 in four seasons in Cuba's top league and just .253/.343/.316 in 27 games over two years of Can-Am play. Cespedes can demonstrate plus straight-line speed in workout settings but has shown mostly average quickness in his Minor League debut. That leaves his ability to remain in center field in doubt, though his plus-plus arm strength would make him an easy fit in right. He's similar to but more athletic than White Sox outfield prospect Micker Adolfo, who has been slowed by injuries since signing for $1.6 million out of the Dominican Republic in 2013.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Céspedes' swing-happy approach would make Adeiny Hechavarria blush, swinging and chasing at a 63% and 45% clip, respectively. It's quantifiably at the very bottom of the 20-80 scale and on its own is a barrier between Céspedes and a sizable big league role. However, he came into 2022 running much faster than the year before and has given himself a chance to play a viable center field. He has enough power to support some kind of weird part-time role despite what is likely to be a very low OBP. His All-World arm gives him another way to impact the game. Maybe the ball/strike recognition piece will still come; because of his defection and the pandemic, Céspedes barely saw pro-quality pitching in his early 20s, not really until 2021. His skill set is similar to that of a righty-hitting Brett Phillips.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: While we continue to be skeptical of Céspedes because of his approach at the plate, his stock is absolutely up this spring because he is running much faster than last year and has given himself a chance to stay in center field. He has viable range out there now, and was posting average run times during the spring, looking plus under way. Céspedes does tend to get himself out by offering at early-count junk (he is running a 60% swing% as of publication, which would have ranked second in the big leagues behind Luis Robert in 2021), but if he can stay in center, even for a little while, he has enough power to support some kind of part-time role despite what is likely to be a very low OBP. His All-World arm gives him another way to impact the game, too. Maybe the ball/strike recognition piece will still come; because of his defection and the pandemic, Céspedes barely saw pro-quality pitching in his early-20s, not really until last year. His skill set is similar to that of a righty-hitting Brett Phillips.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: As you'd expect given his lineage, Cespedes has prodigious physical gifts, including elite arm strength. I do not think he'll hit enough to play a big league role, though. His long, noisy swing causes him to be late on velocity and Cespedes hasn't played or seen live pitching regularly for nearly four years, and when he has played, he's struck out a bunch. The error bar around Cuban players is big because the context in which they're evaluated is often strange, but I'm pessimistic about the bat based on the info I have.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rays signed Colmenarez, a highly regarded Venezuelan shortstop, for $3 million as the headliner of their 2021 international signing class. It’s been a tough road for him so far, with most issues completely out of his control. He couldn’t join the Rays in 2020 because the signing period was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic, couldn’t properly train with them during the shutdown, then fractured his right hamate before his first season began. Still young (he’ll be 19 all season) and plenty raw, Colmenarez will likely be further challenged with a necessary but challenging promotion to Single-A Charleston this year. It's easy to write off the .247/.319/.289 slash line Colmenarez produced as a 17-year-old in the Dominican Summer League, because the hamate injury sapped his strength even after he returned for 26 games. His numbers were better, but not dominant, as he moved to the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. He hit .254/.379/.381, still displaying a sweet left-handed swing, but his 26.8 percent strikeout rate and lack of power inspired some concerns about how he’ll fare against upper-level competition. He should gain more power as he grows into his projectable frame, and that would enhance his overall offensive profile. It's the rest of Colmenarez’s game, though, that suggests he still has a big league future. He looks like an above-average shortstop with soft hands, good actions, a strong arm and impressive instincts. That would make him, at worst, a lefty-hitting utility infielder if he hits enough -- and it’s not hard to find a place for those on Major League rosters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Look no further than his $3 million signing bonus to understand the Rays’ optimism regarding Colmenarez, a highly touted Venezuelan shortstop who headlined their 2021 international signing class. And understand the number of obstacles that he faced leading up to his professional debut: He couldn’t join the Rays during the first summer of the COVID-19 pandemic due to the delayed signing period, couldn’t properly train during the shutdown, then fractured his right hamate bone just before his first season began. With his debut pushed back to mid-August in the Dominican Summer League, Colmenarez hit for essentially no power as the hamate injury sapped his strength. That led to a .247/.319/.289 slash line in 26 games for the 17-year-old, but the Rays remain excited internally about his potential despite those pedestrian numbers. His hamate is not considered a long-term issue, and Tampa Bay expects him to bounce back as he moves to a domestic affiliate this year. Colmenarez is still projectable, listed at 5-foot-10 and 170 pounds. He has a sweet left-handed swing with a balanced profile, a good blend of hitting for contact and power, that should include more pop as his body continues to mature. Colmenarez has displayed soft hands with good actions at shortstop, and evaluators expect he’ll remain up the middle as an above-average shortstop even as he grows. He also has plus arm strength, enhancing his defensive potential. Despite a delayed and disappointing debut, there’s still plenty of reason to believe Colmenarez will develop into a well-rounded shortstop with above-average tools across the board.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: A sweet-swinging, lefty-hitting shortstop with a good frame, Colmenarez was among the highest profile (and most highly paid) prospects in the 2021 international amateur class. A hamate injury cost him all but 17 games in 2021 and likely impacted his performance in those, and he also missed a few weeks of the '22 slate while posting a shrug-inducing .254/.379/.381 line and striking out a lackluster 27% of the time. While the hitters in the 45+ FV tier have offensive tools that might enable them to leap into the Top 100, that is probably not true of Colmenarez, who now has a glove-heavy utility infield profile. He's not only likely to stay at short but might be plus there. He has plus hands and actions, and closer to average range and arm strength. Of medium build, there is probably not going to be impact power here at maturity, so any sort of everyday role will have to be obtained via Colmenarez's hit tool, which looks like a future 40 so far. Still, lefty-hitting shortstops with this kind of athleticism don't exactly grow on trees, and Colmenarez now has the look of a low-end shortstop regular or luxury utilityman, albeit one who's still a great distance from the Trop.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: A sweet-swinging, lefty-hitting shortstop with a good frame, Colmenarez was among the best players in the 2020 international amateur class for quite a while, at times claiming the top spot. His amateur report and how he looks in workouts is still driving his placement here, since a hamate injury cost him all but 17 games in 2021 and likely impacted his on-paper performance in those. He's not only likely to stay at short, where he has plus hands and actions and average range and arm strength, but might be a special defender there. Colmenarez's swing has natural lift out in front of the plate and he has shown feel to hit in games, giving him a good offensive foundation on which to layer strength as his frame fills out and matures. There is a chance he matures in the Goldilocks Zone, where he's filled out enough to have meaningful power but not so much that he can't stay at shortstop. Colmenarez is a caliber of prospect commensurate with a mid-first round pick and a potential impact everyday shortstop.
