mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jensen battled the strike zone for two seasons at Fresno State before winning the Mountain West Conference pitcher of the year and tournament MVP awards in 2019. Though he had one of the best fastballs in that year's Draft, he wasn't a consensus first-round talent, but the Cubs selected him 27th overall and signed him for a below-slot $2 million. He has had only sporadic success as a pro starter and spent six weeks in the middle of the 2022 season changing his mechanics at the club's training base in Arizona. Jensen owns one of the harder two-seam fastballs in the Minors, operating at 94-96 mph and reaching 98 with power sink, and he trusts it more than a four-seamer with more velocity and less life that gets rocked when he doesn't keep it up in the zone. He has yet to find a reliable complement to his heater, with his low-80s curveball serving as his second-best pitch last year. He also has an upper-80s slider and changeup, but the latter lacks movement, and he doesn't throw either for strikes. After shortening his arm action and stride and reworking how he uses his lower half in his delivery, Jensen gained a tick more velocity, but his secondary pitches still weren't effective, and he still struggled with his control and command. Chicago still believed in him enough to add him to the 40-man roster last November, but it may be time to move him to the bullpen. His path to the big leagues is as a fastball-heavy reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jensen struggled to throw strikes in his first two seasons at Fresno State before dominating in his third, winning the Mountain West Conference's pitcher of the year and tournament MVP awards in 2019. Though he was not a consensus first-round talent, the Cubs selected him 27th overall that June and signed him for a below-slot $2 million. He has continued to showcase power stuff and inconsistent control and command in pro ball while reaching Double-A at the end of his first full pro season in 2021. Jensen throws his two-seam fastball with atypical velocity, working at 94-96 mph and topping out at 98 with quality sink, and he trusts it more than a harder four-seamer that lacks life and gets pounded when he doesn't locate it up in the zone. His slider has gotten harder and sharper in pro ball, sitting in the mid-80s and touching 90 mph, and he has added a low-80s curveball to give him a softer option with more downer break. He's still refining a mid-80s changeup with fairly ordinary life. The Cubs still believe Jensen can translate his athleticism into enough control and command to be an effective starter. But he also has a funky delivery with a lot of moving parts that he struggles to keep in sync, preventing him from locating his pitches where he wants on a consistent basis. Most scouts outside of the organization believe he's destined for the bullpen, where he could focus on his fastball and slider and perhaps become a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After recording a 5.84 ERA while battling the strike zone in his first two seasons at Fresno State, Jensen dominated in 2019, winning his final nine starts en route to Mountain West Conference pitcher of the year and tournament MVP awards. He wasn't a consensus first-round talent but the Cubs made him the first Bulldogs arm selected that high since Matt Garza in 2005, signing him for a below-slot $2 million as the 27th overall pick. He comes with a good deal of upside but also a hefty amount of reliever risk. Jensen had the best fastball in the 2019 college class, working with sinking two-seamers and riding four-seamers while sitting in the mid-90s deep into games and peaking in the upper 90s. At Fresno State, he relied heavily on his heaters and his slider, an 82-85 mph offering that got sharper when he altered his grip midway through his junior season. The Cubs have had him develop a curveball with more depth to play off his four-seamer and also have encouraged him to use his changeup more often. Jensen's long-term role and success will come down to his ability to throw strikes. Chicago believes his quality athleticism will translate into control and command and enable him to remain a starter, though he averaged 4.2 walks per nine innings in college (2.4 as a junior) and issued 14 free passes in his 12-inning pro debut. Scouts outside the organization believe his long arm action and the effort in his delivery eventually will land him in the bullpen, where he could become a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jensen compiled a 5.84 ERA in his first two seasons at Fresno State before breaking out in 2019, winning his final nine starts, capturing the Mountain West Conference Pitcher of the Year and tournament MVP awards and flirting with a no-hitter in an NCAA regional playoff game in his final outing. He wasn't a consensus first-round talent, but the Cubs made him the first Bulldogs pitcher selected that high since Matt Garza in 2005 and signed him for a below-slot $2 million. They used the savings to pay top high school catching prospect Ethan Hearn $950,000 in the sixth round. Owner of the best fastball in the 2019 college class, Jensen throws two- and four-seam versions at similar speeds. He can carry 94-96 mph velocity on his four-seamer deep into starts, peaking at 98 with running action. His two-seamer arrives about 1-2 mph slower with heavy sink and plays well off his harder, straighter variation. Though Jensen lacked consistency with his secondary pitches in college, Chicago believes it can help him improve in its pitching lab. His 82-85 mph slider became sharper when he changed his grip midway through his junior season, and using his changeup more often could help it become an average offering. He's not particularly big and doesn't have a long track record of providing strikes, so he comes with more bullpen risk than a typical college first-rounder.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: The Braves tried to use the pool space they would have saved by signing Carter Stewart to an under-slot deal to land Hess in 2018, but he went back to school and got about a quarter million the following year. He has projected as a reliever for pretty much his entire life as a prospect, at times looking like a late-inning weapon. After reaching Double-A and the Arizona Fall League in 2022, Hess seemed tee'd up to reach Detroit in 2022, but instead he blew out during the spring and had TJ before spring training had even begun. Hess was back in time to break camp with West Michigan on rehab assignment, but he was shut down after just five appearances. Other teams' internal systems list his reason as returning to the IL as "right elbow surgery," but it's unclear if Hess has simply had a setback during recovery from the 2022 TJ or if he's gone under the knife again. A Tigers contact did not want to confirm injury specifics for this list. Healthy Hess can touch 97 mph, and his low-80s slider has good sweep to it and is frequently his out pitch. Hess also has a solid low-80s changeup, but he barely threw it in 2021. If it turns out he's had another season-ending injury, then he should probably just be in the honorable mention section of the list since a big part of the optimism around Hess was that he'd race to Detroit once he showed he was healthy.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Hess reached Double-A at the end of 2021 and while he showed a continued propensity for missing bats, his combination of plus stuff and fringy command still indicates a future in middle relief rather than as someone who can be trusted in the later innings. With a long frame and violent delivery, it’s unlikely Hess will ever have anything resembling precision to his game, but he has the weapons to get hitters out simply by keeping the ball in the zone. His lively fastball sits in the mid-90s and can touch 97, while his low-80s slider has good sweep to it and is frequently his out pitch. A part-time starter in college, Hess has a solid low-80s changeup he’s confident using against right-handed hitters, but he barely threw it in 2021. His ability to throw strikes waivers from at-bat to at-bat, and declined overall in 2021, and he has a tendency to aim the ball when he needs a strike, leading to grooved pitches and hard contract. Hess will likely return to Double-A Erie to begin the year, and his future as either a legitimate bullpen piece or run-of-the-mill Quad-A arm-strength reliever will depend on just how much he can harness his arsenal.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Hess always had the stuff to start for LSU, but troubles with command and pitch efficiency led to an inability to maintain a rotation slot while there. Drafted in the seventh round in 2019, the Tigers liked what they saw in him during shorter stings and have developed him as a pure reliever. There’s nothing complicated about what Hess does. He’s a long-levered righty who comes in and tries to miss bats with a traditional fastball/slider combination. While he lacks true smoke, he still can sit in the 94-96 range with his fastball, which features good life, and his velocity-driven low 80s slider has missed bats in the minors. It’s an arm-heavy delivery with little load or lower-half incorporation and a tick of violence, and it’s hard to see him ever being in possession of anything resembling above-average command. Hess has had a velocity dip early this spring, but still could move quickly as a potential bullpen piece whose overall game falls a bit short of late-inning leverage situations. (Alternate site)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Hess was a well-known power arm on the high school summer showcase circuit and into the spring, showing mid-90s heat, a plus power curveball, and a reliever's command and approach in his best stints. Due to the prep righty reliever profile, his price wasn't met and he went to LSU, where they tried to make him a starter after a solid freshman year in relief. The starter role never quite took, as he mostly sat in the low-90s with lesser stuff. His stuff got back to his showcase circuit best in pro ball in short stints, which seems like the best role for him going forward.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Low-90s, average slider as a starter but was mid-90s with a plus slider as a freshan reliever at LSU. If he returns to relief in pro ball, which most teams believe he will, he's a likely relief piece.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tigers general manager Al Avila and LSU head coach Paul Mainieri worked together three decades ago at St. Thomas University in Miami. When Hess had an up-and-down junior season, bouncing between the rotation and bullpen, Detroit saw him fall down draft boards and selected him in the seventh round of the 2019 MLB Draft, believing he could be a solid reliever. After dominating NY-Penn League hitters, his midsummer jump to Class A West Michigan flashed the potential the Tigers believed they could tap, including 22 strikeouts over 21 innings. The combination of Hess’ 6-foot-6 frame and a projectable power fastball tantalized scouts, even if the statistics didn’t back it up. Though Hess started for most of his collegiate career, he was more effective out of bullpen, including a dominant freshman season. His fastball plays more solidly into the mid-90s in shorter stints, pairing with a slider that works in the low to mid-80s with darting movement. He has a changeup but neither needs nor uses it much in relief stints. While his tall frame creates leverage, command has been a challenge throughout his career, including 11 walks at West Michigan. Like former University of Miami closer Bryan Garcia a few years earlier, the Tigers drafted Hess hoping his college experience would allow him to move quickly through the system and reach Detroit sooner than expected. Garcia moved from West Michigan to Triple-A Toledo in his first full pro season; the Tigers would love to see Hess do the same, giving them a middle relief or setup option in 2021.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Grammes would flash two 70-grade pitches in college in his upper-90s fastball and his slider, but he was so comically raw as a strike-thrower that he slid all the way to the fifth round of the 2019 draft. He played two ways at Xavier, and at the time, it seemed possible pro development might make his strike-throwing more consistent and enable him to work in a high-leverage bullpen role. Grammes began the 2021 season with seven good starts, during which he threw strikes at a 40- or 45-grade rate, a shocking development for him if it wasn't a small-sample aberration. Sadly, his UCL blew in June of 2021, he had Tommy John in early July, and he was quite wild when he returned from rehab in 2022. Unlike Justin Martinez (who had a similar rehab timeline), Grammes was not added to the 40-man after 2022 and began 2023 at High-A Hillsboro. He's begun to pitch backwards off his slider more often, using his fastball as a chase pitch. He can't finish his slider as a chase pitch consistently, so even though he has solid middle-inning stuff, the command portion pulls Grammes into an up/down relief projection.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Grammes had two 70-grade pitches in his upper-90s fastball and his slider but was so comically raw as a college strike-thrower that he slid all the way to the fifth round of the 2019 draft. He's athletic and played two ways at Xavier, and at the time, it seemed possible pro development might make his strike-throwing more consistent and enable him to work in an high-leverage bullpen role. That started to occur in the fall of 2020. Grammes' body started to mature and he had better feel for release than he did while in school. He ditched his changeup for a second breaking ball, a nasty low-80s curveball. He began the 2021 season with seven good starts, during which Grammes threw strikes at a 40- or 45-grade rate, a shocking development for him if it wasn't a small-sample aberration. Sadly, Grammes' UCL blew in June and he had Tommy John in early July. He's a 2022 Fall League candidate whose stuff will put him in the conversation for a 40-man spot if he rehab goes well. His surgery's timing and Grammes' inability to build a starter's foundation of innings, combined with his present control issues, all but seal his fate as a reliever, but he could be a dominant one due to the quality of his stuff.

Grammes' body has started to mature and he's got better feel for release now than he did at Xavier, though he's not as balanced over his front side and his lower half has gotten a little stiffer. Grammes has 40+ stuff but I'd like to see an extended stretch of viable strike-throwing before moving him into a tier with guys whose ability to pitch I feel better about. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Grammes was a two-way player at Xavier (he has plus raw power) and we hope the focus on pitching will enable him to eventually have usable control. You could argue he has 20 control/command right now, and despite the electric quality of his stuff, he's a long shot to be a big leaguer. But he was up to 99 in college and would flash an occasional 70-grade slider, so if things come together, he could be a bullpen monster.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Converted infielder is up to 99 mph at times with a plus-flashing slider, but an arm action and feel likely more suited to relief.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Known more for his hitting and wrestling prowess than his pitching in high school in Virginia, Grammes became a two-way player at Xavier and showed enough promise on the mound to become a fifth-round pick in 2019. The four years since have been a rocky road, to say the least. He lost his first full season to the pandemic and then made eight High-A appearances before needing Tommy John surgery in July 2021. Grammes returned to Hillsboro late last July, and while the results were a mixed bag (17 earned runs, 33 strikeouts in 18 innings), his stuff still showed the same promise. The 6-foot-1 right-hander is back up to the upper 90s, touching triple digits, so velocity has not been a concern coming off the elbow procedure and long rehab. His upper-80s slider is a wipeout pitch too, making sure hitters can’t just sit on the heat, and it might be only a touch better than his low-80s curveball, at least when it comes to bite. The deuce is still at least an above-average pitch, which is more than can be said for a changeup he doesn’t use much in relief. Command was a relative difficulty for Grammes before Tommy John, and that continued to be true last year as he tried to play catch-up. In the offseason, the D-backs have worked with him on landing pitches more consistently. If he can, the quality of his arsenal could point to a high-leverage role out of the bullpen. Grammes was already left exposed to the 2022 Rule 5 Draft (and went unselected), so time is ticking.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: More of a power hitter than a pitcher in high school, Grammes won nearly as many Virginia state wrestling titles (two) as he pitched innings (three), and he received a walk-on opportunity at Xavier only after emailing the program. While he has posted much gaudier numbers at the plate than on the mound with the Musketeers, he'll definitely become a full-time pitcher as a pro. He turned down the Orioles as a 35th-rounder last year as a sophomore and should go about 30 rounds higher this June. Grammes offers some of the best fastball velocity in the Draft, working at 95-99 mph as a reliever in the past and at 93-95 as a starter this spring. It doesn't feature a lot of life and he struggles to command it, so his heater can get hit when he leaves it over the plate. Similarly, he can throw some sharp low-80s sliders and also get into trouble when his breaking ball flattens out. Grammes has shown little feel for a changeup while trying to incorporate a third pitch as a starter this year, and he'll probably scrap it as a reliever at the next level. Though he throws with some effort, he has made some progress cleaning up his delivery and has the athleticism to continue to improve. He has little history of providing strikes or consistency, though he never has concentrated solely on pitching either.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Mikolajchak's stuff didn't quite bounce back to the level he showed prior to a late 2021 shoulder injury, and he struggled in '22, regressing from both a stuff and command standpoint. At peak, he was 94-97 mph with a nasty slider, two of a fast-moving four-pitch mix. In 2022, he was sitting 93 and Mikolajchak's cutter was getting slammed by opposing hitters. At one point, he looked like a high-leverage relief prospect, but now he's purely a rebound candidate.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Mikolajchak bounced back and forth between the Sam Houston bullpen and rotation during his final two years there, looking best in relief and projecting there in a big league role. He was 90-95 mph with an above-average breaking ball after signing in 2019. Then Mikolajchak blew up throughout 2020 instructs. He sat 90-92 in his first outing, then wrapped up his year pumping 95-97, which he was blowing past everyone. The two pitchers sounded so different that Eric had to make sure neither of the scouts he spoke to had the wrong player (they didn't). There's also evidence of a leap in Mikolajchak's pitch data: more spin, more induced vertical movement on his fastball and a harder curveball that we now have classified as a slider. We had the expectation that Mikolajchak's repertoire might be pared down as he was being fast-tracked in relief, but he threw all four of his pitches in 2021 (fastball, slider, cutter, and changeup) amid about 40 strong innings at Akron, with his velo settling into the middle range of that crazy 2020 instructs run at 93-95. He had less arm strength this spring, sitting 91-93 in a big league spring training game at Colorado. That pitch has substantial margin for error because of its vertical break and we still view Mikolajchak as more than just a middle reliever, though not quite an elite late-inning option.

fangraphs.text: Mikolajchak bounced back and forth between the Sam Houston bullpen and rotation during his final two years there, looking best in relief and projecting there in a big league role. He was 90-95 with an above-average curveball after signing in 2019. Then Mikolajchak arrived for instructs in the Fall of 2020. I've spoken with scouts who bookended his Fall work and it sounds like he was 90-92 in his first outing, then wrapped up instructs sitting 95-97, which he was blowing past everyone. The two pitchers sounded so different that I had to make sure neither of the scouts I spoke to had the wrong player. There's also evidence of a leap in Mikolajchak's pitch data: more spin, more induced vertical movement on his fastball and a harder curveball. He now has an impact power pitcher's fastball/curveball combo. After he threw four different pitches in college, he projects to work with three (his changeup looks good on paper but the scouts I spoke with didn't see it in the Fall) out of a big league bullpen, and based on how vigorously the arrow is pointing up for him after his Fall in Arizona, he may move very quickly. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.text: Mikolajchak bounced back and forth between the Sam Houston bullpen and rotation during his final two years there, looking best in relief and projecting there in a big league role. He was 90-95 with an above-average curveball after signing.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Plus makeup, low-tomid-90s fastball, average curveball with vertical action. Has bounced back and forth between rotation and bullpen each of the last two years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mikolajchak set a Sam Houston freshman record with 13 saves in 2017 and split the next two seasons between the bullpen and the rotation before the Guardians selected him in the 11th round of the 2019 Draft. They sent him to Double-A for his full-season debut after the pandemic layoff and he responded by posting a 3.18 ERA with a 57/9 K/BB ratio in 39 2/3 innings. Mikolajchak has upgraded his stuff since turning pro, beginning with a fastball that has gone from 92-95 mph in college to 94-97 with riding action and induced vertical break that make it tough for hitters to get on top of. He has turned an average low-80s slider into a plus mid-80s slide piece, and he also can morph it into a shorter, harder cutter. His upper-70s curveball has become an average offering and he also can mix in a low-80s changeup with some fade. Not only does Mikolajchak have more pitches than most relievers, but he also throws more strikes. His biggest need is to find a way to hold left-handers in check after they battered him for an .835 OPS (compared to .555 by right-handers) in 2021. Though he'll open 2022 with just 64 2/3 frames in the Minors, he may not need many more before he's ready to help Cleveland.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Politi redshirted in his first year at Seton Hall and went 6-7 with a 5.04 ERA in the next three seasons. Despite his modest success and fastball velocity, the Red Sox liked his pitch data enough to draft him in the 15th round and sign him for $25,000 in 2018. He acquitted himself well as a multi-inning reliever in high Class A during his first full pro season, then posted a 1.27 ERA in five late-season starts that left Boston rethinking his long-term role. Politi has added 2-3 mph to his fastball in pro ball and now deals at 92-95 mph and reaches 97. His four-seamer features some of the highest fastball spin rates in the system, creating armside run that eats up right-handers. His second-best offering is an upper-80s slider, and he also has made progress with a curveball while continuing to try to refine his changeup. While Politi had success in the rotation last summer, his long-term future likely will be in the bullpen. There's a lot going on in his max-effort delivery, making it difficult to repeat and thus to command his pitches. He projects as a long reliever who may not need much more than another year in the Minors before he's ready for an audition in Boston.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Politi spent late 2019 through early 2021 trying to stretch out as a starter in Boston's system. Late in 2021, he was moved to the bullpen. His changeup has been scrapped, and he now sits 93-96 mph with two distinct breaking balls: a mid-80s slider/cutter and a low-80s curveball. The slider is his putaway pitch versus righties and also works like a cutter in on the hands of lefties, while Politi's curveball is a way to freeze righties early in the count to work ahead of them. He's a pretty standard middle reliever who is likely to stick on Baltimore's roster to meet Rule 5 requirements before settling into an up/down role thereafter.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: The Red Sox stretched Politi out and moved him into the rotation toward the end of his 2019 season at High-A. He performed well in that capacity, putting to effective use a mid-90s fastball/high-80s slider combo that is greatly aided by his deceptive delivery, while working to develop a lower-80s curveball and changeup. As he mixed those other two pitches in more frequently during his first full year as a starter, Politi saw the continuation of a years-long decrease in K-rate, while his walks remained at an uncomfortably high 11%. He also gave up 77 hits in his 75 Double-A innings, 11 of which left the park. As such, by the end of the season, he’d transitioned back into a full-time bullpen role, which he continued in the Fall League. He projects as an up/down relief type.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: A Day Three pick in 2018, Politi pitched well enough out of the bullpen in 2019 that the Sox stretched him out late in the season and gave him a handful of starts. During that stretch he struck out 61 in 47 innings. Then we had to wait until 2020 instructs before anyone saw him again, and there Politi was frustrating due to a lack of command. His delivery is deceptive, his fastball has ride at the top of the zone, when he can command his slider it is quite good, and it seems like there are several other possible pitches in the mix to be a potential tertiary offering (a changeup, curveball, maybe a cutter) if it turns out Politi can actually throw strikes and continue developing as a starter. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: A Day Three pick in 2018, Politi pitched well enough out of the bullpen last year that the Sox stretched him out late in the season and gave him a handful of starts. During that stretch he struck out 61 in 47 innings. Politi is deceptive, his fastball has ride at the top of the zone, and he commands his slider and will flash an occasionally good changeup. It's an interesting package with the arrow pointing up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez signed with the Red Sox for $550,000 in April 2018 -- a few weeks before his 17th birthday -- after getting some pro experience with Aguascalientes in the Mexican League. He dominated out of the gate, allowing just one earned run in 23 innings in the Dominican Summer League that year, and he was showing signs of a full-season breakout at Single-A Salem in 2021 (2.03 ERA, 32 strikeouts in 31 innings) when he was dealt to the Nationals in a July deal straight up for Kyle Schwarber. He had been limited by elbow tendinitis at the time of the trade, and after doing some rehab work in the Florida Complex League, he underwent Tommy John surgery in spring 2022, meaning he still hasn’t pitched for a full-season Washington affiliate. Before the elbow issues, the 6-foot right-hander was showing improved velocity to the 92-95 mph range and was touching the high 90s from a high slot. He also sported a mid-80s changeup with good fade, and while lefties still hit him better than righties at Single-A, it should help fend off the splits from getting too extreme. An upper-70s curveball with depth rounded out his arsenal and gave him the three quality pitches needed to start. Command was rarely an issue for Ramirez pre-Tommy John, though that ability to spot the ball well all over the zone will be tested in his return. He has gotten back to playing catch this offseason, and evaluators will be paying attention to how well his repertoire returns when he retakes the mound throughout the summer of his age-22 campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez had some pro ball experience with Aguascalientes in the Mexican League when the Red Sox purchased his contract for $550,000 in April 2018, just a month shy of his 17th birthday. He dominated the Dominican Summer League that season, giving up just one earned run in 23 innings, and proceeded to strike out 24 percent of the batters he faced at Class A Short Season Lowell a year later. The pandemic delayed a further breakout, but Ramirez showed promise upon his return in 2021 with a 2.03 ERA, 32 strikeouts and eight walks in 31 innings at Low-A. Elbow tendinitis limited his first-half contributions, and he was traded to the Nationals straight-up for Kyle Schwarber at the Deadline in July. He rehabbed in the Florida Complex League late in 2021 and then unfortunately needed Tommy John surgery in the spring of 2022, forcing him out for the entire season. The 6-foot right-hander throws from a high slot and has seen his velocity pick up since entering the Minors to the point where he sits in the 92-95 mph range, touching the high-90s on occasion. The mid-80s changeup is his best secondary with promising fade, and it should help him fight rough lefty-righty splits. He isn’t afraid of going to an upper-70s curve that could be a solid third offering with its downward break. Ramirez’s best asset remains his command and ability to spot the ball both up and down in the zone. On paper, he has all the pieces to be a solid back-end starter, even if nothing is a true plus pitch yet. But the elbow concerns lower that floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez broke into pro ball in the Mexican League as a 17-year-old before the Red Sox purchased him from Aguascalientes for $550,000 in April 2018. He allowed just one run in 23 innings in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League that summer, then ranked sixth in strikeout rate (9.2 per innings) in the New York-Penn League in 2019, when he was the short-season circuit's youngest qualifier at age 18. He used his pandemic downtime to get stronger last year and opened eyes with improved stuff in instructional league. That carried into 2021, when he had a 2.03 ERA with 32 strikeouts and only eight walks in 31 innings at Low-A Salem before hitting the IL in late June with right elbow tendinitis. The injury wasn’t enough to scare off the Nationals, however, as Washington picked him up at the Trade Deadline in a swap for Kyle Schwarber. Ramirez works the top and bottom of the strike zone with four-seam and two-seam fastballs, and his velocity jumped from 91-94 in 2019 to averaging 93.5 mph and topping out at 96 more frequently in shorter stints at instructs. He has advanced feel for a mid-80s changeup that fades and sinks. When he stays on top of his upper-70s curveball, it features nice depth and gives him a solid third offering. The most advanced young pitcher in the Boston system at the time of the trade, Ramirez repeats his clean delivery easily and pounds the strike zone. He has the confidence to throw any pitch in any count, and it's growing as his stuff continues to improve. He has a high floor and the possibility of winding up with a solid fastball and curve to go with a plus changeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramirez pitched in the Mexican League at age 17 before the Red Sox purchased him from Aguascalientes for $550,000 in April 2018. He allowed just one run in 23 innings in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League afterward, then skipped a level and thrived as the youngest ERA qualifier (age 18) in the short-season New York-Penn League last year. Using both two- and four-seamers to work the top and bottom of the strike zone, Ramirez sits at 91-94 mph and peaks at 96 mph with his fastballs. He gets downer action on his upper-70s curveball when he stays on top of it, and he throws hitters off balance with a mid-80s changeup with some fade and sink. Ramirez has precocious feel for pitching that stands out more than his stuff. He has a clean delivery, repeats it easily, pounds the strike zone and possesses the confidence to throw any pitch in any count. Though he doesn't have much projection remaining in his 6-foot frame, he might have three solid pitches if he can find a little more power and consistency.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Acquired from Boston in the 2021 Kyle Schwarber trade, Ramirez didn't pitch in 2022 and hasn't yet in 2023 as he recovers from a TJ. Recall that Ramirez also had arm issues throughout 2021, so it has been a few years since we've seen him totally healthy. Fully-operational Ramirez has a vertical arm slot and hand position that create backspin that will let his fastball play atop the strike zone, though he wasn't working up there as often as he could. His slider has effective, vertical movement, and he has fairly advanced arm-side changeup feel. An average athlete with a smaller frame, Ramirez experienced an unexpected velo bump that began at 2020 instructs, where he was 92-94 mph and topping out at 96 without having lost any command. He was viewed as a changeup/command backend type before the velo bump. Still just 22, Ramirez's injury history is long enough to throttle him down into this FV tier and re-evaluate him when he's finally healthy.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Acquired from Boston in the 2021 Kyle Schwarber trade, Ramirez won't pitch in 2022 as he deals with an elbow issue that has plagued him for huge chunks of the last two years. Healthy Ramirez has a vertical arm slot and hand position that create backspin that will let his fastball play atop the strike zone, though he doesn't work up there as often as he could. His slider has effective, vertical movement, and he has fairly advanced arm-side changeup feel. An average athlete with a smaller frame, Ramirez experienced an unexpected velo bump that began at 2020 instructs, where he was 92-94 mph and topping out at 96 without having lost any command, or having begun to overthrow his breaking ball or anything of that nature. He was viewed as a changeup/command backend type before the velo bump, which moved him into the 40+ tier entering 2021 and through the time of the Schwarber trade. In the little bit of 2021 that Ramirez did pitch, he was again sitting 93-94 mph. His injury creates a somewhat awkward 40-man situation, as Ramirez was a possible post-2022 addition, and his injury arguably makes him easier for opposing teams to Rule 5 stash on their 60-day IL. He's a candidate to be one of the prospects teams request medicals for ahead of the Rule 5.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Here's what I wrote about Ramirez last year when he was coming off a very successful 13-start stretch in the New York-Penn League (61 innings, 63 punch outs, 16 walks): "Ramirez has a vertical arm slot and hand position that create backspin that will let his fastball play atop the strike zone, though he doesn't work up there as often as he could. His slider is average but has effective, vertical movement, and he has fairly advanced arm-side changeup feel. An average athlete with a smaller frame, there's no overt physical projection that allows us to get excited about Ramirez growing into a monster fastball, so instead we think he's a developmental fifth starter." Well, Ramirez started throwing harder. He was sitting 92-94 at Instructional League and was topping out at 96 without having lost any command, or having begun to overthrow his breaking ball, or anything of that nature. Changeup/command guys tend to outpace traditional projections and though the developmental setting could have allowed for a short-term velo bump that won't hold over a long season (I have Aldo sitting 90-94 in 2019), Ramirez is still on track to be a pitcher similar to Seabold by the time his 40-man deadline arrives. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text:
For a long time this system has been lousy with undersized, relatively unprojectable pitchability types, and Ramirez is the strike-thrower du jour. He had a very successful 13-start stretch in the New York-Penn League -- 61 innings, 63 punch outs, 16 walks -- working off of three pitches. He has a vertical arm slot and hand position that create backspin that will let his fastball play atop the strike zone, though he doesn't work up there as often as he could. His slider is average but has effective, vertical movement, and he has fairly advanced arm-side changeup feel. 
An average athlete with a smaller frame, there's no overt physical projection that allows us to get excited about Ramirez growing into a monster fastball, so instead we think he's a developmental fifth starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Barlovento, Venezuela, in 2019 for $775,000, Machado was one of the biggest mysteries in the system entering the 2022 season after appearing in just one professional game. Machado was part of the Venezuelan group who stayed in Florida through the pandemic, but his Rookie-level Florida Complex League debut was cut short by a hamstring injury. In ’22, Machado appeared in 90 games with Single-A Dunedin, where he hit .263 with a .687 OPS. A full, healthy season made ’22 a success to begin with, but the Blue Jays were also encouraged by some of Machado’s physical maturation in their program. As draftees flooded into Dunedin, he raised his game and continued to work through scrappy at-bats, showing a little more pop than his one home run suggests. Machado is a switch-hitter, but put up far better numbers batting left-handed (.300) than right-handed (.146), which will be important to monitor in 2023 and beyond. Machado will continue to split his time between shortstop and second base with a chance to stick at short long term. Part of his offensive game will need to make a jump, whether that be in the power or on-base department, but his defensive fundamentals give Machado a good base to work from. A sample of 91 pro games is very shallow to draw from, though, so Machado could still have plenty of development in front of him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed alongside Rikelbin De Castro in ’19 for $775,000, the switch-hitting Machado remains one of the more tantalizing mysteries in the Blue Jays’ system. Machado was part of the Venezuelan group that stayed in Florida throughout the COVID shutdown, and when he finally had an opportunity to make his pro debut in ’21 in the Florida Complex League, that lasted just one plate appearance -- a single -- before a hamstring injury cut his season short. With just one trip to the plate as a pro entering ’22, Machado needs reps and lots of them. Without much power to speak of, Machado will be more of a spray hitter, but he comes with the potential to make contact consistently enough for that to work with his broader profile. A solid athlete, the Blue Jays like how Machado looks defensively and trust he’ll stay at shortstop long-term with a quality throwing arm. That defensive ability will be valuable to supporting Machado’s floor while his offence develops. We’ll finally see some longer stretches of Machado in ’22, giving him one of the widest ranges of outcomes in Toronto’s system. Hitting for average and working walks will be key to his rise, given the lack of power, but Machado’s glove is what has the organization excited about a full season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Machado was signed in 2019 alongside Rikelvin De Castro, and while Machado received the smaller bonus of the two at $775,000, the switch-hitter already profiles as a better bat. Machado was part of the Venezuelan group who stayed in Florida throughout the shutdown and found creative ways to stay physically engaged and work on his game at the hotel. There will be immediate appeal in an athletic, switch-hitting shortstop, and Machado has some legitimate offensive upside from both sides of the plate. Both swings are quick and compact, and there could be some more power for Machado to grow into as his strength naturally develops. Machado will be given every opportunity to stick at shortstop long term, which the Blue Jays believe he’s fully capable of. His throwing arm will be his strongest tool defensively, but the Blue Jays like his defensive actions, too. There’s still plenty of development ahead for the teenager when he gets into Minor League games, but Machado could start to take some serious strides up the board as he puts together his all-around tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays shelled out nearly $2 million to land a pair of promising 16-year-old shortstops at the outset of the 2019 international period, signing Rikelvin De Castro ($1.2 million) and Machado ($775,000) on back-to-back days. While Castro is viewed as the better defender and more likely of the two players to remain at shortstop, Machado, a switch-hitter from Venezuela, could end up as the better hitter. An advanced approach for his age gives Machado a solid foundation as a hitter, and he makes consistent contact from both sides of the plate with a short swing that has little wasted energy. His bat speed and overall ability to impact the baseball should improve as he begins to grow into his wiry-athletic frame, and there are some scouts who believe Machado will develop double-digit home run power. He’s a dynamic athlete on both sides of the ball with average speed that plays up once he’s underway. Machado’s athleticism, tools and feel for the game will give him a chance to stick at shortstop, where he profiles as an above-average defender with range, dependable hands and an above-average arm. Machado’s ceiling is still coming into view and he’ll need years to develop his game in the Minors, but the final product could be an everyday player who contributes in all facets of the game.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Machado only played one game in 2021 due to a hamstring injury. In 2022, he hit .263/.342/.345 with Dunedin, striking out at a somewhat concerning 25% clip, though his in-zone contact rate was somehow still very strong at 86%. Machado still isn't strong enough to swing with real control of the barrel, let alone any sort of power. We're still bullish about his hit tool projection and think he'll attain viable big league physicality through physical maturity, and that part of his strikeout-rich 2022 was due to missing two of the last three years because of the pandemic and injury. Machado is a smooth defender with great actions and enough arm strength for the left side of the infield. His glove is going to carry him to the upper levels, with a bench infield role his most likely outcome assuming the hit tool improves like we think it will.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Machado only played one regular season game in 2021 due to a hamstring injury, and he wasn't on the Jays' instructs roster, which means the only looks scouts had at him were during extended spring training. Reports from that timeframe are consistent with Machado's amateur reports, indicative of a compact, switch-hitting middle infield defender with a utility floor. Recall that the Blue Jays split their 2020 instructs groups in such a way that their younger players were not involved with scoutable, on-field activity, so it has been especially hard for the industry to see Machado since he signed in July of 2019, and he's now a 19-year-old with just one career game played.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: No change here as, like de Castro, Machado was part of the rookie camp contingent rather than the group subject to traditional instructs. Machado is a very flashy, very compact middle infielder with precocious barrel feel for a young hitter, let alone one who switch-hits. The contact ability and defense may need to carry the whole profile because Machado is a smaller-framed player. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Unsigned during the 2018-19 international period, Dominguez moved from Venezuela to the Dominican Republic to focus on improving his velocity. The venue change paid dividends when the Mets inked the right-hander just before his 18th birthday in November 2019. The 2020 shutdown kept Dominguez from seeing the Minors in his first season, though he did stay stateside that summer and work out with other Venezuelans at the Mets’ Spring Training facility. Dominguez remained in Florida in 2021 but was highly limited, making only 10 appearances (12 innings) in the Florida Complex League while the Mets had him focus on developing routines and getting in better shape to handle the rigors of a starting role. Dominguez underwent Tommy John surgery in March and is in line to return for 2023. There remains ample stuff on which to dream here. Dominguez stands 6-foot-5 and uses every bit of that size to throw in the mid-90s, touching as high as 99. The heater works well up in the zone too, when Dominguez is at his best with his command. A low-80s slider -- previously deemed a curve -- shows promising spin and break, but it lacks consistency compared to the fastball. He technically possesses a changeup with some movement, but it has a long way to go to become an average offering. Between last year’s and this year's surgery, Dominguez’s inexperience could mean there’s still room for ample growth, especially when it comes to his secondary pitches. But early results make the 20-year-old look more and more like a future reliever who relies on his velocity to blow by hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It isn’t often a great sign when an international player (outside of Cuba) signs a year after he is first eligible, but the plan has worked out well for Dominguez so far. Originally eligible for the 2018-19 signing period, the Venezuela native finally inked a deal with the Mets in November 2019 following a move to the Dominican Republic, where he focused on improving his velocity. Dominguez has yet to appear in a Minor League game but has some experience stateside after the coronavirus pandemic forced him and other Venezuelans to work out of New York’s Spring Training facility in Port St. Lucie last summer. The 6-foot-5 right-hander uses his size to his advantage to sit in the mid-90s and has touched as high as 99 in the past. The Mets have been pleased with the way his breaking ball – previously classified as a curveball but now looking more like a slider – has progressed because of the way he can spin it. It shows above-average potential with late break. The changeup made strides in 2020 and now shows promising movement of its own. The command needs to be the next thing to come for the tall righty, and New York hopes improvements with his release point will aide in that category once he is able to get in games more consistently. Dominguez has the pieces and physicality in place to be a starter. He just needs the game action to put all of those into place against actual opponents. If the command doesn’t quite come around, the velocity gives him a good shot at seeing Major League time in a bullpen setting, but as a pitcher still only entering his age-19 season, that conversation remains far off.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he was eligible to sign during the 2018 international period, Dominguez instead decided to move to the Dominican Republic and focus on his training, with the goal of improving his prospect stock. The right-hander did exactly that, as his fastball quickly jumped from the low 90s to the mid-90s in a matter of months. The Mets took notice of the Venezuelan hurler’s rapid velocity gains and signed him a few weeks ahead of his 18th birthday, then watched him run his fastball up to 99 mph during the Dominican instructional league. Dominguez is physically strong and advanced for his age, with a 6-foot-5, 195-pound frame that leaves plenty of room for projection. He already knows how to spin the ball and flashed a plus curveball during the instructional league. Like many tall, hard-throwing young pitchers, Dominguez will need to fine-tune his mechanics and delivery as he begins to develop in the pro ranks. Getting stronger should help him in that process, and club officials already like how his arm works. The Mets believe they found a steal in Dominguez, who will pitch at age 18 for all of 2020. He will need to develop a changeup and continue to add strength, though the final product could be a big league starter with electric stuff.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Dominguez was a known and not all that highly regarded pitching prospect at the beginning of 2019, when he was a 17-year-old Venezuelan righty with some effort who sat 90-93 mph. Then he was 94-97 at an event in the summer, which caused teams to reconsider him, though some clubs wanted to see it another time or two to make sure it wasn't an anomaly. The Mets moved quickly, but Dominguez's $95,000 bonus reflected some level of uncertainty. Between when Dominguez was waiting for his contract to be approved and the end of Dominican instructs, he continued to sit in the mid-90s and hit 99, flashing a plus breaking ball at times. He was then deployed with extreme caution in 2021, working in two-inning relief stints with significant rest between outings, sitting 94-95 with sink. He had Tommy John not long before the 2022 season and was still rehabbing as of list publication. Given how he was deployed before the surgery, it's fair to project Dominguez as a reliever at this point, but he's still a high-priority backfield target in case things have somehow taken a leap coming out of rehab.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There was already a Perez-Brewers connection considering Hedbert’s father, Robert, played for the club in 2001. The younger Perez joined Milwaukee for $700,000 out of his native Venezuela in July 2019, and after the lost pandemic season, he got off to a quick stateside start in 2021, slashing .333/.394/.575 with six homers in 32 games in the Arizona Complex League before a brief promotion to Single-A Carolina. He returned to the Mudcats for his age-19 season last year and showed some pop (15 homers) but struggled overall with a .216 average, .272 OBP and 82 wRC+. There is an obvious positive in Perez’s game in his raw power. He’s bulked up in his 5-foot-10 frame from his days playing back home, and the result has been loud exit velocities and a significant portion of his hits going for extra bases when he puts the bat on the ball. Pitch recognition and selection have been issues at this early stage, and those problems not only led to a 29.9 percent K rate in Carolina, but also have kept him from reaching the hitter’s counts that would allow him to swing away more freely. As Perez has grown out at the lower levels, he’s become progressively less toolsy overall. Once a 55 runner, he’s closer to average now and isn’t likely to be a huge stolen-base threat moving forward. The lack of speed and a weak arm have made left field his primary position, and he’ll face a higher offensive threshold there. There are worse places to start than with plus raw slugging ability, and considering Perez will still only be 20 for the entire upcoming season, he has time to improve his overall approach at the dish.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of six-year Major Leaguer Robert Perez signed with the Brewers -- for whom his father played briefly in 2001 -- for $700,000 out of Venezuela in July 2019. It hasn’t taken Perez long to stand out in an organization getting more loaded with outfielders by the year. In 2021, the left-handed slugger slashed .333/.394/.474 with six homers over 32 games in the Arizona Complex League and earned a bump to Low-A Carolina in his age-18 season. Full-season pitchers were able to keep him much more off-balance (25 strikeouts in 65 PA), thus ending Perez’s 2021 on a sour note. An alternate training site participant at just 17 in 2020, Perez struggled with pitch selection and found himself down in a lot of counts at Carolina, leading him to fight off pitches instead of putting good swings on hittable offerings. He is capable of making good strong contact, and he exhibits a good amount of raw power from a bulky 5-foot-10 frame. It plays in games as well, as he showed in Arizona. The Brewers are hopeful that the Carolina bumps are growing pains because if it does come together, Perez still has the chance to be an average hitter at the top level with the way he can pound the ball on contact. Perez looked toolsier upon signing, but as his body has matured, his power remains his only plus skill. His speed and fielding ability are above-average now, though they could grade downward if he continues to prioritize strength, and his arm isn’t seen as much of a weapon these days. While he has years of development ahead of him, Perez is trending toward becoming a power bat in left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prince Fielder moved fast through the Brewers’ Minor League system thanks to a mix of talent and pedigree; he knew his way around professional baseball because he grew up in the game. Now along comes another left-handed hitter with eye-popping tools and impressive poise for his age in Perez, whose father, Robert Perez, wasn’t a player the caliber of Cecil Fielder but nonetheless logged six seasons in the Major Leagues with five different teams including the Brewers in 2001. Hedbert Perez received the second-highest bonus ($700,000) among players signed by Milwaukee during the 2019-20 international period and immediately made an impact during a batting practice session in Milwaukee, launching a series of long home runs to Fielder’s former landing spots before departing for that fall’s instructional league. Despite being denied his official pro debut in 2020, Perez continued to impress with tools on both sides of the ball. At 17 years old he was the youngest player at the Brewers’ alternate training site, getting experience against far more experienced pitchers and some of the Brewers’ tough left-handed pitching prospects like Antoine Kelly and Aaron Ashby. Perez finished the year in the instructional league, then once again was the youngest player in the room when the Brewers included him among 15 players invited to their Minor League mini-camp at the start of Spring Training. Perez has a quick, compact left-handed swing and advanced plate discipline for his age combined with the raw power. In the field, he has an arm for the corners but the speed and instincts to play center field. The Brewers, who prioritize up-the-middle defenders, believe he will stick in center. If his tools and poise lead to production in his long-awaited pro debut, then Perez could continue to rise to the top of the Brewers’ prospect list.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of Robert Perez, an outfielder who played six Major League seasons (1994-2001) with five different teams, Hedbert Perez received the second-highest bonus ($700,000) among players signed by Milwaukee during the 2019-20 international period after he impressed scouts with his athleticism, tools and advanced feel for the game as a Venezuelan amateur. The Brewers brought him to Miller Park for batting practice after he signed, and Perez made the most of the opportunity by hitting some long, big league-esque home runs before opening even more eyes during instructional league. Across-the-board tools highlight Perez’s impressive profile and fuel his impact potential on both sides of the ball. One of the better pure hitters in his class, Perez has a pretty swing for a player his age, combining bat speed and feel for the barrel with a quick, compact left-handed stroke. Those qualities, along with his discerning eye, have led scouts to project Perez as a future above-average hitter, and the fact that he already shows above-average raw power as a teenager makes it easy to dream on his offensive ceiling. More than just a promising young hitter, Perez has the potential to remain in center field long term with his blend of athleticism, plus speed and range, and it certainly doesn’t hurt that he also has great instincts and gets good jumps. His accurate, above-average arm is a weapon up the middle and qualifies him to play either outfield corner. Overall, Perez has one of the highest ceilings in the Brewers’ system and should offer a glimpse of that potential when makes his highly anticipated debut in 2020.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Cooler heads acknowledged the hit tool risk here, even after Hedbert's fantastic complex-level season, but not even pragmatic prospect prognosticators predicted he'd have such a rude awakening in full-season ball, where Perez hit .216 in 2022. He still has exciting pull-side power for a left-handed hitter, but the track record of prospects who strike out this much at such a low level isn't great, and as a left field-only runner and thrower, Perez doesn't have secondary skills to fall back on.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Perez is a physical, lefty-hitting outfielder with a swing that is compact but still has some lift, especially to his pull side. He runs well, has shown advanced feel to hit as a pro, and is generating more power on contact than is typical for a hitter his age. He doesn't have big, frame-based power projection but already has plenty of pull-side juice. Despite his present physicality, Perez wasn't assigned to an affiliate right away and hung back in Extended until the start of the Complex League season. He crushed it in Arizona, hitting .333/.394/.575 before a September promotion to A-ball, where Perez didn't hit. The combination of Perez's BABIP-inflated line in Arizona, his maxed-out physique, his tiny walk rate (just 4.5%), and the fact that his underlying hit data doesn't support his summer line all create real trepidation among scouts and analysts. Perez is a projectionless left fielder whose early-career on-paper plate discipline is scary. He has the power to carry a corner outfield profile if he can hit enough, but that's far from a foregone conclusion at this point, and there's risk of limited athletic longevity due to Perez's build at this stage. He's a high-risk prospect with the ceiling of an everyday left fielder.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Perez is a physical, lefty-hitting outfielder with a swing that is compact but still has some lift, especially to his pull side. He runs well, showed advanced feel to hit when he first turned pro, and is generating more power on contact than is typical for a hitter his age. He doesn't have big, frame-based power projection but already has plenty of pull-side juice. He swung and missed a lot this spring, which was surprising given his early career output. I also have a 30 on Perez's arm based on my 2020 fall look, which I think limits him to left field only. He and Joe Gray share the power/whiff/corner phenotype but Gray is further along the minor league ladder and has put a favorable plate discipline track record on paper while Hedbert doesn't yet.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Perez is a physical, lefty-hitting outfielder with a swing that is compact but still has some lift, especially to his pull side. He runs well, has advanced feel to hit, and is generating more power on contact than is typical for a hitter his age. He doesn't have big, frame-based power projection but might hit enough that it doesn't matter. He's likely four or five years out, but has the tools of an everyday corner guy if, in fact, the bat is as advanced as it appeared after he signed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates handed out 17 six-figure bonuses during the 2018-19 international signing period. Nolasco was right in the middle, getting $235,000 to sign out of the Dominican Republic. He immediately opened eyes with a very strong Dominican Summer League performance in 2019, finishing with a .302/.373/.472 line. His highly anticipated United States debut was delayed, first by the pandemic in 2020, and then a minor injury in the spring of 2021 that kept him from going to full-season ball. He spent the summer posting a .961 OPS in the Florida Complex League. Nolasco has the chance to be an impact hitter from the right side of the plate. He has ridiculous raw power, with the chance for it to be plus in time as he improves his approach. Already showing present strength, he needs to refine his movements in the box so he can get the bat head out front more, but he does show some strike zone discipline and the willingness to draw walks and work counts to get to pitches he can do damage with. In his short time as a pro, he’s already put up impressive Trackman data in terms of things like exit velocity. Not particularly speedy, Nolasco is limited defensively to an outfield corner. He does have enough arm for the prototypical right fielder and he’ll likely see time moving forward in both spots to see which is a better fit. Wherever he plays, it’s the bat that has the chance to move him up the ladder, with physicality and youth on his side.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Pirates went after talent during the 2018-19 international signing period, they clearly targeted hitters, with 10 of their top 11 bonuses being handed to position players. One of them was Nolasco, a physical outfielder who got $235,000 to sign. He made his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League and immediately showed some of his offensive upside by hitting .302/.373/.472 over 54 games. Nolasco is lean and ripped and can really impact the baseball from the right side of the plate. He makes consistent, really hard contact, recording a maximum exit velocity of 110 mph in the DSL. He has a solid approach at the plate with the chance to hit for average and power. He’s not a burner, but runs well enough and throws well enough to be a solid outfielder, though he’s definitely a corner outfield type. In the end, it’s going to be all about his bat, which he’s bringing to the United States for the first time as an 18-year old.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Nolasco had two years of surface-level statistical success in rookie ball and the huge exit velos to match, but now after three pro seasons, his strikeout rates show a troubling upward trend. They've tripled since his claim-staking 2019 DSL season and Nolsaco K'd at a whopping 34% rate in the 2022 Florida State League. Some of his early-career success seems to have stemmed from his physical maturity. His Adonis-like physique helps him generate plus pull-side power, and he will show it to you without overswinging - he simply lacks bat control and breaking ball recognition. It felt like the Pirates were slow-playing him a little too much after the pandemic (Nolasco was easily physical enough to go to Low-A in 2021), but perhaps they simply knew he wasn't ready to parse full-season pitching. There's still some prospect clout here because of Nolasco's power and long-haul physicality, but at this stage, he should be considered more of power-driven flier than a likely big leaguer. Be warned that he may hit for huge power at Greensboro in 2023, but the key thing to watch is his strikeout rate.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Nolasco built upon his impressive pro debut with a .284/.409/.552 line on the complex. He has an Adonis-like physique, much more physical than the typical pro ballplayer, let alone one his age. Nolasco has sizable present power without overswinging, and his statistical production and underlying TrackMan/Hawkeye data corroborates enthusiasm regarding his raw power. There aren't many teenagers who generate this kind of buzz from eyeball scouts and also perform at this level on paper without an obvious red flag, but Nolasco is also about as old (and in some instances a little bit older) than a bunch of the hitters Pittsburgh pushed to full-season ball at some point in 2021. It's physically exceptional individuals like Nolasco who tend to feast on underdeveloped pitching, and it's possible that's what he's done so far. The 2020 shutdown cost him what would have been his Florida Complex season and he probably should have been in A-ball at some point in 2021, especially if the Pirates wanted to test his hit tool at a pace that better fits with his Rule 5/40-man timeline, which is 2022. Instead it looks like Nolasco will be subject to the slow cooker developmental approach the Pirates seem to be taking with lots of their young players, putting them further away from the big leagues during their Rule 5 year than teams are typically comfortable entertaining with a possible draft pick.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There's no change to Nolasco's blurb. He was at instructs, but I can't find anyone who saw enough of him to have a strong opinion, which may be due to reasons I address in the System Overview: Many of the international prospects Pittsburgh has signed over the last two years have become of interest to opposing teams, and this is especially true of Nolasco, who has quickly added mass to his frame (his shoulders are huge, as if he's got cantaloupe halves perched on either side of his neck) and grown into considerable power. His swing is not presently geared for the kind of in-game power you hope for based on his raw juice, but the barrel feel and ball/strike recognition are fairly advanced for a player this age. Corner outfield profiles are tough but the early indicators here are strong. (Fall Instructional League)

His swing is not presently geared for the kind of in-game power you hope for based on Nolasco's raw juice, but the barrel feel and ball/strike recognition are fairly advanced for a player this age.
