fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: After having missed all of 2021 with an elbow strain, Murray threw just 20 innings at Double-A last season before being shut down for Tommy John surgery in May and is set to miss the first portion of the 2023 season as well. In those 20 innings of work, his fastball velocity was down, living around 86 mph, as opposed to in its previous high-80s/low-90s habitat. He also struggled to locate his slider, throwing it for a strike just 44% of the time, and both pitches fell short of league average in terms of their swing-and-miss metrics. In his four starts in 2022, there was a significant difference between his results the first time through the order compared to subsequent face-offs: in innings one through three, opponents put up an anemic .146/.327/.268 slash line, but in innings four through six, they slashed .312/.395/.750. The optimism surrounding Murray’s future as a big leaguer requires dialing back to the 2020 alt site and his meteoric rise through the system in 2019. If he can recapture that form, he could still slot into a short relief role.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: A high spin rate, backspinning axis and flat approach angle give Murray's fastball big time carry in the zone, and it sneaks past hitters even though it only sits in the 88-91 mph range and tops out at 92-93. It enabled him to reach the upper levels of the minors in just one year, and he finished 2019 having made eight good starts at Double-A, then was part of the Jays' alt site contingent in 2020. He seemed likely to debut at some point in 2021 but instead he missed the whole year with an elbow strain, pitching just two-thirds of an inning during an August rehab outing, after which he was shut down again. Healthy Murray looks like a multi-inning relief piece, as his fastball deception plays best in shorter stints.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: A high spin rate, backspinning axis and flat approach angle give Murray's fastball big time carry in the zone, and it sneaks past hitters even though it only sits in the 88-91 range and tops out at 92-93. It enabled him to reach the upper-levels of the minors in just one year, and he finished 2019 having made eight good starts at Double-A, then was part of the Jays' alt site contingent in 2020. He showed a little bit of a velocity bump there, further bolstering confidence that his fastball will play against big league hitters even though it isn't that hard. He can pair the fastball with both breaking balls, and he throws a lot of strikes, but not with enough precision to start in my opinion. I'm skeptical of it working in a rotation, and instead think Murray will end up working in a long relief role. (Alternate site)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: A high spin rate, backspinning axis and flat approach angle give Murray's fastball big time carry in the zone, and it blows past hitters even though it only sits in the 88-91 range. It has enabled Murray to reach the upper-levels of the minors in just one year, and he finished 2019 having made eight good starts at Double-A. He can pair the fastball with both breaking balls, and he throws a lot of strikes. I'm skeptical of it working in a rotation but a Yusmeiro Petit sort of relief role has precedent.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Murray earned Mid-American Conference pitcher of the year honors as a sophomore and junior in 2017 and ’18 at Kent State, going a combined 15-3 with 251 strikeouts over 170 2/3 innings across the two seasons. After going in the eighth round to the Blue Jays and signing a $169,600 bonus, Murray carried his success right into the Minor Leagues in short-season ball, posting a 1.75 ERA over 25 2/3 innings. In ’19, Murray established himself as a legitimate prospect with a 2.75 ERA over 137 1/3 innings, striking out 169 batters between Low-A, High-A and Double-A. He had a shot at impacting the MLB club in ’21, but elbow issues wiped out nearly his entire season. Those are now behind him entering ’22. The headliner with Murray is the “invisiball,” a fastball with an incredibly high spin rate that allows him to blow hitters away up in the zone despite sitting in the low-90s. Murray’s fastball had ticked up to the 92-93 mph range, but the right-hander could look more natural slightly below that, so his velocity is worth monitoring throughout ’22. A 12-6 curveball is Murray’s second-best weapon while his slider is close behind and the changeup is still developing. There’s certainly bullpen potential for Murray, with a multi-inning role appealing, but the Blue Jays will keep him as a traditional starter to open the ’22 season as he builds back up. Murray’s fastball is an MLB-ready pitch and he’s a proven producer at each level of the Minor Leagues, so even though he was left off the 40-man roster this past offseason, he’ll be a candidate to jump onto it if he’s pitching well at any point in ’22.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After logging 39 innings as a true freshman in 2016, Murray garnered Mid-American Conference pitcher of the year honors as both a sophomore and junior, going a combined 15-3 in 30 starts with 251 strikeouts in 170 2/3 innings between the two years. The Blue Jays selected Murray in the eighth round of the 2018 Draft, signed him for $169,600 and watched him continue to dominate in his pro debut with the Vancouver Canadians. Murray split the ’19 season between three levels, posting a cumulative ERA of 2.75 over 137 1/3 innings with 169 strikeouts. He missed much of the first half of 2021 with an elbow sprain but avoided surgery and returned to the Minor League mound in August. Murray’s greatest tool is his fastball, which has an elite spin rate. This “invisiball” is an excellent weapon up in the zone and has taken another step forward with a recent velocity bump that sees Murray sitting in the 92-93 mph range. This isn’t typically the velocity that would blow hitters away, but the spin rate is what makes it special. A 12-6 curveball with good bite is Murray’s best secondary pitch. Murray will also feature an average slider while his changeup has shown encouraging development, and he's also working on a cutter that's becoming effective. One of the most unique evaluations in the Blue Jays’ system, Murray made great use of the shutdown in 2020 and will now have a shot to prove that his fastball can fool more advanced hitters in the upper Minors, too. A multi-inning relief role is possible, but the Blue Jays still see Murray as a starter, giving him multiple paths to the Major Leagues.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Lewis is an explosive rotational athlete with big, switch-hitting bat speed and poor barrel accuracy. He tends to swing through the center of the zone and misses the stuff he doesn't run into, but it sure does look pretty, and once you watch Lewis lay into a few, you understand why he got nearly $1 million to sign. So far in 2023, Lewis has stopped playing shortstop and instead is playing a mix of 2B/3B, and he's pretty rough around the edges at those spots. Consider him a fairly young late-bloomer with premium athletic traits and very raw baseball acumen at this stage.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: It was first evident that Lewis had taken a sizable step forward in the physicality department (without compromising his twitch and straight line speed) during 2020 instructs. He was weak with the bat as an amateur but showed noticeably more pull-side pop at the end of the year. That has continued, and now Lewis is showing plus-plus bat speed from the left side of the plate. He has a bottom-hand dominant swing from the left side and needs to incorporate his whole body to swing this hard, but Lewis can dial his swing's effort up or down situationally and shows the ability to shorten up and spray all-fields contact against pitches all over the zone. He is an extremely aggressive hitter, perhaps because he can basically hit anything he tries to, and this creates bust risk since indiscriminate approaches have been the undoing of many talented prospects. Across a couple thousand scouting reports I write at this site every year, I probably use the phrase "five-tool potential" fewer than five times. It applies here. Lewis could become a switch-hitting leadoff man with power and speed in the Jimmy Rollins mold (without the 70 arm).

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Much of the focus surrounding the teenage hitters on this list centered on how they looked when they arrived at instructs in the fall, and Lewis is one who took a sizable step forward in the physicality department without compromising his twitch and straight line speed. He was weak with the bat as an amateur but showed noticeably more pull-side pop during 2020 instructs. We still know very little about the feel to hit aspect here, as scattered looks at Lewis in the fall didn't really clarify any of that, but Lewis is an obvious up-the-middle athlete who appears to be growing into some power. The year off arguably hurts him less than others because he was so young to begin with and only now is he close to the age of the average draft-eligible high schooler. He's a priority complex-level follow for clubs. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Quick as lightning, Lewis is a frame/athleticism projection infielder who is currently weak with the bat. Depending on how his swing and power develop as he matures, he could be a well-rounded second baseman with elite speed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of a growing contingent of Bahamians in the Marlins organization, Lewis has drawn comparisons to countryman Jazz Chisholm for his package of power, speed and twitchy athleticism in a compact frame. Signed for $950,000 in 2019, he had his pro debut delayed until 2021 because of the pandemic. Personal issues and a broken hamate limited him to just 51 games in Single-A at age 19 last year and his performance has declined while he has repeated the level in 2023. A switch-hitter, Lewis has good bat-to-ball skills and a decent understanding of the strike zone. He exhibits electric bat speed from both sides of the plate and has gotten considerably stronger since turning pro, but he hits too many groundballs and has yet to figure out how to tap into his plus raw power. He can get overly pull-conscious and needs to make adjustments to better handle breaking balls. Lewis has well-above-average speed and uses it aggressively on the bases, stealing 16 in 17 attempts last season. His quickness doesn't play quite as well in the field, where he has average range at second base and perhaps a tick better than that at third. His average arm is better suited for second, where his fast hands help him turn double plays.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lewis signed for $950,000 in 2019, receiving the highest bonus among Bahamians in that international class. Though the pandemic wiped out the Minor League season and what would have been his pro debut the following summer, he impressed in instructional league that fall. When he finally got a chance to play in 2021, he batted .302/.354/.497 with 18 extra-base hits and nine steals in 43 games as an 18-year-old in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. Lewis is reminiscent of countryman Jazz Chisholm with his combination of twitchy athleticism, power and speed in a compact frame. A switch-hitter with a quick swing from both sides of the plate, he has gotten stronger since signing and opened eyes by displaying at least average power in his debut. His hand-eye coordination and patient approach allow him to make consistent contact, though he'll have to prove he can handle quality breaking balls at higher levels. With his well-above-average speed, Lewis is a base-stealing threat and covers ground in the middle infield. The Marlins believe he has the actions and solid arm strength to handle shortstop, though he probably won't get much of a chance as he rises through the Minors alongside Kahlil Watson and Jose Salas. Lewis spent most of last summer at second base, where his quick hands help him turn double plays, and he can become an average or better defender as he develops more consistency.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Hendrick was drafted as a bit of a developmental project. While he was old for his high school class, the Western Pennsylvania prepster was raw relative to his peers in a few ways. Chief among them, he had some concerning swing-and-miss tendencies and was in flux mechanically, as his swing changed a few times during his pre-draft summer. Because of his location, he basically had no 2020 varsity season since things didn't really get going before the shutdown. The Reds still bet on his power, which was among the best in the entire 2020 draft class, and drafted him 12th overall. Hendrick has swung and missed a ton in two years of pro ball. The entire Florida State League ran exorbitant strikeout rates in 2021, but Hendricks didn't come down upon initial assignment there in '22 and stayed north of 35% when he was promoted from Daytona to Dayton. His swing is explosive but grooved, cutting through the middle of the zone without much variation to match pitch locations. We're talking about a sub-60% contact rate here. Hendrick's saving grace is that when he does make contact, he's doing huge damage. He somehow managed to hit 21 homers in just 109 games in 2022 even while striking out 37% of the time, and his hard-hit and barrel rates are already above the big league average for a right fielder. It's not a good sign to strike out this much in A-ball, though, and if we take a step back and view Hendrick without the context of his draft position, he looks like a low-probability, power-only flier.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Hendrick was drafted as a bit of a developmental project. While he was old for his high school class, the Western Pennsylvania prepster was raw relative to his peers in a few ways. Chief among them, he had some concerning swing-and-miss tendencies, and was in flux mechanically, as his swing changed a few times during his pre-draft summer. Because of his location, he basically had no 2020 varsity season since things didn't really get going before the shutdown. While strikeout rates at Low-A Southeast in 2021 were high across the entire league, Hendrick's 38% punchout rate is a concerning indicator. His swing is explosive, but grooved, cutting through the middle of the zone without much variation to match pitch location. The bat speed and power components of the profile, which drove teams to consider Hendrick in the middle third of the first round, are still evident, and even if Hendrick develops a 35- or 40-grade bat, he'll probably do enough damage on contact to be a platoon bat. That's the role he's tracking toward.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: The Reds have taken several old-for-the-class high schoolers over the last few years and the most recent (and most talented) is Hendrick. It is somewhat concerning that Hendrick was not only older than most of his elite high school peers on the 2020 Draft showcase circuit but that he was older and still swung and missed a lot during that stretch. This, combined with his corner outfield defensive projection, makes him a prospect of extreme variance and risk since he'll need to really rake to be an everyday player. But he also tinkered with his swing during that pre-draft summer and at times it had ridiculous length and noise it's unlikely to once he has received pro instruction for a while. Plus, he was coming from Western Pennsylvania varsity ball, which is not nearly as good as that in the Southeast, Texas or California, which is where most of his opponents were from during the 2020 process. Let's also not lose sight of Hendrick's ability. He was the most explosive rotator in the entire 2020 class (and it really wasn't close) regardless of demographic, and carried among the biggest raw power projections because of his big, square-shouldered frame. He needs reps against good pitching, and time to adjust to what will likely be some initial failure. He got his first exposure to it during instructs and responded pretty well. He'll stay in the 45+ FV tier along with similar high-variance and high-risk prospects until he builds a statistical foundation in pro ball. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020updated
fangraphs.text: Kendrick tinkered with his swing last summer amid his issues making contact with showcase pitching, a dry spell made more concerning by his age relative to the rest of the class. It makes him a high-risk prospect, but Hendrick is the most explosive rotator in this whoe class and it really isn't close. He he among the bst raw power projection in the class and it's possible he just needs reps against good pitching, reps he hasn't had as many of coming up in Western Pennsylvania.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hendrick had an up-and-down summer showcase circuit in 2019, at times looking like one of the top high school power hitters in the country and at times looking lost, though he did play for USA Baseball’s 18U team that won silver at the World Cup in Korea. His 2020 season in the Pittsburgh area was all but wiped out by the pandemic, but the Reds bought his power potential at No. 12 overall that summer and signed him for $4 million. Since then, the outfielder has had trouble finding his groove at the plate. After shaking off an injury-riddled first full season, Hendrick’s prodigious power did show up in games in 2022 as he homered 21 times in 388 at-bats. That unfortunately also came with a 37.2 percent strikeout rate across two levels of A ball, but there were some signs of things clicking, albeit inconsistently, cutting down the swing-and-miss a little and getting to his power over the last month and change of last season. He needs to slow himself down and let his barrel stay in the zone a bit longer, with more than enough strength if he can focus with a left-center-field approach, the left-handed hitter has a chance to produce more regularly. Hendrick is a good athlete who runs pretty well and can steal a base. While he’s best suited in right field -- where his strong arm also profiles well -- he’s shown he’s more than capable of playing center field if needed. He’ll need to find a way to make consistent contact to profile well as a regular in either spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds certainly haven’t been afraid to take hitters with their top pick in Drafts over the years, going the position player route with their first selection in five of the last seven years. Three of those have been college players and two have been high school, with catcher Tyler Stephenson going No. 11 back in 2015 and Hendrick going No. 12 overall in 2020. The Pittsburgh area prep standout’s debut in 2021 was a bit of a mixed bag, showing off some of the offensive tools that made him worth a $4 million bonus, but also struggling to make contact and dealing with a leg injury that limited him to just 63 games in Low-A in 2021. Healthy in 2022, the power showed up, but consistency remained elusive. Hendrick still has the raw tools as a left-handed hitter that got scouts excited when he was in high school, with elite bat speed and strength which leads to tremendous raw power. He showed flashes of getting to that power during his debut, and while he showed patience (19.2 percent walk rate) he also struck out way too much (37.6 percent), a trend that continued in 2022. It was more about focusing too much on launch angle power to his pull side than it was about chasing out of the zone or poor pitch recognition, and there’s hope he can make adjustments to get back to a gap-to-gap approach that allows him to get to his power more naturally. Hendrick has trimmed down and is more agile and mobile than he’d been previously, with some thinking he’s moving well enough to play center field. He likely fits better in right field, where his above-average arm would play well, with the hope that he can find a level of consistency to fit the power profile for the corner spot as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the Pittsburgh area isn’t exactly known as a huge amateur baseball hotbed, there have been some first-round quality bats to come out of the high school ranks in the region. Back in 2003, the Pirates took Neil Walker No. 11 overall and more recently, Alex Kirilloff went 15th to the Twins in 2016. In 2020, it was Hendrick’s turn when the Reds took him at No. 12 and signed him for $4 million, then saw him impress late in the alternate camp and during instructional league play. At his best, Hendrick’s left-handed bat is what stands out the most. He has as much raw power as anyone from the 2020 Draft and when he’s on time at the plate, it’s shown up in games against very good competition. He has very quick hands and plus bat speed, with leverage and loft and the ball jumps off his bat, while the bat head going through the zone sounds like a helicopter. He has, at times, listened to too many people in terms of his setup at the plate, forcing him get out of sync and leading to more swing-and-miss. There’s some rawness to his game, but that will be offset by the plus work ethic that was on display last summer after he signed. Hendrick isn’t a burner, but he is very athletic and runs well. The Reds will let him continue to play center field for now until he shows he can’t handle staying up the middle, but he has the arm and bat to profile well in right, so don’t be surprised to see him get time in both spots in the future.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Greene came over from the Mets in the Francisco Lindor deal and has an interesting blend of soft skills and frame projection. He's an extremely patient (arguably passive) hitter with below-average bat speed and power right now, but he is super lanky and loose and should grow into more strength and power as he matures. Greene's feel to hit is not as advanced as his idea of the strike zone, and because he's so skinny and young, he needs to use his whole body to swing hard and tends to take big rips right through the center of the zone without real feel for the barrel. Scouts don't think he can play center field, which makes it imperative that he start to get stronger and make more authoritative contact. Because he's treaded water in these areas for the last year, Greene is more in a late-projection flier category now than he is a high-ceiling, high-variance prospect. Were he a college hitter, he'd be set to go late in Day Two of the draft.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Greene came over from the Mets in the Francisco Lindor deal and has an interesting blend of soft skills and power projection. He's an extremely patient hitter with below-average bat speed and power right now, but he is super lanky and loose and should grow into more strength and power as he matures. Greene's feel to hit is not as advanced as his idea of the strike zone and because he's so skinny and young, he needs to use his whole body to swing hard and tends to take big rips right through the center of the zone without real feel for the barrel. He glides from gap-to-gap and is a viable center field candidate for now, though at his age and with his frame there's a chance he fills out in a way that pushes him to a corner, but of course that might come with lots of power. Still in very nascent stages of development, Greene is a slow-burning prospect who needs to get stronger to be a big leaguer at all, but he could break out in a big way if that physicality arrives.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Greene was a 2020 draftee out of a SoCal high school, and he's a frame-based projection prospect who may have had a bigger breakout senior year had the pandemic not squashed his pre-draft season. Teams and scouts who liked him best as an amateur thought he had pretty good feel for contact and were projecting on both his broad-shouldered, He's an average athlete who struggled to get over his front side on throws from the outfield during my looks at him in 2019. That's one of a few developmental things to watch as Greene traverses the minors. The big one, though, is his swing. As an amateur (again, going off my 2019 summer looks here) his swing was really long and needed pretty significant polish to be playable, but he wasn't loading his hands quite as deep during his first pro instructs, and he had a better Fall than expected. It's likely that Cleveland's amateur report drove their desire to acquire Greene since he was a recent draftee who only saw instructs action. And in this regard Greene isn't your typical Cleveland prospect in that he was a little older than the typical high school prospect and is already 19 and a half. However, since you're reading this list, you know they have a penchant for SoCal hitters. Some scouts do not agree with me about the swing. They like Greene's cut and had him in the late-first, early-second round mix. I had him in the third round as a higher variance sort, with the speed for center field (for now), considerable body projection (which might impact the range in center), and the need for a swing overhaul. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020updated
fangraphs.text: Greene is a good-framed high school outfielder with a great set of wheels. He has some pull pop and occasionally takes a gorgeous, low-ball swing that shows of power in that direction, but aside from last Area Codes he hasn't had a lot of bat-to-ball success. He's a high-variance high schooler because of the risk associated with the hit tool.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene starred at the 2019 Area Code Games and as part of a scout team that faced the U.S. national 18-and-under squad, propelling him to the Mets in the supplemental second round a year later. New York traded him to the Guardians along with Andrés Giménez, Amed Rosario and pitching prospect Josh Wolf for Francisco Lindor and Carlos Carrasco in January 2021, so his pro debut came with his second organization. He has one of the higher ceilings among the system's outfielders but will require time to develop. Greene has some natural feel for hitting and makes consistent line-drive contact from the left side of the plate. He employed an extremely patient approach in his debut, drawing 35 walks in 43 games while repeatedly using the opposite field. He has enough bat speed and projectable strength to deliver 15-20 homers per season if he looks to turn on more pitches and launch them in the air. While Greene has plus speed, he's still learning how to get the most out of it as a basestealer and center fielder. He's smoothing out his reads and routes in center, where his quickness helps him recover from some of his mistakes. His fringy arm strength is playable in center field but precludes him from right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene's athleticism stood out on the prep showcase circuit in 2019, when he starred at the Area Code Games and as part of a scout team that faced the U.S. national 18-and-under squad. The Mets made him a supplemental second-round pick last June and signed him away from a Missouri commitment for $850,000. His only experience with the Mets came in instructional league before they traded him to the Indians along with Andrés Gimenez, Amed Rosario and pitching prospect Josh Wolf for Francisco Lindor and Carlos Carrasco in January. Greene has the hand-eye coordination and line-drive-oriented left-handed stroke to hit for average. Scouts believe he relied more on natural ability than swing mechanics or approach as an amateur, giving him the opportunity to improve quickly as he gets more instruction in pro ball. He has the bat speed and projectable strength to develop 15-20 home run power, especially if he adds some more loft. With speed that earns plus and even some well-above-average grades from some evaluators, Greene is aggressive on the bases. His quickness helps him outrun some of his mistakes, but he needs to improve his reads and routes in center field. If he doesn't, his fringy arm strength will relegate him to left field.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Burns had a rough season at Akron as he started to move away from his angle-dependent fastball, which he threw about two-thirds of the time in college and in 2021, and leaned more on his secondary stuff, which aside from his slider, isn't very good. Whether he can develop a third viable pitch will dictate whether Burns can stick at the back of a rotation or merely act as upper-level depth.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Burns' college numbers (a 2.86 career ERA notched mostly against the SEC, with a 3-to-1 K/BB ratio) were more impressive than his repertoire, which is spearheaded by an angle-reliant fastball and an above-average slider. While he touched 97 mph at Auburn, he only averaged about 92, and while he fills the zone with it, his command is imprecise. Historically, Burns has leaned heavily on his fastball. He used it 66% of the time at Auburn and 61% of the time last year. Typically, Burns has terrific feel for his slider, which he command consistently to his glove side. His changeup spin rates have changed over time, indicating he has a relatively new grip that better kills the spin on that pitch, though he still barely throws it. His curve and slider have overlapping velocity bands, but they have clear and distinct shape from one another. With all the strikes and a bevy of average pitches, Burns projects as a high-probability backend starter.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: I'm a little lighter on Burns than the industry consensus, which tends to have him as a low variance 45 FV arm. I don't think statistical success for SEC pitching necessarily translates to pro ball (see: Pilkington, Konnor) and Burns is a squat guy with a high-effort delivery whose stuff is just okay. He was up to 97 before his junior year but I have him sitting 90-92 and touching 95 during the college season, then throwing about that hard in a single-inning Fall outing with Cleveland. Burns does have a tight slider in the 78-81 mph range; his curveball velocity band overlaps with the slider a bit but it has distinct shape. He also throws a mid-80s changeup with sink, but worked very, very heavily off the fastball in college. I'd like to see his secondary usage increase in pro ball. Burns also has advanced pitchability elements, and he'll vary his delivery home to mess with hitters' timing. He profiles as a four-pitch rotation piece who'll outpace my projection if he can either a) show he can execute all his secondary pitches consistently or b) add velocity. I think the former is more likely. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020updated
fangraphs.text: Burns is a bulldog righty with running low-90s heat, several quality secondaries and starter command. Was 90-95 t97 in a 2020 pre-season outing, looking very crisp.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burns flashed first-round stuff and won Gatorade's Alabama high school player of the year award in 2017, but dropped to the Yankees in the 37th round because he was strongly committed to Auburn. He succeeded 2018 No. 1 overall pick Casey Mize as the Tigers' No. 1 starter in his final two seasons before signing for a below-slot $1.6 million as a supplemental first-rounder in 2020. He performed well while advancing to Double-A in his first two years as a pro but missed time with a sore elbow in 2021 and a shoulder strain last season. After working with a 92-95 mph fastball and touching 97 with some armside run on his fastball in 2021, Burns spent much of last year operating more at 90-93, though he still commanded his heater well. His most dependable pitch is a mid-80s slider with depth, and he can turn it into a harder, tighter cutter as well. He lands his upper-70s curveball for strikes and also mixes in a low-80s changeup with sink. Burns flashed solid control in the past but his walk rate jumped from 3.4 per nine innings in his first pro season to 4.6 last year, when he didn't challenge hitters as much with slightly diminished stuff. He's small for a starter and has durability concerns that date back to college, where he had shoulder issues in 2019. If he can regain some velocity and stay healthy, he might be a No. 4 starter, though he's starting to trend toward becoming a multi-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burns flashed first-round stuff as Gatorade's Alabama high school player of the year in 2017, but he was strongly committed to Auburn and followed 2018 No. 1 overall pick Casey Mize as the Tigers' Friday-night starter in his final two college seasons. The Guardians selected him 36th overall in 2020, the highest pick they've spent on a college arm since taking Drew Pomeranz at No. 5 a decade earlier, and signed him for a below-slot $1.6 million. They handled him carefully in his successful 2021 pro debut, starting him once a week in High-A and giving him two weeks off when he came down with elbow soreness in midsummer. Burns usually works at 92-95 mph and touches 97 with some run on his four-seam fastball, and his ability to spot it on either side of the plate may be more impressive than its velocity (which fluctuated after his stint on the injured list) or life. His best secondary pitch is his plus slider/cutter, which arrives in the upper-80s and helped him to have more success against lefties than righties in High-A. He also throws a 78-82 mph downer curveball that has gotten more consistent in pro ball and has some feel for a low-80s changeup with some sink. With the ability to throw four pitches for strikes and advanced command of his fastball, Burns has a high floor as well as the upside of a mid-rotation starter. The biggest concern is his durability because he's small for a starter, had shoulder issues in 2019 before his elbow flared up last year and his stuff has declined at the end of his last two full seasons. If he can stay healthy, his biggest backers believe he could be similar to fellow former Southeastern Conference standout Sonny Gray.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Burns flashed first-round stuff when he was Gatorade's Alabama High School Player of the Year in 2017, but worries about his size and signability dropped him to the Yankees in the 37th round. He didn't sign with New York, then worked his way into Auburn's rotation as a freshman and succeeded 2018 No. 1 overall pick Casey Mize as the Tigers' ace during the next two seasons. The Indians signed him for a below-slot $1.6 million as the 36th overall choice last June, the highest they've taken a college arm since grabbing Drew Pomeranz at No. 5 a decade earlier. When he's on, Burns can feature two plus pitches in his fastball and breaking ball. His four-seamer sits at 92-95 mph and tops out at 97 with some run, and he shows the ability to locate it on either side of the plate. His breaker can combine curveball depth with slider velocity in the low 80s at times and devolve into a slurve at others. Burns also has a sinking changeup that can become an average third offering. He throws strikes but comes with some durability concerns because he's 6 feet tall, had shoulder problems in 2019 and his stuff tends to dip late in the season. The highest-ranked college pitcher on this list, he has a higher floor than the high school arms ranked ahead of him and his biggest backers see similarities between him and another smaller former Southeastern Conference standout, Sonny Gray.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: The ultra-lanky Blakely took just shy of $1 million to eschew a commitment to Auburn. Drafted as a raw, long-levered SS/3B from Michigan, Blakely has been barbecuing in the lower levels for the last few years. His strikeout rates are untenable, and after an improvement in 2022, they are back in the 40% range early in 2023. But Blakely is capable of some incredible things over at third base, and I tend to give projectable left-handed hitters like this a little while longer to grow into their bodies and swings. Readers should consider him a low-probability prospect at this point, but he brings potentially elite defense to the table, something none of the other struggling bats at Tri-City can tout.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: The ultra-lanky Blakely took just shy of $1 million to eschew a commitment to Auburn. Drafted as a raw, long-levered SS/3B from Michigan, Blakely spent 2021 on the complex, sandwiching a rough summer between a good-looking Extended and instructs. He's a smooth, loose, lefty-hitting shortstop with an exciting, projectable frame. Blakely has good defensive hands and feet but his internal clock wasn't calibrated for the pace of summer showcase ball, and he's put forth a mixed defensive performance as a pro, often making acrobatic plays to corral the baseball but then failing to make accurate throws to first to complete the play. While Blakely played all over the infield in 2021, he's likely a long-term third base fit. Based on what he showed last year, he has the tools to be plus there with experience, but he needs to throw with more conviction. It doesn't always look pretty, but Blakely can recognize breaking stuff and ball and strikes. His on-paper performance during the ACL season was actually fine until he went 1-for-50 over the last two weeks of the season. There's still quite a bit of variance here, but Blakely projects as a part-time infielder.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: The ultra-lanky Blakely took just shy of $1 million to eschew a commitment to Auburn. He's a relatively raw, long-levered SS/3B from Michigan who is likely to spend all of 2021 in the AZL and then finish up at instructs, which for the last few years has meant Diablo intrasquads for the Halo kids. mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Even though he missed his senior season of high school because of the pandemic, the Angels liked Blakely’s raw tools enough to take him in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft out of the Detroit area high school ranks and give him $900,000 to sign him away from attending Auburn. He didn’t provide much return on the investment during a rough debut in the Arizona Complex League in 2021, but things started to click with a move to full-season ball, though he missed time with a hamstring issue and then a hand injury caused by a hit by pitch. He made up for lost reps as one of the younger players in the Arizona Fall League. With the strides Blakely made in 2022, there’s confidence more people will be talking about him with more reps. While he still struck out in nearly 30 percent of his plate appearances in 2022, that was a big step in the right direction compared to his debut, and he continued to understand the value of seeing pitches and drawing walks. There’s raw power for him to tap into, but he’s yet to grow into his body and needs to add strength to his 6-foot-3 frame. Signed as a shortstop, Blakely moved around the infield during his pro debut, but has settled in at third base, focusing on the hot corner in the California League and the AFL. His defense has been inconsistent, with a strong arm and decent footwork but a tendency to let things speed up on him. Some feel a move to the outfield might make the most sense long term, but if the improvements with the bat are legit, the Angels will find a spot in the lineup for him every day.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels have hit the Detroit area high school scene twice in the last few years to roll the dice on some high risk, high reward types. In 2018, it was two-way player William Holmes in the fifth round. In 2020, they took Blakely, an athletic, but raw infielder who got an over-slot bonus of $900,000 to walk away from his Auburn commitment. He didn’t play his senior year because of the pandemic and struggled for much of his pro debut in the Arizona Complex League, though the Angels saw steady improvement from start to finish last summer. Blakely has some raw tools to work with, starting with his athletic 6-foot-3 frame. His hit tool is fringy -- he struck out in 37.1 percent of his plate appearances during his pro debut -- and he will have to refine his approach to make more consistent contact from the left side of the plate. There’s at least above-average raw power for him to tap into and there could be more if he can add strength. The Angels moved Blakely around the infield during his debut, getting equal time at shortstop, third and second base, largely because of other personnel. He’ll keep getting reps at all three, though he might profile best at third when all is said and done. He let the game speed up on him defensively, but he has a strong arm and good footwork that should allow him to stay on the dirt.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Detroit-area high school scene might not be thought of as a hotbed for baseball talent -- the last prepster from there to make it to the big leagues was Daniel Fields, a 2009 draftee who touched the Majors briefly in 2015. But the Angels feel they may have tapped into a bit of a mine, taking high-risk/high-reward type players in the top five rounds twice in the last three years. In 2018, it was two-way player William Holmes. In 2020, it was Blakely, a super-athletic shortstop who got an over-slot $900,000 to sign in the fourth round and then went to instructs for his unofficial pro debut. Blakeley’s size and athleticism are the first things that stand out. He’s 6-foot-3 and has plus speed, which should help him on both sides of the ball. A left-handed hitter, he’s worked to improve his swing to make more contact with some good results, though there are still swing-and-miss concerns, something that could improve with a refined approach and pitch recognition as he faces better pitching consistently. As he adds strength to that athletic frame, there is some power to come if he can learn to make enough contact to get to it. Despite his size, Blakeley has every chance to stick at shortstop, with outstanding range and enough arm for the premium position. This isn’t going to happen overnight, and Blakely has only about 40 at-bats at instructs on his pro resume, but there’s considerable ceiling for the infielder to try and get to in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Daniels' loud tools stood out much more than his performance in his first two years in college, when he batted .176 with a 38-percent strikeout rate at Tennessee and .168 with a 44-percent whiff rate in the wood-bat Cape Cod League. He did an about-face to hit .357/.478/.750 with 13 extra-base hits in 17 games as a junior in 2020, though scouts still weren't completely sure what to make of him because the shortened season ended before he could prove himself in Southeastern Conference play. He became one of the highest-ceilinged players in the Houston system after signing for $400,000 as a fourth-rounder. Daniels wowed the Astros during instructional league, where he generated impressive exit velocities and displayed the best speed among position players in camp. The ball makes a different sound coming off his bat and he has well above-average raw power, but he still has to show he can erase a history of swinging through hittable fastballs and struggling against breaking balls and changeups. He spent the fall trying to simplify his right-handed swing, starting his hands higher to shorten his first move and elevate more balls. With speed that draws well above-average grades from some evaluators, Daniels could be at least at 20-20 player if he figures things out at the plate. Though he spent much of his final season in college at DH, he has the quickness to stick in center field as a pro if he improves his reads and routes. He has average arm strength and can play all three outfield spots.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: It's not as if hitting prospects with huge power and severe strikeout issues are rare, but what is rare is that Daniels barely performed in college but is still seen as a guy with huge power potential. In part due to injuries and then the pandemic, Daniels never played more than 35 games in a college season and never homered more than five times in a single campaign. He struck out roughly 40% of the time combined between his underclass seasons at Tennessee and the wood bat summer ball he played amid them, then exploded during non-conference play in 2020, walking as much as he struck out while slashing .357/.478/.750 for four short weeks. He draws some Giancarlo Stanton swing comps because of his closed stance/stride and tucked hands, and Daniels' raw power is only a grade shy of Stanton's. Daniels can also really run and has the Michael Vick, sportscar forward tilt and posture as he does. He'll run some plus times straight through the bag and some 70-grade times with the turn on his way to second base. The bust probability here is high because the track record for college hitters striking out this much and succeeding is very sparse, but guys with this kind of power/speed combo don't exactly grow on trees.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres inked Contreras out of Mexico for $50,000 in July 2017, then watched as he became one of their steadiest risers. After posting a 3.61 ERA in 25 appearances (23 starts) at Class A Fort Wayne in 2019, Contreras’ stock continued to trend upward with a very impressive showing at the team’s instructional camp. That is, until he blew out his right arm during his final outing and underwent Tommy John surgery. Added to the 40-man roster last offseason, Contreras is still finding his footing in his post-procedure return to the mound at High-A Fort Wayne. Contreras doesn’t come with much physical projection to his thicker, undersized build, but his stuff has steadily ticked up since he entered the pro ranks. His fastball sits in the mid-90s, and he commands it with ease for a pitcher his age. He uses that heater to help set up one of the best curveballs in San Diego’s system, and he also has a quality changeup at his disposal to combat left-handed hitters. The clean and repeatable delivery that fuels Contreras’ strike-throwing ability also leads evaluators to project him for well-above-average command. Everything sounds promising, but first he needs to get back on the mound. Once he’s able to make up for lost time and get back on track, Contreras has the look of a future back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres inked Contreras out of Mexico for $50,000 in July 2017, then watched as he became one of their steadiest risers. After posting a 3.61 ERA in 25 appearances at Class A Fort Wayne in 2019, Contreras’ stock continued to trend upward with a very impressive showing at the team’s instructional camp. That is, until he blew out his arm during his final outing and required Tommy John surgery in November. Despite the setback, team officials remain high on Contreras, who should still be only 22 years old when he returns. Contreras doesn’t come with much physical projection to his thicker, undersized build. But his stuff has steadily ticked up since he entered the pro ranks. His fastball sits in the mid-90s, and he commands it with ease for a pitcher his age. Contreras uses that heater to help set up arguably the best the curveball in San Diego’s system, and he also has a quality changeup at his disposal to combat left-handed hitters. The clean and repeatable delivery that fuels Contreras’ strike-throwing ability also leads evaluators to project him for well above-average command. First thing’s first: Contreras needs to attack his rehab process. But with a knack for attacking hitters and an impressive blend of big league caliber pitches, Contreras has the look of a future backend starter.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Contreras showed a huge velocity boost during 2020 instructs, where he was up to 97 mph and sitting 93-95 during early innings before settling in the 92-94 range deep into outings. Unfortunately he blew out and needed Tommy John; he would miss all of 2021. The Padres added him to their 40-man to prevent other teams from picking him in the Rule 5 (though we didn't end up having one) and stashed him on the IL while he finished rehab. Contreras re-entered affiliated ball in early May of 2022 and was non-tendered after the season and then re-signed on a minor league deal. Since returning from surgery, his fastball has been sitting 92-94. He has struggled to throw starter-quality strikes (he's walked about a batter every other inning the last two seasons), but he still has a deep enough repertoire to consider him a spot-starting prospect. He needs to keep his frame in check and might even develop better command if his conditioning improves.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Contreras showed a huge velocity boost during 2020 instructs, where he was up to 97 mph and sitting 93-95 during early innings before settling in the 92-94 range deep into outings. He had previously been 90-92 and worked a lot with a plus changeup, and he averaged 10 K/9 and just over 2 BB/9 against low-level hitters at that velocity. During that same instructs window, he blew out and needed Tommy John; he would miss all of 2021. The Padres added him to their 40-man to prevent other teams from picking him in the Rule 5 (though we didn't end up having one) and stashed him on the IL while he finished rehab. (The Padres were burned a little in this case since they added Contreras to the 40-man before they knew there wasn't going to be a Rule 5 Draft, and now he's occupying a 40-man spot despite looking unlikely to impact the big league team this year.) Contreras re-entered affiliated ball in early May of 2022 and made a couple appearances in the weeks leading up to list publication, during which he again sat 92-94 mph, with his changeup not quite as dynamic as it was at peak. It's too early to worry about that, as we're only talking about a few innings at this point. The takeaway is that Contreras' arm strength has basically returned post-op. This doesn't appear to be one of those cases where a guy totally reshapes his body during TJ rehab and comes back shot out of a canon in the direction of the big leagues. Instead, it looks like Contreras will spend his first option year trying to find that changeup and pitch his way into five- and six-inning shape so he can compete for a rotation spot next spring.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: The Padres have recently had several short, stocky, advanced pitchability types in the lowest levels of their system, the kind of pitcher who ends up as a sixth starter if their stuff plateaus. They had so many of these sorts that it seemed possible one might have an uptick in stuff just at random, even though none of them had obvious physical projection. During instructs, Contreras was that guy. I saw him up to 97, sitting 93-95 during early innings and then settling in the 92-94 range later in outings. He had previously been 90-92, worked a lot with a plus changeup, and he averaged 10 K/9 and just over 2 BB/9 against low-level hitters at that velocity. Though less high-profile, he joined the parade of Tommy Johns required of Padres pitchers after blowing out during an instructs game against the Dodgers. It means he'll miss all of 2021. Contreras needs to be put on the 40-man this offseason or be exposed to the Rule 5 Draft, and I think he merits consideration from teams that want their pick to start on the 60-day IL rather than one who can contribute immediately. Several pitchers in a similar TJ rehab boat were picked in the 2020 Rule 5, and I don't think the lag between when Contreras last pitched and when he'll next pitch is a deterrent. The arrow was so firmly pointing up for Contreras last year that I think I'd welcome the post-surgery risk if it meant acquiring an advanced young pitcher with a chance to take the ball every five days. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Leeper had an extreme collection of injury issues as an amateur, including two Tommy John surgeries. He was totally healthy and throwing very hard during his last few seasons at Oklahoma State, but he still ended up being passed over in the shortened 2020 draft and signed as an undrafted free agent. Less than a year after signing, Leeper was at Triple-A blowing upper-90s gas past veteran hitters and working with a plus slider. He seemed poised to debut in Chicago either late in 2022 or sometime in 2023, but he blew out again this spring and had his third career TJ in April. A successful rehab will put Leeper back on the doorstep of a big league relief role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After starring as a Texas prep junior, Leeper underwent two Tommy John surgeries and an ulnar nerve transposition that limited him to 2 2/3 innings over his senior season and first two years at Oklahoma State. He persevered and eventually became the Cowboys' closer before signing with the Cubs for $20,000 as a 23-year-old nondrafted free agent in 2020. He made a spectacular pro debut last summer, recording a 1.29 ERA with 53 strikeouts in 35 innings between Double-A and Triple-A, though he was shut down in August with elbow inflammation. Leeper goes after hitters with two pitches. His four-seam fastball sits at 94-96 mph and touches 99, and it features a flat approach angle and riding life that make it tough for hitters to barrel. If they try to sit on his heater, he can make them look bad with an 86-88 mph slider that features tremendous depth. After averaging 7.0 walks per nine innings during his college career, Leeper more than halved that rate to 3.3 in his pro debut. His stuff is real and if his control is as well, he could help Chicago in the near future and eventually fill a high-leverage role. The biggest question is his health, as he didn't pitch on consecutive days in 2021 before missing the final two months, though the Cubs say his shutdown was precautionary more than anything else.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Kath was absolutely stuffed on FanGraphs' 2021 pre-draft rankings, but it quickly became clear in pro ball that he has severe bat-to-ball issues. In fairness/kindness to the White Sox (and myself), the pandemic disrupted Kath's pre-draft summer. Changes to the schedule and location of showcase events limited his participation in them, making it rare for him to face the top-of-the-class peers who might have exposed these issues sooner. Kath's sweet-looking lefty stroke dominated varsity baseball in Arizona, his frame portended impact power, and he was slick enough as a defender that some scouts thought he might be a long-term fit at shortstop. The latter two elements are still part of Kath's game, positive aspects of his prospect profile. But it was visually evident very quickly in pro ball that he was struggling to parse breaking balls and catch high fastballs, and now that we have a full season of pro data to comb over, the underlying contact metrics here are very scary: 19% swinging strike rate, 59% contact rate. Even if he strikes out a third of the time, if Kath can get to power against righty pitching and take an above-average rate of walks (he did both in 2022) while playing great defense, he'll be a solid (if flawed) big league role player, kind of like late-career Matt Carpenter with a better glove. His footwork, hands, actions, and arm strength are all plus, and it may even be worth running him out as a shortstop just to see how it goes. Of course, because he's already striking out at a 33% clip, there's risk the bottom falls out of the bat so significantly that the other stuff doesn't matter.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text:
The early portion of the pandemic made it hard for Kath to play a lot pre-draft summer showcase ball, as the events that would normally occur in the western portion of the country were moved to the Southeast. Instead he was seen frequently in a wood bat summer league in Arizona, at Area Codes, and at one Perfect Game event in October, before crushing varsity pitching the next spring. Kath has a good looking swing, but he often swung inside and underneath fastballs on the outer third at those showcase events. Because his participation against curated competition was fairly limited, these issues didn't become part of Kath's pre-draft narrative. He had trouble recognizing breaking balls during Eric's in-person looks this spring. We now some evidence that Kath has both a plate coverage issue and potential breaking ball recognition issues, causing an overhaul of how we're projecting him compared to our pre-draft assessment. 
There are still carrying tools here, though. Kath has a big, projectable frame (standing next to Colson Montgomery on the left side of the infield can make this easy to miss) and the long-term power projection that comes with it. He's also a fantastic defensive third baseman already. Because the White Sox have Montgomery playing shortstop, Kath has been strictly limited to third in affiliated ball and in the instances when Eric has seen him during instructs and spring training. His footwork, hands, actions, and arm strength are all plus, and in most circumstances, it'd be worth sending him out at shortstop to see how it goes. While the contact-related warning signs here are worrying, there are still some obvious paths and precedents for Kath to be an integral big leaguer. Matt Chapman is a super-charged version of this overall profile (definitely not a comp), while Ryan McMahon and late-career Matt Carpenter are fair offensive comps, but have inferior gloves.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Kath has one of the sweeter swings in the draft. He was seen a lot in a wood bat summer league in Arizona during the summer before his senior year and led his team to a state title the following spring. Kath has that hitterish, no batting gloves style and a rhythmic, well-timed cut. He can turn on balls with big power and routinely whistles balls to the oppo gap. There's huge disagreement about Kath's ultimate defensive fit. He's a smooth defender but a slow-twitch athlete with a big frame. He doesn't have much room to slow down and remain at short, and it's likely that he'll get bigger as he enters his 20s because he's such a broad-shouldered guy. Teams who like him best at least think he can be a shift-enabled middle-infielder because of his hands and actions. On the low end, teams think he'll end up at first base, and don't see the explosive power package to support that profile. It's likely a team calls Kath's name late in the first round or in the comp, though some have him in round three or four.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox might have taken Kath with their 2021 first-round pick if Colson Montgomery hadn't been available, so they were delighted to grab him as their second-rounder with an over-slot $1.8 million bonus. Gatorade's Arizona player of the year, he led Desert Mountain HS (Scottsdale) to the state 5-A title and crushed a long home run at the Angels' Spring Training stadium in the championship game. He hasn't thrived in pro ball, batting .227/.325/.367 with a 35 percent strikeout rate in his first two pro seasons. Scouts considered Kath one of the more advanced hitters in the 2021 prep class, but he has struggled to catch up to quality fastballs and to recognize breaking balls as a pro. Chicago helped him simplify the load with his left-handed swing, and while he did a better job of drawing walks and avoiding ground-ball contact last season than he did in his debut, his propensity for swinging and missing remains a huge concern. He still has plus raw power that could translate into 20 or more homers per season if he can put the bat on the ball more regularly, but he also needs to add more strength after his bat speed diminished late in the year. Kath played shortstop in high school but his below-average speed and quickness prompted an immediate move to third base in pro ball. He has the potential to become at least an average defender with soft hands and plus arm strength at the hot corner, though he'll have to improve his agility and consistency. He has a ways to go to catch Bryan Ramos as Chicago's third baseman of the future, which eventually could prompt a move to first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kath factored into the White Sox's possibilities for the first round of the 2021 Draft, so they were thrilled to find him available in the second. Gatorade's Arizona player of the year, he carried Desert Mountain High (Scottsdale) to the state 5-A title and smashed a long homer at the Angels' Spring Training park in the championship game. Signed for an over-slot $1.8 million, he hit just .212/.287/.337 with a 37 percent strikeout rate during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League. Kath was one of the more advanced hitters in the 2021 high school crop, employing an easy left-handed swing and a mature approach to make consistent hard contact to all fields. He tried to do too much in the ACL, chasing and trying to pull too many pitches and producing a lot of weak contact when he did connect. If he gets back to focusing on driving the ball from gap to gap and can add some loft to his stroke, he could become a solid hitter with average or better pop. A shortstop in high school, Kath immediately moved to third base after turning pro. Though he's a below-average runner, he has enough range to go with soft hands and plus arm strength at the hot corner. His debut may have been rockier than expected, but the White Sox still envision him and 2021 first-rounder Colson Montgomery locking down the left side of their infield in the future.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Kopps was so dominant as a multi-inning fireman at Arkansas (he had a 0.89 ERA in 2021, working about 90 innings across 33 relief appearances) that he was a Golden Spikes finalist. He signed for $300,000 in the third round and projected as a quick-moving low-leverage reliever. After a 2022 speed bump, Kopps is back on that track. He's sitting 93 (up three ticks from last year) and missing bats at Double-A San Antonio. Kopps has two different breaking balls, but his upper-80s slider is easily his best pitch and he leans on it heavily. His slider quality and execution will enable him to be a viable middle reliever. His 40-man evaluation year isn't until 2024, so he'll likely spend next season as upper-level depth that isn't occupying a roster spot.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Kopps, a Golden Spikes finalist, was a dominant multi-inning fireman at Arkansas and posted a 0.89 ERA in 2021 as a fourth-year junior working about 90 innings across 33 relief appearances. He doesn't throw especially hard (mostly 89-92 mph), but he has a plus slider that he executes with remarkable consistency. He's a quick-moving, high-probability middle-relief prospect.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Golden Spikes finalist Kevin Kopps was a dominant multi-inning fireman at Arkansas. He doesn't throw especially hard (mostly 91-92) but he has a plus slider that he executes with remarkable consistency. He's a quick-moving middle-relief prospect.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Older than most Draft picks, Kopps had to bide his time before bursting onto the radar. He redshirted in 2016, missed 2018 after undergoing Tommy John surgery and then the pandemic shortened his 2020 campaign. However, he was nearly unhittable in 2021, pitching to a 0.90 ERA with a 0.76 WHIP, both of which led NCAA Division I. After racking up 131 strikeouts in 89 2/3 innings, Kopps was named the SEC Pitcher of the Year and also won the Dick Howser Trophy as the College Player of the Year. The Padres grabbed the Arkansas product in the third round and signed him to a below-slot $300,000 bonus. As a result of his workload in college, Kopps only threw 14 2/3 innings in his professional debut, but was just as dominant. Kopps has four pitches in his repertoire, but it’s his cutter that’s been the key to his success. The mid-80s offering has late movement and the right-hander is able to vary its depth depending on whether he wants to throw it in the zone, or try to get a hitter to chase. He also throws a low-90s fastball, an average curveball and a developing changeup. Kopps has shown decent control early in his career, but doesn’t always command his fastball as well as he’d like. Kopps has been 25 for the duration of the 2022 season and hasn’t moved as quickly as many would have hoped coming out of college, having been just OK at Double-A thus far. He’ll need to work on getting more swing-and-misses against advanced bats if he’s going to break through to San Diego as a 26-year-old in 2023.

fangraphs.label: 2023report
fangraphs.text: Marceaux is still only sitting about 90 mph, but his secondaries are all pretty good and he commands them well enough to profile as a spot starter. Breaking ball shape and depth are Marceaux's most impressive traits, and even though they don't have especially different shapes, the gap in speed between his curveball and slider gives hitters different looks. His changeup has also taken a step forward in pro ball. He is currently in the Double-A rotation and is near-ready injury depth.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Marceaux has four pitches and, when you consider how much better he was at limiting walks as a junior, has a pretty good chance to remain a starter in pro ball. Both of his breaking balls flash plus, he has plus raw breaking ball spin, and his slider's angle has back-foot utility against lefty hitters. He needs to polish his breaking balls' shapes so those pitches are more distinct, as Marceaux will likely need to lean heavily on them as a pro, since his fastball and changeup are both below average. He's a high-probability depth starter or bulk middle innings reliever.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
