But his first full season at the upper levels in 2022 -- back with Altoona -- did not go nearly as well. The left-handed-hitting Fraizer still has the ability to hit the ball hard, recording high exit velocities when things are clicking. He really lost his approach in 2022 and it snowballed as he struggled, with the outfielder often trying to do too much. His swing mechanics also went significantly sideways and his tendency to cut himself off on the front part of his swing -- which didn’t hurt him in 2021 -- really caused him trouble against better pitching in 2022. Fraizer’s speed still plays well and he can steal a base, as well as play a very solid center field. He needs to simplify things and just let his natural ability and tools take over. The Pirates didn’t protect him on the 40-man roster last offseason and he wasn’t taken in the Rule 5 Draft. At age 25, the clock is ticking. He may have overperformed in 2021 and underperformed last year; the key will be in finding a middle ground somewhere.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fraizer didn’t have much success in his first two years at the University of Arizona, despite obvious size and athleticism. He was at the start of a breakout season as a junior in 2019 when he broke a hamate, leaving most teams unsure of who he was as a player. The Pirates liked his tools enough to take a flyer on him in the third round of that June’s Draft and he had an understandably rusty return from injury during his pro debut. Unseen by most during the pandemic, Fraizer took off in 2021, going from High-A to Double-A and earning a spot on the second team of MLB Pipeline’s Prospect Team of the Year. Even during his up-and-down days at Arizona, Fraizer has shown an advanced knowledge of the strike zone and a willingness to work counts and draw walks. That continued in 2021 as he walked in over 11 percent of his plate appearances while limiting strikeouts, making consistently hard contact from the left side of the plate. He changed his setup in 2021 with obviously positive effects, spreading out a bit more and staying more balanced, which helped him drive the ball and tap into his raw power. Fraizer’s plus speed is an asset on both sides of the ball, as he continues to learn the craft of stealing bases and covers a lot of ground in center field, where the Pirates believe he can stay long term, though he’s continued to get reps in all three spots. The Pirates saw Fraizer’s confidence soar in 2021 and now that he believes in his own ability to produce, he has the chance to continue developing into a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fraizer had two relatively nondescript years at the University of Arizona before starting to really click at the start of his junior year. His Draft profile was just starting to rise when he suffered a broken hamate, limiting him to just 19 games. The Pirates liked his tools enough to nab him in the third round of the 2019 Draft and signed him for a below slot $525,000 and he shook off the rust during his pro debut in the short-season New York-Penn League. His production was impacted by a scratch in his glasses, making it hard for him to see, but he’s since upgraded to contacts. The left-handed hitter is physical and athletic with plus speed that helps him on both sides of the ball. He needs to clean up some of his movement at the plate and his bat path, some of which he’s already made gains on, and that could give him the chance to be a solid hitter who can barrel up the baseball consistently. Fraizer is strong and he could start tapping into some power as he further refines that approach. With his speed, Fraizer has the chance to play center field with an average arm. He played all three outfield spots last summer, something that’s likely to continue with a likely ceiling of a fourth outfielder type contributor.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Fraizer only really played consistently as a sophomore at Arizona, pencilled into the starting lineup just 23 times combined between his freshman and junior years. The latter was shortened by a broken hamate, but after posting a vanilla sophomore line, Fraizer went bonkers during his shortened 2019 and had an OPS over 1.000 in about five weeks of play. Several teams had him stuffed based on the pre-injury look, and he ended up going in the third round even though his career line was commensurate with that of a traditional fourth outfielder. His post-draft performance (.221/.287/.266 in the Penn League) was in that vein, too, though remember Fraizer was dealing with the backend of a hamate break, which can sap power output for months. Further obscured from evaluation by the pandemic and the loss of the 2020 season, Fraizer made his full-season debut as a 23-year-old at High-A Greensboro in 2021 and obliterated the level, slashing .314/.401/.578 with 20 homers before a month-long promotion to Altoona to finish the year. There's been a swing change here, too. Fraizer's stance has opened up, and his top hand seems to be more involved with a swing that now has more consistent lift and intent to do damage than before. Twenty pumps from a potential center fielder will get your attention, especially when they're climbing the minor league ladder as fast as Fraizer. His numbers against lefties are troubling, as is Fraizer's rather expansive, chase-prone approach, which is at least in danger of diluting his quality of contact. Staying in center field (it's going to be close - he's tightly-wound and has above-average speed but isn't a true burner and he's rapidly filling out) gives Fraizer a shot to be a regular, while settling into a corner gives him more of a platoon projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The vast majority of players to make it to the big leagues from New Hampshire have been pitchers, though Ryan McKenna has spent time in the Orioles' outfield after being a 2015 fourth-round pick out of high school. Lavigne would like to be the next Granite State prep bat to make it. The Rockies went over slot to sign him for $2 million as a Competitive Balance Round A pick in 2018, then saw him have a tremendous pro debut that summer. It’s taken him a while to find his footing since then, though he started figuring some things out in 2021 and hit his way to Double-A for the first time in 2022, finishing things off with a solid Arizona Fall League showing. Lavigne entered pro ball with a definite hit-over-power profile, but he got into trouble when he started to try to sell out for power too much. He got back to a better overall approach in 2022, drawing more walks and showing the ability to make more consistently hard contact from the left side of the plate. The power is going to come thanks to his natural strength and bat speed and the Rockies were pleased with how he adjusted to the Eastern League after his promotion. It’s possible Lavigne will never be more than a fringy defender at first base, one with a below-average arm, but this part of his game improved as well in 2022. He’s a tireless worker, one who will be at the upper levels of the Rockies' system at age 23 for most of the 2023 season and who still has the potential to develop into a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lavigne was a bit of a pop-up prospect from the New Hampshire high school ranks, not exactly a hotbed for professional talent, as the 2018 Draft approached. He landed in the Competitive Balance Round A and the Rockies went over slot to sign him for $2 million. It seemed like a very shrewd investment based on his pro debut in the Pioneer League (.996 OPS), but he really seemed lost for most of his first full season of pro ball in 2019. A return to Low-A in 2021 was a good move as he righted the ship and earned a bump up a level for the final two months of the season. When he was struggling, Lavigne was getting caught between the hitter he’d always been, one focused on contact with excellent plate discipline, and the one he thought he had to be, a power-hitting first baseman. He sold out for power too much in 2019 and got out of his approach. He’s still learning to catch the ball out front and let his natural strength do its thing. In 2021, he started getting much more comfortable with his swing and was adjusting to velocity more consistently. Lavigne is going to have to hit to keep moving up, as he’s a fringy defender at first base with a below-average arm. He’s grown into more of a leadership role, and the Rockies noticed that after he helped Fresno win a ton of games in Low-A, he led Spokane to the High-A West playoffs as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Right-handed pitcher Chris Carpenter is the highest-drafted high school player ever from New Hampshire, taken No. 15 overall back in 1993. After popping up to land in the Competitive Balance Round A in 2018, Lavigne became just the second prep player since Carpenter (Jeff Locke, 2006) to get taken in the top two rounds from the Granite State. He made a very strong first impression when he posted a .996 OPS in his pro debut, but struggled with the move to full-season ball in 2019, though the Rockies were pleased with his adjustments in instructional league play in 2020. At his best, Lavigne’s strengths as a left-handed hitter are his knowledge of the strike zone and his ability to drive the ball to all fields. While he drew a lot of walks in 2019, he was too passive at the plate and missed too many good pitches to hit. He also got pull-happy and tried to sell out for power, leading to a spike in strikeouts, instead of just letting his natural strength and bat speed do the work. At instructs, he looked more like the 2018 version than the lost ’19 edition, making more hard contact and using the entire field more consistently. It will be Lavigne’s bat that will carry him to the big leagues, as he’s definitely a first baseman only with a below-average arm. The Rockies are optimistic he righted the ship last fall and hope the reps of a full season will fully get him back on track.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: How many high school players drafted out of New Hampshire have made it to the big leagues? As of right now, none, but Lavigne is hoping to change that. Taken in Competitive Balance Round A of the 2018 Draft, Lavigne had a huge pro debut that resulted in an All-Star nod in the Pioneer League. He wasn't able to keep that going with the jump to full-season ball in 2019 as he struggled in the South Atlantic League. There's still a lot to like about Lavigne's offensive upside if he can right the ship. He's big and strong, with bat speed and a ton of raw power coming from his 6-foot-4 frame. While he has shown a propensity for drawing walks, he may have been too patient during his first full season, not aggressively going after good pitches to hit. As a result, he didn't drive the ball as consistently as he is able to and he certainly didn't tap into that power, while seeing his strikeout rate spike as well. Given Lavigne's age and experience, some struggles aren't out of the ordinary, and a rediscovery of the balance between being patient and aggressive will allow him to develop into the all-around hitter the Rockies think he can be. Lavigne is a first baseman only on the defensive end of things, and has work to do there, but he's athletic and should be a capable defender, albeit one with a below-average arm. It will be his bat that will carry him and there's confidence in the organization he'll get that going again.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Players from cold-weather Northeast states like New Hampshire aren't supposed to be particularly advanced. There's a reason why a high school hitter from the Granite State has never made it to the big leagues. Lavigne, taken earlier than any prep position player from the state when the Rockies selected him 42nd overall in the 2018 Draft, hopes to be the first and showed that he didn't get the memo about not being prepared for pro ball when he led the Rookie level Pioneer League in on-base percentage and finished third in OPS in his summer debut. Scouts lauded Lavigne's raw power as the Draft approached, seeing his bat speed, strength and 6-foot-4 frame all pointing to future over-the-fence ability, some of which showed up during his first taste of pro ball. There's confidence he'll get to that power because of his advanced approach from the left side of the plate. He works counts, draws a ton of walks and rarely gets fooled, giving him the chance to eventually be a plus hitter with plus power. While his below-average speed does limit him to first base as a pro, he's surprisingly athletic given his size and has the chance to be a solid defender. His bat should profile at the typically run-producing spot as well, with the Rockies excited to see what he can do over a full season.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Lavigne still has a sound approach, a big, strong frame, and a good-looking uppercut swing, but his bat path is grooved and the scouts who saw him at instructs have concerns about how much contact he's capable of making. His swing enables him to turn on fastballs left up and in, which is atypical for a hitter this size, but he struggles to connect with stuff up and away from him and that's where a lot of fastballs live nowadays. His age, approach, present power, and frame have me holding over his FV from last year but this is a prospect whose 2021 on-paper performance feels pretty important. We still don't have a big leaguer born in New Hampshire. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text:
After he looked just okay against his elite peers on the summer showcase circuit, Lavigne generated a ton of buzz as a senior the following spring. Northeast popup high schoolers have a dubious track record (there has never been a major-league hitter from New Hampshire) because they spend all spring mashing bad high school pitching, but lots of teams were in on Lavigne's spike in power and thought he fit in the second tier of high school hitting prospects in the draft behind the likes of Nolan Gorman and Jarred Kelenic. 
Lavigne has not shown that kind of power with the wooden bats in pro ball, both because he's not hitting the ball as hard as we anticipated and because he isn't lifting it. Were Lavigne as physically projectable as his age suggests, this would be less worrisome, but he's a broad-shouldered, imposing presence, so the lack of present thump is somewhat troubling. We're not out on him yet (he's too young), but first base-only prospects need to mash and that hasn't happened here yet.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text:
After he looked just okay against his elite peers on the summer showcase circuit, Lavigne generated a ton of buzz as a senior the following spring. Northeast popup high schoolers have a dubious track record because they spend all spring mashing bad high school pitching, but lots of teams were in on Lavigne's spike in power and thought he fit in the second tier of high school hitting prospects in the draft behind the likes of Nolan Gorman and Jarred Kelenic. 
Lavigne has not shown that kind of power with the wooden bats in pro ball and his exit velos are actually a bit below big league average, though that's less worrisome considering his age. He's a first base-only defender and needs to absolutely mash to profile. We're cautiously optimistic that he can do it, but he's out of the gate a little slower than we anticipated.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: A high-profile $2 million 2019 international signee, Vera's first two years in pro ball really only generated looks on the Tempe backfields, as the first year of the pandemic wiped out what would have been his first full season. Still 18-years-old for most all of 2021, Vera slashed .317/.384/.469 in the Arizona Complex League and was promoted to Low-A for most of the last month of the season. He didn't homer all year. That's less about how much power he has (Vera is pretty physical for a teenage shortstop) and more about his swing's functionality and his style of hitting. His left-handed swing is somewhat long and downward-cutting. This, plus Vera's willingness to offer at pitches out of the zone, has him currently spraying unpredictable grounder/liner contact all over the field. His natural strength and ability to rotate often makes the contact hard enough to slip through the infield. While his righty swing has more pull/lift elements, it is less explosive. Barring an eventual lefty swing change, Vera looks more like a good utility man or low-end regular, the kind of everyday shortstop who hits near the bottom of the lineup, and he's FV'd such that we're projecting that outcome. He has both the athleticism and, based on opinions from outside the org, the baseball aptitude to do that. Because the below-average plate discipline also creates bust risk here, we're more inclined to take a "believe it when we see it" approach regarding the swing change rather than an anticipatory one.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Vera has added considerable mass over the last year or so and has transformed from a rail-thin project into a teenage shortstop with pretty impressive raw power for his age. Vera's lefty swing is short but still has loft, while his righty swing (he ditches his batting gloves from the right side) is a little more erratic but has verve and power potential. Vera doesn't track pitches very well from either side of the plate but that might be because of how hard he swings, which feels excessive at times. My notes from each of the last two instructs periods also indicate I saw high-effort swings, so this has been going on for a while. There's a chance for Vera to age into the Goldilocks Zone, where he stays lithe and athletic enough to remain at short but also grows into impact power. Because they have so many young infielders in Extended to start 2021, Vera has seen action all over the infield and it's been tough to get a feel for his exact defensive ability, but he and Denzer Guzman have the best chance to stay at short of all the system's young infielders.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: It's hard to find prospects who have an infielder's grace and athleticism as well as a big, projectable frame. He's currently skinny as a rail, but Vera is one of these prospects and has a chance to mature in the Goldilocks Zone, where he stays lithe and athletic enough to remain at short but also grows into impact power. He took some good cuts in the Fall during intrasquads, but if Vera worked deep into counts and swung several times during the same at-bat, his later swings weren't as controlled and strong. He needs to get stronger. I'm a bit less confident in Vera filling out than I was with Ronny Mauricio at the same age just because Vera's physical composition is a little narrower and more slender, but if he does, his swing is already in a better spot to hit for power than Mauricio.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: A broad-shouldered shortstop with considerable physical projection. Swing has natural loft from both sides of the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As one of the more highly regarded international prospects available for the 2019-20 signing period, Vera commanded a $2 million bonus in July 2019, then was basically stuck in his Arizona apartment and unable to stay in shape during 2020 because of the pandemic. In 2021, he turned his conditioning around and went out and hit well during his pro debut in the Arizona Complex League to earn a late bump up to full-season ball. The 2022 season, however, was a disaster, as Vera struggled out of the gate and let it snowball. Still only 20, there’s time for Vera to right the ship, but after a year in which he finished with a .572 OPS, he has a lot to work on. A 6-foot-2 athletic switch-hitter, Vera had shown a strong feel for making contact in the past, and there was belief he could tap into some raw power as he added strength. In 2022, he chased out of the zone much more than he should have and didn’t make enough contact to overcome that, with a 27 percent strikeout rate far too high for someone without big-time power. He’ll have to work to make better swing decisions moving forward. Vera is still a good defender with excellent actions and a strong arm, enough for him to play shortstop going forward. For now, the emphasis will be on him finding a better approach at the plate if he’s going to have a chance to fulfill his potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Vera was ranked in the top 10 of MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospect list when the 2019-20 signing period began and the Angels gave him $2 million to join the organization in July of 2019. The pandemic not only kept him from making his debut in 2020, but he was pretty much stuck in an Arizona apartment for an extremely long time and gained weight as a result. He was able to return to his conditioning, shedding those pounds in time to hit .317/.384/.469 in the Arizona Complex League in 2021, earning a late promotion to Low-A ball at age 18. Vera reported to camp this spring in even better shape and the Angels were thrilled with where he was physically, though that didn’t help his offensive profile as he struggled to find consistency in full-seson ball. He’s still hit over power, and has shown the ability in the past to make contact from both sides of the plate. He doesn’t draw a ton of walks and his strikeout rate crept upward in 2022. There’s plenty of bat speed and his added strength should allow him to start tapping into his raw power, even if he always has a contact-first approach. There is a chance Vera’s 6-foot-2 frame will fill out too much and he’ll become too big for shortstop, though he shows very good actions and more than enough arm for the premium position. He could be a plus defender if he eventually has to move to third and there’s confidence the extra-base authority will come to profile well at the corner spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A dozen prospects got bonuses of $2 million or more during the 2019-20 international signing period. Vera, one of two to get seven-figure bonuses from the Angels over that time, was at the bottom of that dozen, getting $2 million even to sign on July 2. The shutdown kept him from making his professional debut in 2020. Because he was stuck in one place, he wasn’t able to work out, so he came to instructs with some added weight. The good news is that he still showed off tremendous tools and already has shed the excess pandemic-induced weight. The Angels gave Vera that kind of bonus because they feel he can be an impact player at a premium position. He swings the bat well from both sides of the plate, with excellent bat speed and an advanced feel for the strike zone that’s geared for contact. There’s definite raw power to tap into, but he’s hit over power for sure, with the chance for him to be a plus hitter in time. While Vera is an average runner, he might be as close to a true shortstop as the Angels have in the system. He moves very fluidly with outstanding actions and instincts, a strong arm and very true hands. The only thing that will keep him from being an above-average defender at short is if he slows down too much in the future, which eventually could necessitate a move to another infield position, though that’s not something being discussed at all internally at this point.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A shortstop out of Venezuela who ranked highly on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects list as the 2019-20 signing period opened last July 2, Vera got $2 million from the Angels to join the organization. With that price tag comes lofty expectations, even if patience is used, and Vera has already stood out at instructs and the Angels’ pre-spring program in Arizona. Vera’s tools and advanced feel for the game, especially given his age, give him the chance to be a true impact player. The Angels love his swing from both sides of the plate and think he could be a plus hitter when all is said and done. He has plenty of bat speed and was already showing plate discipline that belies his age and lack of experience. There’s above-average raw power in there with the chance for it to be at least average game power once he physically matures. The only tool that isn’t going to be above-average is his speed, but he’s a very good defender, with a strong arm, really good hands and excellent range despite the lack of quickness. He’ll have every chance to play shortstop long-term, but will profile just fine at second or third should he outgrow the position. He’ll be 17 as he plays his first professional games in 2020.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Howard skipped Rookie ball, assigned instead to High-A Myrtle Beach to start the season, and he stayed there all year despite lackluster production at the plate. He struck out nearly five times as often as he walked, rarely seeing a three-ball count all season. His steep learning curve in that regard isn't surprising at this stage: While his approach was already advanced when he was drafted, he was a Midwestern high schooler at the time, and as with any cold weather hitter, it’s reasonable to allow some added time for his approach to fully adjust to professional pitching. He best squares up pitches at the bottom of the strike zone, so his adjustment to pro arms has been a challenge given pitchers’ penchant for fastballs up in the zone. Despite his lack of offense, Howard’s defense at shortstop didn't falter, standing out in a system overflowing with middle infielders. He continues to project as a second-division everyday big league shortstop or high-end utility man, and is more likely to reach that outcome than most teenage shortstop prospects because of his defense. We believe a star turn is still unlikely here.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: A player with mature baseball feel who is exceptionally polished for having been a Midwestern high schooler, Howard is a rare sort of high-floor teenage draftee. who is exceptionally polished for having been a Midwestern high schooler, Howard is a rare sort of high-floor teenage draftee. While not exceptionally toolsy nor athletic, Howard is solid in these areas and is advanced defensively as well as from a bat-to-ball standpoint. He best squares up pitches at the bottom of the strike zone, and although he hasn't been tested regularly at the letters, he's shown flashes of being able to either lay off those pitches or pull his hands in and find a way to get the barrel there. Whether Howard is able to do that against big league velocity is tough to predict, but he has promising feel to hit and an advanced approach for a cold weather hitter, as well as perhaps the best defensive footwork from the 2020 draft class. He projects as a solid everyday big league shortstop, and is more likely to reach that outcome than most teenage shortstop prospects. I don't see a star turn here unless I'm underrating how much room for strength-gains Howard has, or how much his feel for contact will buoy his in-game power output.

fangraphs.label: 2020updated
fangraphs.text: Perhaps he would have come out of the 2020 blocks having already filled out and showing more raw power, but Howard answered most relevant questions the previous summer when he performed against the best high school pitching all summer on the showcase circuit. That pitching is much better than what Howard would have seen in Illinois this spring. Howard best squares up pitches at the bottom of the strike zone, and although he hasn't been tested regularly at the letters, he's shown flashes of being able to either lay off those pitches, or pull his hands in and find a way to get the barrel there, and even to catch that high pitch way out in front of the plate and hit it in the air to his pull side. Whether Howard is able to do that against big league velocity is tough to predict, but he has promising feel to hit and an advance approach for a cold weather hitter, as well as perhaps the best defensive footwork in the entire class. He projects as an everday big league shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Howard led his Jackie Robinson West (Chicago) club to the Little League World Series Finals in 2014, six years before becoming just the third local product drafted by the Cubs in the first round. Signed for $3,745,500 as the 16th overall pick in 2020, he struggled offensively and missed time with a hamstring strain when sent to Single-A at age 19 to make his pro debut the following year. He didn't get much of a chance to rebound in 2022, severely injuring his hip in early May and requiring season-ending surgery. Howard's outstanding defense and makeup have prompted Chicago to challenge him with aggressive assignments. He hasn't disappointed with the glove, showing twitchy actions, range to both sides, quick hands and a plus arm capable of making strong throws from a variety of angles. He complements his tools with instincts and intelligence and looks like a future Gold Glover. Though amateur scouts had mixed opinions about Howard's offensive upside and he hit just .229/.287/.315 in 103 games during his first two pro seasons, the Cubs saw some encouraging signs before he got hurt last year. A right-handed hitter, he hit the ball significantly harder and controlled the strike zone better than he did in 2021. He could develop at least 15-homer power to go with his solid speed, but he's going to have to learn to recognize and deal with breaking balls and make adjustments to avoid producing weak ground-ball contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Howard starred at shortstop on the Jackie Robinson West (Chicago) club that advanced to the Little League World Series finals in 2014, six years before the Cubs made him just the third Windy City-area product they've ever drafted in the first round. Signed for $3,745,000 as the 16th overall pick in 2020, he's so advanced defensively that he headed directly to Low-A for his pro debut at age 19 last year. Initially overmatched at the plate before rallying in the final two months, he didn't get much of a chance to develop further in 2022 because he injured his left hip in a baserunning mishap in May and required season-ending surgery. One of the best defenders in the entire Minors, Howard is a legitimate plus-plus shortstop. He has quick-twitch actions, fast hands and a plus arm capable of making quality throws from a variety of angles. He has instincts and intelligence to complement his physical tools, and the only reason he spent time at second base last summer was to give fellow teenager Kevin Made some time at shortstop. After Howard's offensive upside drew mixed reviews on the high school showcase circuit, he didn't answer any of those questions in his debut. He has some promising building blocks in a sound right-handed swing, the bat speed and projectable strength to have perhaps average power and solid speed. But he also has a long ways to go with his plate discipline and pitch recognition, which leads to too many strikeouts and too much ground-ball contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The starting shortstop on the Jackie Robinson West (Chicago) team that advanced to the 2014 Little League World Series finals, Howard became just the third Windy City-area product selected in the first round by the Cubs. The top true shortstop in the 2020 Draft, he followed in the footsteps of Brian Rosinski (1975) and Don Schulze (1980) when Chicago took him 16th overall last June. Signed for $3,745,500, he impressed the Cubs with his physical and mental maturity during instructional league. The best defensive player in the system, Howard is a no-doubt shortstop. He has smooth, athletic actions as well as quick hands and a solid to plus arm capable of making throws from a variety of angles. He has the high baseball IQ to make the most of his tools and the internal clock to slow the game down on both sides of the ball. While Howard drew some mixed reviews as a hitter on the high school showcase circuit and again while making his pro debut with a challenging assignment to Low-A, he has an efficient right-handed swing and mature approach that should allow him to make consistent contact. He generates promising bat speed and is adding strength to his projectable 6-foot-2 frame, so he could develop average power. He's a solid runner who's an asset on the bases.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Valerio has a .302/.399/.443 career line with more walks than strikeouts up through High-A, and he plays an up-the-middle position. Yes, Valerio is small, listed at just 5-foot-7, 165 pounds, but his swing is balanced, and he maintains barrel accuracy despite a high level of effort. Plus, his short levers enable him to get on top of fastballs that many hitters cannot. Based on Valerio's level of in-the-box athleticism, I have big belief in his hit tool, and don't think he is going to bottom out due to a lack of physicality. Landlocked at second base, it's possible Valerio ends up with a trajectory similar to César Hernández's, where at times his lack of versatility puts pressure on other elements of a team's roster.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Valerio (acquired from the Mets in the Keon Broxton deal) is a compact infielder with excellent feel for contact. He has a big, slow leg kick and takes a lot of high-effort swings but it doesn't undermine his ability to put the bat on the ball, and he's currently among the minor league leaders in swinging strike rate. Valerio is neither especially strong nor especially projectable, and he's a better long-term fit at either second or third base. Ideally a player falling in that range of the defensive spectrum would have a better shot to grow into power, and so Valerio projects as a versatile, 1-ish WAR multi-positional infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Things were looking up for Valerio when he went from a $10,000 signing with the Mets in March 2018 to a piece in the Keon Broxton trade with the Brewers in January 2019 to an impressive full-season performer in 2021. Last season, however, changed that narrative when Valerio found himself challenged in the upper Minors for the first time. The Dominican Republic native slashed just .228/.313/.357 with 12 homers in 113 games at Double-A Biloxi. Even with that down year, Valerio still exhibits signs of controlling the zone well. His 16.7 percent K rate may have been a career high, but it was still well above-average by Southern League standards. A 10 percent walk rate was solid too and roughly in line with Valerio’s career marks. He’s added some lift to his swing in the last two years, and while that’s increased his homer output to 23 in that span, a relative lack of overall strength led to some weak fly balls and a .249 BABIP that dulled his whole offensive performance. Valerio needs to hit because he’s yet to lock in as an average defender anywhere. His below-average arm has made second base his primary position, and the Brewers started mixing in more left field last year. Average speed doesn’t help matters at either spot, though he is more aggressive on the basepaths than his raw wheels would indicate with 61 steals on his resume since 2021. Finding the perfect marriage between keeping his K/BB ratio in check and perhaps getting back to what he’s best at with spraying line drives could put Valerio back on track in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Valerio signed with the Mets at 17 years old in March 2018 and immediately took to the pro game with a .319 average and 6.9 percent K rate in that year’s Dominican Summer League. The 5-foot-7 infielder caught the attention of Brewers scouts, and Milwaukee acquired the then-teen in a January 2019 trade for Keon Broxton. After a solid stateside debut in 2019, Valerio’s true breakout came at Low-A Carolina last season as he hit .314/.430/.469 with more walks (54) than strikeouts (49) in 85 games. A late-season promotion to High-A Wisconsin saw more power from the 20-year-old. One thing is abundantly clear in Valerio’s career -- he can hit. His career .302 average entering 2022 speaks to that, and his career 113/120 K/BB ratio highlights his plate discipline and bat-to-ball skills. It’s decent power for a player sized at just 5-foot-7, 165 pounds, given how much hard contact he already makes, but his 11 homers in 2021 likely will be his ceiling at higher levels. Valerio isn’t a burner, but he was an active baserunner in the lower levels (where rule changes encouraged action on the basepaths) with 31 steals in 40 attempts. The Brewers want to find Valerio a defensive home, and that’s their next challenge in his development. He has second, third and short on his Minor League resume, but his below-average arm should keep him at the keystone. Milwaukee hasn’t ruled out trying him in center either to see if that can stick. The Dominican Republic native has gone from a low-level trade pickup to a bat his organization wants in the lineup at every level.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: A fourth round shortstop, Conley originally attended Miami (but never played there), then transferred to Texas Tech, where he only played the 2020 and ’21 seasons, giving him a much shorter runway for evaluation and stat generation than most power conference prospects. He slugged .600 during his career in Lubbock. Conley is a switch-hitter with pull power from both sides of the plate. He looked rough on defense as an amateur and may not have the hands for the infield, but because we're talking about a switch-hitter with power, Conley has some exciting potential outcomes, even if he has to move to the outfield. He has a chance to be a valuable, bat-first utility type.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Fourth round shortstop Cal Conley out of Texas Tech originally attended Miami (but never played there) and transferred to Texas Tech, where he only played the 2020 and ’21 seasons. He slugged .600 during his career there. Conley is a switch-hitter with pull power from both sides of the plate. He looked rough on defense during the college postseason and may not have the hands for the infield. But because we're talking about a switch-hitter with power, Conley has some exciting potential outcomes, even if he has to move to the outfield. He has a chance to be a valuable, bat-first utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Conley was initially slated to head to Miami for college, but he decided to transfer to Texas Tech, sitting out the 2019 season as a result of the NCAA’s transfer rules. He made a strong first impression with the Red Raiders with an OPS over 1.000 in the shortened 2020 season, then backed it up by slashing .329/.393/.587 in 2021, enough to land him in the fourth round of that summer’s Draft. After a very slow start with Single-A Augusta to kick off his first full season of pro ball in 2022, Conley played his way to High-A and performed well in the Arizona Fall League. The son of former Minor Leaguer Brian Conley, Cal is the kind of player who is better than the sum of his parts. A switch-hitter, Conley has displayed a knack for contact, particularly from the left side of the plate. While the undersized infielder is a hit-over-power, gap-to-gap, use-all-fields type, there’s more extra-base pop than you might think, with the 16 homers he hit in 2022 not an aberration at all. While he’s not a burner, Conley does have solid speed and he maximizes it with excellent instincts and aggressiveness on the basepaths, not to mention a “gamer” mentality that has his engine going full throttle at all times. Those instincts help him play a capable shortstop, the spot he’s seen the most time at thus far, but some see a move to second base in his future, where he might have the best chance at being a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 55 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Brian Conley was a Minor League player for the Cubs and Reds in the 1990s and went on to coach in the Cincinnati organization. His son Cal starred at Texas Tech after transferring from Miami, and an uptick in power (15 homers) in 2021 helped land the steady middle infielder in the fourth round of last summer’s Draft, signing for $422,500 and making his pro debut with Low-A Augusta. Conley is a switch-hitter who has very good bat-to-ball skills, though the contact rate is better from the left side and right side features a bit more swing-and-miss. He is hit-over-power, though his added strength did translate into more pop in his last year at Texas Tech and he showed that it translates with a wood bat in his hands during his first full season with the Braves. With above-average speed and very good instincts, Conley is capable of playing a solid shortstop, though his arm might be a bit short for him to be an everyday player at the premium spot. He’s mostly played short as a pro, though he’s gotten times on the right side of second base, and second is the more likely spot where he could develop into a big league regular, with a more likely outcome of being a heady utility type.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Morissette is a compact middle infielder with a sweet lefty stroke, and a hit/power combination that has a shot to play every day at second base. He has terrific vertical plate coverage, able to shorten up and barrel gut-high pitches, as well as drop the bat head and scoop low balls out to his pull-side, and he does most of his slugging damage that way. This can sometimes lead Morissette to pull off of pitches away from him, which might be something upper-level pitchers will start to exploit. Overall, his feel for contact helps weaponize his modest raw power enough that Morissette projects as a core infield role player.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: A sweet-swinging, multi-positional infielder, Morissette bears an eerie resemblance to Rays infielder Joey Wendle. Like Wendle, Morissette's bat-to-ball skills and approach are what will likely carry him to the big leagues; he's currently ranked behind similar hitters who have more power projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boston College's only two-time baseball All-American, Morissette fell short of pulling off the trifecta in 2021 after injuring his hand in a home-plate collision with Louisville catcher and No. 1 overall pick Henry Davis. He did rally to finish his college career with a 16-game hitting streak before Miami selected him in the second round and signed him for $1,403,200. He batted just .234/.312/.401 in his first full pro season, though he did homer six times in June just before fouling a ball off his left ankle and sustaining a fracture that sidelined him for six weeks. After standing out with his bat-to-ball skills in college, Morissette has made changes to his left-handed swing to help him drive the ball more consistently as a pro. Instead of focusing on making line-drive contact and using the entire field, he has concentrated on launching balls to his pull side since joining the Marlins. His new approach might result in 15 or more homers per season, but he also batted just .226/.311/.372 in his first two professional years. That kind of production won't cut it for a player projected as an offensive second baseman. His instincts are more notable than his average speed on the bases and in the field. He has a quick first step and gets the job done at the keystone, but his average arm is stretched at third base and he doesn't have the range desired at shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boston College's only two-time baseball All-American, Morissette didn't put up loud numbers last spring, in part because he injured his hand in a home-plate collision with Louisville catcher and No. 1 overall pick Henry Davis. He rallied to finish the season with a 16-game hitting streak before signing for $1,403,200 in the second round. Former All-Star Joe Panik was his favorite player growing up and Morissette projects as a steady player in the same mold. Though Morissette batted just .204/.308/.299 while making his pro debut in Low-A, the Marlins remain confident in his bat-to-ball skills. He employs a compact left-handed swing with a patient all-fields approach that should enable him to produce high batting averages. His power is more in question because he has solid but not plus bat speed, needs more strength and frequently hits the ball on the ground, which may limit him to 10-12 homers per season. Morissette's instincts on the bases and in the field stand out more than his average speed. After he spent most of his college career at second base while also seeing action at third for the Eagles and at shortstop in summer ball, the Marlins plan on trying him all over the infield. He's a solid defender at second base, but his range is a bit lacking at shortstop and his average arm is stretched on the left side of the infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sequera, a $750,000 signing out of Venezuela in 2019, was one of the surprises of the Tigers' international crop in 2021, when he posted an .823 OPS and 23 extra-base hits in just 46 games to win MVP honors in the Florida Complex League. His promotion to Single-A Lakeland for 2022 left him a bit more exposed, but he still produced 28 doubles and 19 homers in 116 games and had a solid late-season run before fading in the final week. Sequera steps to the plate looking for hard contact to the pull side, an approach that leads to high chase rates and strikeout totals -- though he dropped his strikeout rate 7 percent from 2021 to 2022. He homered on 20 percent of his fly balls in 2021, an unsustainable performance, but answered in 2022 with more line drives and better pitch recognition, if not results. His athleticism has not translated into speed on the basepaths. He moves well at shortstop and has a knack for highlight plays but could eventually shift over to third if he continues to grow. While Sequera has slugged his way alongside Cristian Santana and Roberto Campos to give the Tigers a trio of intriguing international prospects on their way up the system, Sequera is the least heralded of the group. He might never be a high-average hitter, but if he can maintain power numbers, he could work his way into the Tigers’ infield picture. Advanced pitching at High-A West Michigan could temper his aggressiveness.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Roberto Campos was the headline signing of the Tigers’ 2019 international class, Sequera was rather overlooked as a Venezuelan shortstop who received a $750,000 bonus. Despite missing the Dominican Summer League when it was canceled due to the pandemic, Sequera enjoyed an eye-opening pro debut by winning MVP honors in a Rookie-level Florida Complex League well stocked with prospects. He got extra bases on more than half his 42 hits for the season, including 11 home runs, and finished with a flourish, including four long balls, four doubles and 17 RBIs over his final 12 games. Sequera takes an aggressive pull approach at the plate that leads to high strikeout totals but consistently hard contact when he connects. He has enough bat speed to turn on fastballs with authority on different parts of the plate. He shows some pitch recognition, but like many hitters his age looking for power, will also chase breaking balls out of the zone. He moves well at shortstop for his size, especially on balls up the middle, and has worked to improve his range. He could shift to third as his body fills out. The Tigers once had a pipeline of talent coming out of Venezuela, including Avisail Garcia and Eugenio Suarez, but Sequera has the potential to be the best Tigers prospect from the country since those days. He got his first taste of full-season ball with Single-A Lakeland this summer and has shown pop, but little patience at the plate.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Sequera is a barrel-chested teenage infielder who hit for impressive power on the complex in 2021. What he has in present power he lacks in long-term projection, though, as it's likely the muscular Sequera ends up as a shift-aided second baseman, or a third baseman during the bulk of his career. So long as he can keep the strikeouts in check, he has the pop to play a meaningful role at either of those positions at the very least.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: The undersized, athletic Paniagua is leading the org in strikeouts as of list publication, albeit as a 22-year-old at Low-A, a level he is essentially repeating. He only sits 90-92 mph, but Paniagua can vary his fastball's shape, his low-80s curveball has bat-missing finish and depth, and he repeats a simple, balanced delivery with machine-like precision. While unlikely to ever have an impact fastball, Paniagua has the on-mound athleticism to develop plus command and a better changeup, projecting as a backend starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Paniagua was a little older than many international signees when he joined the Cardinals at 17 for $160,000 out of the Dominican Republic in December 2017. He didn’t reach full-season ball until 2021 and was primarily a reliever -- and a successful one with 62 strikeouts in 46 1/3 innings -- during that first spin at Single-A Palm Beach. Paniagua returned to the Florida State League as a starter in ’22 and impressed again with a 2.18 ERA, 0.96 WHIP and 107 K’s in 99 frames. He ended the year with eight more mundane outings for High-A Peoria, and the Cardinals chose to leave Paniagua off the 40-man when he was Rule 5-eligible, though he went unpicked. The 6-foot-1 right-hander works with a four-seamer and a sinker around 91-93 mph, occasionally touching 95, and there’s still the chance more velo could be coming because it looks like he still hasn’t fully grown into his figure. His upper-70s curveball showed great depth and 12-to-6 vertical break, and A-ball hitters -- especially righties -- couldn’t touch it. A mid-80s fading changeup could be helpful against batters from both sides, but lefties still had the lion’s share of success against Paniagua in 2022. Paniagua likely wasn’t much of a Rule 5 threat last year because he lacked success above the Single-A level, but with his three-pitch mix and solid ability to pitch in the zone, there’s still a potential starting pitcher here in the big leagues. That extra velo would go a long way toward helping that projection. Considering Paniagua is entering his age-23 season, the clock is ticking.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in the 2019-20 international class for $290,000 at age-17 out of the Dominican Republic, Sanchez put together his first big year in the system, climbing all the way from the Arizona Complex League to High-A Everett. Why he’s been so under-the-radar and finally found himself is largely rooted in the Mariners’ player development program, which has constantly preached persistence and patience with the middle infielder. After he signed, Sanchez’s hips got a little wider and the defense and range took a dip. But he arrived in 2022 in much better shape, and it translated well into his profile at shortstop. He’s blossomed into a legit defender at the premium position -- arguably the best middle infielder in the system, which could greatly benefit his long-term trajectory. Beyond the glove, a big part of his step forward was simply trusting his approach at the plate. He may not hit for as high of an average as he progresses, but the sneaky power could lead to some surprising production that, coupled with his strong defense, will make up for it, and he’s definitely a high-ceiling player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ovalles signed a little later than many in his class when he joined the Mets in November 2019 out of the Dominican Republic, and he missed out on what would have been his first Minor League campaign due to the pandemic the following year. He got off to a solid start with a 2.83 ERA and 0.69 WHIP (third-lowest among the 257 pitchers on the circuit with at least 30 IP) over 35 frames in the Dominican Summer League in 2021 and took a step forward stateside this past season, posting a 4.05 ERA with 66 punchouts in 46 2/3 frames between the Florida Complex and Florida State Leagues. The 6-foot-3 right-hander gained velocity throughout his second pro campaign and was around 93-95 mph, topping out at 97, during his time with Single-A St. Lucie. If the heat wasn’t enough, Ovalles’ fastball also comes with a healthy amount of spin typically in the 2,500-2,700 rpm range, adding to the hope it can be a true plus pitch. His low-80s sweeping slider actually had a higher whiff rate and was dominant against righties. He’d fold in a get-me-over curveball occasionally, and his 83-86 mph changeup can get some swing-and-miss but was pounded by lefties, who had a .948 OPS against Ovalles in a small FSL sample. Ovalles has started and relieved at this early stage, and despite his improved stuff, he’s exhibited decent control too, adding to the hope the arsenal can play over a larger sample. His projectable frame at 6-foot-3 points to the possibility of another level of a repertoire still to come with more experience as he moves into full-season ball for good in his age-20 campaign.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Santos joined the Mets system for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic just before the 2017-18 international period closed. He has been slowly working his way through the system, playing for one club per season in his last three campaigns. He spent 2022 entirely at High-A Brooklyn, throwing a career-high 116 2/3 innings for the Cyclones. Santos posted a 4.47 ERA with 105 strikeouts in 116 2/3 innings in the South Atlantic League and was left unprotected and unpicked in the offseason Rule 5 Draft. The lack of a stellar strikeout rate doesn’t tell the whole story because Santos was nearly elite at one thing -- keeping the ball on the ground. His 58.7 percent ground-ball rate was the third-highest in the Minors among the 311 pitchers with at least 100 innings in 2022. A 93-96 mph fastball is the main culprit because its impressive sink made it difficult for batters to square the ball up, enabling the pitch to play up to plus level. His low-80s slider shows some promise but still lacks the depth to be more than average, while an upper-80s changeup drops some but didn’t prevent Santos from getting lit up (.295 average-against) vs. lefty hitters. The 6-foot-7 right-hander has always been projectable, and the velocity and movement have certainly come, along with a little better control than many his size. There’s something to be said for a pitcher that elicits ground balls by the bucketful in an age when hitters prioritize lifting the ball in the air, but a lack of surefire secondary pitches -- and the ticking roster clock -- could make 2023 a make-or-break year for Santos.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets signed Santos for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic as part of the 2017-18 international signing period, seeing the 6-foot-6 right-hander as a projectable arm. He ascended quickly stateside after only 11 Dominican Summer League outings as a 17-year-old in 2018 but took a step back at Rookie Advanced Kingsport (5.09 ERA, 36 strikeouts in 40 2/3 innings) the following year. Following the missed 2020 season, Santos saw full-season ball for the first time with Low-A St. Lucie and didn’t miss a ton of bats, striking out 79 in 96 innings. He finished with a 4.59 ERA. Heading into just his age-20 season, projection remains the name of the game for Santos. Previously sitting at 92-93, he added a little velocity to be in the 93-96 mph range with his fastball now. The pitch typically shows promising sink, so it’s not straight velo either. Everything else remains in development. A low-80s slider shows promising spin, but lacks the consistency to be more than an average pitch. An upper-80s changeup does little more than show separation from the heater and remains his third pitch by far. Santos got better at throwing strikes in the second half last season, and with an 8.9 percent walk rate, that remains less of a concern than it did entering '21. The Mets are still working with Santos on developing consistent mechanics to help him command the ball better in general, because as his low strikeout rate proved, he could be quite hittable inside the zone. His size, youth and fastball still give Santos some promise, and discussions about a move to the bullpen remain at least a year away.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets saw plenty to dream on when they signed Santos for $275,000 out of the Dominican Republic in September 2017. At 6-foot-8, Santos stood out in more ways than one in his first taste of pro ball in the Dominican Summer League, prompting a move stateside in the midst of his age-17 season. His results took a step back in 2019 at Rookie Advanced Kingsport – namely his 5.09 ERA, 1.75 WHIP and 25 walks in 40 2/3 innings – and he missed out on more chances to develop due to the pandemic and a broken toe suffered not long after leaving Spring Training. He was healed in time for instructional league in the Dominican Republic and salvaged some time throwing there. As is true of many tall pitchers, Santos’ fastball is the star of his arsenal. It usually sits around 92-93 and can touch 95 and earns extra points for the way he bears down on hitters with it thanks to his massive extension. There could be even another tick of velocity in the tank as he adds more strength to his frame. As he showed in the Appalachian League, control can be an issue at times because of his size, however, and that’s something Santos will have to find the more he throws. The breaking ball and changeups are works in progress. The former was a particular point of emphasis last spring before camp broke and can look the better of the two offerings because of its promising spin, though it’s not yet a plus pitch. Mechanics and secondary pitches will be what decides how much of a role Santos can play in the Majors. If he can only keep the fastball as a plus pitch, then he could head to the bullpen like fellow 6-foot-8 Met Dellin Betances. If he can develop a better breaking ball, then starting could be a real option. With an August birthday, he will still be a teenager for much of the 2021 season, an indication that time is very much on his side.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets handed out a pair of seven-figure bonuses during the 2017 international period, signing shortstop Ronny Mauricio and outfielders Adrian Hernandez for $2.1 and $1.5 million, respectively. Santos, on the other hand, received a $275,000 bonus that's already looking like a bargain for the Mets after the teenage right-hander finished his professional debut at 17 in the rookie-level Gulf Coast League. Long and lanky, Santos has grown since he signed and now stands at 6-foot-8. Unlike many young pitchers of that size, however, he has a very good delivery and knows how to command his developing three-pitch mix. Using a high three-quarter slot, Santos fills up the strike zone with a fastball that sits in the low 90s and touches 95 mph. It has riding life because he generates huge extension toward the plate, while all signs point to the big right-hander adding more velocity to his plus fastball. When he signed with the Mets, Santos didn't have a breaking ball, but he has quickly gotten a good feel for a slider that he throws with power and depth, giving it the look of a future out pitch. His changeup is below average right now, but with his feel for pitching, the Mets are confident it will come on as a third effective offering. Santos' tantalizing combination of youth, size and plus command all point to a career as a strike-throwing starting pitcher, possibly even one who pitches near the front of a big league rotation. So it's been no surprise the Mets have received multiple calls from teams looking to make deals asking about him as his first full season in the United States awaits.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Santos pitches like a XXL José Ureña, with an eerily similar delivery that creates sink (he has a 60% groundball rate, way above his 49% 2021 mark) and tail on his mid-90s fastball, but is tough to repeat. Though he's started throughout his pro career, Santos' general athleticism, maxed-out frame and inconsistent release funnel him to the bullpen with relative certainty. While he lacks the long-term physical projection typical of a 20-year-old, he may yet throw harder in relief. The east/west action on his fastball and slider combo can make him an uncomfortable at-bat for righties even though his slider doesn't have a ton of movement in a vacuum. In essence a "look" or specialist relief prospect at a distance from the big leagues, I've cooled my FV jets a bit here.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There's no change here as Santos was not at 2020 instructs: A slight dip in velo and a strike-throwing regression weren't enough to slide Santos down the pref list at this point last year, not as his age, nor at his size, and especially not when you consider both. This is a giant teenager with a good arm and some breaking ball and changeup feel (for creating movement, not for locating) who was pushed hurriedly to an affiliate when he was still 17. The arm action looked a little less fluid and was a bit compromised in 2019, but I'm still on Santos as a long-term projection arm with an elite frame. (At-home dev)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: A slight dip in velo and a strike-throwing regression isn't enough to slide Santos down the pref list at this point, not as his age, nor at his size, and especially not when you consider both. This is a giant teenager with a good arm and some breaking ball and changeup feel (for creating movement, not for locating) who was pushed hurriedly to an affiliate when he was still 17. The arm action looked a little less fluid and was a bit compromised last season, but we're still on Santos as a long-term projection arm with an elite frame.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Trenta-sized teenagers who throw in the mid-90s don't typically have any idea where its going, but Santos threw strikes so efficiently for two months in the DSL that the Mets thought him fit for an August promotion. He made his stateside debut just before his 17th birthday and walked just six hitters in 50 innings all summer. So Santos has rare size, precocious velocity, and control, though much of the rest of the profile has room for improvement. He exhibits neither notable raw spin nor feel for locating his current breaking ball, a low-80s slurve. There's a strong chance Santos tries several iterations of various breaking balls during the course of his development and the one(s) he ends up with will probably look much different than what he's currently using. At this point in his development, we just care about the raw spin, a trait of limited malleability, and Santos' is just okay. It's reasonable to hope he grows into elite velocity. The fact that he's throwing this hard at this age and at this size is encouraging, though he's less projectable than one would probably assume given his age and height. All talk of Santos' physical progression centers around reshaping his current frame rather than just adding mass, as he's already pretty filled out. This clouds the fastball projection somewhat, but he'll probably still end up throwing really hard. There's need for significant development throughout the rest of the repertoire, and it's more likely that a portion of that happens (resulting in a back-of-the rotation or bullpen role) than it is that all of it does (resulting in stardom). He signed for $250,000 in 2017.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Tresh has above-average pull power and plus raw arm strength. His pop times are often in the 1.9s but his throws tend to sail on him rather than be on the bag, so his effectiveness in stopping the run game plays down a little bit. While Tresh has big power for a catcher, he struggles to cover the outer third of the plate and swings inside a lot of pitches in the strike zone, as well as over the top of a lot of breaking balls, and he's likely to end up as a 20- or 30-grade bat, which is basically par for the course at catcher. Tresh receives on one knee even with runners on base, in a style similar to former Phillies catcher Carlos Ruiz, where Tresh is very low, almost in a half split. This sometimes makes it harder for him to block balls in the dirt but aides his ability to frame low pitches. While he needs polish, Tresh projects as a power-over-hit backup catcher.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: A catcher with plus-plus raw will always appeal to scouts, but many evaluators have put 40 or lower grades on his hit tool, and a lack of accuracy mitigates his plus arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A hamate bone injury caused Tresh to miss the start of his 2020 collegiate season, but he put himself back on the radar at North Carolina State in 2021, when he homered 15 times in 56 games and helped the Wolfpack finish third at the College World Series. The Royals selected him in the 17th round and gave him a high bonus – $423,000 – to sign him away from returning to school. Tresh posted an .828 OPS between High-A and Double-A in his first full pro season in 2022, with 14 homers and 54 RBI. Tresh is a strong hitter who generates impressive exit velocities with his raw power and bat speed. He made more contact in 2022 with a 24.3% strikeout rate between both levels. Tresh is still aggressive, and there are still improvements to be made in his approach, especially with pitches on the outer part of the plate, but he has a lot of power potential. Behind the plate, Tresh showed significant improvement with his receiving last year. He has a plus arm and should become at least an average defender. Tresh receives high marks for his ability to run a pitching staff, a quiet competitor who leads by example. How far he goes and what his ceiling ends up being depends on whether he can continue his improved approach and contact at the higher levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At North Carolina State, Tresh caught sparingly behind Patrick Bailey, the No. 13 pick in 2020, and Tresh missed the start of the 2020 season with a broken hamate bone in his left hand. He put himself back on the radar and filled Bailey’s void in ’21, homering 15 times in 56 games last spring and helping the Wolfpack finish third at the College World Series. It felt like a steal when the Royals selected him all the way down in the 17th round, but Tresh stuck to his signability and wasn’t afraid to go back to school if needed. The Royals were able to sign him for $423,000, roughly the slot of a fourth-round selection. Tresh posted a 1.143 OPS in six games in Rookie ball after he was drafted, earning him a quick promotion to Low-A Columbia, where he struggled more in 10 games. Tresh has obvious raw power and consistently high exit velocities thanks to massive strength and bat speed. He’s aggressive at the plate and will need to do a better job of consistent contact, but the Royals see room for improvement as he spends more time with the hitting development program. Behind the plate, Tresh is inexperienced for a college catcher, but he showed significant improvement as a receiver in the fall. He has a plus arm to keep the running game in check and should become at least an average defender if the Royals keep him at catcher. Tresh earns praise for his leadership, ability to run a pitching staff and his quiet competitiveness. He still has a lot of ceiling for a college player, which was appealing to the Royals in the Draft. How far he will go depends on his improvement with contact and time behind the plate.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Willis is an XXL high school prospect with a much more consistent delivery than most 6-foot-7 prepsters. He sits in the low-90s and has solid curveball feel, projecting as an innings-eating fourth starter. There was a point when Willis was sitting 82-85 mph as an amateur, then came back from ulnar nerve decompression surgery peaking in the mid-90s. He's currently dealing with an arm issue and hasn't pitched in 2022, making him a deep projection prospect.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Willis is an XXL high school prospect with a much more consistent delivery than most 6-foot-7 prepsters. He sits in the low-90s and has solid curveball feel. He projects as an inning-eating fourth starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Willis hasn’t been seen a ton in recent years, both at the amateur and pro levels. He underwent ulnar nerve decompression surgery in July 2020, which knocked him out for many showcase events that summer. The Cardinals still liked enough of what they saw to select the Colorado high-school product in the seventh round of the 2021 Draft and sign him away from a Minnesota commitment with a $1 million bonus. Another arm issue limited him to six appearances (four starts) in the Florida Complex League last season. The 6-foot-5 right-hander has plenty of size on the bump, so while he touches the mid-90s but sits more in the 89-92 mph range these days, there’s still hope he can add a few ticks of velo as he continues to age and mature. (He’ll just turn 20 before Opening Day this spring.) His curveball has long been his preferred secondary, and while he’ll flash an occasional good-looking changeup, it’s still lagging behind the other two offerings. One of the promising signs of Willis’ 2022 was that he walked only two of the 46 batters he faced in the FCL, notable for someone with so much missed time. The Cardinals took it easy with Tink Hence out of the gate too, then watched him blossom into a Top 100 prospect. Willis lacks Hence’s premium stuff and ceiling, but like the other right-hander, he has ample time to blossom into a quality starting prospect, especially if his pitches take a step forward the more he throws them.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Willis underwent ulnar nerve decompression surgery on his right elbow in the middle of July 2020, knocking him out of many showcase events. Almost exactly one year to the day later, he was a Draft pick in his home state of Colorado. The Regis Jesuit High School product showed enough health and stuff in his senior spring to get the Cardinals to select him in the seventh round, and St. Louis coaxed him out of a Minnesota commitment with a $1 million bonus, well above the $211,500 assigned to the slot. The right-hander, who made one appearance in the Florida Complex League, stands out for his size at 6-foot-5, and with some projection remaining, there is hope that he can add even more velocity. As it stands, he’s around 90-94 mph, occasionally touching a smidge or two higher. His curveball looks like a solid secondary already, and he sells a sinking changeup well with his arm speed, though it remains behind the curve. Willis remains a work in progress with his command, perhaps no surprise for such a young pitcher his size. Interestingly, he was the only high school pitcher selected by the Cardinals over last year’s 20-round Draft, so it’s clear they see enough moldable parts in him as he begins his pro career. It wouldn’t be a shock if St. Louis took a conservative approach with him early on, just as they did with Tink Hence in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rojas was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 24 prospect on the 2022 International Top 50, and he received a $1.3 million bonus to sign with the Padres on Jan. 15, becoming San Diego’s second-highest signee of the class behind only Jarlin Susana ($1.7 million). The Cuba native moved to the Dominican Summer League and quickly caught some eyes by walking more times (26) than he struck out (23) while hitting .279/.373/.357 over 46 games. To put that in further context, Rojas’ 1.13 K/BB ratio ranked 16th among 255 qualifiers in the DSL, and he has the advanced knowledge of the strike zone and short left-handed swing to back up those numbers. He also wasn’t afraid of using the whole field, going the opposite way roughly a third of the time, as he tried to protect the plate. Rojas’ performance came with zero homers, but there’s always been a belief that something close to average pop could come as he fills out his projectable 6-foot-1 frame. An average runner, the teenager wasn’t afraid to press the issue on the basepaths with 14 steals, though that will be tested as he gets off the complex. He played only shortstop -- and the Padres believe he can stick there -- but he has the arm strength to handle third, where he might be a better fit long-term. San Diego officials think they might be able to get aggressive with Rojas in year two because of his approach, and he could see full-season ball at some point before 2023 is up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An intriguing combination of power and speed, Rojas signed with the Padres for $1.3 million on January 15, 2022. The 17-year-old, ranked as the No. 24 prospect on MLB Pipeline’s International Top 50, reminds some of a young Yoán Moncada with his projectable 6-foot-1, 190-pound frame. Rojas, a Cuban native, already flashes some power and has a chance to develop into an above-average hitter with his advanced approach and plate discipline. Described as a pure hitter, Rojas has a quick, compact swing and uses the whole field better than most hitters in his age group. An average runner with a strong arm, Rojas will start his career at shortstop, but some feel he may eventually shift to second or third. He has an enticing skill set and there’s a lot to dream on, but he’s still a ways away.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: A physical lefty stick who just signed in January and hasn't yet come stateside, Rojas' carrying tool is his bat. Though he's worked out at shortstop in the past, he may end up trending way down the defensive spectrum due to his size and lack of arm strength. On his way there, he'll likely become a versatile defender, with a combination of second, third, and left field looking most likely.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Urbina was ranked No. 6 on MLB Pipeline’s international prospect list when the 2018-19 signing period began, and the Twins gave the outfielder $2.75 million to sign right out of the gate on July 2, the third-highest bonus given to a player in the signing period. He’s shown some glimpses of ability, especially in terms of his approach at the plate, but it’s come without much impact and his development has been impeded by the pandemic in 2020 and then visa issues that kept him from playing in 2022 until late June. There is no question the right-handed-hitting outfielder knows how to control the strike zone. He makes a ton of contact and draws walks, bringing a 17 percent strikeout rate and a walk rate just over 11 percent with him into the 2023 season. But he’s yet to show a consistent ability to do any damage or tap into any power. He did hit the ball a bit harder in 2022 with more line drives and fly balls, but he’ll have to show more to live up to the initial power projections. Urbina has slowed down some since signing and will have to stay on top of his body and conditioning to maximize his ability. He’s a center fielder by trade, but there is growing concern he won’t maintain his speed to stay up the middle. A move to a corner might be necessary, which puts even more pressure on him to be a more productive hitter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top prospects in the 2018-19 international signing class, Urbina got $2.75 million to sign with the Twins right at the start of the signing period. He showed off his advanced feel to hit and speed during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019 and got pushed up to full-season ball in 2021, an aggressive assignment that didn’t go so well as the outfielder finished with a .585 OPS. His 2022 debut was delayed until late June because of visa issues. Despite the struggles, Urbina still showed off a strong knack for making contact and controlling the strike zone, with a 12.3 percent walk rate and a strikeout rate of just 18.7 percent. The issue was the quality of contact, with a lack of physicality leading to a lack of impact. He did work this offseason in Venezuela on adding strength and engaging his lower half more to give him a more impactful swing. Adding angle to that swing while having better pitch selection in terms of which ones to put into play will also help his offensive upside. While Urbina appeared to slow down a tick, the strength and conditioning work he put in this offseason should help in that regard as well. He has good instincts on defense and can still play center field even if he’s not quite the burner he was when he first signed. Urbina could have benefitted from a summer in a short-season league last year, but given how young he is, there’s time for him to reach the ceiling the Twins thought he had when they signed him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Urbina was ranked No. 6 on MLB Pipeline’s Top 30 international prospects list when the 2018-19 signing period began, and he got the third-highest bonus in the class, $2.75 million, to sign with the Twins. He showed off an exciting offensive skill set in his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019 and continued to impress with how he carried himself during his time at instructs last fall. Though he’ll be just 19 for nearly all of the 2021 season, Urbina really stands out for his feel for the game. He has incredible bat-to-ball skills and controls the strike zone very well, walking more than he struck out in the DSL and whiffing in just 6.5 percent of his plate appearances. He has a good swing from the right side of the plate and tends not to chase out of the zone. The only question is how much impact he’ll have, as he needs to add strength to get to what could be decent power in the future. Urbina is a plus runner right now, but beyond his pure speed, his tempo in the game helps him both be a basestealing threat and to play excellent outfield defense.
