While he played mostly center field during his debut, he looks very comfortable in all three outfield spots, with good instincts and routes, with the Twins thinking he could end up a plus defender in whatever spot he settles into.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As an amateur, Urbina spent several years in the Venezuelan Winter League’s parallel program for young players, showing what he could do against older and more experienced players. That helped make him one of the best players in the amateur crop for the 2018-19 international signing period and led to the Twins signing him for $2.75 million on July 2. He didn’t disappoint in his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019, showing off impressive all-around skills. Urbina has the chance to be an outstanding hitter, one who could eventually develop into a plus hitter in the future. He makes consistent hard contact and can use all fields well. Right now, he’s showing mostly doubles power, more to the pull side, but the right-handed hitter should grow into more pop as he matures, even though he’s not the biggest guy in the world. He has an advanced approach at the plate, walking more than he struck out during his pro debut. Urbina’s plus speed should continue to help him on both sides of the ball. He’s already a basestealing threat, swiping 19 bags in the DSL in 2019, and he has outstanding range in center field, with the chance to be at least an above-average defender there long-term. Urbina is obviously still far away, but the Twins are excited to see what he can do in the United States for the first time in 2020.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the start of the 2018-19 international signing period drew near, Urbina was No. 3 on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 international prospects list. The Twins wasted no time to pounce, inking the talented outfielder for $2.75 million. He'll make his professional debut this season. Urbina has the chance to be a dynamic up-the-middle player who hits at or near the top of a lineup. He's shown an ability to make consistent line-drive contact, performing well against older competition in the Venezuelan Winter League's parallel program for young players over the years. He has plus speed, he's been clocked with premium 60-yard times, that should help him on both sides of the ball. He's already considered an advanced defender who can stay in center field long-term and he continues to make strides with his throwing, with evaluators feeling he'll have an average arm in the future. It will be years before the Twins get a return on their investment with Urbina. But the combination of his instincts, makeup and tools will make it exciting to watch him begin the climb up the Twins ladder in 2019.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text:
It's best to look at Urbina’s atrocious production at Low-A in 2021 with a good amount of context in mind. Urbina was one of the more advanced hitters in his J2 class when he signed in 2018; he played 50 games of Rookie League ball in 2019 and continued to look mature beyond his 17 years as he acclimated to professional pitching. Then came 2020, and with it, both the global pandemic and the contraction of the minor leagues, which meant Urbina not only lost a year of professional development, but when he returned, it was to full-season ball, a zero-to-60 scenario that would make it difficult for any young hitter to find immediate success. And indeed, Urbina’s woes were obvious. When he was dialed in, he showed the explosive rotation in his swing that had garnered him attention as an amateur, but those instances were few and far between. More often, he looked unsure of what to expect, slowly dragging his bat through the zone and seeming to decide mid-swing whether he should’ve offered at the pitch. He went hitless in 48 of his 101 games at Low-A Fort Myers, finishing the year with a wRC+ of just 67 and an anemic .191/.299/.286 slash line. 
But while output like that is by no means good, there were elements to his performance last season that were encouraging. He struck out just 18.7%, significantly less than league average, especially in Low-A Southeast, where the ABS system had K-rates elevated to the extreme, and we still think he has a preternatural ability to catch fastballs at his letters and hit them with power. His speed has diminished a bit and he’s less of a base-stealing threat than he was once was; he stole 16 bags in 2021, compared to the 19 he stole in '19 in less than half the number of games. And scouts see him as a tweener outfield type without the chops to stay in center field; he split his time evenly between center and left (plus a one-game cameo in right field), and if his speed can’t keep him in center, his bat will have to improve to ensure his fit as a corner outfielder, though at just 19, he still has time to get there. The arrow is pointing down and we anticipate we'll have a quick hook with Urbina if he looks like this again in 2022, but we still like the combination of bat speed and lack of swing-and-miss at this age, and with Urbina's pedigree, it makes us want to hold off on sliding him for now.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Urbina was one of the more advanced hitters in his July 2 signing class from both a bat control and physical development perspective, and since he's begun to generate a little bit of stateside data, including during intrasquads against Twins pitching much older than him, he's continued to show an advanced idea for what he should be doing at the plate. Urbina's power projection is somewhat limited by his stocky frame, which may be an issue if he does eventually move to a corner. He's an explosive rotator though, and this guy's power doesn't just come from size and strength, but rather an upper body that unwinds kind of like Yuli Gurriel's does. Currently an above-average runner, there's a fair chance he ends up in left field due to a lack of top-end speed, though it might depend on how his body develops. But what's driving the profile here is the bat. Urbina's timing, hand-eye coordination, and all-fields feel for contact at a young age are all advanced for his age. His level of talent is commensurate with high school outfielders typically taken late in the first or sandwich round of a draft. Because of the potential corner profile and lack of physical projection, Urbina will need to perform on paper to climb the FV scale, but the eyeball reports from his amateur days through this Fall all indicate he will. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text:
Urbina was one of the more advanced hitters in his July 2 signing class from both a bat control and physical development perspective. He was also one of the youngest. Currently an above-average runner, there's a fair chance he ends up in left field due to a lack of top-end speed, though it might depend on how his body develops. 
Urbina's power projection is somewhat limited by his size, which may be an issue if he does eventually move to a corner. He's an explosive rotator though, and this guy's power doesn't just come from size and strength, but rather a an upper body that unwinds kind of like Yuli Gurriel's does. Urbina also has many promising bat-to-ball traits -- timing, hand-eye coordination, all-fields feel -- at a young age. He's one of the high priority Florida minor league/extended spring prospects to see, and we currently have him FV'd just a shade behind the top prep outfielders in the 2020 class.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Urbina was one of the more advanced bats in his July 2 signing class from both a bat control and physical development perspective. He was also one of the youngest. Currently an above-average runner, there's a fair chance he ends up in left field due to a lack of top-end speed, though it might depend on how his body develops. Urbina's power projection is somewhat limited by his size, which may be an issue if he does eventually move to a corner. It would mean he would have to be a high-end contact hitter to profile as an impact big leaguer, but that seems like it's in play because Urbina has so many promising bat-to-ball traits -- timing, hand-eye coordination, all-fields feel -- at such a young age.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Peluse had TJ toward the end of high school and began his Wake Forest career in the bullpen before transitioning into a weekend starter role as a sophomore. He was a pitchability righty with fringe stuff that played up because Peluse’s delivery screws with hitters’ timing, but after undergoing a bit of a physical transformation during the pandemic shutdown period, he was sitting 94-98 during 2020 instructs. He held that velo to start 2021 before backing down into the 93-95 range later in the year, but it's still an impact fastball at the top of the zone at those speeds. His changeup has flashed better movement than in the past, though Peluse tends to decelerate his arm when he throws it. His fastball/slider combo gives him a relief floor (his fastball grades are part of the relief forecast, as we think he'd sit in that peak velo band there), and the changeup progression gives him a shot to start.

fangraphs.label: 2021report

Peluse throws exclusively from the stretch, his fastball/slider combo gives him a relief floor, and the changeup progression gives him a shot to start.

fangraphs.text: Pitchability righty with fringe stuff

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peluse, a ninth-round Draft pick by the A’s out of Wake Forest in 2019, transformed his body during the pandemic by strengthening his legs while also refining his mechanics, leading to a fastball that was up to 98 mph. The increased velocity helped him rack up 109 strikeouts in 101 combined innings between High-A and Double-A in 2021. He regressed a bit last season, posting a 5.38 ERA with only 92 strikeouts in 118 2/3 innings at Double-A Midland. Peluse’s fastball ticked down last season, sitting around 92-94 mph for the most part. He rounds out his three-pitch mix with an above-average slider and decent changeup, though both offerings were likely affected by the decrease in velocity. Command has always been a strength for Peluse dating back to his college days. Even in a down 2022, he only walked 28 batters at Double-A. Between his strong build and ability to consistently pound the zone with strikes, the A’s still see a path for him to stick as a starter, though they hope he can regain some of that lost velocity in the coming season. Given his repertoire, a move to the bullpen could also be in play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A ninth-round pick by the A’s in 2019, Peluse went to the New York-Penn League later that summer and posted a 2.25 ERA. He utilized the pandemic as an opportunity to strengthen his legs and refine his mechanics, and the result was a return to baseball throwing a fastball harder than he’d ever thrown before. After lighting up the radar gun in the instructional league, the increased velocity helped him rack up 109 strikeouts in 101 combined innings at High-A and Double-A in 2021. Peluse’s 95-98 mph fastball is accompanied by a strong slider that has flashed plus at times and a solid changeup that continues to improve, giving him a good three-pitch mix to work with. Command is also a strength, evidenced by his low walk numbers that date back to his college days at Wake Forest. Proving to be durable with a big body and having just thrown by far the most innings over a single season in his baseball career, Peluse is expected to develop into a starter at the Major League level. His advanced repertoire and consistent ability to pound the strike zone should help him knock on the big league door soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A ninth-round pick in 2019, Peluse has put himself on the prospect radar for the A’s after showing up to the instructional league that consistently hit 97-98. The increased velocity was a credit to his hard work during the baseball shutdown in 2020 as he focused on strengthening his legs. Now carrying a power fastball, Peluse also brings a strong slider that flashes plus, as well as a changeup that is still developing. His command has always been solid going back to his days at Wake Forest, and it showed up in his debut season in the Class A Short Season New York-Penn League, walking just six batters across 24 innings. Approaching his first full season in the Minors in 2021, Peluse will get a chance to show what he can do with his improved repertoire. His repeatable delivery projects him to stick as a starter.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Pena is a physical, big-framed third base prospect with a good looking swing and is Arizona's most exciting 2021 international signee. He's shown an ability to pull his hands in and hit inside pitches for power, he's short to the ball but has lift in his swing, and he presents an interesting combination of present physicality (which might enable him to move quickly through the lower levels of the minors) and body projection (which might enable him to grow into power). Pena spent 2021 in the DSL, where he performed at a league-average level. That was it for him, as the D-backs did not have instructs. He remains an exciting, high-variance corner prospect who we were excited about as an amateur.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs signed only one player to a seven-figure bonus when the international window opened in January 2021, and that was Pena, who inked for $1.2 million out of the Dominican Republic. He got off to a solid start at the Dominican Summer League in his first Minor League campaign. Arizona got aggressive with the infielder in 2023, sending him to both the Arizona Complex League and Single-A Visalia in his age-18 season. That aggression caught up to Pena in the California League, where he slashed just .248/.344/.314 in 36 games, but that early taste of full-season ball could set him up well for a return in 2023. The pieces that Arizona evaluators first loved from Pena as an international amateur are still there, for the most part. He shows a smooth swing from the left side, and even when he was struggling with Visalia, he was still taking walks at a 12.7 percent clip. The power remains in the projectable department, considering he homered only four times in 2022 (none of them in Single-A), but his size at 6-foot-1, 170 pounds gives hope that at least average pop is coming. Pena’s lack of speed at this early stage of his career has pushed him from shortstop to second base, and he might end up being average there with the lesser defensive demands. D-backs coaches and evaluators have always loved Pena’s baseball IQ, and that’s part of the reason why they’ve pushed him so quickly to this point. He’ll get a crack at his first full Minor League campaign during his age-19 season in 2023.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Bednar didn’t begin the 2021 season as a potential first-round pick, but he ended up going 14th overall after seeing his stock rise throughout a fantastic spring at Mississippi State that included a big bump thanks to his dominating performance in the College World Series. Bednar’s best pitch is a plus low-80s slider with plenty of bite. He does a good job working the edges with the pitch and can generate swings and misses both in and out of the zone. His fastball sits 92-94 mph with plenty of 95-96 offerings thrown in, and he commands the pitch well, showing the ability to elevate with two strikes while also working both sides of the plate. While his changeup was rarely seen in college, it has good action and shouldn’t be a detriment to his development. While Bednar has a sturdy frame that's built to withstand innings, his delivery is far from pretty, with a quick, violent finish that features a big spin off to the first base side and gives some evaluators reliever vibes. He’ll certainly remain a starter for some time to come, and could move quickly through the system.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Brother of Padres prospect David Bednar, Will is a strong-bodied righty who has been up to 96 and has some feel for a loopy, shapely curveball and a harder slider. He had shoulder tendonitis as a prep senior, which helped push him to school, and he is a draft-eligible sophomore for the Bulldogs. He's not especially athletic but could have a plus fastball/slider combo that enables him to pitch in relief if starting doesn't work out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Pirates All-Star David Bednar, Will was named most outstanding player at the 2021 College World Series after dominating in three starts as Mississippi State won its first national title. After signing him for a below-slot $3,647,500 as the 14th overall pick that July, the Giants expected him to move quickly through the Minors. But his first full pro season in 2022 ended after two months because of a stress reaction in his lower back and related issues have sidelined him for most of this year. When he starred in college, Bednar bullied hitters with a 92-97 mph fastball that could feature either good carry up in the strike zone or heavy life at the knees and an 82-85 mph slider with horizontal and vertical action. Rarely at full health last year, he mostly worked at 90-93 mph with his heater and had less power and movement with the slider. His truncated season gave him little opportunity to work on a low-80s changeup with some fade and sink that he barely used in college and can struggle to throw for strikes. Bednar pounded the strike zone at Mississippi State but his back issues also took a toll on his control and command. He features some effort in his delivery but has a strong 6-foot-2 build that should lend itself to durability. His intelligence and competitiveness should help him get the most out of his ability, though he'll need to regain his health and his college stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Bednar brothers will remember 2021 fondly after David compiled a 2.23 ERA as a rookie reliever with the Pirates and Will won most outstanding player honors at the College World Series after leading Mississippi State to its first national title. The latter struck out 15 in six one-hit innings against Texas in his first CWS start and won the final with six more scoreless frames against Vanderbilt, then went 14th overall in the Draft and signed for an under-slot $3,647,500. His stuff and control haven't been as sharp in 2022 while he has battled some lower back issues. Bednar has spent much of his first full pro season working at 90-93 mph with his fastball after operating at 92-95 mph and reaching 97 in college. He can throw his heater with good carry up in the strike zone as well as with heavy life at the knees. His best offering is a slider that reaches the mid-80s with plenty of horizontal sweep as well as depth when it's on, and he'll occasionally dust off an upper-70s downer curveball to give hitters a different look. Bednar also has the makings of an average changeup with fade and sink, though he's still honing his ability to throw it for strikes. His physical frame should give him the durability to succeed as a starter, though there is some effort to his delivery and his control has wavered at times this summer. He also stands out with his intelligence and competitiveness and could be a late-inning reliever if starting doesn't work out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Webb spent two seasons as a starter at Sinclair (Ohio) CC and two as a reliever at Miami (Ohio) before the Red Sox picked him in the 14th round in 2021. In his first full pro season, he compiled a 3.18 ERA with 88 strikeouts in 56 2/3 innings while rising from Single-A to Double-A. The first pitcher from Boston's 2021 Draft to reach Double-A, he also performed well in the Arizona Fall League. Webb works with two pitches and misses bats with both of them. His fastball sits at 93-96 mph and touches 98 with significant carry and some arm-side run. He backs it up with a low-80s slider that has good sweep at times and is tighter with more depth at others. Physically imposing at 6-foot-5 and 246 pounds, Webb has an extremely low release point for someone so large and creates good extension. There's effort in his crossfire delivery and his short arm action isn't the prettiest, but they provide a lot of deception and his pitches get on hitters in a hurry. He threw strikes in college but has lacked reliable control as a pro, and he could help Boston's bullpen in the near future if he can find the zone more consistently.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Webb has the chance to become the first player in the history of Tabor College, an NAIA school in Kansas, to reach the big leagues. Initially an infielder, he moved to the mound when his bat didn't progress, and he landed in the 18th round of the 2014 Draft after an outstanding spring in Tabor's rotation. He's put 2015 Tommy John surgery in his rear view mirror, moving into the bullpen upon his return and pitching his way up to Triple-A in 2018 to earn a spot on the 40-man roster last offseason. Webb relies on two power pitches to get hitters out as a short reliever. His fastball has ticked upwards in those shorter stints, sitting in the 95-96 mph range, thrown with deception thanks to a quick arm. His breaking ball, a power slider, flashes above-average with good depth, though it's not always consistent. He cut his walk rate down in 2018, but he kept missing bats and carries a 11.1 K/9 rate into the 2019 season. Webb led the organization with 18 saves in 2018, but without further consistency of his breaking ball and command, he's unlikely to close in the big leagues. He does have the stuff to pitch in the seventh inning, at the very least, in the near future.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Webb was a low-bonus, late-round, small school pick who still wasn't really on the prospect radar for most clubs until 2018. His velocity took a step forward (up to 98 mph) and the added armspeed helped his 50 to 55 type stuff grade out a tick better. This improvement made him a lock to be a Rule 5 pick if not protected, so Atlanta added him to the 40-man roster. Like many of the 40 FV-grade relievers on this list, Webb projects as a middle reliever, but he has the best chance to turn into a bit more, and could possibly be a setup man.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Head came over from the Padres as part of the Joe Musgrove trade and had a rough first season in the Pirates system, at times looking totally lost as he brushed up against full-season pitching for the first time. Especially in August, when he struck out 40% of the time, he had trouble making contact with in-zone fastballs at an alarming rate. He ended up striking out 31% of the time across the entire season but still managed to hit 15 bombs and post a line that was above league average, almost identical to Sammy Siani's. Head swings hard and has pop despite being a wiry guy with narrow forearms. He doesn't track pitches well and still has the rather extreme arm bar from his days as a Padre, both of which might be contributing to the whiffs. The overall line was not as rough as some scouts' visual reports would suggest and Head entered the year having barely played high-level baseball since he was a relatively obscure amateur prospect whose pro experience was limited to the complex level and instructs until 2021. There is officially rather extreme bust risk here because of how the bat seems to be trending, but still plenty of other skills to like.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: The big prospect acquired in the Joe Musgrove deal with San Diego, Head's pro experience consists of 32 AZL games the summer after he was drafted in 2019, and two Fall Instructional League camps in '19 and '20. If you've been following both the prospect lists and the site’s analysis of the recent Padres deals, you'll know the Friars have a penchant for taking expensive gambles on pop-up high school prospects. Head, who signed for a record-setting bonus ($3 million, basically slot at 22nd overall) in the third round, was one of their 2019 selections of this ilk. A two-sport athlete whose football exploits (he was in a QB timeshare at a 6A school) cut into his time on the showcase circuit (though he was known in Texas), Head eschewed his commitment to Oklahoma to turn pro. Sometimes prospects who’ve never faced the upper echelon of high school pitching require a prolonged adjustment period upon first entering affiliated ball due to the leap in stuff quality from varsity high school ball, even if that prospect comes from a talent-rich area like Texas or Southern California. But that was not an issue for Head against pro pitching in the 2019 AZL. Despite some clear mechanical flaws, he sprayed hard contact all over the field and hit .283/.383/.417 against the best pitching he’d ever seen in his life. Then we had the long 2020 layoff, and my look at Head in fall instructs after he hadn’t faced live pitching for nearly a year was not as good. He wasn't tracking pitches as well, he was late on some pretty average fastballs, he lacked balance at the plate, and his pitch recognition backed up. His swing does have an arm bar, but that was also true in 2019 when he was letting the ball travel deep and hitting it hard the other way. He added a footwork component that wasn't there in 2019, an extra toe-tap before his stride. I can't outright declare this to have been detrimental, it just wasn't there when he was successful. During the Padres' final day of intrasquads, he (ironically) half-swung at an Omar Cruz fastball that was way inside, which hit Head on the hands (sorry if that’s confusing), causing him to leave the game. None of this is enough for me to move off of where I had Head evaluated last year, though. Because of the lack of minor league season, the 2020 Instructional League was full of pitching that was typically more advanced than what Head would have seen during a normal instructs, and he was dropped into that environment after not playing all year. And let’s not forget that Head has some unique athletic traits. He’s ambidextrous, and swings and throws a baseball with his left hand though he quarterbacked primarily with his right, occasionally using his left when he rolled out that way. I still think he’s a potential traditional big league leadoff hitter, but while some others young kids really blew up on the backfields last Fall, Head struggled. The context for those struggles is important, though. (Alternate site, Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text:
The Padres have been unafraid to stick their necks out and use high picks on high school players who weren't fixtures on the summer showcase circuit for one reason or another (injury, participation in football, etc.), players who may be underscouted (and perhaps undervalued) by clubs who are more comfortable with prep hitters who've performed against curated competition. The results have been mixed. Mason House and Sam Keating are not on this prospect list, while Blake Hunt has climbed it, and Mason Thompson has yo-yo'd. Now 2019 draftees Hudson Head and Josh Mears enter the fray, with Head doing so after receiving a $3 million bonus, a record for a third-rounder. 
The pitching he saw in the AZL was the best he's seen in his entire life, and Head not only allayed concerns about that competition-quality chasm by hitting .283/.383/.417, he also occasionally did some freaky, elite stuff that got me very excited about his prospectdom. Head is ambidextrous, and swings and throws a baseball with his left hand but quarterbacked primarily with his right, occasionally using his left when he rolled out that way. For someone with so little high-level experience, his bat control is remarkable. A pronounced arm bar caused him to be late on some of the good velo I've seen him face but Head's feel for opposite field contact enabled him to strike those pitches with authority anyway. I think he needs polish from a mechanical standpoint, but there's rare natural bat-to-ball proclivity happening here. There's also much more measurable power than I would have guessed -- Head's exit velos last summer were more akin to those of heavy-hitting corner guys his age than someone who looks like a wiry leadoff sort. Still a high-variance prospect because of his short track record of hitting, Head has a shot to be a leadoff-hitting center fielder, an above-average regular.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Popup athlete is now widely known and has gap power, some loft and plus speed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For most of his pro career since the Padres took him in the third round and gave him an over-slot bonus of $3 million to sign, Head has been a bit of a cautionary tale about raw toolsy high schoolers who can’t quite figure things out at the next level. After a pretty solid pro debut after signing in 2019, he reportedly looked good at San Diego’s alternate site, but for most of his two years with the Pirates after they got him as part of the Joe Musgrove deal, it’s been a struggle. There might have been signs of life in 2022, however, as Head slashed a much more solid .264/.355/.472 from July 1 on after posting a .650 OPS in the season’s first three months. Head is a tinkerer at the plate, one who was constantly changing his setup to try to unlock his considerable raw tools. He moved his hands often and found a spot that helped him use his athleticism more, and rather than change it the second something went wrong in the second half of 2022, he stuck with it and found more consistency than he’d had previously. There are still approach issues, as he struck out more than 30 percent of the time, even when things were going better, but there’s a lot of potential impact in his left-handed swing. He also made progress on the other side of the ball. He’s always had good speed, but in 2021, his defensive metrics were not good. In 2022, he graded out very well in center field. It remains to be seen if Head’s mechanical changes and his commitment to his craft will allow him to climb to the next level, but it’s the first glimmer of hope in a while.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Head didn’t have a lot of experience against top competition as a two-sport standout who also was a quarterback at his Texas high school. He did show off some impressive tools as the 2019 Draft approached and the Padres jumped ahead of the industry by taking him in the third round and going way over slot to sign him for $3 million. He had a solid pro debut in rookie ball that summer and impressed the higher ups at the club’s alternate site in 2020. He made his full-season debut with the Pirates, who acquired him in Jan. 2021 as part of the Joe Musgrove trade, and he struggled offensively. The Pirates still feel Head has considerable tools; he just needs to learn how to unlock the shed. His power did show up, as he hit 15 homers, impacting the ball more than you would think someone with his smaller frame should be able to. In 2021, he struggled against good fastballs, leading to a lot of the strikeout issues, and most of his power came off of him crushing secondary stuff. He’s worked to stabilize his stance and let his natural athleticism play so he can more regularly time up velocity. Head also has very good speed, though it’s yet to translate to the basepaths, and his athleticism is a big asset in the outfield. He’s played all three spots thus far and might have the skills to play center field. He does have the arm for right and could have the power profile as well if he can learn to make more consistent contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport standout at his high school in Texas, Head jumped on scouts’ radars when he hit .615 as a senior. The Padres loved his athleticism and set a then-record for third-round bonuses by giving him $3 million in the 2019 Draft, despite his relative lack of track record. His pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League (.283/.383/.417) made it seem like a worthwhile investment, and even though he was slowed by a hamstring issue in 2020, he still showed off some loud tools during his time at the Padres’ alternate training site before joining the Pirates courtesy of the Joe Musgrove trade. Head has now become one of the best athletes in the Pirates' system. The left-handed hitter has tremendous bat speed and raw power, though he’ll have to keep working to rein in his swing to get to it. He does have a good overall approach at the plate with a feel for hitting, but the alternate training site has been the only time he’s really faced advanced competition heading into the 2021 season. With plus speed, Head should provide value on the basepaths, and he has a very good chance to play center field for a long time, especially as he gets more reps to work on his reads and routes. Should a move be needed, his arm, not to mention his potential offensive profile, could work well in right field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Seeing an opportunity to add an ultra-athletic, five-tool player to an already loaded system, the Padres went all-in in their pursuit of Head, taking him in the third round in 2019 and then signing him for $3 million, a record bonus for a third-round pick. A little-known commodity with barely any track record against quality competition, Head batted .615 as a senior at Churchill High School in Texas. After being drafted, he went on to post an impressive .283/.383/.417 slash line in Rookie ball. He impressed as one of the younger players at the Padres’ alternate camp last summer, then was the highest-ranked prospect dealt to the Pirates in the deal for Joe Musgrove in January. Wiry strong with good snap in his wrists, Head brings premium bat speed to the Pirates’ system. He has raw power, too, giving him serious upside from the left side of the plate if he can harness the moving parts in his swing. Head has an advanced feel for hitting, and his ceiling is extremely high. But he’s yet to face serious competition. If Head continues to develop and improve, he could wind up with average or better tools across the board. He has plus speed and should have no problem sticking in center field once he improves his reads and routes. His strong arm will allow him to play anywhere in the outfield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Even though he signed for just $20,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2018, Ventura has been brimming with potential for years, beginning in 2019, when he climbed three levels out of the Dominican Summer League and into stateside ball. He missed all of 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic shutdown and Tommy John surgery respectively, and when he returned last June, it was only for four starts before a pectoral injury ended his 2022 early. Ventura went unprotected in the Rule 5 Draft, and while the Mets were concerned someone would grab and stash him, he went unpicked and stayed in the New York system. The 6-foot right-hander flashed his typical promise during his brief time in the Florida State League, striking out 10 of 29 batters (34.5 percent) before the most recent injury. He topped out at 97.3 mph on the radar gun and sat 93-95 mph from a high release slot. His mid-80s changeup got good separation off the heater, and while it did show some firmness, it projects as a potential above-average offering that got almost as many whiffs as the fastball and curve combined. Speaking of which, after Santos toiled with a breaking ball for years, his 79-81 mph curveball flashed as average with vertical drop, but he used it only 14 percent of the time. Ventura’s athletic delivery has long given Mets officials hope that he can throw strikes, and that didn’t change after the brief look in ’22. The right-hander still has the upside of a back-end starting pitcher, especially if he can lock the breaking ball into place, but he absolutely needs to get innings to meet that ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for only $20,000 out of the Dominican Republic in July 2018, Ventura shot up through three Rookie-level affiliates (one Dominican, two domestic) a year later and finished with solid numbers -- a 3.78 ERA, 54 strikeouts, 19 walks in 52 1/3 innings. Following the missed 2020 season, he had the potential to break into full-season ball last year but underwent Tommy John surgery in the spring, causing him to miss the entire 2021 campaign. The good news: Ventura returned to Single-A St. Lucie this season with a fastball that averages 94 mph. That’s even more promising because the 6-foot right-hander had really leaned on the heater to find his success early in his career. When he was previously healthy, he had also been working on finding a consistent breaking ball instead of one that showed slider shape at times and curveball depth at others. A mid-80s changeup has been his most oft-used secondary in 2022, and while it has a higher whiff percentage than the other two offerings, it does get too firm to be more than an average pitch. Ventura always earned points for an athletic and repeatable delivery that helped him throw strikes at the lower levels, and those characteristics should help him re-find the command post-Tommy John. A pectoral strain suffered in late June has put off that timeline a little further, but it’s less of a concern than the elbow was. Regained health and additional work on the secondaries could push him into becoming one of the Mets’ best prospect arms by the middle of 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ventura signed with the Mets for only $20,000 shortly after his 17th birthday in July 2018 and moved directly to the Dominican Summer League from there. He returned to the DR complex circuit in 2019 but was moved stateside after only three impressive starts. The right-hander climbed to Rookie Advanced Kingsport in that age-18 campaign, finishing with strong numbers (including 54 strikeouts against 19 walks in 52 1/3 innings) across the board at three levels. He underwent Tommy John surgery in the spring and won’t see a Minor League mound again until likely the middle of next summer. The Mets are fans of Ventura’s overall athleticism and repeatable delivery prior to the procedure. He uses both to throw a fastball around 92 mph that features some cut to it. The pitch alone has guided the 6-foot hurler’s early trips to the Minors to the point where he has used it 80-90 percent of the time at the lower levels. That pitch selection will change as he faces tougher bats, and the Mets are optimistic that his other offerings will be good enough to handle more usage. The breaking ball, particularly, will remain a focus. Sometimes, it can come out of his hand with slider-like action. Others, it has the depth of an above-average curveball. The Mets teamed with Ventura to find the breaking pitch that works best off his heater. The changeup can be an out pitch, but like any young pitcher, it needs to be thrown more to complete its true development. It wasn’t killer stuff from Ventura before Tommy John surgery. But it all came from a promisingly athletic frame, and Ventura’s ability to throw strikes across the board was a promising first step. A move away from the fastball and into the secondary pitches needed to get upper-level bats out should come next in his journey to find a spot in the back end of a Major League rotation, once he regains his elbow health.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Mets for $20,000 on July 25, 2018, Ventura made his pro debut two weeks later in the Dominican Summer League. When the right-hander returned to the level in 2019, it took him all of four starts to convince the Mets that he was ready for a greater challenge. A strong performance over 33 innings in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League came next and led to another promotion -- this time to the Rookie-level Appalachian League, where he allowed one run and three hits in two starts to close out the season. Though he lacks the type of size or physicality like some of the other teenage hurlers in New York’s system, Ventura does have some room to grow into his lithe, athletic frame. Those physical gains should help the right-hander add more velocity to a fastball that already sits in the low-90s with natural cutting action. A slider that flashes above average gives Ventura a quality secondary pitch to complement his fastball, and he also shows some aptitude for turning over a tumbling changeup. A good athlete with a quick arm, Ventura already repeats his delivery better than most hurlers his age. That should allow him to develop above-average control and at least average command as he works his way through the Minors. If it all comes together for him, Ventura could be a No. 5 starter at the highest level.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: The athletic little Ventura was coming off TJ and made a handful of Low-A appearances before he was shut down at the end of June with a pectoral strain. He was sitting 93-95 mph during the healthy portion of that small window, but was down in the 92-93 range and getting knocked around in his final outing before hitting the IL. Though he's never had an issue with walks and will show you three above-average pitches, Ventura's recent injury track record (and his inability to build a workload foundation as a result) slides his projection toward the bullpen, where he profiles as a good multi-inning fireman. Ventura's high slot helps him stay on top of his nasty two-planed curveball, and he can turn over a tailing changeup from that slot, though with mixed consistency. How the Mets handle the back half of Ventura's 2022 will be interesting. This is his 40-man evaluation year, he's one of very few pitching prospects in this system with overt big league stuff, and he's badly in need of innings, so extending him into the Fall League makes sense if the Mets are inclined to be bold and give him an opportunity to earn a 40-man spot even though he has very little full-season experience.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Did you mean, "Yordano Ventura?" This Ventura began the 2019 summer in the DSL but had reached Kingsport by August. He doesn't have a big frame to dream on but he's very athletic, his 2019 TrackMan data indicates he can really spin it, and his fastball had plus carry and some cut action. Plus, he already throws pretty hard for someone his age, and he'll show you an occasional plus slider. I did have an in-office source tell me that Ventura's 2020 instructs data was a little below what I have from 2019, which may be the result of poor unit calibration at either site. Right now this is a young, lower-variance pitchability prospect. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Ventura began the summer in the DSL but had reached Kingsport by August. He doesn't have the big frame to dream on but he's very athletic, can spin it, his fastball has life, he already throws pretty hard, and he'll show an occasional plus slider. You can go kind of wild projecting on his command because of the athleticism, but realistically he could be a No. 4/5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite the Mariners’ possible logjam of quality arms competing for just a handful of bullpen spots, the club liked Clarke enough to pry him away from the Cubs in last December’s Rule 5 Draft, making him a strong candidate to contribute ASAP. Clarke’s numbers didn’t jump off the page at Double-A Tennessee last year, but Mariners GM Justin Hollander suggested that the under-the-hood metrics are above average, saying, “This is a guy we feel like there’s some dials to turn” at the Winter Meetings. Entering his age-25 season with three years of Minors experience, Clarke relies on his massive 6-foot-7 frame to his advantage, paired with a low three-quarters arm slot that creates a quirky angle and makes it challenging to decipher out of hand, especially for righties. And given his size, the repeatability of his mechanics and the athleticism and body control also stand out. He throws his fastball in the 92-94 mph range and tops out at 96 mph with much run and sink, making him one of the top ground-ball pitchers in the Minors. His best pitch is an off-the-table curveball, which is effective against both righties and lefties. He complements those with a mid-80s slider that ranks average. And he throws all of them for strikes, which makes him an ideal arm for the Mariners’ mantra of \"Dominate The Zone.\"

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs spent back-to-back 2019 Draft picks on college closers with starter traits, then moved Louisville's Michael McAvene (third round) and Southern California's Clarke (fourth) into the rotation as soon as they turned pro. Clarke got knocked around when he started for the Trojans early in his college career, but recorded a 1.96 ERA and a 26/4 K/BB ratio during his 23-inning pro debut. He participated in instructional league in 2020, making two game appearances there but spending most of his time in Chicago's pitching camp. He then missed the first three months of 2021 with with a hip impingement. Clarke's hammer curveball is the best in the system and works against both left-handers and right-handers while arriving in the low 80s with power downer break. His fastball sits at 92-94 mph and peaks at 96 with run and sink that produce groundouts. His mid-80s slider gives him another solid pitch and is further testament to his feel for spin, and he's refining a changeup with some sink. Clarke's 6-foot-7 frame and low three-quarters arm slot create unusual angle that makes it tough to pick up his pitches, especially for righties. He's athletic and has good body control, allowing him to repeat his delivery and provide consistent strikes. He can't match McAvene's pure stuff but has more polish and a better chance to succeed as a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs used consecutive picks in the 2019 Draft on standout college relievers with starter traits, taking Louisville's Michael McAvene in the third round and Southern California's Clarke in the fourth. Clarke missed his junior high school season following Tommy John surgery and got knocked around while shuttling between roles in his first two years with the Trojans, but he logged a 1.03 ERA in a full-time bullpen role last spring. Chicago eased him into pro ball with short starts and will keep him in the rotation going forward. Clarke's hammer curveball ranks as the best in the system and is effective against both left-handers and right-handers with its powerful downward break. He elicits a lot of ground balls with his fastball, which parks at 92-94 mph and tops out at 96 with run and sink. His feel to spin also translates into a solid slider and he's working on refining his changeup after not using it much as a college reliever. Clarke's 6-foot-7 frame and low three-quarters arm slot create angle that makes it difficult to pick up his pitches, especially for right-handers. He's athletic for his size, repeats his delivery well and provides regular strikes. His pure stuff isn't as loud as McAvene's but he has a better chance to make it as a starter.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Clarke had never thrown more than 50 innings in a single pro season due to a combination of injury and the pandemic, and he entered 2022 (his 40-man evaluation year) as a key upper-level evaluation since, when healthy, he's had the command to pitch at the back of a big league rotation. Clark's fastball averaged about 90 mph during his 2021 post-IL outings, and has been more in the 90-94 range so far in 2022 as he's reached Double-A. Clarke has plus east/east command of four pitches, with his upper-70s curveball the most-deployed, since Clarke uses it as a way to get ahead of hitters (back door) and putting them away (back foot) while his slider and changeup are more used for the latter. His stuff isn't huge, but it plays because of Clarke's command, and he's a good bet to be an efficient fifth starter.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: McMahon was a notable prospect in high school following his pre-draft summer, when he was sitting in the low-90s with a good slider. His stuff didn't spike during his senior year, so he ended up at Miami, where it did. He was consistently touching 96 or 97 mph during his 2019 and '20 outings with the Hurricanes, and averaged 92.5 mph both years. He sat about a tick below that on average during his 2021 pro debut, while throwing many more innings than ever before across about 20 starts. McMahon's fastball has tail and sink, and its movement mimics a still-improving changeup, while his slider remains his go-to finishing pitch. For how violent his delivery is, McMahon fills the zone with his fastball and is pretty good at locating his slider consistently to his glove side, although not always in a precise, enticing location. He often appears to be "underneath" his changeup and creates lateral action on it but inconsistent dive, though sometimes he actually gets impact dive on the change when he releases it late and it ends up glove-side. He's had some injury issues (knee tendinitis in 2018, shoulder soreness in '19) but McMahon has No. 4/5 starter stuff with a chance for more if the changeup keeps coming.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McMahon could have been a pretty high Draft pick out of high school in 2017, but he ended up being just a late-round flier by the Braves because of his commitment to Miami. After missing most of his freshman year with a knee injury, he pitched in the Hurricanes' weekend rotation over the next two years, with his feel enough for the Rockies to take him in the second round of the shortened 2020 Draft. He had a solid first full season in High-A but wasn’t able to build on it in 2022 as a lat strain kept him off the mound for much of the year. There’s confidence that McMahon will bounce back healthy and return to his right-handed pitchability ways. He can get swings-and-misses with all of his offerings, starting with a low-90s fastball that has solid action down in the zone. His changeup is his best secondary offering, with good arm speed and deception, and his slider was tightening up from the slurve he featured in college. While he doesn’t have a true plus out pitch, he doesn’t hunt strikeouts and focuses more on executing pitches. He is willing to throw any of his pitches with two strikes to put hitters away. McMahon’s ability to fill up the zone can hurt him at times because hitters know strikes are coming and he has been too predictable with his pitch usage. Using his changeup more against right-handed hitters, pitching backward occasionally and setting up hitters better in general will help him reach his high floor as a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McMahon went from the Philadelphia high school ranks into the University of Miami rotation, though a knee injury kept him out for the bulk of his freshman year in 2018. He pitched pretty well in the weekend rotation as a sophomore and showed his solid feel for pitching in the shortened 2020 season enough to generate some first-round looks. He landed in the second round to the Rockies, threw well at instructs that fall and had a solid first full season in High-A in 2021. His progress was delayed in 2022 as a lat strain kept him from throwing a competitive pitch until late July. The right-hander has a solid three-pitch mix with a very good idea of how to use his entire repertoire. He pitches to both sides of the plate very well, starting with a fastball that sits low-90s and touches a bit higher, thrown with good late action down in the zone. His changeup is an above-average pitch that he throws with good deception and arm speed, missing bats and getting ground-ball contact with it. His breaking ball can be a bit of a hybrid/slurve type of a pitch, but it’s trending in the right direction towards more of a tight slider. While McMahon can throw strikes and can keep hitters off-balance by mixing his pitches and tunneling his secondary stuff off his fastball well, he still needs to work on his command within the zone. His fastball can flatten out at times, causing him to get hit, but he has the pitching IQ to reach his ceiling as a No. 4-type tarter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A multi-sport standout in high school out of Philadelphia, McMahon was a solid pitching prospect in 2017, but slid deep into Day 3 of the Draft because of his commitment to the University of Miami. After missing a large chunk of his freshman year with a knee injury and serving as the Saturday starter as a sophomore, McMahon pitched very well for Team USA and continued to throw well during the shortened 2020 season. While he did get some first-round buzz, he landed near the top of the second round, where the Rockies went a bit over slot to sign him before watching him throw very well at instructs. During his time in instructional league play, McMahon really stood out with his pitchability, especially his fastball command. He can run it up to the mid-90s with late action when he keeps it down and he’s shown the ability to reach back for a bit more when needed. While he has good feel for spin, his breaking ball can be a bit of a slurvy hybrid, but should be tight slider with good late three-quarters tilt to it, a potential plus pitch. His changeup gets swings and misses as well as generates weak contact. In addition to the breaking ball consistency, he’ll have to continue to work on shortening his deeper arm action to help keep his stuff from flattening out. Thanks to his athleticism and feel for pitching, he has a very good chance to reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation type starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Before Orioles executive vice president Mike Elias took over baseball operations and hired Koby Perez as his international scouting director, the team had long-eschewed Latin America from a scouting standpoint. They were one of the few teams without a presence in the talent-rich region, and their system suffered for it. As it was, the franchise had never given out a seven-figure bonus until Hernandez received one of two in 2020-21, when the 17-year-old Venezuelan signed for $1.2 million. So far Hernandez is yet to deliver on that promise, after struggling in his first two seasons in Rookie ball. Hernandez is tall, graceful and strong at 6-foot-3, with a smooth right-handed swing and an all-fields approach some believe cuts into the raw power he flashes in batting practice. That power is nonexistent in games at this point, with Hernandez going homeless in his first 82 professional contests, but he’s still young enough to grow into more as his body matures. He is an average runner but quick with strong baserunning instincts. Hernandez is more advanced on defense, where his athleticism complements an above-average arm and smooth hands. He cut down his errors significantly in his second year in Rookie ball, without undercutting the good footwork and impressive range that make him a standout defender. There is still a chance he may have to move off the position because of his size, depending on his growth in the coming years. But the bigger question mark right now is whether Hernandez will hit enough to eventually make that a conversation. This is a big year for Hernandez to work on re-setting his ceiling, which when he signed was arguably as high as anyone in the Orioles’ system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles made the international market a priority for the first time under executive vice president and GM Mike Elias and international scouting director Koby Perez, hoping to establish themselves in the talent-rich region after hardly tapping into Latin America for decades. They had a headliner for those burgeoning efforts last year in Hernandez, a lean and athletic shortstop who received one of the first two seven-figure bonuses in franchise history. Hernandez signed for $1.2 million as a 17-year-old out of Venezuela, then showed promise despite choppy results in his first season at Rookie ball. At 6-foot-3, Hernandez is tall, graceful and strong, reminding some scouts of a young Alex Rodriguez or Carlos Correa because of his body type. His right-handed swing is smooth and easy, with flashes of raw power potential that have yet to show up in games. He can hit to all fields, make consistently hard contact and show a prescient understanding of the strike zone. He walked more than expected in the Dominican Summer League despite the lack of power. His discipline, and strength are expected to develop as his body matures. He is an average runner but quick with good instincts on the bases. Tool-wise, Hernandez is more advanced at this point on defense, where his athleticism shows in abundance. He has an above-average arm, smooth hands and good footwork, despite committing his share of errors in the DSL. That’s not uncommon for young infielders with impressive range, and the Orioles don’t want to undercut his aggressive instincts on the dirt. If Hernandez must move off the position eventually it’ll probably be because of his size, depending on his growth in the coming years. But as Correa, Rodriguez and others have shown, there is certainly a place for tall shortstops in the Majors - and their upside often outweighs the risk. Hernandez’s size, athleticism and youth enable the Orioles to dream on him as a player with that kind of ceiling; while his floor is probably as a utilityman at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles were dormant for years in the international market, eschewing it almost entirely before Mike Elias became general manager in 2018 and immediately hired Koby Perez as his director of international scouting. Come international signing day 2021, Hernandez was the main headliner of a record-setting class for which the Orioles shelled out their first two seven-figure bonuses in franchise history. A lean and athletic shortstop, Hernandez, 17, signed for $1.2 million out of Venezuela. At 6-foot-3 and 175 pounds, Hernandez reminds some scouts of a young Alex Rodriguez and Carlos Correa because of his body type. His right-handed swing is smooth and easy, with flashes of raw power potential and an ability to hit to all fields. He already makes consistent hard contact and shows an early understanding of the strike zone, although he would benefit from improving his plate discipline as he develops. Hernandez’s athleticism shows most obviously on defense, where he displays an above-average arm, smooth hands and good footwork. There is belief he’ll stay at the position as he grows, but could require an eventual move to third base depending on how his body matures in pro ball. More important to scouts is the upside, which gives Hernandez the ceiling of an impact regular in the big leagues with a utility man floor.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Hernandez was one of the top players from the Baltimore international class that signed in January of 2021, part of a reinvigorated international operation that lay dormant under the previous regime. While his pro debut failed to impress in terms of performance, scouting the stat line in the DSL is a dangerous undertaking and Hernandez's numbers and underlying data improved throughout the season. Hernandez provides a rare combination of size and athleticism that fits the casting call for a modern, star-level shortstop. He has an eye-popping frame, but there are some concerns as to just how big he will be at physical maturity and if that will lead to him needing to change positions. For now, he’s more than toolsy enough to stay up the middle, with graceful actions, fundamentals beyond his years and a plus arm. Offensively, Hernandez has plus bat speed and power potential as he grows into his frame, but he’s prone to over-swinging at times and has too much pre-swing movement to give him the mechanical consistency he'll need as he moves through the system. Hernandez has a massive ceiling, but we are still years away from knowing what his chances of reaching it are.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies like Williams and his upside so much, they acquired him twice. They first took the Colorado high schooler out of their own back yard in the fourth round of the 2020 Draft, signing him for $450,000. He hadn’t thrown a competitive pitch when the Rockies sent him to the Reds that offseason as part of the deal that netted them Robert Stephenson. He was making his pro debut in the Reds system when he came back to the Rockies in the Mychal Givens trade close to the 2021 deadline. He took a developmental step forward in 2022 across two levels of A-ball before finishing with a 12-strikeout exclamation point in Double-A. Still only 21 for all of the 2023 season, Williams’ projection is looking like it’s starting to turn into performance. The Rockies think he has the chance to have a legitimate four-pitch mix, with all of them being at least average. He’s commanding his low-90s fastball better to both halves down in the zone and showing he can pitch up with it. He’s also learned that he can’t just blow away hitters with his heater and is mixing his pitches much more effectively. He’s always been able to spin a breaking ball with an outstanding power curve and there are makings of a distinct slider. He also started showing conviction in throwing his changeup more consistently. With his delivery more under control, Williams is developing beyond just a thrower, learning to execute his pitches. The next step will be command within the zone but his improved stuff, pitchability and added physical maturity have led to an up arrow next to his name.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Williams was the top high school player in Colorado for the 2020 Draft, though no one got to see him pitch leading up to it because the coronavirus pandemic shut down the season before it began there. So teams interested in the big, physical right-hander had to mostly go on what they saw over the summer. The Rockies saw enough to take the prepster out of their own backyard in the fourth round of the shortened Draft, and they signed him for a below-slot bonus of $450,000. They never got to see him throw a competitive pitch, as they sent him to the Reds, whose scout team Williams played on in the Area Code Games in the summer of 2019, as part of the deal that saw Jeff Hoffman join the Reds and Robert Stephenson head to the Rockies. Williams has all of the elements of a future big leaguer, but they’re a bit raw and undeveloped at this point in time. The Rockies saw a fastball in the 92-95 mph range coming from his 6-foot-3 frame. His secondary stuff is all inconsistent, but he has a good feel to spin his breaking ball with the chance to have a plus curve down the road. He had not thrown his changeup much in high school, so that will be an area of focus developmentally for him as he starts his pro career. Big and physical, Williams is a solid athlete who should be able to eventually command the baseball well enough to give him the chance to reach his ceiling as a mid-rotation starter. Patience will be key as he’s not logged many innings on the mound, knowing that there have been pitching success stories out of the Colorado high school ranks – Roy Halladay, Kevin Gausman and Kyle Freeland as the prime examples – but that Gausman and Freeland went on to college and it took a while for Halladay to figure it out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Having signed for $1 million on Jan. 15, 2021, Montesino was one of the Padres’ two seven-figure additions to begin the 2021 international period, the other being Samuel Zavala, who has become an even more prominent name in the two years since. The Venezuela native got off to a promising start in the 2021 Dominican Summer League but missed the opportunity for his first stateside season after undergoing Tommy John surgery before the 2022 campaign began. The left-handed slugger flashed a good amount of power in the DSL, ranking among the top 15 qualifiers (out of 190) with his .489 slugging percentage and .934 OPS. A selective approach led to a quality walk rate and on-base percentage, but as is true of many young hitters, there was still plenty of swing-and-miss when he did take his hacks, leading many to believe he’ll eventually settle in as a power-over-hit type. Montesino was a defensive question mark even before needing the elbow procedure. Originally signed as an outfielder, he already got the majority of his defensive starts at first base in the DSL, and unless he can improve his routes on the grass, he’ll likely end up at the cold corner long term. Below-average speed and arm strength did him no favors there either. Montesino is still only 19 entering 2023, and it’ll be important for him to pick up right where he left off offensively given how much of his value is tied into his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Montesino, along with Samuel Zavala, is one of two left-handed-hitting outfielders who signed for seven figures in the Padres’ 2020-21 international class. Montesino, who signed for $1 million, projects as a power hitter and showed as much in his professional debut last summer. The Venezuelan slugged .489 over 56 games in the Dominican Summer League. He underwent Tommy John surgery before the season and has missed the 2022 campaign as a result. Montesino’s easy left-handed swing produces plenty of pop, though there’s some swing-and-miss to his game. He’s a strong hitter with a selective approach, but needs to control the strike zone better as he matures. He’s a power-over-hit prospect, but the Padres think there’s still plenty to like about his overall hit tool and the Padres feel he could develop into an above-average hitter. This was an offense-first signing as Montesino’s defensive skill set is a work in progress. He projects as a below-average defender who needs to refine his routes and his reads and is likely to wind up in either left field or first base. His arm and his speed leave something to be desired as well, though they should both be passable. Regardless, his bat is his carrying tool and his offensive development will ultimately determine his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of two lefty-hitting outfielders to sign for seven figures in the Padres’ 2020-21 class, Montesino joins Samuel Zavala as big-time talents out of Venezuela. Montesino, who signed for $1 million, projects as a power-hitting corner-outfield type in the mold of fellow Padres prospect Tirso Ornelas. Montesino’s easy left-handed swing should produce plenty of pop. Though there might be a bit of swing-and-miss to his game, he’s a big, strong hitter with few moving parts and a decent understanding of the strike zone. The Padres expect him to be able to hit for average and power as he progresses. But make no mistake: This was an offense-first signing. Montesino’s defensive skill set is raw, and he projects as a below-average defender who needs work cleaning up his routes and his reads. Montesino’s arm and his speed leave something to be desired as well, though they should both be passable. Still, if the Padres can hone Montesino’s corner-outfield skills toward respectability, they feel his bat will be able to carry him the rest of the way.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Angeles is an interesting player who is set up to succeed statistically and, when combined with his age, perhaps get juiced in a big way by pro scouting models. He is not the sort of player who you notice getting off the bus but Angeles has a track record of hitting in games dating back to his amateur days. He hit well in the 2019 DSL (his traditional stats are supported by the TrackMan data sourced from that year) and forced the Padres to push him to full-season ball with a great 2021 minor league spring training performance at the plate. As an 18-year-old in full-season ball, Angeles hit .343/.397/.461. Some of the power output there is a Cal League mirage, and Angeles 3 homers are more emblematic of hwo much power is actually here right now. There is not overt power projection here, and so unless Angeles turns out to have very special bat-to-ball skills he is more likely to become a contact-oriented utility infielder rather than a true regular.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Angeles is an interesting player who is set up to succeed statistically and, when combined with his age, perhaps get juiced in a big way by pro scouting models. He is not the sort of player who you notice getting off the bus but Angeles has a track record of hitting in games dating back to his amateur days. He hit well in the 2019 DSL (his traditional stats are supported by the TrackMan data sourced from that year) and forced the Padres to push him to full-season ball with a great 2021 minor league spring training performance with the bat. He's now an 18-year-old in full-season ball playing in the ballparks that constituted the old Cal League. He could make a lot of contact, have his power output inflated by the offensive environment, and look like a stud on paper. I saw Angeles twice during the spring but he's not the kind of guy who jumps out at you with big power or speed on a short look; he's a vanilla athlete with very advanced feel for the bat. He's definitely a prospect because hitting, after all, is the most important thing, but I don't get the sense that there's huge upside here. (At-home dev)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Padres out of the Dominican Republic for $300,000 in 2018, Angeles jumped out to a promising start in his pro career by hitting .301/.359/.376 and striking out just 19 times in 44 games the next year in the Dominican Summer League. A continued breakout in 2021 in which he hit a combined .329/.392/.445 between Low-A and High-A made him an attractive prospect for the A’s, who acquired him last March along with Adrián Martínez as part of the Sean Manaea deal. Playing his first season with Oakland at High-A Lansing as a 20-year-old, he hit .278/.316/.353 in 97 games. Angeles is a strong, physical player despite what his 5-foot-11, 175-pound frame might suggest. While there’s not a ton of power to his game, the ball really comes off his bat hard and he uses a quick swing to hit high quality line drives. He has continued to post low strikeout totals, demonstrating good bat-to-ball skills throughout his Minor League career. Angeles can utilize his above-average speed to steal bases. He still plays shortstop and second base, though he does get lackadaisical defensively at times. With an overall talent the A’s remain high on, he’ll get a chance to continue progressing through the system, with second likely his future full-time role should he settle into one spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres, as a penalty for overspending in the 2016-17 international signing period, were unable to sign anyone for more than $300,000 in 2018, but that didn’t stop the organization from inking Angeles. Signed for the full $300,000, the infielder has looked like a bargain and is off to a fast start in his pro career. He hit .301/.359/.376 with only 19 strikeouts in 44 games in the Dominican Summer League during his 2019 pro debut, then raked over 105 games in 2021, hitting .329/.392/.445 over two levels of Class-A ball. The contact skills caught the eyes of the A’s, who acquired him along with Adrian Martinez in the April trade that sent Sean Manaea to San Diego. Listed at 5-foot-11 and 175 pounds, Angeles doesn’t hit for a ton of power, but puts that ball in play with strong bat to ball skills and an aggressive approach. The right-handed hitter hit .354 against right-handers in 2021, suggesting he’ll be tough to match up against as he continues to climb the ranks. There’s some uppercut in Angeles’ quick swing, but that translates more to doubles and triples as he uses his above-average speed to take the extra base. He also knows how to steal a bag when the opportunity presents itself, swiping 36 over his first 149 professional games. While Angeles is most comfortable at shortstop, the position he played prior to signing, it’s likely he’ll wind up at second base. He’s played second, third and shortstop early in his career and that versatility may help expedite his path to the big leagues -- especially if he keeps hitting at his current pace. Angeles has quick feet, solid hands and the arm strength to play anywhere on the infield, though his accuracy needs to improve. Of course, if he continues to rake, the A’s will find a spot for him to play.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Torres put up a bloated stat line during the shortened 2020 college season despite striking out in a third of his at-bats. He brought his strikeout rate down in his 2021 season at NC State, though the rest of his slash line came back to earth a bit as well. College stats are normally pretty meaningless, but in Torres’ case, they're virtually all we have to draw upon, as he’s played very little for a college draftee his age, which may be partly to blame for his overly aggressive approach in the box, where he regularly whiffs on would-be balls – mostly high fastballs and misread breaking balls he can't reach. Defensively, he'll stick at short, but he'll have to improve his bat-to-ball skills and his patience, as his power is underwhelming. His short professional stint to close out the 2021 minor league season was encouraging, as his K-rate dipped into the mid-teens and he launched four homeruns, three triples and four doubles in 25 games at Low-A. 2022 will be his first chance to prove he can sustain quality performance over a full season, and spring looks at him have been encouraging from a bat-to-ball perspective.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Torres was of interest as a high school prospect but his age and rawness pushed him to NC State. He had a strong, surface-level performance as a hitter in the shortened 2020 season but also struck out in nearly a third of his plate appearances. He's a lock to stay at shortstop, with a chance to hit for power so long as the whiffs aren't as much of a problem as they seem. He's played very little for a college player his age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres didn’t have too much time to show what he could do at North Carolina State, with the pandemic shortening his freshman year and him leaving after the 2021 season as a Draft-eligible sophomore. He played enough to convince scouts his glove alone was worth drafting, and his power production as a sophomore helped him land in the third round of that summer’s Draft. After a solid pro debut, his first full season in High-A in 2022 was rough offensively. There are some things Torres can do well from the right side of the plate when he stays within himself. He uses his hands well with some feel for the barrel, with some seeing a little Tim Anderson in his setup and mechanics. At his best, he’s shown good feel for the zone and a gap-to-gap swing, but he doesn’t see enough pitches and gets into trouble when he tries to do too much and sells out for power, leading to too many swings and misses. If Torres can simplify things at the plate, he’ll be able to impact a big league team sooner rather than later because of his glove. He’ll be a shortstop for a long time, with outstanding actions and hands to go along with a plus arm and terrific instincts. He saw a lot of time at second base in 2022, both because of personnel on the same team and the fact that the lack of offensive profile points to a likely career as a defense-first utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Torres was Maryland’s best high school prospect in 2019, but opted to head to North Carolina State for college. The Dominican-born shortstop was Draft-eligible in his second year of college in 2021 and while he didn’t go in the first round, like former Wolfpack shortstops Trea Turner and Will Wilson, he did land in the third round with the Reds, then went out and had an impressive pro debut, mostly in Low-A. Torres’ calling card in defense was, and continues to be, his work at shortstop. Though he’s a fringy runner, he has excellent instincts that help him cover a lot of ground to go along with smooth actions, plus hands and a plus arm. While there were concerns about how his bat would play at the next level, the Reds have been pleasantly surprised with his right-handed swing. He’s always had good bat speed and some sneaky power, but got into trouble in college by getting overly aggressive at the plate. In the brief sample of his pro debut, Torres showed good plate awareness, didn’t chase too often and showed off an excellent gap-to-gap line drive swing. If he can continue to perform offensively like that, he has the chance to be a big league regular at a premium position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Reckley was the best Bahamian prospect and one of the top shortstops in the 2022 international class. He signed for $2.2 million, the largest international bonus paid by the Giants since they gave Marco Luciano $2.6 million four years earlier, though they topped that by giving Dominican outfielder Rayner Arias $2,697,500 in 2023. He played just 11 games in his pro debut last summer because he sustained a hairline fracture of a vertebrae after getting kneed in the back on a freak play. A switch-hitter, Reckley has a good understanding of his swing and the strike zone. He shows more power from the right side of the plate and has enough bat speed and projectable strength to produce 15 homers on an annual basis. He works the ball from gap to gap and could be a future leadoff hitter, thanks to his on-base ability and plus speed. Reckley's quickness makes him a base-stealing threat and gives him good range at shortstop. He has smooth actions and solid arm strength and just needs to develop more consistency with his defense, like most teenagers do. His intelligence and instincts stand out in addition to his tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The latest prospect to come out of the Bahamas, Reckley was one of the top shortstops in the 2021-22 international class.
