San Francisco signed him for $2.2 million in January, giving him its largest international bonus since paying Marco Luciano $2.6 million four years earlier. Reckley should be able to adapt to pro pitchers immediately because he understands his swing and the strike zone. A switch-hitter with bat speed, he shows more pop from the right side and could produce 15 homers per season once he adds strength. He's more of a gap-to-gap hitter who could fit at the top of a lineup with his on-base ability and plus speed. Reckley's quickness is evident on the bases and in the field. He's an athletic shortstop with smooth actions and solid arm strength. Besides his tools, the Giants also praise his instincts and intelligence.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Juan showed an intriguing mix of power and speed as an amateur in the Dominican Republic, where he trained with three-time All-Star shortstop Rafael Furcal. He was ranked as MLB Pipeline’s No. 16 prospect in the 2022 international class and signed with the Mets for $1.9 million -- more than a third of their pool money -- when the window opened on Jan. 15. Juan’s early results didn’t quite meet the hype as he hit .219/.310/.323 with a 77 wRC+ in 53 games in the Dominican Summer League, but his potential remains. The teenager’s plus speed certainly played early in his transition to pro ball, as he swiped 16 bags in 17 attempts and made 45 of his 47 defensive starts in center field. Batting from the right side, the 6-foot-2 slugger shows good raw power with impressive bat speed in his BP sessions. But to this point, that’s where much of his slugging ability remains, in part because he puts the ball on the ground a lot (51.1 percent GB rate in the DSL). Squaring up the ball a bit more and focusing on pitches he can drive should be focuses as he gains experience against pro arms. Juan drew early comparisons to Byron Buxton and George Springer as an amateur, and those certainly flatter him coming off the DSL time. The outfielder will only be the age of an American high school senior in 2023, so he has ample time to sharpen his considerable tools and become a potential everyday player at the top level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Power and speed working in combination will open any scout's eyes. Juan has the potential to show both in the pro game, and training with 3-time All-Star shortstop Rafael Furcal bolstered his case to be MLB Pipeline’s No. 16 prospect in the 2022 international signing period. The Mets made the right-handed slugger their biggest signing of the cycle when they inked Juan to a $1.9 million bonus, using more than one-third of their pool money to haul him in. Juan already shows at least above-average wheels in all aspects of the game, and that should give New York hope that he will be able to remain in center field for the long haul. As if that wasn’t enough, he already shows good power in batting practice, and there remains room for the lanky 6-foot-2 slugger to add more as he matures. His future value could come down to how well his hit tool plays, but early reports indicate Juan could be an average overall hitter if everything clicks. Juan drew initial comparisons to a young Byron Buxton and George Springer. That’s not exactly fair to a 16-year-old just about to get his professional feet wet, but it does paint a picture of who Juan could be at his absolute best in the pros. A word of caution, however: Buxton and Springer overcame severe strikeout concerns early in their careers. If those same issues pop up for Juan and he doesn’t properly adjust, it could be an uphill battle toward Queens, no matter how good the rest of his profile is.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bergner was a highly rated pitcher out of high school who had an up-and-down college career at North Carolina before the Tigers took a chance with a ninth-round pick in 2019. After beginning his pro career as a long reliever, he took advantage of a starting opportunity at High-A West Michigan with a strong stretch run in 2021, building momentum that carried into Double-A Erie with an outstanding first half. He began a late-season stint at Triple-A Toledo with five scoreless innings against Iowa, but largely struggled the rest of the way. Bergner pitches with a polished, easy delivery out of his tall frame. His fastball approaches the mid-90s, but was more often around 91-93 mph last season. His changeup ranges from the low-to-mid-80s depending on whether he’s looking for speed differential or movement. He has a slow, buckling curveball and tweaked his slider last year with help from Tigers pitching director Gabe Ribas to develop more bite. Bergner needs to hit the corners, work ahead and throw his secondary pitches for strikes to be effective at the upper levels, something he struggled to do at Triple-A. The Tigers did not add Bergner to their 40-man roster at season’s end, opting to keep other pitching prospects instead. His arsenal and grasp of pitching give him the potential to take the next step, but this is probably a make-or-break year for him with his 26th birthday in May. With other starting prospects coming, Bergner might be better off with a move to the bullpen to see whether his fastball plays up in shorter doses.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers hit the jackpot with a college pitcher in the ninth round when they drafted Tarik Skubal in 2018, and they’d love to find fortune again with Bergner, their ninth-round pick in 2019. Bergner had been on pro teams’ radars since he was a highly rated pitcher in high school. He followed through on his commitment to North Carolina, but had an up-and-down career with the Tar Heels. He was a high-strikeout long reliever in Low-A Lakeland, posting an 8-for-34 walk-to-strikeout ratio over 24 1/3 innings, then got his opportunity as a starter at High-A West Michigan after Beau Brieske was promoted to Double-A. His performance opened eyes, as did his 110 strikeouts over 83 1/3 innings for the season. On the flip side, he thrived in West Michigan despite high fly-ball and pull rates. Bergner has a nice, easy delivery out of his 6-foot-5 frame. He pitches off a fastball that approaches the mid-90s. As a reliever, he could pair that with a fading changeup and mix in a slow curveball. He later revamped what had been a hard slider, took some velocity off it and added some depth in hopes of making it a swing-and-miss fourth pitch in his arsenal. Bergner has a good understanding of pitch design and mental approach. While Bergner enjoyed a breakout season at West Michigan, he was also older than the vast majority of hitters he faced. He continued to be successful at Double-A Erie to begin this season and is getting a late-season look at Triple-A. Bergner is eligible for the Rule 5 Draft this offseason and just might be on the cusp of pitching his way onto the 40-man roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of two national championship teams at Parkview HS (Lilburn, Ga.) before attending Troy, Cerny was one of the better college athletes in the 2021 Draft. He dropped to the Phillies in the 10th round because of signability concerns, but he turned pro for $146,100, then got traded to the Astros for Garrett Stubbs in November. He slashed .197/.293/.401 in Single-A during the first two months of 2022, then surged to .297/.404/.513 in the next two before getting shut down with a bruised right thumb. Cerny has some of the best all-around tools in the system but he also comes with swing-and-miss concerns. He has a busy right-handed swing geared to hit balls as far as he can, though his bat speed and strength would provide plenty of power even if he didn't swing for the fences. To reach his 25-25 upside, he'll need to learn to stop chasing balls out of the strike zone and figure out how to handle quality offspeed pitches, and he was making some mild progress last year when he got hurt. Cerny's aggressiveness carries over to the bases and the outfield as well. He has plus-plus speed and looks to steal and take extra bases. His quickness and instincts give him the range to remain in center field and his solid arm strength helps make him an asset at all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cerny played on two national championship teams at Parkview High (Lilburn, Ga.) before heading to Troy. One of the better college athletes in the 2020 Draft, he fell to the Phillies in the 10th round because of signability concerns and turned pro for $146,000. A thumb injury restricted him to 13 games in his pro debut, after which Philadelphia dealt him to the Astros for Garrett Stubbs in November. Cerny has 25-25 upside with bat speed and strength that creates legitimate pop from gap to gap. But he also comes with swing-and-miss concerns because he has a lot going on in his right-handed swing and a grip-it-and-rip-it approach. He can crush fastballs but chases too many pitches out of the strike zone and struggles with breaking balls and changeups. With plus-plus speed and an aggressive mindset, Cerny is a basestealing threat. His quick-twitch athleticism and instincts allow him to cover ground and play a quality center field. He also offers solid arm strength and some added intrigue with some catching experience in high school.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Acquired from Philadelphia for Garrett Stubbs, Cerny was the Phils' tooled-up 10th round pick out of Troy, a high-variance scout favorite with rare power and speed for a college prospect. Cerny has strikeout issues because of his high-octane, pull-heavy approach, but unlike lots of the power-over-hit outfielders the Astros have brought into the org, he is actually performing on paper early in his career, and he's on pace for a 20/20 season (he's actually on pace for closer to 40 steals) as of list publication. Cerny has plus bat speed and plus wheels that enable him to play center field, giving him some breathing room on offense. That Cerny is punching out at a 30% clip in A-ball is a bust-indicating red flag, but he has a bigger ceiling than all but a few players in this system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: To be filed under “pitching talent can come from anywhere,” Erla was a 17th-round pick of the Angels in their all-pitching 2021 Draft, signing for slot value ($125,000) after spending five years at Michigan State. The organization first thought that perhaps it had a Draft bargain when he was the most exciting arm at instructs the fall after he signed. He missed the first two months of the 2022 season with a shoulder issue but threw well across 16 starts in Double-A once he was healthy. Erla’s arsenal starts with what can be a plus fastball. He sat in the mid-90s during instructs in shorter stints and was around 93-94 mph, touching 97 with the Trash Pandas last year, but the organization thinks there’s more velocity in the tank. With a lower release, he does a good job of sinking it down in the zone to get ground-ball outs but also can get guys out at the top of the zone because of his unique release height. He flashed a solid mid-80s slider and he’s worked on a new one this offseason in the hopes of finding a true out pitch. He has a changeup that can miss bats and get contact on the ground, though it’s too firm at times. The 6-foot-4 Erla has shown he can repeat his delivery well and fill up the strike zone with all of his pitches. He’ll be 25 for most of the 2023 season, so the clock is ticking, and the Angels will continue to let him start because of his strike-throwing ability and the hope he can sharpen his two secondary offerings, knowing the fastball-slider from his slot could be nasty coming out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Erla spent five years at Michigan State, not getting drafted in 2019 after a rough season in the Spartans rotation and not getting selected in the shortened five-round Draft in 2020. He put up decent numbers in that fifth year to attract a little attention and the Angels made him pitcher No. 17 in their 20-pitcher Draft in 2021. He threw a handful of innings last summer in the Arizona Complex League to get his professional feet wet, then opened some eyes with his performance in instructional league play. The 6-foot-4 Erla may have been the most impressive arm at instructs for the Angels last fall. He’s more about arm strength than anything, with a fastball that sat 95-96 mph and touched 98 at instructs. After that, it’s a bit of a question mark. He showed a good hard slider in the mid-80s that has the chance to be a solid secondary offering and he has a changeup, but it’s well behind the other two as a below-average pitch. While Erla was generally around the plate at Michigan State, he didn’t have great command, but he’s been filling up the strike zone since joining the Angels. He’s already 24, but there’s an interesting combination of velocity and size here. He’ll get the chance to start for now and any future role will depend on the consistency of his secondary stuff and his ability to land them for strikes.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Erla ended up spending five - yes, five - years at Michigan State, passed over in 2019 after a down year and then again in 2020 because of the shortened draft. Sure, he's much older than the typical prospect who has just entered pro ball, but his stuff was resurgent during instructs and he still presents the same amount of roster flexibility to teams that a new draftee does, so he's not a 24-year-old who needs to be 40-man'd soon. Erla sat 90-94 during the 2021 college season, then came out in the 94-97 range during instructs. The volatility present in his health (he had a lat tear in college and his delivery is quite violent) and performance are just part of his profile now, so he'll have to prove he can sustain this across a whole year to move up the list. But 94-97 with tail, and a plus changeup (Erla's short slider has good raw spin but lacks great movement, visually) would make for a good middle-inning relief option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top pitching prospects in the 2020-21 international class -- and also one of the youngest -- Pinto didn’t debut until ‘22 due to pandemic-impacted issues in his first year and minor injuries in his second. The Mariners instead instilled a conditioning-heavy plan for the Venezuela native, which he ate up. And now that he’s better built up his body, the focus transitions to the Mariners’ mantra of 'Dominate The Zone.' Pinto’s numbers weren’t stellar in his first pro year, but much of that was marred by Jekyll and Hyde performances -- he would dominate for 1-2 innings, then lose it. Yet everything from the naked eye to the under-the-hood numbers suggest that he possesses above-average fastball velocity that can continue to grow. The true out pitch is his curveball, which generates comical swings and takes from his three-quarters arm slot. There’s good bend and depth, suggesting it can be a big league offering. He does a solid job of repeating his delivery, which also bodes well. For all these reasons, the lean and loose Pinto will probably require more patience because the delivery isn’t quite there yet. But if he can transform the dominant flashes into consistency, there could be big upside -- because the pure stuff is certainly there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top pitching prospect signed in the 2020-21 international signing period and basically the youngest, Pinto has yet to pitch in a professional game, mostly due to the limited baseball and physical resources where he was stationed during the peak of the pandemic shutdown. So Seattle instead had the 17-year-old focus exclusively on conditioning and getting in better shape last season. Scouts estimate Pinto is up to 6-foot-4 and really lean and projectable, with an incredibly loose delivery. He’s now hitting the low 90s with plenty of opportunity to keep growing into velocity. His best pitch is a curveball, a tight breaking ball with good depth that has a chance to be at least a plus pitch in the future. He already has solid feel for a changeup. Pinto is long and loose and does a nice job of repeating his delivery, which could eventually lead to better-than-average control and command. There’s a long way to go here, but with patience could come a very exciting left-handed starting pitching prospect -- especially since he’ll pitch a full season in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The early returns on the Rangers' 2020-21 international class are promising, with outfielder Yeison Morrobel, third baseman Gleider Figuereo and Cueva all making this Top 30 list and right-hander Leandro Lopez not far behind. Based on his potential at the plate, Cueva landed a $1,025,000 bonus. The Venezuelan finished third in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League batting race (.330) in his U.S. debut last summer. Cueva has a quick left-handed stroke and a knack for putting the bat on the ball and using the entire field. He'll need to improve his swing decisions against more advanced pitching, however, because he chases a lot of pitches and that leads to strikeouts and suboptimal contact. His bat speed already translates into high exit velocities, and if he can add strength and learn to drive ball in the air, he could grow into 15-20 homer pop. Cueva has average speed and isn't particularly adventuresome on the bases. He has worked to enhance his quickness and his chances of remaining at shortstop, where he has good actions, quick hands and solid arm strength. His range may be closer to average, which may make him more of a second baseman in the long run.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cueva received the second-highest bonus in Texas' 2020-21 international class, signing for $1,025,000. He's one of three Venezuelan shortstops on our Rangers Top 30, joining Luisangel Acuna and Maximo Acosta. He batted .282/.375/.381 in his pro debut as a 17-year-old in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. Cueva will require time to develop but could become a solid hitter with average pop. He has a nice left-handed swing and shows the makings of bat-to-ball skills and plate discipline. To reach his power potential, he'll need to add strength and learn to drive balls in the air more consistently. While Cueva can flash plus speed, he'll probably settle in as a solid runner once he matures physically. He has worked hard to improve his quickness and his chances of staying at shortstop, where his actions, hands and arm are all up to standard. If he and Acosta team up this summer in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League, Cueva likely will get much of his playing time at second base.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Cueva has made some noise on the Surprise back fields, whacking hard contact to all fields and showing impressive gap-double power for an 18-year-old infielder. He is big and strong in the lower half, especially in the thighs, which is part of where his power is coming from but also puts Cueva at risk of moving off of shortstop as he continues to mature. His swing has gorgeous natural loft and his lightning-quick hands enable him to turn on the ball with authority, giving him some hit/power skill elements that make him relatively exciting even though he lacks any kind of typical physical projection. He'll need to hit his way to the big leagues but early indications are that Cueva has a shot to.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Murphy pitched with Josiah Gray in the rotation for NCAA Division II Le Moyne (N.Y.) in 2018 and succeeded him as the Dolphins' ace the next two seasons while also winning New England Collegiate League pitcher of the year honors in 2019. Signed for $22,500 in the fifth round of the shortened 2020 Draft, he ranked third in the Minors in strikeouts (164), fourth in whiff rate (13.8 per nine innings) and sixth in K/BB ratio (6.3) while advancing to High-A. He wasn't nearly as effective last year, working just 42 1/3 frames while dealing with back and shoulder issues. Murphy's fastball plays better than its velocity thanks to his command and ability to create carry up in the zone, though it was less effective last season when it mostly parked at 88-92 mph after ranging from 91-95 in 2021. His most reliable offering is a solid low-80s slider with depth that he can turn into a harder cutter with more horizontal life. Both his upper-70s downer curveball and a fading low-80s changeup are decent pitches but nothing special. When he's 100 percent physically, Murphy repeats his compact delivery with ease and exhibits advanced control and command while mixing his pitches well. His ailments detracted from his ability to locate pitches with his usual precision in 2022, and he needs it to succeed with his mostly average stuff. If he can stay healthy and regain his 2021 form, he's a potential back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a freshman in 2018, Murphy was the No. 2 pitcher in NCAA Division II Le Moyne's rotation behind Josiah Gray and threw a no-hitter. He filled the strike zone for three years with the Dolphins and won New England Collegiate League pitcher of the year honors in 2019 before the Giants signed him for $22,500 in the fifth and final round of the 2020 Draft. He boosted his prospect stock immensely during his pro debut, when he ranked third in the Minors in strikeouts (164), fourth in whiff rate (13.8 per nine innings) and sixth in K/BB ratio (6.3) while reaching High-A. Though Murphy's fastball parks at 91-93 mph and tops out at 95, it plays much better than its velocity because he commands it so well and his high spin rates create carry up in the zone. His best secondary pitch is a low-80s slider with some depth, and he also can morph it into a harder cutter with more horizontal action. He also utilizes an upper-70s curveball with downer break and a low-80s changeup with some fade. Thanks to a compact delivery that he repeats with ease, Murphy has advanced control and command. He mixes his pitches expertly and throws them to all four quadrants of the strike zone. He competes and hides the ball well, making him that much tougher to solve, and has a high floor with a ceiling of a No. 4 starter.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Murphy was a money-saving fifth round pick in 2020, but he’s turned himself into a bit of a prospect after putting up one of the best statistical seasons in the system during his pro debut, with a bonkers 164-to-26 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 107.1 innings. Murphy dominated A-Ball mostly as a result of plus command and control. He not only pounds the strike zone but also shows an uncanny ability to locate both north-to-south and east-to-west. That said, scouts still wonder if he has a true in-zone weapon that will work against more advanced hitters. His stuff isn't bad, so much as it’s a kitchen sink of average offerings, including a low-90s fastball, two breaking balls (with the slider exceeding the curve), and a solid changeup. Murphy has put himself on the prospect map and has the potential to assume a back-of-the-rotation spot, but he'll need to prove it at every level.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Mezquita has close to average big league raw power at age 20 and has gotten to it in games throughout the early stages of his domestic career despite some swing-and-miss tendencies. He's of medium build (and that may be generous), but not of medium bat speed and explosion, as his pull-heavy uppercut swing is built to do damage. Mezquita's breaking ball recognition is only fair. If you hang it, he will bang it, but he's also apt to chase ones off the plate. Though he's not built like a prototypical right field prospect, Mezquita's power over hit skill set fits in that mold.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mezquita decided to stick with the Braves and re-sign after his original $300,000 bonus in 2017 was nullified as part of the penalty for international signing infractions. His first two summers in the organization -- the Dominican Summer League in 2018 and the Gulf Coast League in 2019 -- were fairly nondescript, but his tools showed up a bit more consistently after the shutdown in Complex League play during the summer of 2021. He performed decently in his full-season debut in Augusta in 2022, but he scuffled with a promotion to High-A Rome. There are some raw tools for Mezquita to work with, though he’s still learning how to use them on a regular basis. He has good bat speed from the right side of the plate and raw power to tap into, but it’s yet to show up in games. He’s capable of hitting the ball hard but is often too aggressive at the plate, and while he’s willing to draw some walks, his penchant for swinging and missing continues to be a concern. Mezquita runs well and is capable of stealing a base, but he’s not electric when it comes to his speed and athleticism. That could mean that he won’t stick in center field long term, and while he has a strong enough arm for a corner spot, that would put much more pressure on a bat that has yet to come around.

fangraphs.label: 2022draft
fangraphs.text: Though not especially toolsy, Sprinkle is a viewed as a viable defensive shortstop (there are some arm strength questions, though) with a strong statistical track record on offense thanks to his feel to hit. A team who buys that he can stick at short will likely take inside the first 60 picks or so.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After barely playing during the pandemic-shortened 2020 season, Sprinkle was co-Big West Conference freshman field player of the year the following spring and played for the U.S. collegiate national team during the summer. UC Santa Barbara's best position prospect since 2006 third-rounder Chris Valaika, Sprinkle entered 2022 with first-round buzz but slipped to the fourth round after struggling at the plate. He batted .237/.290/.301 in a month in Single-A after signing for $452,900. Scouts considered Sprinkle the best defensive shortstop in the 2022 college class. He's quick with range to both sides and reliable hands, and he increased his arm strength last year to where it now grades as solid to plus. He enhances his throwing ability with a fast release and has a good internal clock. Sprinkle batted .353/.402/.536 at UCSB in 2021 but got out of whack when he added strength and hunted home runs for much of his draft year. He has bat speed but gets overly aggressive at the plate, lengthens his right-handed swing and leaves himself vulnerable to offspeed pitches. He needs to focus on getting on base to take advantage of his plus speed and basestealing aptitude.

fangraphs.label: 2022draft
fangraphs.text: Watters has a power pitcher's mid-90s fastball/curveball combination, and his curve has unusually high velocity for a pitch with vertical shape. He struggled badly with walks during his draft year in Morgantown, but it was his first season as a starter, and he had only thrown about 34 innings prior to 2022. He's likely a relief-only prospect, but he has two plus pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Watters transitioned from pitching in the bullpen his first two years at West Virginia to starting in 2022. The stuff he showed in the Mountaineers' weekend rotation was tantalizing, highlighted by a 15-strikeout performance against Texas, and it was enough for the A’s to take him in the fourth round of the 2022 MLB Draft. Getting his feet wet with a couple of outings at High-A Lansing, he’ll look to begin his ascent as a starter through the system in his first full season as a pro. Watters is a strong presence on the mound at 6-foot-4. His fastball was up to 99 mph during his junior year and touched triple digits in his time as a reliever. He also possesses a plus pitch in his power curve, missing plenty of bats as a true 12-to-6 that sits in the mid-80s. There’s also a mid-80s changeup in there, though it’s less polished compared to his other two offerings. Command will need to improve for Watters to have a chance to start at the next level. While the stuff was high-octane in college, he usually had little idea of how to locate it. Given his track record as a reliever, there’s a strong chance he ends up back in the bullpen, where he can rear back and overpower hitters with two plus pitches.

fangraphs.label: 2022draft
fangraphs.text: Gold has plus bat speed and pull power but he may not have a position due to issues with throwing accuracy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers spent much of the 2022 Draft stocking up on college bats. Gold was among the most polished, a three-year performer at Boston College who posted a .940 OPS as a sophomore and .958 as a junior. The Tigers’ front office has changed since drafting Gold, but his combination of hitting ability and zone control fit the mold of hitter that new president of baseball operations Scott Harris has touted as the model for the organization. Though Gold struggled in a late-season stint at Single-A Lakeland last summer, his quick swing and line-drive approach to all fields is expected to translate well once he gets acclimated to pro ball and develops a routine. The bigger question might be power. He never reached double digits in home runs at BC, and just two of his 13 pro hits last summer went for extra bases, both doubles. He doesn’t tend to chase much. Gold alternated between second and third base in Lakeland, but his strong arm and body frame could work better at third. Gold turned 22 last fall, and the Tigers could aim to push him if he can handle pitching in Lakeland early in the season. He’ll have to fight his way through a crowded group of infielders in the Tigers farm system, but for an organization that badly needs offense, Gold’s hit-first resume should get a fair shot.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Cedeno is a twitchy, compact middle infielder who swings harder than you'd expect someone his size to swing. His short levers make him tough to beat with fastballs, but he lacks deft feel for the barrel and tends to swing through the center of the zone. While we over-projected on Cedeno's hit tool in the past, he's still a viable middle infielder with sneaky pop, though one who has now been left back on the complex after being crowded out by the middle infielders currently at Low-A (Aquino, Ferguson, Merrill). He's an interesting change-of-scenery candidate with long-term utility man projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Padres signed Cedeño for $300,000 out of Venezuela in July 2018, the max they were allowed due to previous overages in the international period. He showed a good approach in the 2019 Dominican Summer League with a nearly equal K/BB ratio but hit just .193 in 47 games. There was hope a breakout would come when he moved stateside in 2021, only for a meniscus tear to limit him to 18 games in the Arizona Complex League. He jumped to a full-season affiliate last year in Single-A Lake Elsinore and produced a .256/.362/.400 line in 71 contests before getting 12 games in during the Arizona Fall League. Because of his distance from the Majors, the Padres left Cedeño unprotected from the Rule 5 Draft. Cedeño is still more about potential than production. To watch him take batting practice and even swing during the game is to see a switch-hitter with a patient approach, promising bat speed and enough power to reach around a dozen homers in a Major League campaign. In reality, he still hasn’t hit above .256 in a season, perhaps because he trades line drives for more catchable fly balls and still looks a little more comfortable hitting from the left side. An average runner with a decent arm, Cedeño has seen time at all four infield spots, including a little bit of first base in 2022. He’s adequate enough with the glove to handle second base, and that would represent his best opportunity to provide value. Cedeño will be 21 for all the 2023 season, and that will be a proving ground to show his physical gifts can turn into actual performance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Florida high school product, Hermann was headed to play college baseball at South Florida before the Yankees took him in the 14th round and gave him a slightly over-slot $135,000 bonus in 2021. Because he was the lightest player in the Draft at 160 pounds, they had him initially focus on adding strength before making his pro debut in 2022. He needed little more than a month before earning a promotion from Rookie ball to Single-A, where he recorded a 2.66 ERA in four starts. Hermann's fastball sits at 89-92 mph and peaks at 94, playing better than its velocity because it has a flat approach angle that produces carry up in the zone. He has advanced feel for a sinking 83-88 mph changeup that yields ground-ball contact, though it could use more velo separation from his heater. He also utilizes a low-80s slider with encouraging shape and spin rates that he can morph into an upper-80s cutter. While he lacks physicality, Hermann is athletic and has projection remaining. He has good extension in his delivery, allowing his pitches to appear quicker than they are, and he provides plenty of strikes. If he can get stronger and add more power to his stuff, he could become a No. 4 or 5 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals signed Rodriguez in July 2019 out of the Dominican Republic, and the start of his pro career was bumpy because of the pandemic. It didn’t seem to slow him down, as he was named the DSL Royals Blue Player of the Year in 2021 and then brought his high energy to the States in 2022, slashing .306/.395/.514 between the Arizona Complex League and Single-A. Rodriguez’s best tool is hitting, with innate bat-to-ball skills, an efficient swing and a simple approach at the plate. He doesn’t fear velocity and has an excellent idea of the strike zone for someone who just finished his age-19 season -- his 10.8 percent walk rate and 16.2 percent strikeout rate were better in Columbia than Rookie ball. The switch-hitter has a good approach from both sides of the plate, but most of his pop -- which is below average right now -- comes from the left side. That could change with more reps on the right side and more strength. Rodriguez is an above-average defender at second base with quick hands and good footwork. Rodriguez has tools and youth on his side right now. The ingredients are there to make good on that upside as long as his contact skills and zone control continue. He seems to be limited to second base right now, but he could probably handle the left side of the infield if needed; certainly if he gets stronger and there’s emphasis on versatility. As a second baseman without a lot of thump, Rodriguez has a high floor as a utility infielder, but if the high average and on-base numbers continue against better pitching, perhaps there’s a leadoff candidate in his future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bradley’s senior year at the University of Georgia got off to a fast start when he had a .397/.513/.730 line through 18 games, only to come to a screeching halt because of the pandemic. The five-round 2020 Draft left him unselected, but he was part of the Royals’ undrafted free agent class that summer. Bradley’s contact rates have fueled his rise, and he slashed .293/.382/.455 with 12 homers at Double-A in 2022. Bradley has a good eye and reacts well to where the ball is thrown, spraying the ball all over the field rather than pulling everything. He uses a slightly open stance and has a smooth left-handed swing, but he doesn’t garner a lot of power, even for an older guy with a bigger frame. He makes up for that with his situational hitting and awareness of the strike zone, lowering his strikeout rate to 18.3 percent in Double-A last year. Bradley has a high baseball IQ, leading to more stolen bases (19 last year) than his average speed originally accounted for. He’s likely limited to left field because of his below-average arm. Bradley has been a solid all-around contributor in his first two years as a Royal. If that continues, he could find a role as a fourth outfielder. Evaluators would like to see a little more power to give him a higher ceiling, but the hit tool could carry him far.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of Pirates shortstop Oneil Cruz, Rafael Cruz signed with the Twins for $500,000 when the 2020-21 international signing period opened up in January 2021. He struggled out of the gate in the Dominican Summer League that year but righted the ship with a return to the DSL in 2022, hitting well enough to earn a trip stateside to finish the year in the Florida Complex League. Most facets of Cruz’s game are still pretty raw. He has tremendous raw power from the right side of the plate and showed he could get to it with a .558 slugging percentage in the DSL last year. He had a tendency to try to hit every pitch hard, which worked in the Dominican, but he scuffled and pressed a bit when he got to the FCL and had to start refining his approach. There’s some swing-and-miss to his game, but more reps against better pitching should help him learn to make better swing decisions. It's a little unclear where Cruz will play defensively long term. He was a shortstop when he first signed, but the Twins moved him to third base before he even played a game. He has a very strong arm that fits the hot corner and he’s continued to work on his throwing and fielding accuracy. He’s played a good amount of first as well, and while it’s way too early to pigeonhole him, some see a future as a first-base/DH type. Wherever he plays, his offensive potential will carry him up the ladder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing high school baseball at Westlake HS (Ga.), Nowlin went to Chipola Junior College in Florida, and while he didn’t throw a ton -- 60 innings in total over two seasons, almost all in relief -- he impressed with his ability to miss bats. The left-hander didn’t hurt his stock by throwing well in the Cape Cod League in 2021, with the Twins taking him in the 19th round of the Draft that year and going a bit over the Day 3 slot to sign him for $160,000. Developing him cautiously, he both started and relieved in his first full season, reaching High-A at the end of the year. Because of Nowlin’s lack of deep resume, he’s still pretty raw, but his performance as a pro has spoken for itself. He struck out about 36 percent of batters he faced in 2022. His fastball averaged around 92 mph and topped out at 95-96 with high spin and good arm side life, with the potential for more consistent velocity as he gets more physical. He missed a ton of bats with both his low-80s slider, which is more of a north-south pitch with depth than a sweeping breaker, and a mid-80s changeup that was effective more because of the velocity differential than the action of the pitch. Nowlin is going to have to refine his command, with an inflated walk rate (4.6 BB/9 in 2022), especially as he moves up the ladder and faces hitters less likely to chase out of the zone. If he does that, he has the chance to start. If not, his stuff could play well as a lefty reliever in a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hamilton played little in his first four seasons at Wright State, redshirting when he arrived, coming off the bench the next two years and having the 2020 season shortened by the pandemic. He finally got a chance to show what he could do in 2021, when he was named Horizon League Player of the Year and ranked third in NCAA Division I in runs scored (78) and OPS (1.306). Signed for a well-below-slot $47,500 in the fifth round that July, he slashed .308/.425/.508 between Single-A and High-A in his first full pro season before dropping to .206/.320/.341 in the final six weeks in Double-A. Hamilton has one of the best approaches among Astros farmhands, controlling the strike zone while making consistent contact and drawing a healthy amount of walks. His left-handed swing is geared more for hitting line drives than launching balls, but he has enough bat speed and strength to generate 12-15 homers per season. He handles same-side pitchers well, adding to his usefulness as a potential fourth outfielder. Hamilton has plus speed and uses it well on bases, swiping 27 bases in 31 tries last year. He possesses average range in center field, where he played most often in 2022, and could be a solid defender on the corners, where he also saw a lot of action. He has average arm strength, gets rid of throws quickly and registered 11 assists last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After three years of relief work at Kansas State, including a junior season that catapulted him onto Draft boards, he went in Round 14 in the Angels’ all-pitching Draft in 2021. Los Angeles challenged him with a Double-A assignment in his first full season and he responded. The left-hander led the Southern League in saves and was named its Reliever of the Year, missing a ton of bats and giving up very few hits in the process. Torres does it from a 6-foot frame and with average stuff, but his combination of a lower slot -- the ball looks like it’s coming from the first-base dugout -- and feel for using what he has helped him strike out 14.3 per nine innings and hold hitters to a .143 average in 2022. His fastball only sits around 90 mph, but the angle and carry up in the zone helped it elicit a 36-percent miss rate last year. His low-80s slider can also miss bats, a sweeping breaking ball that flashes above average. He continues to work on a changeup to give him another look for right-handed hitters, but no one squared him up from either side in the Southern League. The Angels love Torres’ athleticism and competitiveness on the mound, and while he could stand to cut the walk rate down a little, he’s around the zone enough to project future success. The overall stuff might mean he doesn’t get the ball in high-leverage situations in the big leagues, but he’s not far from getting the chance to impact the Los Angeles bullpen and he’s shown he is far from afraid of the spotlight.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels gave seven-figure bonuses to outfielders Nelson Rada and Randy De Jesus at the start of the 2022 international signing period, but they also brought in some intriguing young pitching talent. No one got a higher bonus than Encarnacion, who signed for $500,000 and then struck out nearly 11 per nine innings during his Dominican Summer League debut. A plus athlete on the mound, Encarnacion’s fastball currently sits around 92-93 mph and can touch 96. His slider is his best secondary offering, a low-80s breaking ball that has the chance to be better than average in the future. He’ll throw his changeup up to 87-88 mph, giving him a true three-pitch mix, though he could use some more separation between his heater and the offspeed offering. The two things Encarnacion needs to work on the most are his command and physicality. He walked 5.3 per nine in his debut and adding strength to his 6-foot-2 frame will help him repeat his delivery, which in turn will lead to more strikes. There’s projectability here to go along with some intriguing stuff, giving him the chance to develop into a starting pitcher long term as he comes stateside for the first time in 2023 at age 18.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez flew under the radar in the 2016-17 international class, signing for just $75,000 out of Venezuela. He took a few years to find his footing, but he absolutely wowed in 2022, especially when making the jump to High-A Everett, where he slashed .342/.477/.583 with seven homers and 27 RBIs in 35 games to give him 27 homers and 114 RBIs (second among all Minor League hitters) in total. There’s a chance he taps out because of his speed and defense, but the Mariners are bullish on how he finished the season, which he capped off with time in the Arizona Fall League. The big focus for him into 2023 will be finding better counts to continue to do damage, which should help him better tap into his considerable raw power. He can be aggressive and expand the zone too often at times, though he offsets the swing-and-miss with a willingness to take walks. When he’s putting the ball in play, he’s found far more line drives and fly balls, a big reason why he surpassed his 2021 season home run total by June last year. Likely destined for first base, Perez has legit pop from the right side and the exit velocities to show for it, but he’ll need to continue raking to progress -- his big league trajectory depends on it, especially given the defensive limitations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Munoz joined the Mariners during the 2019-20 international signing period for $195,000, then was among the many impacted by COVID interrupting the following season, which prevented him from pitching competitively until an assignment to the Dominican Summer League, where he spent 2021-22. The first year was inconsistent, but he rebounded in the second and made the midseason All-Star team. A projectable righty with room to keep adding strength, Munoz is another arm that Seattle’s player development staff has been banging the drum on. He’s up to the mid-90s on his fastball with decent arm-side run and above-average hop. He’s also shown flashes of a plus slider that generated a ton of whiffs and strikeouts with. It’ll probably need more depth as he progresses, but, so far, he commands it better than the heater. Now it’s a matter of if he can develop a third pitch and remain a starter, because there were a lot of positive signs with his strike throwing. It’s a changeup right now, but he doesn’t throw it often because of how good the other two have been. If he does go down a relief road, his path to the Majors could be accelerated.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hood overcame some pandemic-impacted challenges at Penn, mainly in that his 2020 season was cut short after just eight games and that it was canceled altogether in ‘21. His performance as the 2019 Ivy League rookie of the year caught some eyes, including those of the Red Sox, who drafted him in the 20th round in 2021. But Hood instead opted to transfer to NC State, where he jumped on Seattle’s radar and prompted the club to take him in the sixth round in 2022 and give him $250,000 to sign. The 22-year-old has above-average raw power and has the chance to remain an infielder, perhaps even at shortstop, though he profiles better at third. He also plays a decent outfield defense, which collectively has drawn comparisons to big league super utilityman Dylan Moore but with more power. That type of versatility could only help his case to ascend quickly. Hood has legit strength and an aggressive approach, with some impressive exit velocities already. But one critique is that he can too often hunt the homer. He’ll also need to make adjustments against secondary pitching, especially as he rises the ranks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Trying to prove that a local kid can make good, Tolve went from the Georgia high school ranks to Kennesaw State for college. He parlayed a solid 2021 season (.319/.393/.498) to get drafted by his hometown Braves in Round 17 of the 2021 Draft. He showed off some interesting tools during a solid first full season with High-A Rome in 2022, but his climb to Double-A in 2023 was interrupted by a quad strain that limited him to just 50 games. He made up for some lost reps in the Arizona Fall League. When he’s healthy, Tolve has been an athletic left-handed hitting catcher, a demographic that’s often in high demand. He is capable of making loud contact, though there’s too much swing-and-miss in his game. He did improve his strikeout rate a bit in 2023 (27.2 percent, compared to 32 percent in 2022), and he will draw some walks. There’s raw extra-base pop there if he can be a bit more consistent in finding the barrel at the plate Tolve runs very well, especially for a catcher, and he’s been athletic enough to play other positions in the past. His agility is an asset as a backstop; he’s a solid receiver with good arm strength. If he can continue to refine his approach at the upper levels, he could be a solid big league backup in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels drafted McIntosh in the 34th round after he swatted 16 homers as a Motlow State (Tenn.) CC freshman in 2018, but he chose to transfer to West Virginia rather than turn pro. He had modest success with the Mountaineers but performed well in the inaugural year of the MLB Draft League in 2021, landing him a $20,000 bonus from the Marlins as a nondrafted free agent. He quickly has become an organization favorite and spent his first full pro season in Double-A, where he helped Pensacola win the Southern League championship. A right-handed hitter, McIntosh produces some of the best exit velocities in the system and works deep counts in search of pitches he can drive to his pull side. Though he fits the power-over-hit profile, he draws plenty of walks and doesn't strike out excessively. He's surprisingly quick for a catcher, can flash solid run times and displays good instincts on the bases. It may be a stretch for McIntosh to remain behind the plate, however. He earns raves for his leadership and preparation skills, but he's a decent receiver at best, struggles to block balls and has below-average arm strength. He surrendered 97 steals (at an 85 percent success rate) in 67 games last year, and Miami plans on giving him time at first base to get him more at-bats in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets signed Consuegra for $500,000 in July 2017, and it took nearly five years for the outfielder to reach somewhere above the Dominican or Florida Complex Leagues due to various injuries and the 2020 pandemic-canceled season. Finally able to hit triple-digit games played for the first time, the Dominican Republic native broke out at Single-A St. Lucie, hitting .251/.324/.431 with eight homers and eight steals in 66 games before coming back to earth at High-A Brooklyn (90 wRC+), where the pitcher-friendly confines of Coney Island may have played a part. He got an 11-game look in the Arizona Fall League ahead of his Rule 5 eligibility but remained unprotected and unpicked in the early winter. What makes Consuegra such a promising talent is that he’s loaded up with tools. His raw power ranks among the best in the Mets system, and it was certainly notable that he finished with eight balls struck at 110-plus mph during his time in the Florida State League (per Statcast). He’s also an above-average runner who can cover good ground from any of the three outfield spots. His plus arm strength, capable of firing 95+ mph missiles from the grass, helped him pick up 13 outfield assists last season (with two more in the AFL). The separator will be Consuegra’s overall performance with the bat. His swing can get too long, and a 25.9 percent K rate in ’22 is likely only to get worse as he dives into the upper Minors. He’ll get much-needed reps to improve the bat in what is still technically his second full season in 2023, and the rest of the profile gives him a shot at being a fourth outfielder down the line.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Atencio joined the Mets in July 2018 at the same time as top New York prospect Francisco Álvarez, but it’s been a much slower road through the system for the southpaw. The Venezuela native pitched in the Dominican Summer League in 2019 and 2021, showing signs of a breakout coming out of the pandemic with 76 strikeouts in 48 innings during the latter season. He jumped to Single-A St. Lucie in 2022 and handled the assignment fairly well with a 2.27 ERA and 48 strikeouts in 39 2/3 innings, though he did walk 23 over that span. The 6-foot left-hander sat in the average velocity range with a 91-93 mph fastball, which did touch 95 at times. He worked hard to establish the four-seamer in his first trip to a full-season affiliate, throwing it 58 percent of the time. His 82-85 mph changeup could get fairly firm but still was average with an ability to get whiffs against righties, while his upper-70s sweeper has enough depth to be a putaway pitch too. Atencio’s 13.6 percent walk rate with St. Lucie marked a career high as he fought wildness. That’s a tough pill to swallow for a hurler without a true plus pitch at present. That said, the three-pitch mix he’s flashed over the past two seasons keeps his starting dreams alive. Despite being passed over for Rule 5 protection in 2022, Atencio enters his age-21 season with a limited workload on his arm, so the potential for further growth certainly exists.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Greene signed for just $17,500 as a South Alabama senior when the Yankees took him in the eighth round of the 2019 Draft. After missing out on his first full season due to the pandemic, he proved to be a steady performer as a reliever at the High-A, Double-A and Triple-A levels in 2021 and 2022. He spent all of last season with Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, posting a 3.42 ERA, .199 average-against and 96 strikeouts in 68 1/3 innings, but he was still left off the Yankees' 40-man roster when he became Rule 5-eligible due to a roster crunch. The Mets swooped in during the Rule 5 Draft, and in order to keep him, Greene must remain in their Major League bullpen for all of 2023. The 6-foot-1 right-hander pitches out of the stretch at the extreme first-base side of the rubber, and he fires in a low-90s fastball that can be deceptive with its apparent rise and cutting action. Despite the fastball being closer to average velo, that ride can make the heater extremely difficult to pick up, and hitters often hopelessly swung below the pitch at Triple-A. An upper-70s slider kept opposing batters from sitting on the fastball and played well into the Yankees’ pitching philosophy of prioritizing sweep on breaking pitches. An upper-80s changeup kept lefties honest but was a distant third pitch. If hitters can learn not to chase the high heat or the solid breaker, they can earn the occasional free pass from Greene, who walked 11.1 percent of the batters he faced in 2022. That control has been one reason why the righty has stayed in relief in the pros, but his two best pitches make him an MLB-ready bullpen option for the Mets.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2019-20 international signing period might always be known for the addition of Francisco Álvarez for $2.7 million in July. One month later -- after New York added international bonus pool money in a deal that sent Jeurys Familia to Oakland -- the club also picked up Lugo for $475,000 as an infielder out of the Dominican Republic. After a mundane introduction to stateside ball, Lugo broke out offensively in 2022 with Single-A St. Lucie, hitting .261/.347/.427 with 10 homers in 84 games before moving up to High-A Brooklyn, where he was also an above-average hitter with a 115 wRC+ in 28 contests. Lugo’s power is better than his Florida State League numbers indicate as he regularly registered exit velocities above 95 mph. His 41.1 percent hard-hit rate on that circuit was on par with Major League sluggers like Ian Happ and C.J. Cron in 2022, and the 20-year-old -- who stands out for his strength more than bat speed -- may only get stronger from here. Batting from a slightly closed stance, Lugo can sometimes expand the zone, leading to strikeouts in about one-quarter of his plate appearances, and hitting for average likely won’t be a strong suit. At 6-foot-3, Lugo was large for shortstop, even by modern standards, and as a below-average runner, he’s a better fit at third base. He has the arm for that spot, and he has enough pop to provide offensive value away from a premium position. The 20-year-old was Rule 5-eligible this offseason but went unprotected and unpicked as he’s at least two years away from the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCollum spent three seasons at Division II Wingate University, pitching almost entirely out of the bullpen and helping the team win a national championship in 2021. He went undrafted, but signed a free agent contract following the Draft and made his pro debut that summer with full-season Clearwater, recording inconsistent results over nine appearances. A return to the Single-A level in 2022 reaped much better results with a 1.45 ERA and a .111 average-against before a bad ankle sprain ended his season at the end of June. The 6-foot-5 right-hander might end up with three quality pitches. He throws his fastball in the 94-97 mph range with solid carry and offers a hard and short slider. His splitter is a developing third pitch, but there’s a chance it could become an out pitch in time. Command and control have held McCollum back, though. He walked more than seven per nine in college and really struggled during his pro debut. But he’s already improved his ability to find the zone since he signed, dropping that walk rate to 4.6 in 2022 while striking out 15.1 per nine. More strides in that direction could give him the chance to impact a big league bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signing as a 17-year-old out of the Dominican Republic in May 2018, Rodriguez began his career in the bullpen because of major control issues (51 walks in 50 1/3 innings) during his first two years in the Dominican Summer League. After the lost pandemic season, he moved into the rotation at Single-A Palm Beach and had success with a 3.36 ERA and 88 strikeouts in 69 2/3 innings. His 2022 season in High-A Peoria (4.59 ERA, 119 strikeouts in 121 2/3 frames) was a bumpier ride, but it was notable that he nearly doubled his previous career-high workload. The Cardinals did not add him to the 40-man when he became Rule 5-eligible in the offseason, and he went unselected in that process. The 6-foot right-hander’s velocity has picked up in recent years as he’s matured and gotten stronger. He can sit 95-96 mph earlier in outings but typically settles in closer to 93-94 as he goes deeper, which makes sense for a pitcher still getting built up as a starter. He’ll showcase a quality mid-80s slider that he can work to either side of the plate while also mixing in an upper-70s curveball offering a slower breaking look. His mid-80s changeup still lacks consistency, and there are the makings of a cutter for another diversified offering. Rodriguez doesn’t have the same control issues he did earlier in his career, but his delivery lacks consistency and can make him to fly open, causing his command to waver. His career might go full circle with a return to the bullpen as a result, which could allow him to open the velo even more.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After two years of inconsistent work at the University of Maryland, Staine transferred to Central Florida for the chance to have a more certain role. While a minor back issue and a blister slowed him down some, his ability to pitch well -- mostly as the Knights’ Friday night starter -- allowed him to land in the fifth round with the Rockies. While he didn’t pitch competitively after signing, he did make a good impression with the club's player development staff during instructs. A 6-foot-4 right-hander with a loose arm and some athleticism on the mound, Staine has four pitches that give him the chance to start. His fastball averages around 93 mph and touches 96 and it features good ride to it, which plays well at the top of the zone when he needs it to. His low-80s slider should be an average breaking ball, and he has a slower curve he can land early in counts. He’ll flash a decent changeup, but will need to commit to it more after not throwing it much in college. More than anything, the Rockies love how Staine goes right after hitters with a repeatable up-tempo delivery. He’ll need to refine his command to remain a starter long term, but the organization feels like he has the mentality to develop into a guy who can navigate through a lineup multiple times and be a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ravelo signed for $545,000 out of the Dominican Republic, landing the third-highest bonus in Boston's 2021 international class. Though he batted just .197/.303/.265 in his U.S. debut last summer, his defense earned him a promotion to Single-A for the final week of the season at age 18. His offensive game needs more work, though he shows some promise as a switch-hitter with bat speed from both sides of the plate. Despite his youth, Ravelo already displays the consistency to make routine plays at shortstop and the tools and instincts to produce web gems. He has twitchy athleticism, classic shortstop actions, quick hands and solid arm strength. He's an average runner at best, but still shows range to both sides and is one of the best infield defenders in the system. More effective as a left-handed hitter, Ravelo needs to make adjustments to his offensive approach. He employs a leg kick and is overly pull-conscious, leading to too many strikeouts and weak ground balls. If he can get stronger and improve his pitch recognition and swing decisions, he could produce 10-15 homers per season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of La Romana, Dominican Republic, in 2017, Nunez put up underwhelming numbers in the Dominican Summer League in 2018 and the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League in 2019, but there was already some early intrigue with his power potential heading into the lost 2020 season. Nunez grew into some of that in 2021, hitting six home runs with an .848 OPS between the Florida Complex League and Single-A, then his breakout finally came in 2022. Last summer, Nunez climbed from Single-A to High-A, hitting a combined 19 home runs with a .304 average and .824 OPS. He carried this into a successful Dominican Winter League stint, showing some of the pop that the Blue Jays have long dreamed on. At 6-foot-3 with a big frame, Nunez is limited to first base, where he’s just an OK defender. He needs to improve his chase rate at the plate and work more walks, but his exit velocities are among the best in the organization. Nunez will be challenged by more advanced pitching, especially as older arms use more polished breaking balls against him, but there’s no denying his pop from the right side. Much like Spencer Horwitz or any other prospect in the organization likely to stick at first base, he’ll need to hit his way up the ladder. The Blue Jays believe there’s far more potential in there physically, though, making Nunez a name many are watching for another potential breakout if he can clean up his plate approach.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Tatum spent his first three seasons at North Carolina State as a part-time player, then hit .317/.423/.543 with 12 homers and 16 steals as the Wolfpack reached the College World Series semifinals in 2021. He hit a massive home run to beat Jack Leiter and Vanderbilt, 1-0, in Omaha shortly before the White Sox made him a 16th-round pick. He played just 42 games in his first full season because he drew a 50-game suspension after testing positive for amphetamines, and an ankle injury limited him to just six contests in the Arizona Fall League. Tatum collected just 600 at-bats in the past five years between college and the Minors, so he has more untapped potential at the plate than most 23-year-olds. He has a quick left-handed swing and a willingness to work counts and draw walks, but he also strikes out way too much (30 percent of his plate appearance in his first two pro seasons), puts the ball on the ground far too often (28 percent) and uses the opposite field almost to a fault. He has enough bat speed and wiry strength to produce at least 15 homers per season but will need to turn on and lift more pitches to get there. With his well-above-average speed, Tatum is dangerous on the bases and covers plenty of ground in center field. His below-average arm is playable in center and left but limits his usefulness in right. His speed and defense could help make him a useful fourth outfielder if he doesn't provide enough offense to be a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The latest Cuban prospect to emerge in the White Sox system, Chapelli was named MVP at the 15-and-under World Cup in 2016 and won rookie of the year honors in the island's top domestic league at age 17 three years later. One of a dozen players to defect from Cuba's 23-and-under World Cup team in Mexico in October, he signed for $500,000 eight months later. He tore up younger competition in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League during his pro debut, finishing third in slugging (.636) and OPS (1.084). Built like a slightly taller Jose Altuve, Chapelli's clean left-handed swing and patient approach produce a lot of hard contact. In two seasons as a teenager in Cuba's Serie Nacional, he batted .304/.419/.438, a stat line that doesn't do justice to his power potential. With his hitting ability, bat speed and sneaky strength, he could hit 15 or more homers on an annual basis. After playing the outfield corners in Cuba, Chapelli switched to second base in the DSL. His solid speed, quick hands and decent arm give him a chance to become an average defender at second. He'll be 21 this season and could make the jump to High-A to show what he can do against more age-appropriate competition.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez didn’t produce much initial hype as a 2017 signing out of Mexico, partly because of his size at 5-foot-8, but he immediately earned some attention in his 2018 debut in the Dominican Summer League. There, Hernandez posted a 2.60 ERA over 55 1/3 innings, striking out 64. That momentum quickly evaporated, though, when Hernandez got rocked in Rookie-level the Gulf Coast League in 2019, posting an 8.02 ERA over 21 1/3 innings. But the up-and-down start to his career continued when he bounced back with Los Mochis in Mexico. That set up Hernandez’s true breakout in ’21. That summer, he climbed from Single-A to Double-A, striking out 108 batters with a 2.74 ERA over 62 1/3 innings. That's when Hernandez’s potentially elite changeup truly began to shine, baffling hitters even when they knew it was coming. He was off to a tremendous start in 2022, with a 1.88 ERA over 24 innings while reaching Triple-A, but his season was slowed by a shoulder issue, and he was hit hard upon his return. The Blue Jays are betting on Hernandez’s upside, though, and after he went untouched in the Rule 5 Draft, he has a chance to make his big league debut as early as 2023. It’s all about the changeup with Hernandez, but can that pitch survive on its own against MLB hitters? That question is why the Blue Jays are working with him to add some bulk and get his fastball up to the 92-93 mph range, which would theoretically keep hitters off the changeup a bit more. He also throws a slider, but that’s more to show hitters a different look than create outs. Hernandez’s changeup is one of the best pitches in the organization, though, and his strikeout numbers prove it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 45 | Slider: 40 | Changeup: 65 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Hernandez signed as an unheralded pitching prospect out of Mexico in 2017, but showed some immediate promise in the Dominican Summer League that year with a 2.60 ERA over 55 1/3 innings, striking out 64. Moving to the GCL in ’19, though, he got tagged with an 8.02 ERA over 16 relief appearances and appeared to lose any momentum. Hernandez embraced that challenge, pitching for Los Mochis in the Mexican Winter League before earning a Low-A assignment to open ’21. He climbed all the way to Double-A, posting a combined 2.74 ERA across the three levels with a whopping 108 strikeouts over 62 1/3 innings, reintroducing himself as one of the best young arms in the system. Hernandez’s changeup is one of the best pitches in the organization. Even with opposing hitters on it, they often struggled to make much contact against it at all. His fastball sits in the low-90s, approaching 92 mph, and he uses that to disguise the changeup. He’s also thrown a bit of a slider, but his changeup was so effective in ’21 that he rarely needed to stray from that in big situations. There isn’t much more physical projection for Hernandez’s 5-foot-10 frame, but as a strict reliever now, he makes it work. Developing his breaking ball will be a key to his long-term sustainability, but his changeup has the potential to be special. Veteran Triple-A pitchers who have seen advanced changeups before will be a great test for that pitch, but now that Hernandez has been added to the 40-man roster this past offseason, he could put himself on the doorstep of the Major Leagues by the end of ’22.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Targeting projectable, tooled-up prospects at premium positions, the Mets handed out a pair of seven-figure bonuses to Dominican amateurs in 2017, signing both shortstop Ronny Mauricio and Hernandez, a center fielder, on July 2. While Mauricio was widely viewed as the better prospect and therefore received a higher bonus, Hernandez signed for $1.5 million after he ranked 19th on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 international prospects list. Hernandez is a premium athlete with a strong frame who has a high-energy style on the field. An aggressive hitter, he has terrific bat speed and outstanding raw power from the right side of the plate. That pop shows up more on the pull side, but he can drive the ball to all fields and should tap into it more consistently as he refines his approach at the plate. Hernandez's plus speed should continue to help him on both sides of the ball. Hernandez is a center fielder for the time being, but there's the chance he could grow and develop more into the prototypical athletic right-fielder mold down the road. Hernandez's power-speed combination has earned him comparisons to Jose Guillen from some scouts, and the Mets would be thrilled if he become that caliber of player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Mets went shopping in the international amateur market last summer, they aggressively went after, and signed, a pair of exciting Dominican position players. One was shortstop Ronny Mauricio; the other was Hernandez, the toolsy outfielder who ranked 18th on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 international prospects list and signed for $1.5 million. Compared to former big league outfielder Jose Guillen, Hernandez has a power-speed combination that could be special one day. He is a premium athlete with a strong frame who has a high-energy style on the field. An aggressive hitter, Hernandez has terrific bat speed and outstanding raw power. That pop shows up more on the pull side, but he can drive the ball to all fields and should tap into it more consistently as he refines his approach at the plate. Hernandez's plus speed should continue to help him on both sides of the ball as he begins his pro career in earnest. Hernandez is a center fielder for the time being, but there's the chance he could grow and develop more into the prototypical athletic right-fielder mold down the road. He has a long way to go, taking his first official steps in 2018.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Like Desmond Lindsay, who is further down this list, Hernandez is muscular, explosive, tightly-wound, and suffered a severe soft-tissue injury (a torn hamstring) that cost him most all of 2019. He wasn't part of New York's 2020 instructs contingent, so we have basically no new information from the last two years. Healthy Hernandez ran well enough to stay in center field and had sizeable raw power for a teenager. The cement on the bod is pretty dry, and while I think that means limited power projection, it also probably means Hernandez's chances to stay in center field may be a little more stable, assuming he has his pre-injury speed when he returns. While his 2018 slash line was strong (yeesh it feels scary to write that -- it's been a long time since this guy has played), there were some underlying swing-and-miss issues that might rear their ugly head in a more meaningful way in 2021. (At-home dev)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Like Desmond Lindsay, who is a ways down this list, Hernandez is muscular, explosive, tightly-wound, and suffered a severe soft-tissue injury (a torn hamstring) that cost him most all of 2019. And so, the scouting report remains the same as it did on last year's list: Hernandez runs well enough to stay in center field and he has sizable raw power for a teenager. The cement on the bod is pretty dry, and while we think that means limited power projection, it also probably means Hernandez stays in center. The exit velos on THE BOARD for both Hernandez and Lindsay are from the 2018 season, when they were healthy enough to generate sufficient data.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Signed for $1.5 million in 2017, Hernandez is a physical power/speed center field prospect who showed proclivity for pull-side lift as an amateur. Built like an M-80 at 5-foot-9, 210 pounds, Hernandez lacks body-based power projection, but he already has some pop, and his frame is so compact that it'd be surprising if he thickened enough to necessitate a move out of center field. He had a pull-heavy, somewhat limited approach to contact as an amateur, but his first pro summer was free of statistical red flags. How his bat-to-ball skills and plate discipline develop will dictate his future role, and it's hard to have great feel for either of those variables. He's here largely because we like the defensive profile and raw power.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Fitterer was an interesting $1 million-ish high school prospect with the traditional fastball/overhand curveball suite and the sort of pitchability you'd expect of an older SoCal high schooler, but because he was older, it was tougher to be confident projecting on his wiry frame. From a velocity standpoint, Fitterer hasn't progressed. He was 90-92 mph and touching 93 during my Fall League looks and has been in that range again in 2022. That pitch does have cut and carry elements that help it play when it's located, but his arm swing and line to the plate were highly variable in Arizona, and his walk numbers have taken a step back in 2022. Both of Fitterer's breaking balls - a mid-80s slider and an upper-70s curveball - are consistently average or better, and give Fitterer the repertoire depth to start. If we assume Fitterer's velocity just is what it is, he'll need to develop better command to hold down a rotation spot. Right now he looks more like a Day Two college arm with a depth starter projection.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Fitterer was often the first player mentioned by sources who saw the Marlins' GCL/instructs group in 2019, as he has a traditional fastball/overhand curveball suite and the sort of pitchability you'd expect of an older SoCal high schooler (he has a four-pitch mix). How much you're willing to project on his frame and fastball will vary depending on how you balance the traditional-looking frame and Fitterer's age. I think he's likely to have a bevy of near-average offerings except for the curveball, which will likely be above. He's tracking like a No. 4/5 starter, and he could be on the Peter Lambert style fast-track. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Fitterer was often the first player mentioned by our sources who saw the Marlins GCL/instructs group, as he has a traditional fastball/overhand curveball suite and the sort of pitchability you'd expect of an older SoCal high schooler. How much you're willing to project on his frame and fastball will vary depending on how you balance the traditional-looking frame and Fitterer's age. We're on the lower end, but feel pretty confident he'll have a third good pitch and starter's command.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Has a low-90's sinker and sharp breaker. Has some surface-level projection, but was drafted at age 19 so we're not as bullish on the velo progressing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts considered Fitterer one of the more polished high school pitchers in the 2019 Draft, and he drew comparisons to Kyle Hendricks with better stuff. Since signing for an over-slot $1.5 million as a fifth-round pick, he has been slower to acclimate to pro ball than expected. He lost the 2020 season to the pandemic and missed time with back and shoulder issues in 2021 before finally getting a full season in High-A last year. Fitterer's fastball usually ranges from 92-95 mph with natural sink and cut, and it stands out more for its ability to generate weak contact than for missing bats. His best secondary pitch is a sinking low-80s changeup that helped him have more success against left-handers than right-handers in 2022. He has some feel for spinning the ball, though his upper-70s curveball and low-80s slider can blend together at times. Fitterer's athleticism hasn't translated into reliable strike-throwing. He doesn't attack hitters, and his average stuff doesn't leave him with much margin for error when he catches too much of the plate. He needs to get stronger and more consistent to make it as a starter, and he faces an important year in Double-A.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more polished prep pitchers in the 2019 class, Fitterer slid to the fifth round amid concerns about his UCLA commitment but signed for $1.5 million (the equivalent of early second-round money). He has been compared to Kyle Hendricks with better stuff, though he has only pitched 53 innings in three years because of the pandemic shutdown in 2020 and back issues last season. The Marlins tried to get him more innings in the Arizona Fall League, only to see him develop shoulder soreness after two starts. Fitterer imparts a lot of natural sink and cut on a fastball that ticked up a bit last year, when it sat at 92-94 mph and touched 96 while generating a lot of weak grounders.
