He has aptitude for spinning the ball, producing solid 78- to 82-mph curveballs with good depth and some tighter sliders in the low 80s. He's also making progress with a sinking low-80s changeup. A good athlete who offered some intriguing right-handed power as a two-way player in high school, Fitterer repeats his delivery with ease and provides consistent strikes. He exudes a calm demeanor on the mound and has a ceiling of a mid-rotation starter with three solid pitches and control to match. To reach it, he'll need to get stronger and prove he has the durability for the role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts considered Fitterer one of the more polished high school pitchers in the 2019 Draft, but his UCLA commitment clouded his signability. He fell to the fifth round before signing with the Marlins for $1.5 million, the equivalent of early second-round money. He posted a 2.38 ERA in his 2019 pro debut in Rookie ball and performed well in instructional league last fall while continuing to draw comparisons to Kyle Hendricks with better stuff. Fitterer uses a fast arm to generate 91-93 mph fastballs and top out at 95 with natural sink and cut that produce weak grounders, and he could add more velocity as he fills out his projectable 6-foot-3 frame. His best secondary pitch is an upper-70s curveball with good shape. He also has a tighter slider in the low 80s and a changeup with similar velocity and some sink. A good athlete who flashed some intriguing right-handed power potential as a prep hitter, Fitterer repeats his delivery consistently and throws strikes. If he adds strength and refines his arsenal, he could fit into the middle of a big league rotation. His polish will help him make the jump to full-season ball in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fitterer caught the attention of scouts with a 12-strikeout complete game at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in October 2018, setting the stage for a strong high school senior season. Signability concerns related to his UCLA commitment knocked him down to the fifth round last June, but the Marlins landed him for a well-over-slot $1.5 million, the largest bonus after the top three rounds. He pitched well in his pro debut, adding to his comparisons to Kyle Hendricks with better pure stuff. With a quick arm, Fitterer produces 91-93 mph fastballs that top out at 95 with natural sink and cut that elicit a lot of weak ground-ball contact. He shows the potential for three solid secondary pitches, headlined by an upper-70s curveball with nice shape. He also utilizes a sharper slider in the low 80s and a changeup with similar velocity and some sink. A good athlete who displayed some interesting right-handed power potential in high school, Fitterer repeats his delivery well and should have no trouble providing strikes. He's more polished than most young pitchers, and his main needs are to get stronger and develop more consistency with his pitches. If that happens, he could blossom into a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since signing for $820,000 in July 2019, Quintana has endured a slow road up the Washington chain. After 2020 was lost to the pandemic, the Venezuela native was limited to only seven games in the Florida Complex League in 2021 due to multiple hamstring injuries. He lasted a full campaign in his FCL return last year and showed some promising results with a .289/.342/.439 line, five homers and a 116 wRC+ in 50 games. Now that Quintana has been able to stay on the field more consistently, we have a slightly clearer view of who he can be in the box. He has plus raw power from the right side and uses it to the pull side as well as right-center. Listed at 6-foot-1, 175 pounds, Quintana’s strength and power production should be his carrying tools on his way to the capital. Though he can make hard contact, he expanded the zone too much last year at the complex and walked only 4.5 percent of the time, lowest in the FCL among those with at least 190 plate appearances. An average runner with just a decent arm, Quintana was moved to first base for Single-A Fredericksburg early in 2023 to get out of the way of an outfield logjam. However, the defensive move may have placed an additional burden on his performance because he started to hit again after moving back to grass. First base would put extra weight on his bat, and he still might need to lock in there long-term if he wants to crack the capital with this core of prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Quintana was the Nationals’ third-highest signee of the July 2019 international class with an $820,000 bonus. (Fellow Venezuelan Andry Lara was part of the same group.) The 6-foot-1 outfielder is still waiting to make an impact in the Minor Leagues. He was limited to instructional-league play in 2020 and played only seven games in last year’s Florida Complex League before suffering hamstring issues that kept him off the field the rest of the way. He’s gotten a lot more playing time this season in the FCL and has taken advantage with strong production across the board. Quintana displays impressive raw power from the right side and doesn’t show much of an issue driving the ball toward right-center. He has shown quality plate discipline in the past, but that hasn’t been a huge part of his game in 2022. An average runner, he was already expected to slow as he aged and filled out his 175-pound frame. That speed will be worth monitoring even more so following the hamstring concerns. Quintana has played right field only during his looks in Minor League Baseball, and that’s where his long-term home was expected to be anyways. His 2022 success establishes a base layer of both health and production, and he could be a breakout candidate over a fuller campaign in 2023.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Quintana was overshadowed by fellow Venezuela native Andry Lara among the Nationals’ July 2, 2019 crop, but he received an $820,000 bonus -- third-highest in the organization’s class. He has yet to play in the Minors in an official capacity, but does have experience in instructional league already, following last year’s cancellation of the season. He got in three games in the stateside Florida Complex League this summer before a significant hamstring injury sent him to the injured list. Quintana draws fullback comparisons for his thicker frame at 6-foot-1, strength and physicality. His raw power, particularly to right-center, already jumps out for his age and experience level, and the Nationals are pleased with the way he has been able to show plate discipline at such a young age against more advanced competition at instructs. His speed is average now but is likely to slow a tick as he matures, meaning a move from center to the corners should be in the cards down the line. His arm is impressive enough to handle such a transition. The right-handed slugger is set to see the Minors at age 18 and could take off once he starts playing against more age-appropriate competition. With no true negatives on the board yet, Quintana has a chance to be a solid Major League outfielder, regardless of which spot he ends up at on the grass. He just needs to start picking up the experience necessary to reach that projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals locked up a pair of promising 16-year-old Venezuelan prospects at the start of last year’s international period in right-hander Andy Lara and Quintana, the latter of whom received an $820,000 bonus that marked the third-largest given out by the organization to a player in the 2019-20 class. Brought to the U.S. to participate in the organization’s fall instructional league, Quintana opened eyes with his physicality and tools on both sides of the ball. An athletic and physically gifted young player, Quintana packs a lot of strength into his thicker frame. That strength shows in his bat speed and ability to impact the baseball from the right side of the plate. He can drive the ball to all fields and impressed club officials last fall with his pop to the opposite-field gap. He has a clean swing and sound approach for a young player, with the potential to hit for both average and power as he matures. Quintana is an average runner and will likely begin his career in center field, though physical development may eventually force him to an outfield corner. His average arm is better suited for left field than right. The Nationals are high on the teenager’s defensive ability and see him as a potentially dynamic outfielder regardless of position.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Quintana signed for $820,000 as one of three high-dollar signings in the Nats' 2019 July 2 class, behind Andy Lara and left-hander Pablo Aldonis. Quintana made a solid first impression stateside in the Instructional League. He's an average runner with an average arm and above-average raw power. He has a well-developed 6-foot, 205-pound frame that reminds some of Marcell Ozuna, making him likely to end up in a corner. He has fair feel for contact and impressive ball-striking power for a hitter his age, though he's been a little over-aggressive at the plate early on in his pro career and the OBP portion of the profile is going to be important here since Quintana is a corner bat. There's still enough of a hit/power combo to consider Quintana a developmental prospect of note.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There's no change here: Quintana signed for $820,000 as one of three high-dollar signings in the Nats' 2019 July 2 class, behind Lara and left-hander Pablo Aldonis. Quintana made a solid first impression stateside in the Instructional League. He's an average runner with an average arm and above average raw power. He has a well-developed 6-foot, 205 pound frame that reminds some of Marcell Ozuna , but Washington thinks Quintana can play center field for a while, maybe even long enough to be an everyday player there in the big leagues. With no organized games to go off of, we're projecting a lot on the bat, but his swing path is direct, there's raw strength, and he's already showing opposite field BP power. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Quintana signed for $820,000 in the Nats' 2019 July 2nd class as one of three high-dollar signings, behind Lara and left-hander Pablo Aldonis. Quintana made a solid first impression domestically in the instructional league. He's an average runner with an average arm and above average raw power. He has a well-developed 6-foot, 205 pound frame that reminds some of Marcell Ozuna or a number of Cuban outfielders, but Washington thinks Quintana can play center field for awhile, maybe even long enough to be an everyday player there in the big leagues. With no organized games to go off of, we're projecting a lot on the bat, but his swing path is direct, there's raw strength, and he's already showing opposite field BP power.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Calabrese is built like a compact little sports car and he's as fast as one, reaching first in about 4.1 seconds after contact. Along with the diminutive frame come very short levers that make Calabrese's swing very minimalistic; he's difficult to beat in the strike zone because of it. The contact and speed combination, along with Calabrese's pre-draft age, made him look like a potential leadoff man as an amateur, but injuries and the pandemic robbed him of valuable reps and he had a rough 2021. The contact piece of his profile is now in question, which puts Calabrese on thin ice since his frame limits power projection.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Calabrese is built like a compact little sports car and he's as fast as one, reaching first in about 4.1 seconds after contact. Along with the Lilliputian frame come very short levers that make Calabrese's swing very minimalistic; he's difficult to beat in the strike zone because of it. The contact and speed combination mean Calabrese has some leadoff man traits. He needs to get stronger, especially in the forearms, and could grow into doubles power if he does. He has a shot to profile as an everyday center fielder if his speed and contact skills hold water. A nagging hamstring injury kept him in Extended to start 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Calabrese was slated to be a part of the 2021 Draft class when he reclassified to be eligible for 2020. He and Owen Caissie were two Ontario high school outfielders who went in the third round of the shortened Draft, the last in a seven-year run of Ontarians in the top three rounds. Calabrese’s debut in the Arizona Complex League didn’t stand out, but he took a nice step forward during his 2022 full-season debut at age 19. A left-handed hitter with a smaller frame, Calabrese has the feel of a potential table-setter if it all clicks. Only his speed is plus, and he can steal a base and cover a ton of ground in the outfield, but he does a lot of other things pretty well too. There isn’t going to be much power to speak of, but a full healthy season after dealing with some injuries in 2021 enabled him to develop a better approach at the plate and make more consistent contact. He cleaned up his bat path over the course of 2022 with outstanding results, slashing .331/.405/.514 from Aug. 1 on. Calabrese spent most of his time in 2022 in center field and he certainly has the ability to stay there. But he also showed he can handle either corner, which could be essential since he may best profile as a fourth-outfielder type, unless he can add strength and impact the ball more as he moves up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Calabrese reclassified to be eligible for the 2020 Draft rather than in 2021, though he couldn’t take advantage of the typical Canada National Team’s trip to Spring Training to raise his Draft profile. Nevertheless, his combination of hitting ability and speed intrigued the Angels enough to take him in the third round and give him full slot to keep him from attending the University of Arkansas. That made him one of three high school outfielders from Ontario taken in the top three rounds in the past two years, joining 2019 draftee Dasan Brown and fellow 2020 draftee Owen Caissie. A 5-foot-10, left-handed-hitting outfielder, Calabrese’s top tool is his speed. It’s received an 80 on the 20-80 scale from some scouts, the kind of top-of-the-scale wheels that should allow him to steal bases and have plus range in the outfield. He definitely has a hit-over-power profile at the plate, with a loose and easy swing that makes consistent hard contact. He should grow into more ability to drive the ball, but is more likely to have gap-to-gap extra-base authority than over-the-fence pop, though some see a little Andrew Benintendi in his profile if he gets stronger. Defensively, Calabrese has an average but accurate arm that works well in center field. He should have no problem staying up-the-middle long term. He’s just 18 for all of the 2021 season with plenty of time for him to develop into a top-of-the-order, table-setting type center fielder at the big league level.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Polcovich checks a lot of the boxes we like here at FanGraphs. He's a short-levered, switch-hitting, up-the-middle player with above-average bat speed. He does not have great tactile feel to hit and just sort of rips the bat through the zone as hard as he can, so his likely ceiling had been as a versatile power-over-hit sort who could hopefully play a passable second base and a good center field based on his speed and athleticism. Polcovich has really bulked up, and now has a lower half that looks like it was designed by an Instagram algorithm, in Anthony Recker territory. His mobility has regressed and he's been limited to 2B/DH duty this year, and there isn't really a path to profiling if he isn't bringing defensive versatility to the party.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There is a difference between being short and being small. Kaden Polcovich is about 5-foot-8, but he's also pound-for-pound the strongest prospect I saw during minor league spring training in Arizona. Polcovich generates big power with a max-effort style of hitting and is a threat to do damage from both sides of the plate. He's also a plus runner with experience at many different positions, including second base and center field. So why was he undrafted for two consecutive years while he was at Northwest Florida State? The max-effort swings have driven swing-and-miss concerns, and while Polcovich has the range for the middle of the diamond, his defensive hands and actions are below-average. So on the one hand, he's a switch-hitting up-the-middle player with power, while on the other, he's a positionless player with strikeout issues. After two years at Northwest Florida, Polcovich was seen on the 2019 Cape, and at Oklahoma State early in 2020. He raked during a non-conference play (the Cowboys had a bold non-conference slate) and buoyed his draft stock into the Day Two mix. He's raw for a player his age, but Polcovich has impact tools. Even with a 30 bat, he projects to play a role similar to the one Sam Haggerty is playing now, expect with more meaningful power. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020updated
fangraphs.text: Polcovich is a switch-hitter with some power, and junior college performer preceding a good Cape and early-2020 with freshly minted Oklahoma State threads. He's a plus runner with below average hands who is not a lock to stay at second base and may have to give center field a try.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners coveted Polcovich enough out of Oklahoma State that they used one of their five picks in the shortened 2020 Draft on him. The immediate transition to pro ball, however, was not seamless, especially after he climbed in the second half of ‘21 to Double-A Arkansas, where he slashed .133/.242/.211 (.453 OPS) and struggled to establish any confidence. But his ‘22 at the affiliate was a big turnaround. He raised his OPS by nearly 300 points and did so with a healthy sample size of 524 plate appearances. He also continued to flash his speed and has drawn praise as one of the best baserunners in the system. He also can play all over the infield and outfield, making him that much more valuable in the eyes of a club that puts a huge premium on defensive versatility all the way up to the Majors. Based on his trajectory, with a few hiccups followed by promise, Polcovich has drawn comparisons to Sam Haggerty. The big thing with him to continue climbing will be showing that his turnaround in ‘22 was legitimate and that he can produce consistently with the bat. The switch-hitter bats more naturally righty, but he’s shown an ability to make enough contact from the left side to continue hitting there. And even with a smaller and stocky build, he’s shown some extra-base potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A promotion to Double-A Arkansas in 2021 was an eye-opening one for the middle infielder, as Polcovich hit .133/.242/.211 (.453 OPS) in 149 plate appearances. The Mariners believe their third-round pick from ‘20 still had a solid process, approach and good pitch recognition, but wasn’t seeing results. As such, it took a mental toll that led him to pressing more. The club has chalked up those Double-A struggles to bad luck. He was much better at High A Everett earlier last season with a .980 OPS. Polcovich has a shorter stature at 5-foot-10, and while his tools aren’t incredibly loud, he profiles with solid on-base potential and he’s a switch-hitter. Though he bats more naturally from the right side, he’s been able to make enough contact from the left to stick with both moving forward. The power profile isn’t exactly strong, but he does have some extra-base potential within the gaps rather than over the wall. He’s also described as a solid runner and smart base runner. Defensively, Polcovich came up as a second baseman at Oklahoma State, but the Mariners have used him all over, including shortstop and center field. He’s dependable with an average arm yet doesn’t necessarily stand out at one spot over the others. The Mariners covet that kind of versatility, which could make him a valued commodity if his bat catches up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The son of a former 10-year pro ball player, Polcovich spent one year at the University of Kentucky then moved on to Northwest Florida State College for two seasons and Oklahoma State after that. He began to catch scouts’ eyes after hitting .305 in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2019, and he was batting .344/.494/.578 with 19 walks and eight steals in 18 games for the Cowboys last spring before the shutdown, which was enough for the Mariners to nab him in the third round and sign him for a below-slot bonus of $575,000. The switch-hitting Polcovich bats more naturally from the right side, but he’s shown an ability to make enough contact from the left side to continue hitting there. Overall, he has a solid approach, and even with a smaller and stocky build, he’s shown some extra-base potential, though his power is more gap-to-gap than over-the-wall at this point. He runs well and is a smart baserunner. At various stops, Polcovich has played a number of positions defensively, including second and third at OSU and center field on the Cape. He’s dependable at a number of spots with an average arm, but he doesn’t necessarily profile at one defensive home. That could lead to a future similar to his dad’s, albeit with a bit more thump in his bat. He made a strong first impression on the Mariners during his time at the alternate training site last summer.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Palmer didn't hold the velo boost he exhibited during the shortened 2020 college season, when he sat 92-96 mph before the COVID shutdown. Instead he sat about 92 across 63 innings of work with Low-A Dunedin. Palmer's body and delivery are both reliever-y, and his early-career strike throwing issues (42 walks in 63 innings) push his ultimate projection further toward the 'pen. But Palmer also has a great split-action changeup and his funky, low-slot delivery helps his slider play up. He still projects as a low-leverage reliever thanks to the quality of his secondary stuff.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Palmer had two dominant starts to close out 2020, including a 13 K complete game versus Illinois State, continuing an ascent that began on the Cape the summer before. He worked 92-96 during his pre-draft spring. Palmer's body and delivery are both reliever-y, though his low-ish slot definitely helps his fringe slider play against righties. His best pitch is a split change with dive and tail. If he can execute that slider consistently then perhaps he'll be able to start. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020updated
fangraphs.text: Palmer had two dominant starts to close out 2020, including 13 K complete game versus Illinois State, continuing an ascent that began on the Cape the summer before. His best pitch is a split, and I have him in as a sinker/splitter reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Palmer helped his Draft stock with a strong showing as a reliever in the Cape Cod League in 2019, and he carried that back to college and into the Jacksonville rotation. The Blue Jays liked him as a starter, though, and selected him in the third round of the 2020 Draft. Palmer’s advanced pitches and deep arsenal helped him to a 3.00 ERA in 2021 with Single-A Dunedin over 63 innings, and he was off to another strong start in 2022, carrying a 3.90 ERA between High-A and Double-A. Unfortunately, Palmer underwent Tommy John surgery late in the season and is expected to miss most or all of the 2023 campaign. It’s a difficult blow for the right-hander, who has one of the most unique mixes of pitches in the organization, creating movement in every direction. That’s helped Palmer post a strikeout rate of 11.6 batters per nine innings in the Minor Leagues, and that should continue to serve him well following his recovery. In a perfect world, Palmer could recover in time to be an Arizona Fall League candidate, which would enable him to see some competitive innings in ’23 and carry momentum into 2024. By then, he should slide right back into the upper Minors and offer the Blue Jays some nice starting depth with the “bulldog” presence on the mound he’s become known for. The surgery is a tough setback, but Palmer remains a unique talent to monitor long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Palmer gained momentum with a strong showing in the Cape Cod League as a reliever, posting a 1.45 ERA over 18 2/3 innings before enjoying a strong start to this junior season at Jacksonville in the rotation. The Blue Jays selected him in the third round of the 2020 Draft, signing him to a slightly-above-slot bonus. His pro debut with Low-A Dunedin saw Palmer struggle with control early, but he turned a corner midseason and pitched two seven-inning no hitters over his final five starts of the season, ending with a 3.00 ERA and 83 strikeouts over 63 innings. That successful first step in the Minor Leagues came thanks to one of the most unique and diverse pitch-movement profiles in the organization. Using his deep arsenal, Palmer can comfortably work all quadrants of the zone and uses an above-average changeup to keep hitters off balance from either side. With a fastball that sits in the 92-93 mph range and reaches a touch higher, Palmer also has a slider that's still ahead of his curveball with some good depth. You’ll hear the “bulldog” tag applied to Palmer often, and while his thick build on a 6-foot-1 frame is unique in the organization, the Blue Jays were pleased with how he improved his physicality towards the end of ’21 and through the offseason. In ’22, Palmer’s first task will be proving that his strong ending to ’21 was the start of something. He still walked 42 batters over those 63 innings, which will need to improve regardless of his role. There’s obviously bullpen potential down the line if the Blue Jays choose to explore that, but he’ll be given more opportunities to start for now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jacksonville University has produced a lot of Draft talent over the past several years, including back-to-back third-round picks Michael Baumann (2017) and Austin Hays (2016), both with the Baltimore Orioles. While Palmer wasn’t as scouted as any of his Dolphins predecessors, his arm strength and strong start to his junior season, not to mention a successful turn as a reliever last summer on the Cape, still earned him a third-round selection by the Blue Jays, along with an above-slot signing bonus. At 6-foot-1, 230 pounds, Palmer is a unique build in a Blue Jays system that’s filled with taller right-handers. Palmer makes up for that with great intangibles and competitiveness, described by some as a “bulldog” on the mound. With a fastball that sits in the 92-95 mph range, Palmer uses his strength to maintain that into starts. It’s a heavy ball with sinking action coming from a relatively low slot, which helps keep Palmer away from hard contact. His split changeup is a strong pitch in the 82-84 mph range while his slider has some good depth to it. Palmer’s curveball is still developing as a fourth pitch. Opening at Low-A Dunedin in his first season, Palmer showed real control concerns and was averaging a walk an inning as late as late July before turning things around in that department in the second half. His swing-and-miss rate took off around the same time, confirming what made Palmer such a promising Draft pick in the first place. It’ll take a longer road for the right-hander to prove the control issues are truly behind him. Until he shows more consistency, questions about his ability to start hold down the profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia was one of the top prospects on the international amateur market when the 2019-20 signing period opened, but it’s taken him a while to sign and really get going in his professional career. Because of an age discrepancy, he didn’t sign with the Phillies until March 2020, getting a bonus of $2.5 million. Then the pandemic-related shutdown happened, so he was stuck in Venezuela for an extended period and played just 18 games with Single-A Clearwater in his official pro debut in 2021. The 2022 season wasn’t much better as a torn meniscus limited him to just 37 total games, depriving him of essential development time. Garcia still possesses the raw tools and athleticism that made him such a coveted prospect in 2019, but he has yet to really have the opportunity to learn how or show them in his performance. He has close to top-of-the-scale speed and is a major base-stealing threat, one who was on pace to steal 100 bases in 2022 before he got hurt. To use that speed he is going to have to work on improving his overall approach and gain strength so he can get on base and impact the ball from the right side of the plate more consistently. His explosive athleticism works very well in the outfield. He’s a plus defender who will be able to play center field for a long time, combining his speed and outstanding reads and routes to cover a lot of ground. There are a lot of similarities between him and fellow Phillies prospect Johan Rojas, both in terms of his tools and what he needs to work on, but he needs to start getting regular reps under his belt to show what he can do.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A discrepancy in his reported age kept Garcia from signing when many thought he’d be able to, in July of 2019, not joining the Phillies officially until March 2020 for $2.5 million. The toolsy outfielder had to stay at home in Venezuela, working out on his own for the rest of 2020, because of pandemic-related travel restrictions. He played just 18 games in his official debut in 2021, with just a .570 OPS to show for it. The Phillies are still very high on Garcia and his quick-twitch athleticism. The right-handed hitter needs reps to help him build focus from pitch-to-pitch and so he can learn a consistent approach. He’s worked to clean up his swing and connect his lower half to the upper half, with a bigger base, while gaining an understanding of the importance of controlling the strike zone. A plus runner who can steal a base, Garcia is a plus defender who can stay in center field for a long time, ranking behind only Johan Rojas in terms of route efficiencies in the outfield. More than anything, he just needs to play every day, something he’ll hopefully do in 2022 at the age of 20.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Garcia was on the map as a prospect eligible to sign when the 2019-20 international signing period began on July 2, 2019, but a discrepancy with his reported age led him to have to wait until 2020. The Phillies were more than happy to be patient, signing the talented infielder for $2.5 million in mid-March of 2020 when he was 18 years old. He wasn’t able to participate in instructional league play in Florida last fall, working out at home in Venezuela. The Phillies love Garcia’s overall tool package, especially what they think he can do with the bat. He has a solid approach with the ability to send line drives to the gap, but there should be more power to come as he fills out. His super-quick hands standout more than anything, where he can let the ball get in on him and make late swing decisions, which should help him hit as he gets moving in the system. Garcia’s speed is currently his lone plus tool, with him having recorded 6.3-second 60-yard dashes in the past. That should help him on the basepaths and it really helps him play a very good center field, where he could be a plus defender in time. He plays with high energy and the Phillies can’t wait to unleash his talents on pro ball in 2021.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Originally slated to sign in 2019, Garcia instead had to wait a year due to age misrepresentation and put pen to paper in March of '20. He then had to wait another year to get into games since he couldn't come to the US for any baseball activity due to travel restrictions, keeping him from instructs. Garcia struggled in 2021, which is perhaps unsurprising for a young hitter who had endured such a long layoff; he slashed a concerning .229/.299/.271 with Low-A Clearwater. Garcia can really fly, and his swing is fairly short back to the ball, but he lacks any real strength and has to round mechanical corners to get the bat around with any sort of authority. He is sinewy and cut and has a very promising athletic foundation on which to build strength, but he desperately needs to build it or else we're talking about a fifth outfielder at best, and only then if Garcia develops into a defensive vacuum. Given the context of the look - fraud perpetrated by adults in his orbit and a prolonged global pandemic cost him multiple seasons - we're not ready to pull all the way off Garcia, though he's not the sort of prospect a team would be interested in acquiring right now. He remains a developmental prospect of extreme variance.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Everything I have on Garcia either comes from the org or from what I've seen on video, which is less than I have on any other player on this list (or any other), which I think it is important for readers to know. Garcia first appeared in the electronic pages of FanGraphs in February of 2019 when Kiley and I wrote up exciting players we expected to sign that July. Instead, Garcia had to wait until March of 2020 to sign due to age misrepresentation, as he was a full year older than indicated. He's now the age of a junior college prospect and has very few in-game reps for a player that age. He is very talented, though, and has one of the better baseball builds in all of the minors, a physique that rivals Luis Robert's. Garcia has plus bat speed and is really short to the baseball despite lots of pre-swing noise in his hands. He's also fast enough to have a shot to be an impact center fielder, though I have no idea what his instincts out there are like. It's tough to line up a player like this on a list; I think I'd take a shot on his upside rather than the major league-ready middle relief/fifth starter/bench role players I have behind him here. But while you could argue Casey Martin is just as toolsy/risky, we have several years of college looks/data to support his tool profile that we don't for Garcia, who couldn't come to the US for any baseball activity in 2020 due to travel restrictions. (At-home dev)

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Shoemaker, a Canadian lefty, experienced a huge velo spike and was into the 93-95 mph range during his draft spring after sitting about 87 during the 2020 summer. He's been back in the low-90s early on during Complex League play in 2022 and remains an physical projection sleeper in the extreme. His delivery is pretty violent, and he struggled to get on top of his upper-70s slider during 2020 showcase play, which caused it to flatten out, but Shoemaker also has a ton of room on his frame for strength and, hopefully, velocity.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Canadian lefty Adam Shoemaker (11th) experienced a huge velo spike and was into the 93-95 range this spring after sitting about 87 during the 2020 summer. His delivery is pretty violent but Shoemaker also has a ton of room on his frame.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the first 10 rounds of the 2021 Draft, the Braves had a little extra bonus pool money to go after some talent on Day 3. That’s how they were able to sign Shoemaker, a native of Ontario, away from his commitment to St. John’s University, with an over-slot bonus of $477,500 in the 11th round. It’s been slow going for the projectable lefty, not surprising given how little he got to pitch in high school, both because of the weather and COVID protocols in Canada, spending the last two summers in the Florida Complex League. At 6-foot-6, Shoemaker is very much a \"baby giraffe\" type on the mound, one who’s thrown just 43 1/3 innings over his first two summers, missing time in 2022 with some minor shoulder issues. There’s plenty of ceiling to reach, with a fastball that touches 94-95 mph but doesn’t live in that range, a mid-80s slider that has the chance to become a solid offering and some feel for a changeup that he needs to throw more. Shoemaker is definitely still growing into his body, and the Braves are hopeful that added strength will lead an uptick of stuff. It will also help him repeat his delivery and command the baseball more consistently. He needs reps more than anything, as Atlanta was very cautious with this project, with the hopes that he can be a late-blooming left-handed starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Big projectable left-handers are often a hot commodity in the Draft, but not as much when they can’t be seen. A native of Ontario, Shoemaker couldn’t pitch much and couldn’t be seen much because of strict pandemic protocols in Canada. He was able to get to the States a bit to show what he could do and the Braves thought his size and potential were enough to go over slot in the 11th round of the 2021 Draft for $477,500 to sign him away from his commitment to St. John’s. While there’s a lot of unknown about Shoemaker, one thing is certain: there is definite upside potential. The 6-foot-6 southpaw can throw his fastball in the 90-94 mph range, shows a pretty solid mid-80s slider and does have some feel for a changeup, but hasn’t thrown it much to date. He attended Braves strength camps during the offseason and if he can keep becoming more physical, those strength gains could translate into more velocity. Shoemaker is a solid athlete with the chance to repeat his delivery and throw a decent amount of strikes. He’s pitched so little over the last couple of years that the Braves are sure to proceed cautiously, with a huge variance of potential outcomes.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Encarnacion has a big, projectable frame that lets you dream on his solid-if-unspectacular current toolset. He signed for $1.1 million in January as Boston's second-highest paid international addition behind Fraymi De Leon (in the Others of Note section below). We think Encarnacion is likely to end up at third base long-term, and on-paper performance is going to be an important part of him climbing the minors (and this list), but his frame supports sufficient projection in the power department for an eventual role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best prospect in Boston's 2022 international class, Encarnacion signed for $1.1 million out of the Dominican Republic. He debuted as a 17-year-old in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, hitting .255/.355/.369 and leading his club with three homers in 41 games. He'll need plenty of time to develop but features some of the best power potential in the system. With a quick right-handed swing and a projectable 6-foot-2 frame, Encarnacion could have at least plus raw power once he matures physically. He can lift pitches without selling out for home runs, and his pop plays to all fields. He also shows promising feel for hitting and managing the strike zone. Presently a fringy-to-average runner, Encarnacion could slow a bit as he adds muscle. Reduced quickness could push him from shortstop, where he spent most of his pro debut, to third base, where he also got some playing time. His quick hands and strong arm would be well suited to the hot corner, and he should be able to fit the offensive profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $195,000 out of Mexico in 2019, Melendez made a strong pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League later that year and opened eyes by coming back from the pandemic layoff to strike out 38 in 18 1/3 Single-A innings to open 2021. He finished that season as a 19-year-old in Double-A, making him the youngest pitcher in the Texas League, and he retained that status when he returned to Corpus Christi for all of 2022. He battled his control and command throughout last season and has missed most of 2023 with elbow issues. Melendez has gained about 5 mph in fastball velocity since turning pro, now dealing at 92-95 mph and touching 98. His 5-foot-8 build and over-the-top delivery created an unusual look for hitters, and the shape and carry on his heater resulted in a 31 percent swing-and-miss rate on his heater in 2022. His 77-80 mph curveball and tight 82-85 mph slider had shown signs of becoming solid pitches in the past, but he didn't throw them for strikes or miss bats with them last year. Melendez's fading low-80s changeup was actually his second-most effective offering in 2022, though he doesn't trust it much. While his delivery provides a lot of deception, he also struggles to keep it in sync and doesn't have a track record of throwing strikes. With his size and control issues, he's more multi-inning reliever than starter, but his fastball is a true weapon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of Mexico for $195,000 in 2019, Melendez made a successful pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League. After his development was limited to instructional league in 2020, he opened last season by dominating Low-A hitters with a 0.84 ERA and 38 strikeouts in 18 1/3 innings. Just 19 years old, he earned a promotion to High-A in June and another to Double-A in September. Melendez has added about 5 mph to his fastball since signing and now operates at 92-95, though the shape and carry on his heater are more notable than its velocity. He backs it up with a pair of solid breaking pitches, with his 78-80 mph curveball slightly more effective than his 83-85 mph slider. His sinking changeup is still a work in progress but he shows some encouraging feel for it. Melendez has an advanced ability to sequence his four-pitch mix and the deception in his delivery helps his stuff play up. He might be more of a multi-inning reliever than a starter, however. He's shorter than desired at 5-foot-8, he doesn't have a track record of filling the strike zone and he has to prove his stuff will hold up over a full pro season.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Melendez, who looks like he'd fit into a child's XL t-shirt, has already reached Double-A as a 20-year-old starter and is punching out over 30% of opposing hitters while struggling with walks. He powers a mid-90s fastball right past hitters at the letters, aided by his lack of height and due north arm slot, which creates enough ride on the pitch for him to miss bats in the strike zone. While his other pitches flash bat-missing movement on occasion, especially his 12-to-6 curveball and his changeup, they are more consistently below average, though Melendez is still only 20, and only one of them needs to become more consistent for him to profile in middle relief.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While it’s too early for the 2018-19 international signing class to have made a big league impact in Colorado, the Rockies' efforts during that period are showing up on the prospect landscape. Warming Bernabel is in the organization’s top 10 and Juan Brito was dealt to bring in Nolan Jones. Guerrero, who signed for $650,000 in July of 2018, is perhaps a step behind Bernabel, but has pretty much hit everywhere he’s been, from his Dominican Summer League debut in 2019 to his United States debut in the Arizona Complex League in 2021 and his step up to full-season ball in 2022. Since signing, Guerrero has displayed a knack for finding the barrel. It’s kind of a controlled aggression at the plate as he’s not one to see a ton of pitches, but he rarely strikes out, with a 15.6 percent K rate heading into the 2023 season. He’s slight and wiry, but he started tapping into some raw power more consistently in 2022, though it still remains to be seen how much strength he can add to maintain that extra-base authority. Though he’s just an average runner, Guerrero is an aggressive baserunner and can steal a base. He’s played all three outfield positions since moving from the infield in 2021, but is mostly likely a corner guy long term and his defense has improved markedly. That puts more pressure on his bat, but the Rockies like his confidence and his response to things like late-game pressure to make them a bit more bullish about his offensive upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies handed out nine bonuses of six figures or higher during the 2018-19 international signing period. Guerrero was closer to the top of the list when he received $650,000 to sign out of the Dominican Republic at the start of the period. Since then, he’s done nothing but hit, with a .319 average in the Dominican Summer League for his pro debut in 2019 and then a .318 average in his United States debut in 2021 in the Arizona Complex League. Guerrero has already shown a very good feel at the plate and even though it’s more of a “see the ball, hit the ball” approach, he’s limited his strikeouts and even drawn some walks. How much he can add muscle to his ultra-lean frame will help determine how much impact he has at the plate, with the Rockies expressing confidence he’s going to grow into more extra-base thump. Signed as a shortstop, Guerrero mostly played third during his DSL debut and shifted to the outfield in 2021 where he used his athleticism more than he exhbited any idea of how to actually play the position. He’s an aggressive baserunner who plays with super-high energy but has average speed, so a corner spot makes the most sense. He might just be scratching the surface, with the ceiling to eventually grow into a big league regular with an exceptional bat.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: The spindly Guerrero has very precocious feel for contact and a swing that is much more elegant and precise than it is explosive. He can hit and has done nothing but since entering pro ball, slashing .319 with an OBP just south of .400 in both of his first two pro seasons. Narrowly built, it's not obvious that Guerrero will develop typical big league strength and power, especially not for a left field, which is where he's trending on the defensive spectrum. He's another very young 2022 40-man eval in this org, so he might move quickly if the Rockies want to stress test his bat to better inform their decision about whether to 40 him or not. He's a very interesting sleeper who could blow up if he comes to camp with more physicality.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: The 19-year-old Batista doesn’t have dominant stuff, but he is a projectable youngster keeping his head above water in full-season ball, and has a chance to carve out a backend rotation spot down the line. His low-90s fastball touches 94 mph and plays best at the letters, living more off of angle than explosive movement. Batista also has an average, low-80s slider and a fringe curveball, both of which could add power as he continues to physically mature. His delivery is balanced and consistent enough to project Batista as a starter, though he hasn't shown any early indicators that he’s going to have special, role-cementing command. For now, he’s a well-rounded developmental starter, probably a lower-variance one likely to mature into a fifth to seventh starter type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the last players the Astros signed in their 2018-19 international class, Batista signed for $25,000 out of the Dominican Republic. His career started slowly, with a pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League followed by the pandemic shutdown and then a 7.46 ERA in a brief stint in the United States in 2021. He took a huge step forward last year, posting a 2.67 ERA with a .178 opponents' average against and 127 strikeouts in 107 2/3 innings while earning a late promotion to High-A at age 20. Batista works at 91-94 mph and tops out at 96 with the projectability to add more velocity, and his fastball also features the flat approach angle with carry and armside run that's in vogue. His best pitch is a plus low-80s slider with two-plane break and he also throws an upper-70s curveball with similar shape. He shows some feel for a low-80s changeup with some fade but it's still a work in progress. More polished than most of Houston's younger pitching prospects, Batista has a sound delivery and generally repeats it well. He could have average control and at least decent command once he's fully developed. He has the ingredients to become a four-pitch starter and also could be a bullpen asset who concentrates on his fastball and slider.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Mooney is a short-arming, low-slot righty with an upshot fastball and two good secondary offerings. His low-80s changeup has enough fade to be weaponized by his consistent arm-side command of it, his low slot helps his sweeping slider play against righties, both as a chase pitch and in the zone, and his fastball angle allows it to do damage at the letters even though it sits in the low-90s. Mooney had Tommy John in college and has had a bunch of injury issues as a pro, but he has legit fifth starter or long reliever stuff and he could be in the big leagues in 2023 if he stays healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mooney spent three seasons in St. John’s rotation and had success right out of the gate. He was putting together a solid junior season to boost his Draft stock when he needed Tommy John surgery after nine starts. The Twins took him in Round 12 of the 2019 Draft and had him rehab with their staff. He’s dominated hitters at the lower levels but also hasn’t been on the mound that much, brought along slowly in 2021 (42 IP) and missing time with a nerve entrapment in his collarbone in 2022 (60 IP). The 6-foot-1 right-hander fools hitters with a bag of fringy-to-average stuff. Thanks to his lower slot and funky arm path, his 90-ish mph fastball plays up with a very flat vertical approach angle. His frisbee 80-mph slider and changeup with good depth might be his best offerings, and the data points to them being more successful than his heater. He also has a low-80s cutter, and when he’s been on the mound, the combination of pitches and deception has been very tough to hit, with a 13.5 K/9 rate and .183 average-against entering 2023. Aside from needing to stay healthy for a full season, Mooney has to land his stuff in the zone more (4.7 BB/9) to have success at the upper levels. He’s been a good strike-thrower in the past, and if he can rediscover that, he has the chance to start. Already 25, the clock is ticking for a pitcher who was not protected on the 40-man roster and not taken in last year’s Rule 5 Draft.

fangraphs.label: 2022draft
fangraphs.text: McKenzie has above-average feel for contact and is a solid bet to stay in center field. A lack of impact power makes his likely outcome more in the good fourth outfielder range.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McKenzie looked like he was well on his way to Draft prominence after hitting .389 his first two seasons at Baylor, only to drop off with a .225 average and .561 OPS in 30 games on the Cape in the summer of 2021. He got off to another slow start back with the Bears before a late surge allowed him to finish with a .288/.388/.517 line in 54 games as a junior, albeit with a 26.3 percent strikeout rate. The Nats grabbed him in the fifth round, and McKenzie looked like his old self by going 28-for-70 (.400) with 10 extra-base hits and 11 steals in 17 games at Single-A Fredericksburg. McKenzie has a sweet-looking swing from the left side, one designed to spray line drives all over the field. That said, the same swing hasn’t done a great job the past two years of generating power, especially in wood-bat leagues, as he seems to prioritize contact over impact. McKenzie can get too aggressive in trying to put his bat on the ball, and that approach found him walking only once in 73 plate appearances with the FredNats. An above-average runner, McKenzie got more aggressive on the basepaths in the Carolina League, and he would be a decent bet to stick in center in most systems because of his instincts and jumps from the grass. However, James Wood’s presence pushed him to the corners last summer, and because of fringy arm strength, he’s a better defensive fit in left.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Antico played four years at St. John's then transferred to Texas where he was a catalyst for a top ten team's offense. He's a physical, 70-grade runner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After spending four years at St. John’s, Antico transferred to Texas as a pandemic senior for the 2021 season and made sure he was on the Draft map this time by hitting .273/.437/.489 with 10 homers while leading Division I with 63 walks and ranking second with 41 steals. The Cardinals took him in the eighth round and signed him well below slot at $20,000. Antico split his first full season between High-A Peoria and Double-A Springfield, hitting .245/.344/.395 with 14 homers, and his 67 steals led all St. Louis farmhands and tied for sixth-most in the Minors. Antico finished up with 23 more games in the Arizona Fall League as a taxi-squad member. Dating back to his college days, Antico’s whole offensive role has been about getting on base. He has a normal, quiet setup at the plate, and the lack of noise helps him see the ball well and take his walks (11.9 percent BB rate in 2022). Standing at 5-foot-10, there isn’t a ton of power, but he could threaten for double-digit homers over a full Major League season with an uphill swing that put the ball in the air 46.7 percent of the time -- the highest fly ball rate among Cardinals full-season qualifiers last year. That also takes away his ability to snap up infield hits, though. A plus-plus runner, Antico’s value will stem from his feet. He’s the perfect type of base runner to take advantage of new rules encouraging stealing, as he proved in 2022, and he can track down balls between the gaps in center too. Because of his extensive collegiate experience, his second full season will be his age-25 campaign, so he’ll need to get to his ceiling as a speedy fourth outfielder soon.

fangraphs.label: 2022draft
fangraphs.text: Boyd is a well-rounded outfielder whose best tool is his speed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2023 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boyd didn't get on the field during the pandemic-shortened 2020 season in his first year at Oregon State and made just 19 starts in his second. But he broke out last spring, hitting .373/.490/.577, and led the Pac-12 Conference with 24 steals before the Reds signed him for a slightly under-slot $847,500 as a supplemental second-round pick. He spent most of his pro debut in Single-A before Cincinnati traded him to Cleveland for Will Benson in February. A disciplined right-handed hitter, Boyd focuses on making contact and reaching base. He features at least plus speed, which he uses to beat out bunts, turn grounders into singles and create havoc on the bases. He has a bit of pull power but makes a lot of ground-ball contact and hasn't shown much power with wood bats, so he could max out at 10-12 homers per season. Boyd's quickness, solid arm strength and keen instincts give him plenty of versatility. Though he played primarily right field at Oregon State, he spent most of his pro debut in center and the Guardians project that he'll develop into a quality center fielder. The Beavers recruited him as a shortstop and it's possible he could handle second or third base in a super-utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic in August 2012, Reyes has pitched to mixed results in his five professionals seasons but continues to flash tantalizing stuff. That was especially true in 2017, when he ranked among the Class A Advanced Carolina League leaders with his 143 1/3 innings pitched (third) and 133 strikeouts (fifth), both far and away his career highs, while posting a 4.33 ERA and a 1.43 WHIP in 26 starts. Reyes' stuff arguably is the best among right-handed pitchers in Washington's system. Combining athleticism with a fast arm, Reyes pitches with a 92-94 mph sinking fastball that nets him both whiffs and ground balls. Club officials rave about his high-spin-rate curveball, a potential plus pitch, and Reyes impressed them with his changeup development in 2017. While Reyes' stuff may already be there, his control and command are not, with both grading as below average. Further experience and maturation should aid him on that front, giving Reyes a chance to serve as a Nos. 3 or 4 starter once fully developed.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Jiménez was picked by San Francisco in the 2019 Rule 5 Draft and by Oakland in 2020, and in both instances he was returned to the Jays, signing again with Oakland on a minor league deal this offseason. He tends to pitch backwards off his inconsistent, plus-flashing curveball. He's a likely up/down reliever with plus arm strength.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Jimenez was picked by San Francisco in the 2019 Rule 5 Draft and by Oakland in 2020, and in both instances he was returned to the Jays. Jimenez also signed late, agreeing to his first pro contract just before he turned 22. He also missed most of 2017 due to injury, and those sorts of factors combined to limit him to just 33 innings above A-ball even though he is about to turn 26. He sits 93-95, touches 97, the heater spins at about 2450 rpm, and Jimenez’s vertical arm slot makes it hard for hitters to discern the fastball and his power breaking ball from one another. He's in the up.down relief bucket.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Jimenez was picked by San Francisco in the 2019 Rule 5 Draft. Like Ramirez, Jimenez also signed late, agreeing to his first pro contract just before he turned 22. He also missed most of 2017 due to injury, and those sorts of factors combined to limit him to just 33 innings above A-ball even though he is about to turn 26. He sits 93-95, touches 97, the heater spins at about 2450 rpm, and Jimenez’s vertical arm slot makes it hard for hitters to discern the fastball and his power breaking ball from one another. I think he’s pretty likely to stick in a relief role.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Jimenez has developed slowly and his slider is inconsistent, but he throws hard and his fastball has bat-missing life and carry. He could be a fastball-heavy middle relief piece.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At nearly 22, Jimenez was ancient by international standards when he signed with the Blue Jays out of the Dominican Republic in 2015. He didn't do much to distinguish himself until the second half of 2019, when he logged a 1.87 ERA with 46 strikeouts in 33 2/3 innings in his first taste of Double-A. When Toronto opted not to protect him on its 40-man roster in November, the Giants nabbed him in the Rule 5 Draft a month later. He was sent back to the Blue Jays last August and was once again left unprotected, leading to the A’s taking him in the 2020 edtion of the Rule 5. Jimenez can overpower hitters with his fastball, which parks at 94-96 mph, peaks at 98 and features above-average spin rates and riding life. He also misses bats with a low-80s slider with two-plane break. He uses a changeup with similar velocity to keep left-handers in check. Jimenez uses his 6-foot-3 frame and high three-quarters arm slot to create downhill angle on his pitches. Though he has three effective pitches and throws strikes, he has been a full-time reliever since 2018 and he should remain in that role. The A’s must keep him on their active big league roster throughout 2021 and can't send him to the Minors without placing him on waivers and offering him back to the Jays for half of his $100,000 draft price.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text:
Preciado set a record for Panamanian prospects when he signed with the Padres for $1.3 million in 2019. He was shipped off to the Cubs as the shiniest prospect in the Yu Darvish deal in December 2020, and spent '21 in the Arizona Complex League, where he slashed .333/.383/.511 and split his time on the infield between third (16 games) and short (17 games). He’s a big-framed (about 6-foot-4) switch hitter who is athletic enough to stay on the infield. Players like this have a wide range of potential outcomes, with one being that their body develops in the Goldilocks Zone where they remain agile enough to stay at shortstop while also becoming big and strong enough to hit for impact power. Size and stiffness in his lower half have us projecting him to third base now. 
Preciado underwent a swing transformation between 2019 and '20, though he is still making noticeable adjustments to it, which indicates that he is working to further develop. Pitch recognition is a concern, and might become more statistically relevant as he faces better pitching. It hasn't caused a ton of swing-and-miss yet; rather it more often manifests as sub-par contact, with Preciado either rolling over grounders or chopping the ball straight into the ground. On occasion, he will add some small but noticeable space (maybe a quarter inch or so) between the top and bottom hand on his bat. While this is likely coming at the expense of his potential power production, moving his top hand up on the bat could help with his barrel control, and allow him to better react, and adjust to ball movement. This may be a temporary developmental tactic rather than a permanent change (he only does it occasionally, and only from the left side), but the takeaway for us is that Preciado, still clearly in a developmental stage, is able to enact adjustments on the field. He remains a prospect of extreme variance with star-level upside.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text:
The Padres gave Preciado a $1.3 million bonus in 2019 -- a record for a Panamanian prospect -- because he had the overt physical traits that teams have traditionally coveted on the international market. He’s a big-framed (about 6-foot-4) switch-hitter who is athletic enough to stay on the infield. Players like this have a wide range of potential outcomes, with one being that their body develops in the Goldilocks Zone where they remain agile enough to stay at shortstop while also becoming big and strong enough to hit for impact power. Though some teams have shown evidence of a philosophical shift in this area, prospects like Preciado are the ones who typically get paid the most money on the international market. 
When Preciado came to the States for 2019 instructs, he looked like you’d expect a 16-year-old his size to look: raw and uncoordinated. He still had not gained athletic dominion over his frame, and he looked much more like a third base defender than a shortstop. Fast forward a year to the fall of 2020 and Preciado came to instructs with a batting stance and swing that look an awful lot like Corey Seager’s. It allows him to be relatively short to the baseball despite his lever length, and whether it had to do with the swing change or not, he looked much more comfortable in the box in the fall 2020 than he did in '19. Because of the missing minor league season, most teams in Arizona brought an older contingent of player to instructs than they usually would, and still Preciado (who is just 17) was striking the ball with precision and power from both sides of the plate when he made contact. He had real issues recognizing breaking balls during the fall and his ability to adjust to those will be key moving forward, but I'm willing to bet it was a symptom of him being so young while facing unusually advanced pitching after not having seen any live pitching at all for much of last year. 
He's been running close to 4.5 times from home to first for me this year, so while he's a developmental fit at shortstop because of his actions, I think Preciado probably ends up at third base. The Cubs need to address the stiffness in his lower half, which is impacting his speed, comfort, and the zip on his throws (I didn't see Preciado really air one out this spring). That makes it more important that his breaking ball recognition improve. His power potential is uncapped because he has such an ideal frame.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: This is what the upper crust of international free agents look like, those for whom a Goldilocks Zone of development exists. Preciado is a strapping 6-foot-4 and has infield hands, feet, and actions, which means he may grow into huge power as that frame fills out but remain agile enough to stay at short, which would make him a superstar. Though that outcome is not the likeliest (based on how Preciado is built, I have him projected to third and think he'll end up there before he reaches the bigs), the several that exists below that optimal scenario are still very good. Preciado has precocious barrel feel for a 16-year-old hitter his size, let alone one who switch-hits. He's not very balanced, especially from the right side, comfort that hopefully comes with reps.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Will be highest paid Panamanian amateur ever, with $1 million to Cubs C Miguel Amaya being the number to beat. 6-4, switch-hittimg shortstop with feel to hit even though he hasn't grown fully into his body. Young for the class and still raw at the plate, with some reports of trouble vs. velocity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Panama's top prospect in the 2019 international class, Preciado set a bonus record for his nation when he signed with San Diego for $1.3 million (later broken when the Cubs signed catcher Adan Sanchez for $1.5 million in January 2022). He participated in two instructional leagues with the Padres but had yet to play in a pro game when they traded him, three other prospects and Zach Davies to Chicago for Yu Darvish and Victor Caratini in December 2020. Preciado debuted by batting .333/.383/.511 in the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League last summer. A switch-hitter, Preciado is still in the early stages of his offensive development but has a chance to hit for average and power. Though he's 6-foot-4, he has a relatively compact swing from both sides, with impressive hand-eye coordination and promising bat speed. His to-do list includes adding strength, improving his ability to recognize pitches, honing his strike-zone discipline and making less ground-ball contact. Though Preciado split his first pro season between shortstop and third base, the Cubs have a logjam of young shortstops and he fits better at the hot corner. He has good body control for such a tall youngster, but he's already a fringy runner who figures to slow down as he matures physically. He has the soft hands and strong arm to play at least an average third base, though he does need to shorten his throwing stroke.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Trained by his father Victor, who played briefly in the Yankees system, Preciado emerged as Panama's top prospect in the 2019 international class. Signed for a Panamanian-record $1.3 million by the Padres, he participated in instructional league the last two falls but never made his pro debut before they traded him to the Cubs last December. He was the best of the four prospects Chicago received along with Zach Davies in exchange for Yu Darvish and Victor Caratini. Preciado will need time to develop but could hit for power and average from both sides of the plate. He has a relatively compact swing for a 6-foot-4 teenager and displays promising bat speed and plenty of projectable strength. His body and offensive potential have led to Corey Seager comparisons since his amateur days. Preciado presently has fringy speed and figures to lose some quickness as he matures physically. Though he has a good first step and better than expected actions at shortstop for a gangly youngster, most scouts project that he'll eventually move to third base. He has the athleticism, soft hands and strong arm to be a solid defender at third base and right field would be his worst-case scenario.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 The best prospect out of Panama in the 2019 international class, Preciado is a lean and athletic shortstop with a large frame and a projectable body. He signed with San Diego for $1.3 million, a record for any prospect out of his nation. The Cubs acquired him in December as the highest ranked of the four prospects they received along with Zach Davies in a trade for Yu Darvish and Victor Caratini. At the plate, the switch-hitting Preciado drives the ball with hard contact from the right side and sprays the ball from gap to gap from the left side. He has a good rhythm and body control from both sides of the plate. For a player so young, Preciado has an excellent feel for hitting and getting bat to ball with authority. There's good bat speed and the potential for power in the future as he adds strength to his highly projectable, 6-foot-4, 185-pound frame. Preciado is a decent runner with long and easy strides and an extra gear when he needs it. As a shortstop, he has soft hands and is light on his feet in all directions. He has shown a quick first step and a strong and accurate arm that projects to be above average in the future. If Preciado continues to grow, he would probably shift away from shortstop, but scouts are confident his athleticism would translate to third base or the outfield. Preciado will need considerable time to develop in the Minors, but the final product could be a player who makes a serious impact on both sides of the ball.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Wolf came over from the Mets in the Francisco Lindor deal looking like a pretty typical seven-figure teenage pitching prospect in terms of size and arm strength, with slightly nastier secondary stuff. After he was dominant on the Mets backfields in 2019, he had just a fair '21 with Cleveland, struggling somewhat with walks and posting a 5.35 ERA. He was inducing a lot of groundballs, though, and is still a pretty projectable 21-year-old pitcher who already sits 92-95 mph, has a great slider (which he used a whopping 40% of the time in 2021) and natural arm-side action on his changeup. Wolf's delivery and rail-thin frame have long put him in a relief risk area, and the early-career walks and a "minor" injury that kept him from breaking camp to start 2022 (Cleveland did not reveal the specifics to FanGraphs) add to that likelihood. Based on the depth of his repertoire, that could be in a multi-inning role.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Wolf was a 2019 high school draftee from Texas who had a velo bump between his showcase summer and senior spring, when he was suddenly 94-97 with a plus breaking ball at times. He does not have your typical starter's build even though his on-paper measurables are pretty standard for a starter. He's very narrow and spindly rather than strapping and broad. Plus, Wolf's arm action is much longer than a starting pitcher's typically is, but that's something that Cleveland has been good at altering. That might aid Wolf's changeup growth. He has nascent feel for locating the change, but not for creating action on it. I think a path to starting more likely means a developmental course that ends with Wolf having two distinct breaking balls. Based on his frame composition, atypical delivery, and style of pitching, I have Wolf projected in relief, but he has high-leverage stuff. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Wolf was a lower-end follow after the summer showcase circuit, then popped up during his draft spring as a high school senior. When making the rounds in Texas, Kiley ran into him with no background; Wolf sat 94-97 with plus life and a plus curveball while there were a couple dozen scouts in the house who were trying to double Wolf up with eventual first round pick Jackson Rutledge (both are based in the Houston area). Wolf's frame and delivery aren't ideal for a 200 inning type, but the stuff is loud, the arm is fresh, the velo is new, and there's no track record of any trouble in the way of injuries, overuse, or walk rate, so at some point we're just nitpicking.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Wolf popped up this spring and is sitting in the mid-90's with a chance to start, slotting just behind Jackson Rutledge, J.J. Goss and Matthew Thompson in the Houston-area pitcher rankings.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wolf opened eyes when he hit 97 mph in his first appearance as a senior at St. Thomas High (Houston) in 2019, and he parlayed a strong spring into an above-slot $2.15 million bonus from the Mets as a second-rounder. He dazzled during his abbreviated pro debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, where he struck out 12 of the 33 batters he faced, and again in instructional league following the canceled 2020 Minor League season. The Indians acquired him as part of a four-player package in the January trade that sent Francisco Lindor and Carlos Carrasco to New York. Adding strength to his 6-foot-2 frame and lowering his arm slot has helped Wolf’s stuff take off. Those changes increased the velocity and movement on his fastball, which ranged from 90-97 mph with armside run during the spring and averaged 94 mph during his pro debut. He has a second future plus pitch in a curveball that registers in the low 80s with 12-to-6 break when he stays on top of it. Wolf's changeup isn't as effective as his other two pitches, though he can flash some solid ones with fade and tumble that point toward it becoming at least average. Wolf’s athleticism, quick arm and clean delivery enable him to pitch to both sides of the plate and all four quadrants of the strike zone, and he earns high marks for his aptitude with regards to making adjustments. He has plenty of room still to add strength to his projectable frame and should continue to get better with those physical gains as well as his development on the mound.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Ramos has electric bat speed and a 70 arm, but also some hit tool questions because of how much effort he swings with. You can't teach this kind of bat speed, and that's the biggest reason Ramos is on our radar as he enters pro ball as our top prospect from the Royals' 2022 international amateur class.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Right around his 16th birthday, Gaston hit 100 mph while working out for teams. That nearly-unprecedented velocity for his age obviously garnered a lot of attention in the scouting community, though Gaston often had 20 control when he scraped triple digits. While he's continued to have some strike-throwing issues as a pro, he has grown three inches, and his frame now resembles that of his Disney villain namesake. Gaston generates upper-90s velocity as a starter with relative ease, and because his strike-throwing gives him relief-only projection, he might sit 100 mph or better once he's moved into a single-inning role. His curveball is also plus but it doesn't always entice hitters due to his lack of command, perhaps because it's nearly 16 mph slower than his fastball on average (which is why we're classifying it as a curveball). His low-to-mid-90s changeup (seriously) also shows bat-missing potential because of its movement. Even with what we consider bullpen-only projection, it makes sense to continue to develop Gaston as a starter so that he gets more reps with his secondaries and can try to refine them. He doesn't have to go on the 40-man until after the 2023 season, after all. If either of his secondaries can become more consistent, then Gaston will likely become a dynamite late-inning reliever.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There are no change to Gaston's report, as he was the same guy during 2020 stateside instructs. Gaston was a 15-year-old Cuban defector who, right around his 16th birthday, hit 100 mph while working out for teams. That nearly unprecedented velocity for his age obviously garnered a lot of attention in the scouting community, though Gaston often had 20 control when he scraped triple digits. He also isn't classically projectable -- his velocity is already at the top of the scale and he has a maturely-built frame at 6-foot, but he's done some arm slot and arm action tinkering over the last few years that has affected his control and command. So while Gaston may get stronger as he physically matures, what's more important is the projection of his feel for pitching, which appears to be more natural at a three-quarters arm slot with velocity more in the mid-90s, where his arm action is also more naturally online, than the higher slot where he was throwing harder and wilder. Gaston's best pitching performance was as the main event on the mound at the Víctor Víctor Mesa workout at Marlins Park, where the better version of his arm slot, arm action, and control was first seen by a large scouting audience. It didn't hold. Gaston walked a batter per inning in his first pro season while sitting in the 93-97 range with the fastball. He's a teenage relief prospect at this point. (Fall Instructional League)
