mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feltman didn't become a full-time pitcher until his senior season in high school but took over as Texas Christian's closer as a freshman, eventually setting school records for saves in a season (17) and career (32). When the Red Sox made him a third-round pick in 2018 following a dominant spring, the consensus was that he'd be the first player from his Draft to reach the big leagues. He breezed through three levels in his pro debut but got knocked around in Double-A last year. When Feltman blew away hitters in college, he operated with a 95-99 mph fastball with running action and a wipeout slider in the mid-90s. In his first full pro season, his heater usually ranged from 93-97 and his slider featured less velocity and bite. When he lost feel for his slider early in the year, he turned to a slower, slurvy curveball, and he also can mix in a decent changeup. Feltman's control and command regressed significantly in the first half of 2019, and then he threw more strikes but got hit harder in the second half. He's small and falls into ruts where he struggles to repeat an effortful delivery that does provide some deception. He's still on the fast track to Boston but the likelihood that he'll become a closer has decreased.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feltman didn't become a full-time pitcher until his senior season as a Texas high schooler, attracting little attention from scouts but earning a scholarship from Texas Christian. He became the Horned Frogs' closer as a freshman, set a program record with 17 saves as a sophomore and posted a 0.74 ERA and tied another school mark with his 32nd career save last spring. Signed for $559,600 as a third-round pick, he reached Class A Advanced in his pro debut but has stalled in Double-A during his first full season. Feltman has a devastating pair of pitches that could make him a closer in the Majors, though neither has been as sharp as usual in 2019. His fastball combines 95-99 mph velocity with running action and deception at its best, though it has sat more at 94-96 this year. The wipeout mid-80s slider he had in 2018 hasn't been as hard or featured as much bite in Double-A. In addition to blowing hitters away, Feltman can also throw them off balance with a decent changeup. Though he has three pitches, he's definitely a reliever because he's relatively small and there's effort in his delivery. After doing a nice job of locating his pitches where he wanted a year ago, he has battled his control and command this season.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Feltman was one of the more dominant college relievers at Texas Christian in 2018, allowing just 12 hits over 24.1 innings to go along with a 46% strikeout rate. That was enough to make him a third round selection, and after showing improved command and control in 2021, he’s on the verge of making his Fenway Park debut. Sitting 92-94 mph while touching 96 with his fastball, Feltman doesn't light up the radar gun with his velocity like he did in college (when he sat in the mid-to-upper-90s), but his overhand release and significant backspin creates one of the more purely vertical fastballs around and allows it to play up. He complements it with a mid-80s slider than has a bit of horizontal sweep to it, but it’s not a knockout weapon and likely leaves Feltman with the ceiling of a seventh-inning type. While Feltman’s stuff has regressed as a pro, he began better locating his stuff and sequencing his pitches in 2021, and had a 1.86 ERA and 0.828 WHIP over the final two months of the season at Triple-A Worcester. The industry was surprised Feltman was left off the 40-man roster at the end of the year, but the lack of a Rule 5 draft means that Boston will get the first shot to see if he can maintain 2021's second-half improvements.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Billed as likely to be one of the 2018 draft's fastest-moving prospects, Feltman's 2019 velocity was down from his customary 95-97 to sitting 92-95 and touching 96. He arrived to 2020 instructs with a slightly different delivery (his shoulders are more relaxed, his glove hand doesn't extend quite as dramatically, his front side clears a little earlier and better) and lived near the top of his 2019 velo band. While it's encouraging that he's regained some arm strength and that his fastball has other traits that will enable it to play up, Feltman still looks like more of a middle reliever rather than an impact one unless all of that pre-draft velocity comes back. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: We tabbed Feltman as the player Most Likely to Be First to the Majors from the 2018 draft class. He spent his entire first full pro season at Double-A missing bats but also missing locations -- a lot -- and his velocity was down a little bit. The fastball still has bat-missing traits, but unless there's a rebound, Feltman is more likely to be a middle reliever than a late-inning arm.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: If forced to pick one prospect from the 2018 draft to throw a big league inning tomorrow, we might pick Feltman, who has an electric fastball/slider combination. As a junior, Feltman struck out 43 batters and walked just six in 24.1 innings, and tied the TCU school record for saves despite being injured for some of his junior year. His fastball is hard and comes in at a tough angle, while his slider has bat-missing vertical action. Barring injury, Feltman should be a quick-moving reliever and has a chance to turn into a late-inning arm.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Johnson comes from a baseball family that includes a father (Marcel) who played three years in the Minors and two cousins (Jimmy Rollins, Tony Tarasco) who enjoyed lengthy big league careers. Signed for $1.35 million as a second-rounder in 2018, he was one of the youngest players in his Draft and still just 17 when the Marlins promoted him to Low-A for the final month of his pro debut. He lost all of 2019 following surgery to repair a tibial stress fracture in his right leg and all of 2020 to the pandemic shutdown, then started to take off last year once he moved from second base to center field. Johnson batted just .146/.214/.215 in Low-A during the first six weeks of last season, but looked like a more relaxed hitter after changing positions and batted .271/.349/.483 afterward (including some time in Rookie ball). With his stocky frame and penchant for hard contact, he has drawn some comparisons to Howie Kendrick. His bat speed and strength produce plus raw power, though his right-handed stroke can look stiff at times and he needs to broaden his approach rather than look to constantly lift balls to his pull side. A solid-to-plus runner, Johnson uses his speed well on the bases and in the outfield thanks to a quick first step and advanced instincts. He broke into pro ball as a shortstop before moving to second base at the outset of 2021, but he never seemed comfortable in the middle infield and committed 33 errors in 69 games. He looks far more natural in the outfield, with the chance to become a solid defender in center with arm strength to match.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the youngest players in the 2018 Draft, Johnson signed for $1.35 million in the second round and was still 17 when the Marlins promoted him to low Class A for the last month of his pro debut. He missed the entire 2019 season after having surgery to repair a tibial stress fracture in his right leg in March but returned for instructional league. He comes from a baseball family, with his father Marcel playing three years of pro ball and cousins Jimmy Rollins and Tony Tarasco reaching the big leagues. With his hitting ability and the way the ball jumps off his bat, Johnson earns some comparisons to Howie Kendrick. He has a quick right-handed swing that repeatedly produced exit velocities in the triple digits during his pro debut, and he has solid to plus raw power that could produce 20 homers per season once he gets stronger. He'll need to refine his aggressive approach to reach his offensive potential. An average runner, Johnson plays a bit faster than that on the bases and in the field thanks to his instincts and a quick first step. He has the arm strength for shortstop but could lose a step once he matures physically, which could prompt a move to third base. Some scouts think he may retain his athleticism but be better suited for center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Johnson comes from a baseball family, as his father Marcel played three years of pro ball and he's a cousin of Jimmy Rollins and Tony Tarasco. He works out with Rollins, who helped prepare him for the mental challenges of pro ball after the Marlins signed him for $1.35 million in the second round last June. One of the youngest players in the Draft, Johnson was still just 17 when Miami promoted him to low Class A for the final month of his debut. He's expected to miss the 2019 season after having surgery to repair a tibial stress fracture in his right leg in late March. Bat speed and natural talent stand out with Johnson, who has the makings of being a 20-home-run player. He regularly produced exit velocities greater than 100 mph in his pro debut, though he also struck out in 28 percent of his at-bats and needs to hone his approach. He has average speed and the savvy to be a threat for double-digit steals. The question will be how long Johnson remains at shortstop. He has a quick first step and enough arm to make plays there now, but his sturdy frame may eventually dictate a move to second base or perhaps the hot corner. Some evaluators believe he has the athleticism to wind up in center field.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Johnson was one of the younger players in the 2018 draft, but a tibial fracture and the pandemic kept him from playing for what would have been his first two full seasons. He was still easily age-appropriate for Low-A in 2021, but flopped there before he was sent down and rebounded on the complex. Back with the Jupiter Hammerheads in 2022, Johnson continues to lack even a modicum of an approach, but still has tantalizing bat speed and power for his age. Playing exclusively center field now, he's a bat speed/power late-bloomer candidate rather than someone who looks like an imminent big leaguer.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Surgery to repair a tibial stress fracture in his elbow meant that Johnson, one of the younger players in the 2018 draft, missed his entire first full pro season rehabbing. He played during Instructional League and had the same rotational explosion that made teams interested in him in high school despite how raw he was in all facets. Kiley and I speculated he'd move to the outfield before the draft but our sources who saw him in the fall thought it was more likely that he'd end up at third base, and that continued to be the sentiment after he was seen in 2020 instructs, as well. He's much more muscular now than he was when he was drafted. We still know next to nothing about Johnson's approach or feel for the strike zone because he hasn't played much pro ball due to his injury and the pandemic, and that's going to be more important if he indeed ends up at a corner, but there's a chance for big offensive impact here because of the bat speed and Johnson's ability to rotate with breathtaking verve. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text:
Surgery to repair a tibial stress fracture in his elbow meant that Johnson, one of the younger players in the 2018 draft, missed his entire first full pro season rehabbing. He played during instructional league and had the same rotational explosion that made teams interested in him in high school despite how raw he was in all facets. We speculated he'd move to the outfield before the draft but our sources who saw him in the fall think it's more likely he ends up at third base. 
We still know next to nothing about Johnson's approach or feel for the strike zone because he hasn't played much pro ball, and that's going to be more important if he indeed ends up at a corner, but there's a chance for big offensive impact here because of the bat speed and Johnson's ability to rotate. He's arguably the prospect with the highest variance in a system full of players like that.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: There are gothic cathedrals in Europe that have smaller gaps between their ceilings and floors than Johnson, who had some of the most explosive but unkempt talent in the 2018 draft class. Johnson's special bat speed and ability to rotate are both evident to the naked eye, and he also has remarkable bat control for a player who takes such high-effort swings. But everything about his game is very raw and he'll likely require years of polish before he's ready for the majors. This is especially evident in his footwork in the box, where Johnson's stride length and direction are both highly variable. At times, this enables Johnson to turn on pitches on the inner half; at others it wrecks his swing's balance and composition entirely. There's also a wide range of potential defensive outcomes for Johnson. He may end up on the middle infield or in center, depending on how his body and infield actions develop, or possibly in an outfield corner. The good news is that Johnson was one of the youngest players available in the 2018 draft and he didn't turn 18 the middle of October. There's a lot of time for both him and the Marlins to figure this stuff out, and he has some unteachable talents (the bat speed and bat control) that could drive an offensive profile befitting any position if he transforms into a hitter instead of a swinger.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rated as the second-best pitcher on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 International prospects list heading into the 2018-19 signing period, Castillo got $1.6 million from the Phillies to sign. Some international scouts thought he had the best arm in the class, and he'll make his official professional debut in 2019 at age 17. While Castillo isn't very tall, he's very physical and has the potential to have a solid three-pitch mix to use against hitters. It starts with his plus fastball, which he throws in the 92-95 mph range, though he's been up to 97 mph at times, throwing it with solid life. His slider should be an above-average breaking ball and while his changeup is behind, there is some projection to it and it flashes average. He has fringy-to-average command, though he can get in the habit of overthrowing, which leads to pitches up in the strike zone. There isn't much physical projection for this 6-foot super-competitive right-hander, but there is more to come as he truly learns how to pitch and control his emotions on the mound. He'll make his first step in that direction this summer.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Castillo underwent season-ending Tommy John surgery in June, so not only did he lose the back half of 2021, he'll also likely miss most of this season with rehab. Before his UCL tear, he pitched 20.2 innings at Low-A with 20 strikeouts and a 1.31 WHIP, sitting about 92-94 mph. His fastball was touching 97 when the maxed-out Castillo was 15 years old, and he received one of the highest bonuses of the 2018 July 2 class, but things had settled into this average velo range long before the stretch immediately preceding his surgery. Already tracking more like a power reliever or backend starter, Castillo is now a wait-and-see prospect in the midst of what will effectively be two lost seasons.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Castillo's fastball was touching 97 when he was 15 years old, and he received one of the highest bonuses of the 2018 July 2 class. He didn't get into games until July 2019, when he was 93-95 with a plus slider in 20-pitch outings, and I have him sitting 92-93 last Fall. He was creating more movement on his changeup during 2020 instructs (his slider was already quite good), so even though there has been a little dip in velocity here, Castillo remains in the 40 FV tier as he's starting to track more like a No. 4/5 starter than a power reliever. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Castillo's fastball was touching 97 when he was 15 years old, and he received one of the highest bonuses of the 2018 July 2 class. He didn't get into games until July, when he was 93-95 with a plus slider in 20-pitch outings. There's no room on the frame (Castillo body comps to Frankie Montas) but there's already plenty of velo, so that's okay. Castillo needs command and a third pitch, both of which are likelier to come with reps he didn't get last year.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Castillo was one of the top pitchers in the 2018 July 2nd market, receiving the second-highest bonus and ranking third in the class for us when he signed. He has a strong, mature and somewhat maxed-out frame, though some similar pitchers have changed their body composition in pro ball and found more velocity and consistency. Castillo was up to 97 mph as a 15-year-old at the highly-scouted MLB international event in February in the Dominican Republic, and has touched higher in private settings. There's still a long way to go, but currently Castillo has rare arm strength, good athleticism, and a good delivery without much else. When projecting someone this young, you can see off-speed pitches that flash average becoming crisper with maturity, and below average command turning into average command, and all of a sudden, you have an average or better MLB starter. Given his precocious skills, this is not completely unwarranted projection, but it's mostly just that at this point, beyond the velocity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at Oregon State, Grenier won the Brooks Wallace Award as collegiate baseball’s best shortstop in 2018, when he helped the Beavers toward a College World Series crown. The Orioles snagged the Las Vegas product with the No. 37 overall pick that June, signed him for $1.8 million and hoped Grenier would adjust to pro pitching enough to keep up with his standout defensive skills. Two seasons in, Grenier’s strong glove, good range, solid arm and strong instincts still make him a plus defender at short. But the bat has been slow to come around, despite the pull side power and solid walk rate he showed in his second run at Class A Delmarva last season. Grenier coupled that, though, with a nearly 30 percent strikeout rate with the Shorebirds, then struck out 34 percent of the time following a promotion to Class A Advanced Frederick. There was some concern Grenier took those struggles with him into the field somewhat, as he uncharacteristically scuffled a bit defensively in 2019 as well. He is also a plus runner who draws praise for the energy he brings to the field. Grenier will always be a glove-first player, but if he can make more contact, he has a chance to fulfill his ceiling as an everyday shortstop in the Majors. If not, he still profiles as a valuable utility-type, someone whose athleticism and solid internal clock allows him to pick it at various points on the diamond. He could benefit from a big year at the plate about as much as any prospect in the Orioles’ system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of prep baseball powerhouse Bishop Gorman High School in Las Vegas, Grenier honored his commitment to Oregon State rather than sign with the Cardinals as their 21st-round pick in the 2015 Draft. He was a three-year starter for the Beavers and helped lead the program to a College World Series title in 2018, when he won the Brooks Wallace Award as college baseball's top shortstop. The Orioles made Grenier the No. 37 overall pick that June, signed him for $1.8 million and then sent him straight to Class A Delmarva for his professional debut. Grenier is a gifted defender at shortstop, with the range, actions and arm strength, as well as the soft hands and outstanding internal clock, needed to stay at the position long-term. There are questions about Grenier's bat, though, and he didn't assuage any concerns by hitting .216 with an elevated strikeout rate in his pro debut. That said, he does have bat speed and a little pop to his pull side, with solid understanding of the strike zone. The Orioles believe Grenier's emphasis on making contact early in the count instilled an element of panic in his swing, and they worked with him in during hitter mini camps in the fall on developing a better foundation to hit. At worst, Grenier has a career as a defensive-minded utilityman ahead of him, with the upside of being a glove-first regular at shortstop. The Orioles believe there's enough bat there for him to grow into the latter role.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: The stout and strong Grenier is a good defensive shortstop with some raw pop and elevated peripherals. His overt physical tools - the power, straight-line speed, arm, and defensive ability - have been well-reviewed since he was in high school, and forced Nick Madrigal to move from shortstop to second base during the last year and a half of Grenier's time with Oregon State. His odd swing hampers his ability to make contact, but because of his feel for the zone and power, Grenier's overall offensive performance has been just shy of league average, which is pretty good for such a sound middle infield defender. He's in a crowded field of role-playing prospects and was left off Baltimore's 40-man, so consider Grenier upper-level depth for now, but gloves like his tend to find their way onto a big league bench.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Grenier was neither at the alt site nor instructs (which perhaps is daming), and I have no info by which to alter his report: Grenier is a good defensive shortstop with some raw pop and elevated peripherals. His overt physical tools -- the power, straight-line speed, arm, defensive ability -- have been well-reviewed since Grenier was in high school, and they forced Nick Madrigal to move from shortstop to second base during the last year and a half of Grenier's time with Oregon State. He was a swing-change candidate for pro ball and his hands do load a little differently now, coming toward his rising front knee before circling back around in a loop toward the ball. This is reminiscent of lots of Donaldsonesque swings in the minors right now. If something clicks, Grenier could be an everyday shortstop. For now, the strikeouts push him toward a lesser, middle infield utility role. (At-home dev)

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Teams had $1 million evaluations on Grenier when he was in high school, just about half a million shy of what it likely would have taken to sign him. He matriculated to Oregon State, where his abilities sufficed to push phenom Nick Madrigal over to second base. Indeed Grenier is the rare college player who scouts saw as capable of playing shortstop. He's a plus-plus runner with a plus arm, and infield-worthy footwork and actions. Neither acrobatic nor sexy in any way, Grenier's look as a defender, and his overall profile, has been compared to J.J. Hardy's. Like Hardy, Grenier also has some power but his college swing likely needs to be altered for him to get to it in games. With player development now firmly ensconced in the era of swing changes, it seems reasonable to anticipate that Grenier will make some adjustments. The track record for college shortstops is not great, but Grenier has everyday tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Green starred at three Knoxville (Tenn.) high schools in four years before the Yankees drafted him in 2018's third round, signing him away from a Vanderbilt commitment with an above-slot $997,500 bonus. His demanding pregame routine often left him worn out during his lackluster pro debut, but he paced himself better and ranked eighth in steals (10) and ninth in extra-base hits (24) in the Rookie-level Appalachian League in 2019. Known for putting on impressive batting-practice displays on the prep showcase circuit, Green generates well-above-average raw power from the right side of the plate with his bat speed and strength. He did a better job of driving the ball in the air during his second pro season after his pull-happy approach led to a slew of rolled-over grounders in his debut. While he has some patience at the plate, he lapses into swinging for the fences and will need to make more consistent contact. Green shows average speed out of the batter's box, is quicker once he gets going and runs the bases aggressively. After spending most of his first pro season in center field, he played much of his second on the corners. He fits best in right field and has the arm for the position, having reached 93 mph with his fastball and backing it up with a hard curveball while pitching in high school.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Green starred at three Knoxville (Tenn.) high schools in four years and consistently put on impressive shows in batting practice on the showcase circuit. A third-round pick in 2018, he leveraged a commitment to Vanderbilt into an above-slot $997,500 bonus. Adhering to a rigorous pregame routine often left him worn out during a lackluster pro debut, but he adapted and ranked eighth in steals (10) and ninth in extra-base hits (24) in the Rookie-level Appalachian League last summer. Green's bat speed and strength combine to give him well above-average raw power from the right side of the plate. He did a better job of tapping into his pop in his second pro season, driving the ball more consistently in the air after his aggressive nature led to too many rolled-over grounders in his debut. He shows some patience at the plate but still swings and misses too much when he gets caught hunting home runs. An average runner out of the batter's box, Green is quicker underway and looks to steal and take extra bases. He spent most of his first pro season in center field but much of last year on the corners, projecting best as a right fielder. He has the strong arm for the position, reaching 93 mph with his fastball and flashing a hard curveball as a prep pitcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2019 Green starred at three Knoxville (Tenn.) high schools in four years while also earning a reputation for putting on some of the best batting-practice displays on the showcase circuit. His commitment to Vanderbilt gave him added leverage in the 2018 Draft, with the Yankees paying him an above-slot $997,500 bonus in the third round. He fits the classic right-field profile but may take a while to develop after striking out at a 37 percent rate in his debut. Green has obvious bat speed and strength that create above-average raw power from the right side of the plate. He has a decent understanding of the strike zone but can lapse into selling out for home runs instead of letting them come naturally. When he did make contact in his first taste of pro ball, much of it came on rolled-over grounders to the left side of the infield. More than a one-dimensional slugger, Green shows average speed out of the batter's box and is a solid runner once underway. Though he began his pro career in center field, his quickness and arm strength fit best in right. As a pitcher in high school, he reached 93 mph with his fastball and flashed a hard curveball.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Like Everson Pereira, Green spent the first part of the season ramping up his game in extended spring training, but unlike Pereira, he didn't explode onto the scene once he was placed on a roster. Green’s combination of brute strength and bat speed generates plus-plus raw power, but he’s still working on getting to it more often in game settings. There are some moving parts to his swing mechanics, including a sizable leg kick and some drifting body movements that prevent him from making consistent contact. His approach waivers, and he became a more aggressive hitter as the season wore on and his performance struggled for it. An average runner, Green is stretched in center field but has a chance to impact the game from right, where he has above-average range and and one of the best outfield arms in the system. Turning 22 in May, Green is a little behind the standard age/development curve, but that's been expected since his draft year. He'll likely move up to High-A to begin the season. He's a player with high variance, but also some breakout potential.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: The one thing to add to Green's report from last year -- remember that this guy was a Pick to Click, meaning I thought he had a shot to be on this year's Top 100 but we lost the season and NYY had no instructs, so he isn't moving -- is that I learned he coaches kids at a hitting facility in Knoxville, so it would appear this guy is a baseball-loving obsessive. The tightly-wound Green has filled out and gotten a little stiffer since he was signed away from a Vanderbilt commitment for just shy of $1 million in the 2018 draft, but he now also has two solid years of statistical performance under his belt, an important feather in the cap of a prospect who had strikeout issues in high school. He still strikes out a lot, but we have two seasons of promising plate discipline results from him to point to, and his speed gives him a shot to stay in center field, both of which make the whiffing less worrisome. He remains a high variance power/speed prospect with the arm for right field should he need to move. (At-home dev)

He still strikes out a lot, but we can point to two seasons of promising plate discipline results from him, and his speed gives him a shot to stay in center field, both of which make the whiffing less worrisome. He remains a high variance power/speed prospect with the arm for right field should he need to move.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: It was widely believed that the Yankees would use their 2018 second or third round pick on an over slot high schooler with a strong college commitment, perhaps someone a bit under the radar, like Adam Hackenberg or Max Marusak. It turned out to be Green, who was signed away from a Vanderbilt commitment for just shy of $1 million. Green ended up transferring to new high schools after his family had issues with the coaching staff in his original district -- issues that ultimately led to a dropped lawsuit and then a countersuit for defamation. But he was an early Vanderbilt commit, scouts knew who he was, and it didn't affect the way he was scouted. He really broke out at the 2017 Area Code games, when he took one of the most impressive BPs there and had among the best outfield arms. He hit several balls hard during the week but was clearly raw from a bat-to-ball standpoint, and many scouts thought he'd end up going to college because apprehension over his hit tool would prevent teams from paying him enough to go pro. Green didn't face a lot of good pitching while he was in high school and his breaking ball recognition is immature. He may be a multi-year rookie ball guy, and he's a high-risk, high-variance prospect whose body and skillset have been compared to Steven Souza's.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Breaux smacked 37 homers in two seasons at McLennan (Texas) CC while also hitting 100 mph with his fastball as a reliever, a combination that made him the best junior college prospect in the 2018 Draft. After signing for $1,497,500 in the second round, he missed half of his first full season with elbow problems that dogged him at McLennan and lost all of 2020 to the pandemic. He returned last year to homer 23 times in 90 games while advancing to Double-A, though the Yankees declined to protect him on their 40-man roster in November. Breaux resembles recently traded Gary Sanchez offensively, defensively and physically. He has a strong presence at the plate, where his well above-average bat speed and extremely aggressive approach create plus-plus raw power but also a propensity to swing and miss. He did a better job of turning on pitches to crush them out of the park last season, but his swing decisions still leave a lot to be desired. His elbow issues prevented him from catching much in 2018 or 2019 before the pandemic wiped out the 2020 season, so Breaux still has considerable work to do behind the plate. He's still raw in terms of receiving and blocking, while his slow transfer and inconsistent accuracy mean that his arm plays down and he threw out just 17 percent of basestealers last year. He's a bottom-of-the-scale runner, so his only other defensive option would be first base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top junior college prospect in the 2018 Draft, Breaux bashed 37 homers in two seasons at McLennan (Texas) CC while also clocking 100 mph with his fastball as a reliever. He went homerless in his 30-game pro debut after signing for $1,497,500 in the second round but bounced back to go deep 13 times in 51 low Class A contests in 2019, missing half the season with elbow problems that also bothered him at McLennan. His on-field development last year consisted of five games in the independent Constellation Energy League. Similar to Gary Sanchez offensively, defensively and physically, Breaux has a lofty ceiling but is a long ways from reaching it. His well-above-average bat speed and strength coupled with an extremely aggressive approach give him the raw pop to deliver 35 or more homers per season. But he also swings and misses excessively, and he'll need to make better swing decisions and loft more balls in the air to fully tap into his power potential. Elbow soreness meant Breaux spent more time at DH than at catcher in 2018-19 and he had next to no game reps last year, costing him the time behind the plate he needs to improve his receiving and blocking. While few catchers can match his pure arm strength, he has a slow transfer and inconsistent accuracy that led to him throwing out just 16 percent of basestealers in his first two pro seasons. He's a well-below-average runner, so his only other position options would be first base or DH.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The consensus top junior college prospect in 2018 after turning down the Astros as a 36th-rounder the year before, Breaux slammed 37 homers in two seasons at McLennan (Texas) CC and also hit 100 mph with his fastball as a reliever. The Yankees used their top two picks that June on catchers with entirely different profiles, taking Anthony Seigler in the first round and signing Breaux for $1,497,500 in the second. Elbow soreness that limited him as a sophomore sidelined him for nearly three months in 2019, though he did homer 13 times in 51 games in low Class A. Breaux resembles Gary Sanchez offensively, defensively and physically. He has huge raw power and an extremely aggressive approach, displaying well above-average bat speed and strength but also swinging and missing excessively. He produces high exit velocities from the right side of the plate and could have 35-40 homer upside if he makes better swing decisions and puts the ball in the air more often. Breaux's elbow problems meant he spent more time at DH than at catcher in 2018-19, and he needs more reps behind the plate to polish his receiving and blocking. Few catchers can match his pure arm strength, though he must quicken his transfer and improve his throwing accuracy after erasing just 16 percent of basestealers in his first two pro seasons. Despite his radar-gun readings at McLennan, pitching isn't really a fallback option because he has a violent delivery that would make it tough to keep him healthy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Yankees used their first two 2018 Draft picks on catchers with different profiles in 2018, a polished athlete (Anthony Seigler) in the first round and a raw slugger (Breaux) in the second. The consensus top junior college prospect after turning down the Astros as a 36th-rounder in 2017, he slammed 37 homers in two seasons at McLennan (Texas) CC. He also reached 100 mph with his fastball as a reliever for the Highlanders, though elbow issues limited him to four innings and prevented him for catching for a month as a sophomore. Extremely aggressive at the plate, Breaux has well above-average bat speed, strength and raw power. While his approach has yet to result in excessive strikeouts, pro pitchers exploited it and held him homerless and to a lot of weak contact in his 30-game debut last summer. He had shown that his pop will play with wood bats and against better competition when he ranked fifth in the Cape Cod League with six homers in 2017. Though Breaux improved significantly behind the plate from his freshman year to his sophomore year at McLennan, he still requires more polish to become a dependable receiver. Despite his pure arm strength, he threw out just nine percent of basestealers in his first taste of pro ball and won't be able to control the running game until he improves his throwing accuracy. Pitching is less of a fallback than it might seem because he has a violent delivery that would make it difficult to keep him healthy.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Breaux has been famous since his Texas high school days and he put up insane numbers at McLennan Community College in his home state, batting .403/501/.800 over two years there and earning a second round selection in the 2018 draft. He’s shown plenty of power as a pro, but at times the positives about his game are limited to his thump. Now that Chris Gittens has gone to Japan, Breaux arguably has the best raw strength in the system. He’s capable of jaw-dropping bombs, but he’s also a mistake-crusher who drives balls from a very small area of the zone, and offspeed pitches give him fits. That leaves him as an all-or-nothing, high home run/high strikeout type of bat, and he doesn't have much in the way of on-base skills thanks to an aggressive approach and some ugly chase tendencies. He’s only been used as a catcher or designated hitter as a pro, but his defense behind the plate is well below average, and while his arm is strong, it’s rarely accurate. Breaux’s power, which is truly special, will get him plenty of time and opportunities, but he needs to find something else to complement it in order to spend time in the TV league.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There's not much to add to Breaux's report since he only ended up playing in five games in the Constellation Energy League before working out at Dynamic Spots Training and taking live BP with a few dozen other pros for the rest of the summer. I'll also note that new catching coach Tanner Swanson (who came over from Minnesota) is a proponent of one-knee catching, so look for Breaux to implement that in 2021. Breaux is a very physical hitter with huge raw power, red flag peripherals, and stuff that might prevent him from catching. When he was a two-way JUCO prospect, he was in the upper-90s on the mound. A sore elbow cost him a bunch of 2019 and may also have sapped some of his arm strength, depending on when you saw him. Even a fully operational Breaux has some footwork and exchange issues that can slow his release or impact throwing accuracy. He's a relatively inexperienced defender so those things may still come, but if not, the K/BB stuff needs to improve because we're talking about a 1B/DH. (Constellation Energy League, at-home dev)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Cue the Pete O'Brien comps. Breaux is a very physical hitter with huge raw power, red flag peripherals, and stuff that might prevent him from catching. When he was a two-way JUCO prospect, he was in the upper-90s on the mound. A sore elbow cost him a bunch of 2019 and may also have sapped some of his arm strength, depending on when you saw him. Even a fully operational Breaux has some footwork and exchange issues that can slow his release or impact throw accuracy. He's a relatively inexperienced defender so those things may still come, but if not then the K/BB stuff needs to improve because we're talking about a 1B/DH.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Nick Swisher's eyes lit up when he was told that the last name of the player he was set to announce as the Yankees' second round pick is pronounced 'bro', a word Swish uses as linguistic filler the way most of us use 'um' or 'like' more than we want to. While some teams preferred him on the mound (Breaux would touch 98 and his sawed off arm action and the cadence of his delivery are reminiscent of Jason Motte, himself a converted catcher) or were inclined to develop Breaux as a two-way prospect, the Yankees selected him to catch. Two-way duty in college means Breaux is currently raw as a receiver and a hitter, but he has a rare opportunity to become an impact bat behind the plate if he can start recognizing pro breaking stuff. If not, the mound is a terrific fallback option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A prototypical projectable high school right-hander, Pipkin's stock initially rose with a big Area Code Games performance in the summer of 2017. An uneven senior season after that hurt, though he was pitching well as the Draft approached. The Phillies nabbed him in the ninth round and went way over pick value to sign him away from his California commitment for $800,000 and sent him out for his debut in the Gulf Coast League. Pipkin has the chance to have three average or better pitches when all is said and done. Tall and lean, the right-hander has a live and loose arm that currently throws a fastball anywhere in the 88-94 mph range. There's plenty of room for him to add strength to his 6-foot-4 frame, so dreaming on more consistent velocity is easy. He mostly threw his slider during his pro debut, and it shows flashes of a plus pitch, and the hope is he'll be able to mix in an average and distinct curveball, as well. He shows some feel for his changeup, but that is also a work in progress. With a free and easy delivery, Pipkin should be able to be a consistent strike-thrower as he gets more reps. It will take patience because he is so far away, but the chance to have a solid starting pitcher profile could be worth the wait.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: The big-framed Pipkin has grown into the sort of velocity hoped of him when he was an amateur prospect, and he sat mostly 94-96 mph when healthy in 2021. He's had trouble developing dynamic secondary stuff (though his relatively new mid-80s slider looked pretty good in its early stages) and staying healthy, dealing with shoulder inflammation during his career. Still notable due to his frame, velocity, on-paper performance (when healthy), and the new hope for a second out-pitch, Pipkin enters his 40-man evaluation year without a starter's innings foundation, having never worked more than 71 innings in a season. It pushes his forecast toward the bullpen.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Pipkin's fastball velocity was very volatile during his amateur and early pro career, but it has been pretty consistent for a while now. After he topped out at 94 in 2018, Pipkin was up to 98 in '19 and sat 94-95 during instructs last Fall. His secondaries are still not very good (I think the changeup has the best chance to be an impact pitch), but he's quite good at killing spin on his changeup (1600 rpm on average) and, as I've written before, I think that's the pitch that has the best chance of developing into a real weapon, while whatever breaking ball he ends up with will need to be hard. He remains a slow-burn frame-based projection arm. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Much of the velocity the industry saw glimpses of at times during Pipkin's amateur career -- and dreamt it would see again once he filled out -- has arrived. After he topped out at 94 in 2018, Pipkin was up to 98 last year. His secondaries are still not very good (I think the changeup has the best chance to be an impact pitch) but one more brick is in place than was there a year ago and I still think Pipkin has a better chance to start than the older arms ranked behind him who admittedly have a greater chance of pitching in the majors at all.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Pipkin is a frame/athleticism developmental project who signed for $800,000 as a ninth rounder. He has a prototypical frame and fluid delivery. He was up to 96 the summer before his senior year but topped out at 94 in pro ball. His feel for spin is just okay, and it's more likely that a plus fastball and a changeup eventually drive his profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An unheralded 20th-round pick as an Alabama high schooler by the Phillies in 2015, Stewart finally broke out when he made his full-season debut in '18. After ranking second in the low Class A South Atlantic League in ERA (2.06) and WHIP (0.98), he went to the Marlins along with Jorge Alfaro and right-hander Sixto Sanchez in exchange for J.T. Realmuto in February. Miami reportedly considered Sanchez and Stewart the two best pitching prospects in Philadelphia's system. Stewart's fastball velocity has been down 2-3 mph in his first season in the Marlins system, as he has worked at 89-91 mph with plus movement. His low-three-quarters delivery creates a lot of sink and run on his heater, leading to a lot of weak contact -- his 2.4 groundout/flyout ratio ranked fifth in the Minors last year. He shows aptitude for throwing his slider and changeup for strikes, though neither projects as more than an average offering at this time. While Stewart significantly improved his command and control in 2018, he still didn't miss a ton of bats, and he hasn't located his pitches as well this year. Whether his sinker-heavy approach will remain as effective against more advanced hitters remains to be seen. If it does, he could blossom into a No. 4 starter.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Acquired as part of the J.T. Realmuto deal, Stewart's velo tanked in 2019, and he topped out at just 91 mph after he sat 88-92 the year before. His groundball rate dropped from 62% to 51%, and he gave up more homers that year than he had in his entire career. He bounced back into his usual range in 2021 and '22, sitting 90-94 mph with a slider and changeup that have lots of lateral action. He's back to generating a ton of groundballs (62% at Pensacola before a promotion to Triple-A) and is in position to be a depth starter.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Acquired as part of the J.T. Realmuto deal, Stewart's velo tanked in 2019, and he topped out at just 91 mph after he sat 88-92 the year before. His groundball rate dropped from 62% to 51%, and he gave up more homers that year than he had in his entire career. He had no true 2020 bounce-back season. A source who saw him during 2020 instructs thought his stuff had recovered enough that he might fit in a low-leverage, multi-inning relief role but left exposed to the Rule 5 Draft, Stewart went unselected even after he was seen in the fall. He certainly fits the bill as a funky, middle-inning long man due to his starter pedigree, four-pitch mix and command. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Acquired as part of the J.T. Realmuto return, Stewart's velo tanked last year, and he topped out at just 91 mph after he sat 88-92 the year before. His groundball rate dropped from 62% to 51%, and he gave up more homers in 2019 than he had in his entire career. He's a bounce-back candidate who projects as a No. 5 starter if his sinker velo comes back.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Stewart was an under-the-radar 20th rounder from an Alabama high school in 2015 and was mostly anonymous his first two pro summers until showing some progress in 2017 during his third summer in a short-season league, then breaking out this year in Low-A. Stewart primarily relies on an above average low-90's sinker that helped him post a 62% groundball rate in 2018, ranking fourth among qualified pitchers in all of the minor leagues. His slider is his best secondary pitch, but all three grade various versions of average, and his control, if not his command, is above average. The main hurdle for Stewart becoming an innings-eating starter is whether there is enough swing-and-miss in his repertoire, and if his strike-heavy approach will need to change in the upper minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There has been a decent amount of pitching from Colombia to impact the big leagues in recent years, with Julio Teheran and Jose Quintana the biggest examples. While he is still very far away, the Pirates did give Florez $150,000 in July 2016 in the hopes he could eventually join his fellow countrymen at the highest level. The right-hander made his United States debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League in 2018, and though he was slowed by an elbow tweak, he's gotten a clean bill of health this offseason. The Pirates love Florez's size and power stuff. He's already gained some velocity in his time in the organization, cranking his fastball up to 96 mph, and there's clearly more in the tank as he adds strength to his 6-foot-5 frame. He can also really spin his breaking ball, with a power curve that could eventually be better than average. His changeup remains a work in progress. There is also much work to be done in terms of his command if he wants to have any chance to start, though his strike-throwing improved from his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2017 and his move to the U.S. The Pirates will let him start for the time being, but seeing him approach triple digits coming out of the bullpen could be fun to watch eventually.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Florez showed a pretty significant velocity spike between 2018 and '19 and was sitting 92-95 mph as a teenager in the Appy League. Because he was so young when he signed, Florez was Rule 5 eligible in 2020, but was passed over because he hasn't been seen much and is still pretty raw from a strike-throwing standpoint. Still just 20, Florez has mid-90s heat and a prototypical frame, but his slider quality is inconsistent and so is his control. His longer arm action may be the culprit here. After a sterling first half at Low-A Bradenton, Florez was promoted to Greensboro and his peripherals regressed to his career norms. The Pirates didn't add him to the 40-man this offseason. He could conceivably enjoy a velo spike in relief and be a good middle reliever.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Florez showed a pretty significant velocity spike between 2018 and '19 and was sitting 92-95 as a teenager in the Appy League. Because he was so young when he signed, Florez was Rule 5 eligible in 2020, but was passed over because he hasn't been seen much and is still pretty raw from a strike-throwing standpoint. Still just 20, Florez has mid-90s heat and a prototypical frame but his slider quality is inconsistent, and so is his control. His longer arm action may be the culprit here. He was seen in the Fall and pitched a little bit in the Venezuelan Winter League and looked very much the same as he did in 2020. He'll likely pitch in 2021 as a starter to develop his command and secondaries, but Florez has long-term relief projection. (Fall Instructional League, Venezuelan Winter League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: His delivery is a little bit clunky, but after experiencing a significant velocity spike last year Florez now has better stuff at a younger age than most of the other prospects in this system. His fastball has grown from the 88-92 range to the 92-95 band in about a year and it has other characteristics that enable it to play in the strike zone. His breaking ball, which has always had length, now has more power and velocity as well. He has some nascent feel for creating sinking movement on a changeup, but he doesn't often locate it competitively right now. That's true for most of his offerings at the moment and there's an awful lot of relief risk here, but the notion that Florez might throw even harder in short bursts combined with a shot to have three major league-quality offerings means that even if he ends up in relief, he could be dominant. His pitch grades assume bullpen projection. Florez is Rule 5 eligible at the end of 2020, which I think increases his chances of being 'penned and pushed quickly.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rivera declined to sign with the Giants as a 32nd-rounder after his freshman season at Wallace State-Hanceville (Ala.) CC, then became the second-highest drafted player in school history (Craig Kimbrel, third round, 2008) when San Francisco landed him in the fourth round for an above-slot $800,000 a year later. With their college connection and his ability to spin a nasty breaking ball that could make him a closer, Rivera has some parallels to Kimbrel. He worked just 94 innings in his first three years as a pro -- he was worn down in his debut, had a lower back strain in 2019 and the cancellation of the 2020 Minor League season restricted him to instructional league -- and missed the first three months of this season with shoulder issues. Rivera's curveball is a legitimate hammer with power in the low 80s, high spin rates and true 12-6 break. His fastball gives him a second plus pitch that touches 97 mph with electric cutting action, though he tends to command it better when he works around 92-93. He also flashes a solid changeup but lacks consistency with his third offering. While he has the upside of a No. 3 starter, Rivera has a long ways to go to get there. He has to prove he can stay healthy, refine his changeup and harness his fastball and curveball to throw more strikes. His stuff could be even nastier if he moves to the bullpen and just airs out his two main weapons in shorter stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Because he attended Wallace State-Hanceville (Ala.) CC and can spin a nasty breaking ball that might make him a closer, Rivera has drawn comparisons to the greatest player in school history, Craig Kimbrel. He turned down the Giants as a 32nd-rounder after his freshman season in 2017, then became the second-highest Lion drafted after (behind Kimbrel) when San Francisco signed him for an above-slot $800,000 in the fourth round a year later. He was worn down in his pro debut and missed time in 2019 with a lower back strain but has shown electric stuff when 100 percent. Rivera owns the best curveball in the system, a true hammer in the low-80s with high spin rates and 12-6 break. His fastball can reach 97 mph with dynamic cutting action, though he commands it better when he works around 92-93 mph. He can flash a solid changeup though it's very much a work in progress. Rivera offers the upside of a No. 3 starter, but to get there he'll have to prove he can stay healthy and do a better job of locating his pitches. His fastball and curveball move so much that he has difficulty finding the strike zone at times. If he can't stick in the rotation, his stuff could become even filthier if he just airs it out in short relief stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Craig Kimbrel spurned the Braves as a 33rd-rounder in 2007 to return to Wallace State-Hanceville (Ala.) CC for his sophomore season, then went 30 rounds higher to the same club the following June. Rivera took a similar path, turning down the Giants as a 32nd-rounder in 2017 to return to the Lions and then becoming the second-highest pick in the program's history when San Francisco redrafted him in the fourth round last June. Signed for a well over-slot $800,000 in the fourth round, he was tired and didn't have his best stuff in his pro debut. When he's fully rested, Rivera has a legitimate out pitch in a low-80s curveball with sharp break. He's also capable of reaching 96 mph with his fastball, though he's most effective when he operates in the low 90s with sink. He began using his changeup more as a sophomore, showing the potential to become a solid third pitch. Rivera has a smoother delivery when he paces himself as a starter but features more effort and some head whack when he reaches back for maximum velocity. He has the upside of a mid-rotation starter if he can get more consistent with his control and changeup. Some scouts who saw him as an amateur liked him more as a late-inning reliever who could focus on his curve and fastball, with one even comparing him to Kimbrel.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: The Giants drafted Rivera out of an Alabama JUCO twice, moving him up the board from a 32nd round selection in 2017 to a fourth round pick 12 months later. As a pro he’s shown good stuff while struggling to locate, and he missed most of 2021 with shoulder issues. Rivera has two plus pitches. His over-the-top delivery generates ideal shape on a 93-95 mph fastball, and once ahead in the count, he can end at-bats both in and out of the zone with a plus power curve than features outstanding spin rates and depth. He’s not wild but he’s far from precise, and his fastball always up/curveball always down approach can become a bit predictable. He can change the grip on his fastball to create more of a two-seamer, but the pitch doesn't really drop as much as it creates a worse shape. He also has a decent change. It’s a bit of a heave in terms of delivery and most scouts think he’d be better off in the bullpen. How the Giants see Rivera will be revealed with his 2022 role, but most see the makings of a future big league reliever within.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Rivera has an Emilio Pagán body and delivery comp, and he has natural proclivity for spin. His power stuff -- 92-96 with cut action and a plus-plus curveball -- fits like a glove in a relief role, projected here as a third banana sort, a single-inning guy you'd see in the seventh or eighth. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Rivera has an Emilio Pagan body and delivery comp, and he has natural proclivity for spin. His power stuff -- 92-96 with cut action and a plus curveball -- might tick up in single-inning stints, so while his command likely pushes him to the bullpen, he might be dominant there.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: The Giants drafted Rivera after his 2017 freshman season, but he went back to school, raised his stock, and was the first JUCO arm off the board the following year. He has power stuff -- 93-96 with cut action at times, and a plus curveball -- but is wild and may be a reliever, though probably a very good one.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Bishop’s exceptionally loud tools made him the 10th overall pick in the 2019 draft despite questions about his ability to make consistent contact. Nearly three years later, those questions remain, mostly because Bishop hasn't been able to get the necessary reps thanks to a global pandemic and a 2021 season that was mostly lost to shoulder issues. Bishop has plus-plus raw power and is capable of moonshots when he gets a hold of one, but that’s rarely been on display as a pro. While he’s exceptionally patient, at times bordering on passive at the plate, he has a grooved swing that just doesn't cover much of the zone and leaves him strikeout prone despite the fact that he rarely chases. He remains a plus or better runner who covers more than enough ground in center field, but his fringe arm dipped to disturbingly below average following his return to action. More than anything, Bishop just needs a full and healthy season to get his development back on track, but it’s now been three years since he was a dominant force, which he really only was for a few weeks of pre-conference play during his draft spring.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Bishop changed his college commitment late (he was originally going to play two sports at Washington), and headed to ASU. After struggling as an underclassman, he arrived for his junior season with a better body and quieter swing, and exploded, slashing .342/.479/.748 in 2019. He sent many non-conference pitches rocketing into Phoenix's midnight sky before he started seeing -- and swinging over the top of -- Pac-12 breaking balls. He was hitting .450 when PAC play began, struck out in 26% of his plate appearances, and finished hitting .342. Whether this was a real problem was the subject of many draft room debates, as was Bishop's relatively short track record of performance. Because the 2020 season was banged due to COVID, we still have very little quantifiable idea of how Bishop will handle a better cross section of breaking balls than he saw early in his junior year. He crushed middle-in pitches at the alt site but continued to waive at back foot breaking stuff. If he can indeed learn to lay off of those or drop the bat head and hit them, then he's going to be a star. Bishop has rare physical tools. He's a plus runner and will post 70 run times to first on occasion, has solid feel for center field and huge, playable power. It's unclear why his arm strength dipped as a junior when it was an asset earlier in his career, but it's not a significant part of the skillset and I heard nothing odd about his pre-draft medical, so for now I'm looking the other way. He's a Pick to Click who just needs to generate a little more confidence in his hit tool. (Alternate site, Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.text:

Bishop has rare physical tools. He's a plus runner and will post 70 run times to first on occasion, has solid feel for center field and huge, playable power. It's unclear why his arm strength dipped last year when it was an asset earlier in his career, but it's not a significant part of the skillset and we heard nothing odd about his pre-draft medical, so we're looking the other way. He'll be a top 100 prospect as soon as we're more confident in the hit tool.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Bishop changed his college commitment late (he was originally going to play two sports at Washington), and headed to ASU. After struggling as a freshman and sophomore, he arrived for his junior season with a better body and quieter swing. He sent many non-conference pitches rocketing into Phoenix's midnight sky before he started seeing -- and swinging over top of -- lots of Pac-12 breaking balls. Whether this is fixable has been the subject of many debates in draft rooms in the early first round. Bishop has rare physical tools for a college hitter. He's a plus runner and will post 70 run times to first on occasion with solid feel for center field and huge, playable power, so there's a chance for stardom here even if Bishop ends up with a below-average hit tool. It's unclear why Bishop's arm strength and accuracy became issues this year after they were assets earlier in his career, but it's such a small aspect of his skillset that it shouldn't be a concern unless his medical indicates it's a chronic issue. Less stable than the college hitters ranked above him, Bishop has as much upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best college athlete in the 2019 Draft, Bishop went 10th overall to San Francisco, signed for a below-slot $4.1 million and had a solid pro debut. But he barely played in the next two years because the pandemic wiped out the Minor League season in 2020, when he came down with COVID-19 during Summer Camp, and he strained his right (throwing) shoulder in his third game of 2021, limiting him to just 16 contests. He's the younger brother of big league outfielder Braden Bishop, who spent most of last season at the Giants' Triple-A Sacramento affiliate. Bishop's bat speed, strength and the loft in his left-handed swing produce well above-average raw power that plays to any part of the ballpark, but he has yet to show that he can make enough contact or stay healthy enough to take advantage of his pop. He always has come with swing-and-miss concerns, and they've worsened in 2022 as he's gotten more aggressive and pull-happy. He also missed another month of needed at-bats with an oblique injury. A wide receiver who originally committed to play football as a recruited walk-on at Washington before deciding to concentrate on baseball at Arizona State, Bishop has plus speed and at least 25-25 upside. He's still learning to make the most of his quickness as a basestealer and a center fielder, and his inactivity hasn't helped. He should be at least a solid defender in center, where his fringy arm is playable and accurate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A wide receiver who originally committed to play football as a preferred walk-on at Washington, Bishop changed his mind and opted to play baseball at Arizona State. The younger brother of Giants Triple-A outfielder Braden Bishop exploded as a junior in 2019, batting .342/.479/.748 with 22 homers and 12 steals in 57 games, which prompted the Giants to draft him 10th overall and sign him for a below-slot $4.1 million. He recorded an .867 OPS in his pro debut, participated at San Francisco's alternate training site and in instructional league last year and missed most of the first three months this season with a right shoulder injury. Bishop had some of the best raw power in the 2019 Draft, with his bat speed, strength and the loft in his left-handed stroke enabling him to crush the ball out of any part of the ballpark. He did a better job of translating his pop into production once he settled down his approach, worked deeper counts and began using the opposite field, but he still comes with swing-and-miss concerns. He struck out in 27 percent of his plate appearances during his debut, though he also had an encouraging walk rate of 26 percent. Add in plus speed that he's still learning how to get the most out of on the bases, and Bishop has 30-30 potential. After playing the corners during his first two college season, he took quickly to center field in 2019 and should be at least a solid defender there. His arm is fringy to average but he makes accurate throws.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 A star wide receiver in high school, Bishop initially committed to play football as a preferred walk-on at Washington before deciding to focus on baseball at Arizona State. After two promising but inconsistent seasons, the younger brother of Mariners outfielder Braden Bishop broke out as a junior last spring by hitting .342/.479/.748 with 22 homers and 12 steals in 57 games. He went 10th overall in June and signed for $4.1 million, then continued to show a blend of power, speed and patience in his pro debut. Bishop's bat speed and strength plus the leverage in his 6-foot-5 frame and the loft in his left-handed swing gave him more raw power than most players in the 2019 Draft. He began to translate it into production more frequently once he calmed his approach, worked deeper counts and became more willing to use the opposite field. He still needs to make adjustments to reduce his strikeouts, but he improved his contact rate last year and offsets his whiffs with a healthy amount of walks. Also one of the best athletes in the 2019 Draft, Bishop has plus speed that he's still learning how to maximize on the bases. His quickness is more obvious in center field, where he already looks comfortable after playing the corners during his first two college seasons. His arm stands out more for its accuracy than its strength, which earns fringy to average grades.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text:
Cavaco is on a similar journey as Urbina, and as such, is facing similar obstacles, making for an interesting comparison. Much like Urbina, Cavaco boasts an impressive profile and pedigree, but lost the 2020 season only to return to a higher level of play than was previously typically for high school prospects of his ilk, who used to be able to adjust to professional pitching more gradually by cutting their teeth in short-season ball. And much like Urbina, Cavaco proceeded to belly-flop in 2021. But while they both posted identically abysmal 67 wRC+ marks during their seasons at Low-A, they did so in very different ways. Whereas Urbina’s mature approach was dampened by a low BABIP, Cavaco displayed the opposite of that, with an unrefined approach that resulted in walk and strikeout rates of 6.9% and 34.2% respectively. 
But when he did make contact, it was impactful; his BABIP on the season was a cartoonish .361, and scouts still love the raw power he brings. It’s very unlikely Cavaco can sustain that BABIP long-term, so improving his feel for the strike zone will be an important piece of his ongoing development. As an amateur, his swing was awkwardly-timed and very uphill, and his performance in 2021 was partially a result of attempts to adjust it (and, of course, him reacclimating to professional pitching). He still has an uppercut swing, though it’s clear he’s working on flattening it, and he’s added elements to his load and his front foot placement that seem geared toward adjusting his timing. As an added hiccup to his progress, Cavaco missed nearly a month with a concussion, disrupting his season just as he seemed poised to turn around his slow start (his June slash line was .344/.400/.438 when he was shut down on the 10th of that month). His 2021 defense at shortstop (24 errors in 60 games) also makes it more likely he eventually moves over to third base, where his plus arm will still play. Cavaco was always going to be a slow burn and his ceiling is still high, depending mostly on his ability to hone his timing to more consistently get to the in-game power that his bat speed/path combo is geared for.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: A growth spurt buoyed Cavaco's tools and draft stock, and he was 2019's most prominent pop-up high school prospect. He may have had the best frame in the entire draft but had already grown into considerable power as a senior, which he got to in games despite an awkwardly-timed stride and very uphill swing. At times clumsy on defense, Cavaco may still be growing into his new body. He was also catching early in high school, and had to move all over the infield during his upperclass days because talented young shortstop Marcelo Mayer (a potential top five pick in 2021) went to the same high school and was playing short. It seemed likely that, considering his absence from the summer showcase circuit (again, this kid had a late growth spurt), Cavaco might struggle to adjust to the quality of pro pitching. But his 2019 summer after signing was worse than anticipated. He hit .172 and struck out in more than a third of his plate appearances. He had no opportunity to rebound in 2020 because of the cancellation of the minor league season, and like many of us, Cavaco's body yo-yo'd between thick and thin during the year. He's certainly a high-risk prospect but his present power, power projection, and the possibility that he plays a premium position with more reps gives him one of the higher ceilings in this system. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of Eastlake High School in Southern California, the same program that produced former No. 1 overall pick Adrian Gonzalez, Cavaco played his way into the first round in 2019 with a big senior season. Since being taken No. 13 overall, the infielder has had some trouble gaining much traction offensively, missing a good chunk of his first full season in 2021 with a concussion. A return to Single-A Fort Myers in 2022 resulted in a bit more power, though he also showed there’s plenty of work to be done. The right-handed hitter continues to show glimpses of the raw tools that made him a first-rounder in the first place, and he’s still learning how to tap into them on a more consistent basis. He has plenty of raw power, and he did set a career high in home runs in 2022 as he worked to correct some mechanical issues with his swing -- including a swing path that is too uphill and a tendency to bail in his stride. While he has had a better bat path at times, he still needs to be more selective at the plate and cut down his swing-and-miss after whiffing in 34.8 percent of his plate appearances in 2022. A shortstop in high school who had some skills to stick there, Cavaco made the move to third in 2022, where his plus arm should work just fine. He doesn’t turn 22 until next June, so there’s time for him to figure things out, with more reps needed for him to find a better level of consistency on both sides of the ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Eastlake High School in Southern California has had two first round picks in its history. The first was Adrian Gonzalez, the No. 1 overall selection in 2000. Cavaco became No. 2 when the Twins took him No. 13 overall in the 2019 Draft before he struggled during his pro debut in the Gulf Coast League that summer. While the shutdown kept him from playing in 2020, the Twins were very happy with the work he put in on his own and how he performed during instructional league play last fall. During Cavaco’s brief debut in 2019, the infield struggled to make consistent contact, with a tendency to get too uphill the biggest contributor to all of the swing-and-miss. During his time at instructs, he worked to flatten his swing a little, stay in the zone more and make more contact, showing promising strides in that area. That should allow him to tap into his considerable raw power more consistently moving forward. Cavaco worked on his body and his conditioning during the shutdown, showing up to instructs much leaner and more athletic. That gives the plus runner a better chance to stick at shortstop, with enough arm to stay at the premium position. There is a chance he’ll outgrow the spot and he could easily handle a move to third, where he played for most of his high school career.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Heading into the fall of his senior year at Eastlake High School in Southern California, Cavaco was a relative unknown on the Draft scene. He started putting himself on the map with a very strong showing at the Angel Elite showcase that fall and kept it going throughout his senior season, making him one of the biggest pop-up prospects in the Class of 2019. The Twins liked what they saw and took him with the No. 13 pick last June, signing him for a bit below pick value. He struggled during his pro debut as a minor quad issue slowed him and he never quite got rolling as a result. While he scuffled in his first summer as a pro, the reasons Cavaco rose into first-round consideration are still very much there, namely his athleticism and his overall tool package. He has the chance to grow into some serious power, with easily plus raw pop now from the right side of the plate. He’s going to have to refine his approach at the plate and his mechanics as there is some swing and miss in his game. He’s also a plus runner who gets down the line in a hurry and that could translate to some stolen bases down the road. Cavaco’s athleticism also helps him on the other side of the ball. He had primarily been a third baseman, and a good one with great hands, footwork and a plus arm. Then he showed he could play shortstop and after sending him out at the premium position during his pro debut, the Twins will keep him there as he begins his pro career in earnest.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Dalquist and Thompson have moved together in scouts' collective consciousness since both were $2 million bonus signees from the 2019 draft with projectable frames and precocious breaking balls. Dalquist's fastball has more natural ride and while he's progressed from a velocity standpoint, he has consistently walked about 14% of opposing hitters in pro ball and is starting to trend toward the bullpen. While his curveball, which has beautiful shape, was his most-used secondary pitch in high school, a mid-80s slider has since come to the forefront and was his most-used secondary in 2021. The combination of fastball carry and his two viable breaking balls give Dalquist a starter's repertoire, but he has yet to show that he can work with a starter's efficiency. It's too early to totally cut bait on him starting since he doesn't have to be put on the 40-man until after the 2023 season and he could still conceivably be deployed as a starter during his first option year. But because Dalquist hasn't made real strides in this area, his forecast is starting to shift toward the bullpen.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: My pre-draft reports on Dalquist suggested he was a relatively advanced strike-thrower, as is typical for a SoCal high school arm, with a shapely curveball and a short arm action suitable for changeup projection. That's mostly held true more than a year after he was drafted, except I saw more release point variability (as if to vary the shape of his breaking ball) and a longer arm action (which makes me less likely to project heavily on the changeup) than was described in my amateur notes. But again, Dalquist's report remains similar to last offseason's write-up. He's well-balanced over the rubber and has advanced fastball and breaking ball control. He'll likely end up with two viable breaking balls even if the changeup doesn't develop, which will be fine for thwarting lefties so long as they're located well, which they project to be. Because Dalquist is of narrow build, he doesn't have the fastball projection of most other, recently-drafted pitchers (especially since he's already 20) and projects toward the back of a rotation. (Alternate site, Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Dalquist has a semi-projectable frame and a graceful, repeatable delivery. He's been up to at least 94, but mostly sits 89-92 and has good feel for a slower, 12-6 curveball. His arm action portends a better changeup. The key variable here is the velo. If it comes, Dalquist has No. 4 starter upside. Pro workloads tend to disallow that, but Dalquist's feel to pitch gives him a shot to be an effective starter even if he only ever sits 90-93.
