mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox more than doubled Dalquist's third-round slot value, paying the California high schooler $2 million to forgo an Arizona commitment. After getting just three innings in his first two years as a pro because the pandemic wiped out the 2020 Minor League season, he stayed healthier and outperformed fellow big-money prep right-handers Jared Kelley and Matthew Thompson at Low-A Kannapolis. He didn't exactly dominate, however, with a 4.99 ERA and 56 walks in 83 innings. Dalquist has added velocity since signing and now sits at 92-94 mph and reaches the mid-90s more often with his fastball, with the extension in his delivery adding deception that's more notable than his heater's life. His low-80s slider with depth has surpassed his mid-70s downer curveball as his best breaking pitch, though he hangs it too often. He's also making progress with a fading low-80s changeup that can get too firm at times. Dalquist stood out more with his polish than his pure stuff as an amateur, but the reverse was true in 2021, when he struggled to harness his improved stuff. Fastball command was a particular problem, as he regularly missed up and to his arm side. He's a potential four-pitch mid-rotation starter if he can figure things out, but he has yet to show many signs of doing so.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox invested heavily in high school right-handers in the last two Drafts, spending $2.1 million on Matthew Thompson and $2 million on Dalquist in 2019 and $3 million on Jared Kelley in 2020. A California high school product, Dalquist received more than double his slot value in the third round to give up an Arizona commitment. He pitched three innings in his pro debut before spending 2020 at Chicago's alternate training site and instructional league program. Though Dalquist stands out more with his polish than his pure stuff, his pitches have gotten better as he has gained strength. He's reaching the mid-90s more often with his fastball and sitting around 92-94 mph, with the extension in his delivery creating deception that's more notable than the life on his heater. His mid-70s curveball and harder slider both have gotten sharper since he turned pro and show flashes of becoming plus offerings. Dalquist also shows some feel for a changeup that he didn't need much as an amateur. More athletic than physical, he has a whippy arm action, repeats his delivery and usually fills the strike zone, though he has had difficulty harnessing his improved stuff in 2021. He has the upside of a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After drafting Spencer Adams in 2014's second round, the White Sox shied away from taking prep arms with early picks until they spent their 2019 second- and third-rounders on Matthew Thompson and Andrew Dalquist. One of the few pleasant surprises in a lackluster California high school class, Dalquist signed for $2 million -- more than double his slot value in the third round. Chicago had him make just three one-inning starts in his pro debut and will turn him loose this year, likely developing him alongside Thompson. Heading into Dalquist's senior season, scouts regarded him as a projectable right-hander who lacked the present stuff to buy him away from a commitment to Arizona. That changed when his fastball velocity jumped to 91-95 mph last spring, with the extension in his delivery creating deception that's more notable than the life on his two-seamers and four-seamers. He has good depth on a mid-70s curveball that will be at least a solid offering once it adds more power, and also has a slider and a changeup that he didn't utilize much as an amateur. While Dalquist isn't physical, he's athletic and has a whippy arm action. He repeats his delivery and provides consistent strikes. His polish gives him a higher floor than most high school arms, and his ceiling could rise because he still has a good deal of projection remaining in his 6-foot-1 frame.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Brewer is the kind of prospect who the lost 2020 season hurt the most: the raw college prospect who needs reps. He was draft eligible at a junior college before matriculating to Michigan, where he broke out at a big program and went in the third round of the 2019 draft. This is a high-risk hit tool prospect with big tools. Unlike a lot of other prospects of this ilk, Brewer has a pretty good idea of the strike zone, he just swings through a ton of in-zone pitches, and has an especially tough time getting on top of high fastballs. He's begun to play some first base (and has actually taken to it pretty quickly) and much more right field than center, as his instincts in center are middling. The strikeout issues and fringe center field ability are enough of an issue to slide Brewer's FV into more of a late-bloomer tier rather than anticipate that he's a big league role player.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There's an injury update at the end of this blurb, which is otherwise unchanged because of said injuries: Brewer was draft eligible in 2018 at Lincoln Trail JC in Illinois and went unselected, but emerged in his season at Michigan due to his huge tools: solid average raw power, plus-plus speed, plus arm strength and good instincts on the bases. In the 2019 draft, Brewer was an outfielder for the College World Series finalist and arguably had the best raw tools in the draft. But he lasted until the back of the third round due to his rawness at the plate, underlined by his 56 strikeouts to 24 walks. At the plate, Brewer's pitch selection is below average and his swing can get long, so the prototypical profile of the below average contact platoon center fielder, like a Jake Marisnick, is the reasonable upside since Brewer is already 23, going on 24, and has barely played during the last two years because of a toe injury, the pandemic, and a knee surgery. (Injury rehab)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Michigan recruited Brewer as a wide receiver until he dislocated his shoulder as a high school senior, which led to him playing two years of baseball at Lincoln Trail (Ill.) CC before joining the Wolverines on the diamond in 2019. He led Michigan to within a victory of a national championship, won Big Ten Conference player of the year honors and went in the third round of the Draft. He played just 81 games in his first three years as a pro because of a toe injury he sustained in college and recovery from left knee surgery that also would have cost him the 2020 season had it been played. One of the best all-around athletes in the system, Brewer has the potential for at least solid tools across the board but needs more at-bats against quality competition to refine his offensive game. His bat speed and strength give him plus raw power, but he doesn't have the smoothest right-handed stroke and will have to make better swing decisions. He does show a willingness to take walks and knows how to make the most of his well above-average speed on the bases. Though he definitely has the speed for center field, Brewer's defense also requires more polish. His reads and routes can get better, though his quickness helps him recover. He has the solid arm strength for right field should he move to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brewer drew interest from Michigan as a wide receiver until he dislocated his shoulder as a high school senior, which led him to spend two years playing baseball at Lincoln Trail (Ill.) CC before joining the Wolverines on the diamond in 2019. The Big Ten Conference player of the year that spring, he led Michigan to a stunning runner-up finish at the College World Series and went in the third round of the Draft. A toe injury he sustained in college limited his pro debut to 16 games, and surgery on his left knee last spring prevented him from attending instructional league. The fastest player and one of the best all-around athletes among Astros prospects, Brewer could have solid tools across the board if he can add some polish at the plate. His quick right-handed swing and strength create plus raw power, but his less-than-smooth stroke and aggressive approach lead to swing-and-miss concerns. He was less refined than a typical player coming out of college and injuries severely restricted his development opportunities in his first year and a half as a pro. Brewer's well above-average speed contributes to the possibility that he becomes a 25-25 player and gives him a chance to play in center field. He played mostly right field and first base for the Wolverines because of team needs, but could be an asset in center if he improves his reads and routes. A rare bats-right, throws-left player, he has the solid arm and the offensive upside to profile in right field as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Until he dislocated his shoulder as a high school senior, Brewer drew interest from Big Ten Conference football programs such as Michigan and Wisconsin. He focused on baseball for two years at Lincoln Trail (Ill.) CC before transferring to Michigan in 2019, when he led the Wolverines to a shocking runner-up finish at the College World Series and was named Big Ten player of the year. A turf toe injury sustained during the spring limited him to 16 games in his pro debut after he signed for $500,000 as a third-rounder. Brewer has some of the best all-around ability in the system with the potential for at least solid tools across the board. He combines plus speed and plus raw power, giving him at least 20-20 upside. A right-handed hitter, he doesn't have the smoothest stroke and comes with some swing-and-miss concerns, but he also has quality bat speed and strength that produce hard contact to all fields. A center fielder in junior college, Brewer played mostly right field and first base at Michigan because of team needs. If he can refine his reads and routes, he has the quickness to be an asset in center. His solid arm and his offensive ability fit the right field profile.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Baylor's ability to rotate with ferocity took a leap sometime between his showcase summer and his senior spring. Teams were not in agreement about where he fit defensively, and some bailed on him entirely early in the process because he didn't look great with the bat during his pre-draft summer, perhaps due to a lingering arm injury. He went bonkers as a senior, not just clubbing bad pitching but looking more explosive to the eye. He was the sort of prospect for whom short season ball is the right developmental temperature, and he didn't get that in 2020 or '21. He still looked sushi raw as of 2020 instructs and struck out 30% of the time on the complex in '21, but Baylor has also shown rare power for a potential middle infielder and was given a new swing this year, with which he hit .303/.436/.584. The strikeouts, an unsustainably high BABIP, and Baylor's groundball rate (51%) all indicate that some amount of regression is coming, and he's a level behind Logan Simmons, who is the same age and also has hit-tool-related flags.

fangraphs.text: Has quietly popped-up in Virginia and is drawing comparisons to Tim Anderson; loud bat speed, but opinions vary pretty widely about where he should have been selected.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Phillies took Baylor in the third round of the 2019 Draft, signing him for a touch over-slot bonus of $675,000, they knew the Virginia high school product would need a lot of reps to sharpen his very raw tools. Those have been a bit hard to come by as he played in just four games in the Gulf Coast League after signing because of a hamstring injury and the 2020 season was wiped out. He did show signs of life in 25 Florida Complex League games in 2021, earning a late promotion to full-season ball, but wasn’t able to build on it much when he got hit in the thumb at instructs last fall. Baylor has a ton of athleticism at his disposal on both sides of the ball. His bat is a work in progress, but he’s made strides forward with his loose right-handed swing and his overall approach, though there are a lot of swing-and-miss and approach issues he needs to keep working on. He does have excellent bat speed and he started to show some ability to tap into his raw power in 2021. A shortstop when drafted, Baylor played on both sides of second base a year ago and his overall defensive play has improved. His arm and plus speed could work from shortstop, but some think he’d be best suited for second if he were to settle in at one position. It’s still too early to know exactly what Baylor could become, with a full year of games likely to help inform that evaluation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baylor had transferred to Benedictine College Prep, a military school in Virginia, a couple of years before the 2019 Draft. He could have been eligible in 2018 as one of the youngest players in the class, but he repeated 11th grade when he got to the school, which helped some of his raw tools come into focus. He moved up Draft boards firmly into Day 2 talk and went in the third round of the ’19 Draft, but hasn’t been able to play much since, with a hamstring injury forcing him out after just four Gulf Coast League games in 2019 and the pandemic wiping out the 2020 season. The missed reps hurt particularly for a player like Baylor, who is brimming with athleticism and raw tools, but still lacks refinement. When he has been on the field at all, he has shown a knack for making contact, with an ability to spoil pitches well. His right-handed swing is loose and athletic, with good bat speed, and there’s a chance he could have good power in the future, especially as he improves his overall approach, something he made strides with this past offseason. A plus runner who should be a basestealing threat, Baylor uses that speed and athleticism well on the defensive end of things. He moves well at shortstop and has an above-average arm that used to fire 92-mph fastballs from the mound in high school. Not everyone is convinced he can stick at short, with second base or perhaps the outfield an eventual home, but more than anything, he just needs to get out and play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Baylor was a bit of a pop-up Draft prospect in 2019, one who had previously teased with raw tools, but he started to put them to more consistent use during his senior season at Benedictine College Prep, a military school in Virginia. The Phillies took him at the start of Day 2 of the Draft, signing him for $675,000 in the third round last June. He only played in four Gulf Coast League games in his debut summer because of a hamstring injury, so he’ll be starting his pro career in earnest in 2020. The infielder has shown the ability to use all five tools on the field, though he has a ways to go in terms of doing that consistently. There was concern when Baylor was on the summer showcase circuit before his senior year about his ability to impact quality pitching, but he answered many of those questions during his senior year and there is hope his right-handed swing will generate solid power in the future. He’s loose and athletic at the plate and he shows good bat speed, though he’ll need to refine his approach as starts facing professional pitching for real. Baylor can really run and has the chance to be a threat on the bases. That speed helps him defensively as well, giving him the chance to stick at shortstop, especially given his strong arm. Second base could be an eventual home and he’s more than athletic enough to play the outfield, but for now, he just needs to start getting reps so he can develop.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Lorenzo got just south of $2 million on the IFA market a couple of years ago and was the youngest Astros prospect in their entire 2020 Instructional League group. He's already become very physical, so much so that there's early concern he won't be able to stay at shortstop. Second base was already squarely in the picture here, as Lorenzo's arm isn't a slam dunk for the left side of the infield. He is repeating the complex level in 2022 and isn't performing on paper so far, but the sample is small and Lorenzo still has impressive physicality for a middle infielder, and there aren't huge hit tool red flags here like there are with other early-career international busts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic for $1.8 million last July, Lorenzo received the largest bonus the Astros have given an international amateur position player since they paid since-traded Gilberto Celestino $2.25 million in 2015. Though he had one of the more advanced bats among middle infielders in the 2019 international crop, he'll likely make his debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League in 2020 and come to the United States at age 18 the next summer. A switch-hitter, Lorenzo has a compact swing from both sides that is built for hitting line drives to all fields. While he's a hit-over-power guy, his bat speed and feel for the barrel could produce 12-15 homers per season once he matures physically. He manages the strike zone better than most youngsters. Lorenzo will flash plus speed on occasion but is more of a solid runner who could slow down as he fills out. Scouts aren't completely sold that he'll stay at shortstop, though his instincts and strong, accurate arm give him a good chance. He's capable of playing second and third base, and his bat could profile at both spots if he develops more power.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Beard remains a long-term project as a hitter, and his crude feel to hit may ultimately prevent him from reaching the big leagues. But he can really fly and that could eventually translate to impact center field defense, which might make him rosterable on its own. His swing is athletic and Beard takes a pretty good rip; he's not a featherweight. He has a propensity to swing over the top of breaking balls, though, and he might eventually do well to become more of a slasher than he's currently trying to be, but it's too early for that. He was sent back to Low-A to start 2022 and needs to show progression from a bat-to-ball standpoint to stay on here.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Beard's report is very similar to last year's but I've upped his FV because while he's as raw as many of the hitters in the 35+ FV tier, the probability that he remains at an up-the-middle defensive position should create some separation between him and the others. At the same time, this is the sort of player who the year away from seeing pro pitching probably hurts the most, and the kind of player who a shorter draft and a more limited number of minor league roster spots will also hurt. As a hitter, Beard is more like a five o'clock shadow, one of the least-experienced bats to appear on a team's list this year. But of all the young hitters in this org, he has the greatest chance of staying up the middle because his speed almost guarantees he'll stay in center field forever. He's a half-decade dev project with the speed to be a leadoff pest. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a high school outfielder from Mississippi who was the fastest player in the 2019 Draft, Beard inevitably drew comparisons to Billy Hamilton. He had almost no history facing quality pitching, so scouts weren't sure what to make of his bat, but his speed and athleticism landed him in the fourth round with a below-slot $350,000 bonus. His first taste of pro ball was a challenge, as he struck out in 39 percent of his plate appearances in Rookie ball. On the showcase circuit during the summer of 2018, Beard ran a 6.21-second 60-yard dash at a Prospect Development Pipeline event and created havoc on the bases at the East Coast Pro Showcase. He's so fast that he can beat out routine grounders, and once he improves his jumps, he could become a dynamic basestealer. If he gets more aggressive, he could become a plus defender in center, where his fringy arm is playable. Beard needs to gain a better understanding of his right-handed swing, improve his pitch recognition and plate discipline and figure out how pitchers are attacking him. Though he mostly hit soft grounders when he made contact in his debut, he has the bat speed, strong hands and ability to backspin the ball to be more than just a slap hitter. Though he'll require plenty of development time, he has the upside of an average hitter with double-digit homers and league-leading stolen base totals.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: When Holland was drafted, his stance was wide and squat, taking up most of the batters box, and he barely lifted his foot as he swung. In his 2019 rookie ball season, he narrowed his stance and toyed with altered timing mechanisms, but the tinkering was to the detriment of his offensive output. In 2021, he was standing almost completely upright in the box with a pronounced leg kick, resulting in what looks like a more comfortable, better-timed swing, more consistent bat speed, and an improved slash line. He’s unafraid to swing early in a count – three of his 10 home runs came on the first pitch of the at-bat, and another three came on 1-0 counts – but he could afford to be more patient in his approach to tamp down an increasing strikeout rate. He tapped into much more gap power in 2021, notching nearly eight times the number of doubles he hit in his pro debut in just over twice the number of games. In the field, he spent most of his time at short, with stints at second, third, and in center field, and while it’s possible he can stick at short, it’s still not clear where his defensive home ultimately lies. We like Holland's athleticism and defensive versatility, and think he has a little extra roster utility due to his speed. We think that his feel for his swing will get dialed in enough for him to be a versatile, low-impact bench piece.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Holland was a toolsy college player who struggled to perform amid constant tinkering with his swing. One scout called him a "bull in a china shop" defensively because while he has the physical ability to play all three up-the-middle positions, he lacks feel and instincts. While it sounds like some of those defensive issues still exist, Holland's swing situation is a little more stable now and he had an encouraging instructs with the bat. He'll need to go out and perform next year but he has a chance to break out, though the Twins will still need to find him a defensive home. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Holland is the classic toolsy college player who hasn't even put things together yet and performed. One scout called him a "bull in a china shop" defensively because while he has the physical ability to play all three up-the-middle positions, he lacks feel and instincts. Holland had lots of trouble hitting during his draft spring due in large part to tinkering with his mechanics, but he was a fringe first rounder before that, so he was a nice buy-low lottery ticket in the fifth round.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Holland is a 70 runner with 50 raw power that can passably play all three positions up the middle but his swing mechanics and skills can't match his tools.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 The 2019 Draft class was deep in terms of college shortstops and the spring began with Holland looking like he could be one of the first ones taken, especially after a very strong Cape Cod League showing the summer prior. But the Auburn product struggled during his junior year, allowing him to slide to the fifth round, where the Twins were able to sign him for $575,000. He continued to scuffle with the bat during his pro debut in the rookie-level Appalachian League. Holland is an impressive athlete with speed and plenty of raw power. His biggest problem is that he hasn’t incorporated his athleticism into his swing. He seemed uncomfortable and unnatural at the plate during his pro debut using a setup some felt was too spread out. He spent the offseason hitting with fellow Twins prospect Brent Rooker in the hopes of finding some rhythm and timing from the right side of the plate. Getting the bat going would allow Holland to become an intriguing all-around player. He plays good defense at short, with a strong arm and his plus speed helping him with enough range. He continued to work on his swing at the Twins’ minicamp and if he can take that into his first full season of pro ball, he could shoot up this list.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Watson has the kinds of tools that would be the envy of many a Top 100 prospect despite a smallish frame, but a miserable approach and ugly swing continue to be his undoing. Watson’s plus raw power and 70-grade speed give him 30/30 potential, as evidenced by his 21 home runs and 24 stolen bases in just 105 minor league games in 2021. He covers tremendous ground in center field, but his arm, while not a liability, is a bit on the fringy side. At the plate, Watson swings at far too many pitches, while his multi-part, disconnected stroke creates additional swing-and-miss issues. He’s an extreme chaser who rarely sees good counts, and his weaknesses will likely be exploited even further by advanced pitchers who are more comfortable attacking out of the zone. Watson’s tools alone make him a slam dunk fourth outfielder, but without some kind of dramatic, unexpected change in his swing decisions, that’s also going to be his ceiling.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: With geyser-like regularity, LSU churns out high-effort, tweener bench outfield prospects like Watson, who hit .311/.373/.484 while in college. He's another of the many 23-year-old 2019 college draftees who has yet to have an upper-level opportunity due to the 2020 layoff. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: With geyser-like regularity, LSU churns out high-effort, tweener fourth outfield prospects like Watson, who hit .311/.373/.484 while in college.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Like most LSU outfield products, Watson profiles as a bench outfielder with speed and arm strength. He's a high-effort tweener.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Watson burst onto the scene in June of his freshman season at Louisiana State, when he homered five times in 12 games to lead the Tigers to the College World Series final. Impressively consistent production defined his next two years in Baton Rouge, and after signability concerns dropped him to the Red Sox in the 40th round as a Draft-eligible sophomore, the Orioles grabbed Watson in the third round for slot value the following June. Watson wasn’t able to duplicate his career .311/.373/.484 collegiate slash line in his first taste of pro ball, hitting just .224/.295/.431 across 36 games between Class A Short Season Aberdeen and Class A Delmarva. A broken finger forced him to miss the Shorebirds’ playoff run. Watson flies. His toolset is anchored by his well above-average speed, which many consider plus-plus. His legs and instincts allow Watson to run down balls in the gaps and make him a threat on the bases, though he can get overaggressive there at times. While a fringy to average thrower, he possesses enough arm strength to stick in center field and potentially be an impact defender. It’s Watson’s offensive game that lends itself to fewer consensuses. An aggressive hitter with sneaky power who likes to attack early in counts, his approach initially translated to hard contact but few results in pro ball, and he had trouble making contact at both levels in 2019. Some believe that was due to an unorthodox swing that puts Watson in a deep hitting position, which he may benefit from refining as he develops. He may need to clean up some plate discipline issues to reach the Majors, where he has an everyday center fielder ceiling and a very good fourth outfielder floor.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: De La Cruz has plus raw power, incredible for a player his age. Poor pitch recognition and a relatively grooved swing drive an awful lot of swing-and-miss, too much to support a right field profile. The hit rate for prospects like this tends to be pretty low, but there's a meaningful plus tool here, and De La Cruz is still very young, so he lines up a tier ahead of the Others of Note.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: De La Cruz has a right field prospect toolkit straight out of central casting -- plus raw power, plus arm, average underway speed, some contact issues at present -- and a year of 2019 DSL statistical performance arguably derived from his burly physical maturity. De La Cruz's 2019 Trackman data is very strong (it's still on The Board), especially for his age, but the look he had at 2020 instructs was one scouts are skeptical of given just how big he is for his age and where his lack of athleticism will likely push him on the defensive spectrum. He has the power to clear the corner outfield bar but will need to perform from a contact perspective to start to satisfy the industry. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: De la Cruz has a right field prospect toolkit straight out of central casting -- plus raw power, plus arm, average underway speed, contact issues at present -- and a year of DSL statistical performance arguably derived from his physical maturity. His Trackman data is very strong, especially for his age. He could be a middle of the order power bat, but he's years away.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Risky, upside traditional RF profile with plus raw power, plus arm, average underway speed, contact issues at present, signed for $1.8 million.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De La Cruz was the 19th-ranked international prospect in the 2018 class, according to MLB Pipeline, before the Tigers signed him for a $1.8 million bonus. His much-anticipated debut in the States was delayed a year by the pandemic and arguably led to him being rushed to Low-A Lakeland, where his .127 average and 74 strikeouts over 158 plate appearances promoted a midseason second-guessing. He had a much more respectable second half one level down in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League. As an athlete, De La Cruz is a physical specimen who keeps getting stronger; he already boasts some of the best raw power in the organization. As a hitter, he’s still unrefined with a violent, uppercut swing. He has enough power to go to all fields. He has shown improvement in his plate discipline but struggles against offspeed pitches. He runs well for his body but isn’t an instinctive base stealer. He has the strong arm to play a corner outfield spot but needs time to hone his accuracy. Considering De La Cruz’s age, he has plenty of time to learn the skills necessary to take advantage of his raw skills, but the Tigers have to avoid the temptation to push the timetable with him. His second chance at the Florida State League hasn’t quite proven that much better than the first, and the 20-year-old is in danger of never meeting his ceiling of a power-first Major League bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Before the Tigers spent just shy of $3 million each to sign Roberto Campos and Cristian Santana, they gave De La Cruz – then the 19th-ranked international prospect by MLB Pipeline – a $1.8 million bonus out of the Dominican Republic. He made a strong first impression in 2019 in the Dominican Summer League, batting .307 with 11 home runs, 16 stolen bases and a .931 OPS in 225 at-bats. He was on track to compete in the Gulf Coast League when the pandemic scuttled the Minor League season. De La Cruz continues to fill out his athletic frame, reporting to instructional ball last fall with more muscle following the shutdown. He has all-fields power with an aggressive approach at the plate, possibly too aggressive given his 75 strikeouts in the DSL. The Tigers believe his approach will mature, allowing him to maintain average while adding power. He played center field in the DSL but will likely shift to a corner as he continues to fill out. Though the recent Campos and Santana signings have overshadowed De La Cruz, the Tigers see similar upside with a stronger body than expected out of a teenager. He opened 2021 at Low-A Lakeland but bounced down to the Florida Complex League in late June to find his offensive stroke.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers’ shift toward bigger-ticket international signings began in 2018, when they signed De La Cruz – ranked 19th by MLB Pipeline in his international class -- out of the Dominican Republic for a $1.8 million bonus, a then-record for the team under the current system. His stint in the Dominican Summer League didn’t disappoint, including 11 home runs, 16 stolen bases, a .307 average and a .931 OPS in 225 at-bats. The physical tools with De La Cruz are evident, from all-fields power in batting practice to a strong outfield arm to surprising speed. His body has filled out well for his age while still providing room to add muscle. He has good instincts for the game, though his 75 strikeouts in the DSL created some concern about his aggressiveness at the plate. Though De La Cruz played center field in the DSL, he’s expected to eventually shift to a corner spot, where his arm could play. He’ll head to the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League in 2020.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Kelly had a rough 2021. His velo fell from the mid-90s to the low-90s and after an aggressive promotion to Double-A, the righty walked more than a batter per inning in Amarillo. As you'd expect based on the numbers, he has buckshot command, with no feel for consistent fastball location and secondary pitches as likely to sail in above the letters as below the knees. It all stems from a violent delivery that features an aggressive drive to the plate that leaves him off balance and a big head whack as he falls toward first. He remains on our list because his stuff still looks quite good. His splitter comes in with nasty late dip and his slider has the same late tumble when he locates it well. His lack of success generating whiffs with those offerings (among Amarillo hurlers with at least 10 innings, he had the lowest SwSTR% on the club) is perplexing, particularly for a pitcher with a decent track record of success before 2022. We're not entirely out on him, but the arrow is trending down here and he needs to throw a lot more strikes to turn things around.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Kelly has a grip-it-and-rip-it style of pitching that fits best in the bullpen, so even though he has a four-pitch mix (headlined by a bastard slider with vertical bite, à la Brad Lidge), I have him projected in a multi-inning relief role. He was up to 96 at the alt site but sat more 90-94 (the same as in 2019, and basically the same since high school) with scattershot control of his fastball, another reason I have him projected in the bullpen. Sometimes that slider comes out of Kelly's hand high and arcs into the strike zone like a curveball; hitters still can't touch it. Sometimes it backs up on Kelly and has changeup movement; it doesn't matter. When executed, it's a big league out pitch right now. If Kelly's going to start he either needs to refine his fastball command or mix his stuff more evenly while developing more consistent feel for locating his splitter. His heater isn't hard enough to live in the zone, and he'll be punished for his mistakes. (Alternate site, Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text:
Even though we saw him up to 96, we were not big fans of Kelly while he was in high school because he had a softer, maxed out frame and a stiff, violent delivery we believed would limit him to a relief role if his arm didn't fall off first. Now, he has arguably the best physique in this system at a svelte 205, and was so dominant during minor league spring training that the org was compelled to send him to full season ball even though he was initially slated to hang back in Extended until short season leagues began after the draft. And Kelly delivered, striking out 126 hitters in 100 Low-A innings. 
Often, a pitcher who remakes their physique will be rewarded with a jump in velocity. This is not the case with Kelly, who we still have averaging about 92 with his heater. What Kelly does have, is one of the better sliders in the minors, with a shape and bite similar to Brad Lidge's diving bastard of a slider. Sometimes it comes out of Kelly's hand high and arcs into the strike zone like a curveball; hitters still can't touch it. Sometimes it backs up on Kelly and has changeup movement; doesn't matter. When executed, it's a big league out pitch right now. Kelly needs to refine his fastball command because it isn't hard enough to live in the zone, and needs to live at the top of it. We think he'll have to nibble with the heater and end up working too inefficiently to start, but we think he'll be an excellent, multi-inning reliever.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Physical righty was famous in high school, but maxed out frame with some effort, flashed 55 to 60 raw stuff at times with below average command; has dialed that in considerably in pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly moved from West Virginia to IMG Academy in Florida after his sophomore year of high school and quickly endeared himself to scouts, showing premium arm strength and performing well against top competition. The D-backs took him in the eighth round of the 2018 Draft, then went $350,000 above slot value to sign him away from a Louisiana State commitment. Kelly made his full-season debut with Class A Kane County and responded to the challenge by posting a 2.15 ERA and a .199 average against, striking out 126 in 100 1/3 innings. Kelly was challenged with a bump up to Double-A in 2021, and after starting the year on the injured list, he struggled to find a rhythm in Amarillo. With his prototypical pitcher’s body and a pair of plus offerings, Kelly looks the part of a future big leaguer. In his first year in the system, he pitched with a low- to mid-90s fastball that hitters struggled to square up due to its angle and late life. His velocity dipped early in 2021, but after making some mechanical adjustments, it came back and even started to tick up to the mid-90s in the second half of the season. His two-plane slider is a legitimate swing-and-miss offering that registers in the low to mid-80s with hard bite and plays well off his fastball. The organization sees potentially three dominant pitches and Kelly has shown a willingness to mix in his split more, key to his possible future as a starting pitcher. Consistency was an issue for Kelly in 2021 as he struggled to throw strikes. The D-backs rave about his work ethic and he’s shown flashes of returning to form. After starting his career in the rotation, Kelly was shifted to the bullpen in 2021. The D-backs aren’t ruling out him developing into a starter, but at the moment, it looks as though Kelly’s future will come in a relief role, where he could play up his fastball/slider combination.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kelly moved from West Virginia to IMG Academy in Florida after his sophomore year of high school and quickly endeared himself to scouts, showing premium arm strength and performing well against top competition. The D-backs took him in the eighth round of the 2018 Draft, then went $350,000 above slot value to sign him away from a Louisiana State commitment. Arizona seldom assigns high school pitchers right to Class A, but Kelly debuted with Kane County and responded to the challenge by posting a 2.15 ERA and .189 opponents’ average, striking out 126 in 100 1/3 innings. Kelly was challenged with a bump up to Double-A in 2021 and after starting the year on the injured list, he struggled to find a rhythm in Amarillo. With his prototypical pitcher’s body and a pair of plus offerings, Kelly already looks the part of a future big leaguer. In his first year in the system, he pitched with a low- to mid-90s fastball that hitters struggled to square up due to its angle and late life. His velocity dipped early in 2021, but after making some mechanical adjustments, it started to come back in the second half of the season. His two-plane slider backed up a bit this season, but at its best, it is a legitimate swing-and-miss offering, registering in the low- to mid-80s with hard bite, and he knows how to use it in concert with his heater. The organization sees potentially three dominant pitches and Kelly has shown a willingness to mix in his split more which is a key if he wants to be a starting pitcher. Kelly made a big impression on the big league staff at the alternate training site in 2020, but consistency has been an issue in 2021. The D-backs rave about his work ethic and he’s shown signs of getting back to who he was in 2019 and ‘20. There are questions as to whether he’ll ultimately wind up in a rotation or a bullpen and his ability to consistently harness his stuff will go a long way toward answering those.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Kelly moved from West Virginia to IMG Academy in Florida after his sophomore year of high school and quickly endeared himself to scouts, showing premium arm strength and performing well against top competition. The D-backs took him in the eighth round of the 2018 Draft, then went $350,000 above slot value to sign him away from a Louisiana State commitment. He was deemed advanced enough to jump straight to Class A Kane County for his first full season -- an assignment Arizona seldom gives to its high school pitchers -- and responded to the challenge by posting a 2.15 ERA and .189 opponents’ average, striking out 126 in 100 1/3 innings. With his prototypical pitcher’s body and a pair of plus offerings, Kelly already looks the part of a future big leaguer. He pitches in and out with a low- to mid-90s fastball that hitters struggle to square up due to its angle and late life. His two-plane slider is a legitimate swing-and-miss offering, registering in the low- to mid-80s with hard bite, and he knows how to use it in concert with his heater. Kelly’s tendency to fall in love with the pitch makes his sequencing too predictable at times, which is why club officials view the right-hander’s changeup development as a key for him to take the next step. While it is currently a distant third pitch, Kelly throws it with splitter-like action that plays nicely off of his fastball. Kelly's max-effort delivery raises questions about his control and command profile and has led some evaluators to peg him as a future bullpen piece. But the big right-hander has already simplified his mechanics and thrown more strikes than expected in pro ball, and the D-backs are quick to praise his determination and work ethic, qualities that could go a long way in helping him remain a starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals took a chance on Haake in the sixth round of the 2018 Draft after the right-hander’s up-and-down college career, which included three different colleges in as many years. Haake responded by being one of biggest surprises of the class when he posted a 2.85 ERA over 18 starts in Class A in 2019. His only 2020 action came during the Royals’ fall instructional program at Kauffman Stadium. Haake dominates with a plus fastball that sits in the mid-90s. It’s a deceptive pitch thanks to his 6-foot-4 frame and features a ton of movement. His changeup plays well off that deception, and the pitch comes in with splitter action. The fastball-changeup combo helps Haake get whiffs from hitters on both sides of the plate and he rounds out his arsenal with an average slider that can flash plus. Haake sometimes struggles with repeating his delivery, and that has led to control issues that he needs to shore up to be successful. Haake missed two months with shoulder issues in 2019 and missed another six weeks with an injury for High-A Quad Cities during the 2021 season. The Royals had hopes he could have made Double-A at least by now, so it’s an open question how much Haake’s health will further hold him back in 2022 and beyond. The stuff, which Kansas City is not concerned about, could work in a relief setting, especially if he squeezes out even more velocity in short spurts. That might be the best role for the right-hander to get him going for good.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Haake pitched for three different colleges in as many years. He put up underwhelming numbers as an Arkansas State freshman in 2016 and again at Kentucky two years later, with an impressive season at John A. Logan Junior College sandwiched between. The Royals took a chance on his power repertoire in the sixth round in 2018, and Haake has responded by being one of the biggest surprises of the class, though some minor shoulder soreness did shelve him for a time during an otherwise impressive first full season at Class A Lexington. The 6-foot-4 right-hander can dominate with a plus fastball that sits comfortably in the mid 90s and routinely touches 97 mph with late life. An above-average changeup that plays nicely off his fastball and with splitter action is Haake’s go-to secondary pitch, and together they help him pile up whiffs against hitters on both sides of the plate. He posted the best swinging-strike rate (16.1 percent) and second-highest strikeout rate (28.6) among Royals farmhands (70 IP min.) in 2019. Club officials are intrigued by Haake’s breaking ball, which can occasionally flash plus, though they haven’t yet pushed it in his development. Haake seemed ticketed for a bullpen role when he began his career, and his shoulder injury in early 2019 did little to change that belief. But the right-hander’s improved command of his fastball-changeup combo that he showed once healthy last year has left club officials increasingly optimistic about Haake’s chance to be starter, especially with his size and remaining projection. If that doesn’t work out, the Royals have zero doubt that Haake has the stuff and natural bat-missing ability needed to be a bullpen force at the highest level.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Haake’s size, along with the nasty stuff he threw when he was at Kentucky, have long inspired intrigue. On the other hand, his inability to hold that stuff into games, combined with a bumpy injury track record, has been less inspiring. Indeed, Haake currently finds himself on the IL with an undisclosed injury (he’s missed time in the past for a flexor strain and shoulder soreness) and before being shut down in late-April, his strikeout rate had taken a significant tumble in 2022. But while these factors have led to an overall cooling on Haake, and the assumption that his potential as a starter has disappeared, some in the scouting community have expressed an interest in his underlying metrics, and he may well have been selected in last year’s Rule 5 Draft, to which the org left him vulnerable, had it not been cancelled.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Haake was in our 2018 draft top 50 coming out of the fall before his junior year because he was working with absolutely nasty stuff while at Kentucky. The next spring, he had trouble holding that stuff deep into starts, creating doubt that he could start at all. A flexor strain (2018) and shoulder soreness ('19) add to that risk, and Haake has fallen behind the college pitchers in his draft class from an assignment perspective. With mid-90s heat and occasionally good breaking stuff, I think he'll be an up/down relief fit eventually. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Be careful with this one. Haake was in our 2018 Draft top 50 coming out of the fall before his junior year because he was working with absolutely nasty stuff while at Kentucky. The next spring, he had trouble holding that stuff deep into starts, creating doubt that he could start at all. A flexor strain (2018) and shoulder soreness (2019) add to that risk. But Haake does indeed have nasty stuff, up to 98 with the fastball and a slider that has plus movement but is rarely well-located. There's late-inning relief potential here, but that was true when Haake was in college and he still fell to the sixth round.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Castaneda pitched in relief during the 2019 regular season and was stretched out as a four-to-five inning starter during the 2019 Fall League, where he retained his velocity and continued to have success. He was again deployed as a starter in 2021 but struggled with walks and the Brewers chose not to add him to their 40-man after the season. His forkball (he has a split and a straight change) is an obvious out pitch and looks incredible on the high speed camera because it comes out of his hand with virtually no spin. Castaneda's get-me-over curveball only works situationally (often to garner strike one) because it's easy to identify out of his hand. He lacks the arm strength of a typical reliever but the repertoire depth and plus secondary pitch make him a likely bulk relief depth option.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Castaneda pitched in relief during the 2019 regular season and was stretched out as a four-to-five inning starter during the 2019 Fall League, where he retained his velocity and continued to have success. His forkball (he has a split and a straight change) is an obvious out pitch and looks incredible on the high speed camera because it comes out of his hand with virtually no spin. Castaneda's get-me-over curveball only works situationally (often to garner strike one) because it's easy to identify out of his hand. As such, I think Castaneda profiles as a reliever long-term. But there are scouts who think he can continue to start, and he has the repertoire depth to work multiple innings if he ends up in the bullpen. I think he'll be good enough to avoid being on the shuttle to and from Triple-A.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Castaneda pitched in relief during the summer and was stretched out as a four-to-five inning starter during the Fall League, where he continued to have success. His forkball is an obvious out pitch and he held his average velo in the longer Fall League outings, but the get-me-over curveball only works situationally (often to garner strike one) because it's easy to identify out of his hand. As such, I think Castaneda profiles as a reliever, long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed as an 18-year-old out of the Mexican League in July 2017, Castaneda didn’t get his first starting experience until the 2019 Arizona Fall League. He held his own as an inexperienced hurler in that prospect finishing school (1.99 ERA, 0.84 WHIP, 29 strikeouts in 22 2/3 innings) and locked in the transition last year. Castaneda struck out 27.7 percent of the batters he faced for High-A Wisconsin, but he proved to be homer-prone, leading to a 5.20 ERA and a 5.07 FIP in 97 innings. Even after a late-season cameo at Triple-A Nashville, he was left off the 40-man roster last November when eligible for the Rule 5 Draft, and he was left off once again this November after another stint in the upper Minors. Castaneda doesn’t tower over batters at just 6-foot-1, but he can show decent velocity with a fastball at 92-94 mph. The heater can also feature decent arm-side run, and that can be a problem for his fellow righties. The splitter is far and away Castaneda’s standout pitch because of the way it divebombs below hitters’ hands with very little spin. He also sports a more traditional changeup, but it’s the split that shows the most promise. A below-average curveball is thrown for little more than show. The Mexico native is coming off his age-23 season, so he has some road ahead of him. He’s a likely two-pitch hurler at the top level, and that would point back to the bullpen. Castaneda might need to add more velocity to be effective there, or else hope the splitter on its own is good enough.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Servideo was a model darling coming out of the University of Mississippi because of his phenomenal on-base skills, and scouts liked him as a legitimate defender in the dirt who could really run. His first 20 pro games produced a bizarro batting line of .246/.489/.312 at Low-A Delmarva before his season was cut short by surgery to repair a sports hernia. Servideo had a walk rate over 20% over his last two college seasons, and that spiked to more than 30% during his brief pro debut. Obviously, he has plate discipline to spare, but he also seems to stand passively in the box looking for a walk at times. Those scenarios lead to pitcher’s counts, and there are questions about what Servideo can do when forced to swing a bat, as his bat-to-ball skills are a bit questionable and his power is well below average. He can provide good defense at both second base and shortstop and will likely play both positions if he gets to the big leagues, where he future is that of a pesky utility player who works the count.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: A defensive nomad early in his career at Mississippi, Servideo moved back to shortstop in 2020 (Grae Kessinger was an early Houston pick in 2019) and added a leg kick that unlocked new power. He is twitchy, athletic, and extremely cocky. His stock had a chance to continue rising as his defensive abilities at short became more clear, and as his bat was stress-tested against SEC pitching, but Servideo never got that chance because of COVID. I think the mechanical changes are evidence that he's made substantive changes, that his 2020 in-game power improvements are real, and that Baltimore got in on the ground floor of a potential everyday player. He struggled to catch fastballs toward the top of the zone during 2020 instructs, and if that's a continuous issue, then Servideo projects as a utility type, and could move quickly since he already has experience at several positions. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020updated
fangraphs.text: A defensive nomad early in his career, Servideo moved back to shortstop (Grae Kessinger was early HOU pick in 2019) in 2020 and added a leg kick that unlocked new power. He is twichty, athletic, and extremely cocky. His stock had a chance to continue rising as his defensive abilities at SS became more clear, and as his bat was stress-tested against SE pitching, but Servideo never got that chance. I think the mechanical changes are evidence he's broken out and ascended. Of not he's still a good utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The maternal grandson of former Orioles outfielder and 1965 AL Rookie of the Year Curt Blefary, Servideo played sparingly as a Mississippi freshman in 2018, then spent most of 2019 shuttling between right field and center field for the Rebels before posting the worst batting line (.149/.228/.277) in the Cape Cod League. He looked like a different player as a junior, starting on Opening Day by singling, doubling and walking against Louisville left-hander Reid Detmers, the eventual No.10 overall pick. Servideo emerged as one of college baseball's better shortstops, slashing .390/.575/.695 in the shortened season. That showed the Orioles enough to take him in the third round and give him a slightly above-slot $950,000 bonus to sign. Servideo’s plus speed and selective approach allowed him to play a table-setting role in college, where he drew 24 walks in 17 games during his junior year and then routinely created havoc on the bases. He’ll need to add strength and cut down his left-handed swing to remain at the top of the order at the next level, where it’ll be necessary to make more consistent contact. He's not big and won't be a slugger, but he displayed more pop as a junior, homering five times after going deep just four times in 100 previous contests. While there are mixed opinions on how much impact Servideo will have at the plate, there are no questions about his ability to play shortstop. He’s a flashy defender, with smooth hands, quick feet and enough arm strength to profile at the position long-term. His athleticism and strong instincts up the middle should give him time to grow into more of an offensive threat. If he doesn't hit enough to be a regular, he'd be capable of playing anywhere in the infield and outfield as a utility man.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Cantrelle is an athletic, switch-hitting infielder with doubles power. He's not an especially deft hitter, he just swings with big effort from both sides of the plate and sprays hard contact to all fields when he finds himself able to make contact. Similarly, as an infielder Cantrelle isn't especially smooth but makes a lot of plays via sheer effort and athleticism. He played short at Lafayette and has played both middle infield spots as a pro, and he could eventually get reps in center field because of his speed. Even in a smaller conference it was clear Cantrelle was pretty allergic to breaking balls, and he'll likely never hit enough to play a huge role. But the fact that he switch-hits and has the speed and projected versatility he does provides other ways for him to impact a game in a reserve role.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
