Reks' 40-man timeline makes him a potential churn trade target for teams that, like San Francisco last year, are cycling through older, upper-level performers to see if any are for real.

fangraphs.label: 2022report
fangraphs.text: Curpa is a plus-plus runner who plays all over the field (mostly second base, but also short, third, and right field) and who has a long track record of reaching base at a well above-average clip. He's not going to slug and is likely a 45 bat, but Curpa's speed, defensive versatility, and control of the strike zone make him a likely 26th man utility type who can pinch run and play other situational roles.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Barrios will sign as a shortstop, but that does not mean he is going to stay there. Either way, the large-framed infielder has tons of potential on defense. He has shown solid defensive actions, quickness and is best described as a “good twitch” athlete. He could move to third base as he continues to grow and develop, but that’s to be determined. There’s plenty of room on his frame to add strength. He has a solid throwing arm so getting the ball across the diamond from the left side with some authority is not a problem. At the plate, Barrios has a compact swing with a good feel for consistent hard contact. The athletic teen already shows signs of being a plus runner. His work ethic, aptitude and overall makeup are noteworthy. Barrios trains with Carlos Yanez. The Brewers are the favorite to sign him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Guzman signed with the Royals for $1.5 million in the 2015-16 international signing period. While he didn’t hit much early in his career, he impressed defensively and the Royals added him to the 40-man roster in 2019, protecting him from the Rule 5 Draft. He was then non-tendered late in 2020, but re-signed with the Royals on a Minor League deal. His bat started to come around in 2021 as he reached Double-A for the first time. He also played for his native Dominican Republic in the Tokyo Olympics and was the starting shortstop in the bronze medal game victory. He elected free agency after the season and signed a Minor League contract with the D-backs in November. Guzman, who used to switch hit as a kid, just started doing so professionally in 2019. It’s still a work in progress, but he hit well at High-A (.289/.352/.465) prior to his promotion last season, showing signs that hitting from both sides of the plate may stick. He added strength and his .401 slugging percentage last season was a career high, but power still isn’t Guzman’s forte and it’s unlikely he’d hit double-digit homers at the highest level. The 23-year-old is certainly a glove-first shortstop and grades out as a plus defender at the premium position. What’s more, he added to his versatility last season, spending time at both second base and center field. With a plus arm and above-average speed, Guzman has the capabilities to play all over the diamond. It remains to be seen how much he’ll develop as a hitter, but his glove gives him a solid floor and the added versatility could help him reach the Majors as a utility option off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals didn’t hold back on the international market for the 2015-16 signing period, handing out a combined $3.75 million to two players: outfielder Seuly Matias and Guzman. The shortstop got $1.5 million to sign and has consistently impressed with his defense in the pro ranks. Though his offense initially struggled to keep up with his slick glove, he showed signs of improvement in 2018, reaching full-season ball for the first time. He made even greater strides back at Class A Lexington in 2019, leading the Legends to a South Atlantic League title. If you remove Guzman’s unproductive April from his final .253/.296/.373 batting line, he was a .273/.313/.404 hitter as a 20-year-old in his first full-season campaign. He’s begun to grow into his projectable frame and was a noticeably stronger player in 2019. The Royals have worked with him to calm down his extraneous movement in the box and give him a more solid base to hit, and the results have been positive so far. Club officials see Guzman’s power starting to come out and note that he drove the ball more consistently as the 2019 season unfolded. He’s also running better than he has in the past, adding speed and being more aggressive on the basepaths. Even if the bat doesn’t come to fruition, Guzman’s glove could carry him up the ladder. He’s capable of making spectacular plays at shortstop thanks to outstanding lateral range and arm strength that’s up there with best in the Royals’ system. His high error totals are a product his range, and club officials think he actually was better on making the types of routine plays he’s struggled with in the past. Whether Guzman will hit enough to be an everyday player remains to be seen, but the Royals are encouraged by the progress he made in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals didn't hold back on the international market for the 2015-16 signing period, handing out $3.75 million to two players, outfielder Seuly Matias and Guzman. The shortstop got $1.5 million to sign and has consistently impressed with his defense, and while his offense has struggled to keep up, he showed signs of improvement in 2018, reaching full-season ball for the first time. There's no question it's Guzman's glove that will carry him up the ladder. He's capable of making spectacular plays at shortstop with an arm that sometimes plays as plus. He has outstanding range, showing he can make the play up the middle or to his backhand side. The organization still believes in his bat from the left side of the plate and thinks he's starting to figure things out. He has had a tendency to get out of his swing, jumping around the box, so the Royals have worked with him to calm things down and give him a more solid base with positive effects. He's also running better than he has in the past, adding speed and being more aggressive on the basepaths. Guzman has the tools to play shortstop defensively without question. Whether he will hit enough to be an everyday player remains to be seen, but the Royals are encouraged by the step forward he made in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals exceeded their international bonus pool for the first time during the 2015-16 signing period, with outfielder Seuly Matias ($2.25 million) and Guzman ($1.5 million) receiving their two biggest bonuses. Part of the same Dominican youth league that spawned Nomar Mazara and Amed Rosario, he batted just .228/.301/.305 in his two years in Rookie ball. Kansas City still likes his potential on both sides of the ball and is encourage that he finished 2017 with his best month as a pro and a strong performance in instructional league. While he has yet to produce much at the plate, Guzman already recognizes pitches and controls the strike zone well for a teenager. A switch-hitter, he has bat speed but needs more strength in order to do some damage. Though he has a groundball-oriented swing, he should grow into some gap power. Though he's not flashy, Guzman has good hands and a solid arm that plays up with a quick release at shortstop. He doesn't have the speed or quickness typical of his position, but the Royals believe his smooth actions will allow him to remain there. They like his maturity and how he has handled adversity in his introduction to pro ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals have invested heavily in international shortstops this decade. They spent $2 million on Raul Adalberto Mondesi in 2011, $1.3 million on Marten Gasparini in '13, $850,000 on Ricky Aracena in '14 and $1.5 million on Guzman in '15. The other three players have louder tools than Guzman, but he might have the best instincts of the bunch. Guzman has a mature approach for a teenager, showing good pitch-recognition skills and patience. A switch-hitter who enjoyed more success from the left side of the plate in his 2016 pro debut, he makes consistent line-drive contact and should have some gap power once he fills out. Presently a fringy runner, Guzman could gain a step as he gets stronger, but he won't ever be a basestealer. Guzman is not a flashy shortstop, but he has good hands and gets the most out of his solid arm with a quick release. Some scouts outside the organization wonder if he's quick and rangy enough to stay at short, but the Royals like his actions and have no such concerns. They praise Guzman's maturity and how well he handled jumping to the United States for his debut.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: I'll speculate that the Royals and Guzmán came to some kind of mutual agreement regarding his roster status, since last winter Kansas City exposed him to free agency in order to clear a 40-man spot but re-signed him to a minor league deal only a week later. He didn't hit during sporadic big league spring training at-bats but has looked fantastic during minor league play this spring, especially on defense. The Royals added Guzmán to the 40-man after his age-20, 2019 season even though he was overmatched at A-ball that year. In the year and a half since then, he has become considerably more physical without really compromising his defensive ability, and he was still making rangy, acrobatic plays this spring. With the strength has come added power, enough that Guzmán is a real threat to do damage when he makes contact. An expansive approach and grooved pair of swings mean he'll likely max out with a 40-grade hit tool, but a plus-gloved infielder with mistake power is still a desirable role-player, and also describes a lot of low-end shortstop regulars. (Alternate site, LIDOM)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Now 21, Guzman has filled out and developed 45 raw power while maintaining excellent defense at shortstop. He has yet to play anywhere else, but because he falls short of profiling as a regular there on the offensive end, it's likely he starts to see time at other positions soon -- especially because he's now on the 40-man -- so he can be a versatile bench infield option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When he was selected in the third round of the 2017 Draft, Tabor was a skinny, baby-faced kid, but the D-backs saw pitchability and the potential for his stuff to tick up. They signed him for an above-slot $1 million. He overcame a shaky start at Class A Short Season Hillsboro in 2018 to finish the season on a high note, and that success carried over into his age-20 campaign at Class A Kane County, where the right-hander compiled a 2.93 ERA, 1.00 WHIP and 101/16 K/BB over 95 1/3 innings spanning 23 starts. Tabor pitched across three levels in 2021, working his way up to Triple-A in the process. His numbers dipped a bit, but the D-backs feel he pitched better than the numbers indicate since pitching in Reno is always tough on the stats. Tabor’s advanced ability and polish are particularly impressive considering his cold-weather background as a Massachusetts prep. A good athlete with a clean delivery, his fastball sits in the low 90s and he can get up to the mid-90s when he needs to. He’s had an advanced changeup since he was drafted and has improved his slider to the point where it can be his best secondary pitch. While he’s capable of missing some bats, Tabor is a command-over-stuff guy and has proved to be an accomplished strike-thrower early in his career. He can pitch to all four quadrants of the zone and features some of the best command in the Arizona system. The D-backs like what they’ve seen from Tabor and believe he has the tools to remain a starter at the highest level. He’s made big leaps over the past four seasons, so as long as Tabor continues on a similar trajectory -- refining his secondary pitches and continuing to gain experience -- it won’t be long until he’s pitching in the back end of a Major League rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Diamondbacks Top 30

The D-backs liked what they saw from Tabor in Instructional League and believe he has everything needed to eventually be a starter in the big leagues, especially with the recent uptick in stuff. Refining his secondary pitches and gaining experience are the keys now.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A growth spurt before his senior year led to a big uptick in stuff for Tabor, sending his Draft stock rising and scouts pouring into New England as the weather warmed. The D-backs took him in the third round, gave him an above-pick value $1 million bonus and then had him throw sparingly during his pro debut. He overcame a shaky start at Class A Short Season Hillsboro in 2018 to finish the season on a high note, and that success carried over into his age-20 campaign at Class A Kane County, with the right-hander compiling a 2.93 ERA, 1.00 WHIP and 101/16 K/BB over 95 1/3 innings and 23 starts. Tabor’s advanced pitchability and polish at a young age is particularly impressive considering his cold-weather background as a prep. A good athlete with a clean delivery, he sits in the low 90s and touches a bit higher with a fastball that could gain a few more ticks as he adds strength to his projectable frame. He lost some feel for what was a plus changeup in 2019 as he worked to improve his breaking ball, and most scouts now view Tabor’s slider as his better secondary pitch. He has proved to be an accomplished strike-thrower early in his career, averaging 1.6 walks-per-nine across his first three seasons, and showed more bat-missing ability in the Midwest League, posting a 26.8 percent strikeout rate with a 15 percent whiff rate. Refining his secondary pitches is a top priority in Tabor's development, and the D-backs believe his athleticism and clean arm action gives him a chance to do so. He shows more of a floor than a ceiling right now, though that could change with an uptick in velocity and better secondary stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A growth spurt before his senior year led to a big uptick in stuff for Tabor, sending his Draft stock rising and scouts pouring into New England as the weather warmed. The D-backs took him in the third round, gave him an above-pick value $1 million bonus and then had him throw sparingly during his pro debut. After getting off to a shaky start at Class A Short Season Hillsboro in 2018, Tabor finished with a 1.74 ERA over his final 33 frames and then continued to pitch well in is first taste of full-season ball at Class A Kane County in 2019. Tabor has impressed with his stuff, pitchability and polish, the latter being particularly impressive given his cold-weather background. Working from an athletic and repeatable delivery, he'll touch 94-95 mph and sit in the low 90s with his fastball, and there's reason to believe there's more in the tank as he fills out his projectable frame. His changeup flashes plus, with the potential to get there long-term, and he also has feel for a slider that can be too slurvy. He threw strikes 70 percent of the time in the Northwest League in 2018, issuing 1.9 walks-per-nine, and should have at least average command in the future. Tabor understands how to change eye levels and keep hitters off-balance using his fastball-changeup pairing. Developing a better breaking ball, whether it's a slider or true curveball, is a top priority in Tabor's development, and the D-backs believe his athleticism and clean arm action gives him a chance to do so.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A growth spurt before his senior year led to a big uptick in stuff for Tabor, sending his Draft stock rising and scouts pouring into New England as the weather warmed. He ended up landing in the third round, where the D-backs gave him an above-pick value $1 million bonus. He threw sparingly during his summer debut, but stood out as the most exciting high school Draft prospect from the D-backs' crop of high schoolers selected. While Tabor has a ways to go as a prep pitcher from the Northeast, the D-backs were pleasantly surprised how polished and mature he was on the mound. He shows three plus pitches at times from an athletic and repeatable delivery. His fastball will touch 95-96 mph and sit in the low 90s and there's reason to believe there's more in the tank as he fills out his frame. He's already tightened up his slurvy breaking ball some into a slider that should be a very good weapon for him and he has feel for a solid changeup. He's around the strike zone and should have at least average command in the future. Showing a good sense of what he needs to do on the mound to improve, Tabor was advanced in his ability to change tempos and deliveries to keep hitters off-balance. The D-backs love his business-like approach to honing his craft and think it will serve him well as he begins his pro career in earnest.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Tabor was once again parked in the 90-93 range during 2020 instructs, so while he's quite athletic and has a good frame, it seems the velocity explosion he experienced late in high school will be the only one he enjoys. Though his arm slot looks like it creates backspin on his heater, his fastball's spin axis is actually closer to the dreaded 1:30 mark, a no-man's land for creating movement, but his fastball also has a ton of spin and slightly above-average measured run and rise. I think it's a viable big league pitch but not an impact one. Instead, Tabor will need to lean on his secondary stuff (and command thereof) to miss big league bats. I've seen plus changeups and average breaking balls from Tabor. He'll need to hit the command grade I have projected for him, but he is tracking like a low-variance No. 4/5 starter. Several arms with greater relief risk (but better stuff) are behind him in this system and might pass him if they prove capable of starting. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: We love how athletic Tabor is and how quickly each of his secondaries became good considering his Northeastern prep school background, but while some of our sources are inclined to continue projecting on his velocity because his build is still young-looking, we think two straight years of 90-93 (Tabor's velo popped late in high school) makes it more likely the fastball settles here. He's athletic, his arm slot creates rise on his fastball and bat-missing, vertical action on his breaking stuff, and Tabor has good changeup. We have him projected as a No. 4/5 starter.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text:
Tabor’s velocity seems to have plateaued after it exploded as his wiry frame filled out later in high school. He’s sitting in the low-90s, with a breaking ball and changeup that each flash above average. He's athletic, his arm slot creates rise on his fastball and bat-missing, vertical action on his breaking stuff, and Tabor has unusually good feel for his changeup, especially for a northeast prep arm. It looks like he's going to move along developmentally 
with the advanced teenagers from last year's rookie-ball group. He's the best long-term pitching prospect in this system, and has a chance to be a No. 4 starter if the velo finds another gear, more likely a No. 4/5 if it does not.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Every year, a college player who was draft-eligible the year before takes a sudden leap, performs at an elite level, and forces teams to consider whether there's been a real uptick in his skill or if he's just beating up on familiar competition, in essence repeating a level. Hoese was the 2019 case. After putting up an .803 OPS in his draft-eligible sophomore year (he went in the 35th round and didn't sign), he put up a 1.276 OPS in his junior year, with 23 homers and a 38:30 BB/K ratio. He was handled with care by the Dodgers after he signed, spending a lot of time in the AZL and DH'ing due to wrist and forearm tendinitis. He dealt with more wrist trouble during the spring of 2020 and had just been totally cleared and begun to throw to bases a week before the game shutdown due to COVID-19. He picked up additional reps during Fall Instructional League. Hoese's exit velo data was way down in pro ball, something I'm dismissing because of the injury and therefore am excluding from The Board until we get a valid sample (his college avg/max was 88/104, pro was 84/100). He's not tooled up and doesn't have huge raw power, even with a healthy wrist. Instead he's a very athletic swinger with a quick bat, whose swing is geared for airborne contact. That should help him get to power in games even though there's not huge raw. Hoese will need to attain a balanced hit/power combination to profile at third base, but the Dodgers have had internal conversations about trying him in the middle infield (they tried him there a bit during the Fall), which is obviously an easier bar to clear. His already odd, slow developmental track was further warped and flagged by the pandemic, and the soon-to-be 24-year-old has yet to see an at-bat above Low-A. (Alternate site, Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Hoese was just a name on a list of guys to monitor this spring unti March when the scouting community sat up and recognized the insane statistical season he was putting up. After putting up an .803 OPS in his draft-eligible sophomore year (he went in the 35th round and didn't sign), he put up a 1.276 OPS in his junior year, with 23 homers and a 38/30 BB/K ratio. While he's 6-foot-4, 200 pounds and a late-bloomer, he projects to be an average defender with an average arm at shortstop and has the bat speed to project continued performance at higher levels. There's a posture issue to fix in his swing, but clubs will be wary of trying to change too much while everything is going well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going deep just five times in his first two seasons at Tulane, Hoese exploded for 23 homers (fourth in NCAA Division I) in 2019 and mashed his way into the first round of the Draft. He had a solid pro debut before spending 2020 at Los Angeles' alternate site and instructional league program, then endured a rough first full season last year. He tried to play through a left intercostal strain before missing nearly two months and batted just .188/.241/.245 with two homers in 59 Double-A games. When he's going good, Hoese displays an athletic right-handed swing and a disciplined approach while driving balls from gap to gap. But for much of 2021, his stroke looked longer and slower and he got too aggressive at the plate, which the Dodgers attribute to his injury and trying to dig himself out of a hole during a challenging assignment to Double-A. He continued to struggle in the Arizona Fall League, but he made some swing adjustments during the offseason that the club hopes can unlock a solid hitter with similar power. Though he moves well for a large man, Hoese is still a below-average runner and a fringy defender at third base. He has decent range and hands, while his arm strength fluctuates from fringy to solid. He'll need more consistency on both sides of the ball to profile as a big league regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hoese didn't homer as a Tulane freshman in 2017 and went deep just five times as a Draft-eligible sophomore before ranking fourth in NCAA Division I with 23 homers in 2019. He set American Athletic Conference records for homers, total bases (183), slugging percentage (.779) and runs (72) while mashing his way into the first round and a $2,740,300 bonus. He batted .299/.380/483 while advancing to low Class A, then spent 2020 in alternative camp and instructional league. Hoese has an athletic right-handed swing, plenty of strength and does a nice job of using the leverage in his 6-foot-4 frame. He's a disciplined hitter who focuses on driving the ball from gap to gap, so he should hit for average as well as power. But he hasn't looked like his normal self in 2021 while battling an intercostal strain and struggling in Double-A. Hoese moves well for his size, though he's still a below-average runner. There's no reason he shouldn't be able to remain at third base, but he'll need to improve the consistency of his defense and his arm strength, which fluctuates from fringy to solid. If he had to move to first base, he still should provide enough offense to profile as an everyday player at the less demanding position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After going homerless as a Tulane freshman in 2017 and going deep just five times as a Draft-eligible sophomore in 2018, Hoese powered his way into the first round of the 2019 Draft by finishing fourth in NCAA Division I with 23 dingers. The American Athletic Conference player of the year, he set league records for homers, total bases (183), slugging percentage (.779) and runs (72). A year after he went in the 35th round to the Royals, he signed for $2,740,300 as the 25th overall choice and hit .299/.380/.483 in his pro debut while reaching Low-A. Hoese displayed a nice right-handed swing and the ability to use the leverage in his 6-foot-4 frame during his first two college seasons, and he began to realize his power potential once he added strength. He drives the ball from gap to gap and employs a disciplined approach. While his power is his most attractive tool, he should hit for average as well. Though he's a below-average runner, Hoese moves well for his size. He has solid arm strength and enough range to remain at third base, though he needs to improve his consistency on defense. If he had to move to first base, he should provide enough offense to profile as a regular there as well.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: I'm hitting the breaks on Pena in a sense. I think he has a chance to be an everyday player but I also think it's very unlikely that he ends up having the sort of meteoric rise some other recent teenage superstar players and prospects have had. When you see Pena in a uniform, you can see where the bonus went and how the hype was born. This is a big, strapping young man built like a Division I safety who stands apart from other kids due to his physicality. That size and strength helps enable Pena to rip the bat through the zone with notable raw power for his age but that hasn't really manifested in consistent in-game production in my scattered looks at him, which date back to 2019 Instructs. Pena's swing is noisy and long. There's plenty of time for that to be tweaked if it turns out to be a statistically-evident problem, but in my looks, it has made it so Pena gets jammed pretty often, and makes him late on pitches he shouldn't be. He's strong enough to yank weaker contact through the infield for hits anyway, even if a pitch really ties him up, but aside from the occasional golf shot homer, I think it's going to be tough for him to hit for in-game power with this swing. Now, while I think this problem creates some hit tool risk, there are still huge tools and projection evident in Pena. He's a big, lefty-hitting teenager with a chance to play center and have impact power. Even if problems with his bat persist, he still has plenty of avenues to a lower-ceiling big league role. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text:
As an amateur, Peña was billed as a well-rounded, instinctive player with a frame that portended a fair amount of additional mass. Though not as overtly projectable as the Kristian Robinson/Alexander Ramirez sorts, Peña was clearly going to grow into some power and, based on how he hit in games and played center field, was thought to have a strong chance to become a well-rounded player, perhaps a five-tool sort, with all the tools close to average. It was surprising then that Peña arrived for his first fall instructional league looking like an NFL cornerback, with one source going so far as to tell me they think Peña has a big league body right now. 
Even though his swing is a bit clunky, and his footwork is perhaps unnecessarily conservative, Peña looked pretty comfortable against pro pitching in the fall, the best pitching he's ever faced in his life to this point; his performance included him roping a single off of Michael Kopech, who was sitting 97 that day. The surprising physicality has already brought about more power and bat speed, and Peña already has the helicopter overhead finish to his swing à la Miguel Andújar and Wander Franco. Once the industry becomes more confident in grading his defense and bat, which will come once he's faced pro pitching for an extended period of time, he could be a global top 50 prospect based on his place on the defensive spectrum and the hit/power combination.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: A well-rounded outfielder with considerable physical projection, Peña has shown all-fields hitting ability in games. He has a chance to stay in center field but, if he doesn't, he'll likely have grown into sizeable power. Bonus is believed to be around $3.5 million.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The No. 5 international prospect in 2019-20, Pena signed with the Royals for $3,897,500 shortly after the signing period started. But the Dominican native didn’t have his first full professional season stateside until 2021 because of the pandemic, although he was able to participate in the Royals’ instructional league against older competition in 2020. Pena struggled in 40 games in rookie ball, hitting just .161/.256/.314 with three home runs, but there were flashes of the dynamic player he can be. Pena’s bat is still his calling card despite the contact issues he faced in Arizona. Strong and physical, he possesses power with a slight uppercut swing that yields hard contact to all fields. The Royals are working on mechanical adjustments that will allow his rhythm and timing to be better, cutting down on the swing-and-miss tendency that saw him strike out more than a third of the time last year. Pena is an average runner and solid defender in center field, and the Royals will continue to let him play there unless he outgrows the position. His arm strength and offensive tools profile well in right field. Only 19 years old, Pena is no doubt still growing into his big, 6-foot-3 frame, and his youth and makeup give the Royals confidence he can bounce back after 2021. He has a long way to go, though, and his bat will have to speed up for him to reach his full potential. If the power doesn’t translate, Pena still has enough tools to be an off-the-bench type player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pena was MLB Pipeline’s No. 5 international prospect in the 2019-20 signing period and reminded scouts of a young Carlos Beltran in terms of skill set and potential. The Royals, the team that drafted Beltran back in 1995, gave Pena $3,897,500 to sign right after the signing period opened. The Dominican native has had a strange start to his career: He’s yet to play a professional season stateside because of the pandemic, but he participated in the Royals’ instructional league in both Kansas City and Arizona last fall, gaining valuable experience against older prospects. Pena’s bat and power are his best tools right now, but the other parts of his game are developing quickly. He has a sound approach with a slight uppercut swing and yields hard contact to all fields. He has some pop and has shown strength and quickness through the strike zone. Pena is an average runner with a solid-to-average arm and good defensive skills, so the Royals are going to let him play in center field for now. But he’s already added to his frame since he was signed and could outgrow the up-the-middle position and move to right field, where he has the offensive tools and arm to profile well. Pena had his moments last summer where he struggled against older pitching. But Royals officials were pleased to see that Pena is open to learning and making adjustments quickly, which could signal a quicker move through the Minors once he actually starts playing games. Despite gaining experiences last summer that someone his age usually doesn’t get, Pena’s still a young player and has a long way to go. But if it all clicks for him on the field, he has to potential to be the face of an organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts who saw Pena, who was MLB Pipeline's No. 5 international prospect for the 2019-20 signing period, were reminded of a young Carlos Beltran in terms of his skill set and potential. Perhaps that's why the Royals, the team that drafted Beltran back in 1995, gave the Dominican native $3,897,500 to sign right after the signing period opened on July 2. He received his first taste of stateside action during instructional league and impressed those who saw him with his athleticism, tools and advanced feel for the game. Pena's bat and power are his best tools at the moment, but the other parts of his game are not far behind. The left-handed hitter has a sound approach with a slight uppercut swing that yields hard contact to all fields. He has shown strength and quickness through the strike zone and the ball jumps off of his bat. He could end up having plus power and does not have a lot of swing and miss. An average runner with a solid-to-average arm and solid defensive skills, he runs well enough to at least be given a chance to stick in center field. He could outgrow the up-the-middle position and move to right field, where he has the offensive tools to profile well. Pena also gets high marks for his baseball IQ, solid instincts and plus makeup. If it all clicks for him on the field, he has the potential to be the face of an organization, much like the player he draws comps to was at one point in his career.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Signed out of Division II Lincoln Memorial University, Elliott is a pitchability lefty with a plus changeup. He's super loose and lanky, his 88-92 mph (that's up, he was 86-88 in 2019) fastball seem to sneak past hitters somehow, and he projects to have plus command. Lefties with a good changeup and command are high-floor types likely to pitch toward the back of a rotation. (Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Elliott starred at Division II Lincoln Memorial University in Tennessee, posting a 2.23 ERA with 134 strikeouts and just 14 walks over 92 2/3 innings during his 2019 senior season. The Padres selected him in the 10th round that summer and inked him to a below-slot $5,000 bonus. The 6-foot-3 lefty posted a 1.77 ERA over 35 2/3 innings in his pro debut then broke out in 2021 as he worked his way up to Double-A. Pitching across two levels last season, Elliott racked up 87 strikeouts and issued just 19 walks over 70 2/3 innings Although Elliott’s velocity has ticked up since college, he remains a command-over-stuff type pitcher. His fastball sits in the low 90s, but plays up because his arm slot creates additional deception. A low-80s changeup, which features good downward action, is currently his best pitch, though there’s a chance his mid-70s slider claims that title in the future. None of Elliott’s pitches will overpower a hitter, but his delivery, coupled with his ability to locate to any corner of the zone helps his stuff play above its velocity. The development of Elliott’s slider may ultimately determine his ceiling. The southpaw has been a consistent performer during his time in pro ball and if the slider comes along, should be able to stick in the back of a rotation. If not, he could profile as an effective longman coming out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best defenders in the 2022 international signing class, Gonzalez signed with Seattle for $1.3 million out of the Dominican Republic and could join a long list of success stories the franchise has had there. A slick-fielding shortstop, he projects to have the most potential to stick there long term as he grows and develops as anyone his age and rank within the organization. Despite being known more for his glove, Gonzalez does make hard contact and has a projectable body expected to add strength, which can ultimately add a little more pop to his bat. What he lacks in power, he makes up for in hitting ability and potential. He’s an average runner. On defense, he shows plus hands with smooth actions and is expected to be a plus defender. He projects to have an average arm and his range is improving. Gonzalez makes playing defense look easy. The Mariners are eager to see what he does in his first season of pro ball in the Dominican Summer League, which could put him on a fast track to the U.S. and the Rookie-level Arizona Complex League come fall.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: It was fascinating to hear scouts who see pro players, specifically the very talented group of teenage shortstops in this system, describe Tucker after I had watched him among domestic high schoolers and discussed him with amateur scouts. After Tucker looked explosive but unpolished to my eye on the showcase circuit, then seemed to take a real leap during an abbreviated senior season, multiple scouts who saw him in Goodyear now consider him a high-floor, lower-ceiling player. It's possible Tucker looks much different in the pro context, or that, like many of us, he was just weary from dealing with months of our earthly reality. I'm inclined to bet on what I saw with my own two eyes when Tucker was an amateur and continue to have him placed as a high-variance, high-ceiling talent. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020updated
fangraphs.text: Twitchy shortstop with explosive hitting hands who needs a swing overhaul in his lower half.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Guardians have an affinity for sweet-swinging infielders and added another with the 23rd overall pick in the 2020 Draft, signing Tucker for a below-slot $2 million. He became part of the 12th sibling tandem selected in the first round, as older brother Cole went 24th overall to the Pirates in 2014. Carson has yet to play much in pro ball because a wrist injury ended his 2021 debut after just six games in Rookie ball. Tucker has a quick right-handed swing with good feel for the barrel and focuses on making line-drive contact to all fields. He boosted his Draft stock when he began to get strong and drive the ball more consistently as a high school senior, and his solid raw power could result in 15 or more homers per season. He also got faster in 2020, consistently displaying plus speed and flashing plus-plus run times, giving him 20-steal potential. With quick feet and hands and solid arm strength, Tucker plays a steady shortstop. He has a chance to become a solid defender there with more experience, and he also has the tools to move all over the diamond if he winds up in more of a utility role. His profile closely resembles his brother's at a similar stage of their careers, though Carson features a bit more pop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Indians selected Tucker 23rd overall last June, six years after the Pirates took older brother Cole at No. 24, they became the 12th sibling tandem selected in the first round. They both were shortstops who boosted their stock with strong senior seasons at Mountain Pointe High (Phoenix). After passing up a Texas scholarship to sign for a below-slot $2 million, Carson saw his first pro action at instructional league. Tucker has good feel for the barrel and makes consistent line-drive contact to all fields. Though his hitting ability stands out more than his power, he has added strength and has driven the ball in the air more regularly in the past year. With some added loft to his right-handed swing, he could deliver 15 or more homers per season. Tucker also displayed much improved speed in 2020, clocking plus to double-plus times after being more of an average runner in the past. He has the quick feet, hands and solid arm strength to remain at shortstop, and those tools also give him the versatility to play all over the diamond if needed. He has a similar profile to his brother at the same stage of their careers, with Carson featuring a bit more pop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Few Brewers prospects have ridden the roller coaster more than Gray in recent years. The 2018 second-rounder missed significant time with pneumonia and a hamstring strain over his first two seasons, both of which were spent in Rookie ball. After the missed pandemic year, he looked like he was finally coming into his own in 2021 with a 289/.407/.632 line and 12 homers in 51 games at Low-A. He hit a wall at High-A Wisconsin, hitting just .219 with a 28.2 percent strikeout rate, and looked gassed in a spell in the Arizona Fall League. When it’s working, Gray shows promise as a hitter who exhibits good raw power and puts the ball in the air often (48.0 percent of the time in 2021). He expands the zone too much at times, leading to the K issues, and that became even more of a concern last summer when it looked like he was pressing to recreate his Carolina success. The 21-year-old still ended up with a 20-20 season (20 homers, 23 steals) because of his above-average speed on top of the pop, and that speaks to his offensive ceiling if he makes enough contact to reach base. Gray played center primarily and mixed in some right field in 2021. The presence of Sal Frelick, Garrett Mitchell and even Joey Wiemer will likely move him to the corner full-time the closer he gets to American Family Field, and he has enough arm to work there. The Brewers hope a full offseason reset gets Gray back on track and helps him show just enough bat to get the rest of his tools in future Milwaukee lineups.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gray emerged as a top prospect for the 2018 Draft as a sophomore, and while he did plateau a bit, there were still few players with better all-around potential in his prep class. After hitting .491 with a .611 OBP and six home runs during his senior year at Hattiesburg (Miss.) High, Gray became the program's first player to be drafted since 2007, going to the Brewers in the second round. He struggled to stay on the field early in his career and move forward with his development as a pro, with pneumonia and a hamstring strain limiting him to just 55 games across his first two seasons, both of which he spent in Rookie ball. Finally able to play regularly in 2021, Gray has taken off, first hitting .289/.407/.632 with 12 homers in 51 games at Low-A prior to a midseason promotion. Gray has two loud tools in his raw power and arm strength. A gifted athlete with a quick right-handed bat, he can hammer balls out of the park to all fields and started to tap into that power more in 2021. The Brewers were most impressed by how he started to make the most of his pop potential and athleticism with an uppercut swing that results in lots of deep fly balls. Though that leads to a good amount of strikeouts, Gray takes his walks as well and now projects as much closer to an average hit tool. Gray’s defense was never in question. His arm strength was among the best among 2018 high-school position players, having been clocked at 98 mph from the outfield at the Perfect Game National Showcase after his junior year. His accuracy sometimes leaves something to be desired, though. He has solid speed and takes good routes in center field, giving him a chance to play there in pro ball. Gray’s advancements in 2021 have made him an even more exciting prospect, and while his profile still comes with risk, his ceiling has jumped to that of a skilled everyday center fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gray emerged as a top prospect for the 2018 Draft as a sophomore, and while he did plateau a bit, there were still few players with better all-around potential in his prep class. After hitting .491 with a .611 OBP and six home runs during his senior year at Hattiesburg (Miss.) High, Gray became the program's first player to be drafted since 2007, going to the Brewers in the second round. But Gray has struggled to stay on the field and move forward with his development as a pro, with pneumonia and a hamstring strain limiting him to just 55 games across his first two seasons, both of which he spent in Rookie ball. Gray has two loud tools in his raw power and arm strength. A gifted athlete with a quick right-handed bat, he can hammer balls out of the park to all fields but lacks feel to hit and is devoid of an approach. Those shortcomings fuel Gray’s swing-and-miss issues, and in turn scouts question whether he will ever make enough contact to unlock his potential at the plate. The Brewers reserve hope that Gray will be able to make strides at the plate as he gains much-needed on-field experience. Gray’s defense comes with fewer question marks. His arm strength was among the best among 2018 high school position players, having been clocked at 98 mph from the outfield at the Perfect Game National showcase after his junior year, though his accuracy sometimes leaves something to be desired. He has solid speed and takes good routes in center field, giving him a chance to play there in pro ball. Gray got stronger during the offseason while training at the Brewers’ complex in Arizona. He still has impressive tools and is young enough to get back on track, though even club officials recognize that 2020 will be a crucial year for the once highly touted prep.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gray emerged as a top prospect for the 2018 Draft as a sophomore, and while he did plateau a bit, there were still few players with better all-around potential in his prep class. After hitting .491 with a .611 OBP and six home runs during his senior year at Hattiesburg (Miss.) High, Gray became the program's first player to be drafted since 2007, going to the Brewers in the second round. He passed on a University of Mississippi commitment to sign for slot value ($1,113,500), and then began his pro career in the Rookie-level Arizona League. Gray has two loud tools in his raw power and arm strength. With his lightning-fast bat and his physical strength, he can hammer balls out of the park to all fields from the right side of the plate. His arm strength was among the best among 2018 high school position players, having been clocked at 98 mph from the outfield at the Perfect Game National showcase after his junior year, though his accuracy sometimes leaves something to be desired. He has solid speed and takes good routes in center field, giving him a chance to play there in pro ball. That Gray has swing-and-miss concerns and has been inconsistent against quality pitchers leads some scouts to question whether he'll ever hit enough to get to his power and unlock his full potential. The guided instruction he'll receive in pro ball could go a long way on that front, though it also means he may need extra time to develop in the Minors.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: I was skeptical of Gray's hit tool when he was an amateur but because he's missed so much time and dealt with the physical aftermath of pneumonia (2018) and a severe hamstring strain (2019), it's premature to declare his hit tool specious. Gray has big present power, power projection, and the instincts to stay in center field despite not being a real burner. He's a high variance prospect but still has everyday talent.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: On the surface, Gray looks like a pretty standard right field prospect. He's a projetable 6-foot-3, has present power and might grow into more, and he has some swing and miss issues due to poor breaking ball recognition. But upon extended viewing, Gray's feel for center field is advanced and he has a better chance to stay there than is typical for a prospect his size. Gray has had strikeout issues in the AZL (he missed AZL time with a respiratory issue, not an injury), during fall instructional league and against good high school pitching. We're skeptical of his ability to make sufficient contact but if he does, he'll be a power-hitting center fielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A Brooklyn native, Palmer attended Holy Cross High School in Flushing, New York, about three miles east of Citi Field. The Mets took the local kid in the 22nd round of the 2018 Draft and bet on his raw skills with a $200,000 signing bonus. After two years at Rookie levels, Palmer finally got to experience full-season ball in 2021 and hit .276/.378/.386 with two homers and 23 steals in 66 games for Low-A St. Lucie. He was promoted to High-A Brooklyn but floundered, hitting .189 with a 38.5 percent strikeout rate in 169 plate appearances. Palmer’s raw power is at least above-average, and he makes hard contact when he puts the bat on the ball. How much that happens remains up in the air. Palmer takes his walks, but his 13.9 percent walk rate in 2021 was also indicative of how much he sat back against certain pitches, rather than being aggressive on the pitches he could drive. His swing can get lengthy at times, too, and that leads to more misses. Seeing more pitching is often what helps players coming out of the Northeast develop the right approach, but it remains a question of whether Palmer will ever be a solid-to-average hitter. Defensively, the homegrown talent has bopped around short, third and second but was primarily an outfielder by the time he reached Brooklyn. His easy plus speed and good arm could make him a serviceable center fielder in time, though he needs more reps to get comfortable out there. There is still a considerable ceiling because of that power-speed combo and the ability to stay up the middle. Palmer just needs to start making contact more consistently to reach it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets didn’t have to go far to find Palmer in the 2018 Draft. The infielder came out of Holy Cross High School in Flushing, New York, about three miles away from Citi Field. Palmer had shown an interesting mix of raw power and athleticism as an amateur in Queens, allowing New York to take him in the 22nd round and offer a $200,000 signing bonus. He held his own with above-average numbers in the Gulf Coast and Appalachian Leagues in 2018 and 2019 and continued to show promise in instructional league ball last fall. Palmer’s power is the standout tool here. It could be a legitimately plus skill in time with the amount of hard contact when he puts the bat on the ball appropriately. What holds him back is his contact rate. The right-handed slugger struck out 39.1 percent of the time in Kingsport in 2019. The Mets believe part of the issue was his getting too heavy on his front side in his batting stance. The organization worked on getting him to stay back more in hopes that he can improve the contact rate and allow the power to play more in games. Palmer is an above-average runner at 6-foot-3, and the Mets believe that athleticism – along with an above-average arm -- will help him play multiple spots since it’s likely he’ll outgrow shortstop in the long term. He played short and third base two years ago and saw some time in outfield corners last fall. The Mets are giving Palmer so many defensive looks because they believe that the bat will someday be valuable enough to get in a Major League lineup every day. The slugger will be 20 for much of the 2021 season, meaning there is plenty of development time remaining, but his first taste of full-season ball should provide some answers on just how far his contact rate can carry him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mets tapped into their own backyard to find Palmer, a product of Holy Cross HS in Flushing, New York. Intrigued by his blend of athleticism and massive raw power, they selected him in the 22nd round of the 2018 Draft and then went above slot value to sign him for $200,000. After a promising pro debut in the Rookie Gulf Coast League, Palmer showcased some of the loudest tools in the Mets’ system at Rookie-level Kingsport in 2019, finishing among the Appalachian League leaders with seven home runs (tied-seventh), 63 hits (tied-fifth) and 100 total bases (tied-fifth). He also led the circuit in strikeouts, fanning 108 times in 62 games. Palmer has premium athleticism and looks the part of a future big leaguer with his projectable 6-foot-3, 195-pound frame. He packs a ton of strength into that frame, and it shows in the form of high-end exit velocities and plus-plus raw power when he does connect. His alarming swing-and-miss issues, struggles against same-side spin and pull-heavy approach lead scouts to question whether Palmer will ever make enough contact to apply his robust right-handed pop. Club officials, on the other hand, think that he’ll improve in that department as he gains experience and learns to harness his athleticism. He is unlikely to be anything more than a below-average hitter, but even a fraction of improvement at the plate could go a long way in helping Palmer reach his power ceiling. Defensively, Palmer split his time in the Appalachian League between shortstop and third base. His speed, range and arm strength are stretched a bit thin up the middle, and both club officials and evaluators tend to agree that Palmer likely is ticketed for the hot corner long term. The Mets believe that his athleticism will translate well in the outfield and could begin to deploy him in either right or left field in 2020. Regardless of which corner he lands at, Palmer is the definition of a high-risk prospect and will need to make significant gains as a hitter to become a big leaguer.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: This is one of the, if not the highest variance prospects in the entire system. Unearthed in the Mets' backyard as an overslot 2018 Day Three pick, Palmer surprised the industry by going to Kingsport and performing well above what was expected of him. There's a gap between the contact performance (Palmer hit .250) and actual skill at this point, but that's okay for such a lanky, cold-weather, out-of-nowhere high school prospect. The measurable power Palmer generates on contact is shocking. He's tied with Mark Vientos and Brett Baty for the highest average exit velo on this list and he's arguably more physically projectable than either of them. His long-term defensive profile is still unclear: the Mets played him all over the field during 2020 instructs and will continue to do so in 2021. Palmer's ability to make contact and recognize offspeed stuff is raw, and like Newton there's a chance that he never makes enough contact to be a viable big leaguer. It's possible he becomes a whiff-prone corner outfielder and falls off the list in two years, but he might also stay on the dirt and develop passable feel to hit and huge raw power. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Like a lot of the Mariners' hitting prospects who you'll read about from here on out, Perez has a high-risk build that might end up at first base rather than third. The difference between Perez and some of the other guys is Milkar's arm, a 60 or 70 on the scale, that might mask future issues with his lateral range. The real reason to like Perez is that he has more of a frame than his measurables suggest, he has advanced feel for the strike zone and for contact, and he has pretty good power for his age, though that's in part because of how physical he is already. He's in the same bucket as Clase: squint hard enough and you can see a future regular, though it's probably a half decade away. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Perez has more of a frame than his measurables suggest, he has advanced feel for the strike zone and for contact, and he might grow into enough power to profile as a well-rounded everyday third baseman. But the frame isn't so overtly projectable as to make it a likelihood.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The switch-hitting Perez made big strides in 2021 to earn a promotion from the Arizona Complex League to Low-A Modesto for the final two weeks of the season, hitting a combined .308/.455/.378 (.832 OPS). This followed a strong impression he made in his age-17 season during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019. The Nicaragua native joined the Mariners’ organization the year prior for $175,000. Perez’s on-base numbers are among the best in Seattle’s system, thanks to an incredibly relaxed and confident approach at the plate and solid barrel control. His flatter-than-usual swing path leads to more quiet contact, which is why his power numbers aren’t off the charts, yet he makes up for it with his high average. For that reason, and given how young he is, the Mariners might opt to let that approach be for the time being. While his hitting profile doesn’t exactly stand out for a third baseman, he does have the chance to play there defensively with a huge arm and decent actions. Though some are worried about his range long-term, the Mariners are bullish on his potential to add more strength, grow into more power and fit the corner infield profile long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The switch-hitting Perez impressed in his professional debut during the Dominican Summer League in 2019, slashing .274/.381/.388 with four homers as a 17-year-old. Though he is so young, there is still plenty of room to grow athletically. He projects more as a third baseman, but he’ll need to show more pop at the plate to wind up there long term. His arm strength could even allow the Mariners to move him to the outfield if needed. Though he’s been more effective from the left side, the uber-confident Perez has shown elite bat-to-ball skills that have led to high line-drive and fly-ball rates, thanks to some quality bat speed. His power could be the determining factor in whether or not he remains at third, though the Mariners are bullish on his potential to rake, particularly after getting more looks at him at the fall developmental league in Arizona in 2020 -- his first reps stateside. Entering 2021, the “next step” phase for Perez will be simply playing. He was one of the many victims of the cancellation of the Minor League season, and the Mariners are excited about getting a clearer scope of how he projects by referring to a more tangible representation of his profile that can only be accumulated with playing time in the Minors.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: Arizona outfielder Ryan Holgate (comp B) has big power. His contact sounds different off the bat than the other U of A hitters from hsi draft class, many of whom also slugged a ton because it was arguably the deepest lineup in 2021 college baseball, and due to the offensive environment in Tucson. Holgate put about a third of his balls in play over 95 mph that year. Realistically he projects as the larger end of a corner outfield platoon.

fangraphs.label: 2021draft
fangraphs.text: Arizona outfielder Ryan Holgate (comp B) also has big power. His contact sounds different off the bat than the other U of A hitters, many of whom also slugged a ton because of the offensive environment in Tucson. Holgate put about a third of his balls in play over 95 mph this year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In a sign of what was to come, Holgate followed up a mundane freshman season at Arizona with a circuit-best 13 homers in the Northwoods League in the summer of 2019. He was off to a hot start before the 2020 shutdown, hit .351/.421/.576 with 11 homers as a junior last spring and mixed in a National Baseball Congress World Series win for the Santa Barbara Foresters in between. The Cardinals selected the slugger 70th overall last July and signed him for just under slot at $875,000. Holgate played 30 games with Low-A Palm Beach in his Draft year but managed just a .193/.279/.289 line and 35.7 percent K rate. The left-handed hitter’s power is what originally stood out to St. Louis, and that remained true in those early Minor League looks, where he maxed out with a 109.2 mph exit velocity. His plus raw power shows up more in batting practice, but it should be at least above-average on the pro side too. A longer swing, designed to make the most of that power, led to the swing-and-miss issues with Palm Beach, and it’s a bigger question now than it was on Draft Day if Holgate will be able to hit for a decent average. A career .314 mark in college provides some hope, and further adjustments to increase the contact rate after last year’s humbling could pay dividends. Holgate played his college position of right field in Low-A, but he projects better in left field due to a fringy arm. The former Wildcat will need to hit to be valuable in either corner outfield spot, and that starts with making more contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Feliz made a strong first impression in 2021 during his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, where he had an .813 OPS and five homers in 46 games. Signed in 2019 for $900,000, the richest contract among that international class for Seattle, Feliz is still growing into his body and filling out, which has made him a more physical player in recent years. As his body continues to mature, it’s possible he can emerge with 55s for his tools across the board. None of those tools necessarily play above the other, making him one of the Mariners’ more well-rounded outfield prospects. Described as very smart and instinctual, Feliz has the potential to stick in center field due to those attributes. At the plate, Feliz’s swing mechanics are somewhat inconsistent and remain a work in progress. It’s not the cleanest or most compact swing and there are a lot of moving parts, especially in his lower half, but despite those hiccups, he showed more feel for hitting than scouts anticipated. However, it’s likely that he profiles more as a power than average hitter long term. Because of all of his tools projecting as above-average, Feliz probably has more upside than floor. But because his swing has a ways to go, his timeline for the Majors is probably a little longer too.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Simmons was so raw that he swung and missed a ton even during high school varsity play, so his 2019 statistical success in the Penn League was surprising and impressive. But an extended look at Simmons during his Australian Baseball League run (which included him struggling to hold on to the bat), has me backpedaling on his placement. It's rare to find infielders with this sort of bat speed but I think it's pretty unlikely that he hits, both due to his breaking ball recognition and a lack of bat control. (Fall Instructional League, Australian Baseball League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Simmons was a toolsy, volatile high school prospect who had strikeout issues against varsity high school pitching. His stride and the way his hands load have both changed since he's entered pro ball, which seems to have improved his timing and general in-the-box comfort. There are still some bat-to-ball issues, but Simmons' raw power/bat speed and rapid improvements are exciting. He could be a multi-positional player with power, the sort Ryan McMahon has been to this point, but with a role that includes some shortstop.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Simmons was a toolsy, volatile high school prospect who had strikeout issues against varsity pitching. The way his hands load and his stride have both changed since he's entered pro ball, which has improved his once putrid timing. There are still some bat-to-ball issues, but Simmons is trending up and has a shot to be a multi-positional infielder with power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A solid Georgia high school prospect, Simmons struggled at the plate a bit during his senior year in 2018 to hurt his Draft stock. The Phillies liked the power potential and overall athlete enough to take him in the sixth round that June and go over-slot to sign him away from his Georgia Tech commitment for $750,000. It’s been a slow development process since, though he did lead the New York-Penn League in slugging percentage in 2019. He did show some glimpses of his offensive upside in his full-season debut in 2021, but injury, a pitch to the helmet and COVID-related shutdowns limited him to just 46 total games. Simmons has always had considerable raw power from the right side of the plate; the question since his high school days was if he’d hit enough to tap into it. He’s had flashes of bringing a solid approach to the plate, with a willingness to draw walks, but he does strike out a fair amount. When he does make contact, it’s loud with good exit velocity and the ability to hit the ball over the fence, especially to the pull side. The Phillies believe his bat is trending in the right direction. The high school shortstop has played three infield positions professionally, but as his body continues to get bigger and stronger, it doesn’t look like he’ll be able to play short long-term. He’s probably best suited for third, where his strong arm plays well, but will continue to get plenty of time at second base as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Simmons entered his senior year of high school in Georgia as an intriguing shortstop prospect with a ton of raw power. He struggled making contact during the spring leading up to the Draft, causing his stock to drop, but the Phillies thought the strength and athleticism were worth taking a chance on in the sixth round and they gave him an over-slot bonus of $750,000 to sign him away from his Georgia Tech commitment. Simmons struggled in his pro debut in the Gulf Coast League and got off to a slow start in the short-season New York-Penn League in 2019, but he found his power stroke and finished as the league-leader in slugging percentage. The Phillies are thrilled with the growth Simmons has shown since starting his pro career. The ball jumps off his bat with solid exit velocity. He’s shown the ability to stay inside the baseball well and nearly all of his home run pop has come to his pull side so far. There are still some swing-and-miss issues, but he offsets them somewhat with a solid walk rate. Simmons is an average runner, but he isn't going to be basestealing threat. Drafted as a shortstop, there are those who think he’d be able to play the premium position long-term, especially because of his strong arm. But the Phillies started having him play second and third in 2019, and he’ll likely continue to move around the infield as his power bat carries him up the ladder.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: A big-bodied, lefty power prospect, Aguilar had among the most present raw power in the 2021 international signing class, but because of how big he is already, there's a real possibility that he ends up at first base. The Mariners know this and want Aguilar to work on his conditioning to give himself the best possible shot to stay at third base, but he's still pretty soft-bodied at the moment. He does have above-average bat speed from the left side and is a fairly short-levered hitter with relatively advanced feel for contact, but the list of hitters who have been in this realm before (Joe Rizzo, Tyler Keenan, Austin Shenton, Keegan McGovern, etc.) have all either been stagnant or regressed physically, so there's no example of these sorts ending up on a more favorable end of the defensive spectrum. (International Signee)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners showed just how much they valued Aguilar when the 2020-21 international signing period opened by making him their highest-priced investment at $1.5 million. The Dominican Republic native hit the ground running in the DSL months later, but his numbers -- a .246/.359/.361 (.720 OPS) slash line with just two homers in 52 games -- didn’t exactly reflect as much. A third baseman by trade, Aguilar has drawn comparisons to Red Sox star Rafael Devers for many reasons beyond his position and left-handed-hitting swing. He worked with Devers’ trainer, the late Rudy Santin, and began living up to that comparison during his pro debut last season. Aguilar has shown an advanced hit tool, and he’s one of the top Minor Leaguers at embodying the Mariners’ mantra of “dominating the zone,” evidenced by a 13.2 percent walk rate. Yet he had just two homers and a .369 slugging percentage, which underscores that he, right now, is more of a hit-over-power type. However, the 17-year-old has decent pop and a 5-foot-11 frame that suggests he could grow into more power. Aguilar moved from shortstop to third after signing, and he worked diligently on his conditioning to handle the hot corner. That work appeared to pay off when he arrived at the Mariners’ high-performance camp in Arizona last fall. Seattle doesn’t necessarily expect him to blossom into Devers’ power profile, but Aguilar nonetheless has the upside to grow into more hard contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles’ second-round pick in 2017, Hall signed for an above-slot $1.3 million bonus after starring for the Canadian junior national team, and seemed to put himself on the fast track with impressive seasons at Low-A Aberdeen in ’18 and Class A Delmarva in ’19. But he was affected more than most prospects by the pandemic, unable to attend Orioles’ secondary site camp in 2020 due to border regulations between the U.S. and Canada. He then experienced a down year at High-A Aberdeen in 2021, hitting .248 with three homers and a .672 OPS as a 22-year-old. The Orioles opted not to protect him from the Rule 5 draft in his first year of eligibility. Hall’s best tool is his plus speed, which he’s used to swipe at least 22 bases in each of his three full professional seasons. He’s more of an all-fields, gap-to-gap hitter than a power threat, with a quick bat and hand strength beyond his physical dimensions. Even so, the lack of power at High-A in 2021 was concerning, given how Hall’s walk rate and extra-base output also slid considerably when exposed to better pitching. Hall's a scrappy hitter who routinely puts together good at-bats, but he might need to add strength to compete more consistently at the higher levels. Hall couples his speed with savvy instincts on the bases, stealing 26 bases in 27 attempts last summer at Aberdeen. He’s also used his quickness to grow into a playable defender at short, though the bat might require him to move around the diamond at the highest level. The arm is good enough to play any of the three infield spots, and Hall also got some experience in center field with the Ironbirds. That versatility helps project Hall to reach the Majors in a utility role, especially if he adds muscle to his wiry frame and can stay out of the trainer’s room. That’s proven challenging in the past, with Hall having three of his four professional seasons disrupted by soft-tissue injuries.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hall has improved steadily since the Orioles, enamored with his play for the Canadian junior national team, landed him with an above-slot $1.3 million bonus in the second round of the 2017 Draft. An oblique injury limited Hall to just two games that summer, and he struggled initially in the New York-Penn League before breaking out down the stretch in 2018. Healthy again, Hall jumped a level and was one of the more productive hitters in the Class A South Atlantic League in 2019, hitting .298/.385/.395 with five homers and 33 stolen bases. He attended O’s instructional camp in 2020 and seems to be a fair bet to begin 2021 at Double-A. Hall benefits from a quick bat and hand strength beyond his physical dimensions, relying more on an all-fields, gap-to-gap approach rather than plus power. There are questions about whether he’ll grow into more, but Hall assuaged some of those doubts by improving his extra-base-hit output and walk rate at each new level. His best tool is his plus speed, which Hall couples with good instincts on the bases. He is a scrappy hitter who consistently puts together competitive at-bats and demonstrates strong on-base skills. He’s also used his quickness to grow into a playable defender at short, where Hall has a chance to stick at the highest level. Whether that’s on an everyday basis depends on how his bat develops as he adds muscle to what is still a wiry frame. Hall possesses enough arm strength to play all over the diamond if not, and has shown capable of handling second base and center field in small samples. This versatility leads him to project to reach the Majors in a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hall has improved steadily since the Orioles, enamored with his play for the Canadian junior national team, landed him with an above-slot $1.3 million bonus in the second round of the 2017 Draft. An oblique injury limited Hall to just two games that summer, and he struggled initially in the New York-Penn League before breaking out in the second half, hitting .358 with a 19-game hit streak down the stretch in 2018. Healthy again, Hall jumped a level and was one of the more productive infielders in the Class A South Atlantic League in 2019, hitting .298/.385/.395 with five homers and 33 stolen bases. Hall benefits from a quick bat and hand strength beyond his physical dimensions, relying more on an all-fields, gap-to-gap approach rather than plus power. There are questions about whether he’ll grow into more, but Hall assuaged some of those doubts by more than doubling his extra-base-hit output and improving his walk rate last season. His best tool is his plus speed, which he couples with good instincts on the bases, and is a scrappy hitter with a tendency to grind out at-bats. He’s also used his quickness to grow into a playable defender at short, where Hall has the chance to stick at the highest level. Whether that’s on an everyday basis probably depends on how his bat develops as he matures and adds muscle to what is now a wiry frame. Hall possesses enough arm strength to play all over the diamond if not, in which case he would project to reach the Majors in a utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After strong performances with the Canadian junior national team had pushed him up Draft boards in 2017, Hall landed an above-slot $1.3 million signing bonus from the Orioles after they took him the second round. An oblique injury limited him to just two games that summer, and Hall struggled at the outset of 2018, hitting .212 with a .524 OPS during his first month in the New York-Penn League. He broke out in the second half, raking at a .358 clip (.913 OPS) over his final 36 contests, and authored a 19-game hit streak along the way. Hall has natural feel to hit, demonstrating good bat speed and the ability to hit to all fields from the right side of the plate, albeit with below-average power. He does have some pop to the gaps, however, and should be a consistent source of doubles and triples as he adds strength to his athletic frame. Plus speed might be Hall's best tool, and club officials rave about his baserunning instincts. Hall's defense and arm have improved considerably in the professional ranks to the point where scouts now view him as an above-average defender who can stick at shortstop. With his slow start and torrid finish, Hall arguably was Baltimore's most improved prospect in 2018. Club officials are quick to praise infield coordinator Dave Anderson and hitting coordinator Jeff Manto for their role in his development, as they each spent a lot of time working with Hall and made him a more confident player overall. He doesn't have a very high ceiling, but the tools and skills are all there for Hall to develop into an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Canada has produced a fair share of Draft talent over the years, with Josh Naylor and Mike Soroka the most recent examples to get taken in the first round (both in 2015). There hasn't been much in the way of middle infielders to come from north of the border, but the Orioles are hopeful that Hall, who signed for $1.3 million as a second-round pick, will be the first to reverse that trend. Hall made his pro debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, where he tallied six hits in nine at-bats before an oblique injury prematurely ended his season. Hall might be a bit unpolished, but he has considerable tools and upside. He has a decent approach at the plate for his age and experience level, with a natural feel to hit and good bat speed. There should be some gap power in the future as well, and he should compile plenty of doubles and triples thanks to his plus speed and sharp baserunning. Hall is capable of making the spectacular play defensively, and while his arm might grade out as average, he can reach back for more when needed and he's usually very accurate. He will struggle at times with the backhand play, but most feel he can stick at short. If not, his tools also would fit nicely at the keystone. Hall needs to add strength to his athletic frame, but that should come as he matures physically. Having turned 18 not long before the Draft, he'll have plenty of time to fulfill his fairly high ceiling.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Hall's speed has put several atmospheres of pressure on low-level minor league defenses. He puts lots of balls in play on the ground and hauls ass to first, to this point running a nearly .400 BABIP as a pro. He has advanced feel for contact for a 20-year-old with an odd developmental path (he left Bermuda as an adolescent to pursue baseball in Canada) and several catalytic qualities that fit in a traditional, perhaps regressive, top-of-the-lineup role. He's stolen 56 bases in 70 career attempts (an 80% success rate) and is fast enough for that skill to keep playing as he climbs the ladder, though he showed up to 2021 spring training having added 15 pounds of muscle during the offseason, which may impact his speed. Hall didn't lack big league physicality and his exit velos were close to big league average in 2019 when he was a little smaller, and he did lift the ball more that year, but power is unlikely to impact the profile. He's tracking like an Everth Cabrera sort of player. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
