fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: For the first time in 2018, the Cardinals deployed scouts dedicated to the lowest levels of the minor leagues and it netted them one of the more explosive physical specimens on last year's desert backfields. Traded in a prospect-for-prospect deadline deal that sent one of the Cardinals' many upper-level outfielders, Oscar Mercado, to Cleveland, Torres dominated rookie ball on either side of the deal and slashed .321/.409/.525 combined in the AZL and GCL. Built like a Division I tight end, Torres' body is a baseball rarity, and he still has growth potential from both a physical and mechanical perspective. Torres doesn't always transfer his weight effectively and his swing can be bottom hand-heavy, but it has a workable foundation and he has the requisite bat speed, strength and hand-eye coordination to hit and hit for power. At maturity, he could be a 6-foot-5, 230 pound power-hitting force in the middle of a lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pérez might still be remembered best as a candidate for the first overall spot in the 2016 Draft. He tested positive for a performance-enhancing substance days before the process began, and MLB Pipeline’s No. 9 Draft prospect fell to the Cardinals at No. 23 overall instead. The Puerto Rico native hasn’t exactly enjoyed a strong offensive start to his career. A broken hand limited him in 2017, and he didn’t see his first full-season action until 2019 with Class A Peoria, where he hit just .269 with a .654 OPS in 118 games. Pérez added strength ahead of 2021 and enjoyed arguably his best offensive season yet at Double-A Springfield with a .265/.322/.339 line and a career-best four homers in 98 games. Pérez’s prospect stock remains in place because of his non-offensive tools. A near-plus-plus runner, he shows excellent range at the demanding position of shortstop and has the hands to handle most anything hit his way. A plus arm makes the defensive profile even better. Pérez has used his speed to swipe 20-plus bags each of his past two seasons, and his performance on the basepaths may be his best offensive asset. Otherwise, he can get too aggressive at the plate. So while his 14.9 percent swinging-strike rate isn’t overly high, he doesn’t quite drive balls adequately when he does make contact. Only 17 of his 86 hits went for extra bases in 2021, and his career full-season high for slugging percentage is a meager .339. Pérez hasn’t been added to the 40-man when he was Rule 5-eligible the past two years, but the glove and speed could get the 23-year-old a Major League look on their own merits, if only as a light-hitting bench option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Not a whole lot has gone right for Perez in the last couple of years. Thought to be a potential top 10 pick in the 2016 Draft, he slid after a positive test for a performance-enhancer. The Cardinals took a chance and drafted him closer to the end of that first round, but while he did show some tools during his pro debut that summer, he struggled in 2017 and his summer ended with a broken hand in early August. That's the bad news. The good news is the shortstop had a productive offseason once his hand healed. That included playing for Team Puerto Rico, and manager Yadier Molina, in the Pan American U-23 Baseball Championship to earn a spot in next fall's World Cup. In addition to getting him more playing time, the Cardinals wanted to make sure he worked on getting more physical. Perez has solid bat-to-ball skills and drew some walks, even when struggling, but a serious lack of strength kept him from impacting the baseball. Some evaluators worry he won't be able to add the strength necessary to hit, but the Cardinals see strength in his hands and forearms and think his build will allow him to add good weight. There's no question about Perez's defense. He has plus speed and outstanding range as a result, to go along with above-average hands and a plus arm when he needs to. Still just 19, there's time yet, but he will have to start showing more at the plate to come close to reaching the potential of a big league regular people saw leading into the Draft.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Perez's road to pro ball was tumultuous, to say the least. Leading up to the 2016 Draft, the Puerto Rican shortstop's name was popping up at the top of the first round. But news of a positive test for a performance-enhancing drug forced his stock to fall. The Cardinals nabbed him with the first of their three first-rounders, giving him full pick value to sign. During his pro debut, Perez showed all of the raw tools that had amateur scouts excited about his upside, all while dealing with the pre-Draft adversity with impressive maturity, though he didn't replicate that performance at the plate in 2017. For now, his defense is ahead of his bat, with no questions about his ability to stay at short long-term. He uses his outstanding speed well to cover a ton of ground and he has excellent hands and a strong arm to boot. He tends to try to do too much at times, something that he will harness as he gets more time under his belt. At the plate, he showed an ability to make hard contact at times, though he'll have to refine his approach and learn to recognize soft stuff better. He should grow into more power as he matures and his speed makes him a base-stealing threat. As time passes, Perez should be able to put his pre-Draft mistake more and more firmly in the rear-view mirror and show who he truly is. It could very well be that misstep allowed the Cardinals to acquire an elite-level player at a premium position.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: As a high schooler in Puerto Rico, Perez looked like he had a chance to be a five-tools monster. He was a svelte-but-strong 6-foot-3 with plus, unpolished bat speed, plus-plus footspeed and every physical trait necessary to stay at shortstop. A positive PED test ahead of the draft tanked his stock, and Perez exhibited a steady physical decline in the year and a half that followed this revelation. Still viable at shortstop, Perez's ability to swing the bat with verve has evaporated. His age and frame are still indicative of physical growth, but unless Perez reclaims some of the offensive explosion he showed in high school, he profiles as a glove-only shortstop prospect.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rincon joined the Dodgers organization for $350,000 as part of a 2015-16 international classic that included Yordan Alvarez, Yadier Alvarez and Yusniel Diaz. He put himself on the map with 13 homers and a 1.044 OPS over 52 games in the Dominican Summer League the following year but trailed off some due to low averages and high K rates in the seasons that followed. At age 23, Rincon looked like he was righting the ship in his second trip to Double-A in 2021 and was moved to the Mets last July in a trade for Billy McKinney. He finished with a .265/.334/.496 line and 22 homers between the two organizations, marking his third Minor League campaign with 20-plus dingers. As you might expect, power is what makes the 6-foot-3 right-handed slugger a notable prospect. Mets officials were quickly impressed by both his raw and in-game pop, and the latter plays so well because of Rincon’s ability to lift the ball, especially to his pull side. His 81 homers since 2017 (his first full season) are 16th-most in the Minor Leagues. Unfortunately, the power comes with whiff concerns; Rincon’s swinging strike rate of 17 percent was 17th-highest among 142 Double-A qualifiers, and it will only get worse at Triple-A or the Majors, barring changes. A below-average runner, Rincon is limited to the corner outfield spots. He has enough arm to play in right, and it was notable that the Mets moved him there after the trade, whereas the Dodgers featured him more in left. He doesn’t add much value defensively beyond the arm, and that places even more emphasis on the slugging ability. The 24-year-old will get to prove he can power his way to Queens with his first assignment to Triple-A in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Yet another recipient of Los Angeles' largesse during the 2015-16 international signing period, Rincon turned pro for $350,000 out of the Dominican Republic. His bonus was an investment in his power potential, which was evident when he homered 13 times in 52 games while batting .328/.383/.661 between two Rookie leagues in his 2016 pro debut. He made his U.S. debut ahead of schedule in late July and went deep twice in the second game after his arrival. Already 6-foot-3 and 190 pounds when he turned pro, Rincon has impressive strength and loft in his right-handed swing. The Dodgers have faith in his ability to hit for average as well as for power, though he'll need to do tone down his extremely aggressive approach to make consistent contact against better pitching. After coming to the States, he drew two walks and struck out 30 times in 105 plate appearances. Rincon moves well for his size, though he may lose some of his presently average speed as he matures physically. He's raw defensively but could become an average right fielder with more experience. He has the solid arm strength desired at his position.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: After posting an uninspiring line over three months of Midwest League play, Rincon went to the Cal League for the season's final month and went nuts. He hit 15 homers in just 29 games, slugging .818 during that span. The hitting environment in California caricatured his pop, but there's impact power here if Rincon can get to enough of it to profile in right. He's posted above-average walk rates over his last 600 plate appearances, which takes some pressure off the hit tool. This is a traditional, power/whiff right field profile who is starting to prove he has an approach.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 60 | Power: 45 | Run: 30 | Arm: 50 | Field: 40 | Overall: 40 Yurchak led NCAA Division I with a 41/12 BB/K ratio in 2017, his lone season at Binghamton after transferring from Wake Forest, prompting the White Sox to sign the redshirt sophomore for an over-slot $150,000 in the 12th round. The Dodgers acquired him in a November 2018 trade for Manny Banuelos that didn't appear to be very significant -- until last year. After going 4-for-42 in May, he batted .403 the rest of the way to lead the Minors in hitting (.365) and finish second in on-base percentage (.443). Thanks to his sweet left-handed swing, uncanny hand-eye coordination and fine command of the strike zone, Yurchak has posted a .321/.421/.466 line while advancing to Double-A in four pro seasons. While he's strong, he doesn't have much loft in his stroke and he doesn't produce high exit velocities. His hit-over-power approach might have him max out at 12-15 homers per season, which would make it difficult for him to profile as a regular at first base. First base and DH are the only realistic lineup options for Yurchak, who has well-below-average speed and athleticism. He's an adequate defender at best at first base, though he does have average arm strength. He has seen brief action at third base and left field as a pro but lacks the range for either position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Yurchak posted an .880 OPS as a Wake Forest freshman in 2015, outperforming future White Sox second-rounder Gavin Sheets, but opted to transfer closer to home to Binghamton. After sitting out 2016, he was a Cape Cod League all-star that summer and led NCAA Division I with a 41/12 K/BB ratio last spring. Signed for an over-slot $150,000 as a 12th-round redshirt sophomore last June, he batted .345/.448/.520 in the Rookie-level Pioneer League during his pro debut and had other clubs ask about him in trade talks. An on-base machine, Yurchak has a pretty left-handed stroke and controls the strike zone exceptionally well. He's strong and could develop average or better power if he adds some loft to his swing, though for now he's content to hammer line drives from gap to gap. He's somewhat of a lefty version of Kevin Youkilis at the same stage of their careers, though the Greek God of Walks demonstrated more pop. Yurchak will really have to hit, because all of his value comes from his bat. He's a well below-average runner and athlete who moved to first base after committing eight errors in 12 pro games at third base. He does have solid arm strength and Chicago hopes he can develop into an adequate defender at first.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One would be hard-pressed to find another pitcher in Seattle’s system who has endured as many obstacles since Draft Day as Carlson. Since being selected in the second round in 2017 out of a Minnesota high school, the righty underwent Tommy John surgery one year later, then came back in an emotional return in Spring Training in ‘20 only to be shut down by the league-wide closure. More than one year after that, he finally began his first full pro season. That topsy-turvy start to his career gave him a more grounded mental approach, and in his first full season, he impressed by making every start. The quirky Minor League schedule actually helped ease him into a no-limits workload, and he reached 100 innings over 19 starts with a 4.77 ERA. Essentially, everything was finally consistent for the 23-year-old, who is in the same age range as some of Seattle’s other top arms, such as George Kirby and Emerson Hancock, who were drafted after him. That gives Carlson a good outlook and strong upside. Before the shutdown in 2020, Carlson had added a lot of strength to his 6-foot-4 frame, which allowed him to reach back into the high 90s on his fastball. His changeup has always been solid and thrown with a ton of fade, and his slider has been above-average at times, though it wasn’t as consistent as the changeup. There’s a lot to like about his future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Carlson was always going to be a case of patience for the Mariners, who selected the righty out of high school in Minnesota in the second round in 2017, given that he was raised in a cold-weather state. But they didn’t anticipate that he would weather the significant setbacks, with just three professional innings so far. He underwent Tommy John surgery in July 2018 and was sidelined all of ’19, but returned in Spring Training in ’20 only to be shut down by the league-wide closure. But Carlson enters 2021 completely healthy – and that will be the biggest thing for the 22-year-old. Beyond the physical toll, there’s the mental factor of being back on a field again consistently. It understandably will take time for Carlson to regain feel for his three-pitch mix, but there is confidence that it all will eventually come back. Before the shutdown, he’d added a lot of strength to his 6-foot-4 frame, which gives the Mariners optimism that he’ll be able to get back up to the 93- to 97-mph range he showed on his fastball as a high school senior. His changeup has always been solid and thrown with a ton of fade, and his slider has been above average at times, though it wasn’t as consistent as the changeup. Carlson is likely headed to High-A Everett or Low-A Modesto to start the regular season. He'll need time to get his command and control back to his pre-injury levels, but the Mariners are excited to finally see what kind of pitching prospect they have on their hands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Mariners knew they would need to be patient when they selected Carlson out of the Minnesota high school ranks in the second round of the 2017 Draft, given he was coming from a northern, cold-weather state. They obviously weren’t thinking it would take him this long to get going, as the big right-hander has thrown just three professional innings from his summer debut. Tommy John surgery in July 2018, before he had pitched that year, then kept him off the mound for all of 2019. The good news is Carlson is 100 percent healthy for 2020, leaving the Mariners facility last fall ready to go. It will understandably take time for him to regain feel for his three-pitch mix, but there is confidence it will all eventually come back. He’s added a lot of strength to his 6-foot-4 frame, so seeing him get back to the 93-97 mph fastball he had as a high school senior doesn’t sound far-fetched. He’s always had a very good changeup, thrown with a ton of fade. His slider also flashed at least above-average at times, though it’s a more inconsistent pitch than his changeup. Carlson had always shown an advanced feel for his stuff, especially coming from cold weather. It will understandably take some time for him to get his command and control back to his pre-injury levels, but the Mariners are excited to finally see what kind of pitching prospect they have on their hands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Minnesota's Gatorade Player of the Year in 2017, Carlson skyrocketed up Draft boards that spring as his velocity improved to go along with his advanced pitchability. Unfortunately, the Mariners haven't gotten to see him pitch competitively much, as he made just a few outings during his summer debut, then needed Tommy John surgery last July without throwing a pitch in a game. Carlson was just finishing his rehab as pitchers and catchers were getting set to report to Spring Training and was playing catch out to 120 feet. The Mariners obviously won't rush the process, but they are eager to see how Carlson's stuff plays, especially because he's filled out his 6-foot-4 frame and is more man than kid now. During that senior year, Carlson's fastball sat in the 93-97 mph range and there's no reason to believe he can't get back to that, if not beyond that once he gets going, and he pairs it well with his fading changeup. His slider would flash plus before the injury, but it was inconsistent, so that will likely be an area of focus, and he always was able to fill up the strike zone with all three pitches. If all goes well, Carlson will get some mound time at the end of the summer in the rookie-level Arizona League. The 2020 season will be the first time the Mariners will get to see exactly what kind of pitcher Carlson might become.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked by MLB Pipeline as the No. 15 prospect in his class, Carlson became the fifth ever Minnesota prep to be taken in the second round when the Mariners selected him in June 2017. Carlson signed for $2 million, well above the recommended value of $1,206,900 for his slot, and made his professional debut the following month in the Rookie-level Arizona League, where he impressed scouts with two strong outings before Seattle shut him down for the season as a precautionary measure. Carlson would end up undergoing Tommy John the following July, effectively wiping out his 2018 season and putting '19 in jeopardy as well. After pitching at 88-92 mph with his fastball on the summer showcase circuit after his junior year, Carlson began to grow into his projectable frame and had his velocity pick up as a result. He sat in the low 90s and touched 95 at the WWBA World Championships in October and then worked at 93-97 mph as a senior during the spring. Scouts expect Carlson to tack on even more velocity in the coming years, while also noting that his heater already plays above its velocity because it has sinking and running life and he commands it well. Carlson also fills the strike zone with his slider, an above-average pitch, and his changeup, which features fade and sink. Unlike most high school pitchers, he trusts his changeup and uses it liberally. Though his future definitely is on the mound, the Florida recruit was also an interesting prospect as a right fielder with bat speed, power potential and arm strength -- a testament to his overall athleticism.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Carlson was a revered two-way high school prospect committed to Florida even though he was from Minnesota. He spent the summer before his draft year sitting in the low-90s and working with a better changeup and better command than is typical for a cold-weather, two-way player. His big, strapping frame portended more velocity. The following year, that velo arrived, and Carlson sat 93-97 for stretches of his pre-draft spring. Seattle drafted him in the second round, gave him $2 million, and Carlson made two starts in the AZL before he was quickly shut down. He had Tommy John and had a season wiped away by the pandemic, all of which piled up to nearly four years between when Carlson threw his last pitch in affiliated ball in 2017 to when he threw his next one, at Low-A in early 2021. His peak velocity has not returned, and Carlson has been more in the 91-93 range, topping out at 94, with some carry and tail. His arm action is still fairly long, his delivery has some head violence, and at a physical 22-years-old, I don't consider him a likely candidate to add velocity. His new-ish curveball has good back-foot angle against lefties and enough depth to miss bats, while his changeup remains a fair offering with tailing action. The entire package looks like a fifth starter (a 40) right now, but the way individuals in baseball either round up or down on that projection depends on what part of Carlson's prospectdom they choose to look at. Look at his draft pedigree and there's hope for more than that; look at his actual performance track record and there's skepticism. He needs to pitch well enough to be added to the 40-man this offseason and nobody is sure how his stuff and health will respond to a full-season workload after he's never even come close to pitching deep into season. I'm inclined to take the under on the hype and justifiably good feelings surrounding his return. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: We're still collectively waiting for Carlson to pitch coming off of Tommy John. At his prep peak, he was into the mid-90s with a good changeup and more strikes than is typical for such a hard-throwing, cold-weather prospect.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text:
Carlson has thrown just three pro innings since signing, as the minor flexor strain that shelved him after his draft turned out to be a prelude to surgery. He was given a PRP injection in an attempt to avoid Tommy John, but it was unsuccessful and he was operated on in early July of 2018. The timing of the surgery may keep Carlson out for all of 2019. When he finally returns, he'll be a 21-year-old with less developmental polish than a lot of teenage prospects from year-round baseball areas like Florida and Texas, as a former two-way, cold-weather high schooler who will have missed about 30 consecutive months of reps. 
The summer before his senior year, Carlson was 88-92 with better command and changeup feel than is typical for a northern prep arm. His velocity ticked up the following spring and he was touching 96, then sat 92-95 in his few pro innings before his injury. If his stuff comes back, he has No. 4 starter upside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Knowles signed with the Angels for $850,000 back in July 2017 out of the Bahamas and it looked like a strong investment when he hit .311 with a .391 on-base percentage in his pro debut across two levels of Rookie ball in 2018. He didn’t perform as well in 2019 and really struggled offensively with a move to full-season ball for the first time in 2021. The fact that Knowles is a super high-energy player is a plus, but it’s also an obstacle. While he’s capable of making hard contact from both sides of the plate, he needs to learn to slow things down and rediscover his approach. Early on, he would draw walks and work counts, but that regressed in 2021, with his strikeout rate ticking up as he chased out of the zone too frequently. There isn’t much power in his profile, so he needs to get back to putting the ball in play and letting his plus speed wreak havoc. On the plus side, the Angels had encouraged Knowles to use that speed more aggressively on the basepaths and he responded by going 31-for-32 in stolen-base attempts last year. He’s a capable defender in center field, but showed that not only can he handle all three outfield spots, but he started getting reps at shortstop as well. If he can get back to more regular contact, he could be an athletic super-utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels handed out bonuses of six figures or more during the 2017-18 international signing period, led, of course, by the signing of Shohei Ohtani. Knowles, a toolsy outfielder from the Bahamas, got the third-highest bonus from the organization that period, $850,000, then made a strong debut in the United States in 2018. His 2019 wasn’t as solid, but he appeared to make some very good strides on both sides of the ball in instructional league play in 2020. While Knowles’ numbers dipped in 2019, he still did show off a good amount of tools to work with. He can make hard contact to all fields from both sides of the plate, and even in 2019, showed an ability to work counts and draw walks. Strong, but not big, he’s not likely ever to have more than fringy power, but should have the ability to drive the ball to the gaps and use his speed to his advantage. The Angels continue to encourage Knowles to use that plus speed more on the basepaths to become a threat to steal, something that improved at instructs. Knowles has the chance to be a very good defensive center fielder, one who could stay there long-term, and he’s shown the ability to play all three outfield spots well. He’s also gotten some time at second base, but it’ll be how much his bat advances that will determine if he can reach his ceiling as an everyday big leaguer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There has been a total of six players from the Bahamas to make it to the big leagues. That’s likely to change as Major League teams have been looking to the Caribbean nation for talent of late, producing bigger-name prospects like Jazz Chisholm and Lucius Fox. Knowles, who signed for $850,000 at the start of the 2017-18 international signing period, isn’t as well-known yet, but has the tools to be part of the next wave of Bahamian big leaguers. As a 17-year old making his pro debut in the United States in 2018, Knowles set the expectations bar very high by putting up ridiculous numbers in two levels of rookie ball. Luck was on his side as he put up very inflated BABIP and that came down to earth with a return to the Pioneer League in 2019. Still one of the youngest players at his level, he did improve his approach beyond those numbers, cutting his strikeout rate and showing progress with his overall plate discipline. As the switch-hitter continues to refine that, he has the chance to be a solid hitter and there’s power to come, with most of it showing up now from the left side of the plate. A plus runner, Knowles is still learning how to steal a base. That speed helps him in the outfield and he’ll continue to get reps in all three spots, though he has the skills to play center full-time if needed. The Angels love his work ethic and his baseball IQ, providing confidence his performance will catch up to his tools as he plays all of 2020 at age 19.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While the Angels have been garnering a reputation of acquiring premium athletes in the early rounds of the Draft, they've also been busy bringing similar players via the international market. At the start of the 2017-18 international signing period, they double-dipped in the Bahamas, signing a pair of outfielders: Trent Deveaux for $1.2 million and Knowles for $850,000. It's been Knowles who broke out of the gate during his pro debut in 2018, earning a promotion from the Arizona to the Pioneer League. Throughout his first summer of pro ball, Knowles showed a solid approach from both sides of the plate, with excellent bat speed. There's emerging power, though it only showed up from the left side during his debut. He's not afraid to draw walks and could be a plus hitter as he continues to refine his approach, perhaps eventually with average big league pop. Knowles has plus speed and loves to use it, though he'll have to learn the nuances of basestealing. The Angels exposed the teenager to all three outfield spots, and he should have the range to play center field and enough arm to man right. Some of that might depend on how he continues to develop as he hopes to join prospects like Jazz Chisholm of the D-backs and the Rays' Lucius Fox in putting Bahamanian baseball more firmly on the map.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Knowles has electric tools -- a plus arm, plus-plus speed, sneaky power for a guy his size -- and until 2021 has been very young for the levels at which he's played (2.5 years younger than average, per BRef), which puts his statline in better context. That's not to say Knowles' bat doesn't need polish. His left-handed swing (this system has a lot of switch-hitters) is pretty grooved and long, leaving him vulnerable on the inner third. I think he's likely to be strikeout prone from that side for good. From the right side, he might be able to do real damage. He has great feel for the zone, his swing is just limited from the left side in an important way. I have him projected as a fourth outfielder.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Knowles has electric tools -- a plus arm, plus-plus speed, sneaky power for a guy his size -- and is the same age as several players who the Angels left back in the AZL. He didn't hit especially well -- .240/.310/.387 -- but was 2.5 years younger than the average player in that league. That's not to say Knowles' bat doesn't need polish. His left-handed swing (this system has a lot of switch-hitters) is pretty grooved, and I think he's likely to be strikeout prone from that side for good. From the right side, he might be able to do real damage. Knowles needs more reps in center as his reads on balls are mixed. Again, Knowles is a 19-year-old switch hitter and it's possible that his feel to hit from the left side still develops. If it doesn't, he easily projects as a fourth outfielder who could be the short half of a platoon at any outfield spot.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Knowles was still just 16 when he came stateside for his first pro instructional league. He was 17 for the entirety of his first pro season, and one of the few bright spots on an underperforming AZL Angels team. A sizable chunk of Knowles' AZL power output was BABIP-driven (his speed is especially meaningful against rookie-level defenses), but despite his measureables, he does have some pop thanks to his explosiveness and ability to rotate, enough that there's little concern about him lacking big league physicality. His footspeed enables projection in center field and while he's had early-career issues with strikeouts, he's not one to expand the zone and instead has the bat-control issues that are typical of early-career switch hitters. Though his bat-to-ball future is cloudy, Knowles' slashing, doubles power as a teen combined with the likelihood he can play center field give him a shot to be an everyday player if he develops as a hitter. If not, he'd be a pretty toolsy fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fourth-round pick in 2018 after he won Big West Conference player of the year accolades at Cal Poly, McKenna slugged a feeble .303 in his full-season debut the following year. He used his pandemic layoff to add strength, hit the ball with more authority than ever in instructional league in 2020 and then got off to a .305/.390/.616 start. He injured his shoulder a week after his promotion to Double-A, missed a month and didn't hit nearly as well once he returned. More of a disciplined hitter who peppered the gaps in college, McKenna now is pulling the ball in the air with more authority. His bat speed and strength give him solid raw pop from the right side of the plate and he's doing a better job of tapping into it. His 34 percent strikeout rate last year leads to question about whether his power-seeking approach will work against more advanced pitchers, and Houston did leave him off its 40-man roster last November. A solid runner, McKenna can steal an occasional base and cover ground in the outfield. While he's not a burner, his quickness and instincts allow him to get the job done in center field. He has solid arm strength and threw out eight runners in 74 games last season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the 2018 Draft's best college hitters on the West Coast, McKenna won Big West Conference player of the year honors last spring after batting .339/.424/.506 for Cal Poly. After signing for $430,000 as a fourth-rounder, he posted similar numbers while reaching low Class A in his pro debut. McKenna used a disciplined approach to drill line drives from gap to gap in college, then made a more concerted effort to drive the ball in his first taste of pro ball. His bat speed and strength give him solid raw power, which translated into more home runs when he added more loft to his right-handed stroke. He has solid speed and runs the bases well but isn't much of a basestealer. McKenna profiles better as a regular if he can stay in center field, where he played in college and most of his debut. His quickness and instincts allow him to cover ground, and his average arm will work on either corner if he has to move or serve as a fourth outfielder.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text:
McKenna had a solid Cape Cod League, putting him on the radar for the top couple rounds, but some scouts thought his lack of patience could be his undoing going forward. McKenna is somewhere around the somewhat classic profile of a power-over-hit center fielder with more tools than skills, but that archetype is in demand now more than ever. McKenna has above average raw power and speed and enough hitting skills to get to around average offensively, and around average defensively in center field. 
At times, he's shown a flat-planed swing that doesn't tap into his power and other times he's over-aggressive, but Houston thinks they can tap into this skillset and thought he was a nice value with performance and low-end regular upside in the fourth round.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez was far from a big name on the international stage when he signed with the Cardinals as a 19-year-old in January 2016, but he commanded attention after hitting .322/.400/.580 with seven homers over 40 games in the Dominican Summer League in his first Minor League season. He climbed steadily through the system and earned a Florida State League midseason All-Star spot in 2019 before jumping to Double-A Springfield. He was set to return to that level in 2021, only to break his hamate bone playing winter ball back home in the Dominican Republic. Following February surgery, he played briefly for Springfield in May, suffered a setback and came back for good in late July. The right-handed slugger hit just .196/.252/.299 with three homers over 29 games in Double-A last season, numbers that were clearly affected by the hamate injury, which can typically sap players of their power in the early stages of recovery. Still, Rodriguez has a history of being aggressive at the plate, and while his bat-to-ball skills keep the strikeout rates from being high, that aggression also keeps him from developing much power. It’s an all-defensive-type profile anyway. Rodriguez’s arm has always been effective at limiting the running game, and even with the hand issues, he threw out 9 of 14 (64 percent) of attempted basestealers with Springfield last season. He’s a quality blocker and receiver out of his 6-foot, 245-pound frame, and it’s clear Cardinals pitchers enjoy working with him behind the plate. It’s a clear glove-first backup profile, and after Rodriguez was passed over twice for a 40-man spot when Rule 5-eligible, a healthy 2022 could get him closer to achieving that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in January 2016 as a 19-year-old, Rodriguez was initially expected to be an organizational roster-filler but has surpassed expectations thanks in large part to his offensive development. He hit .322 with seven homers over 40 games in the Dominican Summer League in his professional debut and has continued his upward trajectory in the Cardinals’ system, including midseason All-Star honors in the Florida State League in 2019. Rodriguez suffered a broken hamate bone after being hit by a pitch in winter ball. He underwent surgery in February and after getting off to a late start in his 2021 campaign, he found himself on the injured list once again, though he returned in early August. Rodriguez’s defensive skillset is what drew the Cardinals to him initially. The backstop has a strong, accurate arm and has thrown out 69% of attempted basestealers over the first four years of his professional career. Offensively, Rodriguez has an overly aggressive approach, but flashes some power -- he hit a combined 16 homers in 2017 and ’18 -- and has made noticeable strides since signing. There’s certainly value to having a defensive-minded catcher like Rodriguez in a system keen on developing pitching prospects. If he continues to improve his overall game and reaches the Majors, it’s likely he’ll do so in a reserve role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An older international prospect whom the Cardinals signed at age 19 in January 2016, Rodriguez was originally viewed as an organizational roster-filler based on his defensive merits. But the Dominican catcher proved a more complete player than initially thought during his pro debut, showing feel to hit and power potential in the Dominican Summer League, and has continued to make strides offensively while incrementally climbing through the Cardinals' system. After a solid first full season at Class A Peoria, Rodriguez moved up to Class A Advanced Palm Beach in 2019 and garnered midseason All-Star honors in the Florida State League before receiving a late promotion to Double-A. Rodriguez's abilities behind the plate are obvious. He does a good job controlling the running game with his plus, accurate arm, and has been praised by evaluators for his catch-and-throw skills, with many noting his consistent footwork and quick release. He moves well in spite of his stocky frame and is regarded as a good receiver and framer who also can handle a pitching staff. Offensively, Rodriguez has feel for finding the barrel and will flash some pull-side power from the right side of the plate, albeit with an overly aggressive approach that can at times undercut his pure hitting ability and on-base skills. Cardinals officials view Rodriguez as a valuable player to have in a system that is always looking to develop pitching prospects. He appears ticketed for a backup role at the highest level if he can continue to make strides on both sides of the ball, and there's a non-zero chance that he will achieve such a role based simply on his defensive chops.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: My pre-draft report on Vogel was light compared to the kind of bonus he got from the Dodgers and what he looked like during Instructional League, so he's moved up a FV tier into the 40s. I initially had him in as a one-tool speedster with some crude bat control, but he hit the ball pretty consistently during the Fall, and against advanced pitching. I'm still skeptical about his power projection but with his speed and the defensive fit it enables in center field, all he needs is a vanilla blend of contact and power to be a useful big leaguer. (Alternate site, Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020updated
fangraphs.text: Vogel is a speedster with some bat control, but his stride could be much more athletic and enable him to get balls near the bottom of the zone more consistently than he did last summer. He's a toolsy developmental project.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Vogel was one of the fastest and most athletic high schoolers in the 2020 Draft, he also came with concerns about his physicality (he was the lightest player selected at 165 pounds), swing and strong commitment to UCLA. That enabled the Dodgers to take the local Southern California product with the 100th overall choice and sign him for a well-over-slot $1,622,500. He spent most of his 2021 pro debut in Low-A, where he hit .231/.323/.339 with a 30 percent strikeout rate and 12 steals in 76 games. Vogel's best tool is his plus-plus speed and he ran the fastest 60-yard dash (6.15 seconds) at the 2019 Perfect Game National Showcase. He's a potentially dynamic basestealer and could become a plus defender in center field once he refines his reads and routes. His plus arm is stronger than most in center. Vogel had an awkward load in his right-handed stroke when he turned pro, and Los Angeles is trying to help him smooth it out with some mechanical changes. He has good hand-eye coordination and can display electric bat speed at times, but he must get stronger so he can impact the ball more regularly. He did add 15 pounds this offseason, though he'll also need to develop a more patient approach to get going at the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Vogel was one of the better athletes in the 2020 Draft, he lasted until the third round because he lacked physicality (he was the lightest player selected at 165 pounds), missed a lot of the summer showcase circuit with a back injury and had a strong commitment to UCLA. The Dodgers pounced on the Southern California prep product with the 100th overall pick and signed him for a well over-slot $1,622,500. He was the youngest player (age 18) at their alternate site during the summer and performed well in instructional league. Vogel ran the fastest 60-yard dash (6.15 seconds) at the 2019 Perfect Game National Showcase and consistently displays plus-plus speed. He uses his quickness to create chaos on the bases and cover a lot of ground in center field, where his instincts could make him a plus defender. He also has a plus arm, stronger than most in center, and can play anywhere in the outfield. Vogel has both offensive upside and work to do at the plate. In addition to his quickness, which should help him get on base, he also can flash some electric bat speed and shows feel for recognizing pitches. He has an awkward load in his right-handed swing that can lead to swings and misses, however, so Los Angeles will try to smooth out his stroke and get him to drive the ball more consistently.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Bacwards guy with a weird swing, but has power and feel for the barrel.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Most colleges recruited Barefoot as a pitcher, so he chose Campbell because it was the lone school that offered him a chance to hit. He missed his first season recovering from ankle surgery before starring as a redshirt sophomore in 2018, winning batting title in the Big South Conference (.364) and Cape Cod League (.379) as well as the Cape MVP award. He had an injury-marred pro debut after signing as a sixth-rounder in 2019, then saw his OPS decline from 1.017 in Low-A to .895 in High-A to .525 in Double-A during his first full pro season last year. A rare bats-right/throws-left player, Barefoot has a busy swing but makes it work thanks to his hand-eye coordination. Predominantly a contact hitter in college, he's now looking to launch balls in the air, which has resulted in inconsistent production and a 30 percent strikeout rate in his first two years as a pro. He was overmatched in his first taste of Double-A and will have to make better swing decisions in order to realize his 20-homer potential. Barefoot is deceptively athletic and can flash plus speed and arm strength. He's an aggressive baserunner who used his quickness to steal 21 bases in 25 attempts in 2021. He can play an average center field but fits better in right, where he's a solid defender and shows off an arm that was clocked up to 94 mph during his brief stints on the mound at Campbell.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hajjar was a solid pitching prospect while in high school in Massachusetts, but opted not to sign with the Brewers as a late-round choice in 2018 to honor his commitment to Michigan. He missed his freshman year after tearing his ACL playing pickup basketball, but came back and led the Wolverines rotation the next two years. While his stuff wasn’t super-sharp, he led the Big Ten in strikeouts in 2021 and landed in the second round of the Draft, where the Twins signed him to full slot. He was missing a lot of bats, albeit with a surprisingly high walk rate, in Single-A when he was part of the crop of prospects the Reds got from the Twins in return for Tyler Mahle at the Trade Deadline. The big lefty didn’t throw an official pitch for the Twins after a full workload at Michigan, but they were thrilled to see his stuff tick up in the short time they worked with Hajjar after he signed. While his fastball averaged around 90 mph in college in 2021, he was more around 93 mph, touching a bit higher, in bullpen sessions with the Twins, though he was averaging around 92 mph in the Florida State League this year. He can miss bats with all of his secondary offerings and he used his plus low-80s changeup with good tumble and his upper-70s curveball effectively last year. He’s been working to add velocity to his low-80s slider and to focus on adding lateral movement to it so it can be a better weapon against left-handed hitters. Hajjar’s overhand delivery creates deception, making him a tougher at-bat. He generally has a good feel for pitching, though he’s struggled with walks during his full-season debut, with a good chance to improve improve his command as he progresses, with perhaps more in the tank as he keeps adding strength to that 6-foot-5 frame.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Endersby was recruited as an infielder but moved to the mound at Cal State Fullerton, where he totaled 16 2/3 innings in three years before transferring to Concordia (Calif.). He made just five starts at the NCAA Division II level during the shortened 2020 season, yet impressed the Astros enough to sign for $20,000 as a nondrafted free agent. He spent most of his 2021 pro debut in Double-A and struck out 110 in 97 innings. Endersby employs the north-south attack pattern that Houston favors. He goes after hitters with a 92-95 mph four-seam fastball with high spin rates and carry up in the zone and an upper-70s curveball with downer break. He also has a harder slider with sweeping action and a nascent changeup that lags behind the rest of his offerings. Endersby lacks physicality but he's athletic and has a quick arm. His control and command come and go, as does the consistency of his secondary pitches, so it's more likely that he winds up as a reliever than a starter. If he moves to the bullpen and concentrates on his fastball and curveball, he could reach the big leagues in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Berryhill's college career took him from Georgia Southern to Walters State (Tenn.) CC to South Carolina before he signed with the Reds for $149,500 as a redshirt sophomore in 2019. After the Astros acquired him in exchange for Cionel Perez in January 2021, he won the organization's Minor League Player of the Year award by batting .295/.413/.562 with 15 homers in 73 games at three levels. An aspiring country singer, he performed the national anthem before games at Low-A Fayetteville and High-A Asheville last season. Berryhill started seeing the ball better last year once he started wearing contacts. His best tools is his plus raw power from the right side of the plate, and he started getting to it more consistently once he started making adjustments to close a hole at the top of his strike zone. He concentrates on launching balls to his pull side, which led to a 30 percent strikeout rate in his first full pro season, but he also draws a healthy number of walks. Surprisingly athletic for a 6-foot-1, 227-pound catcher, Berryhill has below-average speed and runs the bases well. Though he's relatively inexperienced behind the plate, he has soft hands and decent receiving skills, while his arm is fringy. He profiles as an offensive-minded backup who also can handle first base.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Over his four years at Princeton, Smith both relieved and started. He had his strongest year in the Tigers' rotation as a senior, enough for the Angels to take a low-risk flier on the left-hander in Round 18 of the 2019 Draft, signing him for just $3,000. After pitching out of the bullpen during his pro debut that summer, Smith took the opportunity to start in 2021 and ran with it, pitching across four levels to finish in Triple-A. Smith does have four pitches at his disposal, all coming from his strong, though undersized, 5-foot-11 frame. His fastball averaged around 92 mph in 2021, touching 94, but it plays up some because it has good ride up in the zone. His slider, a sweeper with a ton of horizontal movement, is his best secondary offering that can miss bats, a big reason why he struck out 10.6 per nine last season. His slower curve isn’t as good, but serves as a good get-me-over pitch for strike one and he uses his changeup effectively while starting to mix in a new cutter as well. Throughout his college career, Smith struggled with command, walking 4.4 per nine. He threw a ton more strikes in 2021, nearly cutting that walk rate in half. He’s on the map now, with the chance to serve as a No. 5 starter/long reliever type in the big leagues soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed in the 2019-20 international class for $350,000, Labrada made his debut among the Mariners’ Top 30 prospects for the first time in spring 2022 after wowing with his speed the season prior. Though the consensus is that Jonatan Clase might be the fastest player in Seattle’s system, Labrada led all Mariners Minor Leaguers with 32 stolen bases last year over 99 games. At 5-foot-9 and 165 pounds, he may be short in stature but he packs physicality. He possesses a good, compact swing from the left side, but is certainly more of a hit-over-power prospect. With his glove, Labrada profiles in center field given that he has advanced range, great jump, and again, elite speed. After graduating in 2021 from Low-A Modesto to High-A Everett, Labrada saw a dip in offensive production, but not an astronomical one. He still showed decent on-base skills and will continue to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Big league caliber talent can be found just about anywhere and Diaz has the chance to prove that true. Taken in the 27th round of the 2019 Draft out of Michigan State, where he relieved for a year after two years at Iowa Western Community College, Diaz put himself on the map in 2021 with a huge full-season debut that saw him earn a promotion from High-A to Double-A and strike out 16.6 per nine for the year. He wasn’t as dominant post-promotion and he struggled to find the strike zone during his time in the Arizona Fall League, a trend that continued in Double-A in 2022. Diaz is a 6-foot-5 right-hander who profiles as a reliever only. He can get his fastball up to 97 mph, but typically sits around 92-93 mph. It plays up because of its carry in the zone and his extension coming down the mound. His power breaking ball can get slurvy, and it has good depth, but because of the mid-80s velocity, it plays more like a slider. Diaz generally had shown a penchant for throwing strikes somewhat consistently, generally attacking the zone and going right after hitters, but his walk rate continued to climb with Mississippi in 2022. He doesn’t need pinpoint command to fill a prominent role in a big league bullpen, something he should be able to do once he shows he can handle the upper levels of the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Collins starred at McKinney Boyd High School in Texas and looked like he might be headed to Oklahoma State for college ball. The Braves loved his speed and feel to hit enough to nab him in the eighth round of the 2021 Draft, signing him for an above-slot $447,500 and making him the first ever draftee from his school. Collins returned their faith in him by hitting .347/.424/.453 with 12 steals in 23 Florida Complex League games. The left-handed hitting outfielder’s calling card is his speed, which is nearly close to top of the scale. He’s a legitimate basestealing threat who registers very low times from home to first and uses his legs well to stretch singles to doubles and doubles to triples. He can make a lot of contact, but is content to spray the ball around the field. He’s not likely to ever be a big power guy, but added strength will help him impact the ball more consistently. Collins’ speed is also an asset in the outfield and while he’ll need to sharpen his reads and routes, he does have the chance to stick in center field. If he can keep getting on base and get strong enough to drive the ball a little, he could profile as an intriguing table-setting type in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted out of Corona Del Mar High School in California, Schwartz headed to UCLA, where he redshirted his freshman year and only saw 15 games in the shortened 2020 season. His big breakout finally came last spring when he hit .396/.514/.628 with eight homers and a 28/37 K/BB ratio in 44 games for the Bruins. Those numbers made him the Pac-12 batting champion and earned him a spot on the All-Conference Team. The Mets selected Schwartz in the fourth round and went slightly under slot to sign him for $475,000. He walked more than he struck out (13 vs. 12) but otherwise saw minimal results with a .195 average and a .576 OPS in his first 25-game trip to the Minors with Low-A St. Lucie. Despite standing in the box at 6-foot-4, Schwartz isn’t your typical slugging first first baseman. He’s shown an advanced approach everywhere he’s played over the last four years, including in summer-ball circuits, and as he proved in his final season on campus, he makes enough quality contact to sustain a good batting average. However, he doesn’t have a long history of hitting the ball over fences, and before the Draft, some evaluators were concerned that previous shoulder, knee and hip problems would keep him from showing even average power in games. Schwartz is first-base only on defense, and the Mets secured that by giving him all 24 of his defensive starts at the cold corner with St. Lucie. He faces a high offensive threshold there, and simply producing a solid average and OBP might not be enough to meet it. Schwartz is staring up at Pete Alonso on the Mets’ first-base depth chart, so he needn’t press to expedite his route toward Citi Field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Peroza played out of Carlos Guillen’s academy in Venezuela before signing with the Mets for $280,000 on July 2, 2016. He moved stateside in his first Minor League season after a solid debut in the Dominican Summer League, but it was a slow climb from there. Because of late development and the 2020 canceled season, the right-handed slugger didn’t see full-season ball until last year. It was at Low-A St. Lucie that he put up his best numbers yet -- .274/.404/.442, seven homers in 64 games. His numbers after a promotion to High-A Brooklyn were slightly stifled by an extreme pitchers' environment at Coney Island. It’s a classic power-first, corner-infielder profile. Peroza’s top exit velocity at Low-A was 110.6 mph, and he had two of the six hardest hit balls by a St. Lucie batter, despite his limited experience there. He shows natural strength from his 6-foot-1, 221-pound frame, and he plays into it with good lift at the plate. (Of his batted balls in St. Lucie, 42.3 percent were fly balls.) He showed promising patience with a 12.6 percent walk rate between the two levels, but that also led to him striking out in about a quarter of his plate appearances. That K rate could go up as he climbs toward Queens. Peroza’s above-average arm makes him a good fit for third base, though a lack of speed and range may move him to first, especially considering the Mets’ Minor League depth at the hot corner. His trajectory when it comes to getting the raw power to play in games will get him a chance to fight for a place in the New York infield hierarchy.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last 40-round Draft could very well be the 2019 edition. One year before that, the Mets used their 40th-round selection on Metoyer out of NAIA program Louisiana State University of Alexandria. He was dominant in relief for High-A Brooklyn in 2021 with a 2.18 ERA, 0.91 WHIP and 46 strikeouts in 33 innings with the Cyclones and made a late two-game appearance at Double-A Binghamton. The right-hander closed out his age-24 season in the Arizona Fall League, where he fanned 17 but walked 10 while allowing 12 earned runs in 10 1/3 innings. Lanky at a listed 6-foot-3 and 173 pounds, Metoyer earns the biggest praise for his curveball, a plus-plus offering that could play in the Majors right away. The 79- to 81-mph deuce regularly pops 3,000-plus rpm, and he posted the 35 highest spin rates as measured by Statcast in last year’s Fall League. The vertical break toward the bottom of the zone helps generate a high ground-ball rate, and his 69.2 GB percentage was tops among Mets pitchers with at least 30 innings in 2021. The right-hander is typically around 94-96 mph with a cutting fastball, helping keep balls on the dirt. Metoyer went to the AFL to work on a changeup, but that remains a distant third pitch. Because of all the movement, Metoyer can struggle to stay in the zone. That lack of control (along with the lackluster third pitch) keeps him in relief, and it played into the Mets’ decision to leave him off the 40-man roster last November when he became Rule 5-eligible. The velocity and spin of the curveball give him enough of an arsenal to feature in a Major League bullpen, and a back-end role is possible if he can land more strikes in 2022.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Phillies signed Azuaje out of Venezuela for $400,000 as part of an aggressive 2018-19 international signing period for the organization that saw them hand out bonuses of six figures or more to 15 players. He had a solid, if unspectacular, debut in the Dominican Summer League in 2019, missed 2020 because of the shutdown, then came to the United States and the Florida Complex League in 2021, where he swung the bat well, albeit in a 19-game sample. Small and stocky, Azuaje reminds some of former big league infielder Placido Polanco in terms of body type. He makes a ton of contact with a hit-over-power approach from the right side of the plate, showing the ability to send line drives to all fields. He’s had some home run pop show up, with five homers in 45 at-bats in the FCL, but he can get too overly aggressive at the plate and will have to keep refining his approach. When the Phillies first signed Azuaje, he was a plus runner with 6.5 speed. He’s physically matured and slowed down to be more of an average runner, though he’s worked to get in better shape. While he’s played three infield positions in his brief career, his best spot is second, the position he has the greatest chance to become an offensive-minded regular at.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals signed Luis García, Yasel Antuna and Israel Pineda -- one prospect graduate and two Top 30 stalwarts -- as part of their 2016-17 international class. Méndez, a $600,000 signing out of Venezuela, did not quite make the same noise on the professional scene during the early years of his career. That changed in 2021. The 5-foot-10 outfielder hit .287/.343/.440 with five homers, 36 total extra-base hits and 11 steals in 85 games at Low-A and High-A. His 111 wRC+ was third-best among Nats Minor League qualifiers. It’s the hit tool that drives Méndez’s rise to prospect prominence these days. He exhibits a repeatable swing from the left side, allowing him to display strong bat-to-ball skills. While he did strike out roughly a quarter of the time in 2021, Méndez does make decently hard contact when he strikes the ball, leading to an average hit projection. Double-digit homers might be a stretch with the power and launch angle playing more to gaps than over the fence. With above-average speed, Méndez is a threat to steal and can cover ground in the outfield. He played all three spots last year, but his below-average arm plays better in left or center. Nationals officials have drawn comparisons to Grégor Blanco, the 10-year Major Leaguer who was light on power but added speed and defensive value. That would be a positive outcome at its most extreme for Méndez, but it paints a picture of what type of player he could be if the 2021 gains continue.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were certainly bigger names and bigger players than the 5-foot-9 Rivero in the Nationals’ 2018-19 international signing class, and in part because of the 2020 canceled season, it took the shortstop a little longer to prove himself within the system. That opportunity came last summer when Rivero hit .270/.409/.416 with three homers and more walks (19) than strikeouts (17) over 32 games in the Florida Complex League. Rivero was signed in the first place primarily because of his glovework at the premium position of shortstop. He shows exciting fluidity at the six and has looked like a smooth natural at that spot on the diamond ever since he entered pro ball. He gets rid of the ball quickly with a good arm too, giving him multiple ways to impact the game defensively. What earned Rivero his spot on this list, however, was his offensive improvements. He thrives on making a good amount of contact, and the Nationals have been enthused by how well he’s protected the plate at this early stage. The bat doesn’t come with much power, however, and for all Rivero’s defensive strengths, he isn’t much more than an average runner underway. Good, if light, hitters that are also no-doubt shortstops tend to find their ways onto Major League rosters. Rivero’s fit of that profile will be tested when he sees full-season ball for the first time in 2022, just before he becomes Rule 5-eligible in the offseason.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Ueckert logged a 6.17 ERA as a 23-year-old McNeese State senior in 2019, his arm strength intrigued the Cubs enough for them to sign him for $5,000 in the 27th round. He didn't get past Rookie ball in his pro debut and lost a year of development to the pandemic shutdown, so he began 2021 as an almost-25-year-old in High-A. He finished it in Double-A with a combined 1.45 ERA and 37 strikeouts in 31 innings between the two stops and turned himself into a legitimate prospect. Opponents batted just .129/.228/.238 against Ueckert, who took to some mechanical changes and came back from his layoff with dramatically improved stuff. His fastball gained 3-4 mph and now sits at 95-97 mph and reaches 99 with good carry in the zone. He backs it up with a short slider that often climbs into the low 90s and ties up both left-handers and right-handers. Ueckert has gotten stronger and has cleaned up his delivery since signing, which gave a boost to not only his stuff but also his control. He cut his walk rate from 5.7 per nine innings in two years at McNeese State to 4.6 in his debut to 3.5 last season. If he can build off his momentum from 2021, he could pitch in the big leagues this year and develop into a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A .333 hitter over his two seasons as a leadoff man at Texas Tech, Holt inspired something in Brewers scouts because -- despite not being ranked among MLB Pipeline’s Top 200 in the 2019 Draft class -- he signed for $450,000 (the third-highest bonus given out by Milwaukee that year) as a seventh-rounder. After not being an instructional league standout in 2020, Holt certainly played to his strengths in his first full season last year, hitting .283/.403/.341 with 17 steals and a 52/68 K/BB ratio in 97 games at High-A and Double-A. In case that last stat didn’t make it clear, Holt hates to strike out. With two strikes, he will get wide in his left-handed hitting stance and choke up to spray the ball anywhere in play, bucking modern trends. As a result, he fanned only 11.8 percent of the time between Wisconsin and Biloxi last season for the best K rate among Milwaukee full-season qualifiers. Of course, Holt needs to be a big-time contact hitter because he showcases little raw power; only 18 of his 102 hits last season went for extra bases. A part-time outfielder in college, Holt split his time between second and third base in 2021. Despite good speed to help with range, he doesn’t quite have the hands to stick up the middle, meaning he might have to spend more time at the hot corner. He has the arm for the position, if not the traditional offensive profile associated with it. Whether it’s his speed or contact rate, Holt finds little ways to put his stamp on games, and it’s in those margins that he might carve out a Major League infield role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A teammate of fellow Cardinal Lars Nootbaar at USC, Lunn didn’t become a starter until his junior year in 2019, and he posted a 3.69 ERA with 79 strikeouts in 83 innings that spring. The Cardinals selected him in the 11th round and signed him for $125,000 -- the max they could without dipping into their bonus pool. Lunn’s full-season debut had to wait until 2021, and he spent it entirely with High-A Peoria, where he was a strike-throwing machine, especially late. He walked only five batters over his final 10 starts with the Chiefs and finished with a 3.96 ERA with 121 strikeouts and 20 walks over 120 1/3 frames. His 4.1 percent walk rate led Cardinals full-season qualifiers and was second among High-A starters. The 6-foot-3 right-hander won’t necessarily bowl anyone over with stuff. He throws around 90-92 mph with the fastball, though it features good ride at the top of the zone and he spots it well. A mid-70s, loopier curveball tunnels well off the heater, leaving some High-A hitters shaking their heads heading back to the dugout. He’ll throw the occasional low-80s slider as well to give another breaking-ball look, though it doesn’t pop the same way as the curve, and a mid-80s, though occasionally firm, changeup helped him keep pretty solid splits against righties and lefties. The strike-throwing ability is what makes Lunn pop, and it was certainly encouraging the way he grew into that skill as 2021 went on. It’s control over command, though, and he can get occasionally rocked if the stuff is too much in the zone, especially the fastball. The control will keep him in a starting role as he enters the upper Minors, but if the stuff is to truly tick up, a move back to the bullpen for the first time since 2018 might be in the cards down the line.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A late addition to Chicago's 2018-19 international class, Sanchez signed for $80,000 out of Venezuela. He made his U.S. debut in 2021 at age 19, earning a promotion to Low-A after just a month in Rookie ball. He has one of the higher ceilings among White Sox position prospects, though he'll also need plenty of development time. Sanchez's most noticeable tool is his plus-plus speed, which he used to swipe 17 bases in 18 attempts over 53 games last year. After employing a patient, contact-oriented approach in his 2019 pro debut, he got much more pull-conscious and launch-happy last year. A right-handed hitter, he needs to make better swing decisions, focus on getting on base and let his modest home run power come naturally. Sanchez plays with constant energy and is arguably the best infield defender among White Sox farmhands. He's extremely reliable and made just three errors in 70 games at shortstop last season, a remarkable performance for a shortstop. He has the actions, quickness and plus arm to remain at short and the tools to play all over the diamond.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dominguez was ancient by international standards when he signed with the Brewers at age 20 for $7,500 out of the Dominican Republic in February 2016. He had spent three seasons in Rookie ball when Milwaukee flipped him to the White Sox two years later along with outfield prospect Bryan Connell to acquire Xavier Cedeno in August 2018. He pitched at the upper three levels of Chicago's system in 2021, though he got shelled in two Triple-A starts in September and again during the Arizona Fall League. Though he's 6-foot-4, Dominguez utilizes a lower three-quarters arm slot that imparts good induced vertical break on a four-seam fastball that sits at 93-95 mph and reaches 97 with late life. He throws two breaking balls, with his 82-85 mph slider that features more depth than sweep grading better than his 75-79 mph curveball. He can flash some average changeups with fade, but his cambio gets too firm and he has trouble landing it for strikes. After averaging 3.4 walks per nine innings in his first four pro seasons, Dominguez cut that rate to 2.2 in 2021. If his improved control is for real, he has a chance to become a back-of-the-rotation starter. If not, he's likely a fastball/slider middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2022 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Gonzalez didn't attract a lot of scouting attention as a Puerto Rican high schooler, the White Sox liked him enough to sign him for an over-slot $185,000 in the 12th round of the 2019 Draft. After looking overmatched in his pro debut that summer, he fared much better in his return to Rookie ball in 2021, more than doubling his OPS from .483 to .988. He struggled again following a promotion to Low-A, so his development is going to take time. Few White Sox prospects can match Gonzalez's combination of raw power and speed, both of which grade as plus. The right-handed hitter is still unrefined at the plate, focusing more on launching balls to his pull side rather than prioritizing hard contact. He won't make nearly enough of his bat speed and projectable strength unless he reduces his 37 percent strikeout rate from his first two pro seasons. While Gonzalez still is learning how to make the most of his quickness on the bases, it's more apparent in the outfielder. He exhibits solid range and an average arm in center field. He shifted to right field in Low-A in deference to speedster James Beard and is capable of handling all three outfield spots.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: He's been held behind his fellow 2016 class members because Barley's on-field decision-making and consistency are taking longer to cook. He still makes the occasional highlight reel defensive play, runs 4.10, or hits a 420-foot bomb and as long as he's doing that stuff, he'll have a home on these lists. For now, that Barley both went to an affiliate in 2019 and performed there was a big step. He needs to keep doing that. His physical ability is not in question; he needs to level up from a baseball procedure and consistency standpoint. (Fall Instructional League)
