mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Boston gave seven-figure bonuses to three Venezuelans in 2017: catcher Daniel Flores ($3.1 million), who died of cancer four months later; and infielders Flores ($1.4 million) and Danny Diaz ($1.6 million), who quickly emerged as two of the best position prospects in a rebuilding farm system. Flores was advanced enough offensively and defensively to make his U.S. debut at age 17 last summer, though he missed six weeks after straining his left shoulder on a swing. One rival club told the Red Sox they considered him the best prospect in the organization. With a controlled but quick right-handed swing and an advanced approach for a teenager, Flores should hit for a high average. He controls the strike zone and employs the entire field, and his hitting ability and deceptive strength give him the chance to develop 20-homer power. While he's only an average runner and could lose a half-step as he matures physically, he has good instincts on the bases. Flores also shows nice savvy in the field, where he covers more ground at shortstop than his speed might suggest. He's a fluid defender with soft hands and the arm strength to make all the required throws at short. In the event he slows down and requires a shift to third base, he has the offensive potential to profile there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of three Venezuelans to receive seven-figure signing bonuses from the Red Sox in 2017, Flores turned pro for $1.4 million. He's no relation to Daniel Flores, who died of cancer four months after signing for $3.1 million. His tools are fairly similar to those of C.J. Chatham's, Boston's top shortstop prospect, though Flores is much further away from the big leagues. Though Flores receives more praise for his instincts than his tools, he has the ability to contribute both offensively and defensively. He has good actions at shortstop, where his savvy allows him to cover more ground than his fringy speed would suggest. He has the arm strength for the position, though he needs to be mindful not to drop his arm slot and lose accuracy on his throws. With a nice right-handed swing and signs of an advanced approach, Flores should hit for average. He's not very physical but has some loft in his stroke and should develop some gap power once he gets stronger. He won't be a basestealer, but runs the bases well.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Last year, I mentioned that I hoped (and valued him assuming) Flores' lackluster 2019 was a developmental bump rather than the start of a trend. Well, now it's a trend. Flores was generating Willy Adames comps during the Fall of 2018, and has since regressed physically and technically. He no longer looks athletically capable of playing the middle infield and has continued to struggle with the bat. He's in danger of slipping off the list entirely next year unless he performs statistically and looks more athletic early in the year. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Flores was the star of last fall's instructional league in Florida and looked like a potential everyday player in the Willy Adames mold. He skipped the GCL last year and flopped in the Penn League, his body backed up a little bit, and he generally looked less explosive and twitchy. We shaded his FV down a half grade, and consider it more of a developmental bump than the start of a trend right now.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Flores, who received the second highest bonus in the Red Sox 2017 international class at $1.4 million -- just behind Danny Diaz's $1.6 million -- was the buzz of the Southwest Florida instructional league and has exciting potential. After dominating the DSL during the summer, Flores got a late call-up and played two games in the GCL before his summer was shortened by a minor injury. He reminds some scouts of a potential everyday shortstop who takes a few games to grow on you. Unlike many high-bonus, July 2nd prospects, Flores doesn't have loud, flashy tools, or exceptional twitch or physical projection. He's more of the steady, low-key type of player with excellent feel for defense (common among prospects from Venezuela, where there's more of a game-focused development) and high-quality contact. He projects to be an above-average bat with average raw power, and the swing attributes to have a chance to get to most of it. Deceptively quick for his size, Flores has average speed and the defensive instincts to cover more ground than his raw foot speed indicates, as well as a plus arm. There's a chance Flores outgrows shortstop, but he'd likely be at least above-average, if not plus, at third base in that event. It may be a card full of 5's (except for arm strength) on the 2-8 scale, with very little pro experience, but scouts are excited about what little they've seen here and think he could be a first division regular if the bat develops enough.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Quintana was a high school prospect of repute from Las Vegas, then hit .317/.424/.565 during his career at Arizona, squaring up everything but well-located breaking balls, which he tends to swing over top of. His track record of hitting and the likelihood that he'd stay on the dirt had him in teams' late first, early second round mix. He really struggled after the draft, then had no 2020 season to rebound. Quintana is also one of those prospects who had trouble working out and doing baseball activities throughout 2020 because of the safety measures in place in Vegas, and this impacted his fall look. He's still in a holding pattern on this list but could have an average hit/average power combo and play every day at third base. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Quintana had a four-year track record of statistical performance dating back to his senior year of high school, but after the draft he suddenly stopped hitting against Low-A and Short Season pitching. His swing is somewhat grooved, but he has an athletic move forward and should hit a ton of doubles. A well-rounded offensive skillset and above-average defense at third is an everyday profile, but there's some hit-tool risk here.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: A very prominent high school prospect, Quintana matriculated to Arizona and became a core of their lineup almost immediately. Though his swing is somewhat grooved, he's an athletic swinger with power, who is also quite good at third base. He has a shot to be an everyday third baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers had a run of college infielders in the 2019 Draft led by Quintana, a converted shortstop turned third baseman at the University of Arizona, who slugged his way into becoming one of the more productive hitters in the Pac-12 Conference. His 77 RBIs as a junior ranked fifth among NCAA Division I hitters in 2019 to go with a .342 average, 15 home runs and a .626 slugging percentage. After signing for $1.58 million in the second round, Quintana had an encouraging first week as a pro at Class A West Michigan before slumping to a .155 average and 36 strikeouts in July. Once the offensive struggles followed him into the infield, the Tigers pushed him to Short-Season Connecticut to regain his bearings as the season ended. Quintana generates a surprising amount of power for his size. It also leaves him susceptible to all-or-nothing outcomes, which seemed to amass around him in his introduction to pro ball. After hitting his first home run in his fifth pro game, he went 17-for-98 (.173) with 38 strikeouts over his next 106 plate appearances, including an 0-for-12, nine-strikeout stretch over three games in late July. Ironically, both of his home runs at West Michigan and Connecticut came in games in which he didn’t strike out. Defensively, his quick first step and sure hands made him a plus defender in college, with arm strength when needed. The Tigers drafted Quintana early hoping for an eventual quality two-way player for the hot corner. If he’s going to make it, he’ll have to learn to separate the two sides of his game and keep his defense out of slumps. He’ll approach the 2020 season with a fresh start.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Dodgers viewed Estevez as an advanced hitter when they gave him $6 million and paid a $6 million penalty for exceeding their international bonus pool in November 2015. They started the Cuban defector in Class A at age 18 and he didn't take off until the final six weeks of 2018, when he finished the year as the Class A Advanced California League leader in runs (87) and doubles (43). He continued to swing a hot bat in Spring Training and the first month of last season, then lost six weeks to a hamstring injury and tailed off afterward. Estevez employs an open stance with a big leg kick, and he manages to barrel balls despite leaking out early. He has an efficient right-handed swing and recognizes pitches well, but his swing mechanics make it difficult to drive the ball to the opposite field, cutting into his power potential. He's at his best when he's patient and focuses on smoking balls to the gaps. Estevez's quick hands and instincts allowed him to survive two years primarily playing shortstop in high Class A, but he's not suited to do so in the big leagues. His fringy range and arm strength fit better at second base, where he spent most of his time in 2019. He doesn't have the defensive tools desired for a utility role, which puts more pressure on his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Largely on the strength of what they considered an advanced bat, the Dodgers gave Estevez a $6 million bonus and paid a matching amount as a penalty for exceeding their international bonus pool in November 2015. They promoted him aggressively, starting the Cuban defector in low Class A at age 18 and promoting him to high Class A at 19, and he showed little consistency at the plate for most of his first three pro seasons. He seemed to turn a corner when he batted .340/.418/.547 in the final six weeks of 2018, finishing the year as the high Class A California League leader in runs (87) and doubles (43). Estevez has an unorthodox batting style in which his lower half tends to leak out while his shoulders remain square to the ball. During his late-season tear, he was more patient and hammered balls from gap to gap instead of trying to pull everything to left field. With his efficient right-handed stroke and advanced pitch-recognition skills, he could become a .275 hitter with 15 or more homers per year if he can maintain a disciplined approach. Estevez's quick hands and internal clock have helped him survive at shortstop, his primary position in two years in high Class A, but it will be a stretch for him to play there regularly in the Majors. His speed and arm are fringy and better suited for second base, where he can be an average defender. His lack of arm strength restricts his utility value, putting pressure on him to hit enough to become a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Estevez has such an advanced bat that he debuted in Cuba's top league as a 16-year-old. After he defected and Major League Baseball expedited his free agency, the Dodgers signed him in November 2015 for a $6 million bonus and a matching penalty for exceeding their international allotment. Challenged with an assignment to low Class A at age 18 in his pro debut, he hit .293/.340/.458 in the second half of 2016 as the Midwest League's youngest regular but has yet to enjoy similar success in high class A this year. Estevez has one of the best right-handed swings among Dodgers farmhands and precocious feel for the barrel. He's still honing his pitch recognition and can get overly aggressive at times, shortcomings that much older pitchers have exploited in 2017. He has some raw power and the ability to translate it into production, which eventually could mean 12-15 homers per season. An offensive second baseman in the mold of Howie Kendrick, Estevez has fringy speed and arm strength. He has a good internal clock on the field and has shown the Dodgers a little more defensive ability than they expected. He has seen much more action at shortstop than at second base this year, but he's not suited for the left side of the infield and doesn't fit a utility profile.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: He's not a good athlete and at best is only passable at second base, but Estevez can hit, and has a track record of hitting throughout his pro career even though he's been young for every level at which he has played. Still, because he's a shift-enabled second baseman who needs to come off the field late in games, he was unprotected and unpicked in this year's Rule 5. I still think he'll eventually be someone's 1-1.5 WAR shift-enabled infield stick at some point. (Alternate site)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Barely 22 years old, Estevez has already reached Double-A and posted a .268/.322/.405 career line, and he's slugged better than that over the last two years. He has had some injuries, including a shoulder issue prior to baseball's shutdown, and he's already quite heavy-footed for his age. I have him as a 1-to-2 WAR, bat-first infielder.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Estevez was a resounding success repeating Hi-A while still just 20, and coupled it with moments of brilliance with the big league club during the spring of 2019. He continues to split time at both middle infield spots and he's fine at both positions, but what's exciting about Estevez is the bat. He's very short to the ball, but his swing still has natural lift to his pull side, and he can pull most anything because of how short the swing is. He's probably going to get to his raw power in games because of this, which makes him a potential everyday middle infielder despite a lack of physical explosiveness in other areas.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gatorade's 2017 Texas high school player of the year, Scherff went 15-0 with a 0.73 ERA and four no-hitters while displaying first-round-caliber arm strength. Signability concerns dropped him to the fifth round, where the Red Sox signed him for $700,000, more than double his assigned pick value but less than most clubs believed he would accept. His 2018 pro debut was trying, as he got hammered in April while trying to incorporate mechanical changes, found success in May and June after reverting to his high school delivery, then missed two months with an oblique strain. After topping out at 98 mph as an amateur, Scherff sat around 90 mph with his fastball early last season but was back up to 92-93 with a peak of 95 by the end of the year. His fastball is fairly straight, though he commands it well. He gets much more deception with his changeup, which features fade and was considered one of the best in the 2017 Draft. Scherff's biggest need is to find a reliable breaking ball. He can throw his curveball for strikes but it doesn't miss bats, and he worked on a cutter during instructional league. He has the durable frame and control to be a starter, though his lack of an effective breaker and rough delivery could make him a reliever in the long run.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scherff had an outstanding 2017 senior season at Colleyville (Texas) Heritage High, going 15-0 with a 0.73 ERA and four no-hitters to capture Gatorade state player of the year honors. He showcased a first-round arm but worries about his signability and his history of playing for three high schools in four years dropped him all the way to the fifth round. The Red Sox signed him for $700,000, more than twice the assigned slot value but less than most clubs figured he would accept, then had him focus on strengthening his shoulder rather than pitching in game action during the summer. After improving his conditioning and losing 40 pounds, Scherff saw his fastball rise from the upper 80s in the summer of 2015 to the mid-90s a year later, topping out at 98 mph. As he has adjusted to pitching every fifth day in pro ball, he worked at 92-93 mph before straining his oblique in June. He also had one of the best changeups in the 2017 Draft, selling it with deceptive arm speed and creating nice fade. Scherff's breaking pitches aren't as advanced, and Boston has had him shelve his slider to focus on his curveball. While he has a durable frame and throws strikes, his less-than-smooth delivery and lack of a present third pitch lead some scouts to project him as a reliever. He'd be a late-inning option if he moved to the bullpen.

fangraphs.label: 2021updated
fangraphs.text: Once an arm-strength lotto ticket (who worked to reshape his body just to become one), Scherff has developed a plus changeup and now projects as a good middle reliever. His strikeout rate has nearly doubled above his career norms in 2021.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best high school prospect out of Tennessee in the 2017 Draft class, Jennings was a two-sport athlete who got past a torn ACL suffered during his senior football season to pitch his way into the second round of the Draft. The Pirates went over slot to give him $1.9 million to sign rather than head to Mississippi. While the results on paper don't look great, the Pirates are still very bullish on his combination of athleticism and feel for pitching. Jennings will rely on his ability to command his four-pitch mix, rather than be that prototypical projectable power pitcher. Very athletic on the mound, he has the chance to have above-average control of all four offerings. His fastball typically sits around average, though he can reach back for 94 mph on occasion. Without a big frame, there might not be a ton of strength to add, so this might be more or less where he stands velocity-wise. The good news is that he does a nice job using his fastball, two distinct breaking balls -- the Pirates like the slider a little bit more than the curve but they do complement each other -- and his changeup to keep hitters from barreling up the baseball. Some evaluators see some Mike Leake in Jennings as an athletic right-hander with a repeatable delivery who will use command and savvy to get big league hitters out. If he can do that and sharpen a breaking ball to become more of an out pitch, he could profile closer to the middle of a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jennings was a two-sport star at DeKalb County High School in Tennessee, serving as ace pitcher as well as quarterback for the football team. A torn ACL during the fall of his senior year left many wondering how much mound time he'd get, but he turned out to be the best prep prospect in the state. The Pirates went above pick value to sign him for $1.9 million in the second round and he made his pro debut in the Gulf Coast League. Jennings provides an intriguing combination of feel for pitching, projectability and athleticism to the system. He's more of a pitchability right-hander right now, with a fastball he throws 89-92 mph. But he can reach back for more and there might be more velocity to come as he physically matures. He commands the fastball well, moves it in and out and throws it with movement. He'll throw two breaking balls, the slider is liked more by evaluators, and he might focus on just one in the future, and he has good feel for his changeup. The athleticism comes in handy in terms of repeating his delivery and filling the strike zone with all of his pitches. How much his stuff ticks up as he matures and as he focuses on baseball only will determine what kind of starting pitcher he eventually becomes.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Jennings did remote work all year and wasn't seen, so there's no change to his report: How much velocity can we still hope for Jennings to grow into? He's 22 now and isn't especially projectable, but he has had non-arm injuries (an ACL tear in high school, a broken rib) that have cost him reps and compromised his physicality for long stretches. He can still really spin it and his fastball, which was in the 88-92 range in 2019, has other traits that give it some room to breath at lesser speeds. There's a small chance more velo arrives, but I'm more inclined to project Jennings as a strike-throwing fifth starter who relies on his secondary stuff quite often. (At-home dev)

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text:
Jennings was a dual-threat quarterback at DeKalb and was actually the MVP of his high school's classification as an underclassman. He blew out his ACL on the football field the following fall, and yet he was back on the mound the following spring and pitched well enough for the Pirates to offer him $1.9 million as a second rounder (he was committed to Ole Miss). 
Jennings can really spin it but his velocity has waxed and waned as a pro, hovering anywhere between the upper-80s and low-80s. Each of his two breaking balls has premium raw spin, but Jennings release of them, epsecially the slider, hasn't become consistent enough yet for them to play like plus pitches. At age 20, Jennings is still an uncooked, developmental project, but his athletic ability and talent for spinning the ball mean he could really break out if things click mechanically.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Dallas Baptist University has churned out a ton of professional talent over the years, with Ben Zobrist clearly the most successful big league alum in school history, and even had two second-round picks in the 2020 Draft. But only one player, right-hander Vic Black, has been drafted earlier in the June Draft than Hannah, taken No. 50 overall by the A’s in the second round of the 2018 Draft. Since then, the talented outfielder has had to forward his address twice, going to the Reds at the 2019 Trade Deadline in the Tanner Roark deal, then heading to the Rockies along with Robert Stephenson in return for Jeff Hoffman and Case Williams last November. Hannah does have some offensive upside from the left side of the plate. There’s bat speed and the ability to make hard contact, with more gap-to-gap than over-the-fence pop. He’s shown an ability to work counts and take walks, though his approach wasn’t as solid during his first full year. While he’ll record plus run times, Hannah has yet to learn how to use that speed to steal bases. He has shown that his speed plays in the outfield, with a chance to play center field because of how much ground he can cover. He’s seen time at all three outfield spots as a pro, with perhaps a floor as a valuable fourth outfielder. But with a fringy arm, Hannah's best chance at an everyday spot would likely be in center or left.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A second-round pick of the A’s in 2018 after three years as a starter for Dallas Baptist, the Reds acquired Hannah on July 31, 2019, in the trade that sent veteran pitcher Tanner Roark to Oakland. Hannah, the earliest-drafted hitter in his school’s history, was having a decent first full pro season in the California League before the trade and then scuffled at the plate over his 18 games for Daytona in the Florida State League. He was on the move again in late November, when the Reds sent him and Robert Stephenson to the Rockies for Jeff Hoffman and 2020 draftee Case Williams. Hannah has an intriguing offensive profile and the Reds were attracted by his bat and a belief he can be a strong gap-to-gap left-handed hitter. He has good bat speed, makes hard contact and has solid strength. His approach is advanced and allows him to get on base effectively. A plus runner, he needs to get more out of his speed to become a base stealing threat. That speed serves Hannah reasonably well in center field as he can cover a lot of ground and defend well. His arm is below average. He could wind up playing all three outfield spots at some point as he moves up.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at Dallas Baptist, Hannah improved each year in college and as he turned in a huge junior season, his name was popping up in 2018 first-round conversations. The A's were very happy he lasted until the second round, the earliest the Patriots have had a hitter selected, and signed him for an above-pick value bonus of $1.8 million. He was able to show off some of his tools in the short-season New York-Penn League during his pro debut, but a foot injury shelved him for the summer in mid-July. He was having a solid full-season debut in the California League when he was sent to the Reds at the Trade Deadline for right-hander Tanner Roark. While he isn't the tallest guy in the world, he's strong and athletic and has a strong track record of consistent hard contact from the left side of the plate. He has an advanced approach, managing the strike zone well and finding the barrel while being very quick to the ball. His bat speed and strength point to some over-the-fence pop and plenty of extra-base power. He's shown he can handle wood just fine, both in a scorching hot stretch to end his Cape Cod season in 2017 and during his brief pro debut. A plus runner, Hannah is an efficient baserunner with the potential to steal bases and cover a ton of ground in center field. He's a capable defender, albeit one with a fringy arm. He could start to move quickly given his all-around skillset, with a potential future as a No. 2 type hitter in a big league lineup awaiting.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: This is Hannah's third org in less than three years. Drafted by Oakland, he was traded to the Reds for Tanner Roark in 2019 and then was part of a four-player swap with Colorado involving Robert Stephenson and Jeff Hoffman before 2021. Hannah is a contact-oriented outfield prospect with plus speed, more likely to play a bench or part-time role than be an everyday player. He hit .340 in college and has hit .280 in pro ball, with his extra-base hit production consisting almost entirely of doubles. I have him as an average center field defender but think he could be plus in left field. There's clear big league utility here: lefty stick, pinch runner, corner defensive replacement, but I think Hannah needs to develop a nearly elite hit tool to counterbalance his lack of power if he's going to be any sort of regular. He's made a fantastic first impression in purple so far during 2021 spring training. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Acquired last summer for Tanner Roark, Hannah is a contact/speed outfield prospect who will have to make more contact than I have projected in order to play an everyday role. He hit .340 in college and has hit .280 in pro ball, his extra-base hit production consisting almost entirely of doubles. I have him as an average center field defender but think he could be plus in left, a diet Brett Gardner profile lacking the elite plate discipline. It's a bench outfield look.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text:
Hannah had three remarkably consistent years at Dallas Baptist and ended his college career with a .340 average. He has excellent hitter's timing and bat control, and his swing is athletic but compact, enabling not only high rates of contact, but also promising contact quality. That's not to say Hannah will have in-game power. He's a line drive hitter, an old school, two-hole type of hitter, the kind who's sort of an endangered species in the current big league hitting environment. Some teams considered Hannah's lack of power to be a bit of an issue in their pre-draft evals and thought he was more of a tweener fourth outfield type, a projection echoed by pro scouts who saw Hannah in the summer and fall. 
He has plus speed, speed that Hannah exhibited during instructional league even after he had been shut down for the summer with a foot injury. His frame is maxed out and he can't afford to slow down much and still be viable in center field every day, but while this creates some long term risk for his profile, he's fine out there right now. His most likely path to a sizable everyday role involves Hannah out-hitting what we currently have projected for his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hernandez set the amateur scouting world abuzz when he was hitting the upper-90s with his fastball early in his junior season at Texas A&M-Corpus Christi. He wasn’t that electric or as dominant as he was in those first couple of outings all spring, but he showed enough to become the highest-drafted player in school history when the Angels took him in the third round of the 2018 Draft. Sent up to the Class A Advanced California League for his pro debut in 2019, his performance didn’t match the expectations. Part of Hernandez’s issues with Inland Empire stem from the fact his stuff backed up. The upper-90s fastball did not materialize and he tended to sit in the low-90s and couldn’t always maintain his velocity throughout a start. He does have a legitimate four-pitch mix, but it’s now largely average to a tick above across the board. His curve and slider sometimes run into each other, though he still has a feel to spin and he can mix in a solid changeup, but he lacks a true out pitch. In addition to the regression of his stuff, Hernandez’s command, which deserted him in college at times, remained an issue, leading to a 5.7/9 walk rate. He did turn things around with a strong Arizona Fall League campaign as he learned a bit more about what it takes to compete and pitched with a bit of a chip on his shoulder. He’ll need to show that fire on a consistent basis as he moves to the upper levels of the Angels system as a stater.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prior to the 2018 Draft, the earliest a player from Texas A&M-Corpus Christi had been drafted was the ninth round. Hernandez's path to easily beating that hasn't necessarily been straight. He was academically ineligible as a sophomore, but then came out and showed very good stuff early in the spring. While he wasn't as dominant all year, it was still enough for the Angels to take him in the third round and he went straight to the Class A Advanced California League for his full-season debut. Hernandez was up to 98 mph at times during his junior season, sitting more in the 92-95 mph range, throwing the pitch with good sink and showing he could maintain his velocity through starts. He has good feel for his secondary stuff and can throw a distinct curve and slider, though they sometimes blur together into a power slurve. He can really spin it and his breaking stuff does flash plus and he has solid tumbling changeup. Though he has swing-and-miss stuff, Hernandez didn't dominate in college as much as one would think, as he has trouble commanding his pitches both within and outside the strike zone. With a funky delivery, he might best be suited for the bullpen, but he was given a chance to start at the start of his pro career.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Hernandez has good secondary stuff but his control is raw for a 24-year-old, and he hasn't been able to make up the reps he missed in college (he made just 19 starts in three years of college and as of publication, 19 starts in three years of pro ball) due to a 2019 injury and, you know, the pandemic. He probably also needs a bit of a velo boost (he averaged about 92 in 2019), which I think he has a shot to find in one-inning bursts. He's a 40-man candidate this offseason and I hope they 'pen Hernandez at some point late in the year just to see what happens to his arm strength if they do.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Hernandez has good secondary stuff but his control is raw for a 23-year-old, and he hasn't been able to make up the reps he missed in college (he made just 19 starts in three years) due to a 2019 injury and, ya know, the pandemic. He probably also needs a bit of a velo boost, since he averaged about 92 last year, which I think he has a shot to find in one-inning bursts.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text:
One of the least experienced and more polarizing college pitchers available in the 2018 draft, Hernandez has an electric, four-pitch mix and several developmental hurdles ahead of him. At a skinny 6-foot-1, there are scouts who doubt he can start based solely on his frame, though Hernandez held mid-90s velocity deep into games as a junior at Corpus Christi. If amateur scouts are to be believed, any of the following aspects of Hernandez's current profile could change: his stride direction, his arm slot, his breaking ball usage (he has two that bleed together), and the movement profile of his fastball. 
Hernandez was academically ineligible as a sophomore and only started 19 games in three years of college, so there's at least a reason he's behind his peers from a developmental standpoint. He has unteachable arm speed and feel for spin and even if he just ends up as a big league reliever, something that seems pretty reasonable given his talent, it would be a strong outcome for a third round pick. Like Aquino, Hernandez may move up this list quickly with refinement, but we'd like to see it fairly soon given his age.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A teammate of Lucius Fox at American Heritage-Delray Beach High School in Florida, Frank went on to become a three-year starter at Florida Atlantic University and a member of USA Baseball's Collegiate National Team. He boosted his stock with a breakout sophomore campaign that saw him lead the Owls in a host of offensive categories while playing every inning of every game at shortstop. His success carried over to his junior season, while his profile as a college performer only boosted his stock as the Draft approached. The Rays ended up taking Frank in the second round and then saved money by signing him for under slot value. Sent to the New York-Penn League, Frank led the league with a .425 on-base percentage and ranked eighth with a .288 average. Scouts see a future solid, albeit unspectacular, everyday type big leaguer when they watch Frank, in a sort of Mark Ellis type of mold. He has a pro approach to hitting with a good gameplan at the plate, one that led to more walks (33) than strikeouts (28) in his pro debut. He sends line drives to all fields and has a little pop from the right side of the plate. Frank is an average runner who runs the bases well but isn't a threat to steal. Defensively, Frank has a strong arm and good hands that allow him to profile anywhere on the field. His best chance at becoming a regular is at either second or third base, though it's probably more like that Frank serves as a utility infielder.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There's no change to Frank's report since, due to injury, he wasn't seen at all in 2020; I can't confirm it in a concrete way, but it sounds like the same shoulder injury that prevented him from playing in 2019. Remember this was supposed to be a player who moved quickly through the minors, which is part of why he was ranked highly last year. Now he's 24 and has barely played full-season ball. From last year: Frank was first seen by most scouts as a utility player on college Team USA the summer before he was draft eligible. The setting in which you scout a player can do wonders, and the Team USA look didn't give Frank much of a chance to show what he could do. He didn't really stand out, playing all over the field and making contact, but lacking impact tools. He shined much brighter in the spring for Florida Atlantic, with 13 homers and an OPS just shy of 1.000 while playing a passable shortstop. Scouts who saw Frank in pro ball after the Rays popped him in the second round see a slightly lesser version of Taylor Walls, another under-tooled Rays middle infielder with lots of feel. Frank is seen as more of a second baseman going forward and his 45 raw power, 50 speed, and 50 defense still aren't loud, but his ability to hit, take a good at-bat, and have advanced feel for the game give him the look of a potential low-end regular who could move quickly through the minors. He missed almost all of 2019 with a left shoulder strain. (Injured)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With his big body and power potential, Valdez was one of the more physically advanced players in the the 2018-19 international class. Targeting exactly that type of prospect, the Mets inked the then-16-year-old Dominican outfielder for $1.45 million on July 2. Making his pro debut in 2019, Valdez garnered honors as the Mets Dominican Summer League player of the year after slugging .432 with 23 extra-base hits and 36 RBIs in 57 games. He finished the year with a brief but impressive showing in the Gulf Coast League. Listed at 6-foot-3, 212 pounds, Valdez is already a physical specimen and still has plenty of room left to grow into his frame. His bat is his carrying tool, with tremendous raw power that already shows up in games at times. Swing-and-miss issues stemming from an aggressive, pull-heavy approach gives evaluators pause in projecting Valdez as anything more than a below-average hitter, though all agree that the power is for real. He’s a good athlete but a below-average runner and may lose a step as he begins to grow into his body. Valdez has prototypical right-field tools with his power potential and strong arm, but he is going to need many years in the Minors to develop his game.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked No. 28 on MLB Pipeline's list of the Top 30 international prospects for the 2018-19 signing period, Valdez, with his big body and power potential, was viewed by scouts as one of the more physically advanced players in his class. Targeting exactly that type of prospect, the Mets inked the then-16-year-old Dominican outfielder for $1.45 million on July 2. Listed at 6-foot-3, 212 pounds, Valdez is already a physical specimen and still has plenty of room left to grow into his frame. His bat is his carrying tool, with tremendous raw power that already shows up in games at times. In the past, he's been overly aggressive and pull-happy, leading to some swing-and-miss issues, but scouts were pleased with how he improved his overall approach this past year. He's solid athletically, earning at least average grades as a runner, and the Mets view him as a pure center fielder that should stay up the middle. Earning high praise for his makeup, scouts like the way Valdez competes and his joy for the game. That should help him deal with the long road ahead through the Mets' Minor League system, with enough offensive potential to carry him to Citi Field.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Valdez is an absolute behemoth of a corner outfield prospect who is likely to end up in the Franmil Reyes size/strength area at maturity, though right now he's built a little more athletically than that. This guy makes the bat look like a toothpick in his hands and he has thunderous raw power with pretty crude feel for contact coming from a swing that scouts don't really like. His 2019 exit velos are below what you'd probably guess from someone this big and strong who performed the way he did in the 2019 DSL (certainly they're below what I'd guess). I think that's more an in-game contact quality indicator, but a front office source from a team that seems to like contact-oriented players told me they thought Valdez should be higher here. I'm more inclined to move a guy like this after he performs on paper and I think Valdez is physically mature enough to be tested in full-season ball this year. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Valdez got a big bonus as part of the 2018 class and is a beefy power guy who we were a little skeptical of athletically, but he performed in the DSL and was pushed to the GCL last summer. The exit velos are a little lower than we expected given how big and strong Valdez is already.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Big bonus from the 2018 class is beefy power guy that we were a little skeptical of athletically, but he's performing in the DSL and just got a bump to the GCL.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Green was a 14th-round senior sign in 2019 and like most senior signs, had 45/50 stuff in college. He was 90-94 with two average breaking balls and had little college experience because he didn't move into the rotation until his senior season. Last spring, Green's stuff was up -- touching 96 with big sink (he had a 67% GB%), and flashing plus secondaries -- for a while before coming back to Earth during the summer after he returned from biceps tendinitis. He projects as a sinkerballing fifth starter or up/down relief type similar to Peacock, just a few levels behind. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text:
Green was a 14th round senior sign last year and like most senior signs, had 45/50 stuff in college. He was 90-94 with two average breaking balls and had little college experience because he didn't move into the rotation until his senior season. 
This spring, however, Green's stuff was up. He was 92-95, touching 96, and flashing plus secondary stuff including a good changeup. The Dbacks may have found something here, though there's no way to be sure if the velo uptick will hold water or not. He has No. 4 starter stuff if it does, and some scouts with Dbacks coverage this spring prefered Green to several more high-profile arms in the system. He's currently on the IL with biceps tendinitis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Green pitched out of the bullpen during his first three years Southeastern Louisiana before sliding into the starting rotation as a senior in 2018 and showing improved pitchability and control in the new role. The D-backs saw untapped potential in Green as a starter and made him their 14th-round pick in June, signing the right-hander for just $5,000. He impressed during his pro debut that summer, earning All-Star honors as a reliever in the Pioneer League, then opened his first full season as a starter in the Class A Advanced California League. He dominated the hitter-friendly league, going 9-1 with 1 .73 ERA over his first 14 starts to earn a Double-A promotion in July. Green’s calling card is a low- to mid-90s bowling-ball sinker that helps him induce ground balls at an elite rate. After posting a near 68-percent ground-all rate in his pro debut, he led all Minor League hurlers (120 IP min.) in that department in 2019 by inducing grounders at a 67.2-percent clip. Green’s downer curveball is consistently an average or better pitch, and he also throws a slider that has cutter action. A mid-80s changeup gives the right-hander a third usable pitch, though it is behind both of his breaking balls. He issued 1.7 walks-per-nine in 2019, exhibiting above-average control and command. Beyond the effectiveness of his stuff, Green stands out for his stamina and durability. He worked at least five innings in all 22 starts in 2019, averaging better than 5 2/3 innings per turn. Though he did struggle a bit in Double-A (4.28 ERA, .318 BAA) as he attempted to mix his pitches more, the D-backs believe it was a valuable learning experience that will aid him going forward. Green has all the ingredients to become a big league starter, perhaps even a No. 4 if he can trade some of those grounders for a few more strikeouts.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Mendoza had some first round buzz early in his high school career because he had at least 70-grade raw power projection, but he struck out a lot and his stock fell a bit down the stretch while his price tag did not, so he ended up at Florida State. There he continued to strike out while posting relatively modest underclass statlines before exploding as a junior in 2019. He still struck out a ton, but also slugged just shy of .600 and walked 23% of the time. Some scouts describe his approach as more passive than patient, which contributes to a healthy heaping of true three outcomes. There's real risk that Mendoza's hit tool is just a binary "no," and that he ends up flaming out in Double-A. But he also has so much raw power that his swing might be made so simple that he can cut down on the K's and become a viable role player. Because the power here is so titanic, we suppose there's more ceiling than that, but a good realistic outcome for Mendoza would be to become a 1B/DH platoon partner and high-leverage bench bat. (Alternate site, Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Mendoza had some No. 1 overall pick buzz early in his high school senior spring, but ultimately faded a bit down the stretch and his big price tag (plus Scott Boras) led to him enrolling at Florida State, where those concerns played out for three years. Mendoza has massive raw power and a borderline passive late-count approach, which leads to a healthy heaping of true three outcomes. Along with the patient approach, scouts either complain or simply point out Mendoza's on-field demeanor, which runs from "low blood pressure" to "disinterested." He looked less like a third baseman over time at Florida State, and the Nationals plan to play Mendoza at first base most of the time going forward. There's still some projection left: Mendoza could have 70 raw power with a high on-base percentage when he gets to the big leagues, but the margin for error is low and could lead to a platoon role.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Mendoza has huge raw power, a pretty swing, and a shot to stick at third base, but he's regressed since his prep days, losing athleticism, striking out more often, and looking disinterested on the field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mendoza was a highly regarded prospect in the 2016 Draft, but a strong commitment to Florida State led to him being taken by the Tigers in the 36th round. Three years later, after batting .298 with 31 homers and 124 RBIs in 160 games with the Seminoles, he became the Nationals’ third-round pick and signed for above slot value. A successful pro debut at Class A Hagerstown came next, with Mendoza flashing his power potential while making a smooth transition as a first baseman. As a 6-foot-5, 230-pound left-handed hitter, it is easy to dream on Mendoza’s potential at the plate. He gets good leverage in his swing and knows how to impact the baseball, showing plus raw power that should improve as he adds strength. He is still figuring out how to get to that power consistently, though, with swing-and-miss issues and a passive approach currently holding him back. Though he does work his share of walks, the Nationals would like to see him be more aggressive early in the count, viewing it as key for unlocking both his hitting ability and power. Mendoza’s defense at the hot corner with the Seminoles drew mixed reviews from scouts, with most of the concerns stemming from his size and actions. The Nationals immediately moved him to first base in pro ball and have been pleased with the early results, noting that his feet and hands both work well there. They may still offer him reps at third base, where his above-average arm fits well, but their hopeful that Mendoza’s bat will flourish now that he no longer has to focus on improving defensively at third base.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Hearn is a squat but very strong, athletic catcher who has a chance to be an above-average defender with a plus arm (he needs to be more accurate, though) and above average raw power. He needs a reworked swing and may never be more than a 30 bat, which puts him in a likely backup catching bucket. There's definitely more ceiling than that here, it's just dependent on Hearn finding a way to make more consistent contact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ranked as the best high school catcher in a lean 2019 crop, Hearn figured to go in the top three rounds based on talent. Worries about the strength of his commitment to Mississippi State dropped him to the sixth round, though he was still the first prep backstop selected. He signed for $950,000, the equivalent of second-round money, then struck out 36 times in 80 at-bats while hitting .163 in his debut. Hearn offers plenty of bat speed and strength from the left side of the plate. Instead of letting his plus raw power to all fields translate into home runs naturally, he got too aggressive and pull-oriented in his introduction to pro ball, resulting in too many whiffs and rolled-over grounders to the right side of the infield. If he can settle down, he could develop into a decent hitter with 20 or more homers per season. Hearn runs like a typical catcher but moves well enough behind the plate. He had concentration lapses as an amateur but appeared more focused in his debut and should become an average to solid receiver. He has a plus arm with a quick release, and he has recorded 1.9-second pop times to second base.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Williams had one of the biggest frames among the high school prospects from the 2019 draft, standing in at a very projectable looking 6-foot-6. He was much older than the typical high school prospect (he and Adam Kloffenstein, who was drafted the year before, were born nine days apart), which colors his long-term fastball projection, but what is lost there might be gained through a better delivery. Williams had some cross-bodied mechanical violence as an amateur that might be ironed out in pro ball, and already may have been. He had a Mike Clevinger look in the bullpen last spring. The Blue Jays traded Williams to Los Angeles for Ross Stripling during the summer (he was one of two PTBNL in that deal), and he's already a big, strong kid whose fastball has been up to 96 in the past (I have him topping out at 94 during 2020 Fall Instructs), and he creates vertical depth on his 78-81 mph breaking ball. There's sizable relief risk here because of the delivery (and that's ultimately where I have him projected) but there's also a No. 4 starter ceiling if that's corrected or overcome. (Alternate site, Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As one of the more projectable prep right-handers in the 2019 Draft, Williams intrigued the Dodgers, but the Blue Jays beat them to him in the second round and signed him for an over-slot $1,547,500. Los Angeles got him a year later as the first of two players to be named (outfielder Ryan Noda was the other) in an August deal for Ross Stripling. He logged 16 innings in his 2019 pro debut and spent time at the Dodgers' alternate site and instructional league last year. Williams deals at 91-94 mph and peaks at 96 mph with his fastball while using his 6-foot-6 frame and high three-quarters delivery to create a downhill plane that's tough on hitters. Scouts prefer his upper-70s downer curveball over his harder slider, though he made progress with the latter during instructs. He's also gaining confidence in his changeup, which features some tumble and fade. Williams' velocity was up a bit in instructional league and could continue to grow as he matures physically. He has good body control for a pitcher so young and tall, which should help him repeat his delivery, throw strikes and stay healthy. The Dodgers have been working with him to quicken his tempo and make better use of his athleticism.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the more projectable high school right-handers in the 2019 Draft, Williams passed on a Vanderbilt scholarship to sign with the Blue Jays for $1,547,500 in the second round. He posted a 1.13 ERA with 19 strikeouts in 16 Rookie-ball innings last summer, but his full-season debut was delayed until 2021 after the coronavirus shut down the Minors. The Dodgers acquired him as the first of two players to be named in the August trade that sent Ross Stripling to Toronto. Williams presently sits in the low 90s and tops out at 95 mph with his fastball, which plays up because he uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create steep plane and angle. He throws two different breaking balls, with scouts preferring his curveball to his slider because of its spin and his high-three-quarters arm slot. He shows some feel for a changeup that should become an average offering as he uses it more. Williams has more body control than most pitchers his size and age, which bodes well for his ability to repeat his delivery, throw strikes and stay healthy. He'll need time to refine his craft, but if his stuff improves as he gets stronger, he could become a No. 3 or 4 starter.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: A growing number of teams shut down their newly-drafted pitchers during their first pro summer, which is what the Angels did with Stallings, who threw a career-high 103 innings at Tennessee during the spring of 2019. He's 23 and still hasn't pitched in a pro game yet. In 251 career collegiate frames, though, Stallings walked just 37 hitters, and he didn't issue a single free pass during his pre-draft summer on Cape Cod. You'd think an extreme strike-thrower like this would have the most vanilla, stock footage delivery, but Stallings' is actually kind of funky, and helps his stuff (which is very vanilla) play up a little bit. He's a low variance fifth starter prospect who was traded to Baltimore as part of a two-player deal for José Iglesias. (Angels Fall Instructional League)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a high schooler in Virginia, Stallings showed polish on the mound but not enough stuff to really register on the Draft radar, so he went to the University of Tennessee. He was pretty much the same pitcher with the Volunteers, but this time with three years of solid track record in the Southeastern Conference on his resume. That led to the Angels taking him in the fifth round of the 2019 Draft, though after not pitching that summer after a heavy college workload and the 2020 shutdown, he never threw an official pitch for the Angels before he was traded to the Orioles in the José Iglesias deal in early December. None of Stallings' offerings jump off the page, but he has a legitimate four-pitch mix. His fastball will top out at 93 mph and more often comes in at 88-91 mph, but he commands the pitch very well and throws it with a ton of sink. His changeup, which has similar movement, plays off it nicely and he sells it well. His curve got better during his junior year and he also has a slider/cutter at his disposal. Stallings’ stuff plays up because he tunnels his pitches effectively and can throw all four of them for strikes. He rarely hurts himself with walks, allowing just 1.3 per nine innings at Tennessee. That gives him a chance to fit into the back of a big league rotation.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Because he has such advanced feel for pitch location (most notably a tumbling changeup, which is a grade better now than it was when he was drafted), Lewis has a better chance to start than many of the prospects ahead of him in this system. While he repeats his delivery, it is quite stiff, and remember that he's a year removed from a labrum issue. I have him in as a backend starter prospect, and most of the modest variance I associate with him is due to the injury rather than the gap between his ceiling and floor. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Lewis is a classic Texas projection righty: broad-shouldered, sculptable 6-foot-6, with a low-90s fastball and feel for an above average slurve. It's a report that reads an awful lot like Dustin May's did when he was drafted, though Lewis' situation is complicated by a labrum tear that cost him most of 2019.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Lewis is a clasic projection case a 6'6/200 with a 90-92 mph fatball that touches 93 and features plus life, an above average slurve and a rarely used changeup that's at least average. In a loaded Texas prep righty class, Lewis is now seen near the top despite the least present stuff of the group because he has clear starter traits and projection.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lake Travis High (Austin, Texas) had two premium prospects last spring in Brett Baty, the 12th overall pick by the Mets, and Lewis, who went in the second round -- just like his father Jimmy did with the Astros in 1991. The younger Lewis missed the state playoffs with what was believed to be a lat strain but was diagnosed as a partially torn labrum in his shoulder during a pre-signing physical. The Dodgers still signed him for an above-slot $1,097,500 and put his debut on hold. Lewis already demonstrates the ability to carry a low-90s fastball deep into games while topping out at 95 mph, and he should add velocity as he adds strength to his lanky 6-foot-6 frame. He could have a pair of plus pitches if he can develop more consistency with his upper-70s downer curveball. He has some feel for a changeup but didn't have much need for it as an amateur. Lewis's athleticism and strength should help him throw strikes and pile up innings. He has a fairly simple delivery for a tall youngster, using his size and high three-quarters arm slot to create downhill plane. He also intrigued scouts with his hitting ability and power potential, and he might have played both ways had he gone to Louisiana State rather than turning pro.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: McAvene's velo popped late during his draft year and was up to 100 during Louisville's regionals, and he flashed a tight, mid-80s slider. If that holds, he could be a setup type. If not, it's more middle relief. He hasn't pitched in 2021 due to an elbow strain.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The top pitcher in Louisville's 2016 recruiting class, McAvene succumbed to Tommy John surgery in April of his freshman year and returned to the mound 12 months later. He became the Cardinals' closer in 2019 and boosted his Draft stock when his velocity surged during the team's postseason run to the College World Series. Though he hadn't started a game since 2017, the Cubs immediately moved him to the rotation after signing him in the third round. After spending most of his junior season operating at 93-96 mph with riding life on his four-seam fastball, McAvene started hitting 98s and 99s in the NCAA tournament and kept doing so in short starts during his pro debut. His breaking ball shows signs of becoming a plus pitch, combining slider velocity with curveball depth. Now that he's a starter, one of his primary focuses will be to develop his nascent changeup. McAvene has a strong, durable 6-foot-3 frame and is throwing more strikes as he puts elbow reconstruction further behind him. Chicago believes he's equipped to stay in the rotation and plans to develop him alongside 2019 fourth-rounder Chris Clarke, another college closer turned starter. Should he return to the bullpen, McAvene could move quickly and eventually claim a high-leverage role.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: Packard was an interesting buy-low guy in the 2019 draft. His power output dipped during his junior year at East Carolina because of injuries (back and wrist), but he had a stock-up summer after the draft, slashing .296/.392/.422 across three levels. He is patient, swings with verve, has above-average raw power, and looks like a potential Lucas Duda type from a body and swing standpoint. He's sometimes guilty of simply swinging through the center of the zone rather than guiding his barrel to the pitch location, but his hands are really loose and fast. The shaky feel for the barrel slides him below some other role-player types in the system from a certainty standpoint. (Fall Instructional League)

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Packard has above average to plus raw power from the left side, a solid approach and some track record of hitting. That said, he's a left field-only fit and had back and wrist problems this spring that led to a power decline.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers had Packard on an aggressive track after drafting the reigning American Athletic Conference Player of the Year out of East Carolina in the fifth round in 2019. He tore up Midwest League hitting that summer at Class A West Michigan, then had a brief stint of High-A play. The cancellation of the 2020 Minor League season cost him a chance to build upon that momentum and potentially work his way toward the upper levels. Packard has a bat-first profile with a pure, polished left-handed swing and a disciplined approach that keeps him from wandering outside the strike zone. His big frame allows him to produce power without too much vulnerability to strikeouts. His extra-base power beyond home runs is more from exit velocity than his slow foot speed. He has worked on his instincts in left field but has limited range and athleticism, leading some to wonder whether he could eventually shift to first base. The Tigers have found few productive hitters beyond early Draft picks in recent years, but Packard has the skill set and work ethic to potentially contribute at the big league level. His upside will be almost entirely determined by his bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The American Athletic Conference Player of the Year as a sophomore at East Carolina, Packard had the potential to become a first-day MLB Draft pick in 2019 before back issues hampered him as a junior. The Tigers selected him in the fifth round and pushed him aggressively, sending him to Class A West Michigan after he overmatched Short-Season pitching in Connecticut. He responded by tearing up the Midwest League for just over a month, posing an .898 OPS for the Whitecaps before finishing the season at Class A Advanced Lakeland. Packard is a pure hitter with the polish of someone who looks like he has been playing pro ball for a few years. He has raw power to various parts of the field without relying on an all-or-nothing approach, and enough discipline not to chase pitches well outside his zone. His extra bases are based more on power than speed, which he lacks. He’s an adequate defender in left field with limited range, but his value is almost purely offensive. The Tigers have struggled to find Major League hitters in the Draft beyond the first couple rounds, but Packard could end up a value pick if he can stay healthy and continue to learn how to approach advanced pitching. The Tigers could move him up aggressively if he handles the Florida State League.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: There's no change to Locey's report, as he was not at the Cardinals' alt site, they had no instructs, and he was traded after Colorado's was complete: Locey had a rocky end of high school and beginning of college at Georgia, but emerged in a big way in 2019 as the most dependable starter for the Bulldogs down the stretch, ahead of a banged-up Emerson Hancock. Locey would hold mid-90s velo late into games, hitting 97 regularly and landing a solid average breaking ball that dev-minded folks in baseball think has more ceiling. His control is fine, but the command and changeup were both weaker points in a starting role, so relief is a natural fit without a change to that profile. His aggressive, bulldog approach is also conducive to shorter stints. (At-home dev)

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: 2020 Locey teamed with Jake Fromm to help Houston County High (Warner Robins, Ga.) win the Georgia state 5-A baseball championship as a senior in 2016. Both headed to the University of Georgia, where Fromm starred at quarterback while Locey emerged as a key starter on a Bulldogs team that won a school-record 21 Southeastern Conference games in 2019. While there's debate as to whether he winds up as a starter or reliever in the long run, there's no question that his arm was among the best in college baseball's top conference. That arm was part of the package the Rockies acquired as part of the return for Nolan Arenado in early February. A big right-hander who works from a high-three-quarters slot to create angle to the plate, Locey operates at 94-96 mph and can touch 98 mph with his fastball, He maintains his velocity throughout his starts and figures to hit 100 mph if he works shorter stints out of the bullpen. His low-80s slider can be sharp and a solid pitch when he commands it, and he also shows promising shape on a curveball that's a work in progress. As a power pitcher, Locey didn’t have much need for a changeup in college. Locey is strong and physical, though to remain a starter he'll have to do a better job of repeating his delivery and commanding his pitches. If he does become a reliever, he has late-inning potential and perhaps a chance to become a closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a Venezuelan amateur, Cornielly endeared himself to scouts with his clean, athletic delivery and advanced feel for pitching. The Mets signed him for $25,000 at the outset of the 2017-18 international period, and he responded with a strong professional debut the next year in the Dominican Summer League. The right-hander didn’t fare as well last season in his return to the DSL, though he did perform better after a midseason jump over to the Rookie Gulf Coast League, where the 19-year-old impressed club officials with his endurance and aptitude on the mound. With a projectable frame and an innate ability for flooding the zone with strikes, Cornielly has a solid foundation as a starting pitcher. He doesn’t overpower hitters with his stuff, sitting in the low 90s with an above-average changeup and a fringy breaking ball, but he knows how to mix his pitches and commands his fastball better than most hurlers his age. He threw 84 percent of his pitches for strikes and posted a 52/9 K/BB ratio over 46 innings in 2019, all while inducing whiffs at an impressive 23-percent clip. Cornielly’s curveball is his least-advanced pitch, though club officials are optimistic that it will improve as he adds strength and refines his arm action. Cornielly is unique in the sense that he stands out more for his floor than ceiling even though he’s just 19 and has a projectable frame. Adding a bit more velocity could improve the effectiveness of his fastball-changeup combo, but even if he doesn’t, Cornielly still has enough starter qualities to profile to succeed at the back end of a big league rotation.

fangraphs.label: 2021report
fangraphs.text: While he isn't your typical huge-framed teenage arm, Cornielly has a lot of starter traits. He's a plus athlete with a squeaky clean delivery, and advanced changeup feel and fastball command. The breaking ball needs work, but it's a shape problem more than a raw spin one, and I think Cornielly is athletic enough to develop in this area. He has a realistic shot to be a backend starter down the line, and a non-zero chance to develop a premium change, command, or both, and be more. (Fall Instructional League)
