Signed for $2,500 in the 19th round that June, he didn't start to realize his power potential until he slammed 18 homers in Double-A in 2018. He encored with 22 more last year while enhancing his versatility in Triple-A. Though Jones has plenty of strength and leverage in his 6-foot-7 frame, he only began tapping into his power once he did a better job of staying back on pitches and stopped diving so much at the plate. He's driving the ball in the air more often and to all fields. While his size results in a naturally long right-handed swing, he does a good job of making contact and draws walks with a patient approach. Part of a Washington state 4-A basketball championship team at Kentwood High -- where his baseball teammates included future big leaguers Reese McGuire and Austin Voth -- Jones is athletic for his size. He's a below-average runner but not a baseclogger, and he's a quality defender with a strong arm at first base. He also can provide adequate defense on the outfield corners and looked fine in his initial exposure to third base in 2019.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels clearly have a thing for two-way players. We all know about Shohei Ohtani, and Jared Walsh got to the big leagues in 2019. In 2018, they drafted William Holmes and are letting him both hit and pitch as a pro. They took Rivera from the Puerto Rico high school ranks in the fourth round of the 2019 Draft, giving him an above-slot $597,500 bonus to sign him away from his Florida International commitment. He only hit during his pro debut in the Rookie-Level Arizona League, but the plan is to let him follow in Holmes’ footsteps. Rivera has some serious raw power to tap into from the left side of the plate, but there’s question about whether he’ll make enough contact to get to it consistently. There are some swing-and-miss issues -- he struck out in more than 37 percent of his plate appearances during his pro debut -- and he’ll have to refine his approach. But Angels hitting instructors like his swing and think that will come with experience. On the mound, Rivera has been up to 95-96 mph with his fastball, sitting more in the low 90s, with plenty of room to add strength and consistent velocity. He’s shown both feel for spinning his breaking ball and for a changeup, but he’ll need to work on improving his secondary stuff along with his command of all his offerings. Like with his swing, Angels instructors like the biomechanics of Rivera’s delivery, leaving it a bit of a tossup which area he might have the better chance with if he had to choose one to pursue.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In his first two years at the University of Georgia, Elliott pitched as a reliver and a swingman. He got a chance to be a part of the Bulldogs’ rotation as a junior and had a breakthrough season, establishing himself as the best midweek starter in the nation. The Mariners were hunting college pitching in the 2019 Draft and made Elliott the fifth of five college arms they took to kick things off, signing him for a below-slot $400,000 and sending him out for a solid pro debut in the short-season Northwest League. Elliott was a lean 6-foot-1, 170 pounds when he began his college career, but was up to 200 lbs by the time he began his pro career, allowing his stuff to play up. He throws his fastball in the 89-94 mph range and showed he can maintain that velocity deep into starts. He does a nice job mixing in three secondary offerings. His changeup is the best of the lot, an above-average offspeed pitch, and he makes good use of his average slider and even his fringy curve. Command has been an issue for Elliott at times, though he did much better in the strike-throwing department as a starter during his junior year. If he can continue that, with his repertoire, he has the chance to eventually develop into a back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The last catcher from the Southern Indiana to make it to the big leagues was Kevin Brown, a Rangers second-round pick who spent parts of seven seasons in the Majors as a backup. His son Logan followed in his footsteps to USI, starting for the Division II school for two years and eventually being taken in the 35th round by the Braves in 2018. The defensive-minded backstop was a South Atlantic League All-Star and earned a promotion up to the Florida State League in his first full season of pro ball. While Brown hit well in Rome, it’s still his defense that stands out. He has excellent catch and throw skills, throwing out 40 percent of potential basestealers in 2019. He also receives very well and gets high marks for his game-calling, working with pitchers and leadership behind the plate. The left-handed hitter makes a ton of contact, though he doesn’t walk a ton, and hasn’t shown much ability to impact the baseball. The Braves think there’s more bat to come, which would help him develop into a very good glove-first backup catcher at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the youngest players in the 2018-19 international class, Parra was also one of its more physically advanced prospects, showing a promising mix of strength and hitting ability as a Venezuelan amateur. The Brewers signed him for $210,000 on Aug. 30, 2018, Parra’s 16th birthday, and he rewarded the organization by having a successful 2019 pro debut in the Dominican Summer League, where he was nearly two years younger than the circuit’s average player. Listed at 6-foot-2, 184 pounds, Parra has present strength and plenty of room still to grow into his projectable frame. He has impressive natural hitting ability for a young player, with an impactful right-handed swing that already yields hard contact as well as raw power. Parra’s swing can get long at times, resulting in some and miss, though the Brewers think that will be less of an issue once the teenager adds strength and has more experience under his belt. He split time between second and third base in his pro debut but profiles better at the latter position, where his plus arm and below-average speed are fits. Parra offered an early glimpse of his offensive potential when he went 5-for-5 with two home runs, two doubles and five RBIs in his third game as a professional. He improved as the season unfolded, batting .329/.451/.573 with 19 RBIs in July, and finished the year with 23 extra-base hits and a .770 OPS in 65 games. The Brewers are understandably excited about the 17-year-old’s bat and view him as someone who could one day hit in the middle of a lineup.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Popup bat is Canadian that transferred from a Midwest Juco and has put up goofy numbers this spring. It's strength over bat speed and he hasn't been seen versus much velocity, but the raw tools belonged about where he was drafted.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a Nova Scotia high schooler, Sanford drew no scouting or recruiting interest and his only college offer was to play volleyball at Dalhousie University in his home province. He walked on at McCook (Neb.) CC, where he hit 23 homers in two years with wood bats, then transferred to Western Kentucky in 2019 and won the first regular-season triple crown in Conference USA history. After he went undrafted the previous three years, the Yankees made him a third-round pick. One of the best power prospects in the 2019 Draft, Sanford creates well-above-average raw pop with plenty of bat speed, strength and leverage in his 6-foot-2, 215-pound frame. Some scouts worry about the deep load in his left-handed swing and his tendency to get off balance at the plate, though New York believes his hand-eye coordination and quick stroke can make it work. He struck out in 33 percent of his plate appearances while batting .238/.289/.411 in his pro debut at short-season Staten Island, so he has adjustments to make. In addition to his big power, Sanford features plus speed and can flash even faster running times, though he's not much of a basestealer. A first baseman in junior college, he made a nice transition to right field at Western Kentucky. The Yankees deployed him in center field to see how his quickness played there during his first pro summer, and his fringy arm strength likely will land him in left field if he shifts back to a corner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fifth-round pick out of a Virginia high school in 2017, Perry spent most of his first two pro seasons in Rookie ball before breaking out in the New York-Penn League in 2019. He finished second in the short-season circuit in homers and won MVP honors at the New York-Penn all-star game, where he went deep in his lone at-bat. He was slated to finally make his full-season debut in 2020 before the coronavirus pandemic wiped out the Minor League season. Perry stands out with his strength and plus raw power, most of which comes to his pull side. He has a short left-handed stroke with natural loft and enjoyed more success once he realized he didn't need to sell out for home runs. He still needs to make more consistent contact, but he's willing to work counts and draw walks. While Perry shared time behind the plate in the New York-Penn League, that was in deference to 2019 first-rounder Korey Lee, and the Astros believe he can stick at catcher. He has improved as a receiver since turning pro and does a nice job of framing pitches, though he can look a bit stiff at times. He has average arm strength, a quick transfer and makes accurate throws.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brady went from his high school in southern New Jersey to East Carolina University, but after not seeing much mound time as a freshman in 2016, he returned to the Garden State and Mercer Community College. A standout season there in 2017 landed him in the seventh round with the Angels. Some arm issues slowed him early on in his career -- he amassed just 144 2/3 innings over his first two-plus seasons, but he’s healthy now and would have been ready to go for a full 2020 season had it transpired. The 6-foot-1 right-hander has a three-pitch mix and an idea of what to do with it, giving him some starting pitcher qualities. His fastball sits in the 92-93 mph range, and he can reach back for 95 mph on occasion. Depending on who sees him and how he’s throwing it, Brady has either a hard curve or a slider, and a decent slurvy breaking ball that he has a good feel to spin while adding to and subtracting from it. He’ll mix in a changeup that flashes average as well. Despite not having wow stuff, Brady has done a nice job of missing bats while filling up the strike zone fairly consistently. The lack of an out pitch or premium velocity kept him off the radar enough to not be selected in the 2020 Rule 5 Draft, even though he was left unprotected. After a solid showing at instructs this fall, the Angels are intrigued to see what Brady can do in a full healthy season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A starter at California Baptist University, Rinehart pitched well in relief in the Cape Cod League and continued to impress out of the bullpen in his professional debut. After the Mariners grabbed the right-hander in the 16th-round of the 2019 Draft, he pitched his way to full-season ball, where he posted a 3.52 ERA over 10 appearances. Listed at 6-foot-3, 185 pounds, Rinehart showed up to Spring Training in exceptional shape and appeared ready to put together a breakout campaign. Of course, COVID-19 shut down the 2020 Minor League season so Rinehart didn’t get a chance to compete against other organizations, but he did impress at Seattle’s alternate site. The right-hander throws his fastball in the 94-96 mph range and complements it with a trio of secondary offerings. Rinehart has plus control of a changeup that he throws in the upper 70s, a stark separation from his fastball, and also throws both a sweeping slider and a downer curveball that is used as an out pitch early in counts. Rinehart has thrown strikes as a pro, but the improved velocity and usage of the zone has helped him miss more bats. While the Mariners plan to let him start for now, he needs to continue to refine his breaking stuff to remain in the rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: At the start of the 2017-18 international signing period, the Phillies handed out a $2.5 million bonus to shortstop Luis Garcia. Six months later, and at the other end of the bonus spectrum, they inked Martinez for $10,000. Martinez put up pedestrian numbers in the Dominican Summer League in 2018 and while he pitched sparingly in his United States debut in the Gulf Coast League in 2019, he created some buzz with his size, stuff and upside potential. The 6-foot-2 left-hander is lanky and loose and has a legitimate three-pitch mix at his disposal. He can throw his fastball in the 91-96 mph range, throwing it with good late life. His slider has the chance to be a true out pitch, and he has surprisingly good feel for his changeup at a young age, selling it well with good arm speed. Martinez has shown the ability to throw strikes with a clean, easy and relatively effortless delivery that also provides some deception, with an idea of how to mix his pitches. It’s been a very small sample size of performance thus far, but scouts are excited to see what he can do with more time on the mound.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals landed a pair of promising 16-year-old Dominican outfielders at the outset of the 2018-19 international period, signing Marte and Jeremy De La Rosa for $300,000 apiece -- the maximum amount allowed without incurring a penalty -- on July 2. Though both players flashed a collection of intriguing tools during the pro debuts in the 2019 Dominican Summer League, it was Marte who led the team in home runs (tied, 5), slugging (.448) and total bases (94) at age 17, and he was one of Washington’s most impressive prospects during fall instructional camp in 2020. Marte possesses a blend of athleticism and physicality that has already earned him comparisons to an NFL running back. His projectable frame is ideal for adding more strength, and club officials do not expect those physical gains to detract from the plus speed that also enables Marte to play a quality center field. The Nationals believe he has a chance to remain at the position long-term, but his strong arm would more than suffice if he’s forced to move to an outfield corner. Marte’s development as a hitter will be key in unlocking his overall potential. He can do damage from the right side of the plate, combining strength and bat speed into an explosive swing, and Marte already showcases plus raw power to his pull side that should begin to play to all fields more consistently as he gains experience. Marte’s approach and pitch selection will both require considerable refinement (as is the case with most teenage hitters), but the raw ingredients are all there for him to become an impact talent.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals landed two of the top infield prospects in the 2016-17 international class with seven-figure bonuses, signing Yasel Antuna ($3.9 million bonus) and Luis Garcia ($1.3 million) as part of a larger haul. They added another promising infielder the following year in Pena, inking the undersized switch-hitter for $150,000. The Dominican native has done nothing but hit since entering Washington’s system and batted .359/.455/.481 over 37 Rookie-level Gulf Coast League games in 2019, making his stateside debut at age 18. Pena’s ability to repeat his swing and barrel the ball from both sides of the plate already ranks among the best in the organization and could help him develop into an above-average hitter in the big leagues. He has a small frame and will never much in the way of home-run power, he does have the bat speed and strength needed to turn around good velocity and is comfortable hitting to all fields. A solid-to-plus runner, Pena’s quickness and speed help him on both sides of the ball. Though he’s seen time at shortstop, second and third base early in his career, Pena’s best long-term fit might be at the keystone based on his size and offensive profile. If it all clicks, he could develop into a scrappy, top-of-the-order catalyst type who wears out pitchers.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prater was part of a loaded weekend rotation for an Oklahoma squad that also featured 2020 first-round pick Cade Cavalli (Nationals) and fourth-rounder Dane Acker (A’s). However, Prater had the best ERA (3.42) of the bunch and struck out 33 in his 23 2/3 innings before the coronavirus pandemic halted the 2020 season and the Cardinals selected him with the 93rd overall pick (third round) that June. In a more complete sample size, the lefty was named to the 2019 All-Big 12 Second Team and led Sooners’ starters that year with 97 strikeouts and a 3.26 ERA in 80 innings. While there’s still room for growth, Prater did show an ability to miss bats in his professional debut, racking up 83 strikeouts over his first 52 1/3 innings in Low-A. A deceptive, crossfire delivery helps Prater’s stuff play up and makes him hard to hit. He throws his fastball with armside run in the low 90s and sits around 80 mph with his slider. He also throws a changeup around 80 mph that flashes plus, but isn’t always consistent. The development of that pitch, as well as his overall command, will likely go a long way into determining his future role. The Cardinals are giving Prater an opportunity to start as he begins his professional career and he’ll be able to remain there if he’s able to improve upon his control. His delivery features some effort, which may push Prater into a reliever role. He profiles well as a middle reliever and may ultimately wind up in the bullpen, depending on how he develops that third pitch. If he is able to put everything together, his ceiling is likely that of a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2017 Cape Cod League MVP, Jenista's strong summer likely helped his stock avoid falling too much after an uneven junior season at Wichita State, as he landed in the second round with the Braves. He did make it to Double-A and the Arizona Fall League in his first full year of pro ball, but didn’t swing the bat very well and didn’t get any official reps in 2020. The power showed up a bit more in 2021, though he wasn't added to the Braves' 40-man roster in the offseason. There is some juice in Jenista’s left-handed bat, but there are questions as to whether he’ll be able to get to it at the highest level. The power has shown up at times, including hitting 19 homers in a tough hitters' park in 2021. But while he does draw some walks, the swing-and-miss is a real concern, as he has struck out in more than 32 percent of his plate appearances in his first two full seasons of pro ball. Jenista runs well enough for his size and has the athleticism and arm strength needed to play right field well. He saw time at first base in the AFL to close out 2019 and continued to do so in 2021. In the end, though, it will be Jenista’s ability to unlock his offensive potential that will determine his future value.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jenista won the Cape Cod League MVP the summer before his junior year at Wichita State, putting him on somewhat equal footing at the time with teammate Alec Bohm. Bohm went on to have a huge junior year while Jenista was more inconsistent, leading Bohm to be taken No. 3 overall in the 2018 Draft and Jenista sliding into the second round. While he split the year between the Class A Advanced Florida State League and Double-A Southern League, he didn’t swing the bat well, a trend that continued during his time in the Arizona Fall League. Big, strong and athletic, Jenista still has some offensive tools to work with; he just hasn’t figured out how to implement them successfully on a consistent basis. The more he struggled, the more he tried to change his setup at the plate, which rarely works. He did come to the Braves’ hitting camp during the offseason and left it feeling more comfortable than he had all year. There’s definite raw power in his 6-foot-3 frame, but the left-handed hitter had typically been using more of a line-drive, flat bat path. Jenista is fine in an outfield corner with an above-average arm, but he also saw considerable time at first base in the AFL, partially because that’s where he could find at-bats and partially to add to his versatility. If he can get his bat back on track in 2020, he still has the chance to be an everyday hitter in a big league lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A three-year starter at Wichita State, Jenista formed a formidable 1-2 punch with Alec Bohm in the Shockers lineup. Bohm went No. 3 overall in the 2018 Draft, but because Jenista wasn't able to carry over his Cape Cod League MVP performance and turned in a bit of an uneven junior season, he ended up being available for the Braves to select in the second round. He did hit his way up to the Class A Advanced Florida State League in his pro debut. Big and physical at 6-foot-4, Jenista is surprisingly athletic and shows more tools than you might think upon first glance. In college and during most of his pro debut, Jenista showed the ability to consistently barrel up the baseball with a largely line-drive-oriented approach and swing path, while limiting strikeouts and drawing some walks. There's a lot of raw power in his left-handed swing that he hasn't always tapped into, and it could be plus when all is said and done if he can hit enough to get to it. Jenista played first and right field at Wichita State and showed he could do a capable job in center field in the Cape. He'll likely stick at an outfield corner, where he played during his debut, as a pro, but there is pressure on that power bat to progress.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text:
At times, Jenista had mid-first round buzz leading up to his draft year, with a deceptively-athletic body that packed plus raw power, average speed, and an above average arm into a 6-foot-4, 240 pound frame. We dinged him at draft time for having too flat of a swing plane for his type of player, and cautioned that he may age quicker than other similarly-aged and tooled guys. 
He made it to Double-A by age 22 in 2019, but the lack of in-game, over-the-fence-power, along with too many strikeouts as he's reached the upper levels means that real changes need to be made soon to keep his prospect status. His results were stronger in the second half of 2019, and appeared to be BABIP-fueled, but the Braves saw some positive adjustments.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Jenista has a skillset that will be familiar to long-time fans of the game, with some qualities in common with players like Jeromy Burnitz, Adam Dunn, and Lance Berkman. Jenista is deceptively athletic for his size (a 50 runner at 6-foot-4 and 240 pounds) and has big raw power (a 65) along with a right field profile. Jenista is a late-count, power-focused hitter, so his approach will come with some swing-and-miss and some walks. He'll need a slight adjustment to his swing plane, as it's a little too flat for this type of player (he hits more doubles when he makes hard contact than you'd like), and he may age more quickly than player with a slighter build would. The upside is a three-win power-focused corner bat, though a more realistic expectation is probably a low-end regular worth around two wins annually, but he'll need to make some offensive adjustments between now and then regardless.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Feole likely fits in relief due to his average stuff and medium build, but he has a nasty plus curveball that should help him hang around the game for awhile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2021 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As a sophomore at UConn in 2018, Feole collected the second-most strikeouts in school history. When he followed that up with 11 shutout innings for USA Baseball's Collegiate National Team, he looked poised to be one of the more intriguing college lefties in the 2019 Draft class. But a forearm issue slowed him early as his velocity dipped, hurting his stock considerably, and he underwent Tommy John surgery in July after the Padres took him in the 11th round. After completing his rehab process, Feole appeared physically stronger and operated with better stuff when he returned to mound in San Diego’s fall instructional camp. At his best, Feole leans heavily on his fastball-curve combination. The former will sit in the low 90s and was touching higher during instructional league, while the breaking ball serves as his out pitch, flashing plus at times. Feole has a third-pitch changeup that is below average. An unorthodox delivery that includes a head snap makes it difficult for Feole to find the strike zone consistently and portends a full-time move to the bullpen, where his two-pitch repertoire could play up in shorter bursts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chatham was an outfielder who flashed a mid-90s fastball as a reliever at American Heritage High (Plantation, Fla.), which has produced four big leaguers and five first-round picks, including 2018 Red Sox choice Triston Casas. Chatham went to Florida Atlantic, where he moved to shortstop and blossomed into the highest pick in school history (51st overall) as well as the Conference USA player and defensive player of the year in 2016. Persistent hamstring injuries limited him to seven games during his first full pro season, but he stayed healthy in 2018 and finished second in the Class A Advanced Carolina League batting race at .315. Chatham's most valuable attribute is his ability to make consistent line-drive contact. He hinted at average raw power as an amateur that has yet to translate to home run production as a pro, though Boston hopes he can unlock more pop if he adds some strength to his lanky frame and some loft to his relatively flat right-handed swing. He has average speed and is effective on the bases, albeit not much of a threat to steal. His instincts and quick first step allow Chatham to cover ground and get the job done at shortstop. He still has a strong arm and soft hands, and he should be able to play second or third base if needed. He has one of the higher floors among Red Sox position prospects and a decent upside as a reliable if unspectacular regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chatham led Florida Atlantic to its first-ever Conference USA regular-season title in 2016, winning accolades as the league's player and defensive player of the year while playing through a broken hamate in his right hand. The Red Sox made him the highest pick in Owls history, signing him for $1.1 million as the 51st overall choice, but haven't gotten to see much of him yet. The hamate injury hampered him during his pro debut, while repeated hamstring issues limited him to just seven games in 2017. Though he's just an average runner and taller than most shortstops at 6-foot-4, Chatham shouldn't have to move from shortstop. His instincts and quick first step improve his range, and his strong, accurate arm allows him to make all of the throws. If he winds up shifting to second base, he still should provide enough offense to profile as an everyday player. Chatham has a track record of making consistent line-drive contract from the right side of the plate, though he could use some more patience to draw more walks. His size gives him good leverage and more raw power than most shortstops, and he could produce 30 doubles and 12-15 homers annually. He won't steal many bases but is an effective runner.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Despite playing with a right hand injury eventually diagnosed as a broken hamate bone, Chatham led Florida Atlantic to its first-ever Conference USA regular-season title in 2016, earning league player-of-the-year and defensive-player-of-the-year recognition along the way. The first college shortstop drafted in 2016 and the highest pick in school history, he went 51st overall and signed for $1.1 million. His hamate injury hampered him early in his debut but he hit .320 with four homers in his final two weeks, and then he missed most of the first three months of the 2017 season with repeated hamstring issues. Taller than most shortstops at 6-foot-4 and possessing just average speed, Chatham nevertheless should be able to stick at the position. His quick first step and his instincts enhance his range, and he has the strong, accurate arm to make any throw necessary. If he does have to move, he has enough bat to still profile as a regular at second base. Chatham has a track record of making consistent contact and could produce solid batting averages if he improves his patience at the plate. He has more raw power than the typical shortstop, thanks to the leverage in his right-handed swing, and should be good for double-digit home runs and plenty of doubles on an annual basis. He's not a threat to steal but runs the bases well.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Chatham's rather lengthy injury history becomes less problematic when you accept that his likely future role is of a part-time, bench variety. He's a bunch of 45s on offense, he plays a fine shortstop, and last season he started seeing more time at other positions, mostly second base. He played some left field and third base out of necessity in the fall because some of his teammates went home early. He has an outside shot to be Boston's starting second baseman next year, but we have him projected as a utility man long-term.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Chatham played on Miami-area powerhouse high school team American Heritage with Zack Collins, and stood out defensively for being a long-limbed athlete with a plus arm and above average defensive ability. Collins went to Miami and became a top ten pick while Chatham went to Florida Atlanta and became a second round talent. Over 2.5 seasons, Chatham has played only 156 games due to multiple injuries. He has viable infield defensive ability and above-average bat control with some doubles pop, but also has some clear offensive limitations. He had a mostly healthy 2018 at Hi-A, and should begin 2019 on the doorstep of a big league utility role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Cubs ranked second behind only the Dodgers in international spending during the 2015-16 signing period, handing out $16.4 million in bonuses. The best player from that crop is Ademan, who landed a $2 million bonus out of the Dominican Republic. His maturity has led Chicago to push him aggressively, and while he was able to handle low Class A at age 18 in 2017, he scuffled as the youngest regular in the high Class A Carolina League last year. Though he batted just .207/.291/.273 in 2018, Ademan still displayed an efficient left-handed swing and an advanced approach. He recognizes pitches well and uses the entire field, though his rough season demonstrated his need to add strength. He won't ever be a slugger but needs more muscle in order to reach his potential as an above-average hitter with some occasional pull power. Ademan's instincts allow him to play above his average speed on the bases and in the field. He has a good internal clock at shortstop, as well as the solid hands, range and arm to make plays there. His tools should allow him to play second base and third base if he needs to fill a utility role, though he should hit enough to be a regular if he gets the chance to catch his breath.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chicago invested heavily in the international market during the 2015-16 signing period, with Ademan receiving the third-largest bonus in its crop at $2 million. Extremely mature for his age, the Dominican made his full-season debut last August at 18 and didn't look out of place in the low Class A Midwest League. While he may not have as high a ceiling as former top Cubs infield prospects Javy Baez, Addison Russell and Gleyber Torres, he still offers plenty of upside and has a high floor. Despite his struggles in high Class A this year, Ademan is an advanced hitter who already recognizes pitches, uses the whole field and doesn't try to do too much. He makes repeated contact, drilling line drives to all fields while managing the strike zone well. Though he lacks size, he has a quick left-handed swing and some sneaky power that could translate into 12-15 homers annually once he adds some muscle. Ademan has average speed but plays quicker than that on the bases and in the field because of his instincts. He's still learning as a basestealer but already shows a propensity for making plays at shortstop. His hands, range and arm are all solid and should allow him to play a variety of positions if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best prospect from the Cubs' spending spree during the 2015-16 international signing period, Ademan landed a $2 million bonus out of the Dominican Republic. He made his pro debut last summer in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, where he hit .254/.366/.316 with more walks (34) than strikeouts (28). He stood out by showing more polish than a typical 17-year-old. An advanced left-handed hitter with a mature approach, Ademan already recognizes pitches well and uses the whole field. He lacks size and strength but understands his limitations, focusing on stroking line drives and not worrying about driving the ball. With his hitting ability and bat speed, he could grow into double-digit home run power while providing high batting averages and on-base percentages. Ademan has solid speed and already shows some savvy on the bases. He has good instincts in the field as well and should be able to stay at shortstop. He's not the flashiest defender, but his feet, hands and arm all work well.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: I struggled to decide what to do with Ademan. I, like many others, was smitten with his defensive acumen and precocious doubles power during his early days on the complex, but over the last couple seasons, he's gotten heavier and slower without adding any power. He was still young for Hi-A, but he didn't improve in his second year there, and he's in danger of just falling off the radar entirely if he doesn't start performing soon.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: We're chalking up Ademan's terrible 2018 statline to an overzealous assignment. At age 19, the Cubs sent him to Hi-A Myrtle Beach, where he barely hit above the Mendoza Line. He did look a little bit heavier than he had the year before, and his swing was more upright and less athletic than it has been, but all the physical tools to stay at short are still here (quick actions, sound footwork, plenty of arm) for now. Much of Ademan's offensive woes can be explained away by his age relative to the level. He doesn't project to be an impact bat, just one that is better than is usual at shortstop. Ideally he shows up to Mesa in the spring looking a little leaner and twitchier. He'll likely repeat Myrtle Beach (at least for the season's first half) and projects as an average everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2020 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Antone has taken a bit of a circuitous route to pro ball. Initially drafted by the Mets out of the Texas high school ranks in 2012, he opted to attend Texas Christian University. When he didn't get much mound time, he transferred to Weatherford Community College and landed as a fifth-rounder with the Reds. Antone is a big, strong right-hander with some arm strength. He can crank his fastball up to 95 mph. It has some sink to it, eliciting a fair amount of groundball outs. He has thrown both a slider and a curve in the past, with the former being a much more promising option. He's also shown some feel for a changeup, but needs to use it more for it to become a more viable weapon. He's generally around the strike zone, but needs to command the ball better, as he was hit during his pro debut. If the Reds can clean up Antone's delivery a bit and help him keep the ball down in the zone more, his size and arm strength give him the chance to move up the organizational ladder.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Antone's stuff has been steadily improving since he returned from Tommy John, and he was up to 96 as a starter last year. He goes at hitters with the kitchen sink. His flight of fastballs sits in the 89-93 range, he'll cut it and sink it. He also has a slider in the 82-84mph range that has really odd angle running away from right-handed hitters, who struggle to pick up Antone. He'll also drop in an occasional curveball, the changeup lives in the 82-85 range and is viable. He gets ground balls with the fastballs and misses bats with the slider. I think he fits in a multi-inning relief role, maybe the back of a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Selecting players in the Rule 5 Draft is always a roll of the dice. The Pirates knew they were really gambling when they acquired Burdi via a trade with the Phillies, who had taken the reliever in the 2017 edition of the Draft. The former Louisville standout had been a second-round pick of the Twins in 2014, but missed most of '16 with an elbow bone bruise and then was shelved for all of '17 following Tommy John surgery. He did get through the rehab process and made his big league debut last September. At his best, Burdi displayed the kind of power repertoire that plays well in the back end of a bullpen. He's capable of sitting easily in the upper-90s with his fastball and has hit triple digits. His plus slider is nasty and misses a ton of bats, a big reason why he's struck out 12.2 per nine innings in his Minor League career. He will show a changeup against lefties, though he's really just a two-pitch power reliever. Command was never a strength for the right-hander and, not surprisingly, he struggled with his feel upon his return. He'll need to stay on the active roster for 90 days, based on Rule 5 rules, so Burdi will have to stick with the Pirates or get offered back to the Twins. The organization thinks after a real, non-rehabbing offseason, he can get back to showing the stuff that made him an intriguing prospect in the first place.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rule 5 Draft is all about finding a diamond in the rough. That's particularly true in the case of Burdi, who was initially a second-round pick by the Twins in 2014 after a tremendous career as Louisville's closer. He's had trouble staying healthy, however, missing nearly all of 2016 with an elbow bone bruise and then needing Tommy John surgery in May of 2017. The Pirates thought his arm strength was worth the gamble, sending international bonus money to get him from the Phillies, who took him third in December's Rule 5. Burdi rehabbed from surgery and was back on the mound in July, with the Pirates hopeful he can rediscover the nasty power stuff that made him look like a future closer. His fastball sits easily in the upper 90s and has hit triple digits. He backs that up with a nasty plus slider that serves as a true strikeout pitch and can even mix in a changeup against left-handed hitters. Command has been an issue and while hit doesn't have to be pinpoint, his time missed hasn't helped him learn to find the strike zone more consistently. The Pirates are pleased he made it back to competitive pitching in 2018. When he's ready, he'll have to spend 90 days on the big league active roster to get past Rule 5 restrictions.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A lights-out closer at Louisville, the Twins took Burdi in the second round of the 2014 Draft thinking he could be a relatively quick to the big leagues power reliever. He looked poised to prove them right in 2016, but ended up missing all but three outings because of a bone bruise on his right elbow. He was off to a strong start in 2017 when he tore his UCL in May and required Tommy John surgery. Left unprotected, Burdi was selected by the Phillies in December's Rule 5 Draft and then traded to the Pirates. Burdi has a true top-of-the-scale fastball, one that sits easily in the upper-90s, and he complements it with a nasty slider that misses a ton of bats as well when he is healthy. He also has a changeup that could eventually give him a weapon against left-handed hitters. While he doesn't need to have pinpoint command as a short reliever, he does have to find the strike zone more consistently to continue to have success. When Burdi returns, he'll have missed two years of development time, keeping his command and changeup from being refined enough to be ready for primetime. He'll have to spend 90 days on the Pirates' active roster to get past any Rule 5 restrictions and still has closer-type stuff.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Burdi's injury history (a Tommy John and surgery for thoracic outlet syndrome) is a concern, but he's touching 100 mph again, and his lower half is now more involved in his delivery. He'd be in the 40+ tier with Mears if not for his injury rap and age.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text:
A 2017 Rule 5 selection by the Phillies, Burdi was immediately flipped to Pittsburgh for international bonus space and spent much of 2018 recovering from Tommy John. He started a rehab assignemnt in mid-July and made his major league debut in September, his stuff mostly back to pre-TJ form. He topped out at 98 and broke off plenty of nasty sliders, but his command and the quality of break on the slider were inconsistent, which is typical of those returning from TJ. Burdi's delivery is odd. His swivels about an axis created by a stiff front leg. It makes it hard for him to get over his front side and is difficult to repeat. This, combined with his injury history, mean he's perceived as a risk for chronic health issues. 
If he can stay healthy, he could pitch at the back of a bullpen. Rule 5 roster requirements state that a drafted player needs to be on his new team's big league roster for 90 days for his new club to keep him, which means Burdi needs to stay with the Pirates through April and May or else be offered back to the Twins.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After hitting .240 in his first three seasons at Southern California, Stubbs batted .346 with 20 steals as a senior in 2015, when he won the Johnny Bench Award as the top college catcher as well as Pacific-12 Conference defensive player of the year honors. An eighth-rounder that June, he reached Double-A in his first full season but stalled there in 2017. He rebounded last year in Triple-A to claim a spot on Houston's 40-man roster. Stubbs makes repeated contact with a simple left-handed swing and controls the strike zone better than any Astros product. He made a conscious effort to drive the ball more last year, though he's not very physical and his power will come more in the form of doubles than home runs. Extremely athletic for a catcher, he has average speed and knows what he's doing on the bases. Stubbs moves well behind the plate and shows solid receiving skills. He has arm strength to match and it plays up because of his quick transfer, enabling him to throw out 44 percent of basestealers in his first four years as a pro. His biggest drawback is that he's just 5-foot-10 and 175 pounds and wears down over the course of a season, making him more of a backup because he won't hold up as a regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Stubbs hit .240 in his first three years at Southern California before batting .346 with 20 steals as a senior in 2015, winning the Johnny Bench Award as college baseball's top catcher and Pacific-12 Conference defensive player of the year honors. Signed for $100,000 as an eighth-rounder, he opened more eyes by hitting .304/.391/.469 while advancing to Double-A during his first full pro season. He started last year in similar fashion but slumped in May and never snapped out of it, finishing at .232/.328/.321. Stubbs is better than his 2017 numbers and has rebounded this season, but at 5-foot-10 and 175 pounds he's not equipped to handle a full season's workload behind the plate. He also looked worn down at the end of 2016 in the Arizona Fall League and will have to do a better job of managing his strength via nutrition and weightlifting. While he may not have the stamina to be a regular in the big leagues, he has the tools to be a quality backup. Using a simple left-handed swing, Stubbs makes consistent line-drive contact and excels at managing the strike zone. He's not geared for power but does have average speed and provides more value on the bases than a typical catcher. His athleticism pays off behind the plate, where he receives well and enhances his solid arm strength with a quick transfer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After hitting .240 in his first three seasons at Southern California, Stubbs batted .346 with 20 steals as a senior, won the Johnny Bench Award as college baseball's best catcher and was named Pac-12 Conference defensive player of the year. He has continued to impress after signing for $100,000 as an eighth-rounder in 2015, batting .304/.391/.469 and reaching Double-A during his first full pro season. His 5-foot-10, 175-pound frame leads to a lot of questions about whether he'll be durable enough to be a big league starter, but that's the only real concern. His size also makes him the player he is, as he's much quicker and more athletic than the typical catcher. He receives and blocks well, and he enhances solid arm strength with fast footwork and impressive accuracy -- which allowed him to throw out 51 percent of basestealers in 2016. Stubbs excels at making contact at the plate and has walked (64) more than he has struck out (53) in his first two pro seasons. He uses a simple left-handed swing but can drive the ball on occasions and improved his slugging percentage at each of his first four Minor League stops, so he might be able to provide double-digit homers on an annual basis.

fangraphs.label: 2020report
fangraphs.text: Stubbs finally began to see time at other positions in 2019 (the outfield and some second base) and he projects in an interesting 26th man role, which may help keep him healthy and more productive at the plate than he would be if asked to catch everyday.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: After a dour, injured 2017 season, Stubbs had a bounce back 2018 and hit .310/.382/.455 at Triple-A. He spent the offseason adding mass to his little frame, a body scouts have long been skeptical about being able to weather the full-season storm of catching. These doubts have been reinforced by Stubbs' semi-frequent injury issues, which led him to focus on weight gain during the offseason. His athletic capabilities are clear though, and Stubbs is a good ball blocker, an excellent catch-and-throw guy, and his passable framing may benefit from altering the depth at which he sets up. From a skills standpoint, totally ignoring the issue of durability, he looks like a potential everyday catcher. There has been some industry sentiment that Stubbs would be best deployed as a multi-positional bat, perhaps playing third base and the outfield corners as well as catcher. He hasn't played other positions in games but has worked with Matt Chapman at third during the offseason, so perhaps he will be allowed to try new things once the season starts. We have him projected as a contact-oriented, multi-positional bench piece.
