His curveball, typically in the upper-70s, has premium raw spin; that pitch should alone carry him to a role on a big league staff. He spent 2018 with Triple-A Charlotte and is a strong multi-inning relief candidate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Initially plagued by injuries (oblique, elbow) for the first few seasons of his pro career after signing with the A's as a fifth-round pick out of Ole Miss in 2013, Wahl made his big league debut in '17, though he again missed time with a right shoulder injury, ultimately undergoing surgery to address Thoracic Outlet Syndrome. He was back and strong in Triple-A in '18 and made it back up to the big leagues with the Mets after they acquired him in the Jeurys Familia trade. He pitched to mixed results but showcased impressive stuff during his brief time in New York, and the Brewers acquired him in the offseason Keon Broxton trade. Expected to be a big part of Milwaukee bullpen in 2019, Wahl instead suffered a torn ACL in his right knee during Spring Training and missed the entire year. When healthy, Wahl will sit at 95-96 mph and tops out at 98 with his high-spin heater. His power curveball in the mid-80s plays above average and is a true swing-and-miss pitch, though at times it varies in terms of shape and bite. Wahl also has feel for an average cutter that hovers around 89-90 mph and mixes in the occasional changeup, a distant fourth pitch. The effort in his delivery leads to below-average fastball command, but with elite velocity and spin, he also has a larger margin for error. In 2018, Wahl induced whiffs at a 19 percent clip and struck out 40 percent of all batters he faced between the Minors and Majors. The Brewers still view Wahl as a potential late-inning bullpen asset, but after myriad injuries, it's hard to ignore his checkered medical history. Wahl will need to stay healthy first before he gets a chance to contribute, but it's too early to write off the big right-hander given the caliber of his stuff.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Wahl has been plagued by injuries for much of his pro career since signing with the A's as a fifth-round pick out of Ole Miss in 2013. The right-hander was limited by an oblique injury in his first full season, and then underwent season-ending surgery for a nerve impingement in his elbow in July 2015. But Wahl returned as strong as ever last year, showing elite velocity while reaching Triple-A for the first time and setting career bests in appearances (45), innings pitched (54 1/3), strikeouts (65) and opponents average (.194). Wahl's trademark velocity returned in earnest in 2016 as he sat in the upper 90s while touching 100. His power breaking ball plays above average but at times varies in terms of shape and bite, and his seldom-used changeup is a distant third pitch. The effort in his delivery leads to below-average fastball command, but with elite velocity, he also has a larger margin for error. Provided he can stay healthy, Wahl seems poised to log innings out of the A's bullpen in 2017.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Wahl, who turns 27 in March, was part of the two-player package Oakland sent to the Mets for Jeurys Familia last summer. He has just twelve career big league innings at this age mostly because Wahl missed extended development time due to multiple surgeries, including one in 2017 to remedy Thoracic Outlet Syndrome. His stuff was back last year. Wahl's fastball sits in the mid-90s and will touch 99. He has a four-pitch mix but works primarily with the fastball and a power, mid-80s breaking ball that has bat-missing vertical action. A firm cutter and changeup are also folded in on occasion. Wahl has set-up man stuff but below average command and more significant injury risk than most pitching prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Northwest Oklahoma A&M pitching staff in 2014 had a pair of interesting prospects. Dean Deetz started and was an 11th-round pick of the Astros in that June's Draft. Jewell served as the closer that year and pitched well enough in that role to land in the fifth round. Given a chance to start, Jewell took off a bit in '16 and '17, though a return to the bullpen allowed him to make his big league debut last June, three months ahead of Deetz. Jewell's success story was cut short when he fractured his right fibula during a play at the plate, requiring surgery. A move back to the bullpen allowed Jewell to focus on his fastball-slider combination. His hard, sinking two-seamer leads to a ton of ground-ball outs and he can also change a hitter's look with a four-seamer up in the zone that can touch 97 mph. His slider flashes plus and has cutter action to it. He had a changeup he was working on as a starter, but it's not as important in short relief. Neither is the fact that his command has always been far from pinpoint. He does need to throw enough strikes to get high-leverage innings in a big league bullpen, something he'll try to prove he's worthy of as he comes back from his injury.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During his two years at Northeastern Oklahoma A&M, Jewell started one year and relieved the next for the junior college program. He's done a little of both since the Angels took him in the fifth round of the 2014 Draft, almost exclusively starting in the 2016-17 seasons. Able to shake off a rough California League performance in 2016, Jewell moved up to Double-A the following season and showed enough to earn a spot on the 40-man roster. Considering Jewell has some premium power stuff, he hasn't missed as many bats as you'd expect. He's largely been a groundball machine with a hard, sinking two-seamer, then he can turn around and crank a four-seamer up to 97 mph at times. His slider flashes plus with cutter-like movement, and while his changeup is very inconsistent, he is capable of showing a solid one from time to time with split-like action. After his walk rate spiked in 2016, he's gotten back to filling the strike zone more consistently. With a fastball-slider combination that would play up in shorter stints, not to mention a lack of a dependable third pitch and less-than-pinpoint command, there's a good chance Jewell will move back to the bullpen in 2018. That could pave the way to him impacting the big league pitching staff in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The California League has been known over the years to chew up pitchers and spit them out. Jewell, who many thought would have a big 2016 season after a solid first full year of pro ball, definitely struggled in the hitter-friendly circuit, going 2-15 with a 6.31 ERA. Despite that, the Angels feel the junior college product has a good chance to bounce back. Jewell didn't pitch a ton at Northeastern Oklahoma A&M, totaling just 72 2/3 innings over two years, and pitching entirely in relief in his 2014 Draft year. The Angels have worked to stretch him out as a starter and will continue to do so because he has the repertoire necessary to pitch out of a rotation. The 2016 season was his first as a full-time starter and his ability to find the strike zone consistently really backed up. He also lost the feel of his changeup, which graded as the best in the system a year ago internally. His heavy sinking fastball still got ground-ball outs when he kept it down, though that happened less frequently last year. His slider flashes as an above-average breaking ball, but not with any consistency. It's clear the mental wear of the California League got to Jewell. He'll get the chance to wipe the slate clean and the organization is still very much committed to him as a starting pitcher.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: After yo-yoing back and forth between the bullpen and rotation since college, Jewell was finally 'penned in 2018 and had a two-inning sip of coffee with the Halos last June before he fractured his right fibula during a play at the plate. He would need season-ending surgery. Jewell's command has long foreshadowed an eventual permanent move to the bullpen, but he has the stuff to accrue big league outs. He can alter the shape of his mid-90s fastball to sink or cut, has a fine mid-80s curveball, and a power changeup that averages 90mph. He didn't throw his hard cutter/slider during his short appearances with the Angels last year, but we're unsure if the pitch has actually be scrapped. It's an unusually deep repertoire for a reliever, probably one better suited for inducing ground balls than strikeouts, but is possibly enough for Jewell to go for four or more outs at a time.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals signed Agustin out of the Virgin Islands back in October 2013, and he made steady progress at the developmental levels en route to his first taste of full-season ball in 2016. He was overmatched at Class A Advanced Potomac the next year but showed more power and consistency after a demotion to Class A Hagerstown. Taking another crack at Potomac in 2018, Agustin was hitting .386/.411/.659 in the Carolina League before a broken finger suffered in early May disrupted his breakout campaign. Once viewed as a slap hitter with minimal impact potential at the plate, Agustin has since tacked on considerable muscle to his frame. With that improved strength has come a more leveraged swing and an emphasis on driving the ball in the air, something he did nearly 10 percent better last season than 2017. What's more, Agustin was able to make those adjustments while making gains in his approach and improving his strikeout and walk rates. A plus runner who played mostly center field early in his career, Agustin has wheels that now grade out more as above-average, and he's settled in as an average defender who can handle either right or left field. Those positions, of course, come with greater offensive demands, so Agustin will need to hit for both average and power all the way up the ladder to profile as a regular in the Majors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Agustin opened eyes during his impressive professional debut in the Dominican Summer League, one year after the Nationals had signed him out of the Virgin Islands. He performed well in his first stateside action in 2015 between the Gulf Coast and New York-Penn Leagues, but has been inconsistent on both sides of the ball at full-season levels. Agustin did post better numbers during his second tour of the Class A South Atlantic League in 2017, albeit after a demotion from Class A Advanced Potomac. Agustin's quick hands from the left side of the plate fuel his game as a slap hitter who predominantly hits the ball on the ground and sprays it from line to line. He's also an adept bunter and gets out of the batter's box quickly, utilizing his above-average speed. Agustin will never offer much in the way of power, but he makes enough hard contact to accrue his share of doubles and triples while contributing with the occasional home run. A raw defender when he signed, Agustin was one of Washington's more improved outfielders in 2016 after making strides with his routes and angles to the ball. He regressed defensively in 2017, in turn raising questions about his focus and work ethic. Though capable of playing center field, Agustin profiles better in left, where his speed and average arm strength are both fits.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 2013 international signee out of the Virgin Islands, Agustin opened eyes the next year during his impressive professional debut in the Dominican Summer League. That success carried over into his first stateside action in 2015, when he slashed .344/.380/.469 in 45 games between the Gulf Coast and New York-Penn Leagues. Agustin advanced to full-season ball for the first time in 2016, only to miss a portion of the first half with an ankle injury and appear in just 73 games. Agustin's quick hands from the left side of the plate fuel his game as a slap hitter who predominantly hits the ball on the ground and sprays it from line to line. He's also an adept bunter and gets out of the batter's box quickly, utilizing his above-average speed. Agustin will never offer much in the way of power, but he makes enough hard contact to accrue his share of doubles and triples. A raw defender when he signed, Agustin was one of Washington's more improved outfielders in 2016 after making strides with his routes and angles to the ball. He's capable of playing center field but profiles better in left, where his speed and average arm strength are cleaner fits.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: The last time one of us wrote up Agustin he was a skinny, all-fields line drive tweener who looked like a classic bench outfielder. He has put on about 30 pounds since and has undergone a swing and approach change that has him lifting and pulling the ball more often. He's likely limited to left field due to mediocre arm strength, but he may profile as a low-end regular out there if the bat maxes out. Keep an eye on Agustin's walk rate. In 2018 it was a good bit better than his career mark. If that holds, he'll have a better chance of profiling than if it regresses to his career norms.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Finding players who can defend up the middle in the infield can be tough, and that's a big reason why the Pirates took Alemais in the third round of the 2016 Draft following a solid but unspectacular junior season at Tulane. After playing across two levels of A ball in his first full season, he had a strong year playing second base for Double-A Altoona in 2018. There is no question Alemais can defend at the big league level. Alemais has the ability to make flashy plays consistently. He's certainly good enough to play shortstop, then showed in 2018 he could slide over to second in deference to Cole Tucker, and be a plus defender there as well. While Alemais occasionally still tries to muscle up at the plate too much, he has excellent hand-eye coordination and terrific bat-to-ball skills. He rarely strikes out and controls the strike zone well, albeit without any power. The bilingual Alemais has spent the last two offseasons working with Estrellas Orientales in the Dominican Winter League, and it's obviously had a positive impact. It's crowded in the infield in the Pirates' upper levels, but Alemais' glove-first utility profile should help him contribute soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in New York but of Dominican descent, the fully bilingual Alemais had a solid, albeit unspectacular junior season at Tulane. His ability to play up the middle defensively and control the strike zone offensively interested the Pirates enough to take him in the third round of the 2016 Draft. While a thumb injury kept him out of a large chunk of his first full season, he was able to make his way from A ball to the Class A Advanced Florida State League. Despite the missed time, Alemais has shown a bit more bat than expected when he was coming out of Tulane. He has good feel to hit and recognizes pitches well and if he stays within his approach, he has the chance to be a Major League average hitter. Though power isn't a big part of his game, he does occasionally get too big and try to leave the yard, something he didn't do when he moved up to Bradenton in 2017. He has very good hands at shortstop, with solid range, plus instincts and at least a solid average arm, meaning he can play shortstop full time in the future, though he slid over and mostly played second alongside Cole Tucker in Altoona in 2018. Alemais was drafted by Estrellas Orientales in the Dominican Winter League this offseason and the infielder was able to work out with the team for a spell, an experience that must have carried over in 2018. His ability to play on both sides of second might help him fight through the logjam of middle infielders at the upper levels.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Finding college shortstops who can stay at the position isn't always easy. The Pirates did it when they drafted Jordy Mercer in the third round of the 2008 Draft. They're hoping three is their lucky number again as they took Alemais in the same round of the 2016 Draft out of Tulane. There is no question Alemais will stick at the premium position defensively. He has very good hands and an arm that is at least above-average to go along with very good range. All of it plays up because he has outstanding instincts in the field. His ability to be an everyday player at the position will hinge on just how much he'll hit. He didn't produce during his pro debut, albeit in a small sample size, and he missed six weeks of his first full season with a thumb injury, but typically uses a contact-oriented approach with little to no power. He did sneak a few over the fence during instructs and while that will never be a big part of his game, having enough strength to drive the ball on occasion will help keep defenses honest. He's a good athlete with a tick above-average speed. The Pirates love Alemais' makeup, his energy and his intelligence on the field. That with his defensive skills could be enough to get him to the big leagues. If he can swing the bat at all, he could be a glove-first regular.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Alemais is one of the most acrobatic and athletic defensive players in the minors and began seeing most of his reps at second base, not because he's an incapable shortstop, but because he was teammates with Cole Tucker. Alemais' glove is so good that we consider him likely to play some kind of big league role, despite being unlikely to hit. His hands lack life; to Alemais' credit, he's done his best to find a way to hit the ball harder by taking high-effort swings, and he hasn't lost any contact ability in the process. This is an intense, hard-working athlete with some physical shortcomings that will likely limit his role, but he has elite defensive skill and is tough to strike out, which means he has a watered down version of Andrelton Simmons' skillset.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After leading the Cape Cod League with eight homers the summer before, Shaw established himself as the best college power hitter in the 2015 Draft. He has lived up to his reputation since signing for $1.5 million as the 31st overall choice, topping the short-season Northwest League with 12 homers in his pro debut and the entire organization (Majors and Minors) with 24 blasts in 2017 and 25 last season. His first big league homer traveled 468 feet off Seung Hwan Oh in September. Shaw has plenty of strength and leverage in his massive 6-foot-3 frame, giving him huge natural power to all fields. He could hit home runs without trying but sells out too much for power, letting his left-handed swing get too long and chasing pitches out of the strike zone. His whiff rate has jumped from 20 percent in Double-A to 32 percent in Triple-A to 37 percent in his first taste of the Majors, and he's unlikely to hit for much of an average unless he forces pitchers to challenge him more. Mostly a right fielder at Boston College, Shaw broke into pro ball as a first baseman and made himself into an average defender. With Brandon Belt ensconced there in San Francisco, the Giants shifted Shaw to left field in early 2017. His lack of speed limits his range but he does own solid arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The best college power hitter available in the 2015 Draft, Shaw topped the Cape Cod League with eight homers the previous summer and hit 11 in 40 games as a Boston College junior despite breaking the hamate bone in his right hand. He has produced as advertised since signing for $1.4 million as the 31st overall pick, leading the short-season Northwest League with 12 homers in his pro debut and slamming a total of 45 homers in his first two full seasons while advancing to Triple-A. His 24 blasts last year were six more than anyone else hit in the organization in the Majors or Minors. Shaw's massive 6-foot-4 frame affords him plenty of strength and leverage, allowing him to hit the ball out of the park from foul pole to foul pole. Though he recognizes that his raw power means he doesn't have to swing for the fences, his left-handed swing can get long and he gets in trouble when he expands his strike zone. His whiff rate jumped to a career-worst 29 percent in Triple-A last year and he'll have to develop more patience to hit for average against advanced pitching. Primarily a right fielder in college, Shaw spent most of his first two pro seasons at first base and worked diligently to become an average defender there. He's blocked by Brandon Belt in San Francisco, however, so he shifted to left field last May. His lack of speed limits his range, though he does have solid arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Shaw established himself as the best college power hitter available in the 2015 Draft, leading the Cape Cod League with eight homers the prior summer and then hitting 11 in 40 games as a junior despite breaking the hamate bone in his right hand. After signing for $1.4 million as the 31st overall pick, he paced the short-season Northwest League in homers (12) and slugging (.551) during his pro debut. He struggled when he reached Double-A in mid-2016, but he made adjustments and hit well there and in Triple-A this year. Shaw's big 6-foot-4 frame gives him a lot of strength and leverage, and he uses it to crush balls to all fields. His left-handed swing naturally gets long because of his size, so he probably won't hit for a high average, but he doesn't swing and miss excessively for a masher. He ran into trouble when he first got to Double-A when he expanded his strike zone, then showed more discipline in his return in 2017. While he has a strong arm, Shaw's lack of speed limits his defensive value. After spending most of his time at Boston College in right field, he spent his first two pro seasons in first base and worked hard to become an adequate defender. With Brandon Belt ensconced in San Francisco, the Giants have played Shaw mostly in left field this year, but he doesn't have much range.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Shaw is one of many whiff-heavy corner bats with huge power who floats around the upper levels of the minors, putting up big power numbers while struggling to find a big league role if their parent club has someone at 1B/DH. The Giants have tried Shaw in the outfield but scouts don't think he's playable out there. Shaw has the advantage of hitting left-handed, but unless the Giants make a concerted effort to give him reps soon (they demoted him to Double-A to start 2019, so not a great sign) he'll probably bounce around on waivers until a team with 40-man space -- and the time to see whether or not Shaw can hit big league pitching -- gives him a chance. Sometimes this is how clubs fall into Jesus Aguilar and Christian Walker, but it's also the fate of many a Quad-A hitter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As an amateur, Miller drew comparisons to fellow Georgia high schooler Brandon Phillips because they had similar offensive and defensive tools at the same stage of their careers. They went in the same area of the Draft, with Phillips an Expos second-rounder in 1999 and Miller signing for an over-slot $1.1 million as a Giants third-rounder in 2015. While Phillips immediately produced at the plate in pro ball, Miller struggled offensively until he repeated high Class A in 2018. Miller always had an efficient right-handed swing but didn't start making hard contact until he gained more muscle and experience. He has strong wrists and finished fifth in the California League with 51 extra-base hits last year after he started to turn on more pitches. His aggressive approach results in few walks, however, and may require an adjustment against more advanced pitchers. A solid runner, Miller can steal an occasional base. Like Phillips, he was drafted as a shortstop but wound up at second base. His below-average arm limited his effectiveness on the left side of the infield, but his quickness and soft hands make him an asset at the keystone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller has earned Brandon Phillips comparisons because both were Georgia prep products with similar offensive and defensive profiles as amateurs. They went in the same range of the Draft, with Phillips an Expos second-rounder in 1999 and Miller a Giants third-rounder in 2015. Their paths diverge at that point, because while Phillips hit right away in pro ball, Miller batted .222/.277/.304 in his first two seasons. Signed for an over-slot $1.1 million, Miller still offers hope at the plate with his sound right-handed swing and strong wrists. He needs to get stronger, develop better rhythm at the plate and improve his pitch recognition so he can better cope with breaking balls and changeups. He has above-average speed and could reach double figures in homers and steals if he figures things out. Like Phillips, Miller broke into pro ball as a shortstop but was destined for second base. Though his below-average arm isn't suited for the left side of the infield, his quickness and hands could make him a solid defender at second. He needs to get more consistent after topping low Class A South Atlantic League second basemen with 20 errors last year.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Miller's lack of arm strength really boxes him in at second base, which means he has to hit enough to be a regular there because defensive versatility, and therefore a viable utility role, isn't part of his profile. Much of the pressure will be on the bat to ball skills as Miller is a compact guy with average bat speed. He probably needs to be a 60 bat or better to play every day, which is feasible considering that his attributes, dating back to high school, are lead by a short swing and barrel control. He's off to a good start in 2019, walking nearly as much as he has struck out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A $10,000 senior sign as a 14th-rounder in 2015, Poyner pitched on Florida staffs with future Red Sox Brian Johnson and Austin Maddox and five future first-rounders. He has breezed through the Minors with a 2.51 ERA and 5.0 K/BB ratio in his first four pro seasons and made Boston's Opening Day roster in 2018. He spent five separate stints with the eventual World Series champions, logging a 3.22 ERA and a 24/3 K/BB in 22 1/3 innings. Poyner's fastball is tough to grade on the 20-80 scouting scale because it has 40 velocity (ranging from 88-92 mph) with 70 command and 80 deception. Even if it doesn't excite radar guns, his heater plays as a plus pitch, as does his fading changeup. He'll dabble with both a curveball and cutter just to give hitters different looks but both are fringy, and he relies heavily on his main two pitches. Poyner isn't a lefty specialist because he doesn't have a quality breaking ball and actually has been slightly more effective against righties as a pro. He has no margin for error but commands his pitches well and is fearless on the mound. He performed well when the Red Sox trusted him with higher-leverage situations in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Relatively unheralded on stocked Florida pitching staffs that included future Red Sox Brian Johnson and Austin Maddox as well as five first-round arms, Poyner was a $10,000 senior sign as a 14th-rounder in 2015. Other than a rough patch in high Class A during the second half of his first full season, he has carved up pro hitters. He posted a 0.94 ERA after arriving in Double-A last June, lowering his career mark to 2.35 with 168 strikeouts in 149 2/3 innings. Poyner may get more swings and misses on fastballs below 90 mph than any pitcher in the Minors. He usually operates at 88-89 mph but his heater plays as a plus pitch because of exquisite command and a lot of deception. His changeup is also a weapon, and the combination of his two best offerings helped him hold right-handers to a .441 OPS and strike them out at a 35 percent clip last year. Poyner's hybrid breaking ball is closer to a slider than a curveball and doesn't distinguish itself with power or shape, so he's not quite as dominant against left-handers (.654 OPS, 35 percent strikeout rate). He doesn't have much margin for errors but rarely makes mistakes. He doesn't have much left to prove in the Minors and could become a newer version of Craig Breslow for Boston.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Oddly, because four-pitch lefties with command typically find their way into a rotation, Poyner ran the pro ball gamut exclusively as a reliever and has a long track record of performance in that role. His changeup is excellent, but the rest of his stuff is largely enabled by his command. He's a big league-ready middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the top prospects in the 2016-17 international amateur class, Brito got $1.1 million to sign with the A's in July 2016. He made his pro debut the following summer and came to the United States, following that up with a step up to the Short-Season New York-Penn League in 2018. While he hasn't wowed with performance, he has made slow and steady progress. It hasn't shown up on the stat line just yet, but Brito has the chance to hit from both sides of the plate, though he's a touch better swinging the bat left-handed. He's added some strength as he's matured and while he's never going to be a power guy, there should be the ability to impact the ball with some extra-base authority to all fields. Brito initially spent time bouncing between second and third, but it's looking more and more likely that second base is his long-term defensive home with an arm that's a little short for the left side of the infield. He could eventually be a plus defender, though right now he mixes in making the spectacular play with losing concentration and making needless errors on routine plays. Brito will play all of the 2019 season at age 19, so there's plenty of time for his production to catch up to his potential. If it all clicks, he eventually could be a solid every day second baseman in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The No. 26 prospect on MLB Pipeline's list of the Top 30 prospects for the 2016-17 international period, Brito showcased his all-around skills during three games at MLB's International Prospect Showcase in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, in February 2016. The A's liked what they saw from the switch-hitting shortstop and signed him for $1.1 million on July 2, and he made his U.S. debut the following year in the Rookie-level Arizona League. Brito has already made a name for himself as a quality hitting prospect, one who has a short, slight-upstroke swing through the hitting zone. He's shown impressive bat speed and the ability to make solid contact to all fields from both sides of the plate, though some scouts believe the teenager might be a better overall hitter from the left side. Brito has a short frame and a medium build with some physical projection, but he's unlikely to offer much in the way of power. In the field, Brito is a raw defender but has soft hands and clean actions. His average arm strength and speed raise questions pertaining to his ability to remain a shortstop, and he saw the bulk of his playing time at second base during his pro debut while logging the occasional start at shortstop and third base.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text:
A skills-over-tools prospect, Brito is the most well-rounded, technically advanced player of Oakland's splashy 2016 international signees, and the org saw fit to send him to the New York-Penn League as an 18-year-old last summer, where Brito was three years younger than the average regular. 
Brito has enough range for the middle infield and magician's hands around the bag at second base, and while he lacks the max-effort arm strength for shortstop, he throws darts from second to first with a flick of the wrist. His ball/strike recognition is mature for his age and Brito has above-average bat control and hand-eye coordination, but the way his body develops is going to dictate much of what he's capable of doing offensively. He needs to get stronger to be more than a utility option at best. He's a switch-hitting middle infield fit with feel for contact, and that alone makes him one of the more interesting prospects in this system, but there's a sizable gap between where his physicality is now and where it reasonably needs to be for him to punish big league pitching in a meaningful way.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best infield prospects available on the international market at the start of the 2017-18 signing period, Querecuto signed with the Mariners in July 2017 for $1.225 million. The son of former Minor League catcher Juan and younger brother of Juniel, who reached the big leagues with the Rays in 2016 and spent the 2018 season in the D-backs system, the younger Juan will bring his combination of skills and instincts to the United States for the first time in 2019. While his older brother is a 5-foot-8 utility type, Querecuto already stands 6-foot-2, with a lean and lanky frame. His glovework is currently ahead of his bat, partially because of his outstanding defensive skills and partially because of a lack of physicality at the plate. His hands, actions and plus arm all point to a future at shortstop, but a lack of speed and, as a result, range will mean he'll have to use his very high baseball IQ to stick at the premium position, something that is way too early to rule out. He does have a decent approach from the right side of the plate, with a willingness to draw walks. He will have to add strength in order to have any impact as a hitter. He has grown physically and mentally since signing, so the Mariners are hopeful there's more to unlock as he comes stateside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: As the son of Minor League catcher Juan Querecuto and younger brother of Juniel Querecuto, who reached the Majors with the Rays in 2016, the young Venezuelan shortstop has certainly grown up around the game. The No. 26 prospect on MLB Pipeline's list of the Top 30 international prospects for the 2017-18 period, he signed for $1.225 million on July 2. Querecuto is a confident prospect with good plate discipline and good instincts on both sides of the ball. The teen has showed a mature approach, good bat speed and the ability to hit the ball to all fields. Scouts believe he'll add some power as he grows into his projectable frame, albeit mostly to the gaps rather than true over-the-fence pop. Defensively, Querecuto's plus arm strength is more than enough for him to remain at shortstop, where he stands out for his clean actions, soft hands and overall feel for the position. His remaining physical projection could ultimately force him to third base, a position he has the requisite tools for, though it also would place greater pressure on his offensive development.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Querecuto suffered a torn meniscus in February, but his physical immaturity almost certainly had him ticketed for the AZL, so while he may be brought along slowly as minor league spring training gets underway, he should be fine for game action during extended spring training, and when rookie ball starts in June. He's a graceful but unexplosive shortstop, with a limber, projectable frame. His arm and body control are clean fits at short, though his first step leaves a bit to be desired. He may grow into some power as his body matures, which may enable him to play every day, but it's more likely that he becomes a utility type.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After taking a pair of high school pitchers at the top of their 2017 Draft, the Pirates went after prep bats with their next two selections in Calvin Mitchell and Uselton. While Mitchell has started to take off, Uselton has had trouble finding any traction. His debut summer ended after a serious hamstring injury, and he struggled to hit in the Rookie-level Appalachian League in 2018. The 2018 season was meant mostly for Uselton to get his professional legs under him, especially since he completely tore his hamstring the previous summer. It's unclear if there were some lingering effects, but he never could get his right-handed bat going. Uselton is believed to be more power over hit with some strength and leverage to his swing, and the Pirates still hope his power will start to show up the further removed from the injury he is. He'll need to get back to driving the ball to all fields. Uselton is also a former football player, and that athleticism was a plus for him as he entered pro ball. He played center field in high school, but played right in the Appy League in 2018. His arm works from the corner spot and if he can show the power potential he did as an amateur, he could profile well there offensively as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Pirates went high school heavy at the top of the 2017 Draft, taking a prep player with each of their first four picks. Uselton, a former high school quarterback who focused on baseball after his sophomore year, was the fourth of that quartet to be taken. The Pirates only got to see him play two games in the Gulf Coast League during his pro debut with a hamstring injury ending his summer after just seven at-bats. Uselton did return to health in time to head to the organization's instructs in the Dominican Republic, where he was able to play for a couple of weeks before embarking on his offseason plan. The outfielder is more power over hit at this point, with some strength and leverage in his right-handed swing. In the past, he's had some mechanical issues with that swing, but he smoothed some of that during his senior year and showed he is capable of driving the ball to all fields. A solid athlete who runs fairly well, Uselton played center field in high school. He's likely to mostly play in an outfield corner as a pro, where his plus arm, not to mention his power profile, will play very well.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Uselton had a rough first season in pro ball as a 20-year-old in the Appy League. His bat was raw coming out of high school, especially for a hitter who was old for his class, but he was a second round pick because he already had big power and was likely to grow into more. He remains an archtypical right field prospect. There's power, a huge frame, and arm strength. He'd be a sophomore-eligible college player in 2019 had he gone to Oklahoma State and the Pirates typically send newly drafted collegians to the New York-Penn League. That means Uselton will likely begin 2019 in extended spring training and, since he'll essentially be repeating that level until June, he needs to start hitting while he's there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since getting drafted in the 10th round of the 2016 Draft and signing for full pick value out of UC-Riverside, Fernandez has shown he can do a little bit of everything well, particularly hit for power. That's come with a growing strikeout rate and in very hitting-friendly environments has some curious to see if it will work as he attacks the higher levels of the Rockies system. The power was showing up in his first taste of Double-A in 2019 when he was suspended for 50 games after testing positive for an amphetamine. There's no question Fernandez has some raw power from the left side of the plate, and he hit a career high 24 homers in 2018, albeit with some fairly dramatic home-road splits and most of his pop coming in Lancaster's bandbox of a ballpark. His strikeout rate has also crept up in each year of pro ball, though so has his walk rate, and he must cut down on his 34.5 percent strikeout rate from a year ago to have a chance as he advances. Fernandez runs well enough to steal an occasional base and cover ground in the outfield. He's seen almost all of his time defensively in the outfield corners, with enough arm for right. If he can learn to make enough contact, he could be a fourth outfielder type who provides left-handed pop off the bench.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Fernandez showed off his pop by leading the Big West Conference with 112 total bases in 2016. That and his package of decent all-around tools got him drafted in the 10th round out of UC Riverside that June. He finished fifth in the low Class A South Atlantic League with 16 homers during his first full pro season despite missing a month with an oblique injury. He did much more damage at hitter-friendly Asheville (.913 OPS) than he did on the road (.717), however. Though Fernandez has enough raw power to hit at least 20 homers per season, he'll have to tone down his approach at the plate to get there. His left-handed swing is relatively sound but he's overly aggressive, resulting in a 29 percent strikeout rate last year. He has remained productive in 2018 at high Class A Lancaster, perhaps the best hitting environment in the Minors, but his all-out mentality may lead to struggles at higher levels. Fernandez possesses average speed out of the box, is a little quicker once he gets going and can steal an occasional base. He has enough arm strength to play right field, though he spent much of 2017 in left in deference to teammate Willie Abreu.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Fernandez is purported to have been one of Texas' PTBNL options in the Jonathan Lucroy trade, and he's outhit Pedro Gonzalez (whom the Rangers ended up taking) to this point, to the tune of a .275/.365/.520 career line. He's performed up through Double-A, albeit as a slightly old-for-the-level prospect and in hitter-friendly environs. Fernandez strikes out a lot and he only fits in left field, but he is the youngest and most impressive statistical performer of a large group of lefty outfield power hitters in this system. They all realistically project as the larger half of a corner platoon.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Of the shortstops on the main portion of this list, Hernandez has the best chance to stay at the position. His hands and actions are both characteristic of a promising teenage shortstop and he has enough arm for the left side of the infield. Hernandez has also performed reasonably well with the bat as a pro, which is surprising given his clear lack of physical strength. He could have a below-average offensive profile and stay at short, which gives him a chance to be a 50 if he gets stronger into his twenties. If not, he could still be a low-end regular or utiltiy type. He turns 20 in April and should see full-season ball for the first time in 2019.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Encarnacion was a bit of an afterthought when he signed for a $10,000 bonus as a 18-year-old in 2015 and became the DSL Braves everyday shortstop. By that fall's instructional league, the Braves realized they had a prospect on their hands and acted accordingly, pushing Encarnacion to Low-A at age 20 where he put up a 118 wRC+ as an age-appropriate prospect in a full-season league, just two years after he signed for almost nothing. The change was simple: Encarnacion's projection and actions turned into tools with physical development. He now shows 60 raw power in BP, above average arm strength and bat control, and average speed. Encarnacion still has some skills that require growth, as his plate approach is too aggressive to work at the upper levels. And while he has the physical tools to play third base, he's error-prone. The raw tool package and quick-developing statistical performance are a rare combo, so Encarnacion and Cumberland headlined the Orioles' return in the Kevin Gausman trade with Atlanta last summer. It's not a stretch to say Encarnacion has the best tools of any Latin prospect in the Orioles' lower minors, but that's mostly because the Orioles have had a near non-existent international program and their three best international signees (Yusniel Diaz, Encarnacion, Jean Carmona) were all acquired last summer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2019 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taken by the Mets in the 14th round of the 2016 Draft, James is a physical right-hander who compensates for fringy stuff with late movement and advanced pitchability. It's why the organization felt comfortable turning to him when Double-A Binghamton needed a spot start in late May, and again with High Class A St. Lucie the following week. Those two outings aside, James spent his age-20 season in the New York-Penn League, posting a 2.01 ERA over 71 2/3 innings while making 13 starts. James' fastball sits at 89-91 mph with plus sinking action that helped him induce ground-ball contact at a 58 percent clip in 2018. His curveball is an above-average offering as well as a potential out-pitch for him, and he also demonstrates feel for throwing a fading changeup in the mid-80s. James already understands how to sequence his pitches and is consistently around the strike zone. Physically strong and durable, James completed at least five innings in 10 of his 15 starts in '18. The Mets have a track record of developing mid-to-late round high school pitchers that have average stuff but good feel for their craft. James certainly fits that description, and the organization believes he has the qualities needed to reach the big leagues as a back-end starter.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Precipitation and misfortune forced Double-A Binghamton to play three double-headers in a row in late May (not on consecutive days, but still) and, suddenly, the club was in need of pitching reinforcements. The Mets promoted James directly from extended spring training to make a spot start, just three days after his 20th birthday. It's further evidence of James' advanced on-mound craftsmanship, which enables him to succeed with limited stuff. He has now had two strong years of performance at short-season affiliates on the back of a sinking and tailing upper-80s fastball and a slurvy 78-82 mph breaking ball. James' delivery is pretty rough but it doesn't appear to detract from his command, and it may actually help make him tougher for hitters to time. Little things like that are important, as his stuff exists on the margins. If his command maxes out, he'll be a sinker balling backend starter.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Many teams considered English to be one of, if not the best on-mound athletes among high schoolers in the 2018 draft, but many of them also thought he was sushi raw as both a hurler and an outfielder, and that he would end up at the University of Tennessee. A $700,000 bonus brought him to Tempe for a summer free of pitching in games, an approach the Angels have taken with several recent draftees. English did hit, though. While he struggled to perform on paper, he has a pro-quality power and speed combination that enabled him to play center field in high school. He was drafted and will be developed as a two-way player, likely pitching once a week while playing in the outfield once or twice a week and DH'ing the rest of the time as a way to manage fatigue. He arrived for camp having added about 25 pounds of muscle and is one of the more interesting prospects in baseball, let alone in this system, because he's just a very athletic, untouched mass of clay for Angels player development to sculpt.

fangraphs.label: 2019report
fangraphs.text: Northcut drew wide-ranging takes from scouts in the year leading up to signing with the Red Sox as an 11th rounder from an Ohio high school. He played on the Evoshield Canes, the top travel team in the country, and was scouted often, with a decent but not great glove at third base, above average to plus power, and some feel for hitting and game power, but seemed a mid-round prospect. In the spring and into pro ball, Northcut slimmed up a bit and now projects as at least average at third base, with similar raw power, but some pro scouts questioned his feel to hit. All the elements have been there at some point over the past year and some amateur scouts were really in on Northcut -- one said he saw a lot of Austin Riley in him -- but didn't realize his price would end up being as low as it was once he started sliding in the draft.

fangraphs.label: 2019updated
fangraphs.text: Dunn doesn't have exciting upside, but seems likely to have a big league career of some sort. He's a below average runner, thrower and defender, but plays a passable second base for now. Dunn may get shifted to left field or just a general 'bat that you find a spot for' position, because he's one of the few college hitters in his draft class who drew near consensus 60 hit grades. He has average raw power that he doesn't tap into as often as you'd like, so there's some shot for a swing adjustment (think more aggressive mechanics and/or more lofted swing path) that could make him some version of Daniel Murphy. Or, if he continues on this path with only his hit tool rating above average, he could be more of a Tommy LaStella bench bat type. There's obviously plenty of space between those two ends of the spectrum and the Murphy outcome is obviously a longshot, but in today's game, we feel obliged to outline a best case scenario with so many advanced hitters finding game power we didn't foresee.
