mlb_pipeline.text: Sherfy left the University of Oregon in 2013 as the school's all-time saves leader, with 40. Since joining the D-backs in the 10th round of that June's Draft, the right-handed reliever has had an up-and-down path to the top of the system, though he has added 66 Minor League saves, 50 of those coming over the last two seasons as he pitched his way to a 2017 Major League debut and a spot on the D-backs' postseason roster. Sherfy showed exactly what he's capable of doing over the last couple of years after struggling in Double-A back in 2015. He misses a ton of bats, largely with a two-pitch mix. The athletic reliever goes right after hitters with a fastball that sits in the mid-90s and often touches higher, backing it up with a breaking ball that misses a ton of bats and serves as a true out pitch. He has a below-average changeup, but he'll throw it effectively to give hitters a different look. An ability to deliver his two main weapons for strikes more consistently has been the key to Sherfy's success and rise to the big leagues. Perhaps his ceiling is that of a setup man, but he always pitches with intensity and he's clearly not afraid to take the ball in the ninth inning.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thought to be the kind of college reliever who would make a beeline to the big leagues, Sherfy, the former closer at Oregon, hit a stumbling block in 2015 in Double-A. He was able to right himself and pitch across three levels in 2016, then has repeated his dominance in Triple-A in 2017. Aside from that hiccup, Sherfy has been a dominant short reliever with a very high strikeout rate. He does it with a fastball that sits in the mid-to-upper 90s with a ton of life and an above-average slider that is unhittable at times. His changeup is clearly his third pitch, and he's started using it more and throwing it with splitter action. He can miss bats with all three offerings and has shown he can throw multiple innings without losing any of his stuff. Sherfy continues to learn how to prepare himself to pitch every night and maintain his strength for the entire season. He's just about ready to impact the big league bullpen, with the ceiling to close games at the highest level if he can continue to throw enough strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It hasn't exactly been the development path the D-backs envisioned when they gave him $450,000 to sign out of Taiwan back in July 2014, but Huang may have found the right role in a bounce-back 2017 season. The slender right-hander had been a Futures Game participant in 2015, but injuries and a lack of strength necessitated a move to the bullpen, and he was able to dominate two levels of A ball in 2017 pitching in shorter stints. The D-backs had hoped Huang would be able to add strength because he had a three-pitch mix that could work as a starter. But starting with a back injury that hampered him early and followed later by other minor nicks, combined with his relative inability to add strength, the move to the bullpen was necessary. The good news is his stuff really spiked in the role. His fastball sat in the mid-90s and his curve was filthy at times, with straight downer action. He has a good changeup, but didn't throw it as much in this role, with his fastball-curveball combination more than good enough. The D-backs didn't want to limit Huang to just one inning at a time, using almost a modified piggyback system to get him multiple innings every time out. They'd like to keep that ability to go more than one frame as long as they can as Huang hits the upper levels of the system.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Huang had an encouraging debut in the D-backs system, pitching well in the Midwest League and going to the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game in 2015. He got a late start to his second season because of a military commitment back home in Taiwan and never seemed to find his footing, getting shut down after a month in the California League and not throwing particularly well when sent back out to the short-season Northwest League. When he's right, Huang's calling cards are his exceptional command and his plus changeup. He throws a fringy fastball velocity-wise, around 90-91 mph, but it plays up because he can locate it so well. He misses bats with his outstanding changeup and does occasionally show the ability to spin a good breaking ball, though it's very inconsistent. The D-backs feel Huang was trying to play catchup all of 2016 and put too much pressure on himself to do too much, taking him away from his typical gameplan. More concerning is Huang's durability, as he's dealt with back and minor shoulder issues in his two years with the organization. With no military commitment this time around, there's hope he can hit the ground running in 2017 and look more like the back-end starter he was resembling during his debut season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Rockies liked Howard's pitchability enough to draft him in the third round in 2014, then helped him refine a more balanced delivery in hopes of improving his velocity and command. It worked, as he led the low Class South Atlantic League in strikeouts (122) and strikeout rate (8.2 per nine innings) in his first full pro season. He earned mid-season promotions in each of the next two years and was the most successful starter at the hitter's haven that is Triple-A Albuquerque last summer. Howard works at 91-94 mph and can hit 96 with his fastball, though with less sink than he showed early in his pro career. His groundout/airout ratio shrunk from 1.6 in his first two seasons to 0.7 in his next two. There are nights when his deceptive changeup is his best pitch and it's the main reason he has been more successful against right-handers than left-handers. Howard's slider gives him an average third offering. While he provides consistent strikes, his lack of a true plus pitch means he has to be precise with his location. He could be a No. 4 starter if he can improve his slider and command.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Howard worked mostly with an upper-80s fastball at Georgia Southern, the Rockies helped him add more balance to his delivery when he signed as a third-round pick in 2014. The adjustment improved his velocity and command and he responded by topping the low Class A South Atlantic League in strikeouts (122) and strikeout rate (8.2 per nine innings) in his first full pro season. He followed up in 2016 by dominating high Class A hitters in the first half but got hit harder following a mid-June promotion to Double-A. Howard now works at 91-94 mph and touches 96 mph with a fastball that had quality sink in the past, though his groundout/airout ratio shrunk from 1.6 in his first two seasons to 0.7 in his third. His deceptive changeup with fade is the main reason he has been more successful against righties than lefties. He's working to improve his slider to improve that imbalance, and he'll flash some solid ones on occasion. Howard has thrown strikes throughout his pro career, though he learned in a rough pro debut and again in Double-A that he'll get punished if he leaves pitches up in the strike zone. That will be especially true at Coors Field. If he can refine his slider and his command, he could contribute in the back half of Colorado's rotation in the not-too-distant future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Patterson showed off a low-90s fastball as a lefty reliever, but the Rockies preferred the two-way player as a hitter when they selected him in the fourth round of the 2013 Draft. He led the Minors with 45 doubles and 74 extra-base hits in 2015, then went 8-for-18 in a brief stint with Colorado. He has spent most of the last three seasons in Triple-A, smacking a career-best 26 homers in 2017 and matching that in 2018. When the Rockies placed him on waivers in late November, the Mets swooped in and claimed him, only to have the Reds do the same when the Mets put him on waivers a few days later. At 6-foot-4, Patterson has a naturally long left-handed swing but he worked to shorten it when he entered pro ball. He developed a line-drive stroke that didn't take full advantage of his strength and bat speed, then added more loft to his swing and put more balls in the air last season. The added power enhances his profile as a potential regular in the big leagues. Patterson primarily played right field while seeing sporadic time at first base during his first four pro seasons before spending most of his time at first in 2017. He's a capable defender at either spot and his strong arm fits well in right. He got caught up in the Rockies' first base/corner outfield logjam and hasn't gotten back to the big leagues since that 2016 debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way player at South Alabama, Patterson was an effective lefty reliever with a low-90s fastball but showed more promise with the bat. Drafted in the fourth round in 2013, he led the Minors in doubles (45) and extra-base hits (74) two years later. He didn't show as much power while playing in a launching pad at Triple-A Albuquerque last year, then set a new career high for homers by mid-July when he returned there in 2017. Six-foot-4 with long arms, Patterson has worked diligently to shorten his left-handed swing since turning pro. He has succeeded, though his line-drive stroke means he doesn't always take full advantage of his bat speed and strength. He has done a better job of hitting the ball in the air in 2017, showing that he may have enough power to play every day in the Majors. Patterson moves well for his size and offers some defensive versatility. His strong arm makes him naturally suited for right field and he's fully capable in left field and at first base as well. He's blocked at all three spots in Colorado, so he could be destined to repeat Triple-A in 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After playing one year at American Heritage (Plantation, Fla.) High and then moving back to the Dominican Republic, Almanzar ranked No. 4 on MLB Pipeline's list of the Top 30 prospects for the 2016-17 international period. While some teams even viewed Almanzar as his country's top prospect, it was the Padres, as part of their massive international spending spree that year, who ultimately landed him, signing Almanzar for $4 million on July 2. Though he struggled in his 2017 professional debut in the Class A Short Season Northwest League, Almanzar also played the entire summer at 17, making him one of the circuit's youngest players. Almanzar can hit to all fields and has a slightly uppercut swing that causes the ball to jump off his bat, leading scouts to believe that he'll hit eventually hit for average as well as for some power. He's athletic and toolsy, with good footwork and the ability to defend, and he also impresses scouts with his strong and accurate arm. Almanzar's thicker build has already led to reduced time at shortstop and more time at the hot corner, which many believe will be his final defensive home. Should he end up at third base, Almanzar will need to hit for both average and power to accommodate the position's traditional profile. It's early in his career, but Almanzar has shown enough offensive tools to believe that's a real possibility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Almanzar ranked No. 4 on MLB.com's list of the Top 30 international prospects, some teams viewed him as the Dominican Republic's top prospect in the 2016-17 international class. He became a part of the Padres' international spending spree last summer, signing for $4 million on July 2. Almanzar can hit to all fields and has a slightly uppercut swing that causes the ball to jump off his bat, leading scouts to believe that he'll eventually grow into at least average power. He's athletic and toolsy, with good footwork and the ability to defend, and he also impresses scouts with his strong and accurate arm. Almanzar's thicker build has raised doubt among evaluators about his ability to stick at shortstop long term, though there's little doubt that he has the tools and offensive potential to profile at third base. Almanzar has some experience playing in games and showcases in the United States, as he played one season at American Heritage (Plantation, Fla.) High at age 15 before moving back to the Dominican Republic. That experience has aided the teenager this season during his pro debut with Class A Short Season Tri-City.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hinojosa spurned early-round interest from clubs in the 2012 Draft to attend Texas, where he never lived up to his hype outside of playing well at the 2014 College World Series. Signed for $200,000 as an 11th-rounder in 2015, he has been more impressive with wood bats as a pro than he was with metal bats in college. He has plateaued since reaching Double-A midway through his first full pro season and missed the first two months of 2018 after rupturing his left Achilles tendon last September and also getting hit with a 50-game suspension for a second positive test for a drug of abuse. Hinojosa has fared better in pro ball because he shortened his right-handed swing and stopped worrying about hitting home runs. He has a quick bat and makes contact more easily than any Giants farmhand, though that also cuts into his walk totals. He uses the entire field, has some gap power and can hit an occasional homer to his pull side. Though he's a well-below-average runner who lacks the quickness to play shortstop, Hinojosa manages to make plays there thanks to his solid arm and good internal clock. His substandard range won't fly at shortstop in the big leagues, however, so San Francisco began playing him at second and third base last year. There may not be enough impact in his bat to make him an everyday player but he could be a utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hinojosa turned down early-round overtures from clubs in the 2012 Draft so he could attend Texas, but outside of a strong performance at the 2014 College World Series, his Longhorns career was mostly a disappointment. He reversed course after signing for $200,000 as an 11th-rounder in 2015, hitting better with wood bats than he did with metal in college and reaching Double-A midway through his first full pro season. An offensive-minded shortstop, Hinojosa found more success in pro ball after he shortened his right-handed swing. He has a quick bat and controls the strike zone while using the entire field. He's at his best when he focuses on getting on base rather than hitting for power, though he can drive some doubles to the gaps and pull an occasional ball out the park. Hinojosa has the hands and arm to play the infield, as well as a good internal clock that helps him make plays. He has substandard range at shortstop because he's a well below-average runner, however, and fits better at second or third base. A likely utilityman in the future, he'll have to monitor his conditioning to maintain enough quickness for the middle infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Giants gave Beltre their highest bonus in their 2013-14 international class, signing him for $650,000 out of the Dominican Republic. His first two years in the United States were truncated by injuries, with hamstring issues limiting him to 14 games in 2015 and a broken forearm costing him two months in 2016. He finally stayed healthy last season, showing glimpses of talent and also inconsistency in low Class A, but started 2018 on the disabled list with a broken left tibia. Beltre's outstanding bat speed is what initially attracted San Francisco to him and gives him plus raw power from the right side of the plate. He could have 15-homer power if he continues to add strength and refine his approach at the plate. He did a better job of keeping his aggressiveness in check last year, improving his walk (up from 7 to 10 percent) and strikeout (down from 29 to 20 percent) rates compared to his introduction to low Class A in 2016. Beltre has shuffled all over the infield, playing mainly shortstop in his pro debut, shifting to second base in 2015 and third base in 2016, then returning to second last year. He still needs defensive polish and may fit best at the hot corner because his speed and quickness are just average. His strong arm works anywhere in the infield.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Beltre received the largest bonus San Francisco paid during the 2013-14 international signing period, getting $650,000 out of the Dominican Republic. He has yet to complete a fully healthy season, missing most of his 2015 U.S. debut with hamstring issues and losing more than two months last year when an errant pitch broke his left forearm. Beltre originally caught San Francisco's eye with his quick right-handed bat, and his outstanding bat speed gives him plus raw power. He could hit 15 homers per season if he adds strength and tones down his aggressive approach. He lacks polish at the plate, which is understandable considering he's 20 and totaled just 391 plate appearances in his first three pro seasons. Beltre has bounced among different positions, playing mostly shortstop in his pro debut, spending 2016 at third base and settling at second base this season. His strong arm would work anywhere in the infield, but he fits best at the hot corner because his speed and quickness are just average.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the 2015-16 international signing period opened on July 2, the Rangers landed a pair of center fielders. Leody Taveras quickly developed into the organization's top prospect after signing for $2.1 million out of the Dominican Republic. A Venezuelan who landed a $500,000 bonus, Aparicio wasn't ready for full-season ball at age 18 like Taveras was but stands out with the best instincts in the system. Aparicio plays way above his tools as a defender. He has fringy to average speed yet covers a lot of ground in center field because he reads balls well, has a quick first step and takes direct routes. Likewise, he keeps baserunners in check despite a fringy arm because he gets to balls quickly and makes accurate throws. Aparicio displays similar feel for hitting and running the bases. He makes repeated line-drive contact to all fields with his compact left-handed swing and a sound approach. While he's no slugger, he does have bat speed and should produce double-digit home run totals once he gets stronger.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After displaying first-round potential on the high school showcase circuit in 2016, Brannen was hampered by a broken hamate bone in his right hand last spring. The Red Sox took him in the second round and lured him away from a Georgia Southern commitment with an over-slot $1.3 million bonus. He's the best athlete and fastest player in a system thinned by promotions and trades in recent years. Brannen has well-above-average speed and knows how to use it to reach base and create havoc once he does. He employs a compact left-handed swing geared to produce line drives and ground balls that he can beat out. He draws walks but can get too passive at times, and his inability to drive the ball in 2018 points to his need for increased strength. Brannen's quickness also plays well in center field. He could cover plenty of ground on speed alone, but he also has fine instincts and takes good routes. His average arm is better than most at his position.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Given his fastball velocity and the success he has enjoyed early in his pro career, it's difficult to fathom why Martinez had to wait more than three years after he became eligible to land a pro contract. Even then, the Red Sox paid just $5,000 to sign him out of the Dominican Republic in January 2016. He recorded a 1.48 ERA in his first two pro seasons and helped low Class A Greenville win the South Atlantic League championship last September. Martinez worked with a 91-94 mph fastball when he broke into pro ball and boosted his velocity to 95-98 with some armside run during his first full pro season. He also can miss bats with a pair of secondary pitches. His mid-80s slider can be nasty albeit inconsistent, and his low-90s splitter is especially useful against left-handers. Though he has three quality pitches, Martinez will be a reliever. There's effort in his delivery, which also features a long arm action and a lot of moving parts. Though he has a lot going on with his mechanics, they add deception to his pitches and his athleticism helps him throw strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chipola Junior College won the JUCO World Series in 2017 with one of the most stacked rosters in recent junior college history. A total of 11 players from the program were drafted in 2017, led by Rivera, who went No. 57 overall, in the second round. He struggled out of the gate during his debut in the New York-Penn League, showing there's work to be done. Rivera has legitimate raw power, but the question is whether he'll be able to make the adjustments necessary to tap into it consistently. The mechanics of his swing led to him having trouble with balls on the inner part of the plate and a fair amount of swings and misses as a result. He'll have to smooth out those rough edges to become a serious offensive threat from the left side of the plate. Largely a first baseman at Chipola, the Tigers had the Puerto Rico native play a lot of right field during his debut. He'll continue to play both spots in 2018, likely more at first, but it's hard to walk away from his strong arm in an outfield corner. Regardless of his defensive home, it's going to be Rivera's bat that allows him to climb up the Tigers' ladder. How he adjusts in his first pro season should speak volumes about his future impact.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A seventh-rounder as a Puerto Rican high schooler in 2015, Cancel passed on a commitment to Miami Dade JC and signed for $200,000. He spent two years in Rookie ball before moving to low Class A in 2017, when he ranked sixth in the South Atlantic League and first among its middle infielders with 46 extra-base hits. He has a chance to get the job done offensively and defensively and is the organization's top second-base prospect. Cancel is stronger than most second basemen and has the quick right-handed swing to catch up to good fastballs. He's built along the lines of Carlos Baerga and may have some more power he can tap into now that he's hitting more balls in the air. His biggest need at the plate is to add more discipline so he'll be able to handle more advanced pitching. Drafted as a shortstop, Cancel moved to second base two months into his pro debut. He has good hands and turns the double play well, though his fringy speed and average arm limit his ability to play other positions. He'll have to realize his offensive potential to make it as a regular and won't have a utility role as a fallback.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Steele intrigued scouts as a Georgia high schooler in 2015, but his Vanderbilt commitment and rough delivery left him undrafted. He pitched sparingly for the Commodores as a freshman before academic ineligibility prompted his transfer to Chipola (Fla.) JC for 2017. He won Most Valuable Pitcher honors at the Junior College World Series, helping the Indians capture their second national title and then signing for $826,500 as a supplemental second-round choice. Steele's 6-foot-5 frame and low three-quarters delivery allow him to make lefties uncomfortable and get in on the hands of righties. He throws sinking two-seam fastballs in the low 90s and running four-seamers that can reach 95, both of which play up because of the difficult angle his size and arm slot create. His sweeping slider and changeup show flashes of becoming solid secondary offerings but still lack consistency. Though he generally throws strikes, Steele will need to improve his command to remain a starter in pro ball. He missed a month during the spring with a blood clot and worked a combined 52 innings in two college seasons, so he'll need to establish he can hold up over a full pro season. If he's not durable enough to remain a starter, he could be an interesting bullpen option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Chipola College not only won the Junior College World Series in 2017, it had a large chunk of its roster taken in the Draft that June. Bechtold was the third Indian taken, in the fifth round by the Twins, and he went out and had a very strong pro debut in the Appalachian League. Bechtold began his collegiate career at Maryland, but transferred to Chipola after redshirting his sophomore year and being told he would be a part-time player. He put up huge numbers with Chipola, but might have been dinged by some team's models that discount production at the junior college ranks. At least in his debut, Bechtold's approach translated quite nicely to the pro game, making consistent contact and drawing walks in an approach that's still hit over power. A solid athlete with very good range defensively, Bechtold has average speed and likes to run. His plus arm will work very well from the hot corner. It appears that Bechtold has an exciting package of tools to eventually develop into an everyday third baseman. That's starting with full-season ball and the end result could be one of the better steals of the 2017 Draft.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After beginning his college career as a swingman at Louisiana-Lafayette, Marks' transition to the rotation as a sophomore had mixed results. That prompted to a full-time move to the bullpen as in junior in 2017, a role in which Marks thrived. He struck out 100 batters and yielded just 29 hits in 59 1/3 innings to lead all Division I hurlers in both strikeouts-per-nine (15.17) and hits-per-nine (4.40). That overwhelming success earned him a 13th-round selection by the A's in June, and after signing for $110,000, Marks continued to miss bats with ease across two levels in his pro debut. Marks gets the most out of his two above-average pitches, missing bats inside and outside of the zone easily with each. He won't shy away from challenging hitters up in the zone with his low-90s fastball that he can also spot to both sides of the plate. His curveball is a hammer when it's on, registering in the low 80s with tight spin, and it serves as an ideal bat-missing complement to his fastball. Marks has a strong track record as a strike-thrower, but he'll need to improve his fastball command for continued success at higher levels. Though he started seven of his 13 games during his pro debut and has pitched almost exclusively in that role with Class A Beloit in 2018, Marks' future is likely in the bullpen. His fastball-curveball combo gives him upside as a high-leverage reliever, and with improved command of both pitches, he could hop on the fast track to the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After finding one of the game's best defensive catching prospects in Jose Trevino at Oral Roberts in 2014, the Rangers went back to the Golden Eagles for another backstop last June. The Johnny Bench Award winner as college baseball's top backstop in 2017, Whatley signed for $517,000 as a third-rounder. He hit better than expected in his pro debut while providing his usual strong work behind the plate. Whatley was arguably the best all-around defender among college catchers available in last year's Draft. He receives and blocks well, and he's tough on basestealers with his solid, accurate arm. He has more athleticism and speed than most players at his position, though he's still a below-average runner. Questions about Whatley's upside arose when he struggled with wood bats in the Cape Cod League in 2016 and slumped at the outset of last spring. He fared better when he stopped worrying about home runs and focused on sticking with his disciplined approach. He makes consistent contact, owns decent pop and will work counts to draw walks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lugbauer's power output ticked up when he was a junior at Michigan, and he finished with a dozen homers and a .518 slugging percentage. The fact that he does it from the left side of the plate, and perhaps has the chance to catch, made him an intriguing 11th-round pick by the Braves last June. He then slugged his way from the Appalachian League to the South Atlantic League during his pro debut, hitting another 13 balls out of the park. He couldn't quite replicate those results in his first full year, though he did reach double digits in home runs back in the SAL in 2018. It will be Lugbauer's bat that will allow him to continue to move up the Braves' ladder. The power is legitimate, with it perhaps coming more from strength than bat speed, but he did show in his debut that he can hit the ball out to both his pull side and the opposite field, going to left-center field with ease. With the power comes considerable swing and miss, but Lugbauer mitigates that, at times, with a willingness to take walks. While he played several positions at Michigan and saw time at first and third during his debut, Lugbauer committed himself to catching only for the time being. He has work to do on his receiving and he'll have to quicken his release to use his arm strength better, but the Braves like the strides he's made and the work he's put in to improving defensively, with the hopes of finding a power-hitting backup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lee began his college career at Pearl River CC, playing two seasons there before transferring to Mississippi. A strong junior campaign with the Rebels netted him 12th-round selection by the Rays, and Lee rewarded the organization with a successful full-season debut with Class A Advance Charlotte in 2015. A move up to Double-A the following year proved a challenge for Lee but he bounced back to post a Southern League-best .309 average in 2017, and did so despite being traded to Miami in July. He continued to boost his stock in the Arizona Fall League, prompting the Marlins to add him to their 40-man roster, and then made his big league debut with the club in early 2018. His 2016 performance aside, Lee has a strong track record of hitting. He employs a compact left-handed swing that allows him to spray balls across the entire field and fuels his potential to hit for average. His patient approach results in some swing-and-miss but also plenty of walks and solid on-base skills. A plus runner, Lee is aggressive on the basepaths but needs to refine his basestealing technique. Lee's plus-plus speed translates better in center field, where he's a plus defender with good instincts and considerable range. His above-average arm strength is an asset there and allows him to profile at all three outfield spots. That versatility could make Lee a valuable fourth outfielder at the highest level, though an everyday role isn't yet out of the question.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With the trades of superstar prospects Gleyber Torres and Eloy Jimenez, Galindo is the best position player remaining in the organization from the Cubs' $8.2 million international spending binge in 2013-14. He cost just $50,000 coming out of Venezuela but has developed into one of the better hitters in the system. He was thriving in his first taste of full-season ball in 2017 until he broke his leg in mid-June. Galindo has the potential to hit for both power and average. A right-handed hitter, he did a better job of making consistent contact last year. He has impressive strength and raw power, though he needs to curb his tendency to hit ground balls to realize his 20-homer potential. Despite his below-average speed, Galindo moves OK at third base and has the requisite strong arm for the position. Footwork issues and throwing inaccuracies led to 59 errors in his first 146 pro games at the hot corner, however. He could be destined for first base and may be able to handle left field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Harrison turned down a chance to begin his pro career out of high school in 2014, when he opted to honor his commitment to Oregon State rather than sign with the Indians as a 25th-rounder. Known more for his hitting ability and power that produced a .904 OPS with 29 home runs in three seasons with the Beavers, Harrison intrigued teams in the 2017 Draft with his upside as a bat-first catcher. Hoping that his defense would develop, the Brewers drafted Harrison in the third round and signed him for pick value. He made a statement with his bat but struggled defensively during his pro debut in the Pioneer League, and then saw more time at first base with Class A Wisconsin in his first full season before going to the Nationals in the Gio Gonzalez deal at the Aug. 31 Waiver Trade Deadline. Harrison showed the ability to hit for average and power at times for the Beavers, reaching double digits in home runs as both a freshman and sophomore. He added nine more homers as a junior while showing a more refined approach at the plate that carried over into his pro career. Harrison's penchant for striking out, however, has plagued him in his first full season, leading some to question the future utility of his bat. Harrison caught a few times as a junior, but not enough for teams to have a real comfort level with how he looks back there. The Brewers gave him a chance behind the plate early in his career but moved him to first base in 2018 after Harrison struggled to throw out basestealers. Though he could still see some reps behind the plate, Harrison will need to slug his way up the ladder as a first baseman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since signing out of Venezuela back in 2010, all Valera has done is hit. He's finished seven of his eight summers in the Cardinals system with a batting average over .300 and his .314 average in 2017 topped the system, leading to his first big league callup. Valera really knows how to hit and really knows the strike zone. That's led to a career average in the Minors of .303 to go along with a .359 on-base percentage heading into 2018. The switch-hitter has more walks than strikeouts in his career and has the confidence to have tough at-bats against any level of pitching. There isn't power to speak of, though he can find the gaps. An average runner, Valera has increased his positional versatility over time, showing he is capable at three infield positions as well as the outfield. He has good hands, solid range and outstanding instincts that allow all of his defensive tools to play up. That defensive flexibility will be crucial in order for Valera to get more big league time. He'll have to move around as a utility man to get at-bats, but few doubt he'll hit if given the chance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The 2016 Southern Conference pitcher of the year, Gaddis positioned himself as a potential second-rounder when he pitched well in the Cape Cod League and fall practice. His stuff regressed a bit last spring, though he still led the Southern Conference in wins (nine) and ERA (1.89) and became the highest pick in Furman history. After signing for a slightly below-slot $600,000 in the third round, Gaddis looked worn out in his pro debut. Gaddis has heavy sink on his fastball, which sat at 88-92 mph and topped out at 94 in 2017 after reaching 96 previously. He has great feel for his changeup, a plus pitch at times but merely average for much of last year. His curveball and cutter also weren't quite as sharp as usual but show the upside of solid offerings. Gaddis isn't very physical but projects as a starter because he repeats his delivery and pounds the strike zone, efficiently managing his pitching counts. He attacks hitters, even when his stuff is less than its best, and has a higher floor than most of Colorado's starting pitching prospects.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Spanberger homered just six times as a part-time player in his first two seasons at Arkansas, then went deep 10 times in his final 16 games last spring to finish his junior season with 20. After signing for $260,200 as a sixth-rounder, he kept mashing in pro ball. He homered in three of his first games at Rookie-level Grand Junction and ranked second in the Pioneer League with 19 homers, one behind teammate Casey Golden. Spanberger garners some comparisons to Chris Davis because he's a first baseman with big-time left-handed power and swing-and-miss concerns. His bat speed, strength and leverage give him massive raw power to all fields, and he doesn't get cheated with an aggressive approach. While he probably won't hit for a high average, he did make strides with using the entire field and made more consistent contact in 2017. A high school catcher who played some right field early in his college career, Spanberger has well below-average speed that limits him to first base as a pro. He can develop into an adequate defender but has a lot of work to do after committing 10 errors in 54 games during his debut.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since batting .231 in his 2012 pro debut after signing out of the Dominican Republic, Gomez hit at least .305 in his next five years in the Minors. He didn't reach full-season ball until he was age 23 in 2016, but zoomed from low Class A at the beginning of that season to San Francisco last July. He played sparingly in his month with the Giants, though he did go 5-for-16 in the four full games he played. Gomez's simple swing from both sides of the plate and his tremendous hand-eye coordination make hitting a breeze. Besides his pure hitting ability, he also has the solid bat speed and strength to provide 15 homers per season. He's difficult to strike out but also to walk because he puts balls in play so easily. The drawback with Gomez is that he lacks a position because of his well-below-average speed and quickness. He debuted as a catcher, moved to third base three years later, shifted to second base in 2017 and also has seen action at first base and left field. He was too erratic at the hot corner and has substandard range at second, where the Giants will be happy if he can just make all of the routine plays.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A ninth-round pick from Minnesota in 2013, Snelten plateaued as a starter when he got to high Class A but began to take off once he moved to the bullpen in July 2016. He has shown more confidence as a reliever and ranked second among the system's full-season relievers with a 2.20 ERA in 2017. After he had similar success in the Arizona Fall League, San Francisco protected him on its 40-man roster. Snelten's best pitch is his changeup, which dives at the plate and works well against both left-handers and right-handers. He has added fastball velocity since working in shorter stints, now operating at 91-93 mph and peaking at 95 with run and sink. The movement on his fastball and changeup and the downhill plane he creates with his 6-foot-7 frame led to a 2.3 groundout/flyout ratio last year. Snelten has done a better job of maintaining his arm slot as a reliever, allowing him to do a better job of staying on top of his average slider. He has good feel for pitching and some funk in his delivery that adds to his deception. The Giants think he can be more than a lefty specialist, with one club official saying Snelten reminds him of Jeremy Affeldt, a key reliever on their three World Series championship clubs this decade.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A month before the Red Sox spent $63 million in bonuses and tax penalties to land Yoan Moncada, who became the centerpiece in the Chris Sale trade, they signed Cedrola for a bargain $35,000 out of Venezuela in February 2015. After working out for clubs as a shortstop, he moved to center field and was named the organization's Latin American program player of the year in his first taste of pro ball. His U.S. debut in 2016 also went well, as he led the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League in hits (62) and doubles (14). Cedrola has a chance to have four solid or better tools, with his well above-average speed (which projects as plus once he's physically mature) standing out the most. While he's still refining his skills as a basestealer, his quickness already plays well in center field, where he shows advanced instincts. The solid arm strength he showed at shortstop is an asset in center and also will allow him to play either corner. Cedrola has uncanny bat-to-ball skills for a teenager and could develop into a high-average hitter. While he makes easy contact, he could use more patience to improve his on-base ability and maximize the use of his speed. That will be important because he's not very physical and won't ever be a power hitter, though he can sting some balls into the gaps.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Maese was better known for his exploits on the gridiron than the diamond during his time at Ysleta High in El Paso, Texas. That quickly changed in 2015 during his senior year with reports that he was up to 96 mph with a mid-80s slider. He signed for $300,000 as a third-round pick and had an excellent pro debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League. Maese continued to impress the next year, reaching full-season ball at age 19, but was sidelined by shoulder soreness for much of 2017 in his return to Class A Lansing. Maese had surgery in the offseason to address the shoulder impingement, delaying his 2018 season debut. When he's healthy, Maese can run his fastball into the mid-90s but tends to work more in the 90-94 mph range, displaying feel for pitching to both sides of the plate. The pitch features considerable movement, as Maese's fast arm and low three-quarters slot imparts excellent sinking action that has helped him generate more than twice as many ground-ball outs as air outs in his career. His slider is relatively new to his arsenal but shows the makings of a second average-or-better pitch, thrown with power in the upper-80s, and he's also made strides in developing his changeup since signing. Maese's athleticism is special, and it's easy to envision the young righty growing into his projectable frame in the coming years, though first he'll need to get healthy. Maese's sinker gives him potential as either a starter or reliever, but he'll need to refine his secondary pitches and develop better command to stick in the rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Blue Jays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport standout at Ysleta High in El Paso, Texas, Maese was better known for his exploits on the gridiron than the diamond as an amateur. That quickly changed during his senior year in 2015, when droves of scouts filed in to lay eyes on the athletic right-hander amid reports that he was up to 96 mph with a mid-80s slider. He signed for $300,000 as a third-round pick and had an excellent pro debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, capping his season with a 10-strikeout performance over six innings in the GCL playoffs. Maese continued to impress in 2016, beginning the season in the New York-Penn League and advancing to full-season ball at age 19. Though he'll reach the mid-90s with his fastball, Maese tends to work more in the 90-94 mph range, displaying feel for pitching to both sides of the plate. Yet, it's the pitch's movement that makes it so dynamic, as Maese's fast arm and low three-quarters slot imparts excellent sinking action that has helped him generate more than twice as many ground-ball outs as air outs in his career. His slider is relatively new to his arsenal but shows the makings of a second plus pitch, thrown with power in the upper-80s, and he's also made strides in developing his changeup since signing. Maese's athleticism is special, and it's easy to envision the young righty growing into his projectable frame in the coming years. His outstanding sinker gives Maese upside as either a starter or reliever, though he'll need to refine his secondary pitches and develop better command to stick in the rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $350,000 out of the Dominican Republic at age 16 in January 2014, Reyes has long showed big upside but struggled to stay healthy. He missed nearly six weeks with a right thumb injury during his full-season debut and underwent surgery to repair a broken hamate bone in his left hand that fall. Though healthy for all of 2016, Reyes was overmatched as the youngest everyday player in the Class A Advanced Carolina League. His strong start in '17, meanwhile, was derailed by a three-month absence for a broken finger he suffered while punching a wall. Reyes did return to finish his season on a high note, ultimately hitting .302/.333/.434 over 50 Carolina League contests. Reyes generates plus raw power from the right side of the plate with his above-average bat speed and natural feel for driving the ball to all fields. He's shown flashes of applying that power during games, and it doesn't take much to envision Reyes clearing even more fences as he matures. There are questions about his ability to hit for average, though Orioles club officials were pleased with the mechanical adjustments he made late in the season and then during fall instructional league. Reyes has improved his glove work and has the plus arm strength needed for third base, but as a well-below-average runner who will only get bigger, it might be a challenge for him to remain at the position. A move down the defensive spectrum to first base seems likely, though it would place even greater pressure on his offensive tools to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A top prospect in Baltimore's system since he signed for $350,000 out of the Dominican Republic at age 16 in January 2014, Reyes has struggled to stay healthy in recent years. He missed nearly six weeks with a right thumb injury during his 2015 full-season debut and underwent surgery to repair a broken hamate bone in his left hand that fall. Though healthy for all of 2016, Reyes was overmatched as the youngest everyday player in the Class A Advanced Carolina League. And his strong start to the '17 season was quickly derailed when he landed on the disabled list in April with a broken finger suffered while punching a wall. Big and physical, Reyes generates plus raw power from the right side of the plate with his above-average bat speed and natural feel for driving the ball to all fields. He connected on 10 homers in 2016, more than doubling his combined total from the two previous years, and it doesn't take much to envision Reyes clearing even more fences as he develops. Scouts do worry about his ability to hit for average, especially after he regressed last season with his swing mechanics, plate discipline and pitch recognition. Reyes has the arm strength for third base, but as a well-below-average runner, it will be a challenge for him to remain at the position due to his lack of range and quickness. A move down the defensive spectrum to first base appears unavoidable, though it would place even greater pressure on his offensive tools to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Walker broke out in 2014, hitting 26 home runs en route to making his Major League debut with the Orioles, two years after being taken in the fourth round of the 2012 Draft out of South Carolina, where he had helped guide the Gamecocks to back-to-back national titles (2010-11). While he did return to the big leagues briefly in 2015, he's stalled out a bit since then. He's also been on the move quite a bit as the 2017 season approached, being claimed off of waivers by the Braves, Reds and, most recently, D-backs. Coming out of college, Walker profiled as a light-hitting first baseman with an advanced approach and good on-base skills. The Orioles helped him unlock his raw power in 2014 and he's produced at least 18 homers in three straight seasons, but with that improved power has come a pull-happy approach and a penchant for whiffing. Despite being a passable defender at first base, he was blocked with the Orioles by both Chris Davis and Trey Mancini, so Walker started seeing time in left field in 2016, and he spent nearly all of the regular season at the position. With more contact and fewer strikeouts, Walker could find a role coming off the bench at both corner spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Curbelo began his high school career at the Puerto Rican Baseball Academy a year after Carlos Correa departed as the No. 1 overall pick in the 2012 Draft. After performing well on the summer showcase circuit, he moved to Cocoa (Fla.) High as a senior to increase his exposure, though a down spring and strong commitment cause him to slide to the sixth round in 2016. Signed for a well over-slot $700,000 after a strong pre-Draft workout for the White Sox, he played only three games in 2017 before tearing the meniscus in his knee and requiring surgery. Though Curbelo has hit just .242/.322/.354 in Rookie ball during his first two pro seasons, he projects as an offensive-minded infielder. With the bat speed and leverage he generates from the right side of the plate, the ball jumps off his bat and he could produce 20 homers per season in his prime. He'll need to make more consistent contact to get the most out of his pop, and club officials believe he's intelligent enough to make those adjustments. All three of Curbelo's games in 2017 came at shortstop, though it's unlikely he'll stay there. He's an average runner who figures to lose a step as he gets stronger, making second base (where he spent most of his debut) the best-case scenario and third base another possibility. He has reliable hands and the arm strength for the hot corner, where his power projection also fits the profile.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Curbelo entered the Puerto Rican Baseball Academy a year after Carlos Correa left as the No. 1 overall pick in the 2012 Draft. After a strong showing on the summer showcase circuit, he moved to Cocoa (Fla.) High for his senior season in 2016. A lackluster performance and a strong commitment to Miami dropped him to the sixth round last June, where he signed for a well over-slot $700,000. Though Curbelo batted .226/.303/.323 in Rookie ball during his pro debut, he profiles as an offensive-minded infielder. He has good bat speed and leverage from the right side of the plate, and the way the ball jumps off his bat could portend 30 doubles and 15 homers per season in his prime. He has an advanced approach for a teenager but will need to reduce his swing-and-miss tendencies to realize his power potential. A shortstop in high school, Curbelo played there while seeing more action at second base in his debut. Chicago plans on keeping him at second for now, though many scouts believe he'll slow down and wind up at third base once he matures physically. His reliable hands and solid arm would work at the hot corner, and he has the offensive upside desired there as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 65 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 After Reed came out of the University of Oregon and dominated both in his pro debut and in the Arizona Fall League in 2014, he looked poised to get to Minnesota in a hurry. His trip was delayed when he scuffled with a move to Double-A in 2015, though he righted the ship with a bounce-back 2016 season that saw him reach Triple-A for the first time. However, his progress was slowed by a shoulder strain that forced him out for the first two months of the 2017 season. With renewed confidence and a more streamlined delivery that was consistently online, Reed had better results. His velocity ticked upward, sitting consistently in the 94-96 mph range and thrown with good movement to get ground-ball outs. His slider also improved and he continues to refine it. He actually has shown glimpses of a decent changeup, but he doesn't use it enough. His command got better, thanks to his online delivery. He can still get under the ball at times with too much of a low-3/4 slot, which impacts both his command and the quality of his pitches. Hard-throwing right-handed relievers are becoming a depth position for the Twins farm system and Reed once again looks like he belongs in the group that will help out in Minnesota soon.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Back in 2015, Cruz was ranked No. 27 on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 International Prospects list as a potential future shortstop, with strong enough reports to warrant a $2 million bonus from the Braves to sign that July. A strong pro debut in the Gulf Coast League pushed him to the Appalachian League that summer, but he's struggled to find his offensive footing since. The Braves sent Cruz to full-season Rome to start 2017, and it was a mistake. The teenage switch-hitter was in over his head in the South Atlantic League and got sent back down to the Appy League to try to hit the reset button. He still has solid tools and excellent athleticism, with his plus speed his true carrying tool. At his best, he's shown the ability to make consistent contact and spray line drives all over the field, more consistently from the right side than the left. While he was a shortstop initially, he moved over to second when he went back down to Danville a year ago and that's now his likely full-time home, where he should be a capable defender without his fringy arm causing issues. It's hard to put pressure on a 19-year-old by saying that it's a big year for him, but the 2018 season could be a huge one for Cruz. He has plenty of time to develop into a speedy everyday second baseman, but he needs to start showing what he can do.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cruz was ranked No. 27 on MLBPipeline.com's Top 30 International Prospects list in 2015, and the Braves liked him enough to give him $2 million to sign. He hit so well during his Gulf Coast League debut that he earned a promotion up to the Appalachian League at age 17. Cruz didn't continue swinging a hot bat once he got to Danville, but the Braves were impressed with how the teenager maturely dealt with adversity. He's still learning how to switch-hit; he's much better from his natural right side, and while his left-handed swing is workable, there is a chance he'll eventually stick to that side only. He does make consistent hard contact with some extra-base gap power, and he could grow into some more, though it's not likely to be a huge part of his game. His hitting will continue to improve as he refines his approach. He's a plus runner who will be a basestealing threat. His defense at short has improved tremendously, especially after working tirelessly with Luis Lopez. The only thing in question about him staying there is his fringe-average arm, though physical maturity and confidence will aid that particular tool. Cruz is starting to grow into some man strength, which will only help him in all facets of his game. He'll play all of the 2017 season at age 18, already ahead of the curve developmentally.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kolek's big, physical frame and triple-digit fastball made him a legitimate candidate to be the first overall pick in the 2014 Draft. He ended up going second overall to the Marlins and signed for a franchise-record $6 million. He had an inconsistent but promising first full season in the Class A South Atlantic League and showed up to Spring Training in 2016 in better shape, only to suffer an elbow injury that required Tommy John surgery in early April. After a 15-month absence, the big right-hander finally returned to the mound in July 2017 in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, where he issued 14 walks in just 3 2/3 innings. After showcasing elite velocity as an amateur, Kolek worked more in the low- to mid-90s during his full-season debut. He throws his heater with heavy sinking action that leads to many groundouts and few home runs. Both Kolek's slider and changeup are below average, and that lack of an out pitch limits his bat-missing ability. He did make some strides with the former before getting hurt, throwing it with improved depth and power. The Marlins worked with Kolek to refine his delivery during his rehab process with the hope that it would help him regain some velocity, as well as better command. Unhappy with those results, they will now attempt to further simplify his delivery. Kolek still has time on his side, as he'll spend all of 2018 at age 22, but he'll now need to make massive developmental strides to come close to reaching his ceiling.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Kolek's big, physical frame and triple-digit fastball made him a legitimate candidate to be the first-overall pick in the 2014 Draft. He ended up going second overall to the Marlins and signed for a franchise-record $6 million. He had an inconsistent but promising first full season in the Class A South Atlantic League and showed up to Spring Training in 2016 in better shape. However, Kolek's season was over before it started, as an elbow injury suffered during Spring Training resulted in Tommy John surgery in early April. Though he showcased elite velocity as an amateur, Kolek worked more in the low- to mid-90s during his full-season debut. He throws his heater with heavy sinking action that leads to many groundouts and few home runs. Both Kolek's slider and changeup are below average, and that lack of an out pitch limits his bat-missing ability. He did make some strides with the former before getting hurt, throwing it with improved depth and power. The Marlins worked with Kolek to refine his delivery during his rehab process with the hope that it would help him regain some velocity, as well as better command. After a 15-month absence, the big right-hander finally returned to the mound in game action in July 2017. He may be well behind the development curve, but if he can stay healthy and everything clicks, Kolek still could reach his ceiling of a No. 2 or 3 starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox signed Guaimaro, along with several Venezuelan amateurs in 2015, only to have those players declared free agents after Major League Baseball ruled the team had evaded the set limitations pertaining to international bonus pool spending. In July 2016, Guaimaro signed with the Marlins. With present strength to his athletic frame, Guaimaro draws physical comparisons to Marlon Byrd from club officials. He has plus bat speed and impacts the baseball from the right side of the plate, all the while showing the ability to recognize spin and work counts at a young age. He's an above-average runner and plays a strong center field, though further physical development likely will force him to right field, where his plus arm would be a fit. The Marlins have high hopes for Guaimaro, who will be 18 for the entire 2017 season. He'll require considerable time to develop in the Minors, but the final product could be that of an everyday corner outfielder who can hit for average and power.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The way Urena, who signed with the Mets out of the Dominican Republic in November 2011, began his career, he looked like a future impact player. He hit so well in 2013 during his United States debut in the Gulf Coast League and again in the New York-Penn League in 2014, the Mets felt confident in double-jumping him up to the Class A Advanced Florida State League. Two broken hamates derailed him in 2015 and he didn't produce as he had in a return to the FSL in 2016. He did get headed back in the right direction with an All-Star turn back with St. Lucie for a third season. Urena once again looks like his bat could get him to the big leagues. He is capable of driving the ball, finishing the 2017 season with 51 extra-base hits, mostly in the pitching-friendly FSL, and it's easy to see some of the 34 doubles he hit there landing over the fence as he progresses. He'll draw walks and he did make some nice adjustments at the plate last year, though he can get rotational and pull-happy at times, leading to an elevated strikeout rate. The biggest issue is Urena's long-term defensive home. While he made some progress at third during instructs, and has played some first base, his defense has gone backwards as he's filled out. He'll primarily move to a corner outfield spot in 2018, where his plus arm should play.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Urena burst on the scene in 2014 with an outstanding offensive performance in the short-season New York-Penn League. The Mets tried to leap him up to the Florida State League the following year, but the infielder unfortunately broke both hamates. He was relatively healthy in 2016 but didn't come close to producing like he did back in Brooklyn, though he bounced back with a more productive 2017 in his third go-round with St. Lucie. Urena shows a solid approach at the plate, with a good walk rate and not a lot of swing-and-miss to his game. He does, however, get pull happy and needs to find the middle of the field more consistently, though he's been better from the left side than the right thus far in terms of his hit tool. When he gets too big, he gets himself into trouble and needs to trust that his raw power will show up naturally. A fair third baseman with a strong arm, Urena started getting some time at first in 2016, partially because some thought he'd have to move there eventually, and partially to improve his versatility with other more advanced defenders at the hot corner in the organization. On both sides of the ball, Urena needs to find some consistency to reach his ultimate potential. He'll play nearly all of 2017 at age 22, so there's time for him to put it together.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ever since being a highly touted prospect coming from the Dominican amateur ranks, Pujols has carried with him a tremendous amount of offensive potential. While there are still some serious holes to address, his leading the South Atlantic League in home runs in 2016, in his full-season debut, was a very nice step in the right direction. Pujols has as much raw power as anyone in Phillies system, including slugger Jhailyn Ortiz. Proof of that came with that power output in Lakewood, which is not exactly friendly for power hitters. And it's not just pull power for Pujols, who exhibited the ability to drive the ball out in right- and left-center. He needs to vastly improve his strikeout rate -- 32.6 percent in 2016 -- but the Phillies did see progress with his two-strike approach. He's improved his outfield play and has a very strong arm that works well from a corner spot. Just 21 years old for all of the 2017 season, Pujols is as confident as he's ever been in his Phillies career after having sustained success for the first time. The Phillies believe he could be primed for a big year this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 75 | Curveball: 60 | Control: 40 | Overall: 45 Hernandez toiled for five summers in the Giants system but couldn't get out of rookie ball because of an inability to throw strikes. The D-backs signed him out of indy ball, and while the strike zone still wasn't his friend, the Reds rolled very low-risk dice by taking him in the Minor League phase of the 2015 Rule 5 Draft. He pitched across two levels of full-season Class A ball, got added to the 40-man roster at the end of the 2016 season and made his big league debut in 2017. Earlier in his career, Hernandez had some serious difficulty with direction to the plate, contributing to his wildness. That has been addressed with some success, and while he still walks too many, he is able to more frequently attack the zone with his two plus pitches. Even if he's more control over command and getting too much of the plate, he's still successful because of how good his raw stuff is. He'll throw his fastball in the 95-100 mph range, and according to the data the Reds collect, he has one of the best curveballs in the system. Hernandez came back from his 2016 success with a breakout year in 2017 that saw him get big league innings. He has the stuff to pitch in the back of a bullpen, with an ultimate role somewhat dependent on how consistently he can throw strikes.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best defenders in the 2015-16 international class, Brito landed a $2 million bonus to sign out of the Dominican Republic. He spent his first pro season in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League before making his U.S. debut in 2017. That ended in early August when a runner slid into him on an attempted double play and broke his left leg. Fully healthy in 2018, Brito showed improved hitting ability as well as some power en route to both mid-season and post-season All-Star honors in the Pioneer League. The Blue Jays acquired him and right-hander Andrew Sopko for Russell Martin and cash considerations in a January trade. While Brito still needs time to develop more consistency, he has Gold Glove upside at shortstop. He covers plenty of ground at shortstop thanks to his smooth actions, quick first step and keen instincts, and his soft hands and strong arm add to his playmaking ability. His tools will play anywhere in the infield and he saw time at second and third base last year. Brito isn't nearly as advanced offensively as he is defensively. He's a switch-hitter with promising bat speed and solid speed but hit just .232/.324/.362 in his first two pro seasons. He showed some patience in his debut but was overly aggressive last season and struck out in 33 percent of his plate appearances.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best defenders available during the 2015-16 international signing period, Brito signed for $2 million out of the Dominican Republic. His bonus ranked as just the seventh-highest in the Dodgers' global spending spree. He made his pro debut last summer in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, batting .228/.352/.345 but establishing his credentials as the best middle-infield defender in the system. Though he's years away from the big leagues at this point, it's not difficult to project Brito as a possible Gold Glover. With his quick first step, smooth actions and advanced instincts, he covers plenty of ground at shortstop. Soft hands and a strong arm round out a complete defensive package. Once Brito gets stronger, he could provide some offense as well. A switch-hitter, he has a patient approach and solid speed that will help him hit for average. He also has the bat speed to perhaps provide double-digit home run power as well.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Few college middle infielders in the 2017 Draft could match Netzer's track record of hitting. He won the Cal Ripken League batting title at .349 in the summer of 2015, hit .384 as a UNC Charlotte sophomore in 2016 and compiled a .351 average in three college seasons. His prowess at the plate made him a third-round pick, the fourth-highest in 49ers history, and earned him a slightly below-slot $475,000 bonus. He hit his way to Class A four weeks into his pro career. Netzer's bat speed and feel for the barrel allow him to make line-drive contact with ease. He walked almost as much as he struck out in college, though he expanded his strike zone in his introduction to pro ball. He has some raw power, though his left-handed swing is relatively flat and geared more for doubles than home runs. Netzer has average speed, but subpar arm strength, limiting his defensive options. He's an adequate second baseman whose only other position is left field, where he played as a college freshman. His bat-first profile at second base has drawn comparisons to Adam Kennedy and Tommy La Stella.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Indians selected Longo in the 14th round in 2016 out Ohio University, where he had posted a career .355 average over three seasons. He continued to show an advanced bat during his pro debut, but opened his first full season behind schedule due to a wrist injury. When he finally took the field in mid-May, Longo torched Class A Midwest League pitching at a .361/.431/.530 clip to earn a late promotion to Class A Advanced Lynchburg. Longo is a toolsy college product with remaining upside. Hitting from an open stance, he creates leverage to the ball and keeps his barrel in the zone for an extended period of time. It in turn allows him to effectively cover both sides of the plate and use the entire field, something he has always done well. Longo does have some pop in his bat, though it's mostly to the gaps right now. He's an above-average runner who gets out of the box well and finished fourth in the Indians' system with 20 steals in 2017 despite limited action. Longo's speed also plays well in right field, where he spent his entire full-season debut, and his above-average arm strength is a natural fit at the position. While his hit-over-power profile at a corner position might not hold up as well at higher levels, Longo's broad set of skills and solid tools give him a solid chance to consistently outperform projections.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gonzalez was ranked No. 19 on MLB Pipeline's Top 30 International prospects list heading into the 2017 July 2 signing period. His overall tools, particularly at shortstop, stood out enough for the Tigers to give him $1 million to sign and he's starting his pro career in 2018. While player and organization are still getting to know each other, Gonzalez has already made an impression with his glove-work. He has very good actions and a strong arm to go along with outstanding hands, giving him the chance to be an above-average to plus defender when all is said and done. Some felt he might need to move to third in the future because of his age. It's going to take a long time to see if the investment in Gonzalez pays off for Detroit. But the teenager does have all the makings of a big league middle infielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After dealing with Tommy John surgery and thoracic outlet syndrome while at the University of Texas, facing pro hitters late in games may seem like a walk in the park to Curtiss, the Twins' sixth-round pick in the 2014 Draft. After a strong first full season and showing in the Arizona Fall League in 2016, Curtiss pitched his way from Double-A to the big leagues and led the system in saves. He spent most of the 2018 season in Triple-A, though he did return to Minnesota, and was sent to the Angels in January in a Minor League deal. The Twins did give Curtiss the chance to start at the outset of his career, but it's clear the back end of the bullpen, where his fastball-slider combination plays up, is the place for him. He creates angle with his 6-foot-4 frame well, leading to weak contact off of his 94- to 98-mph fastball, though he also misses bats with it up in the zone. His slider has improved to the point of being a true out pitch with hard two-plane break. He's not a big command guy, and while he threw enough strikes previously in his career, his control regressed in 2018. Curtiss wasn't able to establish himself as a Major League reliever with the Twins. He gets a fresh start with the Angels and if he can rediscover the strike zone, he still has the chance to pitch in high-leverage situations in the back end of a bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Marlins have been successful in the past with their international signings, with outfielder Marcell Ozuna and right-hander Jose Urena representing recent examples. The club hopes Marinez can follow in their footsteps after they inked the teenage Dominican shortstop to a $1.2 million deal at the outset of the 2017-18 international signing period. Marinez is very athletic, and some viewed him as one of the best athletes on the market. While some scouts believe his physical development will eventually force him from shortstop to third base, there are others who believe he has the tools to stay in the middle of the diamond. What's more, the teenager has displayed soft hands, good body control and solid range to both sides. He has also shown plus arm strength and impressive actions on defense. A line-drive hitter with some natural loft to his swing, Marinez can spray the ball to all fields. He's still developing as a hitter but has already shown good bat speed and power potential. He destroys fastballs, and like most prospects his age, he's working on hitting secondary pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Herb went 22-9 in four years at Coastal Carolina, three as a starter, before signing with the Mariners for $1,000 as a 29th-round senior in 2014. He didn't do much to distinguish himself in his first three pro seasons before successfully conquering Double-A in 2017, ranking 12th in the entire Minors in both innings (163 1/3) and groundout/flyout ratio (2.0). He came to the Giants in July as the player to be named in a trade for Chris Heston and claimed a spot on the 40-man roster in November. The sink on Herb's 89-93 mph two-seam fastball and the plane he creates with his 6-foot-3 frame generate a lot of ground balls. His secondary offerings all are average, with his slider perhaps the most consistently reliable. He keeps batters off balance by sequencing his pitches well. Herb did a better job of throwing quality strikes last season but has struggled to do so in 2018 while dealing with an oblique issue. He doesn't have a high ceiling but if he can build off the progress he made in 2017, he could be an innings eater at the back of a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A four-sport athlete as an Iowa high schooler, Ziegler struggled to hit NCAA Division I pitching as a Northern Illinois freshman but batted .395 with 22 homers and 31 steals as a North Iowa Area CC sophomore in 2016. Though junior college offensive numbers don't necessarily have much predictive value, the Giants signed him for $100,000 as a 22nd-rounder because they believed in his speed and defense. He's still raw in all phases of the game, and losing nearly three months to an oblique strain while making his full-season debut this year didn't help his cause. Some evaluators have clocked Ziegler with top-of-the-scale run times and he builds his game around his well above-average speed. He can steal bases and chase down balls in center field on sheer quickness alone, though he needs to refine his reads and jumps on the bases and in the outfield. His solid arm strength enhances his defensive value. Ziegler needs to get on base more often to take advantage of his speed. He makes a decent amount of contact from the right side of the plate, but needs to add more strength and patience. His JUCO power doesn't translate to wood bats, though he does have some bat speed and can drive the ball to the gaps on occasion.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Winker was taken in the supplemental first round of the 2012 Draft out of Olympia High School in Orlando, the same school that produced the likes of Brad Miller and Nick Gordon, he was one of the best pure hitters in the class. Despite injuries slowing him down some, he's more than lived up to that reputation and hit his way to Cincinnati for the first time in 2017 at age 23. The two career Minor League stats that explain who Winker is as a hitter are his batting average of .298 and his on-base percentage of .398 through the 2017 season. His advanced approach from the left side of the plate has allowed him to hit for average and draw walks pretty much wherever he's been, including during his time in the big leagues. While the hit tool is ready, it's unclear how much power Winker will have when all is said and done. He definitely has extra-base ability and did show more over-the-fence pop during his time in the big leagues, albeit in a small sample size. Winker's arm is fringy, at best, and he's a below-average runner, so he might fit best in left field long-term. Winker is ready to produce in the big leagues now. With other options in both corners in Cincinnati, the gifted hitter could be asked to rotate between right and left to get that bat into the lineup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A product of Olympia High School in Orlando, alma mater of big leaguer Brad Miller and former first-round pick Nick Gordon, Winker was one of the better pure hitters in the 2012 Draft class. While injuries have slowed his progress somewhat, he still reached Triple-A at age 22 last year and was added to the Reds' 40-man roster this past offseason. He made his big league debut in 2017, riding the Louisville-Cincinnati shuttle on multiple occasions. Winker's best tool is still his bat and approach at the plate. He draws walks and works counts and even while dealing with wrist issues, continues to hit for a high average. His patience has allowed him to post a career on-base percentage of close to .400 while hitting nearly .300 in his Minor League career. His power took a step back in 2016, but he has shown extra-base ability in the past and now past the wrist issues, should be able to add more over-the-fence ability as he continues to mature and learn when he can turn on pitches effectively. A below-average runner, Winker has played both corner outfield spots but is likely a left fielder at the highest level because of his below-average arm, but he should be an acceptable defender there. Adam Duvall's surprising 2016 notwithstanding, Winker still appears to be the future in left for Cincinnati.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Woodruff spurned the Rangers as a fifth-round pick in 2011 to attend Mississippi State, where injuries and role changes led to an unglamorous college career.
