mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Because of a maturity beyond his years, the Mets felt comfortable letting Carpio, who signed in 2013 for $300,000, make his United States debut in the Appalachian League, up a half-step from a typical start in the Gulf Coast League. He responded by hitting over .300, but the excitement from that was tempered when a torn labrum that required surgery forced him out for nearly all of the 2016 season. Because of his plus work ethic, Carpio did make it back for 20 games at the end of the year and was able to participate in instructional league play. After a healthy offseason, he is expected to be ready to go and pick up where he left off. While he doesn't have a ton of power -- there might be some more extra-base pop as he matures -- he does make consistent hard contact and can send line drives to the gaps, employing a solid approach at the plate. He has the defensive skills to stay at short, with good hands and what should be enough arm to stay there if needed, but he'll likely start out at second base, at least to ease his shoulder back into things. Carpio's plus makeup should help ensure he makes it all the way back to his pre-surgery level of play on both sides of the ball. By the time he's ready for New York, he might show he's capable of playing either middle infield position on a daily basis.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic in 2010, Severino reached Double-A for the first time in '15 and received a brief taste of the big leagues that September. He bounced between Triple-A Syracuse and the Majors the next year before taking over as Washington's everyday catcher in late September in the wake of Wilson Ramos' season-ending knee injury. Shuttling between Triple-A and Washington again in 2017, Severino was unable to build on his progress from previous years. Severino is a plus defender behind the plate, with athleticism and agility that fuel his abilities as a blocker. His pitch-framing and overall receiving skills have steadily improved as he's climbed the ladder, and club officials praise his game-calling. Adept at controlling the running game, Severino has posted strong caught-stealing rates throughout his career thanks to a combination of advanced footwork and plus arm strength. Severino's bat, however, still lags behind his glove, as his aggressive approach results in too much forced, weakly hit contact and little in the way of power. It's that lack of impact potential at the plate that likely will limit Severino to backup duties at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic in 2010, Severino reached Double-A for the first time in 2015 and received a brief taste of the big leagues that September. He bounced between Triple-A Syracuse and the Majors last season before taking over as Washington's everyday catcher in late September in the wake of Wilson Ramos' season-ending knee injury. Scouts have long viewed Severino as a plus defender behind the plate, where his athleticism and agility make him an excellent blocker. His pitch-framing and overall receiving skills have steadily improved as he's climbed the ladder, and club officials praise his game-calling. Controlling the running game is where Severino truly shines, as his advanced footwork and cannon arm have helped him post strong caught-stealing rates throughout his career. Severino's bat lags behind his defense and he'll never offer much in the way of power, but he does make a lot of contact and has proved difficult to strike out. With his strong defense chops and some hitting ability, Severino currently profiles as more of a backup than an everyday catcher in the big leagues, thus providing the Nationals with quality depth behind the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Watch Trahan for one day, and you might walk away unimpressed. Watch him over the course of a season and you'll probably understand why coaching staffs wherever he plays love him. A true gamer taken in the third round of the 2015 Draft out of Louisiana-Lafayette, Trahan can do a lot of the little things well to help a team win. One thing he didn't do in 2017 was hit. The shortstop does have excellent contact and on-base skills, keeping his walk rate high and his strikeout rate low. But he tried to do too much at the plate and get too big. Power is never going to be a part of his game, so he needs to get back to the line-drive approach that served him better previously in his Minor League career. Trahan is a very solid defender at shortstop and could stay there if needed, but after seeing time at second base during his stint in the Arizona Fall League, he's going to start moving all over the field more. The Reds are confident that Trahan, a plus-effort, high-energy sparkplug, will play in the big leagues. It's looking likely that it will be as that scrappy utilityman winning teams often need.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Over the last four Drafts, the Reds have taken at least one college hitter in their top four selections. Often it's been the top guy, like Nick Senzel in 2016 and Phil Ervin in 2012. Trahan was the fourth pick the Reds made in the 2015 Draft, but they were pleasantly surprised he was still available in the third round after a solid season at Louisiana-Lafayette. He went straight to the Florida State League for his first full season and more than held his own, though his offensive game took a step backwards with the move to Double-A in 2017. The Reds love Trahan's energy and his defense. Unlike some other college middle infielders who needed to change positions, there is no question Trahan can play shortstop long-term. He's not flashy, but he's an intelligent player who makes all the plays and whose plus speed gives him good range and makes him an effective baserunner. He has shown a decent line-drive approach at the plate overall, with a willingness to work counts and draw walks, though he struggled at the plate in the Southern League. If Trahan hits, he has the chance to be an everyday shortstop. If not, look for him to increase his versatility -- he got time at second base during instructs last fall, but not in games -- with a career as a very valuable utility man as his floor.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Reds knew that patience would be key in developing Hanson after drafting him in the third round of the 2016 Draft. He was, after all, a raw high school arm from a cold weather state in Minnesota. The big right-hander taken in the third round and signed away from his Kentucky commitment was delayed even further when he needed Tommy John surgery and missed the entire 2017 season. The good news is Hanson is back throwing and returned to pitch in the rookie level Arizona League in 2018. He also used his time rehabbing to trim down his 6-foot-6 frame. There's a lot of fastball to come from Hanson, assuming he bounces back to pre-surgery levels, as he was up to 95-96 mph at times with his heater. He also featured a power curve that flashed plus and a changeup that was behind since he didn't need it much in the Minnesota high school ranks. Command was an issue for Hanson, as he struggled to repeat his delivery consistently. The Reds are pleased with where Hanson is and are happy he's back on a mound competitively. It'll be slow going, especially at the start, but the payoff, given his size and chance for two plus pitches, could be big.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Taking a big, raw pitcher from a cold-weather climate might scare away some front offices. But the Reds have had some success patiently shepherding Sal Romano up the ladder slowly, so they didn't shy away from taking Hanson, the Minnesota high school product, in the fifth round of the 2016 Draft. Already faced with a long path to the big leagues, Hanson's journey was forced off-track early when he needed Tommy John surgery in March. Once he returns from the surgery, Hanson has the chance to have really big stuff when it all comes together. He's shown a 92-97 mph fastball and has a power curveball that also could be a plus pitch down the line. The Minnesota Gatorade Player of the Year will have to work to develop his changeup, not needing the offspeed pitch against his high school competition. Command and control are also a work in progress, with mechanics for a 6-foot-5 pitcher tricky to repeat. Once he gets there, he is physical enough to develop into a durable starting pitcher. The Reds feel Hanson is more athletic than Romano was when he started out, though they know he's very much a ball of clay waiting to be sculpted. It will take time post-surgery, but the wait could well be worth it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thanks to the free-agent signing off Zack Greinke before the 2016 season, the D-backs didn't have a first-round pick. Their first selection came in the Competitive Balance Round A and they used the No. 39 overall pick to take Grier out of Auburn. Shoulder soreness kept him from showing what he could do until his first full season and he had a solid performance in the Midwest League, though he faded a bit down the stretch. Grier's carrying tool is his speed. It allowed him to finish second in the organization with 30 steals a year ago and also helps him cover a lot of ground in center field, where he should be able to stay defensively long-term, and where his fringy arm will be fine. He's starting to learn that his profile will likely be at, or close to, the top of a lineup, and with that, on-base skills will be needed. There is swing and miss to his game, but his approach is improving and the D-backs believe he will increase his walk rate and decrease hit strikeout rate as he matures. Better counts will let him tap into some power that's there and allow him to barrel the ball up well even more consistently. Grier's first full season built a good foundation, with strides taken and things still to work on. He'll focus on that as he moves up the ladder in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The D-backs didn't pick until No. 39 overall in the 2016 Draft, courtesy of the Zack Greinke signing. They saw Grier as a rare college up-the-middle player with tools who had performed well at Auburn, though he didn't get to show what he could do in his pro debut as shoulder soreness limited his playing time. Now fully healthy, Grier has shown glimpses of his tools in his first full season. He's very athletic and covers a lot of ground in center field, showing excellent reads and routes. His arm is fringy at best, but it's enough for center. The speed that helps him in the outfield should allow him to be a basestealing threat. At the plate, he can barrel up the ball well when he's on time, though strikeouts have been a concern in the past. He does have some power, with more to come as he fills out. Had this been later in his career, Grier would have likely played through his shoulder issue. The organization, understandably, erred on the side of caution and got to see what kind of player he is this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After taking Dansby Swanson with the No. 1 overall pick in the 2015 Draft, the D-backs went college-pitching heavy, selecting one with each of their next five picks. Young was the first in that group taken, in the second round out of TCU. The lefty made a fairly successful jump to Double-A in his second full season, finishing seventh in the system in ERA. Young relies on a three-pitch mix and his ability to throw them for strikes, rather than any one true out pitch. His fastball is average, thrown around 91-92 mph. His breaking ball, which was more of a slider when he entered pro ball, has morphed into more of a curveball and grades out as Major League average. The lefty has worked on his changeup a lot and it's caught up to his breaking ball, giving him a third average offering. There isn't a whole lot of margin for error for Young, so his ability to command all three is important. He did a much better job of doing that down in the zone in the second half of his 2017 season. Young did pitch out of the bullpen at times with TCU and he looked good doing so during his brief pro debut in 2015. The D-backs plan to continue to let him start and see if he can keep developing into a back-end starter, knowing the stuff would tick up a bit in shorter relief stints.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Like his 2015 Draft classmate Taylor Clarke, Young pitched briefly, and in relief, during his pro debut after being taken in the second round. He spent his first full year as a starter, and outside of what the organization termed arm fatigue that shut him down for a month, he had a successful season. While Clarke passed him a bit by reaching Double-A in 2016, Young got to that level in 2017, though he had more difficulty sustaining that success. He still has the stuff to succeed as a starter at the highest level. Young did see the velocity of his fastball back up a tiny bit as a starter, though he still touched 91-92 mph. His bread and butter is his plus slider, the one offering he has that can miss bats, though he's more of a pitchability, control-type lefty. His changeup improved with the reps he got as a starter, giving him a third average offering. He throws all of them for strikes. Young does have bullpen experience thanks to his time at TCU, but there's nothing that says he can't be a back-end starter at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 Unlike most pitching prospects, Abdullah has more of a golf than a baseball background and didn't take the mound until his junior year in high school. The Dodgers liked his upside enough to give him third-round money ($650,000) in the 11th round of the 2015 Draft and have part-owner Magic Johnson call to welcome him to the organization. They've handled him with care and had him open 2017 in extended spring training to work on his strength and mechanics, then shut him down in July when his shoulder bothered him after just 12 1/3 innings in low Class A. Abdullah's fastball velocity has risen from 88-90 mph when he was a high school senior to 92-94 now with a peak of 97. His heater features run and sink, and it could sit in the mid-90s once he fills out his projectable 6-foot-4 frame. He has a surprisingly advanced changeup with fade, given his background, though he's still learning to maintain consistent arm speed when he throws his curveball. Los Angeles knew Abdullah would be a long-term project when it drafted him and will be patient with his development. He has good athleticism and body control for his size, which bodes well for his future control and command. Club officials praise his intelligence and competitiveness.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Dodgers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Abdullah is fairly new to pitching after focusing more on golf before getting on the mound as a high school junior. He confounded scouts as a senior in 2015, intriguing them with his projectability and pitchability but worrying them with inconsistent velocity and questionable signability. The Dodgers gambled on him in the 11th round, had part-owner Magic Johnson call to welcome him to the organization and inked him for $650,000, the equivalent of third-round money. Los Angeles is handling Abdullah carefully because he's inexperienced and his lanky frame is still growing. After working with an 88-90 mph fastball for much of his senior year, Abdullah now pitches at 92-94 with some run and sink and should gain more velocity as he matures physically. He pairs his heater with an advanced changeup that fades at the plate. Abdullah's curveball is more of a work in progress, and the Dodgers hope it will take off after he experimented with different grips during instructional league. He has good athleticism and body control for a big pitcher, so he repeats his delivery well and fills the strike zone. A tough competitor, he relishes pitching inside.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Concerns about Gettys' hitting ability caused him to fall into the second round of the 2014 Draft, where the Padres signed him for $1.3 million as the 51st overall pick. The North Georgia native struggled with the move to full-season ball in 2015, hitting just .231 with a Midwest League-leading 162 strikeouts at Class A Fort Wayne. Gettys fared much better in his return to Fort Wayne in 2016, however, earning mid-season All-Star honors in the Midwest League before advancing to Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore in late June and finishing in the Arizona Fall League. Returning to the California League in 2017, Gettys continued to show loud tools but regressed overall as he finished as the circuit leader in both strikeouts (191) and strikeout rate (37.2 percent). Gettys' swing is explosive and produces plus raw power that he can apply in games -- he hit a career-best 17 home runs in 2017 -- despite holes in his bat path and overall approach. He continues to strike out at a disconcerting rate, a product of his subpar pitch recognition and strike-zone management, and thus faces questions about the future utility of his hit tool. Plus speed allows Gettys to impact games on the basepaths as well as in center field, where he's a plus defender, with range for days and a cannon arm. With raw power, speed, arm strength and defensive ability that all grade as average or better, Gettys has an undeniably impressive ceiling. The jury is still out on whether he can make the necessary swing adjustments to become an everyday player, but his speed, center-field defense and strong track record against left-handed pitching could still make him a valuable fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Concerns about Gettys' hitting ability caused him to fall into the second round of the 2014 Draft, where the Padres signed him for $1.3 million as the 51st overall pick. The North Georgia native struggled with the move to full-season ball in 2015, hitting just .231 with a Midwest League-leading 162 strikeouts at Class A Fort Wayne. Gettys fared much better in his return to Fort Wayne in 2016, however, earning mid-season All-Star honors in the Midwest League before advancing to Class A Advanced Lake Elsinore in late June and finishing in the Arizona Fall League. Back in the California League in 2017, Gettys has struggled to build on his progress from the previous year despite flashing his usual loud tools. Gettys' swing is explosive and produces plus raw power that he began to show during games last season after making an adjustment in his swing. He continues to strike out at a disconcerting rate, a product of his subpar pitch recognition and strike-zone management, and he faces questions about the future utility of his hit tool. Plus speed allows Gettys to impact games on the basepaths as well as in center field, where he's a plus defender, with range for days and a cannon arm. With bat speed, foot speed, arm strength and defensive ability that all grade as well above average, Gettys has an undeniably impressive ceiling. That is of course is tied to his ability to hit and apply his power, but the speed and strong center-field defense alone could make him a valuable fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Johnson flew under the radar at Cal State Northridge, missing most of his first two seasons with an elbow injury and subsequent Tommy John surgery and logging a 4.33 ERA as a redshirt sophomore in 2014. He created a stir in his first extended pro action the following year, flashing electric stuff while posting a 71/11 K/BB ratio across three levels. He hasn't been able to sustain that kind of success since, never getting into a rhythm in Double-A last season while losing a month to a hamstring injury. Johnson still can flash a three-pitch mix that seems to stamp him as a starter. At his best, he can sit at 92-96 mph with sink on his fastball, confound hitters with plus changeups that tumble and offer some curveballs with power and depth. But he doesn't show that kind of stuff consistently because he collapses on the backside of his delivery, flattening his pitches and leaving them up in the strike zone. While the Giants hold out hope that Johnson can improve his mechanics and become more consistent, they also declined to protect him on their 40-man roster after the 2017 season. He spent most of the season working with a 90-94 mph fastball while his control also regressed. If he doesn't start displaying more consistency, a bullpen move could be in his near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts had a difficult time seeing Johnson at Cal State Northridge, where he missed most of his first two years because of Tommy John surgery and went 3-6, 4.33 as a redshirt sophomore in 2014. The Giants liked his arm action and projectability, so they spent a 23rd-round pick and a $100,000 bonus on him that June. He spent 2016 in high Class A and tired in the second half while working 120 innings -- nearly as many as he pitched in the previous four years combined. Johnson's fastball parked at 93-96 mph and touched 98 while he was averaging an eye-opening 12.3 strikeout per nine innings during his first extended pro action in 2015. Last season, he fell into the bad habit of overstriding and getting under his pitches, which dropped his heater to 90-94 mph and also cost him some sink. He spent the offseason working to correct that flaw yet still is getting hit harder than hoped in Double-A. Johnson trusts his changeup, which can be a plus pitch when it tumbles at the plate, and sells it with deceptive arm speed. San Francisco had him shelve a hard slider that it believes contributed to his injuries, and he has come up with a curveball that has some power and depth. If he can straighten out his mechanics and improve his command, he could become a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Lane spent more time as an outfielder than on the mound in his first two college seasons at Campbell and Lower Columbia (Wash.) CC, then became more of a pitcher at Illinois-Chicago. After he won Horizon League reliever of the year honors in 2016, the Yankees made him a $10,000 senior sign as a 10th-rounder. His control and velocity improved dramatically in his first full pro season, when he logged a 1.52 ERA at two Class A stops to earn a non-roster invitation to Spring Training in 2018. In college, Lane operated with an 89-90 mph sinker and an effective slider. Now he's beating up hitters with a 92-97 mph and a high-spin breaker that looks more like a curveball with its depth. He also has a decent changeup that he can mix in for a different look. Lane also is doing a much better job of locating his pitches in pro ball, reducing his walk rate from 4.1 per nine innings at Illiniois-Chicago to 2.1 in his first two years as a pro. He pounds the bottom of the strike zone, missing bats and creating a lot of weak contact. As a multi-inning southpaw reliever who's effective against both left-handers and right-handers, he may not need much more time in the Minors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Thompson used a sinker/slider approach to great effect in 2017, leading NCAA Division I in victories while going 14-1 with a 1.96 ERA for a 56-6 Oregon State club that finished third at the College World Series. After the Red Sox signed the redshirt junior for a slightly below-slot $350,000 as a fourth-rounder, he told them that though the Beavers had him focus on two pitches, he also threw a curveball and splitter/changeup. He showed the makings of a possible mid-rotation starter during his pro debut but hasn't been as sharp during his first full season. Last summer, Thompson worked with a two-seam sinker at 92-94 mph, touched 98 with his four-seam fastball and flashed a plus slider and split/change. This year, his fastball velocity is down 2-3 mph and his secondary pitches haven't missed as many bats. With a deeper repertoire, Thompson has a better chance of remaining a starter. In college, several scouts projected him as a reliever because he lacks a smooth delivery and didn't have much success in his first three seasons at Oregon State (missing most of 2015 with a back injury). If his stuff doesn't trend back up, he may wind up in the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Red Sox grabbed two Florida two-way players in the 2012 Draft, Brian Johnson in the first round and Maddox in the third. The latter hit 17 homers as a Gators freshman but offers more upside on the mound. After he recorded a 5.05 ERA in his first four pro seasons, he added velocity in 2016 and made his big league debut last year, allowing one run in 17 1/3 innings to earn a spot on Boston's playoff roster. Maddox began the 2018 season on the Red Sox's disabled list with a shoulder strain. Maddox's four-seam fastball averaged 95 mph in his first taste of the Majors and usually ranges from 92-97 mph. He'll throw it up in the strike zone to set up his changeup, a mid-80s weapon with splitter action that also can be a plus pitch at times. He'll keep hitters off balance by mixing in an occasional mid-80s slider that shows some flashes of becoming an average offering. Maddox's control has slipped a bit as he has started throwing harder, and he has to be careful with his location because his reliance on four-seamers has made him a fly-ball pitcher. While he may not be a high-leverage reliever, he made a good first impression in Boston and could be a seventh-inning option.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: De la Guerra was eligible for four straight Drafts from 2011-14 but went unselected as a California high school senior, JC of the Canyons (Calif.) freshman and sophomore and a Grand Canyon junior. He won the Western Athletic Conference batting title with a .373 average in 2014 and encored with a 24-game hitting streak in 2015, when the Red Sox made him a $5,000 senior sign in the 17th round. After not hitting much in his first two pro seasons and fracturing his lower leg in 2016, he batted .283/.361/.437 while advancing to Double-A last season. De la Guerra's instincts and inner drive stand out more than any of his tools, none of which grade better than average. However, he has a knack for making consistent line-drive contract and draws enough walks to post solid on-base percentages. He won't drive many balls over the fence but will lace his share of doubles to the gaps. A second baseman for much of his first two years as a pro, de la Guerra spent most of 2017 at shortstop. He enhanced his utility profile by proving capable at shortstop and also saw action at third base in the Arizona Fall League. He's a steady if unspectacular defender with reliable hands and average arm strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Jerez went in the second round of the 2011 Draft as an outfielder with a big league body and the potential for plus power, speed and arm strength. He batted just .221/.254/.275 in his first three pro seasons, however, so he switched to pitching in 2014. He advanced to Double-A a year after his mound debut, then saw his stuff and command regress in 2016 before righting himself last season. After losing velocity the year before, Jerez regained his 93-97 mph fastball, which features some sink. He also reclaimed the sharpness on his low-80s slider, giving him two pitches to attack left-handers, who posted just a .485 OPS against him last year. He has struggled against righties (.815 OPS in 2017) but hopes that scrapping a changeup for a promising splitter will help him going forward. Jerez also helped his cause by improving his strike-throwing last year. Whether he becomes a situational reliever or something more will depend on his ability to refine his splitter. After outrighting him off their 40-man roster following the 2016 season, the Red Sox added him back last November.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bishop was expected to serve as UC Irvine's Friday night starter until a preseason oblique suffered during a bullpen session prior to Opening Day wiped out his entire junior season. While the Orioles still took a flyer on him in the 26th round in June, it appeared that the two sides were unable to strike a deal prior to the July 7 signing deadline. It later was revealed, however, that Baltimore actually had submitted its $605,000 deal with Bishop nearly five minutes after the deadline had passed, and a corresponding investigation by Major League Baseball determined that the signing was valid because the parties agreed to a contract before the deadline. He spent most of his pro debut with Class A Short Season Aberdeen, pitching to a 0.78 ERA with 38 strikeouts in 35 innings, and continued to impress with Class A Delmarva in 2018. A 6-foot-4, 215-pound left-hander, Bishop can run his fastball up to 95 mph, albeit with little feel for where it's going. He features a pair of breaking balls in a curveball and slider, both of which currently grade as fringe-average but stand to improve with experience. The same can be said for his changeup, too. Bishop's feel for pitching leaves quite a bit to be desired, though he did make gains with both his control and command in his first full season. He has the raw components needed to stick as a starter at the next level, as well as the pure arm strength to become a late-inning reliever should that not work out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fifth-round Draft pick in 2014 out of Tennessee Tech, Hess made steady progress early in his career while reaching Double-A in his first full season. Though he struggled the following year over a full season in the Eastern League, Hess rebounded in his return to the level in 2017, posting a 3.85 ERA and logging a career-high 154 1/3 innings, and the Orioles added him to their 40-man roster after the season. Hess attacks the zone from an over-the-top slot that helps him achieve downhill plane with a fastball that ranges from 89-95 mph and usually sits around 93. Both his slider and curveball are average offerings, with the former currently grading ahead of the latter, though he can get caught between them at times. He also has a serviceable changeup that plays against left-handed hitters and demonstrates average control of his four-pitch mix. Questions remain about whether Hess, with his high-effort delivery and lack of an out pitch, can remain a starter. It's long been thought that his stuff would play up in short bursts out of the bullpen, where his fastball-breaking ball pairing could make him a force against right-handed hitters.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally signed by the D-backs in January 2011, Ramirez spent his pro debut in the Dominican Summer League as an infielder before making the transition to pitching full time the following year. He spent the next four seasons refining his craft in Rookie ball before joining the Yankees via the Minor League phase in the 2015 Rule 5 Draft. Ramirez broke out in his 2016 full-season debut, prompting the Yankees to add him to their 40-man roster in November, and then earned All-Star honors with Double-A Trenton in 2017 before heading to the Orioles in a Trade Deadline deal. After beginning the 2018 season with Triple-A Norfolk, Ramirez was called up for his Major League debut in June and quickly established himself as part of the Orioles' starting rotation. Operating from a high three-quarters slot, Ramirez will sit comfortably in the low-90s with his fastball while bumping 96. A plus changeup and an inconsistent slider comprise his secondary arsenal, and he's capable of generating whiffs against hitters on both sides of the plate with both. Ramirez has good feel for throwing strikes but below-average command. With an intriguing blend of stuff, pitchability and bat-missing ability, Ramirez has all the ingredients needed for him to stick as a big league starter. Should he be unable to do so, the right-hander should have no problem offering value as a long-reliever or swingman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Selected in the 10th round in 2013 following his senior year at Fresno State, Wynns made progress on both sides of the ball during his first two seasons before breaking out in earnest in '17 with a career-best performance across three levels including Triple-A. That across-the-board improvement prompted the Orioles to add Wynns to their 40-man roster after the season, and he rewarded the club by making his Major League debut in June 2018. Wynns is a strong defender behind the plate with above-average arm strength and advanced catch-and-throw skills that enabled him to throw out more than 38 percent of attempted basestealers in 2017. He also made strides with his blocking, and club officials speak highly of his feel for calling a game. No slouch with the bat, Wynns slashed .281/.377/.419 while establishing career highs in home runs (10), doubles (19) and walks (54). Wynns' breakout performance has thrust him into the Major League spotlight, portending a possible backup role for the 27-year-old catcher.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Originally signed by the Cubs in 2011, Araujo spent parts of his first four seasons in his native Dominican Summer League before finally heading stateside in '14. He impressed during his full-season debut two years later and then put it all together in 2017, earning mid-season All-Star honors in the Class A Advanced Carolina League before finishing in Double-A. That success followed Araujo to the Arizona Fall League, and the Orioles liked what they saw enough to take him in the December Rule 5 Draft. Big and physical, Araujo pitches with slightly above-average fastball velocity and pairs it with a plus curveball. Capable of missing bats with both offerings, his 11.6 strikeouts-per-nine innings with Myrtle Beach ranked third in the Carolina League and first among Cubs farmhands. Araujo also features a changeup, while his control of all three pitches helps his arsenal play up. Araujo has shown steady improvement in each season since making a full-time transition to the bullpen. Though he excelled at closing games in 2017, Araujo is more likely to assume a lesser late-inning role should he stick on the active roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles' system had its share of breakout performers in 2017, but Rifaela's was the most unexpected. After scuffling through his first two pro seasons, the Curacao native erupted to slug a Class A Advanced Carolina League-leading 24 homers while slashing .284/.358/.500 en route to circuit MVP honors. A stocky but physically strong player, Rifaela stands out most for his impressive left-handed power. He got to it more than ever in 2017 and also showed improved feel to hit despite striking out in 24.4 percent of his plate appearances with Frederick. Rifaela is a below-average runner but moves well enough to profile as an average defender at either corner outfield spot, even showing he can handle center field in a pinch. It's yet to be seen how Rifaela's game will translate at higher levels against more advanced arms, but there's enough thump in his left-handed bat to peg him as a potential big league contributor in some capacity.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Skoug could have gone in the first three rounds of the 2014 Draft if he hadn't been intent on attending Texas Christian, where he immediately became the Horned Frogs' cleanup hitter and led them to three College World Series in three years. In 2017, he overcame an early slump and 98 strikeouts (one short of the NCAA record) to share the Big 12 Conference player of the year award after leading the league with 20 homers and 71 RBI. He slid to the seventh round of the Draft, where the White Sox pounced on him with an over-slot $300,000 bonus. Skoug has impressive bat speed and strength that create plus raw power. He's at his best when he employs a compact left-handed swing, uses the entire field and lets his pop come naturally, but he fell into a rut at the beginning of his Draft year where his stroke got too long and he got too pull-happy while trying to do to much. He struck out in 38 percent of his plate appearances during his brief pro debut, and while fatigue played a part, he'll need to make adjustments to handle more advanced pitching. Though no one questions Skoug's leadership work ethic, there are concerns about his ability to stay behind the plate. He lacks athleticism and quickness, limiting his effectiveness as a receiver, and might wind up at first base. He compensates for fringy arm strength with a quick release.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After losing his spot at Oregon, Morgan became a walk-on at the University of Washington and was forced to step right into the starting lineup as a freshman. Over his first two years, he was a glove-first backstop, but his Draft profile really jumped when his bat caught up to his defense as a junior, landing him in the third round. He was tired during his pro debut and the Tigers think they'll be getting a look at the real Joey Morgan in 2018. Morgan built a strong defensive reputation at Washington, showing good receiving and blocking skills and an above-average arm. It looked more like average during his summer pro debut, though he still threw out just over 30 percent of potential basestealers in the New York-Penn League. While he was a much better hitter in his junior season, it remains to be seen how the bat will play at this level. He makes consistent contact, but didn't show much in the way of the extra-base ability that raised his profile in college. Morgan will have to show how he can stand up to the rigors of a long season, while continuing to add strength and showing he can be an all-around catcher. If not, a future backup role seems extremely feasible.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Six years after signing for $13,000 out of Venezuela in 2010, Machado still hadn't reached full-season ball. Tommy John surgery that sidelined him for all of 2015 didn't help, but his 5-15, 4.91 record in five seasons in Rookie leagues didn't exactly scream success. His stock changed dramatically in 2017, however, which he began in high Class A and ended with two appearances in Kansas City. Machado sits at 92-95 mph and tops out at 97 with riding life on his four-seam fastball. His changeup shows flashes of becoming a plus pitch but also can get too firm at times and couldn't prevent left-handers from batting .300/.365/.525 against him last year. His mid-80s slider features more velocity than tilt and got hammered during his brief time in the big leagues, when he surrendered nine runs and got 11 outs. Machado's walk rate dropped from 4.7 per nine innings before he had his elbow reconstructed to 2.6 in the first two years afterward. While he's providing more strikes, his command lags behind his control and his delivery lacks deception, so he's fairly hittable. Though he fared well as a starter in Double-A last year, his inconsistencies and the fact that he never has pitched more than 77 innings in a season point to a likely future as a reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: In recent drafts, the Angels had targeted young, athletic outfielders in the early rounds. Pearson, who was Louisiana's Gatorade state player of the year in 2017, fits that description and was taken in the third round, given an above-pick value bonus of $1 million to forego his LSU commitment. After struggling a bit in his pro debut, he was sent to the Twins for international bonus pool money, used to help bring Shohei Ohtani to Anaheim. The Twins liked Pearson in the Draft, but the Angels got to him first, so they're happy to have his athleticism and offensive potential in the fold. There's a power-speed mix to tap into, with 20-20 potential if everything clicks. A left-handed hitter, Pearson utilizes a simple approach with good bat speed and an ability to backspin the ball when he's locked in, pointing to hitting for average and power. He's a plus runner who should be able to steal some bases and cover ground in the outfield. While he played center field in high school, he played left during his pro debut, as his well below-average arm, which is still coming back from labrum surgery after his sophomore year of high school, might be better suited for that corner. Moving to the corner might put more pressure on him to produce offensively, but he has the potential to profile well there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ferguson and Dodgers corner infielder Matt Beaty are battling to become the first Belmont position player to reach the big leagues after teaming up for four years in college. Both parlayed huge senior seasons into pro contracts in 2015, with Ferguson signing with the Astros for $1,000 as a 19th-rounder after hitting .395/.486/.682. He breezed through the Minors before struggling when he got to Triple-A last August. Houston executives rave about Ferguson's baseball IQ, which helps him play above his tools -- not that there are any glaring deficiencies with his tools. He makes consistent hard contact with a sound right-handed swing and a patient gameplan. Though he has a compact build, he has average power and could produce 12-15 homers per year if he tried to drive the ball more often. Ferguson has solid speed and uses it well on the bases and in center field. After getting relegated to the corners in his first two seasons while playing along higher-profile prospects, he showed that he could handle center in 2017. His average arm adds to his versatility, allowing him to man all three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Adcock parlayed three successful years at Michigan into getting drafted in 2016's fourth round, but he didn't make a very positive first or second impression on the Astros. He made just three starts in his pro debut before tearing the meniscus in his knee while fielding a bunt, then arrived at his first Spring Training well over his desired weight. He still made quick work of low Class A, earning a promotion a month into his first full season. Adcock has averaged more than a strikeout per inning in college and pro ball thanks mainly to his breaking pitches. He uses a big-breaking curveball in the mid-70s against left-handers and a sweeping slider in the low-80s, getting lots of swings and misses with both. He sets them up with a low-90s fastball that peaks at 94 mph and features some riding life. After averaging 7.1 walks per nine innings as a Wolverines junior, Adcock has improved his control as a pro by doing a better job of staying online to the plate. He'll need to further refine his control, command and changeup to make it as a No.4 starter. More likely, he'll move to the bullpen and rely even more heavily on his curveball and slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The A's viewed Trivino as a starter when they selected him in the 11th round of the 2013 Draft out of Division II Slippery Rock University. But he pitched to mixed results in the role during his first two seasons, and two years later the A's moved him to the bullpen full-time. Trivino has subsequently blossomed as a reliever, and done so while making a steady climb through the A's system. He pitched to a 3.30 ERA and averaged nearly a strikeout per inning in 2017 while making a career-high 48 appearances across the Double- and Triple-A levels. After the season, the A's added Trivino to their 40-man roster. Listed at 6-foot-5, 225 pounds, Trivino stands out on the mound for his physicality. The big right-hander's stuff is plenty good, too, as he'll run his fastball into the upper 90s while also showing good feel for a low-90s cutter and a quality breaking ball in the low 80s. Meanwhile, after making some key adjustments to his delivery, Trivino made strides as a strike-thrower in 2017 and walked one fewer batter per nine innings than he did the previous year. Trivino's combination of a high-effort delivery and downhill angle to the plate makes his stuff extremely difficult to lift, so much so that opposing hitters have tagged him for just two home runs in 178 1/3 career relief innings, none of which came in 2017. His breaking ball and control both require further improvement, but the raw ingredients are there for Trivino to serve as a late-inning weapon for the A's in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: There were six players from Puerto Rico taken in the top 10 rounds of the 2017 Draft, starting with Giants first-rounder Heliot Ramos. The Angels think they have a real sleeper on their hands with Rivera, the first Puerto Rican taken after the 10th round, an athletic and extremely projectable left-hander they gave $450,000 to sign. Based solely on ceiling, the Angels feel Rivera could be higher on this list. While he entered the Draft as a bit of a soft-tosser, he's already added some velocity to his fastball, with every chance for it to become a plus pitch thrown with good sinking action. His changeup is currently his best secondary weapon and it could be an above-average offspeed pitch eventually, while his curve is a work in progress. One of the more athletic players in the system, Rivera has a strong and repeatable delivery and already has solid fastball command. With a strong foundation to build from with Rivera's athleticism and solid feel for pitching, there was hope he could take a huge step forward in 2018 as he continues to get stronger and refine his delivery. Struggles with command held him back. Still, the final product could be a No. 3 type starter, though it will take patience in the player development department for him to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miller amounted to little offensively during his first four pro seasons before revamping his swing and breaking out in 2017, when he was named as the organization's Ken Griffey Jr. Minor League Hitter of the Year. Opening the season back in the Double-A Texas League, Miller batted .326 to claim a share of the circuit's batting title while also ranking second in on-base percentage (.382) and stolen bases (30). While he didn't fare as well during his first Triple-A exposure after a July promotion, it didn't detract from a career-best year that saw Miller slash .307/.355/.393 with 43 steals and 85 runs across two levels. Miller's speed is his carrying tool, receiving plus-plus grades from scouts, and he's long showed that he knows how to use it on the basepaths. Since the start of the 2015 season, he's posted annual stolen-base totals of 50, 49 and 43, respectively. The left-handed hitter offers little power but uses the entire field well and makes a lot of contact, though at times it can be weak or forced. He continues to draw his share of walks despite an overly aggressive approach that resulted in a career-high strikeout total (102) and rate (18.2 percent) in 2017. Miller's wheels also aid him in the outfield, where he's an above-average defender with an average throwing arm that allows him to play all three spots. He profiles best as an extra outfielder who provides much of his value through his baserunning and defense.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rosario was pure projection when the Mariners inked him for $350,000 at the outset of the 2013-14 international period. He spent the next three seasons playing in his native Dominican Summer League but showed improvement in each campaign before turning in a breakout 2017 campaign with Class A Short Season Everett at age 20. Rosario has impressed club officials with his above-average bat speed and overall feel to hit. He started to grow into his lean, athletic frame in 2017 and in turn saw his power blossom en route to career highs in both doubles and home runs. His swing can get too long at times, however, which leads to some swing-and-miss issues, but also highlights the left-handed hitter's room for improvement. Rosario's athleticism, speed and plus arm strength have netted him time at all three outfield spots, though he spent much of 2017 in center field. He'll need to improve his routes and jumps to remain there, as some evaluators already believe he's best suited for a corner spot long term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A fourth-round pick out of high school by the D-backs in 2012, Taylor spent parts of five seasons in the lower Minors before finally reaching the Double-A level in 2016 during an injury-plagued campaign. The Mariners selected Taylor from Arizona in the Minor League portion of the Rule 5 Draft in December and assigned him to Double-A, where he put together his best and most complete offensive season to date in the Texas League, earning All-Star honors for the first time in his professional career at age 23. Taylor has shown feel to hit throughout his time in the Minors. A switch-hitter, he has good bat speed, makes consistent contact and demonstrates good plate discipline as well as a knowledge of the strike zone. He's equally productive from both sides of the plate, a notion supported by his .286 and .270 averages last season as a right- and left-handed hitter, respectively. His uptick in the power department in 2017 was a major development, though he'll likely always offer more pop to the gaps than true over-the-fence thump. And while he may not be a burner, Taylor does have average speed and earns praise for his baserunning ability. Taylor is best suited for left field defensively on account of his below-average arm strength, though he does have experience at all three outfield positions. That versatility, along with his late-blooming bat, could help him carve out a role as fifth outfielder at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez had a mid-80s fastball when he first became eligible to sign out of Venezuela in 2008, and it took him an additional two years to add enough velocity to entice the Rangers to give him a pro contract. He spent his first two pro seasons and part of a third in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League, then blew out his elbow just when he was starting to gain some momentum in 2015. After missing all of 2016 while recovering from Tommy John surgery, he was spectacular last year, retiring 45 consecutive batters at one point in high Class A before jumping from Double-A to Texas in August. Strictly a reliever, Rodriguez works primarily with a four-seam fastball in the mid-90s and a solid slider in the mid-80s. While he was in the big leagues, his slider wasn't as sharp as it had been in the Minors. He'll occasionally use a low-80s curveball to give hitters a look at something with a little less power. Rodriguez has a clean delivery that has allowed him to fill the strike zone since he entered pro ball. It lacks deception, however, and he'll try to compensate by altering his leg kick or using a slide step. He opened 2018 on the big league disabled list with an elbow injury, but returned to the mound in May.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Since his high school days, Seymour has intrigued with some raw tools, particularly his speed. It's why the Marlins drafted him in the seventh round of the 2014 Draft and signed the Bahamian-born hitter out of Miami-area high school powerhouse American Heritage for an above-pick value bonus of $400,000. It's why the Braves acquired him late in the 2016 season in the Hunter Cervenka trade. Seymour's speed is still very much his carrying tool, and it's top of the scale. He can flat-out fly, though he's still learning to use his speed effectively on the basepaths to be an efficient threat to steal and in the outfield. He is capable of making contact from both sides of the plate, albeit without power, but his approach has not improved over time. Seymour needs to cut down his strikeouts and get on base more frequently so he can use that plus tool to greater effect and allow the run-producers to do their job. A shortstop initially, Seymour has moved to the outfield full-time and is capable of manning all three spots, with a strong arm from his infield days. He'll continue to do that while focusing on his development as a table-setting type of speedster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 40th-round pick of the Giants in 2014, Mahan passed on launching his pro career in favor of attending Kentucky. He made strides in each of his three seasons there and was one of the top performers in the Southeastern Conference as a junior, showing improved hitting ability and power as well as second-base defense. Mahan's breakout campaign in college baseball's best league stood out in a thin crop of college hitters, and the Marlins were thrilled to find him still on the board in the third round. Mahan has a nice left-handed swing, shows good feel for the barrel and drives the ball across the entire field. After totaling six homers across his first two collegiate seasons, Mahan added some loft to his stroke and finally tapped into his raw power in 2017 to finish with 41 extra-base hits, including a team-high 15 home runs. An above-average runner, he moves well once underway but doesn't figure to be a stolen-base threat. Defensively, Mahan has looked comfortable at second base after previously struggling as a shortstop. He profiles as a passable defender there, one who can also play the outfield corners as well as first base. However, any future moves down the defensive spectrum will come with increased offensive demands.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted out of Drury University (Springfield, Mo.), Richards spent two years pitching for the Gateway Grizzlies in the independent Frontier League before inking a deal with the Marlins in July 2016. He's since climbed quickly through the Minors, opening his first full professional campaign with Class A Advanced Jupiter, where he was a Florida State League All-Star, and reaching Double-A roughly a year after signing. He finished his first full professional season with 2.53 ERA and 158 strikeouts in 146 innings, earning Miami's Minor League pitcher of the year award. Richards may pitch with a tick below average velocity, usually sitting 90-92 mph, but his fastball plays up because he creates a good downhill angle to the plate with a deceptive delivery and locates it well. His changeup is above average, features good velocity separation and is effective against hitters on both sides of the plate. A fringy curveball gives Richards a third pitch that club officials say improved in his first full season. Richards gets the most out of his three-pitch mix because he's a consistent strike-thrower who has feel for changing speeds and keeping hitters off balance. And while his stuff may not be overpowering, it hasn't stopped the right-hander from piling up his share of whiffs early in his pro career. He profiles as a back-of-the-rotation starter or a long reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The move to Double-A is often the ultimate test for a prospect, with the general thinking being that if someone can succeed at that level, he can compete in the big leagues. If that's the case, Oswalt should be a big league starter soon after the 2012 seventh-round pick moved to the Eastern League in ERA and promptly led it in ERA and finished in the top 10 in a host of other pitching categories. While the San Diego native took a while to get going, making it to full-season ball in his fourth season, he's moved progressively since, using a solid four-pitch mix to get outs. Oswalt will throw his fastball in the 90-95 mph range and uses his 6-foot-5 frame well, throwing downhill and getting some sink on his heater to get groundball outs. His best pitch is his above-average curve, which has good depth and 12-to-6 shape to it, and he'll mix in a slider and a changeup to keep hitters guessing. Oswalt made a nice adjustment in getting his delivery more in line -- he had been cutting himself off -- and that has led to more consistent quality strikes. Oswalt's ceiling is somewhat limited to that of a back-end starter, but he's very close to reaching that and impacting a big league rotation. The Mets added him to the 40-man roster this offseason as a result.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brodey was a two-way prospect in high school, one some teams liked as a left-handed pitcher, who both pitched and hit in his first year at Stanford. He then focused on being an outfielder and while his junior season wasn't quite as strong as his All-Star turn in the Cape Cod League the summer prior, the Mets still saw enough to take him in the third round of the 2017 Draft and sign him for a slightly below pick value bonus of $500,000. He struggled in his first full season of pro ball, though he did finish with double digits in home runs and stolen bases. While Brodey doesn't possess any plus tools, he can do a number of things well. He had improved his approach and drew more walks during his junior season and showed some feel to hit along with decent strike zone awareness during his pro debut, though that regressed in 2018. He has good bat speed and considerable raw power to tap into, so the more he can work counts the better he will be at reaching that power. While he profiles more as a tweener, Brodey has mostly manned center field as a pro and has impressed the Mets with solid instincts and an average arm. He's likely not a full-time center fielder going forward, but knowing he can handle the position could serve him well as a future fourth outfielder. For him to be an everyday left fielder, he'll have to maximize his hit and power tools from the left side of the plate.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rhame's college career in Oklahoma didn't start so well as a freshman, but he got straightened out with a move to Grayson Junior College. A starter there, he was selected by the Dodgers in the sixth round of the 2013 Draft and his arm strength was immediately moved to the bullpen. He pitched all year in Triple-A in 2017, then was dealt to the Mets in last August's Curtis Granderson deal and he made his big league debut for New York in September. Rhame has, and always will be, primarily about his fastball. It will sit 95-96 mph with plus riding life and he can reach back for upper-90s heat on occasion. That's his go-to pitch, but while his secondary stuff is fringy, at best, he does have two other offerings he uses. His slider will show glimpses of being a sharp breaking ball, but it's been inconsistent. His changeup is below-average, but it has shown improvement. He's generally been around the strike zone throughout his career. It's hard to define a future Major League role for a one-pitch reliever, even if it's a really good pitch. Continued development of his secondary stuff to help keep big league hitters from sitting on his fastball, certainly would help.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: During a breakout performance in his first taste of full-season ball with the Nationals, Mills faced Lakewood, the Phillies' affiliate in the South Atlantic League, four times. He didn't give up a run until his third time around and overall finished with a 1.64 ERA and 28 strikeouts in 22 total innings. It's no wonder, then, the Phillies were glad to add him to their side in late July courtesy of the Howie Kendrick trade. His time in the Phillies' system was ultimately short-lived, however, as Mills was dealt to Miami for Justin Bour in August. Following the trade, the Marlins promoted him to Double-A. Mills has three solid weapons that he is just starting to figure out how to use regularly, not reaching full-season ball until his fourth summer as a pro, but finishing first in the Nats organization in wins and third in strikeouts despite not being there for the season's final month. He has a low-90s fastball with good life to it, an above-average curve and good feel for an average changeup, all coming from a fast arm and deceptive delivery. His improved ability to repeat his delivery greatly impacted his command and control. Mills has shown an ability to set up hitters really well, keeping them guessing and letting his mix of stuff play up more as a result. He has the ceiling of a back-end starter, but there could be more in the tank to unlock.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals have been aggressive with Rodriguez since signing him in January 2012, believing that the ultra-projectable right-hander's performance would eventually catch up to his raw stuff. That finally occurred in 2017, as Rodriguez was in the midst of his best professional campaign and first in the Class A Advanced Carolina League when was he was hit with an 80-game ban in May after testing positive for a performance-enhancing substance. Luckily for the Nationals, Rodriguez's long layoff has had little impact on his performance in 2018. After pitching well early on in Double-A, Rodriguez made the jump directly to the Major Leagues in early June and logged 4 2/3 scoreless frames in long relief in his big league debut. A tall and physical righty with an electric arm, Rodriguez boasts an effortless plus-fastball that touches 97 mph and sits 93-95 with angle and sink. His above-average curveball is a hammer, standing out for its power as well as the late downer action that helps him miss bats. Better control should enable Rodriguez to generate even more whiffs, though he currently struggles to repeat his delivery and arm action. Rodriguez's PED suspension certainly hurt his progress, but the Nationals were still excited by the progress he had made up to that point. Throwing more strikes and developing a serviceable changeup would do wonders for Rodriguez's chances of starting games. A late-inning bullpen role is more realistic, as it would allow Rodriguez's electric fastball-curveball pairing to play up in shorter bursts.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic in 2010, Suero rewarded the Nationals for their patience with a breakout performance in his eighth professional season. Making 54 appearances between Double-A Harrisburg and Triple-A Syracuse, Suero recorded 20 saves, 10 at each level, while pitching to a 1.76 ERA and .209 opponents' average. It netted him honors as the Nationals' Minor League Pitcher of the Year, and they added him to the 40-man roster during the offseason. A raw thrower with little feel for the zone early in his career, Suero has since learned to harness and refine his stuff. He works with a 92-94 mph fastball that has natural cutting action and he locates to both sides of the plate, though it can get flat at times. He complements his heater with an above-average curveball and changeup that he made strides with in 2017. Suero's command leaves something to be desired even though his control has improved in each full-season campaign. The Nationals love Suero's fearlessness on the mound and cite him gaining confidence as a key to his recent progress. While the stuff might not be good enough for him to close games in the big leagues, Suero, with his strong track record against right-handed hitters, should have no trouble carving out a late-inning role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of Washington's 2014-15 international class, Alastre has impressed the club with the quick progress he's made early in his career. After a rocky U.S. debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, Alastre was overmatched with an Opening Day assignment to Class A Short-Season Auburn in 2017. The right-hander fared much better back in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, where he showed improved feel for his promising stuff. Young and projectable, Alastre uses his height to leverage the baseball to the plate, working in the low-90s with his fastball and pairing it with an above-average curveball that features 12-to-6, downer shape. Club officials expect Alastre to add more velocity as he grows into his lean and athletic frame. The Nationals speak highly of Alastre's cerebral approach to pitching and expect his control and command to both improve as he gains experience and develops physically. He's poised to make gains on that front in 2018, in his age-20 season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of the Cubs' 2013 international spending spree, Moreno has posted one of the system's best ground-ball rates since signing for $650,000 out of Colombia. But he also has had a difficult time remaining on the mound, blowing out his elbow and requiring Tommy John surgery after five pro games. He dazzled with a 1.88 ERA and 55/9 K/BB ratio in the lower levels of the system in his first full season back in 2016, but a sore shoulder limited him to 14 starts and diminished his performance in low Class A last year. When he's fully healthy, Moreno can generate groundout after groundout with the power sink and the downhill plane on his 92-96 mph fastball. His secondary pitches are more works in progress but show potential. He has feel for his changeup and while his curveball can get slurvy, he's doing better with it after also trying a slider. Moreno's health history and the effort in his delivery lead to questions about his ability to remain a starter. His walk rate more than tripled from 1.3 per nine innings in 2016 to 4.4 last year, which also doesn't help his cause. He needs innings to refine his repertoire and control, and missing the first two months of 2018 with more soreness means that he has yet to prove he can hold up over a full pro season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For the second time in six Drafts, scouts flocked to see a left-hander at Mundelein (Ill.) High. Ryan Borucki landed late third-round money ($426,000) from the Blue Jays after dropping to the 15th round in 2012 because he needed Tommy John surgery. Murphy, the top prospect in the state of Illinois last spring, received a slightly larger bonus ($500,000) as the Brewers' fourth-round pick. Murphy usually operates at 88-91 mph and tops out at 93 with his fastball. He commands it well, generates some armside run and should have an above-average heater once his 6-foot-4 frame adds muscle. He does a good job of selling his fading changeup, which shows signs of becoming a plus pitch. Murphy exhibits much more feel for his changeup than his slurvy breaking ball. It's more of a soft curveball at this point, and he may be better off working with a harder slider in the future. More strong than athletic, he repeats his delivery and is expected to have at least average control once he's fully developed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A third round pick out of Fresno State in 2014, Luplow, a former college outfield mate of the Yankees' Aaron Judge, had put in a pair of solid, but relatively nondescript full seasons in the lower levels of the Pirates system over his first two full years of pro ball. He surprised many when he moved to Double-A in 2017 and hit his way first to Triple-A and then to the big leagues, leading the organization in home runs and finishing second in batting average along the way. Luplow had always shown glimpses of power, but took a big step forward in turning his extra-base ability into over-the-fence pop in 2017. He can drive the ball to all fields and his continued improvements in terms of pitch recognition and plate discipline have made him a better all-around hitter. He'll have to trust that approach and his bat-to-ball skills to hit more consistently at the big league level. While he tried to play third for a season in 2015, he has settled into the outfield corners, where he has shown he is a capable defender. Luplow still looks like a fourth outfielder type when all is said and done. But he's ready for that role now and given that he's exceeded expectations in many ways, he could hit his way into more at-bats in Pittsburgh.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A supplemental first-round pick back in 2011, Crick was once the Giants' top prospect, a power right-hander with frontline starter potential. A few years later, he appeared on the brink of being another promising prospect lost to control problems when a full-time move to the bullpen sent him in the right direction in 2017. He made his big league debut with the Giants and then was sent to the Pirates in the offseason as part of the Andrew McCutchen trade. Crick still has the premium fastball that made him such a big prospect in the first place, sitting 94-97 mph and flirting with triple digits on occasion, especially in the shorter relief outings. He mixes in a heavy two-seamer with good sink and an above-average slider with excellent bite. He'll even mix in an occasional changeup. While he'll never be a command and control guy, he found the strike zone much more consistently with the move to the bullpen, with a career low 4.0 walks per nine in Triple-A in 2017. As long as Crick can continue to throw strikes with his fastball-slider combination like he did a year ago, he's ready for a full-time gig in Pittsburgh's big league bullpen. After seeming lost, a potential career as a setup man is within reach.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Sherriff has definitely defied the odds. The left-hander started out as a 28th-round Draft pick back in 2011 out of Glendale Community College. Devoloped initially as a starter, he moved to the bullpen in 2014 and started putting up numbers at the upper levels without much fanfare, earning Pacific Coast League All-Star honors in 2016 and '17. Ignored in the Rule 5 Draft, Sherriff finally got added to the roster and called up to the big leagues for the first time in August of last year. He landed on the disabled list in April with a broken toe, but did make it up to St. Louis twice before seeing his season end with Tommy John surgery in May. When Sherriff received his first callup to the big leagues, he largely did what he was supposed to do, keeping left-handed hitters to a .080 batting average over 25 at-bats. That should come as no surprise, given he'd kept lefties to averages under .200 in Triple-A the last two seasons. Sherriff comes at hitters with a funky arm angle that brings in fastballs up to 93-94 mph and thrown with a ton of sink that gets a lot of ground-ball outs. He complements that with a very good slider, which when coming from his lower arm slot, is death to lefties. This has the chance to be one of those outstanding player development stories of perseverance once he returns to health. As long as he keeps throwing his fastball-slider combination for strikes, and he has for most of his career, there's no reason to believe he can't be a big league reliever for many years to come.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After a strong junior season at Maryland that earned him Big Ten Pitcher of the Year honors in 2017, Shaffer entered pro ball as the D-backs' sixth-round pick with a reputation of being a good strike-thrower. Going out and walking just one batter in 24 innings in his pro debut certainly augmented his standing as a right-hander with plus control. Shaffer is going to have to command the baseball well in order to succeed with his largely average stuff. He will touch 94 mph with his fastball on occasion, but it's the sink to it coming from his 6-foot-5 frame that makes it play up and get ground ball outs. His slider is currently his best pitch, a breaking ball that is an above-average offering. His changeup is fringy, but improving, as it'ss a pitch he didn't throw much in college, but was a focal point during instructs. Throwing strikes obviously comes easily to Shaffer. Now he needs to learn how to consistently throw quality strikes, how to game plan and set up hitters. That will be key for him to reach his potential as a back-of-the-rotation starter, something that could happen fairly quickly given his advanced control and feel for pitching.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Ramos jumped on the radar a bit in 2016 after scuffling during his U.S. debut the prior summer, finishing among the Pioneer League leaders in several offensive categories. He hit well in a step up to the Northwest League in 2017, albeit with less power, earning a promotion to the full-season Midwest League. Ramos has plus-plus raw power from the right side of the plate, but aside from the outburst with Missoula, it hasn't shown up in games consistently just yet. He was a better overall hitter in 2017, with fewer strikeouts, and the D-backs love the mechanics of his swing. The next step is for him to learn how to control his effort throughout his swing and be able to find that balance between being a solid hitter and tapping into that power. A below-average runner, Ramos is a fringy defender at third, though he does have a very strong arm. He's an average defender at first. Ramos will continue to see time at both infield corners moving forward, as much to make sure his bat is in the lineup as anything else. It's easy to dream of him fitting the infield corner profile from a run production standpoint, but it's going to take time for him to get there.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: McCullough spent two years relieving for the University of North Carolina, but when he was dismissed from the school for a violation of team rules, he moved to Division II Lander and started there before landing in the fifth round of the 2014 Draft. Putting that adversity behind him, McCullough has been extremely hard to hit as a pro, though he has struggled to consistently find the strike zone. Left unprotected in the Rule 5 Draft last December, McCullough wasn't selected largely because of those command issues. There is absolutely no question about whether his pure stuff can get people out, as evidenced by his career 11.8 K/9 rate and .188 batting average against (14.1 and .158 in 2017 across two levels). His fastball is at least plus, typically in the upper 90s. Hitters don't see his slider and he misses a ton of bats with it. Coming off his best year as a pro, McCullough just needs to keep working on commanding his stuff more consistently. He never has to even have average control given how hard to hit he is. If he can find the strike zone semi-consistently, his fastball-slider combination is good enough to get big leaguers out.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed as a catcher out of Venezuela by the Angels in 2007, Diaz took a while to find success. He hit .157 in two seasons before moving to the mound, then didn't post a sub-5.00 ERA in full-season ball until 2014, when he rose from high Class A to Anaheim before going to the Rockies in a December deal for Josh Rutledge. He appeared to solidify his big league standing when he recorded a 2.37 ERA in 21 appearances with Colorado in 2015, but missed all of 2016 following Tommy John surgery and only briefly surfaced in the Majors last year. Diaz reclaimed his power stuff in 2017. His heavy fastball sits at 96-98 mph and can reach triple digits, eliciting a lot of swings and misses as well as weak ground balls. He gets similar results with his upper-80s slider, which can be nasty with late bite. Diaz does a better job of throwing strikes than he did while struggling early in his career, but he still has lapses where he overthrows. His command still needs more fine-tuning because his pair of power pitches get harder than they should. He might be a setup man if he can do a better job of locating his fastball and slider.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rogers led Spartanburg Methodist (S.C.) to consecutive third-place finishes at the Junior College World Series before signing with the Rockies as a fourth-round pick in 2014. After posting the worst offensive numbers of his career when he got to the Class A Advanced level in 2016, he put up his best when he returned to that level last year, batting .319/.377/.488 with a Minor League-leading 70 steals. He's the premier basestealer in the Minors, swiping 166 bases in his three full pro seasons while succeeding at an 87 percent clip. Rogers wreaks havoc on the bases with his plus-plus speed. It also helps him cover ground in center field, though he played more in left field last season in deference to Yonathan Daza in Lancaster. His quickness also helps him compensate for a below-average arm by getting to balls quickly. Playing in Lancaster, perhaps the best hitting environment in the Minors, helped fuel Rogers' breakout as he batted .356/.418/.589 at home. The right-handed hitter also made a concerted effort to get stronger and hit the ball with more authority, and it showed. He won't ever be a power threat, so he needs to continue to enhance his plate discipline so he can get on base and run wild more often.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2018 Rockies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouts saw plenty of Abreu when they were scouting Albert Almora (the sixth overall pick in the 2012 Draft) at Mater Academy Charter High (Hialeah Gardens, Fla.), and he had the tools to go in the top five rounds the following year. After he turned down the Reds as a 14th-rounder, he never quite put up big numbers in three years at Miami, though he did help the Hurricanes reach a pair of College World Series. A sixth-round selection in 2016, he hit 14 homers and stole 40 bases in low Class A during his first full pro season. Abreu's bat speed, strength and leverage create well above-average raw power from the left side of the plate, but he's not going to get to use all of it unless he improves as a hitter. He's overly aggressive, which leads to swing-and-misses and a lot of weak contact on pitches he'd be better off avoiding rather than putting in play. Whether he can make adjustments and provide more consistent pop remains to be seen. Abreu moves well for a 6-foot-4, 225-pounder but his 40 steals are as much a product of his instincts than his average speed.
