Gordon's father Tom, a former All-Star closer, became his legal guardian at that time, and he's since played an integral role in the young left-hander's development on the mound. The Indians selected Hillman in the second round of the 2015 Draft, making him the fourth Olympia product in as many years to be drafted within the top 60 picks. While the results haven't been there to begin his career, Hillman has made strides with Class A Lake County in 2017 as the season has progressed. Much like his senior year, Hillman sat 89-92 mph with his fastball but wore down physically as the season progressed, pitching more in the upper 80s late in the year. His changeup continues to be his best secondary pitch and has a chance to be above average once developed, while his curveball, which has good shape and depth, projects as at least an average offering. Hillman's quick arm and clean mechanics make him a natural strike thrower, though he'll need to pitch down in the zone more consistently to be effective at higher levels. Hillman's lean, athletic frame leaves room for physical projection, and he'll need to add considerable strength, as well as improve his durability, to stick as a starter. He may not have a high ceiling like some of the Tribe's other young arms, but Hillman has all the ingredients to become a dependable back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 30 | Run: 50 | Arm: 60 | Field: 60 | Overall: 45 In many other organizations, Machado would be preparing to take over as the everyday shortstop, a defensive wizard who has improved enough physically and with the bat to be a big league regular. With the Major League personnel in place in Detroit, however, Machado's role is more up in the air. There is no question Machado could play shortstop in the big leagues, and he's been called upon to do so in short stints over the past couple of seasons. He has terrific hands and more than enough range and arm to play the premium position long-term. He can seamlessly move over to the right side of the infield and play an outstanding defensive second base if needed. While his glove will always be ahead of his bat, he's added enough strength and refine his approach enough where he's no longer an automatic out. There's no power to speak of, but his line-drive approach does have some results. He runs well enough to steal some bases as well. With Jose Iglesias at short and Ian Kinsler at second, Machado's ticket to the big leagues will have to be as a utility guy for the time being. But the Tigers would feel more than comfortable having him step in on either side of second base full-time should the need arise.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The younger brother of former Royal and longtime utility infielder Emilio Bonifacio, Jorge signed for $135,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2009. He hit more for average than power early in his pro career, then swung for the fences and struggled to make quality contact while in Double-A in 2014 and 2015. He finally found a happy medium in 2016, when he set full-season bests with 19 homers and an .812 OPS in Triple-A. Scouts are split on whether Bonifacio has the bat to profile as a regular on an outfield corner. Those who believe in him think that now that he has toned down what had been a pull-happy approach, he has enough bat speed, strength and hitting ability to bat .270 with as many as 20 homers per year. Others question how well his right-handed swing will play against big league pitchers and think he might not produce enough power. Bonifacio has lost some speed as he has matured physically, but he's not a baseclogger and has decent range. His best pure tool is his strong arm, which helped him finish second in the Pacific Coast League with 17 outfield assists last year. He needs to play more under control, however, after leading PCL outfielders with eight errors.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the most fundamentally sound shortstops available during the 2014-15 international signing period, Sierra landed a $1 million bonus out of Venezuela. He made his U.S. debut midway through his first pro season, then homered eight times in the first two weeks of the Rookie-level Appalachian League schedule last summer. He got too power-conscious afterward and tailed off, particularly after making the jump to the Short Season New York-Penn League, where he was the circuit's youngest regular at age 18. Sierra has started to mature physically and has gotten significantly stronger since turning pro, though he projects more as a 15-homer guy than the slugger he looked like last summer. That's still plenty of power for a legitimate shortstop, and he needs to realize he's at his best when he focuses on hitting line drives to all fields. He'll always be an aggressive hitter but will need to make more contact at higher levels. Though he has just average speed, Sierra covers more than enough ground at shortstop because he has keen instincts and a quick first step. A reliable defender with soft hands and an accurate arm, he also has seen action at second base. A utility role could be a fallback, but he has the tools to profile as an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 The Brewers drafted Haniger with the No. 38 overall pick out of Cal Poly in 2012, targeting his natural hitting ability and strong tools. But injuries delayed his progress up ladder, and the Brewers dealt him to Arizona in the Gerardo Parra trade in July 2014. Haniger blossomed in the D-backs' system and reached the big leagues for the first time in 2016 en route to the organization's Minor League Player of the Year Award. However, his time in the desert came to an end in November, when he was traded to the Mariners as part of the deal for Taijuan Walker and Ketel Marte. Haniger generates hard contact to all fields from the right side of the plate through a combination of physical strength, plus bat speed and a sound swing. He tapped into his above-average raw power more consistently last season, setting a career high with 30 home runs between the Minor and Major Leagues after adding a more pronounced leg kick to his swing. He has a good approach, recognizes pitches well and isn't afraid to take a walk. Haniger's athleticism and average speed make him a capable defender at all three outfield positions, and he has the plus arm strength needed for right field at the highest level. Although he has the floor of a productive fourth outfielder, there are many who believe that Haniger's newfound power will thrust him into an everyday role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 45 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 Ibanez was the youngest player (age 19) on Cuba's 2013 World Baseball Classic squad and one of the best young hitters in the island's top league before he defected in 2014. Signed for $1.6 million in July 2015, he made his pro debut in 2016 after a two-year layoff and hit his way to Double-A. The Rangers continued to accelerate his development by sending him to the Arizona Fall League in the offseason. A bat-first infielder, Ibanez has a compact right-handed stroke that produces line drive after line drive. He doesn't try to do too much, focusing on using the middle of the field while controlling the strike zone. He has a knack for barreling the ball but most of his power comes to gaps in the form of doubles rather than home runs. While Ibanez won the Cuban equivalent of a Gold Glove as an 18-year-old in 2011, he has fringy speed and average arm strength. He's a decent defender at second base and also has seen action at third base, though he doesn't have the power to profile at the hot corner. Stuck behind a logjam of middle infielders in Texas, he has drawn comparisons to Howie Kendrick.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic in 2011, Garcia was doing exactly what organizations want to see from pitching prospects: Getting better with age and more experience as he moved up the ladder. After having no problems handling the Florida State League in 2016 and finishing things off with a playoff win in Double-A Reading, he was set to start the year back in Reading, but an 80-game suspension levied at the start of the 2017 season for a performance-enhancing drug put some of that progress in question. Garcia is more or less a three-pitch guy who relies on mixing his pitches well, though he has seen an uptick in the velocity of his fastball. He was up to 95 mph consistently at the end of last summer. He can spin a good curveball and he'll even mix in an occasional slider. His changeup looks like it could give him another Major League average pitch. Garcia's secondary pitches have improved enough that it keeps hitters honest and allows him to get swings and misses on his fastball. Garcia exudes confidence on the mound and stays around the strike zone. His mix is better than any one of his pitches, and he was looking like a future mid-rotation starter, though he'll have to prove himself all over again following his suspension.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals selected Glover in the eighth round of the 2015 Draft out of Oklahoma State on the heels of a dominant junior campaign. He made his big league debut a little more than a year later, earning a callup after excelling at three Minor League levels, and quickly emerged as a key bullpen piece for the Nationals before wearing down in September. A physically imposing right-hander with a power arm, Glover has all the ingredients needed to become a late-inning force. He sits in the mid-to-upper 90s with his fastball and can dial it up to triple digits, while his plus slider, thrown with power at 88-90 mph, is an out pitch capable of missing bats. He also employs a changeup and a curveball, but both lag well behind his other two other offerings and will never be a major part of his arsenal. Glover is a fierce competitor with excellent mound presence, and the Nationals love how he pounds the zone and fearlessly attacks opposing hitters. That mentality, along with the high-octane stuff, could help Glover develop into a big league closer.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Born in New York but raised in the Dominican Republic, Rosario turned pro in 2008 and spent most of his first four years in Rookie ball. He didn't make it to full-season ball to stay until 2014, then missed the following season after Tommy John surgery. He came back better than ever in 2016, rising from high Class A to Triple-A after re-signing with the organization as a Minor League free agent and claiming a spot on the 40-man roster in November. Rosario isn't very physical but has a very quick arm, and he's throwing harder than ever since having his elbow reconstructed. He sits at 96-98 mph and can reach back for 100 and keeps his heater down in the strike zone, generating lots of swings and misses as well as groundouts. His breaking ball has curveball depth and slider power, consistently arriving in the mid 80s. Rosario can flash an average changeup from his days as a starter, though the Cubs made him a full-time reliever last year and will keep him in the bullpen. He has some effort in his delivery, so it's unlikely he'd maintain the same kind of stuff in the rotation. He also lacks the necessary control and command, though he did a better job of throwing strikes in 2016.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: This is Hanson's sixth year on the Pirates' list, ranking as high as No. 3 when his tools and up-the-middle potential landed him in the Top 100 overall list. Those days seem like the ancient past as Hanson is out of options and trying to stick in the big leagues as a super-utility type. Hanson still has some considerable offensive skills. He's hit for average and with some extra-base pop, looking like the type who not only would hit a dozen homers annually, but would also stretch doubles into triples with his speed. The speed plays on the basepaths, as he finished second in the organization in stolen bases in 2016. He hasn't always maintained his approach at the plate or completely embraced a role of being that on-base table-setting type. Initially a shortstop, Hanson played more second base than anywhere else the last two years. He saw time at third and the outfield as well to try to add to his potential versatility. Now it's up to Hanson to own his new identity. His effort level hasn't always been present at all times, but the stakes are higher now that he is out of options. Even after all this time, he's still just 24 years old.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Alvarez jumped onto the prospect radar with a breakout move to full-season ball in 2016 that saw him lead the organization with his .323 average and 36 stolen bases, though he took a step backward in '17, struggling with a move to Double-A before hitting the disabled list with a sprained ankle in May. He had returned and finished the season on a stronger note when he was sent to the Phillies in return for Juan Nicasio. Alvarez had hit for a high average every year since repeating the Gulf Coast League in 2014, using a short, level swing from the left side of the plate to make consistent, hard contact, though his approach did not serve him well initially with the double-jump to the Texas League. He has the chance to grow into more power, but he might be more of a line-drive, doubles-type hitter because of his approach. Alvarez is an above-average runner with excellent instincts that allow him to be a threat on the bases. He has a very strong arm, but he needs to work on his footwork and hands to be a more effective defender at second. The Cardinals added Alvarez to the 40-man roster last offseason, thinking he might be their future second baseman. Now with the Phils, he's blocked by the likes of Scott Kingery, but he has plenty of time to show what he can do in his new organization.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Red Sox for $60,000 in 2013 after they drafted him in the 11th round out of NCAA Division II Nova Southeastern, Asuaje topped the Class A South Atlantic League in slugging (.542) and OPS (.933) in his first full pro season. That success did not translate to Double-A the next year, and the Red Sox traded him, along with Manuel Margot, Javier Guerra and Logan Allen, to the Padres during the offseason in exchange for Craig Kimbrel. Asuaje would get back on track in his first year with the Padres, however, as he was selected to the SiriusXM All-Star Futures Game at PetCo Park, claimed the Pacific Coast League's Rookie of the Year award and made his big league debut in September. Asuaje stands out for his pure hitting ability from the left side. He produces line drives from line to line thanks to a combination of hand-eye coordination and advanced bat-to-ball skills, and he possesses more pop than his size suggests, with the potential to achieve double-digit home runs. Despite being an average runner with good instincts, Asuaje is limited to second base defensively on account of his fringy arm strength and range. To go along with his primary work at the keystone, Asuaje has also seen time at third base and left field. If he's unable to take over at second base in San Diego, Asuaje's bat could help him carve out a utility role in the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed by the Angels out of Venezuela in 2011, Rondon spent three years in Rookie ball before making the jump to the Class A Advanced level for his full-season debut in '14. The Padres acquired him at the Trade Deadline in a prospect package for Huston Street, and Rondon advanced to Double-A the next year, only to have his campaign cut short due to fractured right elbow. Fully healthy in 2016, Rondon was named a Texas League Mid-Season All-Star en route to his Major League debut in late July. Rondon stands out for his floor more than his ceiling, as he's a well-rounded player who projects to have three average-or-better tools. A right-handed hitter, he makes consistent contact, albeit with minimal power, with a flat path through the zone and barrel control that allows him to spray the ball from line to line. While he doesn't strike out much, Rondon can be aggressive to a fault at times and needs to develop more selectivity and learn to work counts in his favor. Rondon's above-average speed shows at shortstop, and he has the necessary range, footwork and arm strength to remain there long term. But despite having all of the defensive tools to be a big league shortstop, he will need to unlock his offensive potential to become an impactful regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Blach's ability to fill the strike zone and pile up innings made him a fifth-round pick in 2012, and he has continued to display those traits in pro ball. He led the Triple-A Pacific Coast League in innings in each of the last two years (165 1/3 in 2015, 162 2/3 in 2016) as well as with 14 victories in 2016. Called up in September, he beat Clayton Kershaw with eight shutout innings on Oct. 1 to clinch at least a Wild Card tie for the Giants. Blach's already impressive pitchability got even better when he repeated the hitter-friendly PCL, and his stuff ticked up a little as well. His fastball now sits at 90-92 mph with sink on his two-seamer and cutting action on his four-seamer, and his curveball got a little sharper. His solid changeup remains his best offering, and his slider gives him a second fringy breaking pitch. With his fairly ordinary stuff, Blach has to do the little things to win -- and he does. He keeps the ball down in the strike zone to generate groundouts and avoid homers, controls the running game, fields his position well and hits better than most pitchers. He lacks a high ceiling but could be an effective innings-eater at the back of a rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After Okert breezed through his first three years as a pro and dominated in the Arizona Fall League after the 2014 season, he seemed poised to help the Giants. Instead he spent all of 2015 getting knocked around in Triple-A while having trouble maintaining his arm slot. He got back on track last year and had three stints in San Francisco, where he posted a 3.21 ERA in 16 appearances. Okert beats up left-handers by throwing fastballs and sliders with a low arm angle and a crossfire delivery. His heater sits at 91-94 and can reach 97 mph but takes a back seat to his sharp slider, a true plus pitch. While the Giants see him as more than just a specialist, he's still looking for a pitch that can truly neutralize righties, and his cutter has replaced his changeup as his best option. Though Okert won't ever have pinpoint control, he cut his walk rate to 2.2 per nine innings in 2016 after averaging 3.6 previously. If he continues to throw strikes, he should serve as San Francisco's No. 2 bullpen lefty this year. If he can reclaim the little bit of velocity he has lost in the last couple of years, he could develop into a set-up man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With a fastball that hit 96 mph and a wipeout slider, Stratton earned Southeastern Conference pitcher of the year honors and worked his way into the first round in 2012. He rarely has shown the same stuff since signing for $1.85 million, however, lowering his ceiling from No. 2 starter to back-of-the-rotation option. He made his big league debut last May as a middle reliever. Stratton has a trio of average pitches and must mix them well to succeed. His fastball sits at 90-92 mph and touches 95 with a bit of sink, his short slider arrives at 82-85 mph and his changeup improved last season. His fringy curveball grades as his worst pitch, yet it was his most effective during his short time in San Francisco. Though he doesn't have the stuff that made him a first-rounder, Stratton compensates by moving his pitches around the strike zone. He has become more willing to challenge hitters and posted the best walk rate (2.9 per nine innings) of his career in 2016. He'll be on call in Triple-A again this season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Holder went to Grossmont (Calif.) JC with the intention of playing both baseball and basketball before deciding to focus on the diamond. That decision paid off as he blossomed into a 2015 first-round pick after a year at Grossmont and two at San Diego. Known primarily for his defense, he raised his OPS from .527 in his pro debut to .669 in his first full season. The athleticism that made Holder a star as a shooting guard in high school also makes him arguably the best defensive player in the Minor Leagues. The best shortstop to come out of college baseball in years, he displays outstanding actions, quickness, range, hands and footwork. He has solid arm strength and is as consistent in the field as he is brilliant. While Holder likely will bat at the bottom of a batting order, he encouraged the Yankees with the changes he was able to implement with low Class A Charleston hitting coach Greg Colbrunn in 2016. He improved his load and took better swings from the left side of the plate. He has ordinary bat speed, however, and rarely drives the ball or draws walks.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-way star at Florida who drew pro interest with his left-handed power potential, Johnson became a full-time pitcher after signing for $1,575,000 as the 31st overall choice in the 2012 Draft. He cruised through the Minors with a 2.32 ERA in his first four pro seasons and made his big league debut in July 2015, but little has gone right for him since. He was shut down shortly afterward with nerve irritation in his elbow amid a downturn in his stuff, which regressed further in 2016, when he missed six weeks to deal with anxiety issues. In 2014, Johnson had a plus curveball, an 88-94 mph fastball with life and premium command and a solid sinking changeup. Last year, his curve wasn't as sharp, his heater ranged from 86-90 mph and his changeup wasn't as deceptive. He also throws a cutter, though its main purpose is just to give batters a different look. Johnson regained his feel for pitching when he returned to Triple-A last July. He can add and subtract from his pitches and locate them down in the strike zone, so he doesn't have to overpower hitters to success. Boston hopes that having a full offseason of work for the first time in three years will help him reclaim his former stuff and upside as a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The White Sox drafted Martin as a sidearming reliever out of Texas A&M in the 35th round in 2012, but he turned them down and then raised his arm angle to high three-quarters and hit 95 mph as a starter in a college summer circuit. When he struggled in the Aggies rotation as a senior the following spring, he returned to a low slot and the bullpen before signing for $10,000 as a ninth-rounder. The Red Sox had him use the higher angle again and deployed him as a reliever, and he made his big league debut in July after averaging more than a strikeout per inning at each of the three highest levels in the system. Atypical for a reliever, Martin features a changeup as his best pitch. Despite their platoon advantage, lefties find him harder to hit because he has such good feel for his circle changeup with fade. He sets it up with a 91-95 mph sinker and uses his 6-foot-7 frame and arm slot to create downhill plane on his heater. Still working to come up with a breaking ball, Martin has a mostly ineffective slider/cutter. He throws strikes but his command isn't as sharp as his control, so he can be hittable at times. Those limitations restrict his ceiling to seventh-inning reliever as opposed to a higher-leverage role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though he was eligible for the Draft every year from 2011-14, Taylor went unpicked each time. Yet he soared to Double-A in less than a year after turning pro in 2015 as a $10,000 senior sign out of South Alabama. After averaging 13.1 strikeouts per nine innings in two years, he recorded a 10.2 whiff rate in his first two seasons as a pro. Taylor misses bats without lighting up radar guns. His four-seam fastball has respectable velocity, sitting in the low 90s and topping out at 95, but hitters don't catch up to it because it has a high spin rate that gives it riding life and creates the illusion that it rises through the strike zone. He changes eye levels by pairing his heater with a changeup that tumbles at the plate. Taylor also uses a short slider to keep hitters off balance. He commands his fastball well and throws strikes with all of his offerings. He made Boston's Opening Day roster in 2017 and has shuttled between Fenway Park and Triple-A throughout the season.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 45 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 60 | Overall: 45 Ynoa's feel for pitching was on full display during his full-season debut in 2013 for the Mets, when he was pitcher of the year in the South Atlantic League after going 15-4 with a 2.72 ERA and 16 walks in more than 135 innings. He's made steady progress since then, albeit with lesser results, reaching Double-A in 2015 and then advancing to Triple-A in last season en route to his big league debut in August. The Orioles acquired Ynoa in February in exchange for cash considerations. Ynoa has long been among the best control artists in the Minor Leagues and entered his first season with the Orioles sporting a career 1.5 BB/9 ratio in more than 795 innings. It helps his average stuff play up, as he'll mix his two- and four-seam fastballs -- the latter registering in the low-90s -- with a pair of breaking balls and a changeup. While he knows how to change speeds and will throw all of his pitches at any point in the count, Ynoa's tendency to nibble at the corners rather than attack hitters has led to harder contact and fewer strikeouts as he's climbed the ladder, while a lack of a put-away pitch makes him particularly vulnerable versus left-handed hitters. After being passed in the Mets' system by the likes of Noah Syndergaard, Jacob deGrom, Steven Matz and Robert Gsellman, Ynoa has been used in a long-relief role with the Orioles. He'll need to improve his breaking pitches and figure out how to neutralize lefties to be an effective starter in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic in October 2010, Tavarez made a slow but steady climb through Boston's system before breaking out in 2016, when he finished second in the Eastern League batting race with a .335 average at Double-A Portland. Impressed by his development, the Orioles selected Tavarez in the Major League phase of the Rule 5 Draft in December. Though undersized and lacking in terms of physical projection, Tavarez is an excellent athlete who has long stood out for his above-average speed and ability to play both outfield corners. He has good bat speed and a short stroke from the left side of the plate, with an approach that has continued to improve as he's climbed the ladder. And while he doesn't offer much in the way of over-the-fence pop, Tavarez's combination of gap power and speed yields plenty of extra-base hits. With his solid collection of tools, Tavarez shows the makings of becoming a fourth outfielder at the highest level, a role that the Orioles hope he can fill for them in 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodriguez has done nothing but impress the Rays since signing for $600,000 out of Venezuela in 2012. His loud tools were on display last year in the Class A Midwest League, where Rodriguez showed improve hitting ability and power while dazzling with his defense behind the plate. He boosted his stock even more during the offseason in the Australian Baseball League, hitting a robust .442/.494/.753 with six home runs in 19 games for the Brisbane Bandits. Rodriguez shows the makings of an impact defensive catcher. His athleticism and agility translate to strong blocking skills, and evaluators raved about his progress as a receiver and framer in 2016. His plus arm strength enabled him to throw out a whopping 56 percent of attempted basestealers in his full-season debut, highlighting his ability to control the running game. Rodriguez requires more work offensively and will need to simplify his swing, but there's enough juice in his right-handed bat to forecast at least average power at maturity. While the Rays are working to develop several young catchers, it can be argued that Rodriguez has the highest ceiling of the group. His electric defense should at least lead to a career as a backup in the Major Leagues, but it will be up to Rodriguez's bat to unlock his everyday potential.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Undrafted out of the Arkansas prep ranks, Wood spent a year at Howard (Texas) JC before going to the Rays in the 29th round of the 2013 Draft. Though he was initially developed as a reliever, Wood made a smooth transition to starting in 2015 and the continued to impress in the role during the Arizona Fall League. He built on that success last season in the Florida State League before moving up to Double-A Montgomery in late May. A broken thumb suffered on a comebacker cost him a month at the level, but, overall, Wood fared well during his time in the Southern League. Though he's an undersized right-hander, Wood's lightning-quick arm generates a fastball that sits 92-95 mph and reaches 97 mph, and he does a good job of locating it to both sides of the plate. He supports his heater with a sharp curveball that has late, 12-to-6 biting action that helps him miss bats. He'll also mix in a decent cutter as well a changeup that could serve as a third average-or-better offering for him with improved feel. Wood's four-pitch mix, track record of being difficult to barrel while missing bats and solid control profile highlight his upside as a starter, but concerns about his durability and a lack of a true third pitch may ultimately force him back into a bullpen role. Should that happen, Wood has the stuff to emerge as an effective setup man for the Rays in the coming years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Harris comes from strong baseball bloodlines, as his father, also named Greg Harris, pitched parts of the 15 seasons in the Major Leagues. The Dodgers drafted him in the 17th round out of the California prep ranks in 2013, and Harris impressed the following year by making a successful jump to Class A Great Lakes for his first full season. Acquired by the Rays that offseason in the Joel Peralta trade, the right-hander made strides last year back at Class A Advanced Charlotte to earn a late-season spot start in Triple-A. Harris saw his velocity tick up in 2016, sitting at 92-95 mph with his running fastball while reaching 97-98, and it made his above-average changeup all the more effective. He also showed better feel for his upper-80s cutter and curveball, with scouts preferring the former to the latter. But while his stuff has improved, Harris remains inconsistent as a strike-thrower because he struggles to repeat his delivery and locate his fastball. Harris' progress as a starter has the Rays encouraged about his prospects of sticking in that role, but there are many evaluators who believe the right-hander will wind up in the bullpen on account of his two above-average-or-better pitches.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: One of the best athletes and biggest enigmas in the 2013 Draft, Engel dropped to the 19th round after batting .265 with two homers in three seasons at Louisville. Since signing for $100,000, he has been one of the best athletes and biggest enigmas in the system. He looked like he might have started to figure things out when he won MVP honors in the Arizona Fall League and led the developmental circuit in all three slash stats at .403/.536/.642 in 2015, but he encored by batting .259/.344/.406 at the top three levels of the White Sox system. After showing a smoother right-handed swing and better rhythm in the AFL, Engel had a busier stroke and worse timing last season. He's equipped with bat speed and strength, he doesn't tap into his raw power because he strikes out too much and hits too many balls on the ground. A top-of-the-scale runner, he's a prolific and success basestealer who would be more of a weapon if he could get on base more often. Now 25 and entering his fifth pro season, Engel is running out of time to show he can produce enough offense to be an everyday player. At the very least, he has the tools to become a speed-and-defense fourth outfielder. He has the speed to chase down balls in both gaps from center field and enough arm strength to handle any of the three outfield spots.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Before the bonus-pool system came into play, the White Sox usually adhered to slot recommendations from the Commissioner's Office. Since the new rules began in 2013, they've picked their spots to spend more lavishly, such as when they paid Michalczewski $500,000 as a seventh-rounder that June. He handled a series of aggressive assignments well until posting career-worst .226/.314/.363 numbers last year in Double-A, where at 21 he was three years younger than the typical position player in the Southern League. A switch-hitter, he has a better swing and is more productive from right side. His bat speed, strength and loft in his stroke creates above-average raw power that he doesn't get to consistently because his swing can get loopy. He'll have to prove he can make enough quality contact against good pitching to become a big league regular. A good athlete for his size, Michalczewski hauled in a 66-yard touchdown pass as a tight end to help win the Oklahoma 6-A football championship game in 2012. A high school shortstop, he has below-average speed but has worked to develop range to both sides at the hot corner. He has a solid arm and led Southern League third basemen with a .951 fielding percentage last year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After the White Sox charged Marco Paddy with rebuilding their international program following a bonus-skimming scandal, his first six-figure signing was Martinez for $250,000 out of Venezuela in December 2011. He hurt his elbow shortly after turning pro and had Tommy John surgery that delayed his pro debut until 2014. He led the low Class A South Atlantic League in 2015 but sliced his ERA from 5.38 to 3.81 and finished third with 141 strikeouts in 137 innings when he returned there last year. As a tall, lanky right-hander with a loose arm, Martinez elicited comparisons to former All-Star Ramon Martinez (no relation) when he signed. His low-90s fastball tops out at 95 mph, with the sink and angle on his heater creating swings and misses as well as groundouts. While his secondary pitches lack consistency, his slider displays some bite and he improved the arm speed on his fading changeup last year Martinez still is learning to repeat his delivery and command his pitches. He did a better job in the second half of 2016, when he recorded a 2.79 ERA and limited opponents to a .202 average in his final 14 starts. If he can build on that progress, he could factor into the back of Chicago's rotation in a couple of years.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Though Peter reached 96 mph with his fastball as a two-way player at Creighton, his elbow often bothered him after he pitched and he preferred playing every day. A White Sox seventh-rounder in 2014, he reached Triple-A midway through his second full season and batted .291/.351/.506 there in the second half of 2017. The Dodgers acquired him in January as part of a six-player, three-team deal that also brought them Scott Alexander from the Royals. In a White Sox system with a lot of high-risk/high-reward bats, Peter stood out for his ability to make consistent line-drive contact at the plate. He did adjust his approach last season, hitting a career-best 13 homers but also striking out a career-high 124 times. He can use his average speed to swipe an occasional base. The versatile Peter has played every position except for pitcher and catcher as a pro. He's fundamentally sound and possesses solid arm strength, though his elbow sometimes bothers him when he has to make longer throws. He profiles best at second base and is most likely to serve as a utility man in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: May is on the verge of giving his family its third big leaguer, following his grandfather Lee and great-uncle Carlos, both of whom were All-Stars. Jacob's tools are similar to those of his father Lee Jr., a 1986 Mets first-round choice who reached Triple-A. May advanced to that level in 2016 but had a rough year while battling an oblique injury. Though the White Sox had hopes that May would develop into a starting center fielder, he now looks like more of a fourth outfielder because he has done little damage against upper-level pitching. A switch-hitter whose game centers around his double-plus speed, he focuses on contact over power and hit just five homers in his first full three seasons after going deep eight times in 66 games during his 2013 pro debut. His plate discipline has deteriorated as he has risen through the Minors, with his on-base percentage sinking to a career-low .309 last year. May does provide some usefulness with his baserunning and basestealing ability and his center-field defense. He has improved his reads and routes since turning pro, making himself into a solid defender. His below-average arm is playable in center.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A freshman set-up man on Kent State's 2012 College World Series team, Clark became the Golden Flashes' closer as a sophomore and a weekend starter as a junior. He has enjoyed success in the rotation as well as the bullpen in pro ball, though he pitched exclusively in relief last year. He's almost impossible to go deep against, having surrendered one homer in 151 1/3 college innings and two in 194 frames through three pro seasons. Clark sits in the low 90s and tops out at 95 mph with his fastball, which features heavy sink and nifty downhill plane. He consistently gets groundouts and also has averaged nearly a strikeout per inning by pairing his sinker with a solid slider. He has improved his changeup, but it's still a fringy offering and he doesn't use it as much in a bullpen role. Clark struggled with his control in 2015 but found the strike zone again last year, halving his walk rate from 3.8 to 1.9 per nine innings. Though he showed some upside as a potential No. 4 starter, the White Sox seem committed to making him a reliever. He gets outs against both left-handers and right-handers, so he can be more than just a specialist.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Mejia has quickly made a name for himself with his elite, 80-grade speed since signing out of the Dominican Republic in 2013. He stole 72 bases in his pro debut and followed it up with 40 steals in his U.S. debut, and then finished second in the New York-Penn League last season with 29, also hitting .322 and earning All-Star honors. Unsurprisingly, Mejia's game is built on his outstanding speed. The switch-hitter makes consistent contact from both sides of the plate, with an approach that's geared towards hitting the ball on the ground and getting on base. Once there, Mejia has proven successful 78 percent of the time, while accruing 140 steals in his first three seasons. Mejia's impressive wheels also translate in center field, where he shows the makings of becoming a plus defender with exceptional range. Mejia has a high ceiling as a potential top-of-the-order hitter who can stick in center. That said, his elite speed alone could make him a big league contributor in some capacity, even if it's just as a pinch-runner or a late-inning defensive replacement.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Indians went well above slot to secure Armstrong, signing him for $325,000 as an 18th-round pick in 2011. A reliever from the outset of his pro career, he made a steady climb through the Minors en route to his big league debut in August 2015. The right-hander dominated at Triple-A Columbus last season, earning All-Star honors in the International League, and he fared well across 10 stints in the Major Leagues. Armstrong has ideal stuff for a late-inning bullpen role. His fastball typically sits between 93-96 mph but has been up to 98. His slider has fastball velocity at 89-92 mph, thrown with tight spin and late, short slicing action that helps him miss bats, and he'll mix in a curveball sparingly to give hitters a different look. The right-hander has some crossfire to his delivery, which gives him natural deception but also hinders his control. Control and command issues aside, Armstrong's knack for generating whiffs with his fastball-slider pairing highlights his late-inning potential in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 45 | Power: 45 | Run: 60 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 For years, Jones has been known as a toolsy, yet raw, player, from his high school days through his career at LSU and even during his pro career. The Tigers liked his upside enough to acquire him from the Pirates in 2015 for Joakim Soria, then saw him miss 50 games in 2016 for a positive \"drug of abuse\" test. The season ended on a much better note, with his big league debut and a strong showing in the Arizona Fall League. After largely playing shortstop with the Pirates and initially some third with the Tigers, it looks like Jones has found a home in center field, where his athleticism really plays well. While he still needs more reps -- that was the main focus for him in the AFL -- it's looking like he could be an above-average defender out there. He has a strong arm and runs well, covering a lot of ground and showing the ability to steal bases. There is no question he has power, both the gaps and over the fence, but there's long been an issue with his strikeout rate and his inability to draw walks. Jones is just about ready to impact the big league club on a regular basis. How much he can refine his approach will go a long way towards defining his future role, with a ceiling of a Mike Cameron-type regular in center field.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 70 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 After a stellar career at Vanderbilt that included closing out the school's 2014 College World Series championship, Ravenelle's pro success after the Tigers took him in the fourth round of the 2014 Draft was initially interrupted by injury. However, pitching across two levels in 2016, reaching Double-A, and throwing in the Arizona Fall League for a second straight season could have him on the path to helping the big league bullpen soon. Ravenelle can hit triple digits with his fastball on a regular basis, but that's not where he's at his best. He tends to give hitters a very good view of his arm slot when he's throwing that hard, leading to him being hit more than he should. When he's sitting 95-96 mph, his fastball has a lot of sink and he'll miss bats and get ground-ball outs. He complements the fastball with a slider that can be nasty at times. He can get too rotational when he overthrows and will then fly out of the strike zone. Command has been an issue for him, even as he climbed to Double-A in 2016. Ravenelle simply has to learn to trust his stuff to have long-term success. Once he realizes he doesn't have to throw 100 mph all the time to get hitters out, his power arsenal should be more than enough to succeed against big league hitters late in ballgames.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: While Ziomek hadn't moved as quickly as some might have expected as a lefty out of Vanderbilt with a good feel for pitching, he was making slow and steady progress up the organizational ladder. Some shoulder discomfort combined with tingling in his fingers in 2016 were tell-tale signs something wasn't right and it turned out he had thoracic outlet syndrome and had surgery last June to try and address it. When healthy -- and reports were that he was and heading in the right direction for 2017 -- Ziomek combines pitchability with solid stuff across the board. He does a nice job commanding his sinking fastball down in the zone, getting groundball outs. His curve, while inconsistent, showed signs of being a very good breaking ball and his changeup was above-average at times. He'd mix in his slider against left-handed hitters mostly. There are have been some marquee names -- most recently Matt Harvey - to be diagnosed with TOS, and the jury is still out about recovery success. If Ziiomek can return to health -- the Tigers will have to play a wait and see game as he gets back out there -- he does have some weapons to work with.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Catchers who show they can catch have the chance to play the game for a long time. On the player development side, patience will always be exhibited to let a backstop's offensive game catch up to his defense, knowing it can take a while. Perez is living proof, moving very slowly in the early stages of his career. Perez's catch and throw skills will always be his calling card. He has a plus arm that shuts down the running game. He has good feet and moves well as he continue to work on blocking and other parts of his receiving. Perez swung the bat better than he had previously in 2016 as he worked to improve his overall approach. That didn't extend to 2017 and he'll need to keep improving his pitch recognition as he advances. There's no real power right now, but he's strong and shows the ability to drive the ball. Perez's defense should be able to carry him up the ladder. He doesn't have to hit much to be a serviceable backup, but the Tigers aren't giving up hope the bat will develop enough for him to be glove-first regular.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After his junior season at Tennessee, it seemed Simcox wanted to return for his senior year. The Tigers, who took him in the 14th round, went way above the $100,000 pick value to sign him for $600,000 and keep him from doing so. Paired with college teammate -- and first-rounder -- Christin Stewart, Simcox helped West Michigan win the Midwest League title in his first summer then moved up to Lakeland with Stewart in 2016. Simcox will have to play catch-up now, as Stewart got promoted to Double-A last season. Unlike his teammate, Simcox does not have one plus carrying tool. He does have excellent contact skills, with a line-drive approach. He'll have to use all fields to be successful as there's not much power there and upping his on-base skills would be a good idea -- he expanded out of the strike zone too much in 2016. Simcox is a solid defender who can stay at short despite having just average speed. He has good footwork, and his angles to the ball have improved. Simcox will reunite with Stewart in 2017. For him to keep up, some added strength would help along with a more refined approach at the plate to show he can perhaps be an everyday player.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals spent $14 million on bonuses in the 2011 Draft, the last one unaffected by bonus-pool limitations, and shelled out $675,000 to land Junis in the 29th round. Because he signed late that summer and spent two years in different Rookie leagues, he didn't reach full-season ball until 2014. Since then, he has improved steadily and developed into one of Kansas City's most reliable starting pitching prospects. As he has added strength and polished his delivery, Junis has gone from sitting in the high 80s with his sinker to operating at 92-94 mph and topping out at 96. His curveball also has added some power and developed into a solid second offering. His changeup lacks consistency but does feature some fade and sink and might become an average third pitch. As a high schooler, Junis averaged 19 points per game in basketball as a senior and displayed intriguing power potential as a third baseman. That athleticism enables him to repeat his delivery with ease, and he has repeatedly pounded the strike zone in pro ball. He was more aggressive and added more plane to his pitches in 2016, enhancing his chances of becoming a mid-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Arguably the best pitcher available in the 2012 Draft, Zimmer rarely has been healthy since signing for $3 million as the No. 5 overall pick. The Royals expected him to reach the big leagues within two years, but elbow, biceps, lat and shoulder injuries restricted him to 222 1/3 innings in his first five pro seasons. He worked just 5 2/3 in 2016 before undergoing thoracic outlet surgery that left Kansas City guardedly optimistic about his future. Before he got hurt, Zimmer could showcase frontline-starter stuff with a 92-97 mph fastball that reached triple digits, a hammer curveball and flashes of a solid slider and changeup. In 2017, he has pitched more at 91-94 mph with his heater and his breaking pitches have yet to regain their former power as well. He opened the year as a starter but came down with shoulder soreness after three outings, and he headed to the bullpen after spending another two months on the disabled list. Originally recruited by the University of San Francisco as a third baseman, Zimmer is a fine athlete who has no trouble repeating his mechanics and delivering strikes. If he has to remain a reliever, he could offer closer upside if he regains his former stuff. His younger brother Bradley was also a first-round pick (2014, Indians) and made his big league debut in 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Royals had two first-round picks in 2015 and spent them both on Indianapolis prep right-handers, Ashe Russell at No. 21 and Watson at No. 33. Signed for $1,825,200, Watson looked so good in his first Spring Training that Kansas City thought he'd have no trouble handling an assignment to low Class A at age 19 in 2016. Hitters have lit him up the last two seasons instead -- although he's still faring better than Russell, who suddenly lost the ability to throw strikes in 2016 and took a leave of absence from baseball this June. Watson still can show the arm strength that helped make him a first-rounder, ranging from 91-95 mph with life on his fastball. Though he showed the potential for a plus slider in high school, it has regressed since the Royals had him curtail its use to focus on his other secondary pitches. He has an average curveball and some feel for a comparable changeup. Watson has had trouble missing bats and has lost some confidence. His high three-quarters arm slot wavers at times, costing him life and command and leaving him vulnerable to walks and home runs. His struggles this year have been compounded by shoulder issues that sidelined him for nearly two months.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Davila impressed scouts with his polish on the showcase circuit during the summer of 2014, but his mid-80s fastballs detracted from his Draft stock. He added about 5 mph while allowing just one earned run in 64 1/3 innings as a senior the next spring, leading the Royals to pay him a well-over-slot $746,000 bonus in the fourth round. They had Davila focus on getting stronger and delayed his pro debut until '16, when he finished second in the Rookie-level Appalachian League in wins (seven) and third in ERA (2.77). Davila has gained 10 pounds since signing and now works with an 87-91 mph fastball that features late sink. He isn't afraid to work inside against right-handers, setting up a fading changeup that has become his most reliable secondary pitch. He has feel for spinning a curveball, though his needs more power to go with its depth. Though he's an advanced pitcher for his age, Davila lacks physicality and got knocked around by low Class A hitters in his introduction to full-season ball in 2017. Once he matures physically, he could have a solid three-pitch repertoire and control and command to match. Kansas City will manage his innings carefully while he continues to add strength.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Duenez was Kansas City's top international amateur signing in 2012, when his hitting ability merited a $425,000 bonus. A third baseman in Venezuela, he moved to first base as a pro and batted .273 with just two home runs in his first three seasons. Duenez broke out in 2016 by hitting .284 with 13 homers and 100 RBIs between three levels, and he slammed three more homers in the Double-A Texas League playoffs. Duenez incorporated more leverage in his left-handed swing during instructional league in 2015, and it paid off with more power last year. He's still much more hitter than slugger, focusing on making contact with a compact stroke and using the entire field. Duenez may not quite fit the power profile at first base, but he could deliver 15 homers per season if he continues to improve his pitch selection. More athletic than most first basemen, Duenez has fringy speed and won't be a big league basestealer, but he managed to parlay his instincts into 26 steals in 30 attempts in 2016. He gets the job done and has some arm strength at first base, though he still must improve his defensive consistency. Duenez moves and throws well enough that he has seen action in left field in the past.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Joining the Twins following the 2015 season, Palka had a strong first season in the organization, especially in the power department. He led the system in both home runs and RBIs while reaching Triple-A, and his left-handed power bat is just about ready to help out in Minnesota, thought that was delayed because of a fractured finger in 2017. Palka has the chance to be a solid overall hitter, but he gives up at-bats too often because he tries to sell out for power too frequently. That leads to high strikeout totals and the inability to string consistent at-bats together. He is always a threat thanks to his well above-average power and plus bat speed, with the ability to turn around any fastball. The Georgia Tech product played right field almost exclusively in 2016 and while he doesn't have great speed, he's fine in the outfield corner and has the skills to play first base as well. As a power-only guy, Palka could profile well on the long end of a platoon at first, right field and DH. If he can elevate his hit skills with better on-base ability, he could become a power-first everyday player. He'll need to find more consistency in his at-bats to succeed in Minnesota, but he's on the verge of getting the chance.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 40 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 60 | Overall: 45 Relievers with low arm slots who don't necessarily light up radar guns can often be underrated and underappreciated. That might be the case for Hildenberger, who has proven to be very difficult to hit wherever he's been and slung his way up to the big leagues in 2017. Outside of a minor forearm issue that shut him down in August, Hildenberger tore through two levels of the Minors in 2016 and finished with an ERA under 1.00. He has enough fastball to be successful, in the low 90s, and he throws it with a ton of sink to be a ground-ball machine. He also can go to a more high-3/4 slot for move velocity when he needs to. He mixes in a good changeup and a slider as well and is an extreme strike-thrower, with a K/BB ratio of over 9.00 in his career. He might not blow you away with stuff, but he can really pitch and has plus mound presence to spare. He's the type who will keep sneaking up on people until he's an established, and very effective, big league setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 When the Twins signed Wells out of Australia in Nov. 2014, he was a scrawny 5-foot-8 lefty who tipped the scales at about 165 pounds. The southpaw with an excellent feel for pitching is now 5-foot-11 and around 180 pounds, and that physical maturity has translated to his performance on the mound, though he spent time on the disabled list in 2017 with a forearm strain. Held back in Extended Spring Training until last June to monitor his workload, Wells' strong performance at age 19 in the Midwest League was one of the pleasant surprises in the Twins' system and enabled him to jump up to the Florida State League in 2017. He has average stuff across the board, starting with a fastball that now sits 90-91 mph. His changeup is a tick above average and his breaking ball should give him a third Major League average offering. All of it plays up because of his outstanding command and an understanding of how to mix his pitches to keep hitters off-balance. Wells isn't going to blow anyone away with his stuff, but there are plenty of lefties in the big leagues who fit a similar profile. Just 20 for all of 2017, his feel for pitching could let him move a little more quickly, with the end result being a back-end starter at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Maxwell led NCAA Division III with 15 homers and a .918 slugging percentage in 2012, when the Athletics made him the highest-drafted D-III player in nearly a decade by taking him 62nd overall. Maxwell struggled to match that level of production early in his pro career, but finally turned the corner last season in Triple-A en route to his big league debut in July and a solid 33-game showing with the A's. It took parts of six seasons for Maxwell to tap into his raw power, but he finally did it in 2016, hitting 11 home runs between Triple-A and the Majors after totaling just 14 during the previous five years. He continues to demonstrate an advanced approach and works deep counts, with a focus on driving the ball from gap to gap from the left side of the plate. He has made significant strides defensively in the Minor Leagues, especially with his blocking and framing, while his strong arm enabled him to post a career-high 39 percent caught-stealing rate in Triple-A. Maxwell proved a more than capable backup in 2016, and he stands to serve a similar role for the A's moving forward.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Brugman and Jacob Hannemann comprised two-thirds of a talented Brighman Young outfield in 2013. While Hannemann was a higher Draft pick that June, going to the Cubs in the third round, it's been Brugman who's had the better career since signing as a 17th-rounder. He continued to climb the ladder in 2016, ranking second in the A's farm system in hits (155), extra-base hits (tied, 52) and total bases (238) while reaching Triple-A for the first time. After being added to the A's 40-man roster last November, Brugman began his 2017 season back in the Pacific Coast League before moving up to Major Leagues in June. Brugman is a mature left-handed hitter who has a knack for staying inside the ball and using the entire field. His surprising raw power shows to his pull side and has produced double-digit home runs in two of the past three years, although it's unlikely to translate to anything more than below-average pop at the highest level. Brugman isn't much of a basestealer despite having average speed, but it does give him sufficient range in center field, and he logged a career-high 103 games there in 2016 while continuing to see time at both outfield corners. Brugman's left-handed bat and his ability to play all three outfield positions is his greatest strength, and the combination gives him the potential to serve as a fourth outfielder in the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: An eighth-round pick out of Furman who got just $12,000 to sign, Smith has already exceeded expectations by pitching all year in Triple-A in 2016. He might have beat projections even further with big league innings, but a mild flexor strain at the end of the season may have derailed hopes for a September callup, and his 2017 season was derailed with a shoulder injury that kept him out for an extended period. On the surface, Smith struggled a bit in his first full season in the Pacific Coast League, a circuit less than pitcher-friendly. But the Angels were pleased overall with his progress, and the southpaw did post both a higher strikeout rate and lower walk rate than he did the year prior. Smith has success largely with average stuff across the board. His fastball will touch 90-91 mph, but it plays up because of his command and his ability to mix in his secondary pitches effectively. His changeup is his best, his one above-average pitch that serves as his top out pitch. His slider has improved and is now his better breaking ball, but he'll still mix in a big, loopy curve as well. Smith does have a limited ceiling because of his lack of plus stuff, but he's just about ready to reach it. He could fill a spot in the back end of the rotation or as a long reliever, if needed.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A two-sport star in junior college, Middleton, a former shooting guard, struggled as a starting pitcher in the Angels system ever since joining it out of the 2013 Draft. The Angels finally pulled the plug and moved him to the bullpen in 2016 and it all clicked faster than anyone could have imagined, with Middleton pitching across three levels, finishing the year in Triple-A. Whenever a pitcher shortens up into a relief role, the hope is he'll pick up a few ticks in velocity. That happened, and then some, for Middleton, who now sports a heater thrown consistently in the 95-99 mph range with plus plus life. His slider also improved and is now an above-average out pitch as well. While his changeup is below-average, it can serve as a weapon against left-handed hitters. His command improved dramatically as well, thanks to some mechanical changes to his delivery and a better understanding of that it takes to fill the role of a short reliever. The Angels give Middleton a ton of credit for buying into the move as he both physically and mentally matures on the mound. He has the right mentality for the bullpen and the swing and miss stuff to pitch meaningful innings late in games.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels know all the history Meyer brings with him, from the injuries to his inability to find the strike zone consistently. They were nonetheless thrilled to get add his arm strength to the system when they acquired him from the Twins for Hector Santiago at the non-waiver Trade Deadline last July. Meyer still has the huge stuff that made him a first-round pick out of Kentucky back in 2011, but he's yet to consistently harness it. He has plus velocity and a high spin rate on his fastball, cranking it up to the upper-90s with extreme ride and sink. His hard breaking ball can miss a ton of bats and his changeup continues to be viable weapon. Over the years, Meyer has struggled with walks and the missed development time because of injuries -- he threw just 64 1/3 innings in 2016 because of shoulder issues -- hasn't helped. The Twins tried him in relief, with some moderate success, but the Angels see him as a starter and he did throw more strikes during his time in their Minor League system. After an offseason working with their staff, the Angels feel, at age 27, Meyer might just be ready to put it together in a big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It hasn't been an easy path for Campos, both in terms of being injured and changing teams. Traded from the Mariners to the Yankees in January 2012, he missed the 2014 season after needing Tommy John surgery. He finally got comfortable in 2016, pitching his way up to Triple-A before he was traded to the D-Backs in the Tyler Clippard deal. He made his big league debut then fractured his right ulnar, leading to Arizona waiving him. The Angels, always on the lookout for pitching depth, took a chance and claimed him. Injuries have followed him to Los Angeles, as a nerve issue in his forearm shelved him in April followed by surgery to remove a bone spur from his elbow in June. The stuff is legit when healthy, with a plus fastball in the mid-90s that has outstanding action to it, thrown with good deception and extension. He can miss bats with both his curve and changeup, both of which are at least Major League average. He throws strikes with all three offerings. After pitching for five minor league teams and briefly for one big league team in 2016, Campos simply needs to stay away from the disabled list. He'll try to make a fresh start in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mariners Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 35 | Run: 55 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 The younger brother of former big leaguer Mat Gamel, Ben signed for $500,000 as a 10th-round pick in 2010 and showed promise in the lower Minors before stalling in Double-A in 2013-14. He got back on track in Triple-A the following year, garnering All-Star honors as well as the circuit's Rookie of the Year Award. Gamel made his big league debut with the Yankees last May but spent most of year back in Triple-A, where he was named International League MVP. In August, the Yankees traded Gamel to the Mariners for right-handed prospects Jio Orozco and Juan De Paula. Gamel started to hit upper-level pitching with more authority once he stopped worrying about hitting for power and focusing on what he does best, using his quick left-handed bat to spray line drives from line to line. He worked with Yankees Minor League hitting coordinator James Rowson to improve his load at the plate and hit a career-best 10 homers in 2015, matching his career total from his first five pro seasons. Gamel has played right field primarily in the big leagues but profiles better in center, where his speed, quickness and instincts translate to above-average defense. He has enough arm strength to play anywhere in the outfield, making him an ideal fourth outfielder.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 40 | Run: 70 | Arm: 40 | Field: 60 | Overall: 45 One of the fastest players in the 2015 Draft, Jenkins hailed from the same West Columbus High (Cerro Gordo, N.C.) program that spawned speedsters Otis and Donell Nixon. Signed for an above-slot $2 million as a second-round choice, Jenkins led the low Class A South Atlantic League and ranked third in the Minors with 51 steals in his first full pro season. But he also scuffled at the plate, hitting .220/.277/.327 with a strikeout rate of 28 percent. Jenkins obviously needs to do a better job of using his well above-average speed at the plate by making more contact. Amateur scouts liked his feel for hitting and he makes an effort to utilize the entire field, but he struggles to handle offspeed pitches. He has some deceptive pull power and could reach double figures in home runs once he makes some adjustments to his approach. Jenkins does a good job of using his quickness. He succeeded on 81 percent of his steal attempts in his first two pro seasons and covers a lot of ground in center field. His arm is below average but isn't a liability.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 55 | Run: 45 | Arm: 70 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 Beras controversially signed with the Rangers for $4.5 million in February 2012 after submitting an older birthdate than he had previously, a move some teams believe was designed to circumvent upcoming bonus restrictions in a new Collective Bargaining Agreement. When MLB couldn't determine his true birthdate, it allowed the deal to stand but suspended him until July 2013. Though his bat has been slow to develop, he started to realize some of his considerable power potential with a career-high 22 homers in Class A Advanced last year. Beras has two well above-average tools in his raw power and his arm, with some evaluators putting top-of-the-scale 80 grades on his arm. He has impressive bat speed and his 6-foot-6 frame gives him terrific leverage, but his long arms also mean he has a long right-handed swing. He has yet to display much consistency at the plate because his aggressive, pull-happy approach has resulted in a 28 percent strikeout rate through his first four seasons. Though Beras moves well for a big man, he has below-average speed that limits his effectiveness on the bases and in the outfield corners. He has a lot of work to do defensively, as his jumps, routes and throwing accuracy all need improvement. Most of his value will come from his bat, and Texas hopes his eight homers last August are a sign that he's about to take off.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Miffed when Coastal Carolina rescinded its scholarship offer when he had a lackluster junior season and subsequent summer, Enright worked to get stronger and improve his mental approach. He led West Orange High (Winter Garden) to its first Florida class 9-A semifinal appearance and boosted himself into the third round of the Draft in 2016. Signed for an over-slot $675,000, he finished sixth in the Rookie-level Arizona League batting race (.313). A switch-hitter who makes line-drive contact from both sides, Enright has a mature approach and doesn't try to do too much at the plate. He doubled 13 times in his 42-game pro debut and could have average or better power once he adds needed muscle to his 6-foot-1 frame. He's an average runner with good instincts but won't steal many bases. Enright has a strong arm spent the majority of his first pro summer at third base while also getting time at shortstop and second base. He focused on second base during instructional league and will see most of his action there in 2017. He projects as an average defender at second and potentially as a solid glove at the hot corner, and he also has the tools to man the outfield corners.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 40 | Power: 50 | Run: 45 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 A Las Vegas high school contemporary of Kris Bryant and Bryce Harper, Robinson eschewed a Nebraska commitment to turn pro as a fourth-rounder in 2010. His career appeared to be stalling when he hit .190/.273/.366 in Double-A in 2014, but he rebounded to hit 41 homers in the next two seasons. The most versatile player in the Rangers system, he enhanced his value by adding center field to his résumé last summer and claimed a spot on the 40-man roster last November. A .245 hitter in his first seven pro seasons, Robinson won't ever hit for a high average because he has a long left-handed swing and strikes out too frequently. He has outstanding secondary skills, however, with his bat speed producing power and his patience allowing him to lead Texas farmhands in walks three times in the last five years. He can look helpless against left-handers but batted .271/.368/.525 against righties in 2016 and has the upside of a platoon player. Robinson plays above his average speed because he's aggressive on the bases and has good instincts on defense. He played all four infield and all three outfield positions last season and impressed with his ability to go get the ball in center field. His best position is third base and he could make for a valuable, offensive-minded utilityman.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rangers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 60 | Control: 40 | Overall: 45 The Rangers signed Dominican right-hander Angelo Leclerc in June 2010 and his younger brother Jose six months later. Angelo isn't much of a prospect and went to the Red Sox in the Triple-A phase of the 2015 Rule 5 Draft. Jose has some of the best pure stuff in the organization and reached the big leagues last July, recording a 1.80 ERA in 12 relief appearances. Leclerc's most effective pitch during his first stint in the Majors was his changeup. He has one version with unusual cutting action that hitters can't help chase out of the zone, as well as a more traditional changeup with fade that he can throw for strikes. His cut changeup plays well off his fastball, which runs from 92-98 mph with running life. Leclerc also can flash a plus curveball but has trouble locating his hard downer and didn't use it much with the Rangers. While he's fairly unhittable and misses a lot of bats, his value is limited because he never has thrown consistent strikes. He issued 13 free passes in his 15 innings with Texas and had a career walk rate of 5.1 per nine innings through six pro seasons, so it's hard to trust him in crucial late-inning situations.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Braves Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: For his first two years at Louisville, Harrington pitched largely out of the bullpen. The left-hander moved to the rotation as a junior and was named the Atlantic Coast Conference's pitcher of the year. His performance moved him into the third round where the Braves grabbed him. He pitched sparingly in his pro debut after the long college season but is ready to attack pro ball as a starter. Harrington is definitely pitchability and command over pure stuff. He'll throw his fastball in the 86- to 92-mph range. It plays up because of its sink and because he locates it so well at the bottom of the strike zone. He has a decent three-quarters breaking ball and a changeup, both of which can grade out as Major League average. There is a ton of deception to his delivery, and he pounds the zone with quality strikes, keeping hitters from squaring up his pitches. Harrington's stuff does play up a tick if he's coming out of the bullpen, but his command, deception and competitiveness all point to him having a future as a back-of-the-rotation starter. If it doesn't work, he could move very quickly as a middle reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It wasn't more than a year after the Marlins made Steckenrider their eighth-round pick in the 2012 Draft that the Tennessee product underwent Tommy John surgery, which cost him the next 18 months. A shift from the rotation to the bullpen during the 2015 season helped Steckenrider get his career back on track and he built on that success in '16, reaching Triple-A for the first time before a strong showing in the Arizona Fall League. A tall and physical right-hander, Steckenrider relies heavily on a 95-98 mph fastball that has a high spin rate, as well as late running action that helps him miss bats inside the zone. He can also generate whiffs with his slider, a hard downer thrown in the mid-80s, and mixes in the occasional changeup. However, it's his fastball-slider pairing that's led scouts to project Steckenrider as a potential late-inning asset. After his breakthrough campaign and impressive performance in the AFL, Steckenrider, now several years removed from elbow surgery, should compete for a spot in Miami's big league bullpen in 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Marlins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Named Mr. Baseball in the state of Kentucky in 2010, Riddle went on to have a solid three-year career at the University of Kentucky before going to the Marlins in the 13th round of the 2013 Draft. Since then, he's advanced through Miami's system at a steady pace, as Riddle earned postseason All-Star honors back in the Southern League in 2016 and finished the year in Triple-A. Riddle is an aggressive hitter with a short left-handed swing that helps him make consistent contact and limits his swing-and-miss. He offers little home-run power but has a knack for pounding the gaps, and he did so more consistently in 2016. Riddle isn't a basestealer despite possessing average speed, though he does receive high marks for his baserunning instincts. A second baseman in college who played mostly third base to begin his pro career, Riddle moved to shortstop full time in 2015 and impressed with his average defense and overall feel for the position. He continued to make strides at short last season, committing just six errors in 84 games, while also seeing some time at the keystone. He has the hands, range and arm strength to play anywhere on the infield, and that versatility should help him carve out a utility role in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cespedes signed for $725,000 out of the Dominican Republic on August 24, 2013, his 16th birthday, because he was too young when the international signing period began on July 2. After debuting in the Dominican Summer League in 2014, his United States debut in the Gulf Coast League the following season was rather ordinary from a production standpoint. He used his considerable tools more consistently and finished sixth in the Appalachian League in hitting in 2016. He reached full-season ball ahead of schedule in May 2017, only to land on the disabled list for six weeks shortly after joining Columbia. While working his way back from injury in late July, Cespedes was dealt to the Marlins with Merandy Gonzalez in exchange for A.J. Ramos. Cespedes has the chance to be a five-tool player. With a loose, whippy bat, Cespedes started showing that he can drive the ball, especially to the pull side. He's shown some occasional power, with more to come as he matures physically. He's played a good amount of center field thus far in his career, and while he could play there, it seems more likely that his home will be in a corner, where his above-average arm would play well -- although there might be more pressure for the power to show up. All teams look for athletes who can grow with experience, and Cespedes looks like he could be that type of player.
