He has a long way to go, but if it all clicks, he could have a future as an everyday right fielder who does everything well at the big league level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Mets Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It's the kind of story tailor-made for a Disney movie. Smoker, a former supplemental first-round pick of the Nationals, has his career derailed by injuries. He eventually pitches a year of independent ball in 2014 then gets signed off of a workout with the Mets in 2015. His velocity returned as a reliever, and he pitched his way to the big leagues in 2016. Smoker has a huge fastball that touches 98 mph and averaged over 95 mph during his time in New York last year. He likes to elevate it and blow it by hitters. The left-hander has an average slider the Mets would love to see him use more. He actually will throw both a splitter and a changeup with tumbling action, but there's been talk about paring the repertoire down, although it's hard to mess with what's worked since he joined the Mets -- he's missed a ton of bats and gotten a lot of groundball outs at all levels. Smoker did give up four home runs in just 15 1/3 big league innings a year ago, a sign that he was too amped up and left his stuff up in the zone more than usual. Given the chance to settle in, Smoker could prove to be a very valuable left-handed setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Appel was taken No. 1 overall by the Astros after a stellar senior season at Stanford, most felt that at the very least he'd make a beeline to the big leagues. After two-plus uneven seasons in Houston's system, he was sent to the Phillies as part of the Ken Giles trade. His first year with his new team was equally frustrating, as surgery to remove bone spurs from his elbow ended his season after just eight starts. Appel remains an enigmatic pitching prospect. When healthy, the pure stuff still grades out pretty well. He'll show a 70 fastball at times, but it doesn't play that way consistently because it flattens out and is too hittable. That was particularly true out of the stretch, when he would lose any angle on his fastball. He still has an solid slider and he'll flash an average changeup. The Phillies feel with his stuff he should be making hitters more uncomfortable, perhaps by using a two-seamer more and by coming inside with more frequency. The injury kept Appel from putting his best foot forward with his new organization and the hope is he can do so with a healthy 2017. He has starter's stuff, but at some point one has to wonder if the fastball-slider combination would do better coming out of the bullpen.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Phillies Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Canelo enjoyed a breakout season in 2015, hitting over .300, making the South Atlantic League All-Star team and earning a promotion while showing off his defensive chops at shortstop. A return to the Florida State League in 2016 did not go as well, leaving his prospect stock somewhat in flux. There is no question Canelo can defend. While he'll still make careless errors at times, he is built to play the premium position with plus range, outstanding hands and a strong arm. Consistency will come as he continues to mature. His plus speed should allow him to be more of a basestealing threat, another skill he'll have to refine as he moves up the ladder. Just how good a player Canelo can be depends on how his bat develops. He has the ingredients to hit, and added strength prior to the 2015 season allowed him to barrel up balls with more authority, although he regressed some in the FSL in that regard. Canelo has plenty of time to get his offensive game back on track and won't turn 23 until September. His glove should carry him up the ladder and make him a utility man at the least. If he gets his bat going, he still could become a defensive-oriented regular at shortstop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Voth ranked third in strikeouts in the Pac-12 Conference in 2013 at the University of Washington before going to the Nationals in the fifth round that June. He continued to pile up K's early in his pro career, leading the Nationals' system in strikeouts for three straight years (2014-16) while reaching Triple-A Syracuse, though a regression of both his stuff and command in '17 led to a demotion back to Double-A in July. He pitched better in his return to Syracuse early in 2018 and earned his first Major League callup in late April. Voth sits at 89-92 mph with his fastball but can run it as high as 93-94 mph. He can impart cutting action on the pitch, and his velocity plays up because he hides the ball well. Voth's slider and changeup give him a pair of Major League-caliber secondary offerings, and club officials were particularly impressed with his development of the latter during the 2016 Arizona Fall League. Pitching with above-average control and command was long viewed as one of Voth's strengths, though he now has much left to prove in that department after struggling in 2017, when he shied away from attacking hitters in the strike zone and spent much of the season nibbling at the corners so as to avoid yielding hard contact. The Nationals are optimistic that Voth will eventually right the ship, and they still view him as a potential back-end starter at the highest level.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Nationals gave Cole an above-slot bonus of $2 million as a fourth-round pick in 2010, only to ship him to the Athletics as part of the Gio Gonzalez trade after the 2011 season. He returned to Washington the following year in a three-team deal for Mike Morse and made a steady climb through the Minors en route to his big league debut in April 2015. He saw even more time in the Majors last season, logging eight starts for the Nationals. Cole sits in the low 90s with his fastball, with a clean arm action and a simple, repeatable delivery that enables him to pitch to both sides of the plate. His above-average changeup is his best secondary offering and plays nicely off his fastball, although it doesn't aid his effectiveness against left-handed hitters. He has good feel for his slider and will mix in a curveball, and club officials were pleased with his improved ability to throw both breaking balls for strikes in 2016. Cole has average control and doesn't issue many walks, but his lack of a plus pitch as well as reliance on location makes him susceptible to hard contact and limits his bat-missing potential. Cole's four-pitch mix and ability to eat innings gives him a solid floor as a back-end starter, but much like Austin Voth, Cole will need something to go his way to crack the Nationals' rotation in 2017.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed out of the Dominican Republic for $7,500 in 2014, Baez struggled in his first full season, beginning the year at Class A Hagerstown before receiving demotions to the New York-Penn and Gulf Coast Leagues. He made some strides in improving his control and missed more bats back with Hagerstown in 2016, only to regress the following year with the move up to the Class A Advanced Carolina League. Baez has big-time arm strength, usually working in the low-to-mid 90s and at times flirting with triple digits, but his velocity isn't consistent because he struggles to repeat his delivery. His curveball has the makings of an above-average pitch, one thrown in the high 70s with decent depth and shape, although his varying release point compromises the pitch's effectiveness. Baez's changeup is a work in progress, and he'll need to develop it thoroughly to remain a starter. Baez's inconsistent mechanics and lack of a third pitch make him to difficult to project as a starter long term, though, at age 22, he still has time on his side. At the worst, the right-hander's impressive arm strength and potential for two average-or-better pitches should allow him to carve out a late-inning bullpen role in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Nationals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Goodwin received a $3 million bonus as a 2011 supplemental first-rounder (No. 34 overall) and impressed in his professional debut the following year, finishing in Double-A. He wasn't able to repeat that success over the next three seasons and appeared to have stalled out in the upper Minors, but he managed to resuscitate his career in 2016 and reached the Majors for the first time in early August. Goodwin showed more of the blend of tools and polish last year that he did at the onset of his career. He has a patient approach, knows how to get on base and, at his best, uses the whole field to hit. His power also has returned, as Goodwin connected on 14 home runs last season after combining for 12 during his two previous years. He creates good bat speed and has improved against left-handed pitching, although there's still a fair amount of swing-and-miss in his game. Defensively, Goodwin's speed, arm strength and instincts make him a solid defender capable of playing all three outfield spots, which he did upon joining the Nationals. He should continue to serve as a fourth outfielder moving forward after getting his first taste of the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Young has an impeccable track record at the plate. He ranked second in NCAA Division I with 105 hits while batting .401 as a sophomore in 2013, and he hit .373 in three years at Mercer before signing for $75,000 as a 14th-rounder in 2014. He won the Class A Carolina League batting title (.321) in his first full year as a pro, ranked second in the Double-A Southern League (.303) in 2016 and batted .351 in the Dominican Winter League during the offseason. Young makes line-drive contact with ease, thanks to his fabulous hand-eye coordination, simple right-handed swing and quality approach. He uses the entire field and walks nearly as much as he strikes out. He offers little power and won't be a stolen base threat with his average speed, though he is aggressive on the bases. A third baseman in college, Young has played all four infield spots and both outfield corners as a pro. His sure hands make him a reliable defender at any spot, though his fringy arm is stretched as a shortstop and third baseman. While he's actually older than Chicago's star double-play tandem of Javy Baez and Addison Russell, Young could help the Cubs as a sweet-swinging utilityman in the near future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Pena ranked second in the Double-A Southern League in strikeouts (140) and strikeout rate (9.7 per nine innings) in 2015, yet the Cubs opted not to protect him on their 40-man roster. After he snuck through the Rule 5 Draft without getting picked, they made him a full-time reliever last year. He missed even more bats as his stuff played up in shorter stints, and he whiffed 13 in nine innings after finally making it to Chicago in his eighth pro season. Pena works primarily with a four-seam fastball and a slider. His heater parks at 93-95 mph and reaches 97, and he can throw it by hitters up in the zone. Hitters had trouble solving his low-80s slider during his brief big league stint. He doesn't use it much as a reliever, but Pena also has a decent changeup that he can throw for strikes. He could help the Cubs in middle relief this year, though he'll need to improve his command to earn a higher-leverage role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cubs Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After losing their top two picks in the 2016 Draft for signing free agents Jason Heyward and John Lackey, the Cubs focused on college arms with 16 of their first 18 selections. The best pure stuff in that group belongs to Clark, a fifth-rounder who signed for an above-slot $450,000. He had a chance to go in the first round after he worked in the mid 90s while dominating his first three starts at Duke last spring, but he pitched his way out of the rotation by midseason after his velocity and command slipped. Clark's fastball operates at 92-96 mph and can reach 99 mph, featuring nice run and sink when he doesn't overthrow. He also can overpower hitters with an 83-86 mph slider when he stays on top of it. He generates his power with a lot of effort in his delivery, however, making it difficult to maintain the velocity, quality and command of his pitches. Clark's changeup isn't as effective as his other offerings and scouts don't like his arm action, so there's a good chance he eventually winds up in the bullpen. If he can build on the consistency he showed in his brief debut, he could become a high-leverage reliever. Chicago will use him as a starter for at least the short term so he can get innings to develop.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 The move to Double-A has derailed the progress of more than one prospect over the years. There were high hopes Travieso was ready for the jump after a solid 2015 season, albeit interrupted by a broken forearm, and a strong Arizona Fall League campaign. Instead the 2012 first-rounder saw his stuff back up and he had an overall disappointing first experience in the Southern League. Travieso got away from what had worked for him in the past, which was trusting his power stuff and filling the strike zone with it. At his best, the right-hander relies largely on his four-seam fastball, which he had been able to get up to 97 mph in the past but largely had it in the low 90s in 2016, and a slider that he's been able to miss bats with in the past. His changeup has improved, but it's still behind the other two pitches. In Pensacola, Travieso's walk rate skyrocketed as he was too fine, perhaps giving the higher-level hitters too much credit. The 2017 season will be all about Travieso re-establishing who he is and going out and proving he can handle the jump. The Reds expect to see a pitcher with a chip on his shoulder, one who still has the chance to develop into a big league starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 60 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 For six years, Brice tried to find a way to harness his excellent stuff as a starting pitcher in the Marlins organization. In 2016, he moved to the bullpen, with a very positive effect, reaching the big leagues for the first time. He was one of three prospects the Reds got in January in return for Dan Straily. Brice is ready to get a full-time shot at a big league relief gig. His heavy fastball plays up in shorter stints, thrown in the low-to-mid-90s from a lower slot, and his power slider has emerged as an above-average breaking ball. He does have a changeup, though it's below-average, and while it would come in handy to keep left-handed hitters honest, it's not as essential as when he was developing as a starter. He's always been at his best when he comes right at hitters, and he found that attack mentality consistently when he changed roles. As a result, he found the strike zone with more regularity while still missing bats. Brice has the look of a future seventh-inning type reliever. His past as a starter could help him be a multi-inning guy out of the pen, but without having to worry about turning the lineup over a few times in an outing.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Reds Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Hit: 50 | Power: 35 | Run: 50 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Elizalde spent parts of four seasons playing in the Mexican League until the Reds signed him in May 2013. Since that time, the unassuming left-handed hitter has swung his way to the upper levels of the system and played on Team Mexico in the World Baseball Classic Qualifier in March 2016. Elizalde is, simply put, a professional hitter. He understands how to take an at-bat with an advanced contact-oriented approach. There aren't many moving parts to his swing, with a low maintenance setup that allows him to get to any fastball. He's a solid outfielder, mostly in right these days, and he has seen some time at first base in the past. He tends to perform well in the Mexican Winter League every year. More than likely, Elizalde profiles as an extra outfielder type at the highest level. Because his swing is so simple, he is the type who could thrive coming off the bench and being ready to swing the bat.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Brewers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Brewers signed Lara for $3.1 million in July 2014, blowing well past their designated bonus pool to land the Dominican shortstop and incurring a penalty tax in the process. So far he's stood out for his defense more than the hitting ability that had originally attracted Milwaukee, although the Brewers remain confident that the teenager's bat will catch up. Lara combines strength and bat speed to generate plus raw power from the right side of the plate, but he's struggled to apply it in games because his swing too often gets long and stiff. The Brewers continue to work with Lara to better isolate and use his hands, which they believe are key to unlocking his offensive potential. Defensively, Lara has surpassed expectations with his glove, range and arm strength at shortstop, though club officials do acknowledge that Lara likely will end up at third base given his current size and remaining physical projection. Lara may not be as advanced as first thought and will need years to refine his game in the Minors, but the foundation is there for him to develop into a big leaguer provided the bat comes around.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Diaz jumped on the true prospect radar with a breakout season in 2014 when he got the opportunity to be a regular behind the plate with Double-A Altoona and reached Triple-A for the first time. This is his third straight year in the Pirates' Top 15, but he has yet to break through to the big leagues, save for six at-bats. Injuries were the culprit in 2016, as an elbow injury kept him out until midseason and then an infected cut forced him off the field at the end. The injury bug even followed Diaz to winter ball as an oblique strain made him shut it down early in Venezuela. When he's healthy, he's one of the best defensive backstops in the Minor Leagues, with plus hands, good blocking and game-calling skills and an absolute cannon for an arm. He's long showed the ability to make consistent contact without striking out much and he's gotten better at controlling at-bats, with some gap power. Diaz used his time rehabbing well, taking on a leadership role and mentoring players while in Bradenton. The Pirates hope he has learned some lessons about taking care of his body and he did report early in the spring in good shape. He might profile best as a backup, one who will wait for his chance for a full-time crack at a big league roster.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Pirates Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Things didn't go so well for the Pirates down the stretch in 2016, with slim postseason hopes slipping away as the second half of the season unfolded. Perhaps the biggest highlight was when Williams, who was acquired as unofficial compensation from the Marlins when they hired pitching guru Jim Benedict away, picked up his first Major League win with his father, who had been battling lymphoma, in attendance. Williams has the chance to contribute more than just one emotional moment. Pitching with largely average stuff, Williams' command, feel for pitching and competitiveness allows it to play up. Velocity-wise, his fastball might be Major League average, but its sink makes it above-average and generates a lot of groundball outs. He used to try to throw two breaking balls, but they ran together, so he's focused on his slider, which is a tighter pitch. He has a fringy changeup but mixes it in well. Williams attacks the zone and follows his gameplan well, going right after hitters and eliciting early contact. His ceiling might be that of a No. 4 type starter, but he's just about ready to fill that role.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: It might seem like a lifetime ago, but it was 2014 when Gonzales zipped to the big leagues less than a year after getting drafted, and he ended up pitching very meaningful innings out of the bullpen in that year's postseason. He had some shoulder soreness impact him in 2015, then came the elbow trouble that required Tommy John surgery and wiped out his 2016 season. But a return to health has Gonzales back on track this season, as he pitched well enough in Triple-A to earn a brief callup with St. Louis in June. The Mariners took notice of the left-hander's progress and acquired him in July in exchange for Tyler O'Neill. All signs point to the 25-year-old getting back to the athletic lefty with plus pitchability he was before he got hurt. Gonzales pitches with an average fastball that plays up because of his command, and because of his plus changeup, he can throw in any count to any hitter. His curve is his third pitch, but it has the potential to be Major League average as well. No longer blocked by the Cardinals' starting pitching depth, Gonzales should be given every chance in Seattle to show he can once again be a reliable mid- to back-of-the-rotation starter. It's in that role where he stands to offer the most value, though a gig as a long reliever is also a possibility.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Cardinals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gant has been on the move quite a bit in the last couple of years. Originally a late-round Draft pick of the Mets, he was dealt to the Braves at the Trade Deadline in 2015. A big spring vaulted Gant onto Atlanta's Opening Day roster a year ago and he was about to make a move from the bullpen into the rotation when an oblique injury knocked him out of action, though he did return to the big leagues. He landed with the Cardinals in December as part of the Jaime Garcia deal. Gant has never been a big stuff guy, but rather has succeeded thanks to his feel for pitching. His fastball might be average, though the velocity has trended up a bit over time, but he can move it to all quadrants of the strike zone. Gant's changeup sinks as well, and both offerings generate weak contact on the ground. His curve is a third average offering that has some good break to it. Gant uses a very unorthodox windup that seems to work for him. Gant doesn't have much projection left, but he does provide some versatility. He could step in and be a solid back-end starter or fit into a bullpen, depending on organizational need.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Diamondbacks Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Koch was a reliever at Louisville when the Mets drafted him in the third round of the 2012 Draft. Getting mound time as both a starter and out of the bullpen, he was making his way up their organizational ladder slowly when he was dealt to the D-backs late in 2015 in the Addison Reed trade. He made his brief, but effective, Major League debut last season. Koch might be the best strike-thrower in the D-backs system, filling the zone with four pitches. None of them are above average, but his ability to throw them to all four corners of the strike zone allow all of them to play up. His fastball is average, but he throws it with a ton of sink to get groundball outs. His slider is the better of his two breaking balls -- he tends to go with a fastball-slider combination when pitching in relief -- but he'll mix in his curve and occasionally his below-average changeup as well. The D-backs love Koch's competitive nature and that he pitched in the big leagues like he belonged. They think he can start as a No. 4 or 5 starter, but also like his versatility and know he can handle any role given to him.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Padres Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Blue Jays' pursuit of Rodriguez during the 2013-14 international period led the club to acquire additional international pool money, which they used to sign the then-16-year-old for $330,000 in January 2014. His rawness showed during his pro debut in the Rookie Gulf Coast League, but he made strides in his second tour of the GCL in 2015 and was continuing to climb the ladder when the Blue Jays dealt him to San Diego for Melvin Upton Jr. ahead of the 2016 Trade Deadline. Rodriguez saw an uptick in velocity in 2015 as he continued to get stronger and grow into his projectable frame. He showed the ability to bump 94 mph with his fastball as an amateur and has continued to sit in the low 90s with good sinking action as a pro. His slider and changeup are below-average pitches for him, though both should improve as he gains better feel for pitching. Learning how to repeat his delivery will be key for Rodriguez, who struggles to keep his body and lightning-quick arm in sync. The right-hander's arm strength offers plenty to dream on, but he'll have to check many developmental boxes before being deemed ready for the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Giants Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Notre Dame's career leader in ERA (1.71) and saves (30), Slania was expected to move quickly as a reliever after turning pro as a fifth-rounder in 2013. That didn't happen, and when he posted a 5.32 ERA in Double-A during the first two months of last season, the Giants decided to shake things up by putting him in the rotation. After he went 8-4 with a 2.42 ERA in 16 starts at three levels, including two strong outings in Triple-A, San Francisco added him to its 40-man roster in November. One of the reasons the Giants changed Slania's role is that he has a deep repertoire and they wanted him to learn how to use it better. He doesn't have a plus pitch but does own three potential solid offerings: a low-90s fastball that peaks at 95 mph with armside run, a low-80s slider with depth and a mid-80s splitter. He also has a decent changeup and a slow curveball at his disposal. Slania did a better job of pitching inside and changing speeds as a starter, and San Francisco will continue to deploy him as one. He has a huge physical presence at 6-foot-5 and 275 pounds, though he works with a shorter arm action and stride than would be expected for his size. His delivery gives him deception and doesn't prevent him from finding the strike zone.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Angels Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Angels obviously believe in Garcia's upside. They wouldn't have given him $565,000 to sign in July 2014 otherwise. But the talented shortstop hasn't been able to take any steps forward as a series of injuries has kept him from important development time. The most recent malady was a fractured cheekbone suffered when he fouled a bunt off his face, limiting him to just 14 Rookie-level Arizona League games in 2016. The adversity has helped Garcia mature, a small silver lining, and he has also grown physically. He looks like a big league shortstop now, with outstanding defensive actions and a strong arm. He has a good swing from both sides of the plate, but hasn't made any progress offensively, largely due to all of the missed time on the field. Still a teenager, Garcia has time to figure things out and get his career moving in the right direction. He's yet to amass a full season's worth of at-bats in his three years in the organization, so staying healthy and putting in a full year will be a good first step.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Yankees Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When the Yankees signed Finley for a well over-slot $950,000 as a third-round choice in 2015, they knew they were getting an advanced high school pitcher. He hailed from a Rancho Bernardo High (San Diego) program that has produced five big leaguers and five first-rounders in the last two decades, most notably Cole Hamels, and grew up around the game as the son of David Finley, who's now Dodgers vice president of amateur and international scouting. Drew's development has yet to take off because he only made six starts in 2016 before he was shut down with elbow fatigue. Finley had one of the best curveballs in the 2015 Draft, a true downer he throws with conviction, but it wasn't quite as sharp last year. His fastball ranges from 89-93 mph and is more effective than its velocity because it has sinking and tailing action, plus he hides and commands it well. His changeup is coming along nicely, showing signs of becoming a reliable offering. Finley has a chance to develop three solid or better pitches with command to match. Thus far as a pro, he has been an extreme flyball pitcher with close to average stuff. That has made him vulnerable to homers, a problem that could be exacerbated when he gets to Yankee Stadium.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cosart went undrafted as a Texas high school outfielder in 2012 and couldn't get on the field as a Duke freshman the following spring. He transferred to Seminole State (Fla.) CC because he wanted to pitch and immediately attracted scouts when he showed arm strength similar to that of his older brother Jarred, who's now with the Padres. The second juco player drafted (third round) in 2014, Cosart dominated Class A hitters when he became a full-time reliever last year but has seen his control disintegrate in 2017. After operating with an 88-92 mph fastball in his two seasons as a pro starter, Cosart recaptured the velocity he flashed at Seminole State when he moved to the bullpen. He now works at 94-97 mph and can hit 99 with some natural cutting action. He has scrapped an ineffective changeup in favor of a splitter that shows potential and is better than his soft curveball. There's a lot of effort in Cosart's delivery, which hampers his control but does bolster his deception. He'll always be much more about power than finesse, but he'll have to find the strike zone much more consistently to realize his upside of a set-up man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed at the relatively advanced age of 20 out of Venezuela by the Giants in 2012, Ysla led the low Class A South Atlantic League with a 2.45 ERA in his introduction to full-season ball two years later. When he got pounded in high Class A in 2015, San Francisco turned him into a reliever before dealing him to the Red Sox for Alejandro de Aza in August. Boston added him to its 40-man roster in November following an up-and-down season in Double-A. Ysla throws harder than any of the Red Sox' lefty bullpen prospects. He operates at 93-96 mph and tops out at 98 with his fastball, which has some natural cutting action. His long-term success depends on his ability to come up with a consistent second pitch, because his slider and changeup lack consistency and aren't more than average pitches at this point. Because he's a smaller guy who works with a lot of effort from a low arm slot, Ysla never was going to last long as a starter. His delivery makes it tough to pick up his pitches but also to land them in the strike zone, limiting his effectiveness. He'll need to transition from thrower to pitcher before he's ready to help in the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Washington's combination of power and speed electrified scouts who attended the Cape Cod League's Fenway Park workout day in the summer of 2014. But he also compiled a 28 percent strikeout rate in three years at Longwood, so he dropped to the 23rd round of the 2015 Draft. Signed for $100,000, he has some of the best raw power in the Red Sox system. With his prodigious strength and the loft in his right-handed swing, Washington generates easy raw power and can hit tape-measure shots to his pull side. How often he'll be able to tap into that pop remains a question because he sometimes struggles to catch up to premium velocity, struggles to identify breaking balls and chases pitches out of the strike zone too often. He won't hit for a high batting average, but if he improves his approach, he could hit deliver 20-plus homers per season and draw walks from pitchers forced to respect his power. Though Washington showed plus speed at the Cape workout, he's more of an average runner now. His quickness plays better on the bases than in the outfield, where he doesn't read balls well off the bat. He's best suited for left field with his so-so range and below-average arm, but he does make accurate throws.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A four-year starter at Florida, Tobias helped the Gators reach the College World Series in 2012 and '15. The leading hitter (.355) on the latter CWS club, which may produce as many as seven position players drafted in the top three rounds, Tobias signed with the Phillies for $10,000 as a 10th-round senior. He batted .301/.362/.439 in his first two pro seasons, reaching high Class A, before Philadelphia traded him for Clay Buchholz in December. Tobias' strong suit is his ability to make consistent line-drive contact. A switch-hitter who's more effective from his natural right side, he can drive some balls to the gaps and has occasional home run power to his pull side. While he doesn't strike out excessively, he would benefit from a more patient approach to bolster his walk totals. Primarily a third baseman in college, Tobias has played mostly second base as a pro. An average runner with arm strength to match, he doesn't quite have the quickness desired at the keystone and is a fringy defender there. He also has seen action in left field and profiles best as a bat-first utility guy who earns raves for his makeup.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Red Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A second-round pick in consecutive Drafts, Stankiewicz spurned the Mets in 2012 when they offered him a below-slot bonus. After a year at Seminole State (Okla.) JC, he agreed to a $1.1 million bonus with the Red Sox that got discounted to $915,000 after a physical revealed he had been born without a right pectoral muscle. His lack of an effective breaking ball resulted in modest success as a pro until he improved his slider late in 2016. Stankiewicz has spent most of his pro career relying heavily on a fastball that sat at 91-93 mph and peaked at 95, commanding it well in part because it lacked life. His velocity ticked up in the second half of last season, and he kept hitters off his heater with a harder, sharper slider in the mid-80s. He also has a curveball and changeup, but both are fringy offerings. Stankiewicz repeats his delivery well and throws strikes, but must pound the bottom of the zone because he lacks a plus pitch that misses bats consistently. He's durable and profiles as an innings eater at the back of a rotation. Boston hopes that his strong finish last year -- he had a 3.15 ERA and 33/7 K/BB ratio in his final six starts, including a complete-game one-hitter -- is a sign that he could become more than that.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Bridwell was a three-sport standout in high school before going to the Orioles in the ninth round of the 2010 Draft. He advanced to Double-A for the first time in 2015, his fifth professional season, and was having arguably his most consistent season before landing on the disabled list with elbow tendinitis in August. Injuries continued to plague Bridwell in 2016, as he missed more than a month of action during the middle of the season as the result of a left rib injury. The Orioles shifted him from the rotation to the bullpen upon his return, and it was in relief that Bridwell made his big league debut in August. He had made two relief outings in 2017 when he was sent to the Angels in mid-April. Bridwell uses his athletic, 6-foot-4 frame to create a steep angle to the plate with his fastball, which has been as high as 94-96 mph but typically sits in the low 90s with good sink. His changeup is a plus pitch and gives Bridwell a weapon against left-handed hitters. He also throws a slider, with the latter slightly ahead of the former. The biggest challenge for Bridwell has been commanding his fastball. When he can throw the pitch for strikes, and complement it with that changeup, he has the potential to dominate. After struggling as a starter for much of his pro career, it looked like Bridwell may have found his calling in the bullpen, but the trade to the Angels gave him another shot and he was taking advantage of it in the big league rotation.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles lost their top two picks in the 2014 Draft as compensation for free-agent signings, making Gonzalez their top selection in the third round. He was part of three Florida state championship teams at Archbishop McCarthy High School, the same school that produced big leaguers Alex Avila and Nick Castellanos. After an inconsistent full-season debut with Class A Delmarva in which he wore down late and finished the year on the disabled list, Gonzalez earned All-Star honors in his second tour of the South Atlantic League as he ranked third in the circuit in both ERA (2.50) and innings pitched (147 2/3). Gonzalez's velocity ticked up in his second full season as he bumped 93-94 mph while sitting comfortably in the low 90s. He struggles to maintain his velocity deep into games, however, and at times will pitch in the upper 80s. The 6-foot-3 left-hander creates a good downhill angle to the plate that gives his heater late life and makes him difficult to lift. Gonzalez's secondary offerings show promise but currently lag behind his fastball. He can flash a plus with his changeup, throwing it with good arm speed and late fading action, and gets good depth to his curveball. Gonzalez struggled with his command in 2015, when he walked 5.0 batters per nine innings, but he improved that number to 3.5 last season and should continue to make strides as he becomes more comfortable repeating his delivery. If all comes together for the left-hander, he could develop into a quality back-end starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Astros took Garcia with the No. 4 pick in the 2014 Rule 5 Draft and then flipped him to the Orioles, whom he had impressed with his arm strength during instructional league a few months prior. He made the Orioles' Opening Day roster as a reliever that year but struggled to stay healthy, with a bout of right shoulder tendinitis in May resulting in a stint on the 60-day DL. He returned to Double-A Bowie in 2016 and spent the entire season in the rotation, albeit with underwhelming results. Garcia showed mid-to-upper-90s velocity coming out of the bullpen but works more in the 92-94 mph range as a starter. His slider has the chance to be at least Major League average, and he's also capable of mixing in a changeup. However, Garcia's below-average control, especially with his fastball, continues to hold him back, as it limits the effectiveness of his secondary pitches as well as his overall bat-missing potential. The Orioles deployed Garcia as a starter so that he could develop his slider and changeup in advance of the right-hander's eventual return to the Orioles' bullpen. While he lacks a late-inning profile, Garcia's two quality pitches and ability to work multiple innings could make him a valuable big league reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles' signing of Ortega flew under the radar, as they inked the Dominican shortstop for just $60,000 in October 2014. He's since impressed club officials with his athleticism, tools and advanced feel for the game at a young age, and he fared well on both sides of the ball last season in the Rookie Gulf Coast League before finishing the year with Class A Short Season Aberdeen. Ortega's defense currently is well ahead of his hitting, but evaluators expect the latter to catch up as he continues adding strength to his athletic and projectable frame. There's little doubt he'll be able to remain at shortstop, where he shows good range and speed as well as an above-average arm. At the plate, the right-handed hitter makes consistent contact but offers little in the way of power. Set to play all of 2017 at age 20, Ortega, who has yet to reach full-season ball, is slightly behind the developmental curve and requires considerable projection. But the Orioles like Ortega's chances of becoming a big league shortstop and believe he's poised to make strides in the coming year.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Orioles Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Orioles knew that Gassaway would need time to develop when they took him in the 16th round of the 2013 Draft out of the Georgia prep ranks. He finally rewarded the organization's patience without a breakout performance in 2016, when he hit a robust .340/.384/.535 with seven home runs in 55 games, and he further rewarded the organization this season by reaching Double-A. A big, physical right-handed hitter, Gassaway began to tap into his plus raw power last season after connecting on just two home runs in his first 126 pro games. He has the strength and bat speed needed to drive the ball out of the park to all fields, and club officials believe he'll develop even more power as he continues to refine his approach and develops physically. Defensively, Gassaway's below-average speed and arm strength limit him to left field. Club officials rave about Gassaway's work ethic and desire to learn, not to mention his promising offensive tools. That combination could make Gassaway an everyday left fielder at maturity, though expectations should remain tempered until he completes a year in full-season ball.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Rays Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Gadea pushed back his signing as a international free agent by a year with the goal of improving his prospect stock by moving to the mound from third base. The decision proved wise, and the Mariners signed the right-hander for $42,000 in November 2012. He was brought along slowly to begin his career before dominating in his first full-season exposure in 2016, when he posted a 2.15 ERA and a 72-to-11 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 50 1/3 innings at Class A Clinton. Intrigued by his combination of size and stuff at a young age, the Rays selected Gadea with the fourth pick in December's Rule 5 Draft. Gadea is both strong and athletic, with considerable room left to grow into his projectable frame. He uses his height to pound the bottom of the strike zone with a fastball that sits 91-94 mph and touches 95, and he pairs it with an above-average changeup that he throws with convincing arm speed. He also exhibits feel for mixing a curveball to keep hitters off balance, although the pitch his least-advanced offering. Gadea's athleticism and smooth delivery give him above-average control at a young age, especially in regards to his fastball, and scouts believe his command could receive a similar grade once he's fully developed. As a Rule 5 pick, Gadea will need to spend the entire season on the active roster to remain in the Rays' system. The club believes he's capable of doing so -- despite having never pitched above the Class A level -- and intend to use him out of the bullpen before resuming his development as a starter in the Minors in 2018.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Nunez signed for $900,000 out of the Dominican Republic, getting the largest bonus in the White Sox's 2014-15 international class. More advanced than most of Chicago's international bonus babies, he made his U.S. debut at age 17 in 2015 but played in just 21 games because of hamstring issues. He stayed healthy and topped the Rookie-level Arizona League with 62 hits when he returned there last summer. Though Nunez is still raw offensively, the tools are there to hit for some average and power from the right side of the plate. He already shows a propensity for using the opposite field and has enough strength and bat speed for 12-15 homers per year once he starts turning and lifting pitches more frequently. He's in the process of figuring out pitch recognition and plate discipline. Most scouts thoughts Nunez would lack the quickness and range for shortstop once he's physically mature, and the White Sox moved him to third base in 2017. He's presently an average runner with nice hands and a strong arm, but he led AZL shortstops with 30 errors in 41 games last year. His bat will profile at the hot corner if it develops like Chicago expects it will.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for a mere $10,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2014, Diaz created a stir when his fastball reached 102 mph during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League the following year. He struggled when he jumped to the United States and low Class A in 2016, though he finished by not allowing a run in his final 16 appearances while striking out 31 in 23 2/3 innings. The White Sox scouted the Red Sox system heavily last summer and noted that he got better every time they went back to see him, so they made sure to acquire him as the fourth prospect in the Chris Sale trade at the Winter Meetings. Diaz's fastball usually sits at 95-98 mph and continues to peak in the triple digits. His heater has some late life to go with its impressive velocity, and it elicits swings and misses in the strike zone -- when he finds the strike zone. He also has a pair of intriguing if inconsistent power secondary pitches in a short slider and a splitter that both range from 88-93 mph. Diaz still is learning to harness his stuff. He has a lot of effort in his delivery, which hinders his ability to repeat his three-quarters arm slot. While there's a big gap between his floor and his ceiling, he does have the upside of a high-leverage reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Prepared to sign with the Brewers as the 14th overall pick in 2010 until a post-Draft physical revealed he had diabetes, Covey opted to stay home and attend the University of San Diego. He had mixed results in three years with the Toreros and in four years in the Athletics' system after Oakland made him a fourth-rounder in 2013. He lost most of the 2016 season to an oblique strain but pitched well in the Arizona Fall League, prompting the White Sox to pluck him in the Major League phase of the Rule 5 Draft in December. Covey showcased a 93-96 mph fastball in high school but now sits at 89-93 mph and tops out at 95 with heavy sink. His most reliable offering is a changeup with splitter action. He utilizes both a curveball and a slider, both of which usually play as average pitches. Covey lacks an out pitch, so he must throw strikes and keep the ball down in the zone to succeed. He doesn't offer a lot of upside as a starter but has a high floor as one who could eat innings in the back of a rotation. Rule 5 mandates that Chicago keep him on its active big league roster throughout 2017, or else it will have to put him on waivers and offer him back to the A's for half of his $100,000 Draft price.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 White Sox Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Cooper spent two years at Bellevue (Wash.) CC before transferring to Hawaii, where he posted a 2.29 ERA in two seasons. Since signing for $5,000 as a 16th-rounder in 2014, he has continued to produce. He dominated as a reliever in his first two pro seasons, pitched well as a starter in high Class A to begin 2016 and thrived back in the bullpen in Double-A. The White Sox will continue to develop Cooper as a starter after he led their farmhands in strikeout rate (10.8 per nine innings) last year while working a career-high 118 2/3 innings. His fastball has improved from 86-90 mph in college to 88-93 mph in pro ball, and it plays up because he commands it well and creates steep downhill plane with his over-the-top delivery. His high arm slot also adds depth to his curveball, his best pitch. Cooper also employs a slider and changeup that give him two additional average offerings. His success is built on pounding the strike zone and keeping batters off balance by throwing any of his pitches in any count. He already has exceeded expectations and could make it as a back-of-the-rotation starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Plutko was overshadowed by 2011 first-rounders Gerrit Cole and Trevor Bauer as a freshman at UCLA, but he emerged as the Bruins ace the following year before leading them to a College World Series championship in 2013. An 11th-round pick that June, Plutko made strides in his second pro season in 2015, finishing at Double-A Akron, and continued to climb through the system en route to his big league debut last September. Plutko's plus control and feel for sequencing are his greatest strengths. The right-hander is adept at painting both sides of the plate with his fastball, which sits around 90-91 mph, but can reach 94. His changeup is his best secondary offering, receiving a plus grade from scouts, and he knows how to keep hitters off balance with both his slider and curveball, with the former currently ahead of the latter. Plutko has been nothing but durable as a pro. After logging a career-high 166 innings in 2015, he ranked second in Cleveland's system in innings pitched (161 2/3) last season, going at least five innings in 25 of his 28 starts. That stamina, as well as his ability to pound the zone with four pitches, could make Plutko a back-end starter in the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Drafted as an advanced lefty out of Wake Forest in 2012, Cooney has been just that, reaching the upper levels of the Cardinals' system quickly. He made his Major League debut in early 2015, stepping into the rotation in July and filling in more than capably. The thought was he'd fill a similar role in 2016, but a bone spur in his left shoulder, which required subsequent surgery, sidelined him for the entire season. In November, Cooney was claimed off waivers by the Indians. Cooney stands out for his overall feel and above-average command of four pitches. His fastball sits at 90-92 mph, a tick above average for a lefty, and he's adept at changing hitters' eye levels with the pitch. His changeup is above average at times and could be consistently so in the future, while his curveball gives him at least a third Major League average offering. He'll mix in a slider as well. As his 1.8 BB/9 ratio throughout his Minor League career attests, Cooney is always around the plate. Cooney continues to be limited as a result of his injured shoulder, and that's likely to carry over into Spring Training. If he can get back to full strength, the southpaw has the potential to provide rotation insurance or serve as a versatile bullpen piece for the Indians.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A 15th-round Draft pick in 2012 out of George Washington (N.Y.) High, Rodriguez broke out in his second full season in '14, hitting 22 home runs to tie for the Midwest League lead. He moved up to Class A Advanced Lynchburg the next year and paced the Carolina League with 17 home runs, though he struggled after receiving a late-season promotion to Double-A. In his return to Akron last season, Rodriguez connected on a career-high 26 home runs, good for third in the Eastern League. A physically strong right-handed hitter, Rodriguez has big raw power that has produced at least 20 homers in three consecutive seasons. Though his power comes with quite a bit of swing-and-miss, Rodriguez has shown a consistent approach at every level, and he paced the Eastern League with 75 walks in 2016. Meanwhile, the Indians are impressed with his progress as a hitter, and praise his improved feel for driving the ball the other way. Rodriguez's size and poor speed limit him to first base, where he is a passable defender. It won't be easy for him to fulfill the right-handed-hitting first baseman profile in the big leagues, though there's little doubt that he has the power to do so.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Big West Conference player of the year as a redshirt sophomore, Calica was unable to build on that success the next year. The Indians still took him in the 11th round in June, and Calica immediately rewarded the organization by hitting .382/.474/.556 with 15 steals over 50 games between Class A Short Season Mahoning Valley and Class A Lake County in his pro debut. An advanced left-handed hitter, Calica has simple, repeatable swing that allows him to make consistently hard contact and spray the ball from line to line. He showed improved gap power upon turning pro, tallying 19 extra-base hits between the two levels, though he likely will never offer much in the way of over-the-fence pop. Calica also stands out for a mature approach that netted him the second-best on-base percentage as a junior, as well as 24 hit-by-pitches. An above-average runner, Calica's wheels play up on the basepaths due to his instincts and because he knows how to read pitchers and picks his spots to run. He's capable of playing center field, but saw more time in left during his pro debut. Regardless of his position, it will be Calica's bat that gets him to the Major Leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Guardians Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Miniard was viewed as a development project when the Indians drafted him in the eighth round out of the Kentucky prep ranks in 2014. As expected, the big right-hander scuffled to begin his career before making strides last year, when, at age 20, he turned in a breakout performance between the New York-Penn and Midwest Leagues. Miniard uses his height (6-foot-7) to his advantage by creating excellent downhill plane to the plate that makes his mid-90s fastball difficult to lift. The pitch also stands out for its natural cutting action, helping him evade barrels and generate plenty of weak contact, especially on the ground. His power curveball projects to be average, while his nascent changeup will need to be developed in the coming years. As is common with young hurlers who have long levers, Miniard struggles to harness his body during his delivery, in turn giving him below-average control. The Indians believe that will improve as he continues grow into his large frame, though it may take time for Miniard to put it all together.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting Grades : Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Curveball: 40 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Sometimes it can take a while for a player to find a home. Jaye was originally drafted by the Blue Jays back in 2010 and has made stops with the White Sox and Rangers - though he never pitched an inning for Texas - before landing with the Tigers just prior to the 2016 season. He reached Triple-A for the first time in his first year with Detroit, topping the system in strikeouts and finishing in the top five in both WHIP and batting average against. Jaye will use four pitches to find ways of getting hitters out. He has good life on his low-90s fastball and generates a good amount of groundball outs. He'll use a curveball on occasion to get over for strike one, but it's his slider, which can be plus at times, that is his true out pitch. It's better than his changeup, which also is a Major League average weapon for the right-hander. He's around the strike zone and cut his walk rate down considerably in 2016. Jaye topped 160 innings in three different Minor League seasons, pointing to the potential to be a workhorse at the back end of a big league rotation. It may not be that high of a ceiling, but he's just about ready to reach it.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Smith had an inconsistent career at Dallas Baptist, but the Tigers, who originally drafted him, don't shy away from plus arm strength when they see it. It's come slowly, with injuries slowing him down some, but the right-hander has proven to be an effective relief prospect in his first year-plus as a pro. In late April, Smith was dealt to the Rays as the PTBNL, completing the January trade that had sent Mikie Mahtook to Detroit. He was on the move again in July as the return sent to the Mets from the Rays for Lucas Duda. Smith is largely a fastball/breaking ball short reliever. His heater will sit comfortably in the 92-95 mph range, and he can reach back for more, all from a clean and easy delivery. He'll show an above-average curveball at times with really good snap to it, but not consistently. Smith doesn't throw his changeup enough, and he'll need to improve his feel for the pitch and use it more in the future, though he did make strides as a strike-thrower in his second full season. That he dealt with some minor arm issues early in his career ended talk about perhaps seeing how Smith would fare in a rotation. He has all the ingredients to be an effective short reliever, with a ceiling of a future setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed back in 2012 as a 16-year-old from Australia, the Tigers took it slowly with Shepherd, letting him start off with a couple of seasons at home in the Australian Baseball League. When he hit over .300 and slugged close to .500 during his United States debut in the Gulf Coast League in 2014, his prospect stock soared. He's moved across two full-season levels the last two years, but hasn't found the same modicum of success. Shepherd hit under .200 in the Florida State League in 2016, though he did show some over-the-fence power. He's always had some swing and miss to his game, to go along with a healthy walk rate. And while he still did pick up free passes, his strikeout rate spiked. As the strikeouts piled up, it snowballed some and he was slow to make adjustments. The Tigers sill believe in his offensive potential, that he will figure it out and develop into the kind of bat that profiles well at third. He's athletic with a good arm and should be able to defend the hot corner for the long term. Shepherd is just 21 for all of the 2017 season, so there's no reason not to give him a mulligan and let him try to get moving in the right direction again. He will have to show he can make adjustments at the plate in order to do so.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Even since his days at the University of Virgnia, Lewicki has shown the aptitude to get hitters out, but staying healthy has always been an issue. He had Tommy John surgery at Virginia in 2013. The right-hander missed two months of his first full pro season with a pectoral muscle injury. The 2016 season saw more of the same, with Lewicki getting shelved for six weeks. A healthy 2017 at the upper levels, however, set him up for his first big league callup last September. Lewicki has shown feel for four pitches at times, all of which he can throw for strikes. His fastball might typically sit around 92 mph, but he gets it up to 95 mph with regularity, throwing it with good sink. His slider will flash above-average and he'll also show an average changeup at times, albeit inconsistently, while mixing in a curveball as well. He doesn't miss a ton of bats, but he also doesn't hurt himself that much with walks. Lewicki had worked some in relief at Virginia, and while he has largely started throughout his Minor League career, he pitched out of the bullpen for Detrot last September (with one start mixed in) and served the same role when he was summoned from Triple-A in 2018. His fastball-slider combination could continue to play up should he stay in a relief gig long-term.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 65 | Slider: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 The Tigers like to draft arm strength. Dallas Baptist University has developed a well-earned reputation as having a pitching staff typically filled with hard throwers. It only stands to reason, then, that the Tigers would look there for talent in the Draft, taking Drew Smith in 2015 and Voelker a year before that. Voelker was making progress up the organizational ladder until he was hit with a 50-game suspension for testing positive for an amphetamine in May. Voelker isn't big and physical, but he's shown that his stuff could play in the back end of a bullpen. He goes right after hitters with a fastball-slider combination. There isn't much angle because of his size, but he does throw it in the mid-90s with regularity and can get a little more on occasion. His slider is a Major League-average breaking ball with good late life and he's even working on a changeup. He's missed a ton of bats wherever he has pitched, though he did get hit a bit more when he first made the move to the upper levels in 2016. Voelker has served as a closer at various stops in the Minor Leagues and he does have the right mentality for such a role. He's probably a touch shy stuff-wise to do the job in the big leagues, but it's clear he won't shy away from the bright lights in whatever role he's given, though he'll first have to get past the inevitable reputation of a positive drug test.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: After barely being able to find any innings as a freshman at Texas A&M, Ecker earned the closer's role as a sophomore and proceeded to save 16 games of the next two years. A completely dominant junior season landed him in the fifth round, where the Tigers gave him full pick value to sign. Ecker is the kind of college reliever who could move quickly though the system. While he's a reliever only, he does have a three-pitch mix he uses effectively. He'll throw his fastball in the mid-90s with good life and he's not afraid to pitch inside with it. His best secondary offering is his changeup, which has splitter action to it and is thrown with good deception. His slider can be nasty at times, but it also can morph into a bit of a hybrid breaking ball at times. He's a bit undersized and can have a long arm action at times, but hitters have never been successful in picking his stuff up. A combination of that kind of stuff with excellent strike-throwing ability often means a quick path to the big leagues. Whether he can close at that level remains to be seen, but the Tigers could get a rapid return on their Draft investment.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: From the start of Alcantara's career with the Angels, there has always been the thought that perhaps he'd be best suited for the bullpen based on his power stuff and command issues. He finally made that move late in the 2016 season, making some strides in adjusting to the role. He was continuing to adjust in the Arizona Fall League when the Tigers acquired him in return for Cameron Maybin. Alcantara's raw stuff certainly works in shorter stints. He'll sit 95-96 mph and touch 98-99 with heavy sink. His power slider is a plus 91- to 92-mph breaking ball at times. He has a below-average changeup, and while he may not need it as much now, the Tigers do preach having one for right-handed relievers to throw to left-handed hitters. Alcantara struggles to find the strike zone consistently and that continued even in the shorter relief stints, though he was very tough to hit. Alcantara gets to settle in to his new organization and his new role in 2017. He doesn't have to be pinpoint with his control, but if he can throw a few more strikes, his stuff should get him to the big leagues, perhaps as a setup man.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Tigers Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: The Tigers liked Pinero in 2015 when he was a Draft-eligible sophomore at Virginia, taking him in the 36th round. A year later, the Tigers nabbed him a lot earlier, in the ninth, and he had a solid pro debut. Pinero's best offensive skill is his plate discipline. He has an advanced approach at the plate and recognizes pitches very well. He can use all fields and while he is not a power guy, tightening up his swing might help him drive the ball, as he can currently get a bit long, making it easier for him to be tied up on inside pitches. At 6-foot-5, he doesn't look like he should be able to play shortstop, but he has surprisingly good actions at the position, with good hands and enough arm. Pinero will be given the chance to play his way off of shortstop. His bat doesn't really profile well anywhere else as an everyday player, so a future as a utility man seems to be the most likely result.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: When Gasparini signed for $1.3 million out of Italy in 2013, he eclipsed the European bonus record of $800,000 set by Germany's Max Kepler four years earlier. Though he has some of the best tools in the system, his first taste of full-season ball last year produced a .196/.256/.293 line with 48 errors -- 10 more than any other Minor Leaguer. He has had more success in 2017 while repeating low Class A and moving from shortstop to the outfield. Given his background and youth, the Royals knew Gasparini would need a lot of time to develop, and they are willing to give it to him because of the potential payoff. A switch-hitter with good bat speed from both sides, he shows better-than-average raw power during batting practice, but he's still extremely raw at the plate in terms of his approach, plate discipline and pitch recognition. Gasparini's most usable tool at this point is his plus speed, though he's still figuring out how to steal bases. His quickness and arm strength are suited for shortstop, but he lacks soft hands and committed 98 errors in 181 games there in his first three pro seasons. He transitioned to center field during instructional league and can become an asset there once he gains more experience.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A full-time starter at Rend Lake (Ill.) CC and Western Kentucky, Edwards became a reliever when he turned pro as a 19th-rounder in 2013. He finished each of his first three years as a pro in high Class A before dominating Double-A and earning a promotion to Triple-A a month into last season. Edwards' velocity skyrocketed in '16 and so did his strikeout rate, jumping to 10.9 per nine innings after he previously averaged 6.5. After ranging from 91-96 mph with his fastball in '2015, Edwards operated at 94-97 and hit 102 with sinking and tailing action last year. His slider improved as well, climbing into the upper 80s and touching 92, though it's still more notable for its power than its break. Edwards destroys right-handers with those two pitches, but he is still looking for a way to solve left-handers, who aren't fooled by his ineffective changeup. Edwards' extra-large frame and the effort in his delivery give him some deception, but they also hamper his control and command. Once he begins finding the strike zone with more consistency, he'll be ready to help the Royals.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Area scout Justin Lehr found two possible big leaguers at Sam Houston State in the 2014 Draft, signing first baseman Ryan O'Hearn in the eighth round and Toups in the 15th. Toups topped the Rookie-level Pioneer League with a .453 on-base percentage in his pro debut and continues to deliver quality at-bats as consistently as any Royals farmhand. He hit his way to Double-A two months into his second full season and surprisingly hit four homers in eight Texas League playoff games. A gamer who plays above his tools, Toups has feel for the barrel and understands that his primary role is to get on base. He has surprising strength for someone generously listed at 5-foot-10 and 170 pounds, but he lets his power come naturally instead of trying to do too much. Toups' strikeout rate did spike to 24 percent once he got to Double-A, so he'll have to make adjustments to handle more advanced pitching. After missing the entire 2013 college season following surgery on his left knee, Toups has regained his average speed and shows good instincts on the bases. A shortstop for the Bearkats and in his pro debut, he now sees most of his action at second base. That's a better fit for Toups' average arm and quickness, and he's a sure-handed defender at either spot.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: MLBPipeline's top-rated high school pitcher in the 2015 Draft, Russell went 21st overall, the earliest the Royals had taken a prep arm since grabbing Zack Greinke with the sixth choice in 2002. Signed for $2,190,200, he was ticketed for low Class A in 2016, but he worked just two innings in Rookie ball as his mechanics and control completely fell apart. When his situation didn't improve this year, he took a leave of absence from baseball in June. As an amateur, Russell used a quick arm and a low three-quarters delivery to generate nasty life on a pair of plus pitches. He sat at 92-95 mph and reached 97 with running action on his fastball and worked in the low 80s with a slider that featured hard bite when he stayed on top of it. Russell's velocity dropped precipitously last year as he battled to find the strike zone. Some scouts thought Russell was destined for the bullpen because his delivery features effort and is long in back, leading to questions about his durability and command. If he can recapture the stuff he had in high school, he'll still need to refine a changeup to be an effective starter.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Royals Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Signed for $850,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2014, Aracena draws comparisons to former All-Star Rafael Furcal because of his size (generously listed at 5-foot-8) and style of play. He came straight to the United States for his pro debut in 2015 and spent last year as the third-youngest regular (age 18) in the Rookie-level Pioneer League. A switch-hitter with a naturally compact stroke, Aracena has had little trouble making consistent contact against more advanced pitchers. He could use more patience to enhance his ability to get on base, where his plus speed makes him a threat to steal. Aracena also has some sneaky power, but he needs to get stronger to hold up over the course of a full pro season. Aracena's biggest need is to settle down defensively after committing a Pioneer League-high 38 errors in just 61 games, the result of concentration lapses more than any glaring flaw. With a well-above-average arm, solid range and good instincts, he should be able to stay at shortstop provided he improves his consistency.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Twins Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Scouting grades : Fastball: 65 | Curveball: 55 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 While the Twins have a fair share of hard-throwing right-handed relievers in their system -- just look up and down this list for proof -- they're not afraid of left-handed power arms, either. Melotakis, drafted back in 2012 as a college reliever but initially developed as a starter, was settling back into a bullpen role when he needed Tommy John surgery and missed all of 2015. He had an encouraging first year back, capped off by a very strong showing in the Arizona Fall League. The key is that Melotakis made it through 2016 healthy, save for one DL stint due to fatigue, as his workload was carefully monitored. The stuff came back, with a fastball that topped out at 96-97 mph and sat at 94 mph to go along with a power curve in the mid-80s. He does have a changeup he worked on when he was starting, but he didn't throw it much last year. His command is a work in progress, but that should improve the further removed from the surgery he gets. The kid gloves will come off now, with Melotakis getting the chance to show how he responds to things like pitching on consecutive nights or multiple innings in one outing. How his stuff holds up then might determine how quickly he gets his first callup to the big leagues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Part of the Astros' franchise-record $8.9 million spending spree during the 2016-17 international signing period, Sierra received a $1.5 million bonus in July. Before he left Cuba, he reached the island's top league at age 18 and had limited success there in three seasons as a part-time player. He batted .316/.465/.506 in his pro debut, though the Rookie-level Dominican Summer League wasn't much of a test for a 22-year-old. Sierra offers intriguing offensive potential for a shortstop. He has bat speed and has gotten stronger since defecting, which could result in 15-homer power if he improves the leverage in his right-handed swing. He's aggressive at the plate but shows a willingness to use the entire field. Houston is confident that Sierra will stay at shortstop despite average speed. His actions and quick first step give him range to both sides. He also played second and third base in Cuba, and he has the soft hands and solid arm to do so if needed in the future.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Rodgers became the best strike-thrower in the Houston system as soon as he signed as a third-round pick in 2012, but he had trouble missing bats and recorded a 4.69 ERA in his first three years in full-season ball. He was a different pitcher in 2016, thanks to an improved slider that Luke Gregerson taught him during Spring Training. Rodgers led the Triple-A Pacific Coast League in ERA (2.86), made his Major league debut in September and won pitcher of the year awards from the Astros and the PCL. Rodgers' slider went from a decent pitch in 2015 to his best offering in 2016. It sits in the low 80s and he has tremendous feel for it, showing the ability to back-door it for strikes or morph it into a cutter to keep left-handers at bay. The threat of his slider keeps hitters from teeing off on the rest of his repertoire: an 89- to 93-mph fastball he commands well, an average changeup and a slow curveball. In order to succeed, Rodgers still has to locate his pitches with precision, a lesson that was reinforced when big leaguers hit .385 against him in the final month. While he lacks a high ceiling, he's a tough competitor capable of helping Houston as a back-of-the-rotation starter or middle reliever. But that won't happen in 2017 after he had Tommy John surgery in May.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: Hoyt's backstory seems almost too incredible to be true. His baseball career appeared over when he went undrafted after posting an 18.82 ERA as a 23-year-old senior at Centenary in 2010. While working as a deckhand on a sailboat in San Diego the following year, he tried out and made an independent league team managed by Jose Canseco. That franchise folded, and Hoyt pitched in two independent league circuits and the Mexican League before the Braves signed him for $500 in November 2012. They sent him to the Astros in the Evan Gattis trade in January 2015, and he finally made it to the big leagues last August at age 29. A rare reliever with three distinct plus offerings, Hoyt led the Triple-A Pacific Coast League with 29 saves last year while inducing strikeouts or groundouts from 69 percent of the batters he faced. His mid-90s fastball features running life, his mid-80s slider can be a wipeout pitch and his upper-80s splitter is almost impossible to lift. He uses his 6-foot-6 frame and high three-quarters delivery to leverage his pitches down in the strike zone. Hoyt battled his control early in his career but has done a better job of providing strikes in the last two seasons. He wasn't as sharp in his first taste of the Majors as he had been in Triple-A, in part because he didn't attack hitters as much and got away from using his splitter. But there's no question that he has the pure stuff to be a late-inning reliever.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A full-time infielder as a sophomore at Howard (Texas) JC in 2012, McCurry transferred to Oklahoma State and set Cowboys records for single-season (19) and career (29) saves, eclipsing Jordy Mercer in the latter category. A $1,000 senior sign by the Athletics in the 22nd round of the 2014 Draft, he came to the Astros in the Jed Lowrie trade in November 2015. He advanced to Triple-A last June and began to push for a bullpen job in Houston, but he'll miss the first 50 games in 2017 because of an offseason suspension for testing positive for a stimulant. Though he's undersized and lacks a true plus pitch, McCurry recorded a 2.18 ERA, 11.0 strikeouts per nine innings and a .205 opponents' average during his first three pro seasons. His pitchability, deception and competitiveness are more impressive than his stuff. He generates swings and misses as well as ground-ball contact, and he breaks more than his share of bats. McCurry has two separate game plans on the mound. He's more effective against left-handers, neutralizing their platoon advantage by using a high three-quarters arm slot to deliver low-90s four-seam fastballs with riding life and solid curveballs with good depth. Against righties, he drops down sidearm and relies on sinking changeups (his best offering) and sweeping sliders.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Astros Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: With a strong summer in the Cape Cod League and tools that fit the center-field profile, Wrenn looked poised to go in the top three rounds of the 2016 Draft. His junior year didn't go as planned, however, because a ball tipped off his glove and broke three bones in his face just before the start of the season and his offensive numbers took a downturn. After the Astros snapped him up in the sixth round, he hit 12 homers and stole 15 bases in 71 games but slumped after a promotion to Class A. Wrenn's most notable tool is his speed, which gets double-plus grades from some scouts. He steals bases with a high success rate, though he should take more opportunities to run. He covers plenty of ground in center field, where he shows a playable arm. Wrenn is still figuring out his identity at the plate. He could parlay his speed into a table-setting role atop a lineup yet also has more pop than Houston expected, especially to his pull side. He gets caught in between focusing on reaching base and trying to drive the ball, leading to some swing-and-miss issues.

mlb_pipeline.label: MLB Pipeline 2017 Athletics Top 30
mlb_pipeline.text: A sixth-round pick by the Indians in 2012, Wendle put himself on the A's radar by winning the Tribe's Minor League Player of the Year award in his first full professional season. Wendle reached Double-A the following year, and Oakland acquired him that offseason for Brandon Moss. He repeated the Triple-A level in 2016 with impressive results, leading the Pacific Coast League and ranking fourth in the Minors in hits (167), and then batted .260 in 28 games with the A's after debuting in late August. Wendle's 2017 campaign began ominously, with a strained right shoulder sidelining him for the first month of the season, though he returned to the field fully healthy in late April. Wendle stands out most for his natural hitting ability from the left side of the plate.
